title: Standard MCQ pool
source: Built by scripts/build-duel-pack.mjs from public/mcq/pool.json and public/duel/mcq/ and data/mcq/high-yield.json and data/mcq/medexpqa.json (MedExpQA, CC BY 4.0, adapted): 1464 ai, 559 open-exam, 144 usmle-resource, 56 amsa.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 9 years attends his annual review. An early-morning urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 5.2 mg/mmol; eGFR is 81 mL/min/1.73m². Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A raised uACR (above 2.5 mg/mmol in men) can be transient, for example after exercise, fever or a UTI. Kidney Health Australia and the RACGP advise confirming albuminuria with 2 of 3 raised samples within 3 months before diagnosing diabetic kidney disease. Once it is confirmed, an ACE inhibitor or ARB is titrated and an SGLT2 inhibitor is favoured.
notes: An ultrasound is for unexplained or progressive CKD, haematuria or suspected obstruction, not for confirming early albuminuria with a normal eGFR.
A timed 24-hour collection is awkward and less reliable than repeat spot uACR, and no longer advised for screening or confirmation.
Electrophoresis looks for a paraprotein (myeloma), which is not suggested by isolated albuminuria in long-standing diabetes.
A biopsy is kept for atypical features such as rapid eGFR decline, active sediment or no retinopathy, not for unconfirmed moderate albuminuria.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is sweaty and disoriented in the emergency department. He refuses treatment for a foot abscess and demands to leave. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Decision-making capacity can only be judged fairly once reversible causes of impairment are excluded. In an insulin-treated patient who is sweaty and disoriented, hypoglycaemia is the most likely and fastest-reversible cause, and a bedside glucose check takes seconds. If he is hypoglycaemic, correcting it may restore his capacity, and his decision about treatment can then be reassessed.
notes: Hyponatraemia can cause confusion, but it does not explain sweating in an insulin-treated diabetic, and the result takes longer than a bedside glucose.
Imaging is not the first step when no head injury or focal signs are described and a reversible metabolic cause is far more likely.
Intoxication is possible, but sweating with disorientation in a person with type 1 diabetes points first to hypoglycaemia, which must be excluded urgently.
A cognitive screen does not assess capacity for a specific decision and is meaningless until an acute reversible cause like hypoglycaemia is ruled out.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man is struck on the chin by a cricket ball. He has malocclusion and a step in his lower teeth. An orthopantomogram shows a displaced left parasymphyseal fracture. Which other fracture is most likely?
questions.why: The mandible behaves like a ring, so it usually breaks in two places. A blow to one side of the chin that causes a parasymphyseal fracture often also fractures the condylar neck on the opposite side. Check the orthopantomogram for this second fracture, and look for pre-auricular tenderness on that side.
notes: The zygomatic arch is part of the midface, and a blow to the chin does not pass force up to it.
Force from a parasymphyseal impact travels to the condyle on the opposite side, not the condyle on the same side.
Orbital floor blowout fractures come from a direct blow to the orbit, not to the chin.
Nasal fractures need a direct blow to the nose and are not linked to mandibular ring fractures.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman, not breastfeeding, has a red retroareolar lump unresolved after five days of flucloxacillin. Ultrasound shows an abscess and a separate irregular, vascular solid mass with angular margins. Most appropriate next step for the mass?
questions.why: The collection is the abscess, but the separate irregular, vascular solid mass with angular margins looks malignant and an abscess cannot explain it. In a non-lactational infection that has not responded to antibiotics, this mass needs a tissue diagnosis, and core biopsy is the preferred method to complete triple assessment.
notes: FNA cytology cannot reliably tell invasive from in situ cancer and gives no receptor status, so core biopsy is preferred.
Waiting for the infection to settle gives false reassurance and delays the diagnosis of a mass that already looks malignant.
Incision and drainage would treat only the collection, and for a small abscess ultrasound-guided aspiration is preferred anyway.
MRI does not give a tissue diagnosis, and tissue is what this suspicious mass needs next.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl is on the paediatric ward of a regional hospital, 6 hours after treatment began for severe diabetic ketoacidosis at the first presentation of type 1 diabetes. At presentation she weighed 40 kg. Her venous pH was 7.02, bicarbonate 3 mmol/L, glucose 41.0 mmol/L, sodium 130 mmol/L and urea 14.2 mmol/L. She received a 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus, then fluids to replace her deficit over 48 hours with added potassium. An insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour was started after the first hour. She now has a severe headache, has vomited once, and is irritable and disorientated. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 64/min (previously 128/min), blood pressure 134/86 mm Hg (previously 106/64 mm Hg), respirations 20/min and SpO2 98% on room air. Her GCS is 13 (E3 V4 M6). Her pupils are equal and reactive. Capillary glucose is 15.8 mmol/L and serum sodium is 134 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT brain before any further treatment
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 1 hour
Increase the fluid rate to replace the deficit over 24 hours
Intravenous mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 20 minutes
questions.why: This girl has cerebral oedema, the main cause of death in children with DKA. She has several risk factors: a first presentation, young age, severe acidosis and a high urea at presentation. It typically appears 4 to 12 hours into treatment. The warning signs are a new headache, vomiting, irritability or confusion, a falling GCS, and a falling heart rate with rising blood pressure (part of the Cushing response). The RCH DKA guideline and ISPAD 2022 say to treat on clinical grounds straight away. Give IV mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 20 minutes, or 3% hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes. At the same time, cut the fluid rate by one third, raise the head of the bed, call senior and intensive care help, and arrange retrieval or transfer. Imaging comes only after she is stable. CT brain should not delay treatment, because a normal early scan does not rule out cerebral oedema and she could herniate while waiting for it. Bicarbonate is itself linked to cerebral oedema and has no role here. Faster fluids would make the brain swelling worse. Her glucose of 15.8 mmol/L rules out hypoglycaemia as the cause of her confusion.
notes: Wrong: imaging must not delay treatment, because cerebral oedema is diagnosed clinically and an early CT may be normal; scan only once she is stable.
Wrong: bicarbonate in paediatric DKA is linked to cerebral oedema and is not indicated; her acidosis is improving with insulin and fluids.
Wrong: giving fluid faster makes cerebral oedema worse; the fluid rate should be cut by one third, not increased.
Wrong: her capillary glucose is 15.8 mmol/L, so hypoglycaemia does not explain her confusion, and the change in her heart rate and blood pressure points to raised intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 35 weeks 4 days' gestation comes to the maternity assessment unit because her baby has moved much less than usual since the previous evening. Two years ago she had a stillbirth at 38 weeks, and that infant was small for gestational age. In this pregnancy she has diet-controlled gestational diabetes. A scan at 32 weeks showed an estimated weight on the 40th centile. She takes low-dose aspirin. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, pulse is 86/min, respirations are 16/min and temperature is 36.7 °C. Symphysis-fundal height is 35 cm. A urine dipstick shows no protein. A 40-minute cardiotocograph (CTG) shows a baseline rate of 135 bpm, baseline variability of 10 bpm, three accelerations of at least 15 bpm lasting at least 15 seconds, and no decelerations. She feels several movements during the trace. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day sonographic biometry and liquor volume assessment
Discharge with routine antenatal review at 37 weeks
Continuation of the CTG for a further 40 minutes
questions.why: Every feature of this CTG is normal by RANZCOG criteria: the baseline is 110 to 160 bpm, variability is 6 to 25 bpm, there are accelerations and there are no decelerations. Her observations and urinalysis show no sign of pre-eclampsia or infection. A normal CTG means the fetus is not hypoxic right now. It does not rule out underlying placental insufficiency or growth restriction, so it does not exclude a later poor outcome. The Stillbirth CRE guideline on decreased fetal movements says that when a woman has risk factors for growth restriction or stillbirth, she should have an ultrasound for fetal biometry and amniotic fluid volume, ideally within 24 hours, along with obstetric review. This woman has a previous small-for-gestational-age stillbirth and gestational diabetes. The scan should be arranged today. She should then be told to come back straight away, at any hour, if movements decrease again.
notes: Sending her home with routine follow-up treats the normal CTG as if it rules out compromise, which is unsafe in a woman with risk factors for stillbirth.
A single episode of reduced movements with a normal CTG and a normal assessment is not a reason for birth at 35 weeks, and preterm induction brings neonatal risks with no proven benefit.
The trace already meets every normal criterion with a good signal, so recording for longer adds no information about her placental reserve.
A Kleihauer-Betke test looks for fetomaternal haemorrhage, which would be suspected with a sinusoidal or abnormal trace, trauma or bleeding, and none of these is present here.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has mild scleral icterus after gastroenteritis with poor oral intake. Bilirubin is 42 µmol/L (unconjugated 38 µmol/L); ALT, ALP, full blood count and reticulocytes are normal. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: His bilirubin is mildly raised and almost all unconjugated. Liver enzymes are normal and there is no sign of haemolysis, and it came on during fasting and illness, so this is Gilbert syndrome. It is benign and needs only reassurance, not further investigation.
notes: Haemolysis would raise the reticulocyte count and usually lower the haemoglobin, but his full blood count and reticulocytes are normal.
Dubin-Johnson syndrome raises conjugated bilirubin, not unconjugated bilirubin.
Acute viral hepatitis would raise ALT sharply and cause a mixed or conjugated rise in bilirubin.
Biliary obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin and ALP, and his ALP is normal.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought in after a high-speed car crash, breathless with BP 82/50 mmHg. Her trachea deviates left and the right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She has a right tension pneumothorax with obstructive shock. This is diagnosed on clinical signs and needs immediate decompression, by needle at the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line or by finger thoracostomy. An intercostal catheter on an underwater seal follows.
notes: Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically, and waiting for a film in a hypotensive patient wastes critical time.
Tamponade does not cause tracheal deviation or a hyper-resonant hemithorax with absent breath sounds on one side.
Positive-pressure ventilation before decompression makes the tension worse and can cause cardiac arrest.
A hyper-resonant chest points to trapped air rather than haemothorax, and fluid will not relieve obstructive shock.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has left-sided ulcerative colitis confirmed on colonoscopy. Symptoms began 3 months ago. Liver function tests are normal. She asks about bowel cancer risk. When should surveillance colonoscopy begin?
questions.why: Colorectal cancer risk in ulcerative colitis goes up with how long the disease has lasted and how much of the colon is involved. Australian guidelines (Cancer Council Australia, GESA) advise a first surveillance colonoscopy about 8 years after symptoms began. The interval after that depends on her risk, for example whether she has PSC, active inflammation, strictures or a family history.
notes: Yearly colonoscopy from diagnosis is for patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal liver tests make PSC unlikely.
Waiting 15 years would miss the period when dysplasia and cancer risk are already rising.
Age 45 is the starting age for average-risk population screening, and it does not apply to colitis-related risk.
Age 50 is an older population screening age that ignores how long she has had colitis, so cancer could be found late.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man who smokes has had a painless, indurated ulcer on the lateral tongue for 5 weeks, persisting after an adjacent sharp tooth was smoothed. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: An indurated oral ulcer that has not healed after 3 weeks, even once the possible cause of trauma is removed, is treated as squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. The diagnosis is made on tissue. An incisional biopsy taken from the edge of the lesion gives the histology and is the definitive test, ideally performed after urgent referral to oral and maxillofacial surgery or head and neck surgery.
notes: Brush cytology is only an adjunct: a negative result does not exclude cancer, so tissue histology is still needed.
Toluidine blue staining helps choose where to biopsy but is not specific and cannot confirm a diagnosis.
CT of the neck is used for staging once cancer is confirmed and does not give a tissue diagnosis.
Herpes simplex ulcers are painful, multiple and short-lived, not a single painless indurated ulcer lasting 5 weeks.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents in labour at 39 weeks' gestation. An endocervical NAAT taken two days ago is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and she has not been treated. Which neonatal complication is most likely?
questions.why: The baby can catch gonorrhoea during a vaginal birth. The main risk is gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, a heavy pus-filled conjunctivitis that usually starts 2 to 5 days after birth and can quickly damage the cornea. To prevent it, treat the mother and give the exposed newborn a single dose of ceftriaxone, as eTG and RCH advise.
notes: Afebrile pneumonitis at 4 to 12 weeks is typical of chlamydia caught at birth, not gonorrhoea.
Chorioretinitis is a feature of congenital toxoplasmosis or CMV, not gonococcal infection.
Sensorineural hearing loss is the classic long-term result of congenital CMV.
Snuffles (syphilitic rhinitis) is caused by congenital Treponema pallidum infection, not gonorrhoea.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with confusion and petechiae. Platelets are 18 x 10^9/L and haemoglobin is 82 g/L; the blood film shows schistocytes. Coagulation studies are normal. Most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Low platelets, haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes on the film, neurological signs and normal coagulation point to thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), which is a medical emergency. Urgent plasma exchange, usually given with corticosteroids, should start without waiting for the ADAMTS13 result, because untreated TTP is often fatal.
notes: Platelet transfusion can make the clotting in small vessels worse in TTP, so it is avoided unless there is life-threatening bleeding.
Intravenous immunoglobulin is used for immune thrombocytopenia, which does not cause schistocytes or haemolytic anaemia.
Corticosteroids are given alongside plasma exchange, but on their own they are not enough for acute TTP.
Eculizumab treats complement-mediated atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, which usually causes severe kidney injury rather than mainly neurological signs.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is hypotensive (BP 78/50 mmHg) with a rising central venous pressure six hours after coronary bypass grafting. His mediastinal drain output has suddenly stopped after heavy bleeding. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Low blood pressure and a rising CVP after heavy bleeding that suddenly stops draining point to cardiac tamponade from clotted blood after cardiac surgery. The definitive treatment is emergency resternotomy, done at the bedside if the patient is crashing, to remove the clot and control the bleeding.
notes: After cardiac surgery the tamponade is usually clotted and loculated, so a needle often cannot drain it and the bleeding is left uncontrolled.
A vasopressor does not relieve the mechanical blockage to cardiac filling and only delays definitive treatment.
Correcting clotting may reduce ongoing bleeding but does nothing for blood that is already compressing the heart.
A balloon pump supports a failing left ventricle but cannot overcome external compression of the heart in tamponade.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man ran a petrol generator inside a closed shed and was found unconscious. After oxygen therapy he is now alert with normal neurological examination and carboxyhaemoglobin 4%. Which complication is he most at risk of?
questions.why: After significant carbon monoxide poisoning, especially with loss of consciousness, delayed neurological sequelae can appear days to weeks after apparent recovery. They include memory loss, cognitive and personality change, and parkinsonism. He should be counselled about these symptoms and arranged neurocognitive follow-up, even though he is well at discharge.
notes: Pulmonary fibrosis follows paraquat or chronic dust exposure, not carbon monoxide poisoning.
Peripheral neuropathy is a feature of chronic lead, arsenic or solvent exposure, not a typical result of acute carbon monoxide poisoning.
Posterior subcapsular cataracts are linked to radiation, corticosteroids or electrical injury, not to carbon monoxide.
Acute kidney injury can occur from rhabdomyolysis during the event, but chronic kidney disease is not the expected long-term risk in a patient who has recovered.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has two days of sharp chest pain eased by sitting forward, following a cold. ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression; troponin is normal. Ibuprofen is started. Which added drug most reduces recurrence?
questions.why: Recurrence is the commonest complication of acute pericarditis and happens in up to about 30% of patients. Under eTG and the 2025 ESC guidelines, colchicine for 3 months is added to an NSAID: 500 micrograms once daily under 70 kg, or twice daily from 70 kg. It roughly halves the recurrence rate and speeds symptom relief.
notes: Corticosteroids are not first-line, and early use in viral or idiopathic pericarditis actually raises the risk of recurrence.
Hydroxychloroquine is used for lupus serositis, which has not been shown here, and it does not prevent recurrence of viral or idiopathic pericarditis.
Beta-blockers may ease the tachycardia, but they do nothing to the pericardial inflammation or the recurrence risk.
A proton pump inhibitor is given as gastroprotection with the NSAID, but it does not change the risk of recurrence.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer on regular oral morphine has two days of drowsiness and multifocal myoclonus. Creatinine is 240 µmol/L (baseline 80 µmol/L); corrected calcium 2.40 mmol/L. Most likely cause?
questions.why: The creatinine has risen sharply from baseline, which means acute kidney injury. The kidneys clear morphine's active metabolites (morphine-3- and morphine-6-glucuronide), so these build up and cause drowsiness and myoclonus. Management is to reduce or stop the morphine and switch to an opioid less affected by kidney function, such as fentanyl or hydromorphone, while treating the cause of the kidney injury.
notes: A corrected calcium of 2.40 mmol/L is normal, so hypercalcaemia does not explain her drowsiness.
Leptomeningeal disease usually causes headache, cranial nerve palsies or nerve root signs, and it would not explain symptoms that appeared alongside the kidney injury.
A creatinine of 240 µmol/L is rarely high enough to cause uraemic encephalopathy, and her opioid use is a far more likely explanation.
Serotonin toxicity needs a serotonergic drug and causes clonus, high temperature and agitation, not sedation linked to kidney injury.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has central chest tightness, now settled with GTN. BP 136/80 mmHg. ECG shows new lateral ST depression; hs-troponin T rises from 40 to 115 ng/L. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She has a high-risk NSTEMI: no ST elevation, but dynamic ST depression and a rising troponin above the 99th percentile. Australian ACS guidelines recommend invasive coronary angiography within 24 hours, alongside aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor and an anticoagulant. Her pain has settled and she is haemodynamically stable, so the very-high-risk 2-hour pathway does not apply.
notes: The 2-hour pathway is for very-high-risk features such as refractory pain, haemodynamic instability, acute heart failure or a life-threatening arrhythmia, and she has none of these.
Thrombolysis is used only for STEMI when PCI cannot be done in time, and it does not help in NSTEMI.
Stress testing is for low-risk chest pain with negative troponins and a normal ECG, not for a confirmed NSTEMI.
CT coronary angiography is used to rule out disease in low- to intermediate-risk patients, not to plan revascularisation in a confirmed NSTEMI.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after vomiting about 400 mL of bright red blood at home. He has passed black stools for 2 days. He has drunk about 10 standard drinks of beer daily for 20 years, and his last drink was last night. He takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse is 116/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. He is alert and oriented. He has spider naevi on his chest and palmar erythema. The abdomen has shifting dullness, and the spleen tip is palpable. Two large-bore cannulas are inserted and a crystalloid bolus is started. Laboratory studies show: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130–180) Platelets 74 x10^9/L (150–400) INR 1.9 (0.9–1.2) Urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5–7.5) Creatinine 90 µmol/L (60–110) Albumin 26 g/L (35–50) The gastroenterology registrar plans endoscopy within the next few hours. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR
Pantoprazole infusion as the only drug therapy
Red cell transfusion to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L
questions.why: This man has an upper GI bleed with features of decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis and portal hypertension: ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of chronic liver disease, low platelets, a raised INR and a low albumin. His tachycardia and borderline blood pressure point to significant blood loss. The bleed should be treated as variceal until endoscopy shows otherwise. Under Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) and Baveno VII, a vasoactive drug (terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 hours, or octreotide) should start as soon as a variceal bleed is suspected, before endoscopy. It lowers portal pressure, improves control of bleeding and reduces mortality. Patients with cirrhosis and GI bleeding should also get antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily). This reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and death. Endoscopic band ligation should follow within 12 hours. Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis, and the extra volume can raise portal pressure. A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does nothing for a variceal bleed and would delay vasoactive therapy and antibiotics.
notes: Fresh frozen plasma is wrong because the INR does not predict bleeding in cirrhosis, eTG advises against routinely correcting it, and the extra volume raises portal pressure.
A pantoprazole infusion alone is wrong because it does not lower portal pressure or treat a variceal bleed, and it leaves out the vasoactive drug and antibiotics the guidelines require.
Transfusing to a haemoglobin above 100 g/L is wrong because the restrictive target is 70 to 80 g/L, and over-transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding.
Balloon tamponade is wrong because it is only a temporary rescue for bleeding that cannot be controlled after drug and endoscopic therapy, and endoscopy is already planned.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy is brought in drowsy and vomiting. His father says he rolled off a couch. He has a bulging fontanelle and bruises on both upper arms. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A drowsy, vomiting infant with a bulging fontanelle, grip-type bruising and a history that does not fit the injuries suggests abusive head trauma. Urgent non-contrast CT brain is the first investigation. It quickly detects subdural haemorrhage that may need neurosurgery and records the injuries for child protection. Under RCH guidance, skeletal survey, eye examination and a mandatory report follow once the child is stable.
notes: A skeletal survey is part of the workup for suspected abuse, but it should not delay brain imaging in an infant with signs of raised intracranial pressure.
MRI is better for dating injuries and finding subtle damage, but it is slower and usually needs sedation, so it is a later test and not the first in an unstable infant.
Cranial ultrasound misses many subdural and convexity bleeds, so it cannot safely rule out an intracranial injury.
Lumbar puncture is dangerous when there are signs of raised intracranial pressure and would not show the injury.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and newly diagnosed Hashimoto thyroiditis reports fatigue. Haemoglobin is 101 g/L and MCV 120 fL. B12 and folate results are pending. Greatest risk of starting folic acid alone?
questions.why: An MCV of 120 fL is too high to blame on hypothyroidism alone. Her two autoimmune diseases make pernicious anaemia likely. Folic acid alone can correct the anaemia while the B12 deficiency goes on damaging nerves, so subacute combined degeneration of the cord can appear or get worse. B12 deficiency must be excluded or treated before folate is given.
notes: Hypokalaemia comes from the rapid red cell production after B12 replacement in severe anaemia, not from folate given to a patient with a mild anaemia.
A rise in platelets during recovery from megaloblastic anaemia is a harmless lab finding, not the main danger.
Folic acid has no effect on glucose levels or insulin needs, so it does not cause hypoglycaemia.
Folic acid has no effect on the thyroid; thyrotoxicosis would come from too much levothyroxine, not from folate.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man has had three spontaneous attacks of spinning vertigo, each lasting 4 hours, with fluctuating left-ear hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness. Examination between attacks is normal. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: His spontaneous vertigo attacks lasting hours, with fluctuating ear symptoms on one side, point to Ménière's disease. The Bárány criteria for definite Ménière's disease need a low- to medium-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the affected ear, documented on audiometry. Pure-tone audiometry is therefore the test that confirms it.
notes: MRI is used to rule out a vestibular schwannoma once audiometry shows an uneven sensorineural loss; it cannot confirm Ménière's disease.
The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre tests for BPPV, which causes positional vertigo lasting seconds, not spontaneous attacks lasting hours.
Caloric testing may show reduced function on one side, but it is not specific and is not part of the diagnostic criteria.
CT scanning is poor at showing the posterior fossa and inner ear, and nothing here suggests stroke or another central cause.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with newly diagnosed ileocolonic Crohn's disease has haemoglobin 118 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 16 µg/L, transferrin saturation 8% and CRP 28 mg/L. Most likely cause of his anaemia?
questions.why: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so inflammation pushes it up. A ferritin of 16 µg/L with a CRP of 28 mg/L therefore confirms true iron deficiency, and the microcytosis and low transferrin saturation support this. In active IBD, IV iron is preferred.
notes: Anaemia of inflammation is usually normocytic with a normal or high ferritin (often above 100 µg/L), not a ferritin of 16 µg/L.
Thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis with normal iron stores, so it would not explain the low ferritin and transferrin saturation.
Ileal Crohn's disease can cause B12 deficiency, but that gives a macrocytic anaemia, and here the MCV is 76 fL.
Sideroblastic anaemia shows iron overload, with high ferritin and transferrin saturation, which is the opposite of these results.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with 18 years of type 2 diabetes has night forefoot pain eased by hanging his foot over the bed. Pedal pulses are absent; ankle-brachial index is 1.40. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Rest pain eased by dependency and absent pulses point to peripheral arterial disease. In long-standing diabetes, an ABI of 1.3 or more usually means calcified, incompressible tibial arteries, so the ABI cannot be trusted. Diabetes Feet Australia guidelines recommend toe pressure or toe-brachial index (with Doppler waveforms), because digital arteries are rarely calcified.
notes: Repeating the test gives the same falsely high reading, because the calcified ankle vessels still cannot be compressed.
An exercise ABI still relies on compressing the calcified ankle arteries, and it is unsafe and unnecessary in a man with rest pain.
Plain x-ray may show calcified arteries or bone changes but does not measure limb perfusion or confirm ischaemia.
Neurogenic claudication causes pain on walking, not night forefoot pain eased by hanging the foot down with absent pulses.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man presents to a general practice in Perth with a 7-week history of cough productive of yellow phlegm. For the past week the phlegm has been streaked with blood. He reports drenching night sweats and has lost 6 kg without trying. He was born in the Philippines, moved to Australia 4 years ago and works as a cleaner. He has no medical history, takes no regular medicines and has never smoked. His temperature is 37.9 °C, heart rate 96/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There are crackles over the left upper zone, and there is no clubbing or lymphadenopathy. White cell count is 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), CRP is 41 mg/L (<5) and HIV serology is negative. A chest X-ray shows patchy opacification with a small cavity at the left apex. He has been given a surgical mask and moved to a separate room. Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Interferon-gamma release assay on peripheral blood
Tuberculin skin test read at 48 to 72 hours
Three sputum samples for acid-fast smear, culture and NAAT
Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest
questions.why: This man has had a productive cough for more than 3 weeks, with haemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss. He was born in a country with high TB rates, and his chest X-ray shows a cavity in the upper lobe. This is active pulmonary tuberculosis until proven otherwise. The X-ray supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm it. Confirmation needs microbiology. The Australian guidelines (CDNA SoNG, the state TB programs and eTG Antibiotic) recommend 3 sputum samples collected at least 8 hours apart, with at least 1 taken first thing in the morning. Each sample has acid-fast bacilli smear microscopy, mycobacterial culture and a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT, such as Xpert MTB/RIF). Smear microscopy and NAAT give a quick answer. NAAT also tells M. tuberculosis apart from non-tuberculous mycobacteria and detects rifampicin resistance. Culture is the gold standard and gives full drug-susceptibility results. A cavity usually means a high bacterial load, so expectorated sputum is very likely to be positive. The samples should be collected outdoors or in a well-ventilated room, away from other people. He also needs urgent referral to the state TB service and notification.
notes: An interferon-gamma release assay shows immune sensitisation to M. tuberculosis, but it cannot tell latent infection from active disease, and a negative result does not exclude active TB.
A tuberculin skin test cannot tell latent infection from active disease, can be falsely positive after BCG vaccination (common in people born in the Philippines), and needs a second visit.
CT shows the cavity and the extent of disease in more detail, but it provides no microbiological confirmation or susceptibility results and does not change the need for sputum testing.

Bronchoscopy with lavage is invasive and carries a risk of spreading infection to staff, so it is kept for patients who cannot produce sputum or whose sputum samples are negative despite strong suspicion.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with one previous vaginal birth is being induced at 40 weeks. Cervix 3 cm dilated, vertex 4/5 palpable at station -3. Amniotomy is planned. Which complication is she at greatest risk of?
questions.why: If the membranes are ruptured while the presenting part is high and not engaged, the cord can slip past the head and be compressed. Queensland induction guidance and the RCOG cord prolapse guideline advise against amniotomy with a high head where possible. If it must be done, the fetal heart should be checked straight afterwards, and any sudden deceleration needs a vaginal examination to look for the cord.
notes: Abruption after amniotomy mainly happens when a lot of fluid drains suddenly in polyhydramnios, and she has no polyhydramnios.
Uterine rupture is mainly a risk with a uterine scar or obstructed labour, and she has only had a vaginal birth.
Amniotic fluid embolism is very rare and unpredictable, so amniotomy does not make it the main risk for her.
Tachysystole is caused by too much oxytocin or prostaglandin, not by amniotomy itself.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man, a retired boilermaker, has 3 months of worsening right shoulder pain. Chest X-ray shows a 5 cm right apical mass eroding the first rib. Which deficit is most likely to develop?
questions.why: A superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumour spreads upward into the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8 and T1), which runs over the first rib. This causes pain along the inner arm, wasting and weakness of the small hand muscles, and numbness on the ulnar side. Examine the hands and eyes of anyone with an apical mass, and refer urgently.
notes: Shoulder abduction is supplied by C5 through the upper trunk and axillary nerve, which lie higher up and away from the superior sulcus.
Wrist drop comes from a radial nerve or C7 lesion, usually compression in the spiral groove, and is not a typical sign of an apical tumour.
Elbow flexion is supplied by C5 and C6 through the musculocutaneous nerve, so it is spared until much later than the lower roots.
The lateral forearm is C6 skin (lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve); Pancoast tumours cause numbness of the medial forearm and ulnar hand (C8 and T1).

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 2 days of left-sided temporal headache. She has pain when brushing her hair and jaw pain that builds while chewing and settles at rest. This morning she woke with a grey shadow over the lower half of the vision in her left eye. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and has never had regular headaches. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse is 82/min, respirations are 16/min, blood pressure is 148/86 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. The left temporal artery is thickened, tender and pulseless. Visual acuity is 6/6 in the right eye and 6/24 in the left. There is a left relative afferent pupillary defect, and fundoscopy shows a pale, swollen left optic disc. ESR is 92 mm/h (reference <30), CRP is 64 mg/L (reference <5) and platelet count is 498 × 10^9/L (reference 150–400). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain
Oral aspirin 300 mg as a single dose
questions.why: This woman over 50 has a new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, a thickened pulseless temporal artery, raised ESR and CRP, and thrombocytosis. This is giant cell arteritis. Her left eye shows reduced acuity, an inferior field defect, an RAPD and a pale (chalky) swollen disc, so she already has arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Without treatment, the other eye can lose vision within days. Therapeutic Guidelines (Rheumatology) advise that suspected GCA with any visual symptom or sign is a sight-threatening emergency. It should be treated at once with IV methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days, then high-dose oral prednisolone, with same-day ophthalmology review. Treatment should never wait for a biopsy or imaging. Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily is the starting dose for GCA without visual involvement and is not enough once the optic nerve is ischaemic. A temporal artery biopsy confirms the diagnosis, but it stays positive for 1 to 2 weeks after steroids start, so waiting for it only risks the other eye.
notes: Oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg is the right start for GCA without visual involvement, but she already has ischaemic optic neuropathy and needs IV pulse therapy.
A biopsy stays diagnostic for 1 to 2 weeks after steroids start, so it should be done after treatment begins, not before.
A gradual-onset headache with no focal neurological signs and classic GCA features does not need CT, and scanning first would delay sight-saving treatment.
Aspirin does not suppress the granulomatous vasculitis and cannot replace urgent high-dose corticosteroids.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has 3 months of loose stools, bloating and fatigue. Ferritin is 5 µg/L. tTG-IgA is 180 U/mL (normal <20) with normal total IgA; she still eats gluten. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A strongly positive tTG-IgA with normal total IgA makes coeliac disease very likely. In Australian adults, GESA and Coeliac Australia still require confirmation by gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies (at least 4 from D2 and 1 to 2 from the bulb) while the patient is eating gluten, before a lifelong gluten-free diet is started.
notes: Colonoscopy does not sample the proximal small bowel, where coeliac disease causes its damage.
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing is mainly useful to rule coeliac disease out, because many healthy people carry these alleles, so a positive result cannot confirm it.
Faecal calprotectin helps tell inflammatory bowel disease from IBS, and it does not confirm coeliac disease.
Capsule endoscopy is kept for complicated or refractory coeliac disease, or for patients who cannot have a gastroscopy, and it does not give tissue for histology.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with Crohn's disease is due to start infliximab. Screening shows HBsAg positive, anti-HBc positive, HBeAg negative and HBV DNA 400 IU/mL. ALT is normal. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She is HBsAg positive, which means chronic hepatitis B, and anti-TNF therapy carries a high risk of hepatitis B reactivation. Australian guidance is to start entecavir or tenofovir before immunosuppression and keep it going during treatment and for at least 12 months after. A low viral load and normal ALT do not remove the need for this prophylaxis.
notes: Vaccination does nothing for someone who already has the infection; it is for people with no markers of infection or immunity.
Monitoring without treatment is an option only for low-risk HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc-positive patients, not for HBsAg-positive patients starting anti-TNF therapy.
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin is for post-exposure protection, such as in newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers, and does not prevent reactivation.
Infliximab can still be given safely with antiviral cover, so denying effective Crohn's treatment is not justified.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman is reviewed in the coronary care unit 3 hours after emergency coronary angiography. She came to the emergency department with central chest pain, fever and a productive cough 2 days after her sister's funeral. Her ECG showed ST elevation in V2 to V4. Angiography showed no obstructive coronary disease, and left ventriculography showed apical ballooning. Her chest X-ray shows right lower lobe pneumonia, and she is receiving ceftriaxone and azithromycin. She has had 1 L of crystalloid since arrival. Temperature is 38.2 °C, pulse 108/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 95% on 2 L/min oxygen. She has a new harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Her JVP is not raised, and there are crackles at the right base only. Bedside echocardiography shows an LVEF of 35%, apical akinesis with hyperdynamic basal segments, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and a peak left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 70 mmHg. Serum lactate is 2.9 mmol/L (reference below 2.0). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing her low blood pressure?
questions.why: This woman has Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: two stress triggers (her sister's death and pneumonia with sepsis), apical ballooning, and no culprit lesion on angiography. She now has one of its most dangerous complications, dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. The basal segments contract too hard, which pulls the anterior mitral leaflet into the outflow tract (systolic anterior motion, SAM). That causes the new systolic murmur, a gradient of 70 mmHg and hypotension. The obstruction gets worse with anything that empties the ventricle or makes it contract harder: low preload, low afterload, tachycardia or inotropes. Her JVP is not raised, she has no pulmonary oedema, and sepsis has left her relatively low on fluid, so the first step is a cautious crystalloid bolus to fill the LV and widen the outflow tract. Reassess after each bolus. If hypotension persists, the next options are a pure vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine, a short-acting beta-blocker if she can tolerate it, or mechanical support that does not lower afterload. Inotropes are avoided.
notes: Wrong: dobutamine is an inotrope that makes the basal segments contract harder and speeds the heart, which worsens SAM, raises the LVOT gradient and can deepen the shock.
Wrong: a nitrate dilates veins and arteries, lowering preload and afterload, which narrows the outflow tract, worsens the obstruction and would drop her blood pressure further.
Wrong: a diuretic lowers preload in a woman with no pulmonary oedema and a JVP that is not raised, so the LV cavity shrinks and the obstruction gets worse.
Wrong: a balloon pump lowers afterload, which can increase the LVOT gradient, so it is not recommended in Takotsubo with outflow obstruction.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of burning central chest pain that began 90 minutes after a large dinner. For 6 weeks he has had similar pain on most evenings. It is worse when he lies flat and partly eased by over-the-counter antacids, and he has acid regurgitation. For the past month, bread and steak have felt as if they stick behind his sternum. His weight has fallen from 84 kg to 79 kg over 3 months without dieting. He drinks about 4 standard drinks daily, stopped smoking 10 years ago and takes no regular medicines. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 98% on room air. He has mild epigastric tenderness and no palpable lymph nodes. A 12-lead ECG recorded during pain is normal. High-sensitivity troponin I is 2 ng/L at 0 hours and 2 ng/L at 2 hours (99th percentile 26 ng/L). Haemoglobin is 136 g/L (reference 130 to 180 g/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Eight-week trial of a proton pump inhibitor
Urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori
questions.why: The ECG taken during pain is normal, and high-sensitivity troponin is very low and unchanged at 0 and 2 hours, so acute MI is ruled out and this man is at low risk of acute coronary syndrome. His symptoms fit gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: burning retrosternal pain after meals that is worse lying flat, with acid regurgitation. He also has two alarm features. One is new dysphagia to solids. The other is unintentional loss of 5 kg, which is about 6% of his body weight. Daily alcohol and past smoking add to his risk. Under Therapeutic Guidelines (Gastrointestinal), alarm features call for an urgent gastroscopy rather than empirical treatment. The aim is to find or rule out the serious complications of reflux, such as peptic stricture, Barrett's oesophagus and oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and to take biopsies. The most important thing to prevent here is a missed or late diagnosis of cancer. A PPI can be started after the scope is booked, but it does not replace the scope.
notes: An empirical PPI trial is only for reflux without alarm features, and it can ease symptoms and heal the mucosa, which delays and hides the diagnosis of cancer.
A normal ECG during pain and unchanged troponin well below the 99th percentile mean he is low risk, and his symptoms are not cardiac, so coronary imaging does not deal with the main danger.
A barium swallow can show narrowing but cannot take a biopsy, and it is not first-line for dysphagia with weight loss, so it would only delay the gastroscopy he needs.
Test-and-treat for H. pylori is for dyspepsia without alarm features, and it does not investigate dysphagia or weight loss.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with asthma cannot complete sentences. After one hour of salbutamol and ipratropium via spacer plus oral prednisolone, she remains breathless with widespread wheeze; venous pCO2 34 mmHg. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She has severe acute asthma that has responded poorly to an hour of salbutamol and ipratropium plus a systemic steroid. The Australian Asthma Handbook adds IV magnesium sulfate, 10 mmol over 20 minutes, at this point. Her low pCO2 shows she is not yet tiring, so the next step is to escalate drug treatment rather than intubate.
notes: Aminophylline is not recommended routinely in acute asthma because it adds little benefit and has a narrow therapeutic index with toxicity, including arrhythmias and seizures.
Montelukast is a maintenance controller with no role in treating a severe acute attack.
Inhaled corticosteroids do not replace systemic steroids or bronchodilators in the acute attack, and she has already had prednisolone.
There are no features of infection, and antibiotics are not part of routine management of an asthma exacerbation.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman admitted with cellulitis refuses intravenous antibiotics. She is drowsy, with fluctuating attention and no focal neurological signs. She recently started hydrochlorothiazide alongside her usual sertraline. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Fluctuating attention and drowsiness suggest delirium, which may be impairing her capacity to refuse treatment. A thiazide combined with an SSRI is a classic cause of hyponatraemia. Checking serum sodium looks for a reversible cause, because capacity should be optimised and reassessed rather than her refusal simply being accepted or overridden.
notes: With no focal signs and an obvious metabolic cause from her medications, brain imaging is not the first investigation.
A cognitive screening score cannot identify the cause of delirium and does not decide capacity for a particular decision.
An EEG is for suspected non-convulsive seizures and is not a first-line test for delirium with a clear metabolic cause.
Her infection is already known to be cellulitis, and the drug history points to hyponatraemia rather than a urinary infection.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with a glass laceration over the right external jugular vein becomes breathless sitting upright after her dressing slips. Wound re-occluded, oxygen on: BP 84/50 mmHg, SpO2 88%, mill-wheel murmur. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Sudden breathlessness, hypoxia, hypotension and a mill-wheel murmur after air gets into an open neck vein mean venous air embolism. Once the wound is occluded and high-flow oxygen is running, the next step is to put her head-down on her left side (Durant manoeuvre). This keeps the air in the right atrium and away from the right ventricular outflow tract. In trauma, turn her by log-roll with in-line stabilisation, and call senior help.
notes: Lying on the right side lets the air move into the right ventricular outflow tract and pulmonary artery, which makes the air lock worse.
Nothing here suggests tension pneumothorax: there is no tracheal deviation or one-sided loss of breath sounds, and the murmur points to air in the heart.
A mill-wheel murmur fits intracardiac air rather than tamponade, which gives muffled heart sounds and a raised JVP.
She is talking and her airway is not threatened, and positive-pressure ventilation would not move the air lock, so positioning comes first.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has a PSA of 8.6 ng/mL at a check-up and 8.9 ng/mL on repeat six weeks later. Urine culture is sterile and digital rectal examination is normal. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: His PSA has stayed raised on repeat testing, infection has been excluded, and a normal DRE does not rule out cancer. Australian practice is therefore to do a multiparametric prostate MRI before any biopsy. The MRI gives the lesion a PI-RADS score, which decides whether to biopsy and which area to target.
notes: Biopsy comes after the MRI, which decides whether a biopsy is needed and where to target it, so going straight to biopsy is premature.
PSMA PET/CT stages cancer once intermediate- or high-risk disease is confirmed on biopsy; it is not a test used to make the diagnosis.
A bone scan is a staging test for advanced disease and has no role before cancer has been diagnosed.
Transrectal ultrasound alone cannot reliably tell cancer from benign tissue and has been replaced by MRI for this purpose.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man has 6 hours of fever 39.5 °C, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. GCS 15, no focal signs or papilloedema. Blood cultures taken, ceftriaxone and dexamethasone given; coagulation normal. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Suspected bacterial meningitis is confirmed by CSF analysis (cell count, protein, glucose ratio, Gram stain, culture, PCR). Under eTG, a CT before LP is needed only if GCS is reduced or there are focal signs, seizures or papilloedema. He has none of these and his coagulation is normal, so the next step is lumbar puncture, done after the antibiotics and dexamethasone he has already had.
notes: CT before LP is needed only for reduced GCS, focal signs, seizures or papilloedema, and here it would only delay the diagnosis.
MRI cannot confirm meningitis or identify the organism, and getting it in the ED delays the diagnosis.
Angiography looks for an aneurysm in subarachnoid haemorrhage, but his headache built up gradually and he has a high fever.
EEG helps with seizures or encephalitis, but he has no confusion, seizures or behaviour change.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old medical student gets a hollow-bore needlestick injury during venepuncture. He has washed the site and reported it. He is hepatitis B immune. The patient's blood-borne virus status is unknown. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: After first aid and reporting, the next step is to test the source patient for HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C, with their consent. This is done urgently because the result decides whether the student needs HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, which works best within hours and must start within 72 hours. The student also has baseline serology taken, but the source result is what guides immediate management.
notes: Culturing the needle tip is unreliable, potentially hazardous and not recommended in any Australian exposure guideline.
An HIV PCR on the student at baseline cannot show infection from an exposure minutes ago, and it does not guide the decision on prophylaxis.
Baseline liver function tests are only relevant later if hepatitis C or prophylaxis toxicity is a concern, and they do not assess the exposure risk.
A CD4 count measures immune status in known HIV infection, so it cannot tell you whether the source patient is infected.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman, day 4 after total knee replacement, has sudden breathlessness. BP 130/80 mm Hg. CTPA: segmental emboli, normal right ventricle. She is on prophylactic enoxaparin. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She has a pulmonary embolism provoked by surgery. She is haemodynamically stable and her right ventricle is normal, so eTG recommends therapeutic anticoagulation (for example enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily in place of the prophylactic dose, not on top of it) for 3 months. Thrombolysis and other reperfusion treatments are kept for high-risk PE with shock.
notes: Thrombolysis is only for PE with shock, and surgery 4 days ago puts her at high risk of major bleeding.
An IVC filter is only used when anticoagulation cannot be given or fails, and neither applies here.
Catheter-directed treatment is for high-risk PE when thrombolysis cannot be given or has failed, not for a stable patient with a normal right ventricle.
A prophylactic dose has already failed to prevent this clot and is too low to treat an established PE.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old man from a nursing home has three days of absolute constipation and abdominal distension. He is haemodynamically stable without peritonism. Abdominal X-ray shows a coffee-bean loop arising from the pelvis. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is sigmoid volvulus without signs of ischaemia or perforation. First-line management is flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression with a flatus tube left in place. Because the volvulus often recurs, elective sigmoid colectomy is considered during the same admission if the patient is fit for surgery.
notes: Emergency resection is for gangrene, perforation, peritonitis or failed endoscopic decompression, and none of these is present.
A contrast enema is only needed when the diagnosis is unclear, and here the X-ray already shows it.
Neostigmine treats acute colonic pseudo-obstruction and should not be given in mechanical obstruction such as a volvulus.
Colonic stenting is for malignant large bowel obstruction and does not untwist a volvulus.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 2 days of fever and constant, diffuse abdominal pain. Over the past 3 weeks his abdominal girth has increased. Alcohol-related cirrhosis was diagnosed 3 years ago. He has not attended follow-up and drinks about 10 standard drinks daily. He has never had abdominal surgery and takes no regular medicines. Temperature is 38.4°C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 20/min. He is jaundiced. His abdomen is distended, with shifting dullness and mild diffuse tenderness but no guarding or rigidity. Serum results: albumin 24 g/L, glucose 6.1 mmol/L, LDH 190 U/L (reference less than 250 U/L) and creatinine 124 µmol/L. A diagnostic paracentesis under ultrasound guidance yields cloudy, straw-coloured fluid. Fluid results: white cell count 2100 x10^6/L with 75% neutrophils, total protein 8 g/L, albumin 5 g/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L and LDH 105 U/L. The Gram stain shows neutrophils and no organisms. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the paracentesis results?
options: High-gradient ascites with infection and no Runyon criteria for a surgical source
Low-gradient ascites with infection suggesting tuberculous peritonitis
High-gradient ascites with infection meeting Runyon criteria for perforation
High-gradient ascites with a polymorph count below the threshold for infection
Low-gradient ascites with infection suggesting peritoneal carcinomatosis
questions.why: Read the fluid in three steps. First, the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is 24 − 5 = 19 g/L. A gradient of 11 g/L or more means the ascites is due to portal hypertension, which fits his cirrhosis. Second, the absolute neutrophil count is 2100 x 0.75 = 1575 x10^6/L. Anything at or above 250 x10^6/L confirms ascitic infection, so IV antibiotics and IV albumin should start without waiting for the culture. Third, look for a surgical source using the Runyon criteria: protein above 10 g/L, glucose below 2.8 mmol/L, or LDH above the serum upper limit. His protein is 8 g/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L and LDH 105 U/L, so he meets none of them. The Gram stain shows no organisms, and he has no peritonism. Together these point to spontaneous rather than secondary bacterial peritonitis. The low protein (below 10 g/L) is also a risk factor for SBP, and he will need long-term prophylaxis after this episode.
notes: Wrong: tuberculous peritonitis gives a low gradient (below 11 g/L), lymphocyte-rich and protein-rich fluid, but his gradient is 19 g/L, the cells are mostly neutrophils and the protein is 8 g/L.
Wrong: secondary peritonitis needs at least two Runyon criteria, and his protein (8 g/L), glucose (5.6 mmol/L) and LDH (105 U/L, below the serum limit) meet none, with no organisms on Gram stain.
Wrong: the absolute neutrophil count is 1575 x10^6/L, far above the diagnostic threshold of 250 x10^6/L, so this misreads the 75% as the count or ignores the threshold.
Wrong: peritoneal carcinomatosis gives a low gradient and high protein, whereas this fluid has a gradient of 19 g/L and protein of 8 g/L, which point to portal hypertension.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman slashed with a broken bottle sits upright in the emergency department. A wound over her right sternocleidomastoid oozes dark blood and hisses on inspiration. Most appropriate immediate step?
questions.why: A hissing neck wound over the external jugular vein means the vein is being held open by fascia and is drawing in air, which risks venous air embolism. Under EMST principles, first press on the wound and put on an occlusive dressing, then lie her flat or head-down with in-line stabilisation to raise neck venous pressure. Give high-flow oxygen and call senior help.
notes: Probing a wound that breaches the platysma can dislodge clot and let in more air or restart bleeding, so it should only be explored in theatre.
CT angiography is right once she is stable, but it does nothing to stop air being drawn in now.
Raising the head lowers venous pressure in the neck, which makes it more likely that air is drawn into the open vein.
Blindly clamping in the emergency department can injure nearby structures and delays the simple, effective step of occluding the wound.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man, a retired boilermaker without symptoms, has a preoperative chest X-ray. It shows bilateral calcified plaques along the diaphragmatic pleura, with clear lung fields. What does this finding most likely indicate?
questions.why: Calcified pleural plaques on both sides, especially on the diaphragm, are the classic sign of past asbestos exposure, usually 20 or more years earlier. They are benign and do not reduce lung function. They do not turn into cancer, but they show the exposure that raises his risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer, so he needs advice on quitting smoking and on compensation.
notes: Mesothelioma usually causes a one-sided pleural effusion or lumpy pleural thickening with chest pain, not neat calcified plaques in a man without symptoms.
Asbestosis is fibrosis of the lung tissue, usually in the lower zones, so it would not leave the lung fields clear.
Pleural calcification after tuberculosis is usually on one side and follows an old effusion, not plaques on both sides of the diaphragm.
Silicosis affects the lung tissue, with nodules in the upper lobes and eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes, not pleural plaques.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man is reviewed on the surgical ward on the morning he is due to go home. Two days ago he came to the emergency department after suddenly passing a large volume of painless maroon blood with clots. He had one more small bleed in the department and none since. He has type 2 diabetes and knee osteoarthritis. He takes metformin. For the past 3 months he has also taken an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory tablet most days for knee pain. He takes no other medicines. Today his temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. His abdomen is soft and not tender. Haemoglobin is 118 g/L (his baseline is 138 g/L; reference range 130 to 180 g/L). Colonoscopy after bowel preparation showed many diverticula in the sigmoid and descending colon, with no inflammation, active bleeding, polyp or tumour. He asks how he can lower the chance of this happening again. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to reduce his risk of recurrent bleeding?
questions.why: This man had a self-limiting diverticular bleed. It was sudden, painless and large, with maroon blood and clots, and colonoscopy showed diverticulosis with no other source. Diverticular bleeding often recurs, in roughly 20 to 40% of patients over the following years. Non-aspirin NSAIDs are a well-established risk factor that can be changed. They raise the risk of a first diverticular bleed and of a repeat bleed. The British Society of Gastroenterology lower GI bleeding guideline advises stopping non-aspirin NSAIDs after a diverticular bleed, and Australian guidance (eTG) also advises avoiding NSAIDs in diverticular disease. The over-the-counter anti-inflammatory he takes every day should therefore be stopped, and regular paracetamol used for his osteoarthritis pain instead. Other sensible advice is a high-fibre diet with enough fluid, and returning urgently if he bleeds again. Avoiding nuts and seeds is an old myth, and large cohort studies show no added risk of bleeding or diverticulitis. Mesalazine does not prevent diverticular bleeding or recurrent diverticulitis.
notes: Studies show nuts, seeds and popcorn do not raise the risk of diverticular bleeding or diverticulitis, so this restriction does not help.
Mesalazine has no proven role in preventing diverticular bleeding or recurrent diverticular disease.
A proton pump inhibitor protects against upper GI bleeding from NSAIDs but does nothing for bleeding from colonic diverticula.
Elective colectomy is kept for recurrent or uncontrollable bleeding and is not offered after a first bleed that stopped by itself.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman having chemotherapy for breast cancer presents 9 days after her last cycle with a temperature of 38.6 °C. Neutrophils are 0.3 × 10^9/L. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is febrile neutropenia: a temperature of at least 38 °C with neutrophils below 0.5 × 10^9/L. It is a medical emergency. eTG advises starting empirical IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam therapy, usually piperacillin-tazobactam, within 60 minutes of triage, after taking cultures but without waiting for the results. Her blood pressure is normal, so she does not need broader cover.
notes: Waiting for culture results delays antibiotics, and each hour of delay in febrile neutropenia increases deaths.
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate does not cover Pseudomonas, and oral treatment is only for selected low-risk patients after assessment, not as the first step.
Filgrastim is not routine treatment for established febrile neutropenia and does not replace urgent antibiotics.
Adding vancomycin and escalating to meropenem is for sepsis with shock, suspected line infection or MRSA, none of which she has.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, comes to the fetal medicine clinic at 17 weeks pregnant to discuss her amniocentesis result. She conceived naturally. At 10 weeks, whole-genome cell-free DNA screening (fetal fraction 11%) showed a low chance of trisomies 21, 18 and 13 and of sex chromosome conditions, and a high chance of trisomy 16. A 7-week scan had shown one gestational sac. The 12-week scan was normal, with a nuchal translucency of 1.4 mm. Amniocentesis at 16 weeks, with QF-PCR and chromosomal microarray, showed a normal female result with no trisomy 16. Both of her previous pregnancies were uncomplicated. She has no medical history, does not smoke, and takes folic acid and iodine. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Ultrasound today shows a single live fetus with biometry consistent with dates, no anomaly seen, normal amniotic fluid and a high posterior placenta. She is blood group O RhD positive, and her antibody screen is negative. This patient is at greatest risk of which of the following complications later in this pregnancy?
questions.why: The screening result was valid (adequate fetal fraction) and showed a high chance of trisomy 16, but amniocentesis found a chromosomally normal fetus. The vanishing twin explanation is unlikely because she conceived naturally and an early scan showed one sac. The most likely explanation is therefore confined placental mosaicism (CPM): the trisomic cells are in the placenta, which supplies most of the cell-free DNA. RANZCOG/HGSA (C-Obs 59) and ISPD advise amniocentesis rather than CVS for rare autosomal trisomies for exactly this reason, because the placenta itself is likely to be abnormal. CPM involving chromosome 16 is strongly linked with placental dysfunction, which raises the risk of intrauterine growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and stillbirth. A normal amniocentesis result means the fetus is reassuring, but the pregnancy is still high risk. She needs continued care with a fetal medicine or obstetric team, serial growth and Doppler scans in the second half of pregnancy, blood pressure monitoring, and counselling to report reduced fetal movements. Many units also consider low-dose aspirin.
notes: Her only risk factor is mild advanced maternal age, with a normal BMI and uncomplicated previous pregnancies, and placental mosaicism does not cause gestational diabetes.
After amniocentesis, leaking of fluid is uncommon and usually happens within days, so a procedure done a week ago with normal fluid today adds little later risk.
Placental dysfunction from trisomy 16 mosaicism tends to reduce amniotic fluid rather than increase it, and no fetal anomaly or diabetes is present to cause polyhydramnios.
She is RhD positive with a negative antibody screen, so the invasive procedure carries essentially no risk of clinically important sensitisation.

questions.stem: A 20-month-old boy has a femoral shaft fracture after a reported fall from a couch. He is alert with normal neurology, and has bruises of differing ages on his back. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A big fracture from a minor fall, together with bruises of different ages, in a child under 2 years should raise suspicion of physical abuse. RCH and state child protection guidelines say a full skeletal survey should be done to look for hidden or healing fractures, which provides evidence for the mandatory report and the forensic record. Neuroimaging is mainly for infants under 12 months or children with neurological signs.
notes: CT brain is advised for suspected abuse in infants under 12 months or children with neurological signs, and this alert 20-month-old has a normal neurological examination.
A nuclear bone scan is only an add-on to the skeletal survey, it is poor at dating fractures and needs sedation and radiation, so it is not the first test.
Bone densitometry is not validated in toddlers and does not look for the other fractures that abuse would cause.
Genetic testing for osteogenesis imperfecta is only considered if clinical or radiological features suggest it, and it does not explain bruises of different ages.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man comes to his general practitioner because he has had attacks of severe right-sided pain around his eye for 3 weeks. The attacks start about 1 hour after he falls asleep. He has one every night, sometimes with a second in the afternoon, and each lasts 45 to 90 minutes. During an attack, his right eye goes red and waters and his right nostril blocks. He walks around the house because he cannot settle. He had an identical 2-month bout 18 months ago that resolved completely, and an MRI of the brain with contrast at that time was normal. Home oxygen, started a week ago, stops most attacks within 15 minutes, but he is exhausted from losing sleep. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and takes no regular medicines. Between attacks, his pulse is 68/min and his blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg. Neurological examination is normal. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm at 68/min, PR interval 150 ms and QTc 400 ms. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to reduce how often his attacks occur during this bout?
options: Verapamil 80 mg orally three times daily
questions.why: This man has episodic cluster headache and is in the middle of a bout. The diagnosis rests on strictly one-sided orbital pain lasting 45 to 90 minutes, attacks at the same times each day (often soon after falling asleep), same-sided tearing, red eye and nasal blockage, restlessness, and an earlier bout that ended with full remission. An MRI from his first presentation already excluded a structural mimic. Oxygen is treating each attack, but attacks are still happening at least daily, so he needs preventive treatment for the rest of the bout. Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) recommends verapamil as first-line prevention, starting at 80 mg orally three times daily and increasing every 1 to 2 weeks according to response. Verapamil can cause bradycardia and atrioventricular block, so record an ECG before starting and before each dose increase. His baseline PR interval of 150 ms is normal, so verapamil is safe to start. A short course of oral prednisolone can bridge him until verapamil takes effect. Amitriptyline is used to prevent tension-type headache and migraine and has no established benefit in cluster headache.
notes: Amitriptyline helps prevent tension-type headache and migraine, but there is no good evidence that it reduces cluster attacks.
Carbamazepine treats trigeminal neuralgia, which causes stabbing pain lasting seconds, not 45 to 90 minute orbital attacks with autonomic features.
Pizotifen is a migraine preventive with no proven benefit in cluster headache, and it causes sedation and weight gain.
Propranolol is a first-line migraine preventive, but it is ineffective in cluster headache.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has recurrent painful left submandibular swelling that comes on at mealtimes and settles within an hour. Between episodes, examination is normal and he is afebrile. Most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.why: Swelling of the submandibular gland at mealtimes that settles on its own suggests a stone blocking the salivary duct (sialolithiasis). Ultrasound is the first-line test: it is cheap, quick, uses no radiation and finds most stones. It also shows whether the duct is widened and whether the gland itself is normal.
notes: A CT scan with contrast gives a radiation dose, and the contrast can hide a stone; it is kept for suspected abscess or deep neck infection.
MRI sialography is expensive and hard to access, and is a second-line test when ultrasound does not give an answer.
Conventional sialography means putting a tube into the duct, gives radiation and can push a stone further in, so it is not a first-line test.
Fine-needle aspiration is used for a solid gland lump that may be a tumour, not for swelling that comes and goes with meals.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman has been on the stroke unit for 2 days. She woke on the day of admission unable to see objects on her right. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and is otherwise well. Atorvastatin 80 mg daily was started on admission. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 86/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 142/84 mm Hg and weight 68 kg. Each eye tested separately shows a congruous right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. She has no limb weakness, sensory loss or dysphasia. MRI brain shows a 30 × 20 mm acute infarct in the left medial occipital lobe with no haemorrhage on susceptibility-weighted imaging. MR angiography shows an occluded left P2 segment and no carotid stenosis. ECG shows atrial fibrillation; an ECG 3 years ago showed sinus rhythm. Echocardiography shows no valve disease. Haemoglobin is 134 g/L, platelets 241 x10^9/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L (eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73m²) and INR 1.0. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy to reduce her risk of recurrent stroke?
options: Aspirin 100 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg orally daily
Enoxaparin bridging to warfarin, target INR 2 to 3
questions.why: This woman has had a cardioembolic posterior cerebral artery infarct caused by newly found non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is at least 5 (age 75 or over, hypertension, stroke), so her biggest risk is another embolic stroke. The Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management and eTG recommend oral anticoagulation, preferably with a DOAC rather than warfarin, for ischaemic stroke with AF. The stroke team times the start by infarct size, and with no haemorrhage on MRI an early start is reasonable. Apixaban is reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily only if two of these apply: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more. She meets none, so she needs the full dose of 5 mg twice daily. Underdosing is a common error that leaves patients unprotected. Antiplatelet therapy, alone or in combination, does much less to prevent AF-related stroke and does not replace anticoagulation. Bridging with heparin raises the risk of bleeding, including haemorrhagic change in the infarct, and gives no extra protection.
notes: Wrong: she meets none of the criteria for the reduced dose, so 2.5 mg twice daily would underdose her and leave her poorly protected from another embolic stroke.
Wrong: short-term dual antiplatelet therapy is for minor non-cardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA, and it prevents AF-related stroke much less well than anticoagulation while still causing bleeding.
Wrong: aspirin alone gives little protection from cardioembolic stroke in AF and is not a substitute for anticoagulation in a patient without contraindications.
Wrong: DOACs are preferred to warfarin in non-valvular AF, and heparin bridging after an acute infarct raises the risk of haemorrhagic transformation without lowering early recurrence.

questions.stem: A male infant born at 39 weeks in a birth suite after 8 minutes of fetal bradycardia is floppy and apnoeic. His heart rate rises from 70 to 140/min with mask ventilation. Which investigation best quantifies the hypoxic insult?
questions.why: After a baby needs resuscitation at birth, paired arterial and venous cord blood gases give an objective, immediate measure of perinatal acidaemia (pH, base excess, lactate). Cord gas results within the first hour, such as pH 7.0 or below or a base deficit of 12 mmol/L or more, also help decide on therapeutic hypothermia.
notes: Cranial ultrasound detects haemorrhage or structural lesions but is insensitive to early hypoxic-ischaemic injury and does not measure the insult.
aEEG assesses how severe an encephalopathy is in a baby being considered for cooling, but it does not measure the hypoxic insult itself.
MRI brain shows the pattern of hypoxic-ischaemic injury best after several days, not at birth.
Placental histopathology may suggest a cause but takes days and does not measure fetal acidaemia.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man admitted for cellulitis develops tremor, sweating and agitation 36 hours after his last drink. Heart rate is 118/min; CIWA-Ar score is 17. Liver function is normal. Most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: This is moderate to severe alcohol withdrawal (CIWA-Ar above 10), so he needs a benzodiazepine. eTG recommends oral diazepam, given in doses guided by symptoms, when liver function is normal. A long-acting benzodiazepine also helps prevent withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens.
notes: Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat the withdrawal itself; it is only added to a benzodiazepine for hallucinations or agitation that persist.
Clonidine can blunt the fast heart rate and sweating but does not prevent seizures or delirium tremens, so it may hide a worsening withdrawal.
Acamprosate is used after withdrawal to help keep people abstinent and has no role in treating acute withdrawal.
Baclofen is a second-line drug for relapse prevention and is not recommended for treating acute alcohol withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner because of headaches for 7 weeks. They began when she started working 12-hour shifts at a desk to meet the end-of-financial-year deadline at her accounting firm. Before this she had only occasional mild headaches. The headache is a bilateral, band-like tightness that builds through the afternoon. She rates it 4/10. It now comes on every afternoon. She has no nausea or photophobia, and climbing stairs does not make it worse. She takes paracetamol 1 g about five times a week and ibuprofen 400 mg once or twice a week, which takes the edge off it. She drinks four standard drinks a week and does not smoke. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse is 74/min and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Her trapezius and temporalis muscles are tender. Passive neck flexion is full and painless. Fundoscopy shows sharp discs with venous pulsations, and the neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to prevent progression of her headache disorder?
options: Switch to paracetamol with codeine on headache days
Take ibuprofen 400 mg regularly three times a day
Start amitriptyline 10 mg each night as prevention
Use sumatriptan 50 mg at the onset of each attack
Limit acute pain relief to fewer than 10 days per month
questions.why: This woman has tension-type headache: it is bilateral, pressing, mild to moderate and not made worse by activity, she has no nausea or photophobia, her pericranial muscles are tender, and it started with a clear trigger (long hours at a desk under deadline stress). Her examination, including fundoscopy, is normal. The main risk for her is medication-overuse headache. She is already taking simple analgesics on about 25 to 35 days in every 4 weeks. ICHD-3 defines medication-overuse headache as headache on 15 or more days a month with regular overuse for more than 3 months. The threshold is 15 or more days a month for simple analgesics, and 10 or more days a month for triptans, opioids or combination analgesics.
