At 7 weeks she has not met the time criterion yet, but she is well over the frequency threshold. Following eTG, she should keep acute treatment to fewer than 10 days a month (roughly 2 to 3 days a week), keep a headache diary, and avoid codeine. Treatment should be mainly non-drug: posture and ergonomics, regular breaks, sleep, exercise, physiotherapy and stress management.
notes: Codeine-containing combination products cause medication-overuse headache at a lower threshold (10 or more days a month), cause dependence, and eTG advises avoiding opioids in tension-type headache.
Taking ibuprofen regularly every day guarantees analgesic overuse, which raises her risk of medication-overuse headache as well as gastrointestinal and kidney harm.
Preventive amitriptyline is kept for established chronic tension-type headache that has not responded to non-drug measures, and it does nothing about her current analgesic overuse.
Triptans do not work for tension-type headache and cause medication-overuse headache at only 10 or more days a month, so taking one with every daily attack would make things worse.

questions.stem: On the paediatric ward, a 3-year-old boy recovers after bronchoscopic removal of a peanut that caused chronic cough and left-sided wheeze. His parents ask how to protect him and his 14-month-old sister. Most important prevention advice?
questions.why: Inhaled foreign bodies are most common between 1 and 3 years of age, and nuts are the classic culprit. Australian advice (RCH, Kidsafe) is to give no whole nuts or similar hard, small foods to children under 5 years, and to supervise them seated at meals. Nut allergy prevention still uses smooth nut pastes, not whole nuts.
notes: ASCIA advises introducing peanut early as smooth paste to prevent allergy, and delaying it adds allergy risk without reducing choking risk.
Puréeing everything is not needed and holds back feeding development; the aim is to avoid hard, small, round foods.
ANZCOR advises encouraging a child who is coughing effectively to keep coughing, and back blows are only for an ineffective cough.
Once the object is removed and the child recovers, routine serial X-rays do not prevent another inhalation.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a 1-day history of worsening headache, fever, vomiting and photophobia. For 5 days before this he had right ear pain. He has no medical history, takes no medicines and has no allergies. His temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, respirations 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. He is alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. He has neck stiffness, no rash, sharp optic discs and no focal neurological deficit. The right tympanic membrane is red and bulging. Blood cultures are taken and a lumbar puncture is done. Ceftriaxone 2 g and dexamethasone 10 mg are given straight after the procedure. Results: Blood: leucocytes 19.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 185 mg/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L CSF: turbid; opening pressure 28 cmH2O; white cells 1900 x10^6/L (90% polymorphs); red cells 6 x10^6/L; protein 2.1 g/L (0.15 to 0.45); glucose 1.2 mmol/L; Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
questions.why: The CSF is turbid, with many polymorphs, a high protein and a CSF:serum glucose ratio of 1.2/6.0 = 0.2 (below 0.4), so this is bacterial meningitis. Gram-positive diplococci mean Streptococcus pneumoniae, and the probable source is his right acute otitis media. Some pneumococci have reduced susceptibility to penicillin and ceftriaxone. So eTG advises adding vancomycin to ceftriaxone as soon as Gram-positive diplococci are seen, and continuing both until susceptibility results are back. Treatment is then narrowed to suit the organism. Dexamethasone should continue for 4 days, because it gives the most benefit in pneumococcal meningitis. Amoxicillin covers Listeria and is added only for patients at risk: those over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised or with alcohol dependence. He has none of these risks, and Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus, not a diplococcus. Aciclovir is not needed: he has no confusion, seizures or focal signs, and the CSF picture is clearly bacterial with organisms seen. Changing to benzylpenicillin before susceptibility is known risks undertreating a resistant strain.
notes: Amoxicillin covers Listeria, which shows as Gram-positive bacilli and is a risk only in people over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised or alcohol-dependent, and he is none of these.
Aciclovir treats HSV encephalitis, but he has no encephalitic features and the CSF is clearly bacterial, with organisms seen.
Dexamethasone should continue for 4 days in pneumococcal meningitis because this is the organism where it most reduces death and hearing loss.
Narrowing to benzylpenicillin is done only after susceptibility testing confirms a sensitive strain, so changing now could undertreat a resistant pneumococcus.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man who smokes has 4 weeks of constant left forefoot pain at night, eased by dangling the leg. His second toe is dry and black; left ABI is 0.32. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia: he has had ischaemic rest pain for more than 2 weeks, has dry gangrene and an ABI below 0.4. The limb is at high risk of amputation, so he needs to be discussed with the vascular team the same day, with a view to imaging and revascularisation. Meanwhile, give analgesia, keep the leg dependent, protect the foot and start an antiplatelet and a statin.
notes: Supervised exercise is used for intermittent claudication, but he now has rest pain and tissue loss, so exercise therapy is not appropriate and would delay revascularisation.
The gangrene is dry and shows no signs of infection, such as redness, pus or fever, so antibiotics do not treat the underlying ischaemia.
A routine outpatient referral is too slow for a threatened limb with established tissue loss, and the delay risks a major amputation.
Cilostazol only improves walking distance in claudication; it does not save a limb with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and should not replace urgent referral.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man develops headache and nausea after running a petrol generator in a closed garage. He is alert, with a normal neurological examination. Carboxyhaemoglobin is 18%. Most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: This is mild to moderate carbon monoxide poisoning with no neurological features. The treatment is 100% oxygen through a non-rebreather mask as soon as possible, which shortens the half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin from about 5 hours to about 1 hour. Continue it until he has no symptoms and his carboxyhaemoglobin is below about 3–5%. Hyperbaric oxygen is only discussed with a hyperbaric unit for severe cases.
notes: Hyperbaric oxygen is considered only for severe poisoning, such as loss of consciousness, neurological deficit, cardiac ischaemia or pregnancy, and this patient has none of these.
Hydroxocobalamin is the antidote for cyanide poisoning, as in smoke inhalation with high lactate, and does nothing for carbon monoxide.
Low-flow nasal oxygen gives too little oxygen to speed up carbon monoxide removal much, and a normal pulse oximetry reading here gives false reassurance.
Methylene blue treats methaemoglobinaemia, such as from nitrites or dapsone, and does not treat carboxyhaemoglobinaemia.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with heart failure on furosemide and perindopril took naproxen for a week; now breathless and oedematous. BP 152/88 mmHg, warm peripheries. Creatinine 151 µmol/L (baseline 92). Most likely cause of his AKI?
questions.why: He is taking a diuretic and an ACE inhibitor, and adding an NSAID makes the "triple whammy". The NSAID blocks the prostaglandins that widen the vessel into the glomerulus, while the ACE inhibitor stops the vessel out of it from tightening, so filtration falls and the creatinine rises. The same drug also makes him hold onto salt and water, which explains why his heart failure got worse, so stopping the NSAID is a key part of treatment.
notes: Low-output cardiorenal syndrome needs poor perfusion, but his BP is 152/88 mmHg and his peripheries are warm.
He is fluid overloaded, not dry, so volume depletion does not explain the creatinine rise.
Nothing in the case points to urinary retention, and a recent NSAID gives a clearer explanation.
Renal artery stenosis shows up as a creatinine rise when an ACE inhibitor is started, not during a stable long-term course after an NSAID.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with a dry cough that has been getting worse for 4 months. He also has breathlessness when walking uphill, a hoarse voice and a constant dull ache below his right clavicle. He has lost 5 kg without trying. He is a retired electrician who worked around asbestos lagging in the 1970s, and he has never smoked. He takes perindopril for hypertension. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 136/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. The right apex is dull to percussion. He has no clubbing, lymphadenopathy or conjunctival pallor. A chest X-ray shows a 5 cm rounded opacity at the right lung apex. Blood results are: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (130 to 180) MCV 87 fL (80 to 100) White cell count 8.1 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) Platelets 438 x10^9/L (150 to 400) Bilirubin 11 µmol/L (less than 20) Creatinine 95 µmol/L (60 to 110); eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2 Corrected calcium 2.40 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.60) ALP 98 U/L (30 to 110) Albumin 32 g/L (35 to 50) CRP 18 mg/L (less than 5) Which of the following best explains the abnormalities in these blood results?
options: Bone marrow infiltration by metastatic tumour
Erythropoietin deficiency from chronic kidney disease
Anaemia of inflammation due to an underlying malignancy
Haemolysis from a paraneoplastic autoimmune process
Vitamin B12 deficiency from poor dietary intake
questions.why: The bloods show a mild anaemia with a normal MCV (normocytic), a mildly raised platelet count, a mildly raised CRP and a low albumin. In an older man with weight loss and a 5 cm apical mass that is lung cancer until proven otherwise, this pattern fits anaemia of inflammation (anaemia of chronic disease). Tumour-driven cytokines such as IL-6 raise hepcidin, which traps iron and suppresses red cell production. The same cytokines cause a reactive thrombocytosis, a raised CRP and a low albumin. In lung cancer, thrombocytosis and hypoalbuminaemia also point to a worse prognosis. The normal results matter too. The corrected calcium is normal, so there is no hypercalcaemia (from PTHrP or bone metastases). The normal ALP and bilirubin give no blood evidence of bone or liver spread, although normal bloods do not rule out metastases. Renal function is adequate for contrast CT. None of these results changes the plan: he still needs an urgent CT of the chest and upper abdomen and urgent referral to a lung cancer multidisciplinary team, with the aim of being seen within 2 weeks (Cancer Australia; Optimal care pathway for lung cancer).
notes: Wrong: marrow infiltration lowers the counts or gives a leucoerythroblastic picture, often with a raised ALP or calcium, but here the white cell count is normal, the platelets are high and the ALP and calcium are normal.
Wrong: an eGFR of 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2 is too high to cause erythropoietin deficiency, which usually appears only when eGFR falls below about 30 to 45.
Wrong: haemolysis would raise the bilirubin (and LDH and reticulocytes), but his bilirubin is normal.
Wrong: B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia, often with low platelets, but his MCV is 87 fL and his platelets are raised.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 50 minutes of heavy central chest pain that began while she was watching television. Over the past fortnight her known angina has come on with less exertion, and she now needs glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) most days. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, and takes metformin, perindopril, atorvastatin and aspirin. In the ED she has received aspirin 300 mg, three sublingual GTN doses and intravenous morphine, and an intravenous GTN infusion has been titrated for the past 20 minutes. She still rates the pain 7/10 and is diaphoretic. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg in both arms, respirations 18/min and SpO2 96% on room air. Two 12-lead ECGs taken 15 minutes apart show sinus rhythm with no ST-segment or T-wave changes. High-sensitivity troponin I, taken 40 minutes after onset, is 9 ng/L (99th percentile for women 16 ng/L). Chest X-ray is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: This woman has a non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome. She has crescendo angina and prolonged rest pain. Her pain is still going after aspirin, repeated sublingual GTN, opioid and a titrated IV GTN infusion. The 2016 National Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS guideline, which eTG follows, classes ongoing or recurrent ischaemic pain that does not respond to medical treatment as very high risk. This applies whatever the ECG or troponin shows. Very high-risk patients need invasive coronary angiography, with revascularisation if indicated, within 2 hours. Arrange this urgently with cardiology, including the choice of P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulant. A normal ECG and a normal troponin taken 40 minutes after onset do not lower her risk, because both can be normal early in a myocardial infarction. Repeat troponin, CT coronary angiography and stress testing are for patients whose pain has settled and who are at low or intermediate risk. Fibrinolysis is only for STEMI.
notes: Serial troponin helps decide between unstable angina and NSTEMI, but the result would not change her management, because refractory pain already makes her very high risk.
Fibrinolysis gives no benefit and may cause harm in non-ST-elevation ACS, and her ECGs show no ST elevation.
CT coronary angiography is for stable, pain-free patients at low or intermediate risk, not for ongoing ischaemia that needs treatment in the catheter laboratory.
Stress testing is contraindicated while rest pain continues, and putting off assessment until tomorrow is unsafe in very high-risk ACS.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old boy has 4 days of projectile non-bilious vomiting. Ultrasound shows pyloric wall thickness 4.5 mm. Venous bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, chloride 90 mmol/L. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis, and he has the typical hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, which makes this a medical emergency but not a surgical one. Following RCH guidance, keep him nil by mouth and give IV 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose, adding potassium once he passes urine. Pyloromyotomy waits until bicarbonate and chloride are back to normal.
notes: Wrong: thickened feeds and GP review suit reflux, but this is confirmed pyloric stenosis with dehydration and alkalosis, so he needs admission and surgery.
Wrong: operating before the alkalosis is corrected risks post-anaesthetic apnoea, because the breathing has slowed to compensate for the alkalosis.
Wrong: a wall thickness of 4.5 mm on ultrasound already confirms the diagnosis, so a contrast study only adds delay and radiation.
Wrong: atropine is a rarely used medical option that works less reliably and is not standard Australian care; pyloromyotomy is the definitive treatment.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has a 2.5 cm painless nodule in the right thyroid lobe, with palpitations and weight loss. TSH is 0.02 mIU/L (normal 0.4 to 4.0). Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: If a thyroid nodule comes with a suppressed TSH, the next step is a radionuclide scan (technetium or iodine-123) to find out whether the nodule is hyperfunctioning ("hot"). Hot nodules are very rarely cancerous and usually don't need FNA. Only cold nodules, or nodules with a normal or high TSH, go on to ultrasound-guided FNA based on ultrasound risk features.
notes: FNA comes after scintigraphy when TSH is suppressed, because cytology of a hot nodule can look suspicious and lead to needless surgery.
Calcitonin screens for medullary carcinoma and is not a routine first test, especially when the clinical picture is thyrotoxicosis.
CT is used to stage retrosternal extension or airway compression and does not show nodule function or risk of cancer.
Thyroglobulin is used to monitor for recurrence after thyroidectomy for differentiated cancer and cannot tell benign nodules from malignant ones.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on warfarin needs two simple dental extractions tomorrow. His INR measured today is 2.6. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: An INR of 2.6 is in the therapeutic range and below the usual cut-off of about 3 for simple dental extractions. The extractions can go ahead without stopping warfarin, using local haemostatic measures such as packing, sutures and tranexamic acid mouthwash. Stopping warfarin raises the risk of stroke and gives little benefit, because bleeding after an extraction can be controlled locally.
notes: Stopping warfarin for 5 days leaves the patient without anticoagulation and at risk of stroke, and it is not needed when the INR is therapeutic for a minor oral procedure.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin and is kept for very high INRs or active bleeding, not for a planned extraction with a therapeutic INR.
Bridging is only needed when warfarin has to be stopped, and here it does not have to be.
Waiting for a normal INR means stopping anticoagulation, which puts the patient at risk of stroke for no benefit because the current INR is already safe for extraction.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic squamous cell lung cancer presents with confusion and polyuria. His corrected calcium is 3.6 mmol/L and he is clinically dehydrated. Most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.why: Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia of malignancy causes volume depletion. Per eTG, the first step is IV rehydration with sodium chloride 0.9%, which restores kidney perfusion and calcium excretion. An IV bisphosphonate is given once the patient is rehydrated.
notes: Zoledronic acid is needed but takes 2 to 4 days to work, and it is nephrotoxic if given before the patient is rehydrated.
Denosumab is kept for hypercalcaemia that does not respond to bisphosphonates or for severe kidney impairment, not for first-line acute treatment.
Furosemide worsens dehydration and is only used for fluid overload after rehydration, not as a routine calcium-lowering drug.
Corticosteroids help mainly in calcitriol-driven hypercalcaemia, such as lymphoma or granulomatous disease, not PTHrP-mediated squamous cancer.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 5 months of worsening breathlessness. Over this time he has lost 20 kg, has coughed up blood-tinged sputum and his voice has become hoarse. He has COPD, and his triple-therapy inhaler has not helped. He has smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 50 years and worked for decades as a mechanic. His temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse is 110/min, respirations are 29/min, blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg and SpO2 is 92% on room air. He has finger clubbing and a hard right supraclavicular lymph node. On the right side of the chest, expansion is reduced, percussion is stony dull and breath sounds are absent. The trachea is deviated to the left. An erect PA chest X-ray, not rotated, shows a large right effusion with a meniscus reaching the 2nd anterior rib, which obscures the right heart border and hilum. The trachea and mediastinum are displaced to the left. The left lung is clear. Which of the following best explains the position of the trachea and mediastinum on this film?
options: Paratracheal nodal mass displacing the airway
questions.why: The film shows a large right effusion with the trachea and mediastinum pushed to the left, away from the fluid. Being pushed away from the fluid means the effusion has a mass effect: the fluid takes up enough space in the right hemithorax to move the mediastinum across. For this patient, it means the shift is not explained by a major right-sided collapse, so a central obstructing tumour has not pulled the mediastinum back towards the right. It also means the mediastinum is not held in place by pleural tumour. So ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration (no more than about 1.5 L at a time) is likely to ease his breathlessness, and it also gives fluid for diagnosis. A contrast CT chest should ideally be done before the effusion is fully drained. If a very large effusion had no shift, or the mediastinum had moved towards the effusion, that would suggest lobar or lung collapse from an endobronchial tumour, or a mediastinum fixed by mesothelioma or malignant nodes. In that case drainage would help less and could cause problems, and bronchoscopy should be considered. Tension pneumothorax is ruled out because the film shows a meniscus, not air.
notes: Collapse causes volume loss, which pulls the trachea and mediastinum towards the affected (right) side, not away from it.
A mediastinum encased by pleural tumour, as in mesothelioma, cannot move, so a large effusion would cause little or no shift.
Hyperinflation in COPD affects both lungs and does not push the mediastinum sideways, and the left lung is described as clear.
A paratracheal nodal mass widens the mediastinum and may narrow the trachea, but it would not shift the whole mediastinum away from a large right effusion.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with CT-confirmed subarachnoid haemorrhage deteriorates in the ED. GCS falls from 14 to 10 and pulse to 46/min; BP rises to 210/110 mmHg, with irregular breathing. What do these findings most likely indicate?
questions.why: Rising BP, a falling heart rate and irregular breathing (Cushing's triad), together with a falling GCS, mean raised intracranial pressure and impending coning. After SAH this is often caused by acute hydrocephalus. Call a rapid response, protect the airway, get an urgent neurosurgeon for an external ventricular drain, and do not chase the BP down.
notes: The BP rise is a Cushing reflex that keeps the brain perfused against high intracranial pressure; it is not the main problem, and lowering it hard would worsen ischaemia.
Delayed cerebral ischaemia typically happens on days 3 to 14 after the bleed, not within hours of it.
Non-convulsive seizures can lower consciousness, but they do not cause hypertension with bradycardia and irregular breathing.
Neurogenic stunned myocardium causes ECG changes, arrhythmias, hypotension or pulmonary oedema, not hypertension with bradycardia and a falling GCS.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner to discuss blood test results. She has had four months of tiredness, cold intolerance, constipation and weight gain of 5 kg. She has had type 1 diabetes since age 11 and uses insulin glargine and insulin aspart. She drinks about 4 standard drinks a week and rarely eats fresh vegetables. Her pulse is 58/min and blood pressure 114/72 mm Hg. She has a diffuse, firm, non-tender goitre and delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes. Vibration sense, joint position sense and gait are normal. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115–165) MCV 116 fL (80–100) TSH 38 mIU/L (0.4–4.0) Free T4 5.1 pmol/L (10–20) Anti-TPO antibodies strongly positive Morning cortisol 430 nmol/L (normal) Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L Serum folate 4.0 nmol/L (above 7) Serum vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor antibodies: pending Levothyroxine is started. A colleague suggests also starting oral folic acid 5 mg daily today. Starting folic acid on its own before the pending results return puts her at greatest risk of which of the following?
options: Adrenal crisis from unmasked cortisol deficiency
Secondary iron overload from rapid erythropoiesis
Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
questions.why: She has autoimmune (Hashimoto) hypothyroidism and type 1 diabetes, so she is at high risk of pernicious anaemia, another autoimmune disease. An MCV of 116 fL is too high to blame on hypothyroidism alone, and her B12 result is still pending. Folic acid alone can correct the blood count in B12 deficiency, but it does nothing for the nerve damage. So the anaemia looks better while B12-related demyelination of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts (subacute combined degeneration) gets worse, and that damage can be permanent. Australian guidance (eTG) says folate must not be given alone until B12 deficiency has been ruled out or is being treated. A low folate with a normal neurological examination does not remove this risk, because she could be low in both. Safe options are to wait for the B12 result or to give B12 alongside folate.
notes: Low potassium from rapid red cell production happens mainly when severe megaloblastic anaemia is treated with B12, and it is unlikely with her mild anaemia and normal potassium.
Adrenal crisis is the risk when levothyroxine, not folic acid, is started in untreated Addison disease, and her normal morning cortisol and electrolytes make adrenal insufficiency unlikely.
Correcting megaloblastic anaemia uses up iron and can cause iron deficiency, not iron overload.
Gastric cancer is a long-term risk of pernicious anaemia itself, and starting folic acid neither causes it nor speeds it up.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is four days after an oesophagectomy. Since jejunal feeds began, his right chest drain has put out 1200 mL/day of cloudy fluid. The drain fluid triglyceride is 4.8 mmol/L. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: A pleural fluid triglyceride above 1.24 mmol/L (110 mg/dL) confirms chyle. This is thoracic duct injury, a known complication of oesophagectomy, and output rises once enteral feeds start. Management begins with stopping enteral fat (nil by mouth or a medium-chain triglyceride diet, or TPN) and draining the chest. High-output leaks usually need thoracic duct ligation or embolisation.
notes: An anastomotic leak shows saliva, high amylase or enteral feed in the drain with sepsis, not a raised triglyceride.
Pseudochylothorax is a chronic effusion with high cholesterol and cholesterol crystals, not an acute high-triglyceride leak after surgery.
Empyema is pus with low pH, low glucose and organisms, and does not raise the fluid triglyceride.
Haemothorax is blood-stained drainage with a fluid haematocrit over half the blood value, not cloudy fluid high in triglyceride.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department of a regional hospital with 2 days of lower abdominal pain and swelling. The pain began as intermittent cramps in the left lower quadrant and is now constant. She has passed no stool or flatus for 36 hours and began vomiting bile this morning. Eight years ago, two tubular adenomas were removed at colonoscopy, and she did not attend the surveillance colonoscopy she was booked for. She takes metformin for type 2 diabetes. Her temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and respiratory rate 20/min. Her abdomen is grossly distended and tympanic, with mild generalised tenderness, no guarding and tinkling bowel sounds. The hernial orifices are normal. Digital rectal examination shows an empty rectum. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (115–165), white cell count 12.1 x 10^9/L (4.0–11.0), creatinine 84 µmol/L (45–90), eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m2 and venous lactate 1.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0). Fluid resuscitation, analgesia and a nasogastric tube have been started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
questions.why: This woman most likely has a large bowel obstruction. She has early obstipation, gross tympanic distension, vomiting that came late, an empty rectum and tinkling bowel sounds. The most likely cause is an obstructing sigmoid cancer, given her previous adenomas, the surveillance she missed and her mild anaemia. Diverticular stricture and sigmoid volvulus are the other main causes. Her rising pulse and pain that has become constant raise concern for ischaemia or impending perforation, so she needs a definitive test now. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast is the investigation of choice in Australian emergency surgical practice and in the WSES guidelines. It confirms a mechanical obstruction and shows where it is and what is causing it (tumour, stricture or volvulus). It separates true obstruction from pseudo-obstruction and detects caecal distension, ischaemia, perforation and free gas. It also stages a tumour, which guides the choice between a stent, a defunctioning stoma and resection. Her eGFR of 72 allows contrast; withhold metformin around the scan.
notes: A plain radiograph can suggest a dilated colon, but it cannot reliably find the level or cause, tell mechanical obstruction from pseudo-obstruction, or show ischaemia, so it does not replace CT.

A water-soluble contrast enema can confirm a distal colonic block, but it gives no information on ischaemia, staging or anything outside the bowel, so it is kept for when CT is unavailable or inconclusive.

Colonoscopy in an acutely obstructed, unprepared colon risks perforation from air insufflation and is not a first-line diagnostic test, although an endoscopist may later place a stent or take biopsies.
Gas in a grossly distended colon scatters the ultrasound beam, so ultrasound cannot reliably show the level or cause of a large bowel obstruction.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman collapses without warning while gardening and recovers fully within a minute. Her pulse is 36/min, regular and large volume, with intermittent cannon a waves in the neck. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A sudden blackout with no warning, a slow regular large-volume pulse and cannon a waves points to complete heart block (a Stokes-Adams attack). Every blackout needs a 12-lead ECG, and here it is the quickest bedside test to confirm AV dissociation and show whether the escape rhythm is narrow or broad. This then guides atropine, pacing and cardiology referral.
notes: Ambulatory monitoring is for intermittent arrhythmias that the ECG has not caught, but this bradycardia is ongoing and an ECG will show it now.
CT brain is not a routine test for syncope with full recovery and no focal signs, and it will not explain a pulse of 36/min.
Postural blood pressure tests for orthostatic hypotension, but she collapsed with no warning and her pulse is 36/min, so this is cardiac until proven otherwise.
Echocardiography looks for structural heart disease later, but it does not diagnose the conduction block that needs urgent treatment.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia after a festival. He was given IM ceftriaxone 3 hours before lumbar puncture, which shows turbid, neutrophilic CSF. Test most likely to identify the organism?
questions.why: Antibiotics given before the lumbar puncture quickly sterilise CSF and blood cultures. PCR picks up N. meningitidis DNA whether or not the bacteria are still alive, so CSF meningococcal PCR stays positive and is the best way to confirm the organism (and its serogroup) after early antibiotics. That is why antibiotics should never be held back to get samples first.
notes: Culture needs live bacteria, and the CSF is often sterile within hours of a parenteral third-generation cephalosporin, so it is likely to grow nothing.
Blood cultures taken after an antibiotic dose usually grow nothing, and they are positive less often than CSF tests in meningitis even before treatment.
Antibody serology takes paired samples weeks apart, so it is too slow and too insensitive to confirm acute disease.
A positive throat swab may only show carriage, which is common in young adults, and a negative swab does not exclude invasive disease.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with asthma presents to the emergency department breathless after a cold. She speaks in phrases, using accessory muscles. SpO2 is 93% on room air. Breath sounds equal bilaterally. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Speaking only in phrases, using accessory muscles and an SpO2 of 90 to 94% mean acute severe asthma. The first step is repeated inhaled salbutamol by spacer (12 puffs every 20 minutes in the first hour), given with ipratropium, oral prednisolone and oxygen titrated to 92 to 96%, as in the Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG.
notes: IV magnesium is kept for patients who do not respond to the first round of inhaled bronchodilators, so it is not the first step.
A chest X-ray is not routine in acute asthma and is only needed if pneumothorax or pneumonia is suspected; her breath sounds are equal.
IM adrenaline treats anaphylaxis or peri-arrest asthma that is not responding to treatment, and she has neither.
An arterial blood gas is not needed before treatment at SpO2 93%; it is for life-threatening features or a patient who is getting worse.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has 2 hours of crushing chest pain and sweating. His ECG shows ST elevation in V2 to V5, I and aVL, with ST depression in lead III. What does the lead III change most likely represent?
questions.why: Lead III looks at the heart from roughly the opposite direction to aVL, so ST elevation in I and aVL shows up as ST depression in III. This is a mirror image of the anterolateral injury, not a second ischaemic area. Reciprocal depression makes a true STEMI more likely (and pericarditis less likely), and it supports immediate reperfusion.
notes: Separate inferior ischaemia is not the best explanation: a single depressed lead facing opposite aVL during a high lateral STEMI is reciprocal, and II and aVF are not involved.
Posterior infarction causes ST depression with tall R waves in V1 to V3, not isolated ST depression in lead III.
Digoxin causes diffuse, scooped ST depression without territorial ST elevation, and nothing suggests he takes digoxin.
Left ventricular strain causes asymmetric ST depression in the lateral leads (V5, V6, I, aVL) with LVH voltages, not depression in III with lateral ST elevation.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man has an acute right occipital infarct on MRI. Formal perimetry shows a complete, congruous left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. He asks about driving his car. Most appropriate advice?
questions.why: A complete homonymous hemianopia does not meet the Austroads visual field standard for a private licence. He must stop driving and tell the state licensing authority. Only the authority can consider a conditional licence later, on specialist advice.
notes: The one-month stand-down after a stroke is for people with no lasting deficit, and his persistent hemianopia fails the visual field standard.
A daylight-only condition is for poor vision in low light, and it does nothing for a lost half-field.
Wide-angle mirrors do not make up for a homonymous field defect, and they are not an accepted way to meet the Austroads standard.
Anticoagulation lowers the risk of another stroke but does not bring back the lost visual field, so he still fails the driving standard.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has had three throbbing one-sided headaches with nausea over two months, each preceded by 20 minutes of spreading zigzag lights. Neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Recurrent, stereotyped attacks of pulsatile, unilateral headache with nausea, after a gradually spreading, fully reversible visual aura, are typical of migraine with aura. With a normal neurological examination and fundoscopy, eTG advises no brain imaging. A headache diary confirms the pattern, counts days of acute medicine use and guides the decision to start prevention.
notes: CT brain is wrong because there are no red flags (thunderclap onset, focal signs, papilloedema), so imaging is not indicated and adds radiation without benefit.
MRI brain is wrong because a typical migraine history with a normal examination does not need imaging, and it often finds incidental lesions that cause worry.
Lumbar puncture is wrong because there is no thunderclap onset, fever or meningism to suggest subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis.
ESR and CRP is wrong because temporal arteritis is a diagnosis to consider in new headache after age 50, not in recurrent headaches with aura at 27.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 3 days of worsening breathlessness. He now sleeps on three pillows instead of one, wakes at night gasping, and has swollen ankles. He has gained 4 kg. He has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation and gout. His medicines are furosemide 40 mg daily, candesartan 16 mg daily (dose unchanged for 2 years), bisoprolol 5 mg daily and rivaroxaban 20 mg daily. Five days ago he started over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for a painful left big toe. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 108/min and irregular, blood pressure 144/86 mm Hg, respiratory rate 26/min and SpO2 91% on room air. His peripheries are warm. He has a raised JVP, bibasal crackles and pitting oedema to the shins, and no rash. Investigations show: sodium 134 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 4.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.2), urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5–8.0), creatinine 132 µmol/L (60–110; 86 µmol/L eight months ago), eosinophils 0.2 x10^9/L (less than 0.5). Urinalysis shows no blood, protein or leucocytes. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the change in his renal function?
options: Efferent arteriolar dilation from angiotensin II receptor blockade
Afferent arteriolar constriction from loss of prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation
Acute tubular necrosis from renal hypoperfusion in cardiogenic shock
Acute interstitial nephritis from a drug hypersensitivity reaction
Intratubular crystal deposition from urate released in the gout flare
questions.why: His creatinine has risen from a baseline of 86 to 132 µmol/L, about 1.5 times baseline, and urea is up out of proportion. This is a stage 1 acute kidney injury (KDIGO) that developed alongside his heart failure decompensation. The only new factor is 5 days of ibuprofen. In heart failure, kidney perfusion depends on prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole, and an NSAID removes this. He is also on a loop diuretic, which reduces circulating volume, and an ARB, which stops angiotensin II from constricting the efferent arteriole. With all three, glomerular filtration pressure falls (the 'triple whammy'). The NSAID also causes sodium and water retention and blunts furosemide, which explains the weight gain and congestion. The urinalysis shows no blood, protein or leucocytes, which fits a haemodynamic (prerenal) cause rather than damage within the kidney. For this patient, the result means he needs admission, the ibuprofen must be stopped and not restarted, his gout flare should be treated another way (for example colchicine or prednisolone, used with care), and he needs IV diuresis with daily electrolytes and creatinine.
notes: Wrong: ARB-related efferent dilation adds to the effect, but his candesartan dose has been the same for 2 years with a stable baseline creatinine, so it does not explain a new rise.
Wrong: he has no cardiogenic shock (BP 144/86 mm Hg and warm peripheries), so he has not had the poor perfusion that causes tubular necrosis.
Wrong: there is no rash, fever, eosinophilia or white cells in the urine to suggest interstitial nephritis, and the bland urinalysis fits a haemodynamic cause.
Wrong: urate crystals block the tubules only after massive urate release, as in tumour lysis, not in a gout flare of one joint.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is admitted with pneumonia. On day two he becomes agitated and frightened by visual hallucinations despite reorientation, family presence and a quiet room. Which drug is most appropriate?
questions.why: This man has hyperactive delirium with distressing symptoms, and non-drug measures have failed, so a short course of an antipsychotic is reasonable. In Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia, strong dopamine D2 blockers can badly worsen parkinsonism or cause neuroleptic sensitivity reactions. Australian guidance (eTG) recommends low-dose quetiapine because it blocks D2 receptors only weakly.
notes: Haloperidol is the usual delirium antipsychotic, but its strong D2 blockade worsens rigidity and immobility in Parkinson's disease.
Droperidol is a strong D2 antagonist (a butyrophenone) with the same risk of worsening parkinsonism, and IM sedation is not needed in a patient who will accept oral medicine.
Benzodiazepines worsen and prolong delirium and increase falls and respiratory depression, so they are kept for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
Risperidone blocks D2 receptors strongly enough to cause dose-related extrapyramidal effects, so it is avoided in Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: A final-year medical student notices a 34-year-old male surgical registrar slurring his speech and smelling of alcohol as he scrubs in for an emergency appendicectomy. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: The patient is at immediate risk, so the first step is to raise the concern straight away with the senior clinician responsible, so the registrar is stopped from operating. Under the Medical Board of Australia Good Medical Practice code and the Ahpra notification guidelines, a notification about impairment may follow, but it does not replace acting now to stop the harm.
notes: Notifying Ahpra may be appropriate later, but it does nothing to stop the operation that is about to start.
Talking to the registrar after surgery lets an impaired doctor operate on the patient first.
Emailing the medical school is slow and goes to the wrong people, so it cannot prevent harm in the operating theatre.
Watching and taking notes leaves the patient exposed to a known, immediate risk.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill has a proximal left leg DVT on compression ultrasound. Rivaroxaban is started for 3 months. She wants ongoing contraception. Most appropriate contraceptive advice?
questions.why: After a VTE, oestrogen-containing contraception should be stopped (UKMEC 4) and replaced straight away with a non-oestrogen method such as a progestogen implant, LNG-IUD or copper IUD. Rivaroxaban must not be taken in pregnancy, so she needs effective contraception throughout anticoagulation.
notes: A progestogen-only implant is highly effective, carries no meaningful VTE risk, and protects against pregnancy while she takes a DOAC.
The combined pill's oestrogen provoked this clot, and continuing it carries an unacceptable risk of recurrent VTE.
The vaginal ring contains ethinylestradiol and carries the same VTE risk as the combined pill.
Any dose of ethinylestradiol is contraindicated after VTE, so a lower-dose combined pill is still unsafe.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man is cut on the left neck with a broken bottle. The wound breaches platysma; bleeding stopped with pressure. No stridor, expanding haematoma or haemoptysis. HR 92/min, BP 128/80 mmHg. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: If a neck wound goes through platysma, assume deep injury until proven otherwise. In a stable patient with no hard signs, EMST guidance is CT angiography of the neck. It shows the vessels, airway and oesophagus, so you can decide between theatre and watching him.
notes: A plain X-ray can show surgical emphysema or a foreign body, but it cannot rule out injury to the vessels or the airway and gut.
Duplex ultrasound depends on the operator, cannot see well near the skull base or behind the clavicle, and does not assess the airway or oesophagus.
Catheter angiography is invasive. It is kept for unclear CT results or for treatment, not used as the first test.
Probing or exploring a wound through platysma in the ED can dislodge a clot and cause sudden bleeding or air embolism, so it is not done.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is given intravenous cefazolin 2 g prescribed for another patient. He has no allergies, normal observations, and is unaware of the error. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Under the Australian Open Disclosure Framework, a patient harmed or exposed to harm by an incident should be told promptly, ideally within 24 hours, with a sincere apology and a factual explanation. The incident is reported internally at the same time. Australian civil liability laws protect an apology from being treated as an admission of liability.
notes: The incident review runs alongside open disclosure, so delaying disclosure until it finishes breaks the requirement to tell the patient promptly.
Getting legal advice before disclosing delays the patient's right to know, and an apology is legally protected and not an admission of liability.
One medication error without concerns about impairment, misconduct or a pattern of practice does not meet the threshold for notification to Ahpra.
He is competent and has a right to confidentiality, so the error must be disclosed to him directly rather than to relatives.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back. His BP is 168/94 mmHg. CT aortogram shows a dissection flap in the ascending aorta. Most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.why: A dissection involving the ascending aorta is Stanford type A. Untreated, mortality rises about 1-2% every hour from rupture, tamponade, coronary occlusion or acute aortic regurgitation, so it needs emergency open surgical repair by cardiothoracic surgery. Heart-rate and blood pressure control with an IV beta-blocker is only a holding measure until theatre.
notes: Endovascular stent grafting is used for complicated type B (descending) dissection, not for the ascending aorta.
Medical anti-impulse therapy alone is definitive treatment for uncomplicated type B dissection, but for type A it only bridges to surgery.
Thrombolysis can cause fatal bleeding or rupture in aortic dissection, so it is contraindicated.
This is not a primary coronary occlusion, and the heparin and antiplatelet drugs given with angioplasty would delay surgery and could be catastrophic.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought in after a car crash with a ruptured spleen and blood pressure 70/40 mmHg. His parents, devout Jehovah's Witnesses, refuse blood transfusion. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Australian state laws let doctors transfuse a child without parental consent if it is needed to prevent death or serious harm. Examples are the NSW Human Tissue Act 1983 s20B and the Victorian Human Tissue Act 1982 s24. The child's best interests come before the parents' religious refusal, and treatment must not be delayed in a life-threatening emergency.
notes: A Supreme Court order is used for non-urgent or planned treatment, and getting one here would delay life-saving treatment.
Crystalloid alone will not replace oxygen-carrying capacity in severe haemorrhage, and giving more of it makes dilutional coagulopathy worse.
Parents cannot lawfully refuse life-saving treatment for a child when the refusal is against the child's best interests.
A child protection report may follow, but it is not the immediate step when the child is in life-threatening shock.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to a rural emergency department with 3 weeks of constant burning pain in her right forefoot. The pain is worst at night when she lies flat, so she has been sleeping in a recliner with the right foot hanging over the edge. For years she has had calf pain after walking short distances. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, a previous myocardial infarction and an ischaemic stroke. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 88/min and regular, blood pressure 164/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 96% on room air. The right great, second and third toes are black, shrivelled and hard, with a sharp line of demarcation and no discharge, swelling or erythema. The fourth toe is dusky. The right popliteal and pedal pulses are absent. The right ankle-brachial index is 0.28, and both ankle pressures are below 50 mmHg. WCC is 8.9 x10^9/L and CRP is 12 mg/L. The tertiary vascular unit has accepted her, and transfer is booked for tomorrow morning. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to reduce her risk of further tissue loss while she waits for transfer?
options: Raise the limb on pillows above heart level
Warm the limb with an electric heat pad
Apply hydrogel to the blackened digits under a film
Hold the limb below heart level, padded with loose dry gauze
Apply graduated compression bandaging from toes to knee
questions.why: She has chronic limb-threatening ischaemia: rest pain for more than 2 weeks, dry gangrene of three toes, an ABI below 0.4 and ankle pressures below 50 mmHg. She is awaiting revascularisation. Until then, the aims are to keep as much blood as possible reaching the threatened tissue (the dusky fourth toe) and to stop the dry gangrene turning into wet, infected gangrene. Letting the leg hang below heart level helps perfusion pressure by gravity, and it is also the position that eases her rest pain. A dry, loose, non-adherent dressing protects the foot from pressure and injury and keeps the dead tissue dry and mummified. Moisture would encourage bacteria and liquefaction. Debridement or amputation is left until after the vascular team has revascularised and assessed her.
notes: Wrong: raising the leg lowers the perfusion pressure in a foot that is already critically ischaemic, which worsens the rest pain and puts the dusky fourth toe at further risk.
Wrong: heat raises the metabolic demand of tissue that cannot increase its blood flow, and a numb, ischaemic diabetic foot is easily burnt, so external heat can speed up tissue loss.
Wrong: hydrogel moistens the wound, which suits sloughy wounds with good blood supply, but it softens dry gangrene and can turn it into wet, infected gangrene.
Wrong: compression is contraindicated in severe arterial disease (ABI below 0.5) because it further cuts arterial inflow and can cause pressure necrosis.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man has had dysuria and purulent urethral discharge for 3 days after condomless sex with a new female partner. A urethral Gram stain shows intracellular Gram-negative diplococci. Most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Intracellular Gram-negative diplococci in a man with urethral discharge mean gonorrhoea. The Australian STI guidelines and eTG recommend ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose. Collect a sample for culture and sensitivities, start partner notification and test for other STIs.
notes: Neisseria gonorrhoeae in Australia is often resistant to ciprofloxacin, and doxycycline does not reliably cure gonorrhoea.
Doxycycline treats chlamydia but does not reliably cure gonorrhoea, so used alone it would leave the infection untreated.
Azithromycin alone is not recommended because gonococcal resistance to azithromycin is increasing and it fails more often.
Benzathine penicillin IM treats syphilis, not gonorrhoea, which is widely resistant to penicillin.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with lung adenocarcinoma is breathless again two weeks after aspiration of a cytology-positive right pleural effusion. Post-aspiration X-ray showed the right lung had not re-expanded. Most appropriate management?
questions.why: This is a symptomatic malignant effusion that has come back, and the lung did not re-expand (trapped lung). Pleurodesis needs the two pleural layers to touch, so the treatment of choice is an indwelling pleural catheter, which allows repeated drainage at home (BTS 2023, eTG).
notes: Wrong: talc pleurodesis needs the visceral and parietal pleura to touch, and a trapped lung that will not re-expand makes this likely to fail.
Wrong: the fluid came back within two weeks, so repeated aspirations mean repeated procedures and only short relief, where a definitive approach is better.
Wrong: decortication is major surgery that is not suitable as palliation for a malignant trapped lung in a frail man with advanced cancer.
Wrong: a malignant effusion is an exudate, so diuretics do not reduce it and would only risk dehydration and electrolyte problems.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl is being treated for diabetic ketoacidosis. Five hours into the insulin infusion she develops headache and irritability. Her heart rate falls from 130 to 60/min. BGL 13 mmol/L. Most likely complication?
questions.why: Cerebral oedema is the main cause of death in children with DKA. It usually appears 4 to 12 hours into treatment, with headache, irritability or a falling GCS, and a falling heart rate (Cushing response). The RCH guideline calls for hourly neurological observations. If signs appear, give mannitol or 3% saline straight away and reduce the fluid rate.
notes: Insulin does lower potassium, but hypokalaemia causes weakness and arrhythmias such as U waves, not headache with a falling heart rate.
Her BGL is 13 mmol/L, so she is not hypoglycaemic.
Osmotic demyelination follows rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia days later, not headache within hours of insulin in DKA.
DKA can make clots more likely, but venous sinus thrombosis is rare and develops more slowly; this early pattern points to cerebral oedema.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 2 days of colicky central abdominal pain and repeated bilious vomiting. She has not passed stool or flatus for 30 hours. She had an open hysterectomy 12 years ago. She takes amlodipine for hypertension. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse is 112/min, blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Her mucous membranes are dry. The abdomen is distended, with tinkling bowel sounds and mild generalised tenderness but no guarding. The hernial orifices are normal. She has not passed urine in 3 hours. Results are: Na+ 132 mmol/L (135–145) K+ 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2) Cl− 89 mmol/L (95–110) Urea 13.6 mmol/L (2.5–7.5) Creatinine 118 µmol/L (45–90) Venous gas: pH 7.48, pCO2 47 mm Hg, HCO3− 33 mmol/L, lactate 1.2 mmol/L CT shows dilated small bowel with a transition point under the scar and no features of ischaemia. A nasogastric tube is placed. Which of the following is the most appropriate intravenous fluid to start?
questions.why: This woman has adhesive small bowel obstruction. Her blood results show a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis: pH 7.48, HCO3− 33 mmol/L, Cl− 89 mmol/L and K+ 3.1 mmol/L. The anion gap is normal (132 − [89 + 33] = 10), and the pCO2 of 47 mm Hg is the expected respiratory compensation (about 0.7 × 9 ≈ 6 mm Hg above 40). She also has a prerenal acute kidney injury, with urea raised out of proportion to creatinine, a tachycardia and no urine output. This pattern comes from vomiting and nasogastric loss of gastric acid (HCl) together with fluid loss. The kidney then holds on to sodium and bicarbonate and loses potassium (contraction alkalosis with secondary hyperaldosteronism). The alkalosis is chloride-responsive: it corrects only when chloride and volume are replaced. So the right fluid is 0.9% saline (154 mmol/L chloride) with potassium chloride added, usually 20 to 40 mmol/L, for both resuscitation and replacement, with fluid balance and electrolytes monitored. Hartmann's and Plasma-Lyte contain less chloride and carry anions that the body turns into bicarbonate (lactate, acetate, gluconate), and 5% glucose and albumin do not replace what she has lost.
notes: Hartmann's has less chloride (111 mmol/L) and only 5 mmol/L potassium, and its lactate is turned into bicarbonate, which makes the alkalosis worse.
Plasma-Lyte 148 has even less chloride (98 mmol/L), and its acetate and gluconate are turned into bicarbonate, so it does not correct a hypochloraemic alkalosis.
Albumin replaces neither chloride nor potassium, has no proven benefit over crystalloid for this kind of volume loss, and costs more.
5% glucose is mostly free water that does not stay in the circulation, so it will not correct her volume loss, and it will make her hyponatraemia worse.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has been ventilated in ICU for 30 hours after a severe traumatic brain injury. He has no brainstem reflexes and no spontaneous breathing. Core temperature is 33.8°C. What does this temperature mean?
questions.why: Under the ANZICS Statement on Death and Organ Donation, core temperature must be above 35°C before brain death can be determined, because hypothermia itself depresses brainstem function. He must be rewarmed, and the clinical tests done only once all preconditions are met.
notes: Hypothermia can mimic absent brainstem function, so these findings cannot count as evidence of brain death.
The apnoea test is part of the clinical examination and also needs the preconditions met, including temperature above 35°C.
Perfusion imaging is used when the clinical exam cannot be done or trusted for lasting reasons, not for hypothermia that can be corrected.
A reversible cause is present, so the coma cannot be called irreversible at this point.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 2 days of lower abdominal colic, gross tympanic distension and no flatus since yesterday. He vomited once today. Rectum is empty. Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: Early obstipation, marked distension and late vomiting point to large bowel obstruction. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the key investigation. It confirms the obstruction and shows its level and cause (cancer, diverticular stricture or volvulus), and it picks up complications such as caecal dilatation, ischaemia or perforation.
notes: A plain radiograph may show dilated colon, but it is less sensitive and cannot reliably find the cause or detect ischaemia.
Colonoscopy is not used to diagnose acute obstruction because insufflating an obstructed, distended colon risks perforation.
Ultrasound is limited by gas in a distended bowel and cannot reliably show the level or cause of a colonic obstruction.
A water-soluble contrast enema can show the site of blockage but has mostly been replaced by CT, which also assesses the rest of the abdomen and complications.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man who etches glass has severe throbbing pain in two fingertips after hydrofluoric acid leaked into his glove. Skin is only mildly red and has been irrigated with water. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Hydrofluoric acid soaks deep into tissue, and its fluoride ions bind calcium. This causes pain far worse than the skin looks, plus deep tissue death. After water irrigation, apply 2.5% calcium gluconate gel and massage it in repeatedly until the pain goes; if pain persists, give calcium by local injection or by intra-arterial infusion.
notes: Silver sulfadiazine is for infection in thermal burns and does nothing to neutralise fluoride ions.
Putting a base on the skin to neutralise an acid is not recommended, because the reaction gives off heat and does not bind fluoride.
Opioids only mask pain, so you lose the main sign that guides calcium treatment, and the fluoride damage keeps going.
Debridement is reserved for clearly dead tissue after calcium treatment has been given, not as first-line care.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man is ready for discharge after IV diuresis for decompensated heart failure from ischaemic cardiomyopathy, LVEF 30%. He asks how to detect fluid reaccumulation early at home. Most appropriate advice?
questions.why: Recurrent congestion is the main early risk after a heart failure admission, and fluid builds up in the body before symptoms appear. The Heart Foundation/CSANZ guidelines advise weighing every morning after voiding, on the same scales, and seeing the GP promptly if weight rises by more than 2 kg over 2 days or swelling or breathlessness gets worse. Chest pain or severe breathlessness means calling 000.
notes: Measuring the ankles once a week picks up oedema late and gives no reliable number to act on.
Oxygen saturation usually falls only once pulmonary oedema is established, so it does not give early warning.
NT-proBNP guides diagnosis and specialist review; a monthly test is too infrequent for home monitoring and not practical.
Blood pressure checks help with titrating drugs, but blood pressure does not track fluid build-up reliably.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to his general practitioner to review his test results. For 18 months he has had worsening breathlessness on exertion and now has to stop after about 200 m on flat ground. He also has a daily cough with clear sputum. Last winter he had one flare-up, treated in the community with oral prednisolone, and he has never been admitted to hospital. He has a 45 pack-year smoking history. He started varenicline 2 weeks ago and has set a quit date. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He uses salbutamol 200 micrograms via a spacer as needed, now on most days, and his technique is good. Temperature is 36.6 °C, pulse 84/min, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 94% on room air. Air entry is reduced and there is scattered expiratory wheeze. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.56 and FEV1 is 55% of predicted, with no significant bronchodilator response. Blood eosinophils are 0.15 x10^9/L (reference 0.0 to 0.5). He has been referred to pulmonary rehabilitation. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his medicines?
questions.why: This man has spirometry-confirmed COPD: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is below 0.7. His FEV1 of 55% predicted puts him in the moderate range in COPD-X (40 to 59%). His breathlessness persists despite a short-acting reliever, and he already has the non-drug measures under way: varenicline with a quit date, and a referral to pulmonary rehabilitation. COPD-X and eTG recommend adding a long-acting bronchodilator for persistent symptoms. A long-acting muscarinic antagonist such as tiotropium, taken once daily and kept alongside the as-needed reliever, is a standard first choice. It improves breathlessness, exercise tolerance and quality of life, and it reduces flare-ups. Inhaled corticosteroids are added only for repeated flare-ups despite long-acting bronchodilators, especially when eosinophils are raised. He has had one community-treated flare-up and his eosinophils are 0.15 x10^9/L, so a steroid is not indicated. Triple therapy, theophylline and long-term macrolides belong to later steps, if at all. Recheck his inhaler technique and review his symptoms after starting the new inhaler.
notes: Wrong: guidelines do not recommend an inhaled corticosteroid alone in COPD, because it does not help breathlessness and raises the risk of pneumonia.
Wrong: triple therapy is for people who keep having flare-ups despite dual long-acting bronchodilators, and he has had one mild flare-up and his eosinophils are low.
Wrong: theophylline is a late add-on with a narrow therapeutic range, many drug interactions and less benefit than inhaled long-acting bronchodilators.
Wrong: long-term macrolide treatment is a specialist option for frequent flare-ups despite optimal inhaled therapy, and it carries risks of resistance, hearing loss and QT prolongation.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man, a retired plumber with asbestos exposure, has right shoulder pain and weight loss. CT shows a 5 cm peripheral right apical mass without mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Best test to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: A peripheral apical (superior sulcus) mass suspicious for lung cancer needs tissue for diagnosis. With no enlarged nodes, a percutaneous CT-guided core biopsy gives the highest yield and enough tissue for histology and molecular testing. This follows the Australian optimal care pathway for lung cancer.
notes: Bronchoscopic biopsy has a low yield for peripheral apical lesions, which lie beyond the reach of the bronchoscope.
Sputum cytology is insensitive for peripheral tumours, and a negative result would not exclude cancer.
EBUS sampling is used for enlarged mediastinal or hilar nodes, and none are present here.
PET-CT is used for staging and cannot give a tissue diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 4 days of thirst, polyuria and weight loss, and 1 day of vomiting. He has no past medical history. He weighs 36 kg. His first venous blood gas shows pH 6.98, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L, glucose 34.0 mmol/L and sodium 131 mmol/L. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is 6.8 mmol/L and urea is 13.2 mmol/L. Fluid replacement is started, and 1 hour later an insulin infusion is started at 0.1 units/kg/h. Five hours after arrival he says he has a severe headache, vomits, and becomes irritable and confused. His pulse is 58/min (130/min on arrival), blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg, respirations are 26/min, SpO2 is 98% on room air and temperature is 36.9 °C. GCS is 11 (E3 V3 M5). His pupils are equal and reactive. Repeat glucose is 15.2 mmol/L and sodium is 129 mmol/L. The head of the bed is raised and the fluid rate is reduced. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain now
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV over 1 hour
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Cease the insulin infusion until review
questions.why: This boy has severe DKA as his first presentation of type 1 diabetes. He has the main risk factors for cerebral oedema: young age, new diagnosis, pH below 7.1, a high urea, and a sodium that is falling instead of rising as the glucose comes down. Several hours into treatment he has a headache, vomiting, a falling GCS and a new low heart rate with high blood pressure (Cushing response). This is a clinical diagnosis of cerebral oedema. The RCH DKA guideline says to treat it straight away, without waiting for imaging. Raise the head of the bed, reduce the fluid rate, and give mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg (2.5 to 5 mL/kg of 20%) IV over 20 minutes. Hypertonic 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg is an alternative. Call ICU early for airway support, and do a CT only after he is stable, to look for other causes such as a clot or bleed. CT now is wrong because imaging delays treatment that can save his life, and cerebral oedema is diagnosed clinically. Sodium bicarbonate is wrong because it does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself linked to cerebral oedema. Dexamethasone is wrong because steroids do not help this kind of brain swelling and they make hyperglycaemia worse.
notes: Wrong: CT delays urgent treatment for a diagnosis made clinically; image only once he is stable.
Wrong: bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA and is itself a risk factor for cerebral oedema.
Wrong: corticosteroids have no role in cerebral oedema from DKA and would worsen his hyperglycaemia.
Wrong: insulin is still needed to clear the ketosis, and stopping it does not treat the raised intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with adhesive small bowel obstruction is managed with nasogastric decompression and IV fluids. Overnight her colicky pain becomes constant, with localised tenderness, heart rate 124/min and temperature 38.1°C. Most likely complication?
questions.why: In adhesive small bowel obstruction, colicky pain that becomes constant, together with localised tenderness, tachycardia and fever, points to strangulation with ischaemia. A normal lactate does not rule it out. She needs urgent CT with IV contrast and an early surgical review for laparotomy, because conservative management has failed.
notes: Aspiration can cause fever and tachycardia, but it would give respiratory signs, not constant pain and localised abdominal tenderness.
Perforation usually comes after ischaemia and causes generalised peritonitis with free gas, not localised tenderness alone.
Paralytic ileus gives painless or mildly uncomfortable distension with absent bowel sounds, not fever and constant localised pain.
Mesenteric venous thrombosis is a separate cause of ischaemia in prothrombotic patients, not the usual complication of a mechanical adhesive obstruction.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after a sudden, severe occipital headache that began while he was jogging. Two weeks ago he had a severe headache that settled within 30 minutes. He has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and hypertension, treated with perindopril. On arrival, his temperature is 37.3 °C, pulse 82/min, respirations 16/min, blood pressure 140/85 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13 (E3 V4 M6). He has neck stiffness and bilateral subhyaloid haemorrhages on fundoscopy, and no focal deficit. INR is 1.0 and platelets are 245 x10^9/L. Non-contrast CT shows diffuse blood in the basal cisterns, spreading into the ventricles, with dilated temporal horns. CT angiography shows a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Forty-five minutes later he vomits. His GCS is now 11 (E3 V3 M5), pulse 48/min, blood pressure 204/96 mm Hg and respirations 12/min and irregular. His pupils are still equal and reactive. Which of the following best explains the change in his vital signs?
questions.why: This man has an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Blood has spread into his ventricles, and the dilated temporal horns show early hydrocephalus. Since arrival his GCS has fallen. He now has a rising systolic pressure, a slow heart rate and irregular breathing. This is Cushing's triad, a late sign that intracranial pressure is raised and the brainstem is being compressed, which means coning is imminent. Equal pupils do not rule this out, because pupil changes can come late. Do not read the rising blood pressure as something to treat on its own. It is the brain's attempt to keep up cerebral perfusion pressure, and lowering it hard could make ischaemia worse. Under eTG guidance and the Between the Flags criteria, this needs an immediate rapid response call, airway assessment, the head of the bed raised to 30 degrees, and an urgent neurosurgical review for an external ventricular drain. Delayed cerebral ischaemia usually happens on days 3 to 14, not within hours of the bleed. A hypertensive emergency does not explain the slow heart rate or the fall in GCS, and on arrival his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg.
notes: Wrong: delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm typically happens on days 3 to 14 after the bleed, not 3 hours after the headache began.
Wrong: a hypertensive emergency would not cause a falling heart rate or irregular breathing, and his blood pressure was only 140/85 mm Hg before his GCS fell.
Wrong: a vagal response to vomiting slows the heart but lowers the blood pressure, and it would not cause a lasting fall in GCS or irregular breathing.
Wrong: neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge usually causes a fast heart rate, low blood pressure and pulmonary oedema, not a slow heart rate with severe hypertension.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with COPD and 50 pack-years presents with a large right pleural effusion. SpO2 is 89% on room air. A non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min is applied. Greatest risk of this treatment?
questions.why: In COPD, high-concentration oxygen can cause hypercapnic respiratory failure and acidosis. This happens because of worsening V/Q mismatch, the Haldane effect and reduced respiratory drive. TSANZ guidelines advise titrating oxygen with nasal prongs or a Venturi mask to a target SpO2 of 88 to 92%.
notes: Re-expansion pulmonary oedema follows rapid drainage of a large effusion, not giving oxygen, and no fluid has been removed.
Absorption atelectasis from a high FiO2 does occur, but it matters much less clinically than CO2 retention in COPD.
Pulmonary oxygen toxicity needs prolonged exposure to a very high FiO2, usually over 24 to 48 hours, so it is not the immediate risk.
Supplemental oxygen does not cause pneumothorax; pleural aspiration is the procedure that carries that risk.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is on the cardiology ward of a regional hospital, waiting for transfer for coronary angiography. He was admitted 18 hours ago with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and has no pain now. Overnight telemetry has shown frequent multifocal ventricular ectopic beats and two runs of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, each 5 to 7 beats long. He has hypertension treated with indapamide. Since admission he has been given aspirin, ticagrelor, therapeutic enoxaparin, metoprolol and atorvastatin. His blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, pulse 78/min and regular, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Heart sounds are normal and the chest is clear. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm, 1 mm ST depression in V4 to V6 and a QTc of 470 ms. Results: hs-troponin I 1960 ng/L (less than 26), K+ 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), Mg2+ 0.58 mmol/L (0.70 to 1.10), creatinine 90 µmol/L (60 to 110). Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to reduce his risk of ventricular fibrillation before angiography?
options: Intravenous amiodarone loading dose, then maintenance infusion
Intravenous magnesium sulfate, then potassium chloride infusion
Intravenous lidocaine bolus, then prophylactic infusion
Oral slow-release potassium chloride tablets alone
Oral flecainide twice daily until angiography
questions.why: This man has an evolving NSTEMI and is waiting for angiography. Ventricular ectopy and non-sustained VT on telemetry, a borderline long QTc, and low potassium and magnesium from his thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide) put him at high risk of ventricular fibrillation. In acute coronary syndrome, Australian ACS guidance and ANZCOR advise correcting electrolytes promptly, aiming for potassium of at least 4.0 mmol/L (4.0 to 5.0) and magnesium of at least 1.0 mmol/L. Give magnesium first, for example magnesium sulfate 10 to 20 mmol IV over about an hour. Low magnesium makes low potassium hard to correct, because the kidneys keep losing potassium, and magnesium also stabilises the myocardium when the QT is long. Then give IV potassium chloride at a safe ward rate (for example 10 mmol/h through a peripheral line) with ECG monitoring, recheck the levels, and stop the indapamide. Keep him on continuous monitoring, continue the beta-blocker, and arrange early angiography to treat the ischaemic cause. Prophylactic antiarrhythmic drugs are not recommended in ACS.
notes: Prophylactic amiodarone for asymptomatic non-sustained VT after myocardial infarction does not lower mortality and is not recommended; amiodarone is kept for sustained or recurrent haemodynamically important VT, or for refractory VF during cardiac arrest.
Prophylactic lidocaine in acute myocardial infarction reduces VF but increases mortality, mainly from asystole, so it is no longer used.
Oral potassium alone works too slowly in a patient at high arrhythmic risk, and it does not correct the low magnesium that will keep the potassium from rising.
Flecainide, a class Ic drug, is contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease because it increased arrhythmic death after myocardial infarction in the CAST trial.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with hypertension has sudden, severe, tearing pain between her shoulder blades that was worst at onset. Left arm BP is 164/90 mmHg and right arm BP is 132/80 mmHg. Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: Sudden tearing interscapular pain with a difference of more than 20 mmHg between the arms gives a high aortic dissection detection risk score (ADD-RS). In a haemodynamically stable patient, the next step is urgent CT angiography of the whole aorta, which can show the intimal flap, its extent and branch involvement. A D-dimer result should not be used to rule out dissection at this level of risk.
notes: With an ADD-RS of 2 or more, D-dimer cannot exclude dissection and adds delay; CT angiography is needed whatever the result.
A chest X-ray may show a widened mediastinum, but it is often normal in dissection, so it cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis.

A CT pulmonary angiogram is timed for the pulmonary arteries, so it may not opacify the aorta well enough to assess it, and pulmonary embolism does not cause a difference in blood pressure between the arms.
Coronary angiography is invasive and does not image the aorta; it can delay surgery and may extend a dissection.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has recurrent renal calculi. Corrected calcium is 2.84 mmol/L (2.10–2.60), PTH 9.5 pmol/L (1.6–6.9) and 24-hour urinary calcium is elevated. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: High calcium with a PTH that is raised, or even just inappropriately normal, means PTH is being made without control, which is primary hyperparathyroidism. This is usually from a parathyroid adenoma. High urinary calcium and kidney stones rule out familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, and stones are a reason to refer for parathyroidectomy.
notes: In secondary hyperparathyroidism PTH rises in response to low or low-normal calcium, so calcium would not be high.
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia causes low urinary calcium and seldom causes stones, but here urinary calcium is elevated.
Malignancy raises calcium through PTHrP or bone destruction, which would suppress PTH rather than raise it.
Too much vitamin D raises calcium through gut absorption, which would suppress PTH rather than raise it.

questions.stem: A 4-week-old breastfed girl has had jaundice since day 3. She is feeding and gaining weight well. Her stools are pale cream and her urine stains the nappy yellow. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Jaundice lasting past 2 weeks (3 weeks if preterm) with pale stools and dark urine suggests cholestasis, such as biliary atresia. Australian guidelines (RCH, state guidelines) say the first test is a total and conjugated (split) bilirubin, done urgently. A conjugated level above 20 micromol/L, or above 20% of the total, confirms cholestasis and needs same-day referral to a paediatric gastroenterology or hepatology service.
notes: Ultrasound is part of the cholestasis work-up once conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is confirmed, but it does not come before the split bilirubin.
Hepatobiliary scintigraphy is a second-line specialist test for biliary atresia, used only after cholestasis is confirmed.
Hypothyroidism causes unconjugated prolonged jaundice and is part of the wider screen, but pale stools and dark urine point first to cholestasis.
Liver biopsy is an invasive specialist test used late to diagnose biliary atresia, not a first-line investigation.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man, an electrician, sees his general practitioner because of 5 months of daytime sleepiness. He dozes off while watching television and in the afternoons, and he wakes unrefreshed despite 8 hours in bed. His wife reports loud snoring every night, with pauses in his breathing followed by gasping. He has had no sudden muscle weakness with laughter or anger, and he denies sleepiness while driving. He drinks 3 standard drinks most evenings and does not smoke. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. Blood pressure is 146/92 mm Hg, heart rate 76/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. BMI is 34 kg/m2, neck circumference is 44 cm and the oropharynx is crowded. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 13 (normal 10 or less), STOP-Bang score 6/8 and OSA50 score 7/10.
