Full blood count, TSH and electrolytes are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: This man very probably has obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). He snores, his wife has seen him stop breathing, he is sleepy in the daytime, he has obesity with a large neck and a crowded oropharynx, he has hypertension, and he drinks alcohol in the evening. Before treatment starts, the diagnosis has to be confirmed and graded by the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI). His Epworth score is 8 or more and his STOP-Bang (4 or more) and OSA50 (5 or more) scores are high-risk. This meets the MBS item 12250 criteria, so a GP can refer him directly for an unattended Level 2 polysomnography done at home. Australasian Sleep Association and eTG guidance say this test is the right one for a patient with a high pre-test probability and no major other illness. Treatment then depends on the AHI: CPAP is first line for moderate to severe OSA, and everyone gets lifestyle measures (weight loss, less alcohol, side sleeping) and advice on driving. Overnight oximetry alone misses hypopnoeas that do not lower oxygen levels and cannot measure the AHI, so it is not enough to diagnose OSA. CPAP, a splint or a wake-promoting drug should not be started before the diagnosis and severity are known.
notes: Oximetry alone cannot measure the AHI and misses hypopnoeas that do not lower oxygen levels, so it is not recommended for diagnosing OSA.
CPAP is first line only once a sleep study has confirmed moderate to severe OSA, and it should not be started on screening scores alone.
A mandibular advancement splint is an alternative for confirmed mild to moderate OSA or for people who cannot tolerate CPAP, so it is not a first step before diagnosis.
Modafinil is used only for sleepiness that persists despite adequate treatment of confirmed OSA, and it does nothing for the airway obstruction.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman, 2 hours after hysteroscopy and curettage, has severe lower abdominal pain and guarding. Curettings contained yellow fatty tissue. BP 90/55 mmHg despite 1 L crystalloid. Which investigation will most likely confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: Fat in the curettings means the curette went through the uterine wall into omentum or bowel fat, so this is uterine perforation until proven otherwise. She is still shocked after fluids and has peritonism, so the senior gynaecologist should do urgent laparoscopy (or laparotomy). It confirms the perforation, looks for bowel, bladder or vessel injury and allows the bleeding to be controlled at the same time. CT is only for stable patients, when the senior asks for it.
notes: CT can be used in stable patients, but sending a shocked woman who is not responding to fluids out of the clinical area for a scan delays surgical control of the bleeding.
Transvaginal ultrasound may show free fluid but cannot reliably show the perforation or rule out bowel injury, and it delays definitive management.
FAST may show free fluid, but the source is already clear from the procedure, and FAST cannot confirm perforation or rule out bowel or bladder injury.
Putting fluid back into the cavity at repeat hysteroscopy risks making the perforation worse and pushing fluid into the abdomen, and it cannot assess injury outside the uterus.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman has three weeks of new left temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw pain on chewing. Her vision and fundoscopy are normal. ESR is 74 mm/h. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She most likely has giant cell arteritis without visual involvement. Under eTG, she should start high-dose oral prednisolone (40 to 60 mg daily) straight away, without waiting for a biopsy or imaging, to prevent visual loss. IV pulse methylprednisolone is for patients with visual symptoms or signs.
notes: IV pulse methylprednisolone is for giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms or signs, and her vision and fundoscopy are normal.
Steroids should not be held back for a biopsy, which stays diagnostic for 1 to 2 weeks after treatment starts.
Aspirin is not a proven treatment for giant cell arteritis and does not replace corticosteroids.
Tocilizumab is a steroid-sparing add-on for relapsing or refractory disease, not the first treatment.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man taking ramipril has routine bloods at his GP. Potassium is 6.8 mmol/L, and the laboratory reports marked haemolysis. He feels well, and his ECG is normal. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Haemolysis releases potassium from red cells, so a haemolysed sample can show falsely high potassium. In a well patient with a normal ECG, the right step is to repeat the sample urgently, taken with good technique, before starting treatment. If the repeat result is still high, it is managed as true hyperkalaemia.
notes: IV calcium gluconate protects the heart in true hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, but this ECG is normal and the result is probably false.
Insulin and dextrose moves potassium into cells in confirmed hyperkalaemia, and giving it on a false result risks hypoglycaemia.
A potassium-binding resin is slow-acting and should only be used once hyperkalaemia is confirmed on a reliable sample.
Stopping ramipril because of a probably false result could harm the patient without need; first confirm the potassium level.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father with 4 days of forceful vomiting after every feed. The vomit is milky and has never been green. He feeds eagerly straight after vomiting and has had 2 wet nappies in the past 24 hours. He was born at term and is formula fed. He weighs 4.5 kg, down from 4.9 kg 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 172/min, respirations 38/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is drowsy but rouses to voice. His hands and feet are cool and capillary refill time is 3 seconds. A peripheral cannula is placed. Venous gas: pH 7.53 (7.32 to 7.42), bicarbonate 37 mmol/L (20 to 28), lactate 1.1 mmol/L (under 2.0), Na 133 mmol/L (135 to 145), K 2.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), Cl 86 mmol/L (95 to 110), glucose 4.3 mmol/L. Ultrasound shows a pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm and a channel length of 18 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: 0.45% sodium chloride with 2.5% glucose at 18 mL/h intravenously
0.9% sodium chloride 45 mL intravenously over 15 minutes
Potassium chloride 2.25 mmol intravenously over 1 hour
Hydrocortisone 25 mg intravenously as a single dose
Laparoscopic pyloromyotomy on the next available list
questions.why: This boy has hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. The ultrasound shows a muscle wall of 5 mm or more (abnormal is 3 mm or more) and a channel of 18 mm (abnormal is 15 mm or more), and he has the typical hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. He is also in compensated shock: he is tachycardic, drowsy and cool at the hands and feet, with a capillary refill time of 3 seconds, while his blood pressure is still normal. Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency but a surgical urgency, not a surgical emergency. The first step is to treat the shock. Keep him nil by mouth and give a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride (45 mL for 4.5 kg), then reassess. After that, give 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose for maintenance plus deficit, and add potassium once he is passing urine (RCH Pyloric stenosis, Dehydration and Intravenous fluids guidelines). Surgery waits until the bicarbonate and chloride are back to normal, because operating while he is still alkalotic risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.
notes: Correct: compensated shock needs a 10 mL/kg isotonic bolus first, here 45 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride, with reassessment afterwards.
Wrong: potassium is replaced only after perfusion is restored and he is passing urine, and it does not treat the shock.
Wrong: his low potassium and alkalosis are the opposite of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which causes a high potassium and an acidosis, so steroids are not needed.
Wrong: pyloromyotomy should wait until shock and the alkalosis are corrected, because operating sooner risks apnoea after the anaesthetic.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with small cell lung cancer has two weeks of facial swelling, morning headache worse on bending forward, and dilated veins over his upper chest wall. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Facial swelling, headache that gets worse on bending and dilated chest wall veins in a patient with lung cancer point to superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO). Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest confirms it by showing where the obstruction is and what is causing it: tumour compression or clot. The CT also guides the next steps: stenting, radiotherapy or chemotherapy, and anticoagulation if there is thrombus.
notes: A chest X-ray may show a widened mediastinum or a mass, but it cannot show or exclude obstruction of the vein, so it does not confirm SVCO.
An echocardiogram looks for pericardial effusion or tamponade, which raises the JVP but does not cause facial swelling and chest wall collateral veins.
Duplex ultrasound of the neck shows the jugular and subclavian veins but cannot properly see the vena cava inside the chest, where the blockage is.
Brain metastases can cause morning headache but do not explain the facial swelling and dilated chest wall veins that show the venous outflow is blocked.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old Aboriginal woman from a remote Kimberley community is about to start high-dose prednisolone for lupus nephritis. Her eosinophil count is 1.4 × 10^9/L (normal <0.5). Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Strongyloides stercoralis is endemic in remote Aboriginal communities. Corticosteroids can set off a hyperinfection syndrome that is often fatal. Australian guidelines (eTG, NT/WA health) advise Strongyloides serology before immunosuppression in anyone at risk, especially with eosinophilia, and ivermectin treatment if it is positive or if steroids cannot wait.
notes: Larval shedding in stool is low and intermittent, so faecal microscopy misses most chronic Strongyloides infections and cannot rule it out.
Hydatid disease is linked to sheep-farming areas and does not carry the risk of steroid-triggered hyperinfection that makes Strongyloides urgent here.
Total IgE is a nonspecific marker of atopy or parasitic infection and will not identify the organism or guide treatment before immunosuppression.
A blood film only repeats the finding of eosinophilia and does not find the parasitic cause that is most likely here.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman in the birth suite loses 800 mL of blood 15 minutes after vaginal birth despite oxytocin 10 units IM. Pulse 108 bpm. Placenta complete; fundus soft and boggy. Most appropriate immediate step?
questions.why: A soft, boggy uterus with a complete placenta points to uterine atony, the "Tone" cause in the 4 Ts. Per RANZCOG and state PPH guidelines, the first step is to rub up a contraction with fundal massage, alongside calling for help, emptying the bladder and giving more uterotonics and tranexamic acid. Second-line drugs and mechanical or surgical steps follow only if bleeding continues.
notes: Ergometrine is a reasonable next uterotonic, but it comes after massage and is contraindicated in hypertension.
Carboprost is a second-line uterotonic, kept for atony that keeps going despite massage, oxytocin and ergometrine.
Intrauterine balloon tamponade is used for atony that does not respond to massage and uterotonics.
Examination under anaesthesia is for suspected trauma or retained tissue, and here the placenta is complete and the uterus is clearly atonic.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman, a school teacher, returns to her general practitioner for review of a duodenal ulcer. Last month she presented with burning epigastric pain that woke her at night. She had been taking naproxen 500 mg twice daily for low back pain over the previous 6 months. Gastroscopy showed a 7 mm clean-based duodenal bulb ulcer with mild antral gastritis. The rapid urease (CLO) result was positive, and antral biopsies showed Helicobacter pylori with no intestinal metaplasia or dysplasia. She ceased naproxen and yesterday completed 14 days of esomeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin. She is now pain-free and is taking esomeprazole 20 mg daily to complete ulcer healing. She has no melaena or weight loss. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse 74/min and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and nontender. Haemoglobin is 136 g/L (reference 115–160 g/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm eradication of the infection?
options: Urea breath test now, continuing the proton pump inhibitor throughout
Helicobacter pylori serology in 4 weeks, continuing the proton pump inhibitor
Faecal antigen test in 1 week, continuing the proton pump inhibitor
Repeat gastroscopy with biopsy in 8 weeks, off proton pump inhibitor
Urea breath test in 4 weeks, off proton pump inhibitor for the final 2 weeks
questions.why: Under eTG guidance, everyone treated for Helicobacter pylori should have eradication confirmed, because clarithromycin resistance means first-line triple therapy fails in a significant minority. The preferred test of cure is the carbon-13 urea breath test. It must be done at least 4 weeks after the antibiotics finish, and the proton pump inhibitor must be stopped for at least 2 weeks before the test. Antibiotics, bismuth and PPIs all suppress the bacteria's urease activity and bacterial load, which can give a false-negative result. She can finish her PPI course for ulcer healing and then stop it 2 weeks before the test. An uncomplicated duodenal ulcer with benign biopsies does not need a repeat scope. A breath test done now while she is still on the PPI and only one day after the antibiotics could falsely reassure. Serology stays positive for months to years after successful eradication, so it cannot confirm cure. A faecal antigen test is a valid alternative only with the same timing rules, and at 1 week while she is still on the PPI it is unreliable. Repeat gastroscopy is mainly for gastric ulcers, to confirm healing and exclude cancer, or for complicated or non-healing ulcers.
notes: Testing one day after the antibiotics while she is still on a PPI suppresses urease activity and is likely to give a false-negative result.
Antibodies persist long after eradication, so serology cannot tell a cured infection from an ongoing one.
Testing 1 week after the antibiotics while she is still on a PPI is too early and risks a false-negative stool antigen result.
An uncomplicated duodenal ulcer with benign histology does not need repeat endoscopy; this invasive test is reserved for gastric or complicated ulcers.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman has perioral and fingertip tingling on day 1 after total thyroidectomy for multinodular goitre. Corrected calcium is 1.88 mmol/L and PTH is 0.4 pmol/L (1.6–6.9). Most likely cause?
questions.why: Low calcium with an inappropriately low PTH soon after total thyroidectomy means hypoparathyroidism, usually transient, caused by injury to or loss of blood supply to the parathyroid glands. Treat with oral or IV calcium, adding calcitriol if needed, according to severity.
notes: Hungry bone syndrome mainly follows parathyroidectomy for long-standing hyperparathyroidism, and PTH is usually normal or high, not suppressed.
Vitamin D deficiency causes a raised PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), not a suppressed one.
Low magnesium can reduce PTH, but nothing here suggests it, and it is much less likely than direct parathyroid injury after this operation.
Dilution from IV fluids causes only a mild fall in total calcium, does not suppress PTH, and is accounted for by using corrected calcium.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man on methadone treatment, who previously injected heroin, has a reactive hepatitis C antibody test at a routine review. He feels well and examination is normal. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A reactive HCV antibody test only shows past exposure. About a quarter of people clear the virus on their own, so Australian consensus guidelines recommend HCV RNA testing to confirm current infection before direct-acting antiviral treatment. Fibrosis is assessed only after viraemia is confirmed.
notes: Genotyping is not needed to start pangenotypic direct-acting antivirals and does not confirm current infection.
Antibodies stay positive for life after exposure, so repeating the test cannot tell current infection from cleared infection.
Liver biopsy is invasive and is not used to diagnose HCV, and fibrosis is assessed non-invasively once viraemia is confirmed.
Fibrosis staging with elastography or APRI comes after HCV RNA confirms current infection, not before.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with hypertension has two months of sudden-onset palpitations. An ECG during an episode showed atrial fibrillation, and he is now in sinus rhythm. Echocardiogram and eGFR are normal. Most appropriate treatment to reduce stroke risk?
questions.why: His CHA2DS2-VA score is 2 (age 65 to 74 and hypertension). Australian guidelines (NHFA/CSANZ, eTG) recommend oral anticoagulation at this score, and the risk is the same whether the AF is paroxysmal or persistent. Without mechanical valves or moderate to severe mitral stenosis, a DOAC such as apixaban is preferred over warfarin.
notes: Aspirin barely prevents stroke in AF and its bleeding risk is close to that of anticoagulation, so it is not recommended.
Warfarin works but is second line to a DOAC in nonvalvular AF, because it causes more intracranial bleeding and needs INR monitoring.
Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet with no established role as a single agent for stroke prevention in AF.
Dual antiplatelet therapy prevents fewer strokes than anticoagulation and causes about as much bleeding, so it is not a substitute.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman taking naproxen for osteoarthritis vomits fresh blood. HR 108/min, BP 118/76 mmHg. Hb 96 g/L, platelets and INR normal; no stigmata of liver disease. IV fluids are started. Which drug is most appropriate now?
questions.why: An NSAID user with haematemesis, a normal INR and platelets, and no signs of liver disease most likely has a bleeding peptic ulcer, which is a non-variceal bleed. Australian guidelines (eTG, ACI) advise resuscitation, an IV proton pump inhibitor such as pantoprazole, and endoscopy within 24 hours. Drugs for varices are not given.
notes: Tranexamic acid is not recommended in upper GI bleeding: the HALT-IT trial showed it did not reduce deaths and raised the risk of venous clots.
Terlipressin lowers portal pressure and is used for suspected variceal bleeding, which nothing here suggests.
Octreotide is a splanchnic vasoconstrictor used for variceal bleeding, and it is not indicated in a presumed peptic ulcer bleed.
Prophylactic ceftriaxone is given to cirrhotic patients with a variceal bleed, not to someone with a presumed NSAID-related ulcer.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a 45 pack-year smoking history has 4 months of increasing breathlessness and 12 kg weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a large left pleural effusion. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A new unilateral effusion in a smoker with weight loss suggests malignancy. The first investigation is ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration, which both diagnoses and treats. Send the fluid for protein and LDH (with serum levels for Light's criteria), pH, glucose, cell count, cytology, and microscopy and culture including AFB. Ideally, a contrast CT chest is done before the effusion is fully drained.
notes: Bronchoscopy has a low yield when there is no visible endobronchial lesion, and it comes after pleural fluid analysis and CT.
Sputum cytology has low sensitivity and does not explain the effusion, so it does not replace sampling the pleural fluid.
Pleural biopsy is kept for exudates where cytology is negative or nondiagnostic, after aspiration and contrast CT.
PET-CT is a staging test, used once a malignancy is confirmed, and does not give a tissue or fluid diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with a painless penile ulcer has reactive treponemal serology, RPR titre 1:64. He asks that nobody, including his partner, be told. What does this result require?
questions.why: A reactive treponemal test with a high RPR titre and a chancre confirms active infectious syphilis. Syphilis is a notifiable condition in every Australian state and territory, so the doctor must notify public health by law, whatever the patient wants. He should still be encouraged and supported to notify his partner himself.
notes: Partner notification should first be led by the patient, with support from the doctor or a public health contact tracer; telling the partner directly without his consent is not the first step.
Confidentiality is not absolute, and the law requiring notification overrides his request.
A reactive treponemal test plus an RPR of 1:64 with a typical ulcer already confirms active infection, so waiting for a repeat test only delays notification and treatment.
Notification is required by law whether or not the patient agrees, so asking for his written consent does not apply.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is stabbed in the right chest. Pulse 118/min, BP 100/65 mmHg, SpO2 92%. Right breath sounds are absent with dull percussion; trachea midline. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Absent breath sounds with a dull percussion note after penetrating chest trauma point to a haemothorax. The next step is a large-bore intercostal catheter, which drains the blood, lets the lung re-expand and shows how much blood is being lost. Thoracotomy is needed if the drain returns more than 1500 mL straight away, keeps draining more than 200 mL/h, or the patient stays unstable.
notes: Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax, which gives a hyper-resonant note and a deviated trachea, not dullness with a midline trachea.
Thoracotomy is kept for a large first drain output, continuing blood loss, or ongoing instability, none of which is known before a drain goes in.
CT would delay treatment in a tachycardic, hypoxic patient whose clinical signs already need a drain.
Pericardiocentesis treats tamponade (raised JVP, muffled heart sounds), not one-sided dullness with absent breath sounds.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy is 5 hours into treatment for severe diabetic ketoacidosis at first diagnosis. He develops headache and confusion, with heart rate 58/min (was 125) and BP 142/90 mmHg. Most appropriate immediate step?
questions.why: Headache, confusion, a slowing heart rate and rising BP during DKA treatment mean cerebral oedema. This is the main cause of death in paediatric DKA. The RCH guideline says to treat it straight away with mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg (or 3% saline), cut the fluid rate and raise the head of the bed, without waiting for imaging.
notes: The diagnosis is made clinically, and waiting for a CT delays treatment that saves lives; imaging comes only after treatment has started.
A faster insulin infusion lowers osmolality more quickly and does nothing for raised intracranial pressure.
Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA and is itself linked to cerebral oedema.
More fluid could worsen cerebral oedema; the fluid rate should be reduced, not increased.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has newly confirmed HIV-1 infection and feels well. Her CD4 count is 520 cells/µL, her viral load is 40,000 copies/mL, and her genotype shows no resistance. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: ASHM's Australian commentary on the DHHS guidelines recommends starting antiretroviral therapy soon after diagnosis for everyone with HIV, whatever the CD4 count. Early treatment protects the immune system and lowers the risk of illness. Once the viral load has been undetectable for 6 months, she cannot pass HIV on through sex (U=U).
notes: Waiting for the CD4 count to fall is an outdated approach: the START trial showed that waiting causes more serious illness than treating straight away.
Pneumocystis prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole is given when the CD4 count is below 200 cells/µL (or below 14%), and hers is 520.
Her infection is already confirmed and her baseline viral load is known, so repeating it adds nothing and only delays treatment.
Azithromycin prophylaxis against Mycobacterium avium complex is only considered when the CD4 count is below 50 cells/µL and ART is not yet working, which does not apply to her.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has had 3 months of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss, and has a perianal fistula. Faecal calprotectin is 640 µg/g, and stool pathogen PCR is negative. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: Right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea, weight loss and perianal disease point to Crohn's disease. A high calprotectin with negative stool tests means the bowel is inflamed and infection is unlikely. Ileocolonoscopy, which intubates the terminal ileum, with biopsies from several sites is the key test: it shows skip lesions and cobblestoning, and histology can show non-caseating granulomas.
notes: CT can show a thickened ileum or a complication such as an abscess, but it cannot give a tissue diagnosis, and repeated scans in young people with IBD add radiation.
MR enterography is used after diagnosis to stage small bowel disease and strictures, but it cannot take tissue to confirm Crohn's disease.
Capsule endoscopy is kept for suspected small bowel Crohn's disease after a non-diagnostic ileocolonoscopy, and it carries a risk of capsule retention if there is a stricture.
A faecal immunochemical test detects blood, not inflammation, adds nothing once calprotectin is raised, and does not confirm the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman, day 7 after coiling a ruptured anterior communicating aneurysm, becomes drowsy with new left arm weakness. Sodium 138 mmol/L; CT shows no new blood or hydrocephalus. Most likely cause?
questions.why: A new focal deficit or drop in consciousness between days 3 and 14 after aneurysmal SAH, with no new blood, no hydrocephalus and a normal sodium on testing, is delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm. Oral nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days and keeping the patient euvolaemic lower this risk (eTG). Confirm it with CT angiography or perfusion imaging and involve neurosurgery or neurointervention urgently.
notes: The aneurysm has been coiled, and CT shows no new blood.
CT shows no ventricular enlargement, so hydrocephalus does not explain the decline.
A sodium of 138 mmol/L rules out hyponatraemia from cerebral salt wasting.
Thromboembolism from coiling happens during or within hours of the procedure, not on day 7.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has cut engineered stone kitchen benchtops for 15 years. HRCT shows multiple small upper-lobe nodules with eggshell calcification of the hilar lymph nodes. Which infection is he at greatest risk of?
questions.why: These findings point to silicosis from respirable crystalline silica in engineered stone. Silica damages alveolar macrophages, so the risk of tuberculosis rises a lot, and it keeps rising as the disease gets worse. Australian guidance therefore advises screening for latent TB and staying alert for active TB in people with silicosis.
notes: Pneumocystis pneumonia happens with severe T-cell immunosuppression, such as advanced HIV or high-dose steroids, not with silicosis alone.
Legionella comes from contaminated water systems or potting mix, and silica exposure does not make it notably more likely.
Psittacosis is caught from infected birds and has no link to silica or stone work.
Q fever comes from contact with livestock and abattoirs, not from cutting engineered stone.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman whose son died three days ago has chest pain and BP 80/50 mmHg. Angiography shows unobstructed coronaries; echocardiography shows apical ballooning and an LVOT gradient of 60 mmHg. Which drug is most likely to worsen her shock?
questions.why: In Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, the base of the heart contracts harder than normal and can cause a dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction, which leads to shock. Inotropes such as dobutamine make the base contract even harder and raise the gradient further, so they should be avoided once an echo shows obstruction. Treatment aims to increase preload and afterload and slow the heart rate.
notes: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-agonist that raises afterload without an inotropic effect, which reduces the LVOT gradient and helps.
A cautious fluid bolus increases preload and LV cavity size, which reduces dynamic outflow obstruction.
A short-acting beta-blocker slows the heart and reduces contractility, which lengthens filling time and can lower the gradient.
Vasopressin raises systemic vascular resistance without stimulating beta-receptors, so it supports blood pressure without worsening the obstruction.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female accountant has had a daily bilateral band-like headache for 2 months during tax season. She takes paracetamol on 6 days a week. Neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal. Greatest risk if this pattern continues?
questions.why: She has tension-type headache and takes a simple analgesic on more than 15 days a month. If this continues for more than 3 months, it causes medication-overuse headache. eTG advises keeping acute treatment to fewer than 10 days a month, avoiding codeine, and treating mainly without drugs (posture, breaks, stress management).
notes: Paracetamol at therapeutic doses in a healthy adult does not cause liver injury; hepatotoxicity needs overdose or major risk factors.
Analgesic nephropathy follows years of heavy combination analgesic or NSAID use, not a few months of therapeutic paracetamol.
Analgesic use does not cause idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and her normal fundoscopy argues against raised pressure.
Her headache has tension-type features, and analgesic overuse makes the existing headache worse rather than turning it into migraine.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department of a rural hospital by her daughter. She has had 4 days of worsening headache and, since this morning, new confusion. One week ago she tripped on a rug and hit the left side of her head on a door frame. She did not lose consciousness. She has atrial fibrillation and hypertension. Her medicines are rivaroxaban 20 mg daily, last taken at 07:00 today, and amlodipine. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 76/min and irregular, blood pressure 166/88 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Her GCS is 14 (E3 V5 M6) and falls to 13 (E3 V4 M6) over the next hour. Pupils are equal and reactive. She has a mild right pronator drift. INR is 1.2 (reference 0.9 to 1.3), APTT 32 seconds (reference 25 to 38), platelets 236 ×10^9/L and eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m². Non-contrast CT brain shows a crescentic, mixed-density left subdural collection 14 mm thick with 7 mm of midline shift. Neurosurgical retrieval has been requested. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management while she waits for transfer?
questions.why: This woman has an acute-on-subacute subdural haematoma while taking a factor Xa inhibitor. Her GCS is falling, she has a focal deficit and the CT shows mass effect. The biggest immediate risk is that the haematoma keeps growing and she herniates before she reaches neurosurgery. Reversing the anticoagulant is the most important step to prevent this. A normal INR and APTT do not rule out a clinically significant rivaroxaban effect, especially when the last dose was taken only hours ago and renal function is preserved. For life-threatening bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban, Therapeutic Guidelines recommend andexanet alfa where it is available and local protocol allows. Otherwise, give prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg IV) with haematology advice. Andexanet is rarely stocked in rural Australian hospitals, so Prothrombinex-VF is the appropriate choice here. Idarucizumab is wrong because it is a specific antibody fragment against dabigatran and has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors. Phytomenadione (vitamin K) is wrong because it reverses warfarin by restoring vitamin K-dependent factor synthesis, and it does nothing to a direct factor Xa inhibitor.
notes: Idarucizumab binds only dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, so it would not reverse rivaroxaban.
Vitamin K restores the synthesis of factors depleted by warfarin but has no effect on a direct factor Xa inhibitor.
Fresh frozen plasma gives too little factor concentration to reverse rivaroxaban, carries a large volume load and is slow to prepare.
Tranexamic acid does not reverse anticoagulation, and its benefit in head injury is limited to the first 3 hours after trauma, not a week later.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old female medical student sustains a hollow-bore needlestick from a consenting 40-year-old man of unknown blood-borne virus status. The wound is washed and the incident reported. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: After first aid and reporting, Australian occupational exposure guidelines call for urgent testing of the source patient for HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C, with consent. The result decides whether the student needs HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, which works best if started within 2 hours and no later than 72 hours. The student also has baseline serology, and must not be the one to ask the source patient for consent.
notes: A baseline HIV RNA PCR in the student would only show infection she already had, so it does not guide prophylaxis now; baseline antibody serology is enough.
A viral load only helps once the source is known to be HIV positive, and here his status is unknown.
Culturing the needle has no role, as it cannot reliably detect blood-borne viruses and does not guide management.
Baseline liver function tests are not the deciding test, as they do not show transmission risk or the need for prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with three attacks of spontaneous spinning vertigo over the past 4 months. Each attack lasted 3 to 5 hours, with nausea and vomiting. Before each attack, his left ear felt blocked and he heard a roaring tinnitus. Afterwards, his hearing in that ear was muffled for several days and then improved. He feels well between attacks. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and drinks four cups of coffee a day. Today he is between attacks. Temperature is 36.7 °C, blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg and pulse 72/min, regular. Otoscopy is normal on both sides. The Weber test lateralises to the right, and the Rinne test is positive on both sides. There is no spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus. The head impulse test is normal, and the Dix-Hallpike test is negative on both sides. The corneal reflexes, facial movements, gait and coordination are normal. Audiometry shows a left sensorineural loss of 40 dB at 250 and 500 Hz with normal thresholds from 2000 Hz. The right ear is normal, and tympanometry is type A on both sides. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain and posterior fossa
Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre on the affected side
ENT referral and gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal acoustic meati
Referral for intratympanic gentamicin injection into the affected ear
Duplex ultrasound of the carotid and vertebral arteries
questions.why: This man meets the Bárány Society criteria for definite Ménière's disease of the left ear. He has had two or more spontaneous attacks of vertigo, each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours. Audiometry documents a low-frequency sensorineural loss in that ear, and his aural symptoms fluctuate. However, the criteria also require that no other diagnosis explains the picture better. Any asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss needs a retrocochlear lesion excluded, especially a vestibular schwannoma, which can cause unilateral tinnitus, hearing loss and vertigo. The investigation of choice is a gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal acoustic meati, arranged through an ENT surgeon. While he waits, attacks can be treated with a short course of prochlorperazine (eTG), and he can be advised to cut down on salt, caffeine and alcohol. Prophylaxis and ablative treatments are a matter for the ENT surgeon once the diagnosis is secure. A non-contrast CT brain can miss small tumours in the internal acoustic canal or cerebellopontine angle. The Epley manoeuvre treats BPPV, but his attacks are spontaneous, last hours and come with a negative Dix-Hallpike test.
notes: Non-contrast CT is not sensitive enough to exclude a small vestibular schwannoma in the internal acoustic canal or cerebellopontine angle, so it would not settle the question raised by the asymmetric loss.
The Epley manoeuvre treats posterior canal BPPV, which causes brief positional vertigo with a positive Dix-Hallpike test, not spontaneous attacks lasting hours with ear symptoms.
Intratympanic gentamicin destroys vestibular function and can worsen hearing, so it is kept for disabling disease that has not responded to conservative treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed.

Posterior circulation TIA is unlikely because the attacks last hours, come with fluctuating one-sided ear symptoms and leave a normal neurological examination, and duplex ultrasound would not exclude the retrocochlear lesion that needs ruling out.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has an emergency splenectomy for a shattered spleen after a motorcycle crash. He recovers well and is planned for discharge on day five. Which lifelong risk is most important to counsel about?
questions.why: After splenectomy, patients carry a lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection, usually from encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b), and it can kill within hours. Australian guidance (eTG, Spleen Australia) covers vaccination, ideally about 14 days after an emergency splenectomy, prophylactic or standby antibiotics, and telling the patient to seek urgent care for any fever.
notes: A pancreatic tail injury can cause a fistula, but this happens early after surgery and is not a lifelong risk.
Portal or splenic vein thrombosis is an early complication, mainly after elective splenectomy for blood disorders with a high platelet count.
A subphrenic abscess is an early complication that appears within weeks of surgery, not a risk that lasts for life.
An incisional hernia is a common long-term problem after laparotomy, but it is far less dangerous than post-splenectomy sepsis.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with subarachnoid haemorrhage has dilated ventricles on CT. Over one hour her GCS falls from 14 to 10. BP is 210/100 mmHg, heart rate 46/min. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She has subarachnoid haemorrhage with acute hydrocephalus, a falling GCS and a Cushing response (high BP, low heart rate), which means raised intracranial pressure and impending coning. The urgent treatment is for a neurosurgeon to insert an external ventricular drain to drain the CSF.
notes: Her high BP is a Cushing reflex that keeps blood flowing to the brain, so lowering it aggressively before treating the raised intracranial pressure can cause brain ischaemia.
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with a reduced GCS and obstructive hydrocephalus because it can cause the brain to herniate (cone).
Nimodipine is given to prevent delayed cerebral ischaemia but does not treat acute hydrocephalus, and it should not be given by mouth when the GCS is falling.
Corticosteroids are not helpful in subarachnoid haemorrhage and do not lower intracranial pressure caused by hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man who drinks heavily daily is brought in confused and unsteady, with no head injury. He has horizontal nystagmus and a broad-based ataxic gait. Capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Confusion, nystagmus and ataxia in a heavy drinker point to Wernicke encephalopathy. This is a medical emergency, and eTG advises giving high-dose parenteral thiamine straight away (for example 500 mg IV three times daily) to prevent permanent Korsakoff syndrome. Do not wait for imaging or other tests before giving it.
notes: Diazepam treats alcohol withdrawal, but it does nothing for thiamine deficiency and he shows no clear signs of withdrawal.
His blood glucose is normal, and giving glucose before thiamine in a thiamine-deficient patient can bring on or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.
With no head injury and a classic presentation, a CT scan should not delay thiamine and would not show Wernicke encephalopathy reliably.
Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed by heavy drinkers and is not enough for acute Wernicke encephalopathy, which needs parenteral dosing.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with breast cancer bone metastases has received monthly intravenous zoledronic acid for two years. She needs extraction of a carious lower first molar. Which complication is she most at risk of?
questions.why: High-dose intravenous antiresorptive therapy for cancer, given over a long time, puts her at high risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ). Dental extraction is the main trigger, and the mandible is the most common site. The risk is much higher than in patients taking oral bisphosphonates for osteoporosis. Australian guidance says to avoid extraction where possible, for example by root canal treatment instead. If extraction is needed, it should be done with minimal trauma, under an oral surgeon, with antimicrobial rinses, after counselling about the risk.
notes: Dry socket is a common but self-limiting complication after any extraction, and nothing in her history makes it especially likely.
She has no anticoagulant use or bleeding disorder, so delayed bleeding from infection is no more likely than usual.
Lingual nerve injury is mainly a risk when lower third molars are removed, not first molars.
Fracture during extraction is rare and mainly happens with deeply impacted third molars in an atrophic jaw.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old tall, thin man who smokes has sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness while studying. The right chest is hyper-resonant with reduced breath sounds; BP 122/76 mmHg. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A tall young male smoker with sudden one-sided pleuritic pain, hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds most likely has a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. His normal BP shows no tension, so there is time for imaging. An erect chest X-ray confirms the pleural line, measures the size and checks for mediastinal shift, which guides whether he is observed, aspirated or drained.
notes: A CT pulmonary angiogram looks for pulmonary embolism, but the one-sided hyper-resonance points to a pneumothorax, which a plain film can confirm without contrast or a large radiation dose.
A D-dimer can only help exclude PE in a low-risk patient and cannot confirm a pneumothorax, which is the likely diagnosis here.
An arterial blood gas measures how much gas exchange is impaired but cannot show the cause or size of a pneumothorax.
A troponin looks for myocardial injury, which is unlikely in a 20-year-old with one-sided pleuritic pain and signs of air in the pleural space.

questions.stem: A 22-month-old boy is brought to a general practice in regional Victoria with a 6-week history of cough. The cough is wet and happens by day and by night. It has not improved with 7 days of amoxicillin or with inhaled salbutamol through a spacer. His mother remembers that the cough started on the evening of a family barbecue. While eating popcorn there, he coughed and gagged for a short time and then settled. He has no eczema and no previous wheeze. He is fully immunised and has had no contact with tuberculosis. He is playful. His temperature is 37.3 °C, pulse 120/min, respirations 38/min, and SpO2 96% in room air. On examination there is reduced air entry and a fixed monophonic wheeze over the left lower zone only. A chest X-ray shows a hyperinflated left lung with the mediastinum shifted to the right. No radio-opaque object is seen. If the underlying cause is not treated, this child is most at risk of which of the following complications?
questions.why: This toddler has an inhaled foreign body, most likely a popcorn kernel, in the left lower lobe bronchus. The clues are a choking episode at the start, a cough that has lasted weeks despite antibiotics and bronchodilators, one-sided monophonic wheeze with reduced air entry, and air trapping on the same side with the mediastinum pushed away. Organic objects are radiolucent, so a normal-looking X-ray does not rule out the diagnosis. Organic material left in the bronchus causes ongoing local inflammation, granulation tissue and infection beyond the blockage. This leads to recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe and then permanent damage to the airway: bronchiectasis. The risk goes up the longer the object stays in. This is why the RCH guideline recommends prompt rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia at a paediatric centre, rather than more courses of antibiotics or inhalers. Tension pneumothorax is a rare acute event, not the expected result of an object left in place. Tracheo-oesophageal fistula is a complication of an oesophageal foreign body, especially a button battery, not a bronchial one.
notes: Wrong: air trapping can rarely rupture into the pleura, but this is an uncommon acute event and not the usual consequence of a retained object.
Wrong: a fistula forms when an oesophageal foreign body such as a button battery erodes into the trachea, not from an object in the bronchus.
Wrong: pulmonary arterial hypertension needs widespread lung or vascular disease, and one blocked lobe does not cause it.
Wrong: a foreign body does not cause atopic asthma, and this child has no atopy, no earlier wheeze and no response to salbutamol.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old girl has a spiral humeral fracture after reportedly falling from a low chair. She has bruises of differing ages on her back and ears. Neurological examination is normal. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A spiral long-bone fracture from a minor fall, along with bruising of different ages on protected sites such as the ears and back, points to non-accidental injury. In children under 2 years with suspected physical abuse, guidelines (RCH, state child protection guidelines) call for a full skeletal survey to find hidden fractures. A child protection notification is also mandatory.
notes: Routine CT brain is recommended for infants under 12 months with suspected abuse, or when there are neurological signs, and this child is older and neurologically normal.
Bone density scanning does not diagnose abuse, and the history and bruising pattern do not suggest fragile bones.
Abdominal ultrasound is not first-line here because she has no abdominal bruising, distension or tenderness suggesting internal injury.
Rickets does not explain bruising of different ages on protected sites, so vitamin D testing would not confirm the main diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man who injects drugs has had jaundice for 5 days after a prodrome of joint aches. ALT is 1820 IU/L, INR is 1.0 and he is alert. HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc are positive. Most appropriate management?
questions.why: This is acute hepatitis B. His INR is normal and he has no encephalopathy, so his liver is still working. More than 95% of immunocompetent adults clear the virus on their own, so management is supportive care with repeat LFTs and INR, notification, contact tracing and a repeat HBsAg at 6 months. Antivirals are kept for severe or fulminant acute disease (rising INR, encephalopathy or a long-lasting severe course).
notes: Entecavir is kept for severe acute hepatitis B (for example a rising INR or encephalopathy) or for chronic infection, and he has neither.
Interferon is not used in acute hepatitis B and may make liver inflammation worse.
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin is post-exposure prophylaxis for non-immune contacts and has no role once infection is established.
Transplant referral is for fulminant liver failure, and his normal INR and clear mental state show his liver is still working.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of yellow eyes and dark urine. Two weeks ago he developed fever, anorexia and aching wrists and knees, which have since eased. He had unprotected sex with a new partner 3 months ago. He takes no medicines and drinks 6 standard drinks a week. Temperature is 37.6 °C, BP 124/78 mmHg, pulse 88/min and respiratory rate 14/min. He is alert, with scleral icterus, a tender smooth liver edge and no asterixis, and he is tolerating oral fluids. Bilirubin is 142 µmol/L (<20), ALT 2140 U/L (<40), ALP 165 U/L (30–110) and INR 1.1 (0.9–1.2). Paracetamol is undetectable. Ultrasound shows a 4 mm common bile duct without stones. HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc are positive, anti-HBs is negative, and hepatitis A IgM and HCV antibody are negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Supportive care and repeat hepatic testing in clinic
questions.why: This man has acute hepatitis B. He had a likely sexual exposure within the 1 to 6 month incubation period, then a prodrome with arthralgia, then jaundice. His tests show a hepatocellular pattern, and HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc are positive. His liver is still working well: INR is 1.1, he is alert with no asterixis, and he is drinking. So he has no features of severe hepatitis or acute liver failure. More than 95% of immunocompetent adults with acute hepatitis B clear the virus on their own. Therapeutic Guidelines and ASHM recommend supportive care for these patients. That means avoiding alcohol and liver-toxic drugs, and repeating LFTs and INR regularly until they improve, with safety-netting advice to return if he becomes confused, starts bleeding or vomits persistently. The doctor must also notify the case, arrange contact tracing (testing, vaccination, and HBIG for non-immune contacts), and repeat HBsAg at 6 months to check for chronic infection. Antivirals are only for severe acute hepatitis B: INR above 1.5, encephalopathy, or jaundice lasting more than about 4 weeks.
notes: He has acute hepatitis B with a normal INR, no encephalopathy and good oral intake, so supportive care with regular LFT and INR checks is correct, because the infection usually clears on its own in adults.
Tenofovir (or entecavir) is reserved for severe or protracted acute hepatitis B, such as INR above 1.5 or encephalopathy, and he has neither.
Interferon is contraindicated in acute hepatitis B because the immune flare it causes can tip an inflamed liver into decompensation, and it has no role in this self-limiting illness.
Acetylcysteine treats paracetamol toxicity or early acute liver failure, but his paracetamol level is undetectable and his INR and mental state are normal.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man who cuts engineered stone benchtops has six months of exertional dyspnoea and dry cough. Spirometry is mildly restrictive and chest X-ray is normal. Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: Engineered stone workers are exposed to very high levels of respirable crystalline silica and are at risk of accelerated silicosis. A normal chest X-ray does not rule this out. Australian respiratory health surveillance guidance recommends CT, which is far more sensitive for early nodular disease, to confirm the diagnosis.
notes: A repeat chest X-ray is not sensitive enough for early silicosis, so it would add little to the normal film he has already had.
Serial peak flows at work and away from work are used for occupational asthma, which would cause variable obstruction rather than restriction.
Serum ACE is neither sensitive nor specific, and it cannot tell silicosis apart from sarcoidosis.
Bronchoalveolar lavage is invasive and does not diagnose silicosis; it is kept for excluding infection or other diagnoses.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 3 hours of central chest pressure that spreads to her left arm. It started while she was gardening and has not eased with rest. She is sweaty and nauseated. She has type 2 diabetes and hypertension, treated with metformin and perindopril. She has been given aspirin 300 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg, enoxaparin, sublingual and then intravenous glyceryl trinitrate, and intravenous fentanyl. Forty minutes later her pain is still 7/10. Temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 106/68 mm Hg in both arms, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Her chest is clear and she has no murmurs. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia with new horizontal ST depression of 2 mm in V4 to V6, I and aVL, and no ST elevation in any lead. High-sensitivity troponin T is 88 ng/L, rising to 296 ng/L at 1 hour (99th percentile 14 ng/L). Her chest X-ray shows clear lungs and a normal mediastinum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: This woman has an NSTEMI. She has ischaemic chest pain, new ST depression without ST elevation, and a rising high-sensitivity troponin above the 99th percentile. Her pain continues despite full medical treatment: aspirin, a P2Y12 inhibitor, an anticoagulant, sublingual and intravenous nitrates, and opioid pain relief. The 2016 NHF/CSANZ Australian ACS guidelines and eTG classify refractory ischaemic pain as a very high-risk feature of NSTEACS. Other very high-risk features are haemodynamic instability, acute heart failure, life-threatening arrhythmia and mechanical complications. Any of these calls for an immediate invasive strategy, meaning angiography with a view to revascularisation within 2 hours. If the hospital has no catheter lab, she needs urgent transfer. Angiography within 24 hours is the right timing only for high-risk patients who are stable and pain-free. Fibrinolysis has no role without ST elevation. Non-invasive tests are not appropriate because the diagnosis is already confirmed and she is still having ischaemia.
notes: Angiography within 24 hours is the timing for high-risk NSTEACS (rising troponin, dynamic ST changes) once pain and haemodynamics have settled, but her pain has not settled, so 24 hours is too long to wait.
Fibrinolysis has shown no benefit in NSTEACS and adds bleeding risk, especially as she is already on dual antiplatelets and enoxaparin; it is only for STEMI when PCI cannot be done in time.

CT coronary angiography is for ruling out coronary disease in low- to intermediate-risk chest pain with a normal troponin, not for a confirmed NSTEMI with ongoing ischaemia, where it delays revascularisation.
Stress testing is contraindicated during active, unstable ischaemia and adds nothing once the troponin and ECG have confirmed the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is hit by a car. Blood pressure 78/45 mmHg and heart rate 132/min despite two units of blood. FAST shows free fluid in the hepatorenal pouch. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: After blunt trauma, free fluid on FAST means haemoperitoneum. In a patient who stays hypotensive despite blood transfusion, this means bleeding inside the abdomen. Under EMST/ATLS principles he needs immediate laparotomy for haemorrhage control, without further imaging.
notes: CT is only for haemodynamically stable patients, and taking an unstable patient to the scanner delays haemorrhage control.
Repeating FAST helps when the first scan is negative or unclear, but this scan is already positive and the patient is unstable.
DPL is a fallback when FAST is unavailable or unclear, and here it would add nothing to an already positive scan.
Angioembolisation suits selected stable or transient responders with solid organ injury on CT, not a non-responder whose bleeding source has not been defined.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after collapsing while walking to his letterbox 1 hour ago. His wife saw him fall with no warning. He was unresponsive for about 20 seconds, did not jerk, and was fully alert within a minute. A few minutes before he fell, he felt a fluttering in his chest. He has no chest pain, headache or incontinence, and he did not hit his head. He has hypertension, treated with atenolol and perindopril. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 38/min and regular, blood pressure 112/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Large waves appear intermittently in the jugular venous pulse, and the loudness of the first heart sound changes from beat to beat. The neurological examination is normal, and his tongue is not bitten. Capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: This man had sudden syncope with no warning, palpitations just before it, and a quick, full recovery. He takes a beta blocker. At the bedside he has a slow, regular pulse, intermittent cannon a waves and a first heart sound that varies in loudness. Together these signs point to AV dissociation, most likely from complete heart block, which makes this a Stokes-Adams attack. Australian syncope guidance (eTG Cardiovascular) says every patient with transient loss of consciousness needs a 12-lead ECG straight away. Because the bradycardia is still present, a 12-lead ECG will show it now. It can confirm complete heart block (regular P waves marching through a slower, independent escape rhythm with no fixed PR interval), show whether the escape rhythm is broad (infranodal and unstable), and look for ischaemia or other conduction disease. It is fast, cheap, non-invasive and decides the next step: pacing pads, atropine or an infusion, stopping AV nodal blockers, and cardiology referral for a permanent pacemaker. A Holter monitor is for intermittent symptoms with a normal resting ECG. Echocardiography looks for structural disease but cannot identify the rhythm.
notes: Ambulatory Holter recording is for intermittent symptoms when the resting ECG is normal, so it is the wrong first test while the arrhythmia is present now and could be recorded in minutes.
Echocardiography can assess structural heart disease once the rhythm is known, but it cannot diagnose the conduction disorder causing his syncope.

CT of the head is not indicated because he did not strike his head, has no headache and has a normal neurological examination, and an intracranial cause would not explain the slow pulse or cannon waves.
Electroencephalography is for suspected seizures, but he had no jerking, no tongue biting, no incontinence and no post-ictal confusion, and his clinical signs point to a cardiac cause.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is recovering on the ward on day 2 after elective coronary artery bypass grafting. He has COPD and a dilated left atrium on echocardiography. Observations are stable. Which complication is he most at risk of?
questions.why: Atrial fibrillation is the most common complication after cardiac surgery. It affects about 20-40% of CABG patients and peaks on days 2 to 4. Older age, COPD and a dilated left atrium raise the risk further. So keep him on telemetry, keep potassium and magnesium in range, and continue or restart his beta blocker.
notes: Tamponade happens in only a few per cent of patients and usually occurs early with bleeding, so it is much less likely in a stable man on the ward.
Deep sternal wound infection (mediastinitis) affects only about 1-2% of patients and usually appears after the first week.
Stroke after CABG affects only about 1-3% of patients and is most often present when the patient wakes from surgery, so it is far less common than AF.
Sustained ventricular arrhythmias after CABG are rare and are usually linked to ischaemia or electrolyte problems, neither of which he has.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl with croup in the emergency department had stridor at rest and recession. Thirty minutes after dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline, she has no stridor at rest; SpO2 98%. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Nebulised adrenaline works within minutes but wears off within about 2 hours, and stridor can come back. The steroid is not yet working fully, so the RCH guideline says to observe for at least 3 hours after the last dose. She can go home only if she still has no stridor at rest.
notes: Sending her home 30 minutes after adrenaline risks stridor returning at home, even with good safety-netting advice.
Adrenaline is repeated only if severe signs come back, and she has no stridor at rest now.
Intensive care is for a child with low oxygen, a tiring child or one needing repeated adrenaline, and she is settled with normal oxygen saturation.
Typical croup is diagnosed clinically, so an X-ray would not change management and may upset her.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has two days of painful vulval blisters and dysuria. Examination shows multiple shallow, tender ulcers on the labia with tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which test most likely confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: Multiple painful, shallow vulval ulcers after blisters, with dysuria and tender lymph nodes, point to a first episode of genital herpes. Australian STI guidelines (ASHM) and eTG recommend a PCR (NAAT) swab taken from the base of the lesion to confirm HSV and identify the type. Syphilis testing is still added alongside it.
notes: Serology can be negative early in a first episode, and a positive result cannot show that HSV caused this particular ulcer.
A Tzanck smear is insensitive, cannot tell HSV from varicella zoster virus, and has been replaced by PCR.
Syphilis usually causes a single painless chancre, and dark-field microscopy is rarely available, so PCR and serology are used instead.
First-void urine NAAT tests for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, which do not cause genital ulcers.

questions.stem: A 26-hour-old term boy is feeding well and has no respiratory distress. Routine pulse oximetry on room air shows right hand saturation 98% and foot saturation 90%. Most likely explanation for this result?
questions.why: Normal oxygen saturation in the right hand (pre-ductal) with lower saturation in the foot (post-ductal) is a failed newborn pulse oximetry screen. It points to a duct-dependent left heart obstruction such as coarctation, where deoxygenated blood flows right to left through the duct into the descending aorta. A foot reading below 95%, or a hand-foot gap above 3%, needs urgent review and an echocardiogram.
notes: Transposition typically gives the reverse pattern, with the foot saturation higher than the right hand, or both low, rather than a normal right hand.
Tetralogy of Fallot causes cyanosis from mixing inside the heart, so the hand and foot readings are both lower and similar.
Transient tachypnoea causes respiratory distress and lowers the hand and foot readings equally, and this baby has no distress.
By 24 hours a normal baby reads 95% or more in both limbs with a gap of 3% or less, so a foot reading of 90% with an 8% gap is not normal.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash. His airway and chest are clear. Heart rate 132/min, blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg; pelvis is tender with perineal bruising. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Suspect a pelvic fracture with haemorrhagic shock. During the circulation step of the primary survey, apply a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters straight away to close the pelvic volume and tamponade venous bleeding, alongside massive transfusion. Angiography or packing comes after the binder.
notes: A patient who is unstable and not responding should not go to the CT scanner before bleeding control has been started.
Perineal bruising suggests a urethral injury, so a urethral catheter is contraindicated until imaging rules it out.
Laparotomy does not control retroperitoneal pelvic bleeding, and nothing here shows bleeding inside the abdomen.
Angioembolisation is a later step for arterial bleeding after the binder and resuscitation, not the first action.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old breastfed girl, born at term, has persistent jaundice. She is feeding well, but her mother reports pale stools and dark urine. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Jaundice lasting beyond 2 weeks in a term baby, with pale stools and dark urine, suggests cholestasis, for example biliary atresia. RCH guidelines say the first test is a split bilirubin to confirm a conjugated fraction above 20% or above 25 micromol/L. If cholestasis is confirmed, the baby needs urgent hepatology referral, because the outcome of a Kasai procedure depends on how early it is done.
notes: Hypothyroidism causes prolonged unconjugated jaundice, which does not explain pale stools and dark urine.
A direct antiglobulin test looks for immune haemolysis, which causes unconjugated jaundice in the first days of life, not cholestasis at 3 weeks.
Hepatobiliary scintigraphy is a specialist test that comes after cholestasis is confirmed and an ultrasound is done, so it is not the first test.
A liver biopsy is invasive and is only used later, in specialist care, to tell biliary atresia apart from other causes of cholestasis.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old Aboriginal man from a remote Northern Territory community attends for his annual health check and feels well. Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs 85 mIU/mL. What do these results indicate?
questions.why: A positive anti-HBc means he has been infected with hepatitis B at some point. A negative HBsAg with protective anti-HBs (10 mIU/mL or more) means he has cleared the infection and is immune. He needs no vaccination and no ongoing liver cancer surveillance for hepatitis B, though reactivation is possible if he is later heavily immunosuppressed.
notes: Chronic hepatitis B needs HBsAg to stay positive for more than 6 months, and his HBsAg is negative.
Vaccination produces anti-HBs only, so a positive anti-HBc shows he has had a natural infection.
Acute infection usually shows a positive HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc, without protective anti-HBs.
Isolated core antibody means anti-HBc is positive with no anti-HBs, but his anti-HBs is clearly protective.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 2 days of worsening generalised headache, fever, vomiting and photophobia. She has Crohn disease and has been taking prednisolone 25 mg daily for 6 weeks for a flare. Her temperature is 39.1 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has marked neck stiffness, a GCS of 15, no focal neurological signs and no rash. Blood cultures are drawn. She is given intravenous dexamethasone, ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin. A non-contrast CT brain is normal. A lumbar puncture is done 1 hour after the first antibiotic doses. CSF results: Opening pressure 28 cmH2O (10 to 20) Appearance: turbid White cell count 1200 ×10^6/L (below 5), 85% polymorphs Red cell count 3 ×10^6/L Protein 1.6 g/L (0.15 to 0.45) Glucose 1.5 mmol/L; paired plasma glucose 8.0 mmol/L Gram stain: no organisms seen Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the Gram stain result?
options: A bacterial cause is excluded, and the antibiotics can be stopped
A viral cause is confirmed, and aciclovir alone should be given
A fungal cause is suggested, and amphotericin should be added
The sample is probably contaminated, and the procedure should be repeated
A bacterial cause remains likely, and the present therapy should continue
questions.why: This CSF has a bacterial pattern: it is turbid, with a raised opening pressure, a white cell count of 1200 ×10^6/L that is mostly polymorphs, protein of 1.6 g/L and a CSF:plasma glucose ratio of about 0.19 (normal is above 0.6). A negative Gram stain does not rule out bacterial meningitis. Even before antibiotics, the Gram stain finds organisms in only about 60 to 90% of cases. That rate drops after antibiotics have been given, as here, and Listeria monocytogenes shows on Gram stain in only about a third of cases. Listeria is a real concern because she has been on corticosteroids for 6 weeks. Under eTG, she should stay on empirical ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin (for Listeria), with dexamethasone, until the culture and bacterial PCR come back. Treatment can then be narrowed or stopped on those results, not on the Gram stain.
notes: Wrong: the Gram stain is not sensitive enough to rule out bacterial meningitis, and stopping antibiotics in this neutrophilic, low-glucose CSF could be fatal.
Wrong: viral meningitis usually gives a lymphocyte-predominant CSF with a normal glucose ratio and only mildly raised protein, and a negative Gram stain cannot confirm any diagnosis.
Wrong: cryptococcal and other fungal meningitis usually cause a lymphocytic CSF with a slower onset and are diagnosed by cryptococcal antigen or India ink, not by an absent Gram stain result.
Wrong: contamination would add organisms rather than hide them, the very low red cell count rules out a traumatic tap, and repeating the lumbar puncture would add risk without changing management.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is brought by ambulance to the emergency department of a metropolitan hospital with 50 minutes of heavy central chest pain and sweating. Paramedics gave aspirin 300 mg and two doses of sublingual glyceryl trinitrate, and afterwards he became light-headed. He has type 2 diabetes and takes metformin. His pulse is 64/min and regular, blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg (138/86 mm Hg at first paramedic contact), respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. He is pale and clammy. His jugular venous pressure is raised at 6 cm above the sternal angle, his lung fields are clear and his heart sounds are normal. The 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with 3 mm ST elevation in II, III and aVF, greater in III than in II, and 1 mm ST elevation in V4R. Bedside echocardiography shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle, preserved left ventricular function and no pericardial effusion. The cardiac catheterisation laboratory has been activated. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment for his hypotension while he waits for transfer to the catheterisation laboratory?
questions.why: This man has an inferior STEMI with right ventricular infarction, which points to a proximal right coronary artery occlusion. The evidence is ST elevation in II, III and aVF that is greater in III than II, ST elevation in V4R, a raised JVP with clear lungs, and a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle. An infarcted right ventricle depends on preload. Nitrates dilate the veins and reduce preload, which is why his blood pressure fell after the sublingual GTN. Primary PCI has already been arranged, so the immediate priority is to restore right ventricular filling. Give cautious IV crystalloid in small boluses (such as 250 mL of 0.9% saline) and reassess blood pressure, perfusion and lung fields after each one. This follows the Australian ACS guidelines and eTG: in inferior STEMI with hypotension, avoid nitrates, record right-sided leads and give fluid first. Use inotropes or vasopressors only if hypotension persists despite adequate filling. Use atropine or pacing only for symptomatic bradycardia or AV block, which he does not have.
notes: Wrong: a loop diuretic would reduce preload further and worsen hypotension, and his clear lung fields show no pulmonary oedema to treat.
Wrong: nitrates are contraindicated in hypotension and right ventricular infarction, and the GTN he has already had probably caused his fall in blood pressure.
Wrong: an IV beta blocker is contraindicated in a hypotensive patient at risk of cardiogenic shock, and inferior infarction makes bradycardia and AV block more likely.
Wrong: a vasopressor is reserved for hypotension that persists after adequate filling, and he has not yet had any fluid.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old woman has had fluctuating confusion and inattention for 3 days, starting after her GP began oxybutynin for urge incontinence. Examination, urinalysis and electrolytes are normal. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is delirium that began soon after she started a strongly anticholinergic drug, and no other cause has been found. Australian delirium guidance says to treat the cause first, so oxybutynin should be stopped. If her bladder still needs treatment, non-anticholinergic options such as mirabegron or bladder training can be used.
notes: Solifenacin is still an antimuscarinic and adds to her anticholinergic load, so it keeps the cause going instead of removing it.
Antipsychotics are kept for severe distress or danger that does not settle with other measures, and they do not treat the cause.
Donepezil does not prevent or treat delirium, and dementia should not be diagnosed during an acute confusional state.
Imaging is not needed when there are no focal neurological signs and the drug explains the delirium.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department 2 hours after a punch to the face. He has nasal obstruction, no clear rhinorrhoea, and bilateral fluctuant, red-purple septal swellings unchanged by decongestant. Without drainage, which complication is most likely?
questions.why: This is a bilateral nasal septal haematoma, which separates the septal cartilage from its blood supply in the overlying mucoperichondrium. Without same-day drainage, the cartilage dies (often after an abscess forms), so the nasal bridge collapses into a saddle nose and the septum may perforate. Treatment is urgent incision and drainage, packing or splinting, and antibiotics.
notes: A cerebrospinal fluid leak comes from a skull base or naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture, not a septal blood collection, and there is no clear rhinorrhoea here.
Orbital cellulitis usually spreads from the ethmoid sinuses and is not the expected result of a septal haematoma.
A sense of smell lost after trauma is caused by shearing of the olfactory nerve fibres, not by septal cartilage necrosis.
Recurrent nosebleeds come from the mucosa of Little's area and are not the main danger of an undrained septal haematoma.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman has sudden tearing chest pain radiating between her shoulder blades. BP is 168/94 mmHg in the right arm and 138/86 mmHg in the left. ECG shows lateral ST depression. Which drug is most likely to cause harm?
questions.why: Tearing pain through to the back with a BP difference of more than 20 mmHg between the arms means aortic dissection until proven otherwise. Treating the ST depression as an acute coronary syndrome with anticoagulants, antiplatelets or thrombolysis can cause rupture, tamponade or catastrophic bleeding. These drugs must be held until dissection has been excluded.
notes: IV opioid analgesia is recommended in suspected dissection because it relieves pain and reduces the sympathetic drive that raises heart rate and blood pressure.
In a hypertensive patient, an IV beta blocker is the first-line anti-impulse treatment, aiming for a heart rate of about 60 and a systolic BP of 100 to 120 mmHg.
An antiemetic is safe here and helps prevent vomiting, which would otherwise raise blood pressure and the stress on the aortic wall.
Paracetamol is a safe extra pain reliever with no effect on bleeding or blood pressure in a dissection.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman admitted to the ward with HSV-1 encephalitis confirmed on CSF PCR starts IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly. She is drowsy with poor oral intake. Creatinine is 72 µmol/L. Most important adverse effect to monitor?
questions.why: High-dose IV aciclovir can crystallise in the renal tubules and cause crystal nephropathy and acute kidney injury. The risk is higher in older patients, with dehydration such as her poor oral intake, and with other nephrotoxins. eTG advises keeping her well hydrated, checking creatinine regularly and adjusting the dose to renal function, which also prevents aciclovir neurotoxicity that could be mistaken for worsening encephalitis.
notes: QT prolongation is linked to macrolides, fluoroquinolones and antipsychotics, not to aciclovir.
Aciclovir rarely causes clinically important liver injury, so liver function is not the main thing to monitor.
Ototoxicity is a typical adverse effect of aminoglycosides and loop diuretics, not of aciclovir.
Severe hypokalaemia is typical of amphotericin B, not of aciclovir.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old boy has had four days of projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds and has lost weight. Venous gas: pH 7.52, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, chloride 88 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: The gas shows a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, caused by repeated loss of gastric acid from projectile non-bilious vomiting. In a 3-week-old boy this points to pyloric stenosis. Confirm it with pyloric ultrasound, and correct fluids and electrolytes before pyloromyotomy.
notes: A salt-wasting crisis in congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, not a hypokalaemic alkalosis.
Malrotation with volvulus causes bilious vomiting and, if bowel becomes ischaemic, metabolic acidosis, so neither the history nor the gas fits.
Reflux causes effortless small vomits in a baby who is thriving and does not upset the acid-base balance.
Cow's milk protein allergy usually causes blood-streaked stools, eczema or irritability, not projectile vomiting with a marked metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is about to start work at a cattle and sheep abattoir in rural Queensland. He is well and has had only the routine childhood vaccines. Which vaccine is most important before he starts?
questions.why: Abattoir workers are at high risk of Q fever (Coxiella burnetii), which they catch by breathing in material from cattle, sheep and goats. It can cause acute febrile illness, endocarditis and chronic fatigue. The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends Q fever vaccination for these workers, after a skin test and serology to exclude past exposure, ideally before they start work.
notes: Rabies vaccine (for Australian bat lyssavirus) is for people who handle bats, not for livestock abattoir workers.
Bovine tuberculosis has been eradicated in Australia, and BCG is not recommended for abattoir work.
Hepatitis A vaccine is recommended for jobs such as sewage work and childcare, not for livestock slaughter.
Typhoid vaccine is for travellers to endemic areas and laboratory staff, not for abattoir workers.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man, a retired plumber exposed to asbestos, has four months of cough, shoulder pain, hoarseness and 7 kg weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a 5 cm right apical mass. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: An apical mass on chest X-ray in an older man with red-flag symptoms is suspicious for lung cancer (a superior sulcus tumour). Cancer Australia and the Optimal Care Pathway advise an urgent contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen, then urgent referral to a respiratory specialist. The CT findings decide which staging tests and which biopsy route come next.
notes: Sputum cytology often misses cancer, especially a peripheral apical lesion, and is not recommended as the first test.
