PET-CT is for staging once CT has shown the lesion and the specialist team has asked for it, not the first test from general practice.
Bronchoscopy is a tissue-sampling test planned after CT, and a peripheral apical lesion is often hard to reach with it.
MRI of the brachial plexus is used to plan surgery for a superior sulcus tumour after CT and tissue diagnosis, not as the first test.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents after her partner manually strangled her last night until she briefly lost consciousness. She has neck bruising and facial petechiae; neurological examination is normal. Which delayed complication is most important to exclude?
questions.why: Non-fatal strangulation with loss of consciousness is high risk. Carotid or vertebral artery dissection can be silent at first and cause a stroke hours to days later, so she needs CT angiography of the neck vessels. She also needs careful forensic documentation and a family violence risk assessment, because strangulation strongly predicts later homicide.
notes: Hyoid fracture is uncommon in survivors, is mainly a forensic finding, and rarely causes a delayed life-threatening problem.
Manual compression of the neck does not usually break the spine, and she has no mechanism of axial loading or acceleration.
Laryngeal fracture shows up straight away with hoarseness, stridor or crepitus, not as a silent delayed problem.
Vocal cord palsy would cause hoarseness and is not the dangerous or delayed threat to her life.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman without diabetes on a surgical ward is accidentally given 10 units of rapid-acting insulin meant for another patient. Twenty minutes later she is sweaty and drowsy. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: When a medication error happens, patient safety comes first. A drowsy, sweaty patient who has wrongly been given insulin needs a bedside glucose test straight away so hypoglycaemia can be confirmed and treated. Escalation, an incident report and open disclosure follow once she is stable.
notes: Insulin can lower potassium, but this is a later check and not the cause of her acute drowsiness.
C-peptide helps tell external insulin from the body's own, but here the source is already known and the result would delay treatment.
A blood gas does not directly show the hypoglycaemia that needs urgent correction.
The insulin dose is already known, the result takes time, and it would not change immediate treatment.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman, a former shipyard worker, has a 3-month dry cough, 5 kg weight loss and hoarseness. She takes perindopril. Chest X-ray shows a 5 cm left hilar mass. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: A suspicious mass on chest X-ray, together with red-flag symptoms, should be treated as lung cancer until proven otherwise. The Cancer Australia guidance and the optimal care pathway say the next step is an urgent contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen, with urgent referral to a specialist. Asbestos exposure raises the risk of lung cancer even in someone who has never smoked.
notes: Sputum cytology often misses cancer, and a negative result would not change the need for CT.
ACE inhibitor cough is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not explain weight loss, hoarseness or a mass.
There is no sign of infection, and waiting 6 weeks for a repeat X-ray would delay the diagnosis of a likely cancer.
PET is a staging test that the specialist arranges after CT, not the first test from general practice.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman at 17 weeks' gestation had NIPT showing a high chance of trisomy 16. Amniocentesis shows a normal fetal karyotype, and her ultrasound shows normal fetal anatomy. Which complication most warrants surveillance?
questions.why: A high-chance trisomy 16 NIPT result with a normal fetal karyotype on amniocentesis suggests confined placental mosaicism. Trisomy 16 confined to the placenta is linked with placental dysfunction. RANZCOG and HGSA guidance therefore advises serial growth scans for fetal growth restriction, along with watching for pre-eclampsia.
notes: Placental mosaicism does not raise the risk of gestational diabetes, which is screened for routinely at 24 to 28 weeks.
Poor placental function tends to cause too little amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios), not too much.
Placenta accreta is caused by a previous uterine scar or a low-lying placenta, not by a chromosomal change in the placenta.
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is a liver condition caused by bile acids and hormones, and is not linked with confined placental mosaicism.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has had 18 hours of vomiting and watery, non-bloody diarrhoea after minding her unwell grandson. She takes perindopril and metformin. HR 118/min, BP 98/60 mmHg; her abdomen is soft. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: She has a viral-pattern gastroenteritis with clear hypovolaemia while taking an ACE inhibitor and metformin. The test that changes her management is urea, electrolytes and creatinine, to look for a prerenal AKI and hypokalaemia and to guide fluids, potassium replacement and sick day rules. Under eTG, stool testing is not routine for acute watery diarrhoea without red flags.
notes: Stool testing is not routine in acute watery diarrhoea without blood, high fever, prolonged illness, immunosuppression or an outbreak, and a viral result would not change her care.
A soft abdomen with diffuse crampy pain and a clear sick contact does not justify CT, and contrast would add a kidney risk in a dehydrated patient.
She has had no recent antibiotics or hospital stay, and a sick contact with the same illness points to a viral cause rather than C. difficile.
Blood cultures are kept for high fever, sepsis or suspected invasive bacterial disease, which this low-risk watery diarrhoea does not suggest.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man sees his general practitioner about 4 months of looser, more frequent stools, now three times daily. On several occasions there has been dark red blood mixed through the stool. He reports tiredness but no weight loss or abdominal pain. He had rubber band ligation of internal haemorrhoids 5 years ago. A National Bowel Cancer Screening Program kit arrived last week, and he asks whether he should complete it; his kit 2 years ago was negative. He takes no regular medicines, including no aspirin or anti-inflammatory drugs. Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. Abdominal examination is normal. Digital rectal examination and proctoscopy show small, non-bleeding internal haemorrhoids and no mass. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (130–180) MCV 74 fL (80–100) Ferritin 6 µg/L (30–500) TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4–4.0) Tissue transglutaminase IgA negative Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Complete the immunochemical faecal occult blood test kit
Oral iron and a repeat blood count in 8 weeks
Repeat rubber band ligation of the internal haemorrhoids
CT colonography as the first investigation
questions.why: This man has a new, ongoing change in bowel habit at 66, blood mixed through the stool, and iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 104 g/L, MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 µg/L). He takes no NSAIDs and has no other obvious source of blood loss. Colorectal cancer must be assumed until it is excluded. The Cancer Council Australia optimal care pathway says a symptomatic patient should be referred for urgent diagnostic colonoscopy. GESA guidance on iron deficiency says a man or a postmenopausal woman with iron deficiency anaemia needs both colonoscopy and gastroscopy (bidirectional endoscopy), because there can be a lesion in both the upper and lower gut. A negative coeliac test does not remove the need for gastroscopy. Small haemorrhoids that are not bleeding do not explain the change in habit or the anaemia, and a normal rectal examination does not exclude a lesion higher in the colon. An FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms. A negative result would falsely reassure him, and the negative kit 2 years ago tells us nothing about his current symptoms.
notes: An FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms; he has red-flag symptoms and anaemia, so he needs a diagnostic test, and a negative result would falsely reassure him.
Giving iron alone without finding the source would delay the diagnosis of a likely gastrointestinal cancer, and a rise in haemoglobin would hide the problem.
Small haemorrhoids that are not bleeding do not explain blood mixed through the stool, the change in habit or the iron deficiency, so treating them misses the likely cause.
CT colonography is a second-line option when colonoscopy cannot be done; it cannot take a biopsy or examine the upper gut, which this patient's iron deficiency anaemia requires.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old Aboriginal girl from a remote community has facial swelling and cola-coloured urine three weeks after infected scabies. BP 130/85 mmHg. Urinalysis shows red cell casts; serum C3 is low. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Red cell casts show a nephritic picture. With a low C3 two to four weeks after a streptococcal skin infection, this points to acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is common in remote Aboriginal communities where scabies and impetigo are endemic. Confirm with ASOT and anti-DNase B, recheck C3 at 6 to 8 weeks to make sure it has returned to normal, and notify public health so household contacts can be screened and given treatment or prophylaxis.
notes: IgA nephropathy causes haematuria within a day or two of a sore throat (synpharyngitic), not weeks later, and the C3 is normal.
Minimal change disease causes nephrotic-range proteinuria without red cell casts, and the complement level is normal.
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome follows a diarrhoeal illness and shows haemolytic anaemia and low platelets; it does not cause a low C3 with casts after a skin infection.
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis also lowers C3, but the C3 stays low beyond 8 weeks; a typical post-infective onset makes it far less likely.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 70 minutes after the sudden onset of right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. She was last seen well at 08:10. She has atrial fibrillation and hypertension, treated with apixaban 5 mg twice daily and perindopril. Her last apixaban dose was at 07:30 today. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 92/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 168/94 mm Hg, respirations 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has non-fluent aphasia, a right facial droop and right arm power of 1/5 (NIHSS 15). Capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L, platelets 241 x10^9/L (150-400), INR 1.1 (0.9-1.2) and APTT 30 seconds (25-38). Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage. CT angiography shows a left M1 occlusion, and CT perfusion shows a 10 mL core within a 90 mL perfusion deficit. An apixaban-specific anti-Xa level is pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: This woman has an acute left middle cerebral artery stroke from a proximal (M1) large vessel occlusion. She is within 6 hours of last known well, has a disabling deficit (NIHSS 15), and has a small core with a large salvageable penumbra. The Stroke Foundation Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines recommend endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion in this setting, whether or not the patient can have thrombolysis. Anticoagulation does not rule it out. She took apixaban about 2 hours ago, well within 48 hours, so IV thrombolysis is contraindicated unless a drug-specific anti-Xa level shows no meaningful anticoagulant effect. A normal INR and APTT do not exclude a clinically relevant apixaban effect. Do not wait for the pending level before the clot retrieval pathway is started, because every minute of delay costs brain tissue. Other care in the meantime: keep her nil by mouth until a swallow screen, and do not lower blood pressure routinely. The value of 168/94 mm Hg is already below the 185/110 threshold used for reperfusion therapy.
notes: Wrong: she took apixaban within 48 hours, and a normal INR and APTT do not exclude a significant apixaban effect, so thrombolysis carries an unacceptable risk of haemorrhage until a drug-specific level shows no effect.
Wrong: idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran and has no effect on apixaban, a factor Xa inhibitor.
Wrong: guidelines do not support reversing a DOAC with prothrombin complex concentrate so that thrombolysis can be given, as this adds thrombotic risk and delay without proven benefit.
Wrong: aspirin gives no reperfusion for a salvageable M1 occlusion, and adding an antiplatelet in a fully anticoagulated patient before reperfusion is decided raises bleeding risk.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 6 hours of worsening breathlessness, chest tightness and wheeze. She had an upper respiratory tract infection 4 days ago. She has had asthma since childhood. She uses only a reliever inhaler and has never been prescribed a preventer. On arrival she speaks in short phrases and is using her accessory muscles. Pulse is 118/min, respiratory rate 28/min, blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg, temperature 37.4 °C and SpO2 91% on room air. There is widespread expiratory wheeze. The trachea is central and air entry is equal on both sides. Over the first hour she receives oxygen by nasal prongs, salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes, ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes and oral prednisolone 50 mg. She is still alert but still speaks only in phrases. Pulse is 122/min, respiratory rate 27/min and SpO2 93% on 2 L/min oxygen. Wheeze persists. A chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with no pneumothorax or consolidation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: This woman has acute severe asthma. She speaks only in phrases, uses her accessory muscles and has an SpO2 of 91% on room air. She has no features of life-threatening asthma: she is alert, with no cyanosis, no silent chest and no exhaustion. She has had an hour of optimal first-line treatment: repeated salbutamol by spacer, ipratropium, oral prednisolone and oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%. She is still in the severe category. The chest X-ray rules out a pneumothorax and consolidation. The Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG advise IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes for severe acute asthma that has not responded to first-line bronchodilators. She should keep having frequent salbutamol, and senior and ICU staff should be told. Aminophylline is not recommended as routine treatment because it adds little and causes arrhythmias and vomiting. IV hydrocortisone works no better than the oral prednisolone she has already had. IV salbutamol is kept for life-threatening asthma that does not respond, in a critical care setting. Nebulised adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction, not acute asthma.
notes: Aminophylline is not recommended as routine treatment for acute asthma: it adds little bronchodilation to inhaled therapy and has a narrow therapeutic index, with arrhythmias, seizures and vomiting.
She has already had oral prednisolone 50 mg and can swallow, so IV hydrocortisone gives no extra benefit and repeats her corticosteroid.

An IV salbutamol infusion is kept for life-threatening asthma that does not respond to other treatment, in a critical care setting; it causes more tachycardia, lactic acidosis and hypokalaemia, and she has no life-threatening features.
Nebulised adrenaline treats anaphylaxis or upper airway obstruction such as croup, and she has no urticaria, angioedema, allergen exposure or stridor.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man comes to his general practitioner for review of heartburn. For 9 years he has had burning retrosternal pain after evening meals on most days, with sour fluid coming up into his throat when he lies down at night. He has treated it with over-the-counter antacids and has never seen a doctor about it. He has no difficulty swallowing, vomiting, black stools or weight loss. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 25 years and stopped 5 years ago. He drinks about 10 standard drinks of alcohol a week. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg. His BMI is 33 kg/m2 and his waist circumference is 110 cm. Abdominal examination is normal. A resting 12-lead ECG is normal. Haemoglobin is 146 g/L (reference 130–180 g/L) and ferritin is 120 µg/L (reference 30–500 µg/L). Which of the following conditions is this patient at greatest risk of developing?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus
questions.why: This man has had untreated gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) for 9 years, with typical burning retrosternal pain after meals and regurgitation at night. He also has most of the recognised risk factors for Barrett's oesophagus: male sex, age over 50, reflux for many years, nocturnal symptoms, central obesity and a history of smoking. In Barrett's oesophagus, repeated acid injury replaces the squamous lining of the distal oesophagus with columnar epithelium showing intestinal metaplasia. It causes no symptoms of its own, but it can progress through dysplasia to oesophageal adenocarcinoma, so it is the key complication to look for and counsel about. Cancer Council Australia and eTG guidance support gastroscopy for a man over 50 with chronic reflux and several Barrett's risk factors, even without alarm features. Management alongside this is lifestyle change (weight loss, smaller and earlier evening meals, raising the head of the bed) and a standard-dose PPI. If Barrett's is found, he needs endoscopic surveillance. Squamous cell carcinoma is linked to smoking and heavy alcohol use, not reflux. Eosinophilic oesophagitis and achalasia are not complications of GORD.
notes: Wrong: squamous cell carcinoma is mainly caused by heavy smoking and alcohol use, not acid reflux, and his moderate drinking and past smoking make it much less likely than reflux-driven metaplasia.
Wrong: eosinophilic oesophagitis is an allergic disorder that usually affects younger atopic men with dysphagia or food bolus impaction, and it is not a complication of long-standing reflux.
Wrong: achalasia is a primary motility disorder caused by loss of myenteric neurons, and it presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids rather than developing from reflux.
Wrong: adenocarcinoma of the distal stomach is mainly linked to Helicobacter pylori and atrophic gastritis, not to acid reflux into the oesophagus.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man at a rural hospital, 3 hours from a PCI centre, has 2 hours of crushing chest pain and no bleeding history. ECG shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is an inferior STEMI that began less than 12 hours ago. Primary PCI cannot happen within 120 minutes of first medical contact, so Australian ACS guidelines advise fibrinolysis (ideally within 30 minutes of arrival) once contraindications are excluded. He is then transferred for angiography (a pharmaco-invasive strategy).
notes: A 3-hour transfer puts primary PCI well past the 120-minute limit, so he should have fibrinolysis first and be transferred afterwards.
STEMI is diagnosed from the ECG and the clinical picture, so reperfusion should not wait for troponin results.
GTN only relieves symptoms and does not reperfuse, and in inferior STEMI it can cause severe hypotension if the right ventricle is involved.
Nothing here suggests dissection (no tearing pain to the back), and imaging would only delay time-critical reperfusion.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man is leaving the surgical ward on day 2 after laparoscopic appendicectomy with oxycodone 5 mg up to four times daily. He takes oral iron. Bowels not opened; abdomen soft. Most appropriate laxative to co-prescribe?
questions.why: Opioids predictably cause constipation, and oral iron and reduced mobility after surgery add to it, so a regular laxative should be prescribed whenever an opioid is supplied at discharge (ACSQHC 2022). eTG recommends a regular osmotic and/or stimulant laxative for opioid-induced constipation, usually both, such as macrogol with senna. A soft abdomen with no signs of obstruction makes this safe to start now, and it prevents hard stools, straining and anal fissure.
notes: Bulk-forming laxatives are not recommended with opioids because they can make hard stools and faecal loading worse when gut transit is slowed.
A stool softener used alone does not counter the slowed gut movement caused by opioids, so it is not enough as prevention.
Peripheral opioid antagonists are kept for constipation that persists despite regular conventional laxatives, not for routine prevention.
A suppository is a rescue treatment for rectal loading, not a regular preventive regimen started with a new opioid.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with severe traumatic brain injury has fixed dilated pupils and no brainstem reflexes. He received a thiopentone infusion until yesterday; serum levels remain high. Which test best confirms brain death?
questions.why: High levels of a sedative like thiopentone mean the clinical brain death tests cannot be relied on. The ANZICS Statement on Death and Organ Donation then requires imaging that shows no blood flow to the brain, such as radionuclide perfusion scintigraphy or four-vessel catheter angiography. Sedatives do not change cerebral blood flow, so these tests still work.
notes: EEG measures cortical activity, which thiopentone suppresses, so it cannot separate drug effect from death, and ANZICS does not accept it.
Transcranial Doppler depends on the operator, can miss flow when the skull blocks the ultrasound, and is not accepted by ANZICS for brain death.
MRI shows structural damage, not whether blood is flowing through the brain, so it cannot confirm that all brain function has stopped.
Evoked potentials test only some sensory pathways, not the whole brain, and are not accepted for diagnosing brain death in Australia.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man collapses in the emergency department waiting area 20 minutes after triage. He had come in with 4 hours of central chest heaviness and nausea. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia, and takes metformin, perindopril and atorvastatin. His first rhythm is ventricular fibrillation. He receives CPR, three shocks, adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV. Spontaneous circulation returns after 12 minutes. He is being ventilated with a bag-valve-mask on 15 L/min oxygen. Pulse is 112/min, blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg, temperature is 35.6 °C and SpO2 is 97%. GCS is 3. A 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in V1 to V5. A venous blood gas taken 5 minutes after return of circulation shows: pH 7.09 (7.32 to 7.42); pCO2 62 mm Hg (41 to 51); bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22 to 28); base excess -11 mmol/L (-2 to +2); lactate 9.2 mmol/L (below 2.0); potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2); glucose 15.1 mmol/L (4.0 to 7.8). Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base disturbance?
options: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Acute respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Metabolic acidosis with coexisting metabolic alkalosis
Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
questions.why: The pH of 7.09 shows a severe acidaemia. There are two causes, and each one lowers the pH. First, the pCO2 of 62 mm Hg is high even for a venous sample, so there is a respiratory acidosis. This comes from low cardiac output during the arrest and poor ventilation with the bag-valve-mask. Second, the bicarbonate of 18 mmol/L, base excess of -11 and lactate of 9.2 mmol/L show a lactic metabolic acidosis from 12 minutes of low tissue perfusion. If the lungs were compensating for the metabolic acidosis, Winter's formula (1.5 x 18 + 8 = 35 +/- 2 mm Hg) says the pCO2 should be low. Instead it is high, so a second, respiratory process is present. This matters for his care. ANZCOR post-resuscitation guidance asks for normocapnia, so his ventilation should be increased and adjusted to arterial gases. Do not give bicarbonate routinely. The lactate should clear once perfusion improves with reperfusion and blood pressure support (MAP at least 65 mm Hg). The mild rise in potassium and the high glucose are expected after an arrest.
notes: Wrong: if the lungs were compensating, the pCO2 would be about 35 mm Hg, but it is 62 mm Hg, so there is also a respiratory acidosis.
Wrong: renal compensation would raise the bicarbonate, and the kidneys need days to do this, but his bicarbonate is low at 18 mmol/L.
Wrong: he has nothing that causes a metabolic alkalosis, such as vomiting or diuretics, and his low bicarbonate and base excess show only a metabolic acidosis.
Wrong: in chronic respiratory acidosis the bicarbonate is raised and the pH is close to normal, but he has a low bicarbonate and severe acidaemia after an acute event.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old retired plumber with a 6 cm right apical lung mass on chest X-ray develops thoracic back pain and bilateral leg weakness with a T6 sensory level. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: New back pain, leg weakness and a sensory level in a man with a probable apical lung cancer suggest malignant spinal cord compression, which is an oncological emergency. He needs high-dose dexamethasone straight away and same-day transfer for an urgent MRI of the whole spine, so that radiotherapy or surgery can preserve neurological function.
notes: CT chest stages the primary tumour but does not show the cord, and an outpatient timeframe delays emergency care.
A bone scan shows skeletal metastases but cannot show cord compression, and it delays the MRI needed.
Waiting a day risks irreversible paraplegia, because outcome depends on neurological function at the start of treatment.
Specialist referral is right for the lung mass, but the new neurological deficit needs same-day emergency management.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with diabetes who smokes has a painful punched-out ulcer on her left fifth toe and night foot pain eased by dangling. Toe pressure 22 mmHg. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She has rest pain, tissue loss and a toe pressure below 30 mmHg, which means chronic limb-threatening ischaemia. Diabetes Feet Australia guidelines call for urgent vascular imaging and assessment for revascularisation. Wound care, stopping smoking, antiplatelet therapy and a statin run alongside the referral but do not replace it.
notes: Compression lowers blood flow to an already ischaemic limb and is contraindicated in severe arterial disease.
There is no sign of infection, and antibiotics do not treat an uninfected ischaemic ulcer.
Supervised exercise is for claudication, not for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia with rest pain and tissue loss.
Elevation worsens arterial perfusion and rest pain, and dressings alone will not heal an ulcer the limb cannot perfuse.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, para 2, is on the birth suite 25 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 38 weeks' gestation. Her labour was induced for pre-eclampsia. She received oxytocin 10 units at the birth, and the placenta and membranes were complete. She is now bleeding heavily with clots, and the measured loss is 1,300 mL. Bimanual compression has been done, a catheter has drained 450 mL of urine, an oxytocin infusion is running, and tranexamic acid 1 g IV was given 10 minutes ago. In labour she took oral labetalol and had a magnesium sulfate infusion. She has no history of asthma. Pulse is 122/min, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg (158/102 mmHg before the birth), respirations 24/min and SpO2 98% on oxygen 15 L/min by mask. The fundus is soft and above the umbilicus. Speculum examination shows no cervical or vaginal tear. Haemoglobin is 95 g/L, platelets 146 x 10^9/L and fibrinogen 3.4 g/L. Crossmatched blood has been requested. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: This is a major primary postpartum haemorrhage (1,300 mL with tachycardia) caused by uterine atony. The fundus is soft and high, and the other Ts have been checked: no tear (trauma), a complete placenta (tissue) and normal fibrinogen and near-normal platelets (thrombin). First-line measures are already done: uterine compression, an empty bladder, oxytocin IM then by infusion, and tranexamic acid. RANZCOG C-Obs 43 and Queensland Clinical Guidelines say the next step for ongoing atony is a second-line uterotonic. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia because it can cause a hypertensive crisis, stroke or eclampsia, even though her BP has fallen from bleeding. Magnesium sulfate also adds to atony. She has no asthma, so carboprost (15-methyl PGF2-alpha) 250 micrograms IM is the right choice. It can be repeated every 15 minutes up to 8 doses (2 mg). Balloon tamponade and surgery are for bleeding that continues despite uterotonics.
notes: Wrong: ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia and hypertension because it can cause severe hypertension, stroke or eclampsia, and her current lower BP is from blood loss, not a resolved disease.
Wrong: misoprostol is slower in onset and less effective than other uterotonics, so guidelines keep it for when carboprost or ergometrine are unavailable or contraindicated.
Wrong: balloon tamponade is the next step only once uterotonics have failed, and she has not yet had a second-line uterotonic.
Wrong: laparotomy with a B-Lynch or similar suture is for haemorrhage that continues despite uterotonics and tamponade, so it is premature here.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of non-itchy facial and hand swelling with colicky abdominal pain, without urticaria. Her father had similar episodes. Antihistamines have not helped. Most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.why: Recurrent angioedema without urticaria, with abdominal attacks, a family history and no response to antihistamines suggests hereditary angioedema, which is bradykinin-mediated. Serum C4 is the recommended screening test because it is low in most patients, including between attacks. If C4 is low, C1 esterase inhibitor level and function are measured to confirm the diagnosis.
notes: Tryptase rises in mast cell-mediated reactions such as anaphylaxis, but hereditary angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, so tryptase stays normal.
Total IgE reflects atopy and does not identify complement-mediated hereditary angioedema.
Skin prick testing detects IgE-mediated allergy, which would not explain inherited attacks without urticaria that do not respond to antihistamines.
Thyroid autoimmunity is linked with chronic spontaneous urticaria, but this patient has no hives and an inherited pattern.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman taking rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation presents drowsy, GCS 13, two days after a fall. CT brain shows a left acute subdural haematoma. Her last dose was 4 hours ago. Most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.why: She has an intracranial bleed and took a factor Xa inhibitor 4 hours ago, so the anticoagulant must be reversed straight away. Under eTG, the reversal agent is prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF, about 50 units/kg IV), given with haematology advice while urgent neurosurgical referral is arranged. Andexanet alfa is an option only where local protocol allows it.
notes: Vitamin K works by restoring vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, so it reverses warfarin but has no effect on rivaroxaban, a direct factor Xa inhibitor.
Idarucizumab is a specific antibody fragment that reverses only dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, and does not bind rivaroxaban.
Fresh frozen plasma needs a large volume and takes a long time to thaw, and it does little to reverse a factor Xa inhibitor.
Protamine reverses heparin, and partly low molecular weight heparin, but has no effect on direct oral anticoagulants.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 30 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain. It began after a fried dinner and radiates to her right shoulder. Over the past 8 months she has had brief, similar episodes after meals. Her temperature is 38.7 °C, pulse 106/min, blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. She is not jaundiced, and Murphy's sign is positive. Investigations show: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) CRP 88 mg/L (<5) Total bilirubin 24 µmol/L (<20) ALP 440 U/L (30-110) GGT 210 U/L (<40) ALT 31 U/L (<35) Lipase 30 U/L (<60) Ultrasound shows a gallbladder wall thickened to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid and a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. The common bile duct measures 5 mm, but bowel gas hides its distal end. She is given analgesia, IV fluids and IV antibiotics, and is admitted for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation before surgery?
options: Repeat liver function tests in 6 weeks
questions.why: The ultrasound and inflammatory markers already show acute calculous cholecystitis. The question is what the liver function tests mean for her. A stone stuck in the cystic duct on its own usually causes only mild LFT changes. Her ALP and GGT are about 4 to 5 times the upper limit, with a normal ALT and a bilirubin that is only slightly raised. This cholestatic pattern suggests a common bile duct stone causing partial or intermittent blockage. A 5 mm duct and a bilirubin of 24 make complete obstruction unlikely, but they do not rule out a stone, especially since the distal duct could not be seen. That puts her at intermediate risk of choledocholithiasis. Guidelines (eTG, ASGE) recommend non-invasive duct imaging before cholecystectomy, either MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound, or else an intraoperative cholangiogram. ERCP is kept for a duct stone that has been confirmed, or for cholangitis that needs urgent drainage.
notes: ERCP carries a risk of pancreatitis, bleeding and perforation, so it is used to treat a confirmed duct stone or cholangitis needing drainage rather than to look for a stone in a woman who is not jaundiced and has a non-dilated duct.
A HIDA scan tests whether the cystic duct is patent to diagnose cholecystitis, which the ultrasound has already confirmed, and it does not show stones in the common bile duct well.
CT misses many bile duct stones because cholesterol stones are often isodense with bile, and it adds radiation without answering the question the LFTs raise.
Waiting 6 weeks to repeat the LFTs would leave a possible duct stone unchecked through cholecystectomy during this admission, risking a retained stone, cholangitis or pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man presents 2 weeks after coronary artery bypass grafting with fever and pleuritic chest pain eased by leaning forward. ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Concave ST elevation across many leads with PR depression is the ECG pattern of pericarditis. With fever and positional pleuritic pain weeks after the pericardium was opened, this is postpericardiotomy syndrome. It is treated with NSAIDs or colchicine, and an echo is needed to look for an effusion or tamponade.
notes: Graft occlusion causes convex ST elevation in one coronary territory, often with reciprocal depression, and not widespread PR depression.
Pulmonary embolism usually shows sinus tachycardia or right heart strain on ECG, not diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.
Mediastinitis causes fever and sternal pain with wound discharge or an unstable sternum, but it does not give a pericarditic ECG.
Type A dissection causes sudden tearing pain and, if it reaches the coronary arteries, ST elevation in one territory, not diffuse PR depression.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with a splenic laceration from a bicycle fall remains hypotensive at 70/40 mmHg despite fluid boluses. His Jehovah's Witness parents refuse blood transfusion. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Parents cannot refuse life-saving treatment for a child. In an emergency, Australian state and territory laws let doctors transfuse a child without parental consent (usually with a second doctor agreeing), and this is recorded in the notes. A child in haemorrhagic shock needs blood straight away.
notes: A court order is the right route when treatment is not urgent, but getting one now would delay transfusion while he is in shock.
Parents' authority is limited to decisions in the child's best interests, so they cannot refuse treatment that would save his life.
An ethics committee is too slow for an emergency and has no legal power to authorise treatment.
Erythropoietin takes days to raise haemoglobin and does nothing for acute haemorrhagic shock.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man had sudden left sensorineural hearing loss two weeks ago, confirmed on audiogram. After oral prednisolone, his hearing has returned to normal. Neurological examination is normal. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Any unilateral sudden sensorineural hearing loss needs gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma. Hearing recovery after steroids does not rule out a schwannoma, so the MRI is still needed.
notes: Discharging him now could miss a retrocochlear tumour, because recovery after steroids does not exclude one.
CT of the temporal bones shows bone and middle ear disease but misses small schwannomas in the internal auditory canal.
A cochlear vascular cause would involve the posterior circulation, so carotid imaging does not help, and he has no stroke features.
Repeating the audiogram tracks hearing but cannot detect or exclude a retrocochlear lesion.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man comes to a suburban general practice with 16 hours of abdominal pain. It started overnight as a vague ache around his umbilicus and has since moved to the right lower abdomen. He has vomited twice, has not eaten since yesterday, and says the walk from the car park jolted the pain. He has no diarrhoea and no urinary symptoms. He has no past medical history and takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 38.1 °C, heart rate 106/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He lies still on the couch. He is tender at McBurney's point with guarding, and pressing on the left iliac fossa causes pain on the right. Bowel sounds are present. A urine dipstick shows ketones 1+ and is negative for blood, leucocytes and nitrites. He asks if he can go home and see how he feels tomorrow. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Arrange an outpatient abdominal ultrasound and review the result tomorrow
Start oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review him in 24 hours
Withhold all analgesia until a surgeon has examined his abdomen
Give analgesia, keep nil by mouth and arrange same-day hospital referral
Request faecal calprotectin and refer him to a gastroenterologist
questions.why: This young man most likely has acute appendicitis. He has periumbilical pain that has moved to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, vomiting, fever, tachycardia, pain when jolted, guarding at McBurney's point and a positive Rovsing's sign. A normal urine dipstick does not rule it out. When appendicitis is suspected in general practice, he needs same-day transfer to an emergency department or surgical unit. The GP should phone a handover, keep him nil by mouth in case he needs theatre, give adequate analgesia, record his allergies and arrange safe transport. Giving analgesia does not hide the diagnosis or delay it. If the diagnosis is confirmed, antibiotics are given in hospital under eTG guidance, alongside appendicectomy or, for some patients, supervised non-operative care. Sending him home raises the risk of perforation, peritonitis and abscess.
notes: An outpatient scan with review the next day delays surgical assessment in a febrile, tachycardic patient with localised peritonism, and a normal scan would not exclude appendicitis.
Treating suspected appendicitis with oral antibiotics in the community, without imaging or surgical review, can mask a progressing or perforating appendix and does not follow eTG advice.
Withholding pain relief is outdated, because analgesia does not reduce diagnostic accuracy and leaving pain untreated causes avoidable suffering.
Ileocaecal Crohn's disease is unlikely after a 16-hour illness with no diarrhoea, weight loss or bleeding, and an elective gastroenterology referral would miss a surgical emergency.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has had worsening thoracic back pain for three days and new weakness in both legs. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: New back pain and leg weakness in a patient with cancer that spreads to bone means suspected malignant spinal cord compression, which is an emergency. eTG advises giving high-dose dexamethasone (16 mg orally or IV) straight away, while urgent whole-spine MRI and oncology review are arranged. How well he walks after treatment depends on how well he walks when treatment starts.
notes: A plain X-ray can miss cord compression, and getting one delays the steroids and MRI that are needed.
More opioid treats the pain but does nothing for the cord compression causing the new weakness.
Radiotherapy is a definitive treatment, but it needs MRI first to find the level, so it is not the first step.
Bisphosphonates help with bone pain and high calcium but do not relieve acute cord compression.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man, a delivery driver, has had months of daytime sleepiness and loud snoring. BMI is 34 kg/m2, Epworth score 14 and STOP-Bang 6. TSH and full blood count are normal. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: His high Epworth and STOP-Bang scores, with obesity and snoring, make obstructive sleep apnoea likely, and he meets the criteria for a GP to refer him directly for an unattended home polysomnography (MBS 12250). The study confirms the diagnosis and grades severity by AHI, which then guides treatment such as CPAP.
notes: CPAP is started after a sleep study has confirmed OSA and shown it is moderate to severe, not before.
Overnight oximetry alone is not an adequate diagnostic test for OSA: it misses hypopnoeas with arousal and cannot grade AHI.
Modafinil does not treat the airway obstruction and is only for residual sleepiness in OSA that has been confirmed and treated.
Upper airway surgery is a later option for selected patients with confirmed OSA who cannot tolerate CPAP, not a first step.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has 4 months of crampy lower abdominal pain eased by defecation, with alternating loose and hard stools. No bleeding or weight loss. FBC, CRP and coeliac serology are normal. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: In a young adult with suspected IBS, loose stools and no red flags, faecal calprotectin is the first-line test to separate IBD from IBS once FBC, CRP and coeliac serology are normal. A result below 50 µg/g makes IBD unlikely and means colonoscopy can be avoided.
notes: Invasive and not needed first in a young patient with no red flags; it is kept for a raised calprotectin or red flags.
FIT is used for bowel cancer screening in people without symptoms aged 45 to 74, not to assess IBS-type symptoms in a 24-year-old.
May suggest lactose intolerance or bacterial overgrowth but does not exclude IBD, and is not a routine first-line test.
Gives a radiation dose with low yield for mucosal disease, and is not part of the first-line work-up for suspected IBS.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner because of 6 weeks of yellow eyes, generalised itch, dark urine and pale stools. She also has a dull epigastric ache that goes through to her back, poor appetite and a 6 kg weight loss. Type 2 diabetes was diagnosed 8 months ago and she takes metformin. She has a 45 pack-year smoking history. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse is 82/min and blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg. She has scleral icterus and excoriations on her forearms. A smooth, non-tender mass is palpable below the right costal margin. Results: total bilirubin 164 µmol/L (reference less than 20), ALP 540 U/L (30–110), GGT 690 U/L (less than 38), ALT 118 U/L (less than 35), INR 1.2, white cell count 7.1 x10^9/L, CA 19-9 860 U/mL (less than 37). A pancreatic-protocol CT shows a 26 mm hypoattenuating mass in the pancreatic head with dilated common bile and pancreatic ducts, no vascular involvement and no liver metastases. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Urgent referral to a hepatobiliary surgical unit
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography with stent insertion
Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy of the mass
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography of the biliary tree
Repeat CA 19-9 and liver function tests in four weeks
questions.why: This woman has obstructive jaundice. She has a conjugated, cholestatic picture with ALP and GGT raised far more than ALT, pale stools, dark urine and itch. She also has a palpable non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign), weight loss, back pain, new-onset diabetes, heavy smoking, a CA 19-9 of 860 and a pancreatic head mass with a double duct sign. This is pancreatic head adenocarcinoma until proven otherwise. The CT shows no vascular involvement and no metastases, so the tumour looks resectable, and surgery is the only potential cure. The Australian optimal care pathway for pancreatic cancer says a GP who suspects pancreatic cancer should refer the patient urgently to a specialist centre with a hepatopancreatobiliary multidisciplinary team, to be seen within 2 weeks. That team decides on further staging, tissue sampling, biliary drainage and timing of surgery. She is afebrile with a normal white cell count, so there is no cholangitis needing emergency drainage or antibiotics.
notes: Routine biliary stenting before resection raises infective and surgical complications, and it is only needed for cholangitis, long delays to surgery or neoadjuvant therapy, which the specialist team decides.
A tissue diagnosis is not required before resecting a lesion that looks resectable on imaging; biopsy is arranged by the specialist team, for example before neoadjuvant or palliative chemotherapy.
The pancreatic-protocol CT has already shown the cause and the level of obstruction, so MRCP adds delay without changing the need for specialist referral.
Watching and repeating tests delays the only potentially curative treatment, and CA 19-9 trends do not replace imaging and specialist assessment.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with diabetes walks into a general practice with 40 minutes of central chest heaviness spreading to her jaw, with sweating. BP 138/84 mmHg, SpO2 97%. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Australian ACS guidelines say anyone with possible acute coronary syndrome needs a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact. The ECG finds STEMI, which needs a 000 call and urgent reperfusion. A troponin or other tests must not delay this.
notes: A troponin can be normal early and takes time, so it must not delay the ECG or the transfer of a possible STEMI.
A chest X-ray can help with other causes, but it cannot show an acute coronary occlusion and comes after the ECG.
Stress testing is unsafe during ongoing ischaemic pain at rest and is only for stable patients once ACS has been ruled out.
CT coronary angiography is for stable, lower-risk chest pain and is not the first test for ongoing pain that may be ACS.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic for screening. He recalls no hepatitis B vaccination. Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs 85 IU/L. Most likely interpretation?
questions.why: A positive anti-HBc means he has been infected with hepatitis B at some point. With HBsAg negative and protective anti-HBs (10 IU/L or more), the infection has cleared and he is immune. He does not need vaccination, but the result should be recorded because the virus can reactivate if he is later immunosuppressed.
notes: Vaccination produces anti-HBs only, so anti-HBc would be negative.
Chronic hepatitis B needs HBsAg to stay positive for more than 6 months, and here HBsAg is negative.
Acute infection shows positive HBsAg or IgM anti-HBc without protective anti-HBs, not high anti-HBs with negative HBsAg.
A susceptible person has negative anti-HBc and anti-HBs, but here both are positive.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after vomiting dark, coffee-ground material three times this morning. She has had black, sticky stools for 3 days. She has knee osteoarthritis and has taken naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 2 months. She also takes aspirin 100 mg daily because of a previous transient ischaemic attack. She does not drink alcohol. On arrival, her pulse is 106/min, blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg (usually 145/85 mm Hg), respirations 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air and temperature 36.8 °C. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease. The abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no guarding. Rectal examination shows melaena. Two large-bore cannulas are inserted and 500 mL of crystalloid is given. Her pulse falls to 92/min and her blood pressure rises to 124/74 mm Hg. Haemoglobin is 97 g/L (baseline 131 g/L), platelets 302 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, urea 13.9 mmol/L, creatinine 81 µmol/L, albumin 39 g/L and bilirubin 9 µmol/L. Gastroscopy is booked for the next morning. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug to give now?
questions.why: This woman has a non-variceal upper GI bleed, most likely from a peptic ulcer caused by naproxen and aspirin together. She has coffee-ground vomiting, melaena, a 34 g/L fall in haemoglobin and a urea raised out of proportion to her creatinine. She has responded to fluids. She drinks no alcohol, has no stigmata of liver disease, and her platelets, INR, albumin and bilirubin are normal, so varices are unlikely. Her Glasgow-Blatchford score is high, so she needs admission and gastroscopy within 24 hours. Her haemoglobin is above the restrictive transfusion threshold (below 70 g/L, or below 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease), so she does not need red cells. eTG and the NSW ACI guidelines recommend an IV proton pump inhibitor (for example, pantoprazole 80 mg IV) while she waits for endoscopy. Before endoscopy it reduces the number of high-risk stigmata seen and the need for endoscopic therapy. After endoscopic haemostasis of a high-risk ulcer, high-dose IV PPI lowers the risk of rebleeding. The naproxen should be stopped for good. The decision on aspirin is made with gastroenterology, and it is usually restarted within days.
notes: Terlipressin is used for suspected variceal bleeding, and she has no alcohol use, no liver stigmata and normal liver function and coagulation results.
Tranexamic acid does not reduce death from GI bleeding and increases venous thromboembolism (HALT-IT trial), so guidelines advise against using it.
Prophylactic antibiotics such as ceftriaxone lower infection and mortality rates in variceal bleeding in cirrhosis, not in non-variceal ulcer bleeding.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin or treats a deficiency-related coagulopathy, and her INR is normal and she takes no vitamin K antagonist.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a painful, swollen right knee that came on suddenly overnight. Two years ago he had an attack in his left big toe that settled on its own. He has hypertension and stage 4 chronic kidney disease. He takes amlodipine, irbesartan and furosemide, and has no drug allergies. He recalls no injury. His temperature is 37.2 °C, pulse 88/min and blood pressure 148/86 mm Hg. The right knee is hot, red and tensely swollen with a large effusion, and the skin is intact. Investigations show: Serum creatinine 245 µmol/L (60–110) eGFR 23 mL/min/1.73 m² (>90) Serum urate 0.52 mmol/L (0.20–0.42) CRP 64 mg/L (<5) Synovial fluid: white cell count 22 000 ×10^6/L with 80% neutrophils; needle-shaped, negatively birefringent intracellular crystals; Gram stain shows no organisms; culture pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this attack?
questions.why: The aspirate shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, so this is an acute flare of gout. He is afebrile with a negative Gram stain. An NSAID, low-dose colchicine and a corticosteroid work about equally well for a flare, so the choice depends on comorbidities. This man has severe chronic kidney disease (eGFR 23) and takes an angiotensin receptor blocker and a loop diuretic. That makes an NSAID unsafe, and colchicine can build up to toxic levels. A short course of oral prednisolone (eTG) is the safest effective option. Intra-articular corticosteroid is another option, but only once infection is reasonably excluded, and the culture is still pending. Culture must be followed to its final report, because crystals do not rule out coexisting infection. Allopurinol is not used to treat the attack itself. Antibiotics are not indicated when the patient is afebrile, the Gram stain is negative, the synovial count is below 50 000 and urate crystals are present.
notes: Allopurinol is urate-lowering therapy for long-term prevention; it does not treat a flare and is started later, at a low dose for his eGFR, with flare prophylaxis.
Colchicine is cleared by the kidneys and builds up in severe chronic kidney disease, causing toxicity such as diarrhoea, myopathy and bone marrow suppression, so a corticosteroid is the safer choice.
An NSAID given with an angiotensin receptor blocker and a diuretic (the 'triple whammy') in someone with an eGFR of 23 risks acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia.

Empirical antibiotics for septic arthritis are not needed: he is afebrile, the Gram stain is negative, the synovial white cell count is below 50 000 and urate crystals are present, though the culture should still be followed up.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has 4 months of thirst and nocturia. BMI is 36 kg/m2 with acanthosis nigricans. Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+, ketones negative, specific gravity 1.022. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: Thirst and nocturia with heavy glycosuria in urine that is not dilute, in an obese man with acanthosis, suggest type 2 diabetes with an osmotic diuresis. Under RACGP and eTG guidance, an HbA1c of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more confirms diabetes. Because he has typical symptoms, one abnormal result is enough.
notes: An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for borderline fasting or random glucose results, and it is unnecessary and slow when hyperglycaemia is clearly likely.
A water deprivation test looks for diabetes insipidus, which gives dilute urine without glucose, not concentrated urine with glucosuria.
GAD antibodies help tell autoimmune from type 2 diabetes once diabetes is confirmed, but they do not diagnose diabetes itself.
C-peptide measures how much insulin the body still makes, which helps classify diabetes after diagnosis, but it does not confirm hyperglycaemia.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors and yellow eyes. Today his wife noticed he was muddled. He has untreated gallstones and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. On arrival he is jaundiced and disoriented to time. Temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 122/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 95% on room air. The right upper quadrant is tender. Results: total bilirubin 104 µmol/L (reference <20), conjugated bilirubin 82 µmol/L, ALP 438 U/L (30–110), GGT 590 U/L (<50), ALT 112 U/L (<40), lipase 52 U/L (<60), white cell count 19.1 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), creatinine 139 µmol/L (60–110), INR 1.2 and venous lactate 3.8 mmol/L (<2.0). Ultrasound shows gallbladder calculi with a 3 mm wall and a common bile duct of 12 mm containing a distal shadowing calculus. Blood cultures are taken, and he is given IV amoxicillin, IV gentamicin and 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. His blood pressure is now 98/60 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: This man has Reynolds' pentad: jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, confusion and hypotension. Under the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 this is severe (grade III) acute cholangitis, because he has neurological and cardiovascular dysfunction. It is caused by a stone in a dilated common bile duct, with a cholestatic liver test pattern, and he also has sepsis with hypoperfusion (lactate 3.8 mmol/L and acute kidney injury). The eTG and the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard say to take blood cultures, give IV antibiotics within 60 minutes (amoxicillin plus gentamicin for biliary sepsis) and give fluids, all of which has been done. Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus from a blocked duct. Once he has been resuscitated, he needs urgent source control by decompressing the bile duct with ERCP (sphincterotomy and stone extraction, or a stent if he is too unstable), and his care should be escalated to ICU. Cholecystectomy should follow once he has recovered, ideally during the same admission. A normal lipase and a thin gallbladder wall make gallstone pancreatitis and acute cholecystitis unlikely.
notes: Wrong: cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder but does not clear the stone blocking the common bile duct, and operating on a septic, hypotensive patient is high risk. It is planned after the duct has been cleared and he has recovered.
Wrong: ultrasound has already shown a dilated duct with a stone in it, so MRCP would only delay drainage in a deteriorating septic patient.

Wrong: cholecystostomy drains the gallbladder, not the blocked common bile duct. It is used for acute cholecystitis in unfit patients, whereas percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage is the fallback if ERCP fails.
Wrong: delaying drainage by 72 hours is acceptable only in mild cholangitis that responds to antibiotics. In severe cholangitis with hypotension and confusion, this delay increases the risk of death.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old retired electrician is reviewed on day 3 of admission to the general surgical ward. He came in with 2 days of constant left iliac fossa pain, loose stools and a temperature of 38.4 °C. On admission, CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast showed multiple sigmoid diverticula and a 5 cm segment of sigmoid wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding. There was no abscess, extraluminal gas, fistula or obstruction. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics, fluids and paracetamol. He is now afebrile, eating normally and has minimal pain, and he has been switched to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. He has hypertension treated with perindopril. He has never had any lower bowel investigation and did not return his last two national bowel screening kits. There is no family history of bowel disease. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 72/min and blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg. His abdomen is soft, with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no guarding. Haemoglobin is 141 g/L (130–180), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0) and CRP 34 mg/L (<5). He is to be discharged today. Which of the following is the most appropriate follow-up investigation?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis in 48 hours
questions.why: This man has CT-confirmed acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis and is getting better on treatment. CT cannot reliably tell inflamed diverticular wall thickening from a sigmoid carcinoma. He is 67, has never had his colon examined and has not done his bowel screening, so cancer in the thickened segment has to be excluded. Colonoscopy should be done once the inflammation has settled, usually about 6 weeks after recovery. CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy are alternatives if colonoscopy is unsuitable. Scoping during acute inflammation is avoided because inflating the bowel with air and passing the scope through the inflamed segment risks perforation. A repeat CT is only needed if he fails to improve within 48 to 72 hours or gets worse. Tumour markers such as CEA are not used to diagnose or screen for colorectal cancer. A faecal immunochemical test is a screening tool for people without symptoms. It cannot replace looking directly at a segment that CT has already shown to be abnormal.
notes: A repeat CT is only indicated if he does not improve within 48 to 72 hours or gets worse, and he is clearly improving.
Colonoscopy during or just after acute diverticulitis risks perforating the inflamed colon and is harder to interpret while the inflammation persists, so it should be delayed.
CEA is not sensitive or specific enough to diagnose or exclude colorectal cancer and is used only to monitor known disease.
A faecal immunochemical test is a screening test for people without symptoms and cannot exclude cancer in a sigmoid segment that CT has already shown to be abnormal.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is a primary school teacher comes to her general practitioner with a 5-month history of crampy lower abdominal pain and loose stools. She opens her bowels three to four times a day, mostly in the morning, with urgency, and the pain eases after defecation. She is bloated most afternoons. She has had no rectal bleeding or weight loss, and she does not wake at night to open her bowels. She has not travelled overseas. No family members have bowel disease. She takes no regular medicines. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse 76/min, blood pressure 114/70 mm Hg and BMI 23 kg/m2. The abdomen is soft, with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no masses. Rectal examination is normal. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 131 g/L (115–165) Ferritin 62 µg/L (30–300) C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5) Total IgA 2.0 g/L (0.7–4.0) Tissue transglutaminase IgA 1 U/mL (<7) Stool microscopy, culture and PCR: no pathogens detected Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: This young woman has symptoms that fit irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea. She has recurrent lower abdominal pain that eases after defecation, a change in stool frequency and form, and bloating. She has no red flags: no rectal bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, fever, mass or family history. Her full blood count, ferritin and CRP are normal. Coeliac serology is negative and valid, because her total IgA is normal. Stool tests show no infection. The main serious condition left to exclude is inflammatory bowel disease, because loose stools with urgency in a young adult can be early Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, and a normal CRP does not rule it out. The first-line test before making a positive diagnosis of IBS is faecal calprotectin, as recommended in eTG and Australian gastroenterology practice. It is cheap and non-invasive. A result below 50 µg/g makes IBD unlikely and avoids colonoscopy. A raised result calls for gastroenterology referral and colonoscopy. Colonoscopy is wrong at this stage because it is invasive and kept for red flags or a raised calprotectin.
notes: Colonoscopy is invasive and kept for red flags or a raised calprotectin, neither of which she has yet.
Duodenal biopsy is not needed because a negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA makes coeliac disease very unlikely.
A lactose hydrogen breath test cannot exclude inflammatory bowel disease, and a trial of avoiding dairy is preferred over formal breath testing.
A faecal immunochemical test is a population screening tool for people aged 45 to 74 without symptoms and is not used to investigate symptomatic young adults in Australia.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man has three months of lower back pain and fatigue. Haemoglobin is 96 g/L, corrected calcium 2.88 mmol/L, creatinine 165 µmol/L, and globulins 58 g/L. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Bone pain with hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia (the CRAB features) and a raised globulin gap point to multiple myeloma. The first test is serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, plus serum free light chains, to find a paraprotein. Bone marrow examination comes after that to confirm the diagnosis.
notes: Bone marrow biopsy is needed to measure clonal plasma cells, but it is invasive and is done after a paraprotein has been found.
Primary hyperparathyroidism does not explain the anaemia, renal impairment and high globulins, which together point to a plasma cell disorder.
Prostate cancer metastases usually cause sclerotic bone lesions and do not raise globulins, so PSA does not test the leading diagnosis.
Myeloma lesions are purely lytic with little osteoblastic activity, so an isotope bone scan often misses them and does not identify a paraprotein.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman, five days after hip arthroplasty, suddenly becomes breathless and confused. BP 76/48 mmHg despite a fluid bolus, SpO2 85% on oxygen, JVP raised, lungs clear. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: After surgery, sudden shock with hypoxia, a raised JVP and clear lungs suggests high-risk (massive) pulmonary embolism. When the patient is too unstable for CT, bedside echocardiography showing right ventricular dysfunction is enough to justify immediate reperfusion therapy such as thrombolysis.
notes: CTPA is the test of choice once the patient is stable, but moving a hypotensive, hypoxic patient to the scanner risks arrest and delays treatment.
A V/Q scan takes too long, needs transfer, and is less useful in an unstable patient.
D-dimer is raised after surgery and can only rule out PE in low-risk patients, so it adds nothing in suspected high-risk PE.
Leg duplex may find a DVT, but it does not show whether PE is causing the shock, so it should not delay decisions about reperfusion.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man comes to his general practitioner with 3 weeks of sharp anal pain. It starts with each bowel motion and lasts about 2 hours afterwards, and there is a small amount of bright red blood on the toilet paper. The pain began after a week of hard stools while he was driving long-haul freight. For the past 2 weeks he has taken psyllium daily, increased his fluid intake, used warm sitz baths and applied lidocaine gel. His stools are now soft, but the pain has improved only slightly. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and erectile dysfunction treated with tadalafil 5 mg daily. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 84/min and blood pressure 134/82 mmHg. With a chaperone present, inspection shows a single linear tear in the posterior midline of the anal margin with clean, soft edges. There is no sentinel tag, induration or swelling. He is too tender for a digital rectal examination, so it is not done. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% applied to the anal margin
Diltiazem 2% applied to the anal margin
Hydrocortisone with cinchocaine applied to the anal margin
Botulinum toxin injected into the internal sphincter
questions.why: This man has an acute primary anal fissure. The fissure is in the posterior midline, has soft edges and no sentinel tag, and has been present for less than 6 weeks. The pain causes spasm of the internal anal sphincter, which reduces blood flow to the posterior anoderm and stops the tear healing. His stools are now soft, but he is still in pain after 2 weeks of conservative care, so the eTG recommends adding a topical drug that relaxes the sphincter. The two choices are glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% and diltiazem 2%. GTN is contraindicated in anyone taking a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor. He takes tadalafil daily, and its long half-life means simply skipping doses would not make GTN safe. Topical diltiazem 2% twice daily for 6 to 8 weeks heals about as many fissures as GTN and causes fewer headaches. He should keep using fibre, fluids and sitz baths. If the fissure becomes chronic, he should be referred to a surgeon. Any bleeding that continues after the fissure heals needs investigation.
notes: GTN with a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor such as daily tadalafil can cause severe, possibly fatal hypotension, so it is contraindicated for him.
Codeine causes constipation, and hard stools would reopen the fissure and keep the pain and spasm going, so it should be avoided.
A topical corticosteroid with local anaesthetic does not relax the sphincter and does not speed fissure healing, and long-term use thins the perianal skin.

Botulinum toxin is a specialist second-line treatment for chronic fissures, or for fissures that have not responded to topical sphincter relaxants, so it is not the next step for an acute fissure that has not yet been treated with one.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with active rheumatoid arthritis has haemoglobin 98 g/L and MCV 84 fL. Iron studies: low iron, low transferrin, transferrin saturation 12%, ferritin 420 µg/L. Most likely cause of anaemia?
questions.why: Her anaemia is normocytic, with low serum iron and low transferrin saturation, but transferrin is low and ferritin is high. In active inflammatory disease, this pattern points to anaemia of inflammation (anaemia of chronic disease). Hepcidin traps iron in macrophages, and ferritin rises because it is an acute-phase reactant.
notes: In iron deficiency, transferrin is high and ferritin is low (under about 30 µg/L), so these results argue against it, although inflammation can raise ferritin and hide a coexisting deficiency.
Beta thalassaemia trait causes marked microcytosis with normal iron studies, not a normal MCV with low iron and low transferrin.
Sideroblastic anaemia causes iron overload with high serum iron and high transferrin saturation, not low saturation.
Folate deficiency (for example from methotrexate) causes a macrocytic anaemia and does not explain the abnormal iron studies.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man who strips old paint from heritage homes has 3 weeks of colicky abdominal pain, constipation and fatigue. Haemoglobin is 104 g/L with basophilic stippling on the film. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: Stripping old paint exposes workers to lead dust. Abdominal colic, constipation, fatigue and anaemia with basophilic stippling suggest lead poisoning. A venous blood lead level confirms it, and Safe Work Australia requires blood lead monitoring and removal from exposure at set levels.
notes: Ferritin detects iron deficiency, which does not explain basophilic stippling, colic or the paint-stripping exposure.
Electrophoresis looks for thalassaemia, which does not explain new colicky pain in a worker exposed to lead.
Porphobilinogen is raised in acute intermittent porphyria, but it is usually normal in lead poisoning, where ALA builds up instead.
An abdominal X-ray can show swallowed lead flakes in children, but it cannot measure body lead load or confirm poisoning.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had 3 days of progressive leg weakness and numbness. She has brisk lower limb reflexes, upgoing plantars, a T8 sensory level and a palpable bladder. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Upper motor neuron signs in the legs, a sensory level on the trunk and urinary retention mean an acute myelopathy. This is cord compression until proven otherwise. Urgent gadolinium MRI of the whole spine rules out compression and can show an inflammatory myelitis.
notes: CSF studies (oligoclonal bands, cell count) help confirm demyelination, but only after imaging has ruled out compression or a mass lesion.
Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerves and roots, which fit lower motor neuron signs such as Guillain-Barre syndrome, not brisk reflexes with a sensory level.
A T8 sensory level with upper motor neuron signs puts the lesion in the thoracic cord, so lumbosacral CT would miss it, and CT shows the cord poorly anyway.
A brain MRI can help with MS dissemination criteria, but it does not exclude cord compression or show the thoracic lesion causing her signs.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman has a dilatation and curettage for heavy menstrual bleeding. The scrub nurse notes yellow fatty tissue in the curettings. Afterwards she is stable with mild lower abdominal pain. Which complication must be excluded?
questions.why: There is no fat inside the uterus, so fat in the curettings means the curette has gone through the uterine wall and into omentum, mesentery or bowel fat. Bowel injury must then be excluded urgently with senior gynaecology review and usually laparoscopy, even if she looks stable. A missed bowel injury can show up days later as peritonitis.
notes: Intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) are a late complication of vigorous curettage and do not explain fat in the specimen.
A cervical tear causes vaginal bleeding during dilatation; it does not put fat in the curettings or cause intra-abdominal injury.
Endometritis is an infection that develops days later; it would not explain fat seen in the operating theatre.
Cervical stenosis is a long-term consequence of cervical surgery and has nothing to do with acute perforation.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 1 hour after sudden, severe, tearing chest pain that radiated between her shoulder blades while she was gardening. She fainted briefly when the pain began. She has hypertension and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Her medicines are perindopril and amlodipine. On arrival, her blood pressure is 168/94 mmHg in the left arm and 136/80 mmHg in the right arm, pulse is 104/min and SpO2 is 96% on room air. An early diastolic murmur is heard at the right sternal edge. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy and no ST elevation. CT angiography shows an intimal flap that starts just above the aortic valve and extends into the descending thoracic aorta, with a moderate high-attenuation pericardial effusion. Twenty minutes later she becomes pale and confused. Her blood pressure is 82/54 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, jugular venous pressure is raised 6 cm and her heart sounds are muffled. Two large-bore cannulas are in place and crossmatched blood is available. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Immediate open repair in the operating theatre
questions.why: This woman has an acute Stanford type A aortic dissection, because the flap starts in the ascending aorta. She now has the complication most likely to kill her: cardiac tamponade from bleeding into the pericardium. The high-attenuation (blood-density) pericardial effusion, low blood pressure, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and confusion are the Beck triad with shock. Type A dissection is a surgical emergency. When it is complicated by haemopericardium and shock, the 2024 ESC guidelines and the Heart Foundation/CSANZ guidance used in Australia say she should go straight to theatre for open replacement of the ascending aorta, with blood products given while she is moved. Draining the pericardium only fixes the tamponade, and the blood pressure it restores can make the aorta bleed again. Lowering the heart rate or blood pressure is wrong while she is hypotensive. Anticoagulants make the bleeding worse.
notes: Metoprolol is the anti-impulse drug used for a dissection with high blood pressure, but in tamponade and shock it removes the compensating tachycardia and can cause cardiac arrest.

Percutaneous pericardiocentesis raises the blood pressure, which can restart bleeding from the aorta into the pericardium, so it is kept for controlled, small-volume drainage only when theatre cannot be reached in time.
Endovascular stent-graft repair is used for complicated type B (descending) dissection and cannot treat a tear in the ascending aorta just above the valve that is bleeding into the pericardium.
Heparin speeds up bleeding into the pericardium and the false lumen; giving antithrombotics because of the low-grade suspicion of a coronary syndrome is a known harmful error in dissection.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man walks into his general practice without an appointment. He has had chest discomfort for 40 minutes. It began while he was gardening and has not eased with rest. He describes a heavy band across his chest that spreads to his neck and both shoulders, and he feels nauseated and clammy. For the past 2 weeks he has had similar but brief tightness when walking uphill, which settled within minutes of stopping. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension, and takes metformin and perindopril. He smoked for 35 years and stopped 2 years ago. He is pale and sweaty. Temperature is 36.6°C, pulse 92/min and regular, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg in both arms, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. The heart sounds are dual with no murmur, and the chest is clear. Both calves are soft and non-tender. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: This man has ongoing ischaemic-type chest pain at rest. The pain is heavy, spreads to the neck and shoulders, and comes with nausea and sweating. It follows 2 weeks of new exertional angina, and he has several risk factors: diabetes, hypertension and a long smoking history. This is a possible acute coronary syndrome. Australian guidelines (National Heart Foundation/CSANZ ACS guidelines, eTG Cardiovascular, and the ACSQHC Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard) say a 12-lead ECG should be recorded and read within 10 minutes of first medical contact. It is the single test that sorts the patient into the right pathway straight away. New ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads (or LBBB with ongoing symptoms) means STEMI. In that case, call 000 for ambulance transfer for primary PCI or fibrinolysis, and do not wait for any blood result. If the ECG does not show STEMI, the patient still needs urgent transfer for serial troponins. Equal arm pressures, no aortic regurgitation murmur, normal oxygen saturation and normal calves make aortic dissection and PE less likely, so the ECG comes first.
notes: Troponin may still be normal early in infarction and must never delay reperfusion, so it comes after the ECG and should not hold up transfer.
A chest radiograph does not diagnose acute coronary syndrome and would delay the test that decides immediate management.
A D-dimer is used for low-risk suspected pulmonary embolism, and this man has ischaemic-type pain with no PE risk factors, normal SpO2 and normal calves.
CT coronary angiography is for stable, low-to-intermediate-risk chest pain and is not appropriate for ongoing ischaemic pain at rest.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with 3 months of tiredness and breathlessness when climbing stairs at the café she manages. Her cycles are regular every 28 days. Over the past year her periods have lengthened to 7 days. On heavy days she changes a super pad every 2 hours, floods overnight and passes large clots. She has no bruising, nosebleeds or change in bowel habit. She and her partner stopped using condoms 2 months ago and hope to conceive within the next year. Her only medicine is folic acid 0.5 mg daily. Her blood pressure is 114/72 mmHg, pulse 98/min and temperature 36.7 °C. She has conjunctival pallor. Abdominal, speculum and bimanual examinations are normal.
