Investigations show: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115–165) MCV 71 fL (80–100) Platelets 438 x10^9/L (150–400) Ferritin 5 µg/L (30–300) CRP 3 mg/L (<5) TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4–4.0) Urine β-hCG negative Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral iron and a levonorgestrel intrauterine device
Oral iron and the combined oral contraceptive pill
Intravenous iron and tranexamic acid during menses
Oral iron and tranexamic acid during menses
Oral iron and referral for diagnostic hysteroscopy
questions.why: She has iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 92 g/L, MCV 71 fL, reactive thrombocytosis, ferritin 5 µg/L with a normal CRP) caused by heavy menstrual bleeding. Management must replace the deficit and treat the cause. Under eTG and the National Blood Authority guidance, oral iron is first line in a stable patient who has not yet tried it. Daily or alternate-day dosing works, and alternate-day dosing may improve absorption and tolerance. Recheck the FBC in 2 to 4 weeks (expect a rise of about 20 g/L by 3 to 4 weeks) and continue for about 3 months after the Hb normalises. The levonorgestrel IUD is usually first line for heavy menstrual bleeding (ACSQHC Clinical Care Standard), but it and the combined pill both prevent pregnancy, and she is trying to conceive. Tranexamic acid (1 g orally three to four times daily for up to 5 days during heavy bleeding) is a non-hormonal option. It reduces menstrual loss by about 40 to 50%, is taken only while bleeding and does not affect fertility. She has a normal pelvic examination and no risk factors for endometrial pathology, so invasive investigation is not needed yet. B: the LNG-IUD is contraceptive and does not suit a woman trying to conceive.
notes: Wrong: the levonorgestrel IUD is contraceptive, so it conflicts with her wish to conceive, even though it is often first line for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Wrong: the combined oral contraceptive pill suppresses ovulation and prevents the pregnancy she is trying for.
Wrong: intravenous iron is reserved for oral intolerance, failure, malabsorption or a need for rapid repletion, and she is stable and has not tried oral iron.
Wrong: hysteroscopy is not indicated in a 24-year-old with a normal pelvic examination, no endometrial risk factors and no failed medical treatment.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman comes to a rural emergency department with a racing heart and mild central chest tightness. Both started suddenly 70 minutes ago while she was watching television. She has never had this before. She has hypertension treated with perindopril and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Her pulse is 138/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air and temperature 36.7 °C. Her chest is clear and she has no peripheral oedema. A 12-lead ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 140/min, a narrow QRS and no ST-segment or T-wave change. Blood was taken on arrival, 75 minutes after symptom onset: high-sensitivity troponin T 9 ng/L (99th centile 14), creatinine 84 µmol/L (eGFR 66 mL/min/1.73 m^2), potassium 4.4 mmol/L and TSH 2.1 mIU/L (reference 0.4 to 4.0). Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of her troponin result?
options: Myocardial infarction cannot yet be ruled out at this point
Acute myocardial infarction is excluded by this single value
Rate-related type 2 myocardial infarction is confirmed
Chronic myocardial injury from renal impairment is shown
Unstable angina is excluded by this normal value
questions.why: Her high-sensitivity troponin T of 9 ng/L is below the 99th centile, but it was taken only 75 minutes after her symptoms began. Troponin takes time to rise after myocardial injury, so one value taken this soon can miss an evolving infarction. The NHFA/CSANZ ACS guideline accepts a single-sample rule-out only when the hs-troponin T is very low (below about 5 ng/L) and symptoms started more than 3 hours before the sample. Otherwise, the test is repeated using an accelerated protocol (usually at 2 hours, or at 1 hour with validated algorithms) and the change between the two values is assessed. Her chest tightness, age, hypertension and diabetes make ACS an important alternative cause and a possible trigger for her AF. So this result does not yet rule out myocardial infarction, and she needs a repeat troponin while her AF is rate-controlled. A: A value below the 99th centile does not rule out infarction when it is taken less than 3 hours after onset and is above the very-low threshold. C: A type 2 infarction needs troponin above the 99th centile with a rise or fall, and her value is normal.
notes: Correct: a single hs-troponin T below the 99th centile but above the very-low rule-out level, taken under 3 hours after onset, cannot rule out infarction, so a repeat is needed.
Wrong: a type 2 infarction needs troponin above the 99th centile with a rise or fall, and her value is normal.
Wrong: chronic myocardial injury means a stable troponin above the 99th centile, and her near-normal renal function does not explain any rise.
Wrong: troponin is normal in unstable angina by definition, so a normal value cannot exclude it.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, distension and repeated vomiting, which is now faeculent. She has passed no flatus for 24 hours. She has known gallstones and has never had abdominal surgery. Her medicines are perindopril, metformin and ibuprofen. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse is 108/min, blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg and respiratory rate is 16/min. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her abdomen is distended, with high-pitched bowel sounds and no peritonism. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated small bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels. Venous blood results: pH 7.43 (7.32 to 7.42) pCO2 46 mmHg (41 to 51) Bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22 to 28) Base excess +6 mmol/L (-2 to +2) Lactate 1.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0) Sodium 136 mmol/L (135 to 145) Potassium 2.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2) Chloride 93 mmol/L (95 to 110) Creatinine 128 µmol/L (her baseline is 78) Which of the following best describes these blood gas findings?
options: Respiratory acidosis with renal bicarbonate retention
Lactic acidosis from metformin and kidney injury
Normal anion gap acidosis from small bowel losses
Metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid and volume loss
Mixed high anion gap acidosis and alkalosis
questions.why: The pH is at the alkalaemic end, and bicarbonate (30 mmol/L) and base excess (+6) are both raised. That means the main problem is metabolic alkalosis. The low chloride (93 mmol/L) and low potassium (2.8 mmol/L) show it is hypochloraemic and hypokalaemic, the typical picture with vomiting. Losing gastric hydrochloric acid produces the alkalosis. Losing volume then keeps it going: it causes a prerenal acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.6 times her baseline) and switches on aldosterone, so the kidney holds on to bicarbonate and loses potassium. A venous pCO2 of 46 mmHg is within the normal range and fits mild respiratory compensation, not a primary respiratory problem. The anion gap is normal (136 - (93 + 30) = 13) and lactate is normal, so there is no hidden acidosis, although a normal lactate does not rule out bowel ischaemia. In practice she needs IV 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride, magnesium checked, and her perindopril, metformin and ibuprofen withheld.
notes: Wrong: a primary respiratory acidosis needs an acidaemic pH and a raised pCO2, but her pH is high and her venous pCO2 is normal, so the raised bicarbonate is the primary change.
Wrong: metformin and the kidney injury make this a tempting choice, but her lactate (1.8 mmol/L), anion gap (13) and pH are all normal, so there is no lactic acidosis.
Wrong: losing alkaline small bowel fluid can cause a normal anion gap acidosis, but her bicarbonate is raised and her pH is not acidaemic.
Wrong: with a normal anion gap of 13 and a normal lactate, there is no evidence of a second, high anion gap acidosis alongside the alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man diagnosed with HIV 8 months ago has had an undetectable viral load for 6 months on dolutegravir plus tenofovir-emtricitabine. He feels well and asks to stop treatment. Most likely result of stopping?
questions.why: ART suppresses HIV but does not cure it. Latent virus persists in reservoirs such as resting memory CD4 cells, so viral load usually rebounds within weeks of stopping. He then loses U=U protection and his CD4 count starts to fall again, so ASHM-endorsed guidance is to continue ART for life.
notes: An undetectable viral load does not clear the latent reservoir, so suppression lasting after ART stops is very rare and is not an expected outcome.
Once HIV infection is established, antibodies last for life and do not disappear when viral load is suppressed or ART is stopped.
Dolutegravir has a high genetic barrier, and stopping all three drugs together rarely selects resistance, so rebound of wild-type virus is the expected result.
CD4 counts fall over months to years after stopping, so rebound viraemia comes well before any AIDS-defining illness.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has an excisional biopsy of a changing pigmented lesion on his back. Histopathology shows superficial spreading melanoma, Breslow thickness 1.6 mm, without ulceration. His regional nodes are impalpable. Most appropriate addition to wide excision?
questions.why: A Breslow thickness of 1.6 mm without ulceration makes this a pT2a, clinically stage IB melanoma. Australian melanoma guidelines (Cancer Council) recommend discussing and offering sentinel node biopsy for melanomas thicker than 1 mm, because it gives accurate staging and prognosis. It is done at the same time as the wide excision.
notes: Routine imaging finds little in stage I-II melanoma with impalpable nodes, so PET-CT is not recommended at this stage.
Adjuvant immunotherapy is reserved for resected stage IIB-IV disease, and pT2a with no known nodal spread does not qualify.
Elective dissection of clinically negative nodes gives no survival benefit and causes significant morbidity such as lymphoedema.
Adjuvant radiotherapy is not used after excision of a thin, non-desmoplastic primary melanoma with clear margins.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has 8 weeks of neck pain radiating to the thumb despite physiotherapy. Elbow flexion weakness progressed to 3/5; biceps reflex is reduced. MRI shows concordant C5-6 foraminal stenosis. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Most cervical radiculopathy gets better with analgesia, physiotherapy and changes to activity. Here, though, there is a worsening objective motor deficit and a matching root compression on MRI, so she needs referral to a spinal surgeon to consider decompression.
notes: Oral steroids may ease radicular pain for a short time, but they do not deal with a fixed compression causing worsening weakness.
Conservative care alone is suitable only when there is no motor deficit, or the deficit is stable or improving, and her weakness is getting worse.
Clinical signs and MRI already agree on the diagnosis, so nerve studies would only delay the referral she needs.
A soft collar does not relieve root compression, and wearing one for a long time leads to stiffness and deconditioning.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites vomits 400 mL of fresh blood. His pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Endoscopy is being arranged. Which drug is most appropriate now?
questions.why: In cirrhosis, haematemesis should be treated as a variceal bleed until endoscopy shows otherwise. eTG and Baveno VII advise starting a vasoactive drug such as terlipressin (or octreotide) straight away, together with IV ceftriaxone, before band ligation within 12 hours. Terlipressin lowers portal pressure, which reduces bleeding and improves survival.
notes: In the HALT-IT trial, tranexamic acid did not reduce deaths from GI bleeding and it increased venous clots, so it is not recommended.
Non-selective beta-blockers prevent variceal bleeding, but they are withheld during an acute bleed with hypotension because they worsen shock.
Vitamin K does not correct the clotting problem of cirrhosis quickly or reliably, and it does nothing to lower portal pressure.
A diuretic would worsen low blood volume and kidney blood flow in a patient who is bleeding and in early shock.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has fever, headache and neck stiffness after a week of right earache. CSF shows 1900 x10^6/L polymorphs and Gram-positive diplococci. Dexamethasone and ceftriaxone have been given. Which drug should be added?
questions.why: Gram-positive diplococci in a neutrophilic CSF mean pneumococcal meningitis, here probably spreading from otitis media. eTG advises adding vancomycin to ceftriaxone until susceptibilities are known, because the organism may be resistant to ceftriaxone. Treatment is then narrowed once susceptibilities are known.
notes: Benzylpenicillin is used only after the isolate is shown to be penicillin-susceptible, so it is not a safe empirical addition.
Aciclovir treats HSV encephalitis, but a polymorph-rich CSF with visible organisms points to bacterial meningitis.
Amoxicillin is added for Listeria in adults over 50, pregnant or immunocompromised patients, and this man has none of these risks.
Meropenem is not recommended as empirical cover for pneumococcus, and ceftriaxone plus vancomycin is the eTG regimen.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man wakes with sudden right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. Audiometry shows a 40 dB sensorineural loss across four contiguous frequencies, and tympanometry is normal. Prednisolone is started. Most appropriate further investigation?
questions.why: Confirmed unilateral sudden sensorineural hearing loss needs gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma. MRI is still needed if hearing recovers with steroids, because recovery does not rule out a lesion.
notes: CT shows bony and middle ear disease well but can miss small soft-tissue lesions in the internal auditory canal, so it is not recommended routinely.
Carotid disease does not cause isolated sudden hearing loss, and the posterior circulation is not assessed this way.
A routine autoimmune screen is not recommended without features of systemic or bilateral progressive disease.
Auditory brainstem response is less sensitive than MRI for small tumours and is kept for patients who cannot have MRI.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain through to his back and collapsed briefly. BP is 78/50 mmHg and HR 124/min, with distended neck veins and an early diastolic murmur. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Tearing pain through to the back, syncope and aortic regurgitation suggest a type A aortic dissection. Hypotension with distended neck veins points to tamponade. In a patient this unstable, current guidelines (ESC 2024) recommend bedside echocardiography to look for pericardial fluid, an intimal flap and aortic regurgitation while cardiothoracic surgery is called, rather than sending him to the CT scanner.
notes: A widened mediastinum is neither sensitive nor specific, and a normal film does not rule out dissection, so it would only delay decisive care.
Pulmonary embolism fits poorly with tearing pain to the back and a diastolic murmur, and moving an unstable patient to CT for the wrong scan is unsafe.
Troponin can be raised in dissection and cannot diagnose or exclude it, and waiting for serial results wastes time in a surgical emergency.
D-dimer is not used to rule out dissection when clinical probability is high, and a raised result would not show tamponade or the type of dissection.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 3 days of tingling that started in her feet and has spread up to her waist. Over the same time her legs have become steadily weaker. Since this morning she has been unable to pass urine. She has had no back pain, fever, trauma or weight loss. Eighteen months ago she had 2 weeks of blurred vision and pain on moving her left eye, which got better without treatment. She takes no medicines. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 80 beats/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Cranial nerve and upper limb examination is normal. Tone is increased in both legs. Hip flexion and ankle dorsiflexion are 3/5 on the left and 4/5 on the right. Knee and ankle reflexes are brisk, and both plantar responses are extensor. Pinprick sensation is reduced below the umbilicus. A bladder scan shows 900 mL. Full blood count and C-reactive protein are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands
Nerve conduction studies of both lower limbs
Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine only
Urgent gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the whole spine
questions.why: Both legs are weak with spastic tone, brisk reflexes and extensor plantars, so this is an upper motor neuron lesion. The arms and cranial nerves are normal, and there is a sensory level at the umbilicus (T10) with urinary retention, so the lesion is in the thoracic spinal cord. An acute myelopathy with a sensory level and loss of bladder control is cord compression until proven otherwise. The next step is an urgent MRI of the whole spine with gadolinium. Imaging the whole spine matters because a sensory level only gives the lowest possible level of the lesion, and there can be lesions at more than one level. The same scan separates a compressive cause (disc, tumour, abscess, haematoma) from an inflammatory myelitis. Her past episode of painful vision loss suggests optic neuritis, so this may be a second demyelinating attack (multiple sclerosis). A brain MRI is usually done at the same time. CSF and antibody tests come after imaging has ruled out compression.
notes: CSF oligoclonal bands help confirm multiple sclerosis, but a lumbar puncture should not be done before imaging has ruled out cord compression, and it would delay the time-critical scan.

Nerve conduction studies look for a peripheral process such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, which causes floppy weakness with absent reflexes, not spastic weakness with brisk reflexes, extensor plantars and a truncal sensory level.
A lumbosacral scan only looks at the cauda equina and would miss the thoracic cord lesion suggested by upper motor neuron signs and a T10 sensory level.
Aquaporin-4 antibodies help tell neuromyelitis optica from multiple sclerosis, but the result takes days and does not rule out cord compression, so it is not the next investigation.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man is reviewed on the surgical ward at 08:00. He was admitted overnight with 26 hours of central abdominal pain that moved to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia and nausea. The emergency theatre list was full, so he is booked for laparoscopic appendicectomy this afternoon. He is fasting and receiving maintenance Hartmann's solution, and regular paracetamol is his only charted medicine. He has no past medical history and no allergies. His temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 90/min, blood pressure 128/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is tender at McBurney's point with localised guarding, and there is no generalised rigidity. White cell count is 14.1 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), neutrophils 11.6 x10^9/L (2.0–7.5), CRP 52 mg/L (<5) and creatinine 80 µmol/L (60–110). CT of the abdomen with contrast shows a 10 mm appendix with an enhancing wall and periappendiceal fat stranding, with no appendicolith, free gas or collection. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management while he awaits surgery?
options: Repeat CT scan with oral contrast today
Withhold opioid analgesia until surgical review
questions.why: This man has acute uncomplicated appendicitis. He has the classic migrating pain, McBurney's point tenderness, neutrophilia and a raised CRP, and his CT shows an inflamed appendix with no appendicolith, free gas or collection. He is stable and booked for appendicectomy, but there has already been a delay of many hours and he has had no antimicrobial cover. eTG (Antibiotic: Intra-abdominal infections, Appendicitis) advises starting empirical intravenous antibiotics when surgery for appendicitis is delayed. This treats the infection and lowers the risk of the appendix progressing to gangrene or perforation before theatre. Surgical prophylaxis is still given within 60 minutes before incision. The delay should also be flagged to the registrar. Percutaneous drainage is only for an appendiceal abscess, and he has none. Repeating the CT adds nothing, because the diagnosis is already confirmed. Treating him with antibiotics alone at home is not the standard for a patient who is booked for and agrees to surgery, and about 3 in 10 such patients need an appendicectomy within a year. Withholding pain relief is outdated: analgesia does not mask the signs of appendicitis or delay the diagnosis.
notes: Wrong: percutaneous drainage treats an appendiceal abscess or collection, and his CT shows neither.
Wrong: the contrast CT has already confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis, so another scan delays treatment and adds radiation without changing management.

Wrong: treating with antibiotics alone at home is an alternative only after a shared decision, and about 3 in 10 patients still need an appendicectomy within a year; he is booked for and agreeable to surgery, the standard treatment.
Wrong: giving opioid analgesia does not mask the signs of appendicitis or worsen diagnostic accuracy, so leaving him in pain is not appropriate.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has her fifth stereotyped left-sided throbbing headache, preceded by 20 minutes of zigzag lines. Examination is normal. Urine beta-hCG is negative with a valid control line. Most appropriate acute treatment?
questions.why: The valid negative pregnancy test shows she is not pregnant, so the treatment choice for her migraine attack is not restricted. eTG first-line acute treatment is aspirin or an NSAID taken early with metoclopramide, which helps absorption and treats nausea. A triptan is used if this fails.
notes: Codeine and other opioids are not recommended for migraine because they work poorly and carry a high risk of medication-overuse headache and dependence.
Ergotamine is no longer recommended because it is less effective than other options and its vasoconstriction is a concern in migraine with aura.
Metoclopramide is a sensible add-on, but oxycodone is an opioid, which is not recommended for migraine and promotes medication-overuse headache.
Tramadol is an opioid with no place in migraine treatment, and ondansetron does not have the prokinetic benefit of metoclopramide.

questions.stem: A 20-hour-old girl is reviewed on the postnatal ward because the midwife reports that she has stopped feeding and started grunting. She was born vaginally at 39+2 weeks, weighing 3.4 kg, with Apgar scores of 8 and 9. She fed well for the first 12 hours. Her mother carried group B streptococcus and received intravenous benzylpenicillin 90 minutes before the birth. The membranes had ruptured 22 hours before delivery, and the mother's temperature in labour was 38.4 °C. On examination, the baby is lethargic and mottled. Temperature is 38.3 °C, pulse 184/min, respirations 72/min, systolic pressure 55 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds. She has subcostal recession and grunting. Heart sounds are normal and the femoral pulses are palpable. Capillary glucose is 3.9 mmol/L. Intravenous access has been obtained, and antibiotics are about to be given. Which of the following investigations is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: This term baby has early-onset neonatal sepsis with shock. She has a fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, grunting, a capillary refill time of 4 seconds, mottling and lethargy. She also has four risk factors: maternal GBS carriage, intrapartum antibiotics given less than 4 hours before birth, membranes ruptured for 18 hours or more, and maternal fever in labour. A positive blood culture is the reference standard for confirming early-onset sepsis. It identifies the organism (most often GBS or E. coli) and its antibiotic sensitivities. Under the RCH Neonatal antimicrobial guidelines and Queensland Clinical Guidelines, at least 1 mL is taken before the first doses of benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, but antibiotics are not delayed to get it. The culture result and the baby's condition are then used to review antibiotics at 36 hours. CRP and procalcitonin are nonspecific markers that can support the diagnosis but cannot confirm it. Urine culture has little value in early-onset sepsis. A chest X-ray shows lung involvement but does not show what organism is causing it.
notes: CRP takes 12 to 24 hours to rise and can be raised by non-infectious causes, so it helps to monitor or rule out infection but cannot confirm sepsis.
Procalcitonin rises normally in the first 48 hours of life, and it is not a confirmatory test in Australian neonatal sepsis guidelines.
Early-onset sepsis comes from maternal flora at birth, not from the urinary tract, so urine culture is not recommended in the first 72 hours and would rarely be positive.
A chest X-ray may show pneumonia, but GBS pneumonia can look the same as surfactant deficiency or transient tachypnoea, and the film cannot identify an organism.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman who works as a hairdresser sees her general practitioner with 10 weeks of right neck pain. The pain runs down the back of her arm to her middle finger and is worse when she looks up. Eight weeks ago she started regular paracetamol and ibuprofen and a supervised physiotherapy program. The pain has eased only a little, and she still drops her hair dryer. She has no hand clumsiness, change in gait or bladder symptoms. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine. Temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 74/min and regular, and blood pressure 134/80 mmHg. Right elbow extension and wrist flexion are 4-/5, the same as 8 weeks ago, and the right triceps reflex is reduced. Sensation is reduced over the right middle finger. Tone, coordination and the lower limb examination are normal, and Hoffmann's sign is absent. MRI of the neck shows severe right C6-7 foraminal stenosis compressing the right C7 nerve root, with a normal cord. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day transfer to an emergency department
Outpatient referral to a spine surgeon
questions.why: This is a right C7 radiculopathy from cervical spondylosis. The radicular pain runs to the middle finger and gets worse on neck extension. There is weakness of elbow extension and wrist flexion, a reduced triceps reflex and C7 sensory loss, and the MRI shows concordant C6-7 foraminal stenosis. Most cervical radiculopathy settles with analgesia, physiotherapy and modified activity. This patient has had 8 weeks of conservative treatment and still has an objective motor deficit, a matching MRI lesion and pain that limits her work. That combination warrants referral to a spine surgeon to assess her for decompression. Urgent assessment is not needed: there are no myelopathic symptoms, no upper motor neuron signs, her weakness is not getting worse and the cord is normal. She still needs safety netting to seek urgent review if weakness progresses, or if hand clumsiness, gait disturbance or bladder symptoms develop. Continuing physiotherapy alone delays treatment of a persisting motor deficit. Transfer to the emergency department is for myelopathy or rapidly progressive weakness. Carotid imaging investigates a TIA, which this fixed lower motor neuron deficit with radicular pain is not.
notes: Continuing physiotherapy alone and waiting 3 more months is wrong because she still has an objective motor deficit with a matching MRI lesion after 8 weeks of conservative care, so she needs a surgical opinion now.

Same-day emergency transfer is for suspected cord compression, myelopathy or rapidly progressive weakness, and she has none of these: there are no upper motor neuron signs, the cord is normal and her deficit is stable.
Carotid duplex ultrasonography is part of the workup for a TIA, but she has a fixed lower motor neuron deficit in one root pattern with radicular pain, not transient episodes of focal weakness.
Immobilising the neck in a rigid collar for weeks has no proven benefit in cervical radiculopathy and causes stiffness and muscle deconditioning.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with ISUP Grade Group 3 prostate cancer, localised on PSMA PET/CT, chooses robotic radical prostatectomy. He is sexually active and fully continent. Most common long-term adverse effect to counsel about?
questions.why: Erectile dysfunction is the most common long-term adverse effect of radical prostatectomy, even with nerve sparing, and age over 65 makes lasting loss of erections more likely. Australian prostate cancer guidance says this risk should be discussed before he consents, along with penile rehabilitation options.
notes: Urinary leakage is common early on, but most men regain continence within a year, so lasting incontinence affects only a minority.
Radiation proctitis follows external beam radiotherapy, not surgery.
Bladder neck contracture does occur after prostatectomy but is uncommon, especially after robotic surgery.
Hot flushes come from androgen deprivation therapy, which is not part of surgery alone for intermediate-risk disease.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy was hit in the mouth by a cricket ball 10 minutes ago. His permanent upper central incisor is on the grass, intact. He is alert and cooperative. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: For an avulsed permanent tooth in a cooperative child, replant it immediately at the scene. Hold it by the crown, rinse it for a few seconds in milk, saline or cold water, put it back in the socket, and have him bite on gauze. Then arrange urgent dental splinting and check his tetanus status. Survival of the periodontal ligament cells drops quickly once the tooth has been out of the mouth for more than about 60 minutes, so every minute counts.
notes: Milk is the right storage medium only when the tooth cannot be replanted, and transport wastes time when replanting at the scene is possible.
Scrubbing the root destroys the periodontal ligament cells and leads to the root being resorbed or fusing with the bone.
Water is hypotonic, so it makes the ligament cells swell and burst, which makes it a poor storage medium.
Waiting until tomorrow means a long dry time out of the mouth, which kills the ligament cells, so the replanted tooth is unlikely to survive.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is anaesthetised for laparoscopy. Her consent form does not mention students. The registrar asks the medical student to perform a pelvic examination. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: An intimate examination of an anaesthetised patient for teaching needs her prior, specific and informed consent, so without it the student should politely decline. If needed, the student can raise the concern later with a supervisor or placement coordinator. Supervision, telling her afterwards or asking a relative cannot replace her own consent.
notes: Supervision makes sure the examination is done competently, but it does not make up for the missing consent.
Telling her afterwards is disclosure, not consent, and the examination would still have been done without her permission.
A spouse cannot consent for a competent adult who will soon be able to decide for herself, and this examination is not urgent or needed for her treatment.
Going straight to Ahpra is out of proportion as a first step; the immediate priority is to decline, then raise the concern through local supervisors.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old girl presents with vomiting and irritability. Her father says she rolled off a couch yesterday. Coagulation studies are normal. CT brain shows bilateral subdural haematomas of differing densities. Most likely cause?
questions.why: Bilateral subdural haematomas of different densities point to bleeds of different ages. That means repeated injury, which a single short fall cannot explain, so this is abusive head trauma. The doctor must make a mandatory report to child protection and arrange an ophthalmology review for retinal haemorrhages and a skeletal survey.
notes: A short fall from a couch rarely causes bilateral subdural haematomas, and it cannot explain bleeds of different ages.
Subdural bleeds from birth usually clear within the first one to three months and would not look new at 4 months.
Glutaric aciduria usually comes with a large head and widened Sylvian fissures, and it is a rare diagnosis made only once abuse has been ruled out.
Normal coagulation studies make a bleeding disorder such as vitamin K deficiency unlikely.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman attends for preconception advice. She was treated for chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease twice, at ages 19 and 22. Pelvic examination today is normal. Which pregnancy complication is she at most increased risk of?
questions.why: Pelvic inflammatory disease scars the fallopian tubes and damages the cilia, and the risk goes up with each episode. This makes ectopic pregnancy (and tubal infertility) the main reproductive risk. She should be told to have an early pregnancy test and an early ultrasound to confirm where the pregnancy is, and to get help urgently if she has pain or bleeding.
notes: Placenta praevia is linked to previous caesarean section, multiparity and assisted reproduction, not to tubal scarring after PID.
Pre-eclampsia is linked to first pregnancy, chronic hypertension, renal disease and antiphospholipid syndrome, not to past PID.
Gestational diabetes is linked to obesity, ethnicity, family history and previous GDM, not to past pelvic infection.
Placental abruption is linked to hypertension, smoking, cocaine use and trauma, not to past tubal infection.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old intern confides that she has written herself temazepam prescriptions for insomnia after night shifts for three months. She has no general practitioner. Most appropriate advice?
questions.why: The Medical Board of Australia's Code of Conduct says doctors should have their own GP and should not prescribe for themselves, especially drugs of dependence. Self-prescribing a benzodiazepine risks dependence, impairment and undiagnosed mental illness. An independent GP can assess the cause of her insomnia and manage it safely.
notes: Changing to another self-prescribed drug still leaves her treating herself, and the cause of her insomnia goes unassessed.
An informal script from a colleague skips a proper assessment and continuity of care, which the Code of Conduct also discourages.
Tapering is reasonable but should be supervised by her treating doctor, not run by herself.
Changing her roster deals with a work factor but leaves the unsafe self-prescribing and any underlying problem unaddressed.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has had left iliac fossa pain for 3 days and a temperature of 38.4 °C. He has left iliac fossa tenderness with guarding, and his CRP is 140 mg/L. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Suspected acute diverticulitis with localised peritonism needs CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast. CT confirms the diagnosis and shows complications such as abscess or perforation, which guide whether he needs antibiotics, drainage or surgery. Colonoscopy waits about 6 weeks, once the inflammation has settled, to exclude cancer.
notes: Colonoscopy during acute inflammation risks perforation, so it is deferred for about 6 weeks after recovery.
Ultrasound depends on the operator, is limited by bowel gas, and stages complications such as abscess or free air less reliably than CT.
An erect chest X-ray can show free air under the diaphragm but cannot confirm diverticulitis or find an abscess, and CT detects free air better.
A contrast enema during acute inflammation adds risk and shows less than CT, because it cannot show what is happening outside the bowel wall.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department of a regional hospital. She has had 2 days of colicky periumbilical pain and bilious vomiting, and she has passed no flatus. She has had two caesarean sections and an open appendicectomy. Adhesive small bowel obstruction is diagnosed. She is treated with nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids with added potassium. Eight hours later her pain is constant and severe despite intravenous morphine. Temperature is 38.1°C, pulse 126/min, blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg and respirations 22/min. The abdomen is distended, with localised tenderness and guarding in the right lower quadrant, and bowel sounds are reduced. Nasogastric output so far is 1.4 L. Leukocyte count is 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0). Venous lactate is 1.5 mmol/L (less than 2.0). CT of the abdomen with intravenous contrast shows a closed loop of small bowel with reduced wall enhancement and fluid in the mesentery. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: The most serious risk in adhesive small bowel obstruction is strangulation, where the bowel loses its blood supply and dies. This patient has the warning signs. Her pain has changed from colicky to constant and is not controlled by morphine. She has a fever, a rising heart rate, localised guarding and a raised white cell count. CT shows a closed loop with reduced wall enhancement and fluid in the mesentery. The WSES Bologna guidelines say that strangulation, a closed loop, peritonitis or ischaemia on CT are reasons to stop non-operative management and operate straight away. This lets the surgeon release the bowel and remove any dead segment before it perforates and causes sepsis. Lactate often rises only once bowel has already died, so a normal value does not exclude ischaemia and should not delay the operation. In a regional hospital this means calling the surgeon now and, if no one there can operate, arranging urgent transfer. Resuscitation and antibiotics should continue while this happens.
notes: A water-soluble contrast challenge is used to predict which uncomplicated obstructions will settle without an operation, and it is not appropriate when CT shows strangulation.
Lactate rises late in bowel ischaemia, so waiting for a repeat value delays the operation while more bowel dies.
Conservative management for up to 72 hours is only for uncomplicated adhesive obstruction without signs of ischaemia, and continuing it here risks perforation.
Colonoscopic decompression treats large bowel problems such as sigmoid volvulus or pseudo-obstruction and cannot reach or relieve an obstructed small bowel loop.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has right face and arm weakness and aphasia that began 90 minutes ago. She took apixaban 3 hours ago. CT shows no haemorrhage; CT angiography shows left M1 occlusion. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She took apixaban within the last 48 hours and has no drug level showing it has worn off, so thrombolysis is contraindicated. Taking an anticoagulant does not rule out clot retrieval, and the Australian and New Zealand stroke guidelines recommend urgent endovascular thrombectomy for a proximal large vessel occlusion such as M1.
notes: Taking apixaban 3 hours ago, with no apixaban-calibrated anti-Xa level showing no effect, contraindicates thrombolysis.
Idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran, so it has no effect on apixaban and does not make thrombolysis safe.
Antiplatelet therapy is delayed until reperfusion is complete and is started after a swallow screen; it does not treat a large vessel occlusion.
Urgent heparin in acute ischaemic stroke raises the risk of haemorrhage without improving outcome, and it delays reperfusion.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 2 days after a day-surgery hysteroscopy and dilatation and curettage for heavy, irregular bleeding. Since yesterday evening she has had worsening lower abdominal pain, nausea and anorexia. The operation record describes a retroverted, bulky uterus and a view partly obscured by blood, and lists the procedure as uneventful. The histology report, released this morning, describes disordered proliferative endometrium with fragments of mature adipose tissue. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and her body mass index is 42 kg/m2. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 97% on room air. The lower abdomen is tender with voluntary guarding but no rigidity, and bowel sounds are reduced. There is scant brown vaginal loss. White cell count is 15.6 x 10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C-reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5) and lactate 1.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0). Fluids, analgesia and antibiotics have been started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
MRI of the pelvis with gadolinium
questions.why: There should be no fat inside the uterus. Adipose tissue in the curettings means the curette went through the uterine wall into omentum, mesentery or bowel fat, so this is uterine perforation until proven otherwise. A perforation like this can injure bowel without anyone noticing, and the injury often shows itself days later. That fits this patient: fever, lower abdominal guarding, reduced bowel sounds and high inflammatory markers 2 days after surgery. She is haemodynamically stable, her lactate is normal and she has no generalised peritonitis, so there is time to image her before deciding on surgery. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the best test here. It can show free fluid, free gas, a collection or abscess, bowel wall thickening or a leak, and bleeding, and it is not limited by her body habitus. A senior gynaecologist and the general surgeons should be told now. If the CT shows a visceral injury, or if she deteriorates, she needs laparoscopy or laparotomy. Erect chest X-ray: free gas under the diaphragm is not reliable after recent uterine instrumentation, and the film shows nothing about the pelvis, collections or bowel.
notes: Free gas can enter the peritoneum through a uterine perforation during hysteroscopy, so finding it does not tell you the bowel is injured, and the film cannot show collections or pelvic disease.
With a body mass index of 42 the views are limited, and ultrasound cannot reliably find bowel injury, free gas or collections higher in the abdomen.
MRI is slow and less available as an emergency test, covers only the pelvis and is poor at showing free gas or a bowel leak in a febrile, acutely unwell patient.
She has no chest symptoms and normal oxygen saturation, and her fever, tachycardia and lower abdominal guarding point to an intra-abdominal source rather than pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: A 12-hour-old term boy is grunting and floppy. His mother was GBS positive and febrile in labour. Temperature 38.3 °C, heart rate 186/min, capillary refill 4 seconds. Most appropriate investigation before antibiotics?
questions.why: This baby has suspected early-onset sepsis with shock, most likely from Group B streptococcus. Under the RCH neonatal guidelines, a blood culture (at least 1 mL) is taken before benzylpenicillin and gentamicin are started, and it is the test that confirms the diagnosis. Other investigations must not delay antibiotics.
notes: CRP takes 12 to 24 hours to rise, so a normal value this early does not exclude sepsis, and it cannot confirm infection.
A lumbar puncture is deferred in a baby with shock and must not delay antibiotics; it is done once the baby is stable.
Early-onset sepsis reaches the baby from the mother and spreads through the blood, so urine culture has a low yield in the first 72 hours.
A chest X-ray may show pneumonia but cannot identify the organism or confirm sepsis, and it does not need to come before antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman comes to a metropolitan emergency department 2 hours after sudden sharp left-sided chest pain began. The pain is worse on deep inspiration, and she is short of breath. Her left calf has been swollen and aching for 3 days. Five days ago she flew from Los Angeles to Sydney. She takes oral oestradiol for menopausal symptoms and smokes. She has no history of bleeding, peptic ulcer or stroke. Temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 114/min, blood pressure 128/82 mm Hg, respirations 26/min and SpO2 93% on room air. Her left calf is swollen and tender. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia only. hs-troponin I is 4 ng/L (99th percentile for women, 16 ng/L), haemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L and creatinine 70 µmol/L. A CT pulmonary angiogram shows filling defects in the left lower lobe segmental and subsegmental arteries and in a right middle lobe segmental artery. The RV to LV diameter ratio is 0.8, with no septal bowing and no contrast reflux into the hepatic veins. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge home with apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily
Catheter-directed thrombolysis of the pulmonary arteries
Insertion of an inferior vena cava filter
Admission and apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily
questions.why: The CT pulmonary angiogram shows emboli in both lungs. However, it shows no right ventricular strain: the RV to LV ratio is below 1, and there is no septal bowing or contrast reflux. She also has a normal blood pressure and a normal hs-troponin. So this is not high-risk (massive) PE, and clots in both lungs alone do not justify thrombolysis. Her pulse of 114/min (at least 110) gives her an sPESI score of 1. She is therefore not low risk. She has intermediate-low risk PE, which needs hospital admission for monitoring, not outpatient care. Her bleeding history, platelets and renal function are reassuring. The THANZ guideline and eTG recommend starting a direct oral anticoagulant, such as apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days and then 5 mg twice daily, for at least 3 months for provoked VTE. Her oestrogen should be stopped.
notes: Outpatient treatment is only for low-risk PE with an sPESI of 0, and her pulse of 114/min gives her an sPESI of 1.
Systemic thrombolysis is for high-risk PE with sustained hypotension or shock, and she is normotensive with no RV strain.
Catheter-directed therapy is for high-risk PE when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed, or for intermediate-high risk PE that is getting worse, and neither applies to her.
An IVC filter is used only when anticoagulation is contraindicated or has failed, and she has no bleeding risk factors.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman on apixaban struck her head in a fall four days ago. CT shows a left subdural haematoma; GCS has fallen from 15 to 13. INR is 1.1. Most appropriate reversal agent?
questions.why: This is an intracranial bleed on apixaban, and her GCS is falling. The urgent priority is to reverse the factor Xa inhibition so the haematoma stops expanding and she does not herniate. eTG recommends prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF, about 50 units/kg IV) with haematology advice, or andexanet alfa where it is available. A normal INR does not rule out apixaban effect.
notes: Vitamin K reverses warfarin by restoring vitamin K-dependent factor synthesis, but it has no effect on a direct factor Xa inhibitor.
Fresh frozen plasma needs a large volume, takes time to thaw, and does not reliably reverse apixaban.
Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody that reverses dabigatran only, not factor Xa inhibitors.
Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin (and partly enoxaparin) and has no effect on apixaban.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has episodic right upper quadrant pain and is afebrile. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a 9 mm common bile duct without visible stone; bilirubin is 42 µmol/L. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: She has gallstones, a dilated common bile duct and raised bilirubin, but no cholangitis and no duct stone seen on ultrasound. That puts her at intermediate risk of a common bile duct stone. MRCP is the non-invasive test of choice to confirm or exclude the stone before deciding on ERCP or cholecystectomy.
notes: ERCP is used to treat high-risk patients (cholangitis, a stone seen on imaging, or very high bilirubin) and carries a risk of pancreatitis, so it is not the first diagnostic test.
A HIDA scan looks for cystic duct blockage in suspected acute cholecystitis and cannot show the anatomy of a duct stone.
CT often misses stones that do not contain calcium and is less sensitive than MRCP for common bile duct stones.
A plain abdominal X-ray shows few gallstones and cannot assess the common bile duct.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old baker has had six months of wheeze and chest tightness. It gets worse during work shifts and settles on holidays. Spirometry shows reversible airflow obstruction. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Spirometry has already confirmed asthma, and the symptoms improve away from work, which suggests occupational asthma such as baker's asthma. The next step is to show the link to work objectively. This is done with serial peak flow readings, taken several times a day for about 3 to 4 weeks, both at work and away from it. Confirming the diagnosis matters because it drives decisions about removing the worker from exposure and about workers' compensation.
notes: A raised flour-specific IgE shows sensitisation only, which is common in exposed workers, and it does not prove that the asthma is caused by work.
Methacholine challenge shows airway hyperresponsiveness, but reversible obstruction has already confirmed asthma, and a single test cannot show a link to work.
Exhaled nitric oxide shows eosinophilic airway inflammation but cannot tell occupational asthma from asthma that is not related to work.
A chest X-ray is usually normal in asthma and does not help confirm an occupational cause.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old truck driver dozes at traffic lights. Polysomnography shows an apnoea–hypopnoea index of 48/hour; Epworth score is 17. He is untreated. What does this result mean for his driving?
questions.why: He has severe obstructive sleep apnoea (AHI over 30/hour) with excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth over 16), and he is already dozing at the wheel, so he meets neither the commercial nor the private standard in Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive. He should be told not to drive and that he must tell the licensing authority. A conditional licence can be considered only once treatment such as CPAP is shown to work and he sticks to it.
notes: Annual review applies to a conditional licence after treatment works, not to an untreated driver who is falling asleep.
Untreated sleep apnoea with excessive sleepiness also fails the private vehicle standard, so a lower licence class does not make driving safe.
Austroads has no daytime-only exemption for sleepiness, and he is already dozing at traffic lights in the day.
He is unfit now, while waiting for specialist review, because the result already shows a serious crash risk.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has 3 months of fatigue and heavy periods. Pulse is 84/min and blood pressure 118/72 mmHg. Haemoglobin is 88 g/L, MCV 67 fL and ferritin 5 µg/L. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She is stable, and her iron deficiency anaemia is explained by heavy menstrual bleeding. eTG recommends oral iron first line, which can be given on alternate days, alongside treatment of the heavy bleeding. Recheck the FBC and iron studies in 2 to 6 weeks.
notes: IV iron is for patients who cannot tolerate oral iron, do not respond to it, have malabsorption or need rapid repletion, and none of these applies yet.
Transfusion is not needed for a haemodynamically stable young woman with chronic anaemia at Hb 88 g/L.
Endoscopy is not first line for a 23-year-old with no GI symptoms whose heavy periods explain the loss; it is for those who do not respond.
Haemoglobin studies for thalassaemia trait are for persistent microcytosis once iron is replete, and a ferritin of 5 already confirms iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and bone pain is started on modified-release oxycodone 10 mg twice daily. His bowels currently open daily without difficulty. Which adverse effect most needs prophylaxis?
questions.why: Opioid-induced constipation affects nearly all patients on regular opioids, and tolerance does not develop to it. Australian palliative care guidance (eTG) therefore advises starting a regular laxative, such as a stimulant with a softener or macrogol, at the same time as the opioid. The other adverse effects are less common, or tolerance to them develops.
notes: Nausea usually settles within about a week as tolerance develops, so it is treated if it occurs and is not routinely prevented.
Respiratory depression is rare when opioids are started at a low dose and titrated in patients with pain, because pain counteracts it.
Sedation is usually mild and fades within a few days as tolerance develops.
Urinary retention is an uncommon opioid effect and does not need routine prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old Aboriginal man from Arnhem Land with type 2 diabetes presents in February with fever, productive cough and confusion. Temperature is 39.2 °C; chest X-ray shows right upper lobe consolidation. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: This is wet-season pneumonia with sepsis in a man with diabetes from the Top End, so melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei) is the leading diagnosis. Culture of the organism confirms it. Take blood cultures, plus sputum, urine and throat swabs, before starting meropenem, as eTG and NT guidelines advise.
notes: Serology has poor sensitivity, and many people in endemic areas already have antibodies, so it cannot confirm acute melioidosis.
A Gram stain may show gram-negative bacilli with a safety-pin look, but it cannot identify the species or confirm the diagnosis.
The Legionella urinary antigen test detects only L. pneumophila serogroup 1, so it cannot confirm the most likely pathogen here.
CT shows how far the lung disease has spread, but imaging cannot identify the organism causing it.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden severe breathlessness that began overnight. For 3 weeks he has needed three pillows to sleep, and his ankles have become swollen. He had an anterior myocardial infarction treated with a stent 9 years ago, and he has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. He has had no cardiac imaging since the infarct. On arrival, pulse is 112/min, blood pressure 178/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min and SpO2 86% on room air. His jugular venous pressure is raised, there is a third heart sound, crackles reach the mid-zones and there is pitting oedema to the shins. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with Q waves in V1 to V4, unchanged from 2 years ago. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines and small bilateral pleural effusions. NT-proBNP is 5800 ng/L. hs-troponin I is 42 ng/L, and 45 ng/L 3 hours later (99th percentile below 34 ng/L). He improves with non-invasive ventilation, glyceryl trinitrate and IV furosemide. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation to establish the underlying diagnosis?
questions.why: This man has acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, which is acute decompensated heart failure. The supporting findings are orthopnoea, leg oedema, a raised JVP, an S3, a chest X-ray showing oedema and effusions, and an NT-proBNP well above the rule-in threshold for his age. His old anterior infarct points to an ischaemic cardiomyopathy. The 2018 NHFA/CSANZ heart failure guideline recommends transthoracic echocardiography for every patient with suspected heart failure. It confirms the structural or functional cardiac cause. It measures LVEF, which separates HFrEF from HFpEF and decides which disease-modifying drugs to use. It also shows regional wall motion abnormalities, valve disease, filling pressures and pulmonary pressures. It is non-invasive and can be done at the bedside once he is stable. The troponin is raised but nearly flat (42 then 45 ng/L) with an unchanged ECG. That pattern fits myocardial injury from heart failure, not an acute MI. Bilateral effusions with pulmonary oedema are expected transudates that settle with diuresis.
notes: Coronary angiography is not the next test: the troponin is flat and the ECG is unchanged, so there is no acute coronary syndrome needing urgent invasive assessment, and angiography does not define ventricular function or the type of heart failure.
CT pulmonary angiography is not indicated: heart failure explains the whole picture, the leg swelling is bilateral, and IV contrast adds risk without addressing the likely diagnosis.

Diagnostic pleural aspiration is not needed: small bilateral effusions with pulmonary oedema in heart failure are presumed transudates and are managed with diuresis, with aspiration kept for atypical, unilateral or non-resolving effusions.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is a second-line test, used when echocardiography images are inadequate or a specific cardiomyopathy needs characterising, and it is not the first investigation.

questions.stem: A term newborn boy is delivered by emergency caesarean for fetal distress. After drying and stimulation at 30 seconds, he is apnoeic and floppy, with a heart rate of 80/min. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Under the ANZCOR neonatal resuscitation guideline, a newborn who is still apnoeic or has a heart rate below 100/min after drying and stimulation needs positive pressure ventilation, started in air for a term baby. Most newborn bradycardia comes from poor breathing, so good ventilation is the key step that brings the heart rate back up.
notes: Bag-mask ventilation is right because an apnoeic newborn with a heart rate under 100/min after initial steps needs positive pressure ventilation within the first minute.
Free-flow oxygen does not help a baby who is not breathing, because it gives no ventilation, and term resuscitation starts in air.
Adrenaline is only for a heart rate below 60/min despite effective ventilation and compressions.
Routine tracheal suctioning is not advised and delays ventilation; it is only for a blocked airway.

questions.stem: A fit 68-year-old man has an impalpable prostate cancer. His PSA is 8.6 ng/mL and biopsy shows Gleason 4+3=7 in five left cores. PSMA PET/CT shows no nodal or distant disease. Most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Gleason 4+3=7 (ISUP Grade Group 3) is unfavourable intermediate-risk disease, and PSMA PET/CT has shown it is localised. A fit man with a long life expectancy should be offered curative treatment, either radical prostatectomy or external beam radiotherapy with short-course androgen deprivation.
notes: Active surveillance is for low-risk disease (Grade Group 1, or selected low-volume Grade Group 2), not for predominant pattern 4 disease.
Watchful waiting suits men with limited life expectancy or serious comorbidity, and he is fit.
Androgen deprivation alone does not cure the cancer and is used for metastatic disease or men unfit for local treatment.
Docetaxel is used for metastatic disease, and PSMA PET/CT has shown no spread.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with breast cancer and extensive liver metastases has early satiety, bloating and large vomits of undigested food after meals. Abdomen soft; bowels open daily, no colic. Which antiemetic is most appropriate?
questions.why: Early satiety, fullness and large vomits of undigested food point to gastric stasis, here from a stomach squashed by hepatomegaly. A prokinetic is first line. Metoclopramide is safe because nothing suggests complete bowel obstruction: the bowels are open and there is no colic.
notes: Haloperidol is the choice for chemical or metabolic causes of nausea, such as opioids or hypercalcaemia, and does not improve gastric emptying.
Cyclizine is an anticholinergic antihistamine best for vestibular or raised intracranial pressure nausea, and its anticholinergic effect can make gastric stasis worse.
Ondansetron is mainly used for chemotherapy- and radiotherapy-related nausea, does not help gastric emptying, and causes constipation.
Hyoscine butylbromide reduces gut movement and secretions, which suits colicky malignant bowel obstruction but would make gastric stasis worse.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man woke yesterday with hearing loss and tinnitus in his right ear. Otoscopy is normal, Weber lateralises left, and audiometry shows a 40 dB right sensorineural loss. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Sudden one-sided sensorineural hearing loss that began within the last 72 hours is a time-critical emergency. Start high-dose oral corticosteroids promptly and contact ENT the same day, then arrange an MRI of the internal auditory canals to exclude a retrocochlear lesion.
notes: Guidelines advise against routine antivirals for sudden sensorineural hearing loss, as they add no benefit over steroids alone.
Normal otoscopy rules out wax, and the loss is sensorineural rather than conductive, so microsuction will not help.
Nothing suggests a bacterial infection: otoscopy is normal and there is no middle ear effusion.
Intranasal steroids treat Eustachian tube dysfunction, which causes a conductive loss, and this is a sensorineural loss.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man has fatigue and arthralgia of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints. Fasting transferrin saturation is 68% and ferritin 950 µg/L. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A raised fasting transferrin saturation (above 45%) together with a high ferritin points to hereditary haemochromatosis. Arthropathy of the second and third MCP joints is a classic sign. HFE genotyping for C282Y homozygosity is the next test to confirm the diagnosis, and it is Medicare-rebated when iron studies are abnormal.
notes: Liver biopsy is now used mainly to stage fibrosis when ferritin is above 1000 µg/L or liver enzymes are raised, not as the first confirmatory test.
MRI iron quantification is useful when genotyping is negative or to measure iron load, but it is not the first test to establish the diagnosis.
Caeruloplasmin is used to investigate Wilson disease, which causes copper overload, not a high transferrin saturation with high ferritin.
Bone marrow iron staining assesses iron stores in anaemia and does not diagnose hereditary iron overload.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has an excisional biopsy of a changing pigmented lesion on his back. Histopathology shows invasive melanoma, Breslow thickness 3.2 mm, with clear deep margin. Recommended wide excision margin?
questions.why: Breslow thickness sets the wide excision margin for primary melanoma. In the Australian Cancer Council guidelines, melanoma thicker than 2 mm needs a 2 cm clinical margin. A tumour this thick also calls for a discussion about sentinel lymph node biopsy.
notes: A 2 mm margin is the margin used for the first diagnostic excisional biopsy, not for definitive treatment of invasive melanoma.
A 5 mm margin is recommended for melanoma in situ, not for a tumour 3.2 mm thick.
A 1 cm margin is for melanoma up to 1 mm thick, so it is too narrow here.
Margins wider than 2 cm do not improve survival and only add morbidity, so 4 cm is not recommended.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 12 years, taking metformin, has five months of symmetrical burning and numbness in both feet. Ankle reflexes are absent; plantars are flexor. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Symmetrical distal sensory loss with absent ankle reflexes in a person with diabetes is typical of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Before accepting that diagnosis, treatable mimics should be excluded. Long-term metformin can cause vitamin B12 deficiency, so serum B12 is the key next test, alongside TSH and other screening bloods.
notes: Nerve conduction studies are kept for atypical cases, such as asymmetry, rapid progression or marked weakness, and are not needed for a typical length-dependent pattern.
Creatine kinase helps assess a myopathy, which causes proximal weakness rather than distal sensory loss and burning pain.
Lumbar spine imaging fits radicular or cauda equina symptoms, not a symmetrical stocking pattern without back pain or sphincter symptoms.
Antinuclear antibodies are not a routine screen for distal symmetrical neuropathy, and there are no features suggesting a connective tissue disease.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man has clinic blood pressure 152/94 mmHg on repeated readings. His home diary averages 123/77 mmHg: single evening readings, mostly after coffee, on an unvalidated device. No end-organ damage. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: His home diary suggests white coat hypertension, but the protocol is not valid: one reading per session, evenings only, after caffeine, on an unvalidated device. So it can neither confirm nor exclude hypertension. With grade 1 clinic readings and no end-organ damage, the Heart Foundation advises confirming the diagnosis out of the office, ideally with 24-hour ABPM, before labelling or treating him.
notes: Starting treatment before the diagnosis is confirmed risks treating white coat hypertension, and nothing here, such as very high readings or end-organ damage, justifies treating straight away.
Testing for primary aldosteronism is not the next step: his potassium is normal, there is no resistant hypertension and hypertension is not yet confirmed.
Echocardiography is not routine in this work-up, and the ECG already shows no left ventricular hypertrophy.
His home readings are invalid and cannot exclude hypertension; even confirmed white coat hypertension still needs follow-up.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man has finished inpatient alcohol withdrawal and wants help staying abstinent. He takes methadone 60 mg daily for opioid use disorder. His eGFR is 85 mL/min/1.73 m2. Which drug is most appropriate?
questions.why: Acamprosate and naltrexone are the first-line drugs for preventing alcohol relapse. Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist, so it is contraindicated in a patient on methadone because it would cause severe precipitated withdrawal. That leaves acamprosate, which is safe with his normal kidney function.
notes: Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors, so it would cause precipitated withdrawal and stop his methadone working.
Disulfiram is a second-line drug that depends on supervised dosing and close adherence, and a drink taken with it can cause a dangerous reaction.
Baclofen is a second-line, off-label option that is kept for when first-line drugs fail or cannot be used, and it adds to sedation alongside methadone.
Benzodiazepines are only for short-term withdrawal management, and using them long term with methadone raises the risk of dependence and fatal breathing depression.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has fever, rigors, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. Bilirubin is 72 µmol/L (mostly conjugated), ALP 310 U/L, GGT 402 U/L and ALT 150 U/L. Which jaundice pattern is shown?
questions.why: Bilirubin that is mostly conjugated, with ALP and GGT raised more than the transaminases, is a cholestatic pattern and points to post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice. With fever and rigors, it suggests a blocked and infected bile duct (cholangitis). The next step is ultrasound to look for a dilated common bile duct.
notes: In hepatocellular injury the transaminases are raised much more than ALP, often into the high hundreds or thousands.
Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and leaves ALP and GGT normal.
A conjugation defect such as Gilbert syndrome raises unconjugated bilirubin and leaves ALP and GGT normal.
Synthetic failure shows up as a raised INR and low albumin, which are not given here and do not explain the cholestatic enzymes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has had a productive cough for a week and a temperature of 38.4 °C. Chest X-ray: retrocardiac opacity obscuring the left hemidiaphragm, with a sharp left heart border. Where is the consolidation?
questions.why: The left lower lobe sits behind the heart and touches the left hemidiaphragm. When it consolidates, it shows as a retrocardiac opacity and the outline of the left hemidiaphragm is lost (silhouette sign). The left heart border stays sharp because the lingula is clear.
notes: Lingular consolidation touches the heart, so it would blur the left heart border, and here that border is sharp.
Left upper lobe consolidation causes upper-zone opacity or a hazy veil over the left lung, not a retrocardiac density hiding the hemidiaphragm.
Right middle lobe consolidation blurs the right heart border and sits on the right, not behind the heart on the left.
Right lower lobe consolidation hides the right hemidiaphragm, not the left one.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman, four hours after total thyroidectomy, develops stridor and a tense, enlarging neck swelling. SpO2 is 91% on 6 L/min oxygen. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She has a neck haematoma after thyroidectomy that is blocking her airway. This is an emergency, and the first step is to open the wound at the bedside: cut the skin sutures or clips and open the strap muscles to let the clot out (the SCOOP approach). Once the pressure is relieved, she goes back to theatre for haemostasis, and her airway is secured if she still needs it.
notes: Imaging delays treatment in a patient whose airway is closing, and the diagnosis is already clear on examination.
Intubating through a swollen larynx that is being compressed by a haematoma is likely to fail, and the haematoma should be released first.
Low calcium after thyroidectomy usually appears after 24 to 48 hours with tingling or tetany, not with a tense, growing neck swelling.
Nebulised adrenaline treats swelling of the upper airway lining, as in croup, and does nothing about a haematoma pressing on the trachea from outside.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with urosepsis is still hypotensive (MAP 55 mmHg) after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid and intravenous antibiotics. Her lactate is 5 mmol/L, and she has bibasal crackles. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is septic shock: she stays hypotensive despite adequate fluid resuscitation, and her lactate is raised. The crackles suggest she is becoming fluid overloaded. Surviving Sepsis and Australian guidance recommend noradrenaline as the first-line vasopressor, targeting a MAP of at least 65 mmHg. It can be started through a peripheral line until central access is available.
notes: She has already had 30 mL/kg and now has bibasal crackles, so more crystalloid risks pulmonary oedema without fixing her vasodilatory shock.
Hydrocortisone is only added when shock persists despite moderate- to high-dose vasopressors, not before a vasopressor has been started.
Dobutamine is an inotrope for heart dysfunction with low cardiac output, and its vasodilating effect could make her hypotension worse.
Albumin is still a volume load, so it shares the fluid overload risk and does not treat vasoplegia, and 20% albumin is not a resuscitation fluid.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man has a transperineal biopsy showing Gleason 4+3=7 prostate adenocarcinoma. His PSA is 11 ng/mL, and MRI shows a 10 mm right peripheral zone lesion without extraprostatic extension. He has no symptoms. Most appropriate staging investigation?
questions.why: Gleason 4+3=7 (ISUP Grade Group 3) with a PSA of 10 to 20 ng/mL is unfavourable intermediate-risk disease, so it needs staging before curative treatment. In Australia, Medicare funds PSMA PET/CT for this. The proPSMA trial showed it is more accurate than CT plus bone scan for nodal and distant metastases.
notes: A bone scan shows only skeletal disease, misses nodal spread and is less sensitive than PSMA PET/CT.
Conventional CT misses small or normal-sized involved lymph nodes and is less accurate than PSMA PET/CT.
MRI has already staged the local tumour; repeating it cannot detect nodal or distant metastases.
Most prostate adenocarcinomas take up little FDG, so FDG PET/CT is not used for primary staging.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman woke with a left homonymous hemianopia. MRI shows a small acute right occipital infarct without haemorrhage. ECG shows atrial fibrillation, previously unknown. Which long-term therapy best prevents recurrent stroke?
questions.why: Her biggest risk is another cardioembolic stroke from atrial fibrillation. The Australian stroke guidelines and eTG recommend long-term oral anticoagulation, preferably a DOAC such as apixaban, over antiplatelet therapy. The stroke team times the start by infarct size, often within a few days for a small infarct.
notes: Aspirin prevents far fewer AF-related emboli than anticoagulation, so it is not a substitute in a patient who can take a DOAC.
Clopidogrel is antiplatelet therapy for non-cardioembolic stroke and does not adequately prevent clots forming in the left atrium.
Short-term dual antiplatelet therapy is for minor non-cardioembolic stroke or TIA, and is inferior to anticoagulation in AF.
Aspirin plus dipyridamole is an option for non-cardioembolic stroke but does not protect against embolism from AF.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to a rural emergency department with 18 hours of fevers and shaking chills and 6 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain. This morning her partner noticed that her eyes had turned yellow. She reports dark urine and pale stools. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and has no other medical history. Her temperature is 39.4 °C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She is alert and oriented. She is jaundiced and tender in the right upper quadrant. Investigations show: white cell count 16.4 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0); platelets 240 x10^9/L (150–400); total bilirubin 61 µmol/L (<20); ALP 310 U/L (30–110); GGT 402 U/L (<40); ALT 160 U/L (<35); albumin 37 g/L (35–50); creatinine 68 µmol/L (45–90); INR 1.0; venous lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2.0). Ultrasound shows a 10 mm common bile duct with a calculus in its distal end. Which of the following best describes the severity of this patient's condition according to the Tokyo Guidelines 2018?
options: Mild (Grade I), as organ dysfunction is absent
Moderate (Grade II), owing to the serum bilirubin level
Moderate (Grade II), owing to leucocytosis and pyrexia
Severe (Grade III), owing to the raised venous lactate
Severe (Grade III), owing to tachycardia and tachypnoea
questions.why: This woman meets the TG18 criteria for a definite diagnosis of acute cholangitis. She has systemic inflammation (fever with rigors and a raised white cell count), cholestasis (conjugated-pattern jaundice with ALP and GGT raised more than ALT) and imaging findings (a dilated common bile duct with a distal stone). Severity is graded from the results. Grade III (severe) needs dysfunction of at least one organ system: hypotension needing vasopressors, a reduced level of consciousness, PaO2/FiO2 below 300, oliguria or creatinine above 176 µmol/L, INR above 1.5, or platelets below 100 x10^9/L. She has none of these, because her blood pressure, mental state, oxygenation, creatinine, INR and platelets are all normal. Grade II (moderate) needs any two of: white cell count above 12 or below 4 x10^9/L, temperature of 39 °C or more, age 75 or more, bilirubin of 85 µmol/L or more, or low albumin. She meets two (white cell count 16.4 and temperature 39.4 °C), so she has Grade II cholangitis. For her, this means she is at risk of getting worse.
notes: Wrong: having no organ dysfunction only rules out Grade III, and she meets two Grade II criteria, so she is not Grade I.
Wrong: a bilirubin of 61 µmol/L is below the 85 µmol/L TG18 threshold, so it does not count towards Grade II.
Wrong: lactate is not one of the TG18 organ dysfunction criteria; a mildly raised lactate supports sepsis escalation but does not make her Grade III.
Wrong: tachycardia and tachypnoea are not TG18 organ dysfunction criteria, and her blood pressure and oxygenation are normal.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops generalised urticaria, wheeze and lip swelling five minutes after intravenous cefazolin. Blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg. The infusion has been stopped. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Skin and mucosal signs with wheeze and hypotension straight after a drug is given means anaphylaxis. ASCIA and eTG guidance is to lay her flat and give IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (maximum 0.5 mg) into the anterolateral thigh without delay, repeating every 5 minutes if needed. Adrenaline is the only first-line drug. Antihistamines, steroids and bronchodilators are only add-ons.
notes: Corticosteroids take hours to work and do not treat the immediate shock or airway compromise, so they are not first line.
ASCIA advises against sedating antihistamines such as promethazine in anaphylaxis because they can worsen hypotension, and they do not treat shock.
Salbutamol may help wheeze that persists after adrenaline, but it does not treat hypotension or airway swelling.
Oral non-sedating antihistamines only relieve skin symptoms and have no role in treating shock or airway compromise.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with intellectual disability and minimal speech has two weeks of aggression, hitting his lower abdomen and new daytime wetting. He is afebrile; abdomen soft, no masses. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A sudden change in behaviour in a child with intellectual disability should be treated as pain or illness until proven otherwise. New wetting with lower abdominal distress points to a urinary cause. A clean-catch urine dipstick, sent for culture if positive, is the quick first-line test that rules a UTI in or out before any behavioural explanation is accepted.
notes: RCH guidelines say constipation is diagnosed clinically and an abdominal X-ray is not recommended, and here there is no faecal mass.
Thyroid disease causes gradual change and would not explain new wetting with lower abdominal pain over two weeks.
Imaging the renal tract comes after a UTI is confirmed, not before a simple urine test.
Nothing in the history suggests seizures, and an EEG does not explain the urinary or abdominal features.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old nulliparous woman with obesity and type 2 diabetes has eight months of heavy, irregular menstrual bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a homogeneous 15 mm endometrium without polyp or fibroid. Which test will most likely confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: This woman is at least 45 and has persistent abnormal bleeding, obesity, diabetes, nulliparity and a thickened endometrium, so endometrial hyperplasia or cancer must be excluded. Only a tissue sample can confirm it, so under RANZCOG guidance she needs an endometrial biopsy (pipelle, or hysteroscopy with directed biopsy or curettage).
notes: Histology of an endometrial sample is the only test that confirms or excludes hyperplasia or cancer in a high-risk woman with a thickened endometrium.
Saline sonohysterography shows the shape of the cavity and finds polyps, but it gives no tissue, so it cannot confirm hyperplasia or cancer.
