CA-125 is not sensitive or specific for endometrial disease, and it is used mainly when assessing ovarian masses.
Cervical screening looks for HPV and cervical disease, and it is not a reliable way to sample the endometrium.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops generalised urticaria, wheeze and blood pressure 78/45 mmHg ten minutes after intravenous cefazolin at anaesthetic induction. She improves with IM adrenaline. Most appropriate investigation within the next hour?
questions.why: A raised mast cell tryptase supports the diagnosis of anaphylaxis during anaesthesia. ASCIA and ANZAAG advise taking it as soon as possible (ideally within 1 to 2 hours, and up to 4 hours) and repeating it after 24 hours or more as a baseline. Testing to find the drug responsible is done later at a specialist allergy or anaesthetic clinic.
notes: Skin testing is unreliable straight after anaphylaxis because mast cells are depleted, so it is deferred for about 4 to 6 weeks.
Drug-specific IgE for cefazolin is poorly validated and not widely available, and it does not confirm that anaphylaxis happened.
Total IgE is nonspecific and neither confirms anaphylaxis nor identifies the trigger.
Histamine has a half-life of minutes, is hard to handle in the lab and is not routinely available, so tryptase is preferred.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man on methadone 150 mg daily, recently prescribed clarithromycin for pneumonia, has palpitations and then collapses briefly at home. He is now alert with normal observations. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: High-dose methadone together with a CYP3A4 inhibitor that also prolongs the QT interval (clarithromycin) puts him at risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, which fits palpitations followed by collapse. A 12-lead ECG to measure the QTc is the key first test. Australian opioid treatment guidelines advise ECG monitoring when methadone doses are high or QT-prolonging drugs are added.
notes: A urine drug screen shows recent drug use but cannot find the arrhythmia, which is the dangerous cause here.
Serum methadone levels are not used routinely, results are slow, and they do not measure the QT interval or risk of arrhythmia.
CT brain is not indicated for a brief collapse after palpitations with full recovery and no head injury or focal signs.
An echocardiogram looks at heart structure and may come later, but it does not find the QT prolongation that is most likely here.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer takes controlled-release oral morphine 60 mg twice daily. Pain is controlled at rest, but she has incident pain when showering. Most appropriate breakthrough dose?
questions.why: The breakthrough dose is an immediate-release form of the same opioid at one-sixth to one-tenth of the total daily dose. Her daily dose is 120 mg oral morphine, so 12 to 20 mg is right, and 15 mg is a sensible dose. She can take it about 30 minutes before showering for incident pain.
notes: 5 mg is about 4% of her daily dose, so it is too small to relieve breakthrough pain.
60 mg is half her daily dose, which is far above the recommended range and risks opioid toxicity.
Controlled-release morphine takes hours to reach peak effect, so it is not suitable for episodic breakthrough pain.
Subcutaneous morphine is two to three times as potent as oral, so 20 mg equals about 40 to 60 mg oral and is too high.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man has two weeks of worsening breathlessness and orthopnoea, a month after an anterior myocardial infarction. He has bibasal crackles and an S3; NT-proBNP is 8400 ng/L. Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: Orthopnoea, an S3, crackles and a very high NT-proBNP after a recent MI point to heart failure. The Australian heart failure guidelines (NHF/CSANZ) recommend echocardiography for every patient with suspected heart failure. It confirms the diagnosis, measures the ejection fraction (which decides treatment) and looks for wall motion problems or mechanical complications after the MI.
notes: A CT pulmonary angiogram looks for pulmonary embolism, which orthopnoea, an S3 and a high NT-proBNP do not suggest, and the contrast is a risk to kidneys already under strain.
Coronary angiography assesses whether ischaemia is causing the heart failure; it does not confirm the heart failure or measure how well the heart pumps.
Cardiac MRI is a second-line test, used when echo images are poor or the cause of a cardiomyopathy is unclear; it is not the first test.
Serial troponin helps tell whether there has been a new infarct, but it cannot confirm heart failure or show the ejection fraction.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has 2 months of weight loss, tremor and palpitations. Pulse is 112/min and irregularly irregular; BP 124/78 mmHg. TSH is <0.01 mIU/L and TSH receptor antibodies are positive. Most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.why: She has Graves' disease with thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation and is haemodynamically stable. Per eTG, a beta blocker such as propranolol is first line: it controls the ventricular rate and eases adrenergic symptoms while antithyroid treatment starts. AF often reverts once she is euthyroid, so rhythm control is deferred.
notes: Digoxin works poorly in thyrotoxicosis because clearance is higher and sympathetic drive is high, so it is not first line.
Amiodarone is very rich in iodine and can make thyrotoxicosis worse, so it should be avoided here.
Rhythm control with flecainide usually fails while she is still thyrotoxic, and AF often reverts once she is euthyroid.
She is stable, and cardioversion is deferred until she is euthyroid because AF very often comes back before then.

questions.stem: A 20-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her father 70 minutes after an episode at day care. Staff saw her go stiff and unresponsive with her eyes rolled back, then she had rhythmic jerking of all four limbs for about 2 minutes. She was sleepy for about 30 minutes afterwards. She has had a runny nose and cough for 2 days. She has never had a seizure before. She is fully immunised, her development is normal, and she takes no medicines. Her mother had a febrile convulsion as a child. Temperature is 39.0 °C, pulse 145/min, respirations 32/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, SpO2 98% in room air and capillary refill 2 seconds. She is now alert, playing and interacting normally. She has clear rhinorrhoea and an injected pharynx. Her tympanic membranes are normal and her chest is clear. There is no rash and no neck stiffness. Neurological examination is normal. Capillary blood glucose is 5.1 mmol/L. She has been given oral paracetamol. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge with parental education and safety-netting advice
Admission to the ward for overnight observation
Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis
Regular alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen for 3 days
questions.why: This is a simple febrile seizure. The RCH Febrile seizure guideline defines this as a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting under 15 minutes, with full recovery within 1 hour and no repeat seizure in the same illness, in a child aged 6 months to 6 years. She has a clear viral upper respiratory source, a normal blood glucose, no signs of meningitis and a normal neurological examination now that she is back to baseline. Once she is back to normal and the source is found, she can go home. Her father needs to hear that the outlook is good: there is no brain damage, the chance of later epilepsy is about 1 to 2 in 100, and the chance of another febrile seizure is about 1 in 3 (higher here because of the family history). He also needs to be taught seizure first aid: time the seizure, put her in the recovery position, put nothing in her mouth, and call an ambulance if it lasts 5 minutes. He should bring her back if she becomes drowsy, gets a rash or neck stiffness, has another seizure, or he is worried. Admission is not needed because she has recovered fully and the source is benign. Lumbar puncture is only for meningism, ongoing drowsiness or a very young or unwell child.
notes: Wrong: admission is for complex seizures, slow recovery, a worrying source or concern about how the family will cope, and she has none of these.
Wrong: she has no meningism, no rash and no ongoing drowsiness, and she is not very young or unwell, so lumbar puncture is not indicated.
Wrong: EEG does not predict recurrence or later epilepsy after a simple febrile seizure and is not recommended.
Wrong: antipyretics are given for comfort only, do not prevent febrile seizures, and an alternating schedule raises the risk of dosing errors.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 38 weeks' gestation is in spontaneous labour on the birth suite. An ultrasound at 34 weeks showed polyhydramnios (amniotic fluid index 27 cm), normal fetal growth and a fundal placenta. Ten minutes after spontaneous rupture of the membranes, with a gush of clear liquor, the CTG shows a sudden fall in the fetal heart rate from a baseline of 135/min to 75/min, which has lasted 4 minutes. She has no epidural, and no oxytocin is running. Her pulse is 88/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, respirations 16/min and temperature 36.9 °C. The abdomen is soft and non-tender between contractions, which come 3 times in 10 minutes. On vaginal examination the cervix is 6 cm dilated, the vertex is at station -3, and a pulsating loop of umbilical cord is felt in the vagina. Help has been called and theatre is being prepared for a category 1 caesarean. While she waits for transfer to theatre, which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Manual replacement of the loop back into the uterus
Digital elevation of the head with knee–chest posture
Fetal scalp blood sampling for lactate measurement
Forceps-assisted vaginal birth in lithotomy position
Left lateral tilt with intravenous crystalloid bolus
questions.why: This is umbilical cord prolapse. Her risk factors are polyhydramnios, a high vertex and recent rupture of the membranes, and the fetal heart rate has dropped and stayed down. The cord is being squeezed between the fetal head and the pelvis. The aim while waiting for a category 1 caesarean is to take that pressure off. The RCOG Green-top Guideline 50, used with RANZCOG guidance in Australian units, advises pushing the presenting part up off the cord by hand through the vagina. The woman is placed knee–chest, or head-down in the left lateral position, so gravity helps. An alternative is filling the bladder with 500 to 750 mL of saline through a urinary catheter. The cord should be handled as little as possible to avoid spasm of its vessels, and tocolysis such as terbutaline can be considered. Elevation continues until the baby is delivered. Delivery should not be delayed for any other test or procedure.
notes: Pushing the cord back into the uterus (funic reduction) is not recommended, because handling the cord causes its vessels to spasm, and it delays the definitive caesarean.
Fetal blood sampling is not appropriate for a prolonged deceleration or bradycardia that is not recovering, and it would delay a birth that is already known to be needed.
Forceps need a fully dilated cervix and an engaged head, but here the cervix is 6 cm and the vertex is at station -3.
Left lateral tilt and fluids treat maternal hypotension, but her blood pressure is normal, and neither measure relieves the mechanical squeezing of the cord.

questions.stem: A 4-day-old term boy, feeding well until today, has three episodes of green vomiting. He is alert with soft, non-distended abdomen. Abdominal X-ray shows a normal gas pattern. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise, even when the baby looks well and the abdominal X-ray is normal. An urgent upper GI contrast study is the investigation of choice. It shows where the duodenojejunal flexure sits and whether there is a volvulus, so surgery is not delayed.
notes: Ultrasound can suggest malrotation (whirlpool sign, reversed SMA/SMV) but depends on the operator, and a normal scan does not exclude it.
A contrast enema looks for distal obstruction such as Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus, which is unlikely with a non-distended abdomen.
CT gives a high radiation dose and is not the standard way to diagnose malrotation in neonates.
A blood gas helps judge how unwell the baby is but cannot diagnose or exclude a surgical cause of bilious vomiting.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with two days of new left temporal headache, pain on chewing, and transient visual loss today. Her temporal artery is tender; ESR 92 mm/h. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She has a new headache after age 50, jaw claudication, a tender temporal artery, a very high ESR and transient visual loss. This is giant cell arteritis with visual involvement, which threatens her sight. Give IV methylprednisolone (500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days) straight away and arrange same-day ophthalmology review, without waiting for a biopsy.
notes: Oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg is right for GCA without visual symptoms, but visual involvement needs IV pulse steroids.
A biopsy confirms the diagnosis but must not delay steroids, and it stays positive for 1 to 2 weeks after they start.
CT brain does not diagnose GCA, and this gradual headache with jaw claudication does not suggest a bleed or mass.
Aspirin treats embolic amaurosis fugax from carotid disease but does not treat the arteritis itself.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has newly confirmed HIV-1 infection. His CD4 count is 520 cells/µL, viral load 64,000 copies/mL, genotype shows no resistance and eGFR is above 90 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Most appropriate initial regimen?
questions.why: ASHM-endorsed guidelines recommend offering ART to everyone with HIV, whatever the CD4 count. The preferred first-line regimen is an integrase inhibitor plus two NRTIs, such as dolutegravir with tenofovir-emtricitabine. His genotype shows no resistance and his kidney function is normal, so tenofovir can be used.
notes: Two NRTIs alone are a PrEP regimen, not treatment, and would not fully suppress the virus, so resistance would likely develop.
Nevirapine can cause serious liver toxicity in men with CD4 above 400 cells/µL, and zidovudine causes anaemia, so this older regimen is no longer recommended.
Boosted protease inhibitor monotherapy suppresses the virus less reliably than triple therapy and is not a recommended starting regimen.
This two-drug combination is not a recommended first-line regimen, and maraviroc needs a tropism test because it only works against CCR5-tropic virus.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman with hay fever has chest tightness and cough beginning minutes after netball training, settling within an hour. Examination and spirometry with bronchodilator testing are normal. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Her symptoms point to exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, but normal resting spirometry with no bronchodilator response does not rule it out. The Australian Asthma Handbook advises confirming it with a bronchial provocation test, such as a mannitol or exercise challenge, before starting an inhaler.
notes: Starting salbutamol on suspicion alone, without confirming the diagnosis, risks mislabelling her and missing other causes such as exercise-induced laryngeal obstruction.
Daily preventer therapy is not warranted when the diagnosis is unconfirmed and symptoms occur only with exercise.
She has no features of pulmonary embolism, so a CTPA would add radiation and contrast without changing management.
Her typical symptoms, together with atopy, make exercise-induced bronchoconstriction likely enough that it should be tested for, not dismissed.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with hypertension has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back. ECG shows tall QRS voltages with lateral downsloping ST depression and asymmetric T inversion, unchanged from 2023. Most likely explanation of the ECG?
questions.why: High QRS voltages with lateral downsloping ST depression and asymmetric T inversion that match an earlier ECG are a long-standing strain pattern from hypertensive left ventricular hypertrophy, not acute ischaemia. A non-ischaemic or non-specific ECG does not rule out aortic dissection, so get a CT aortogram and hold off aspirin, heparin and thrombolysis until dissection has been excluded.
notes: Acute ischaemia should be new or changing compared with the old ECG, and it does not explain the high QRS voltages.
Posterior STEMI shows ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves there, not lateral changes with LVH voltages that match an old ECG.
Digoxin causes a scooped (reverse tick) ST depression across many leads, without high voltages, and he has no history of taking it.
Hypokalaemia gives flattened T waves and prominent U waves with widespread ST depression, not LVH voltages with a fixed lateral pattern.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a PSA of 8.8 ng/mL on two occasions. Digital rectal examination is normal. MRI shows an 11 mm left peripheral-zone lesion; targeted biopsy confirms Gleason 4+3=7 adenocarcinoma. What is his clinical T stage?
questions.why: Clinical T stage depends on the digital rectal examination. A tumour that cannot be felt and was found by needle biopsy because of a raised PSA is cT1c. A one-sided MRI lesion does not raise the clinical T stage.
notes: The tumour cannot be felt and was found by needle biopsy after a raised PSA, which defines cT1c.
cT2a needs a tumour that can be felt in half of one lobe or less; his DRE is normal, and MRI findings do not change the clinical T stage.
cT2b needs a tumour that can be felt in more than half of one lobe, but nothing is felt here.
cT3a means extension outside the prostate, which neither the DRE nor the MRI shows.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman develops lip swelling, a hoarse voice and wheeze 15 minutes after eating a cashew stir-fry. Her blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is anaphylaxis: sudden swelling of the lips and airway, wheeze and low blood pressure after eating a nut. ASCIA and eTG say the first step is IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg, up to 0.5 mg for an adult, injected into the outer thigh and repeated every 5 minutes if needed. She should be laid flat, given oxygen and IV fluids alongside this.
notes: Wrong: corticosteroids act too slowly to treat anaphylaxis and do not reliably prevent a second-wave reaction, so they must never delay adrenaline.
Wrong: antihistamines only help the skin symptoms and do not reverse airway swelling or shock.
Wrong: salbutamol can be added for wheeze that persists after adrenaline, but it does not treat the airway swelling or the shock.
Wrong: a 1 mg IV bolus is the cardiac arrest dose and can cause arrhythmias or myocardial ischaemia. IV adrenaline infusions are reserved for shock that does not respond to IM doses.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has an itchy rash of grouped, excoriated vesicles on both elbows. tTG-IgA is 140 U/mL with normal total IgA, and duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy. Most appropriate long-term treatment?
questions.why: Biopsy-confirmed coeliac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis is treated long term with a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet, supported by a dietitian. The diet heals the bowel and the skin and lowers the risk of complications. Dapsone only controls the itch for the months it takes the rash to respond to the diet.
notes: Dapsone is a short-term bridge for the itch while the diet takes effect, needs G6PD testing and blood count monitoring, and does nothing for the bowel.
Topical corticosteroids give little relief in dermatitis herpetiformis and do not treat the underlying gluten-sensitive enteropathy.
Budesonide is kept for refractory coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease, and is not first-line treatment for newly diagnosed coeliac disease.
A low-FODMAP diet is for irritable bowel syndrome and still contains gluten, so it does not treat coeliac disease.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman is intubated in the ICU for pneumonia with respiratory failure. Immediately afterwards, breath sounds are faint bilaterally and her oxygen saturation falls to 84%. Which test best confirms tracheal tube position?
questions.why: Possible oesophageal intubation is an emergency. Under ANZCA and ANZICS guidance, a sustained waveform of exhaled carbon dioxide on capnography is the standard test to confirm the tube is in the trachea. If there is no sustained waveform, the tube is assumed to be in the oesophagus ("no trace, wrong place") and is removed.
notes: A chest X-ray shows how deep the tube sits, but it cannot tell tracheal from oesophageal placement and takes too long in a desaturating patient.
Arterial blood gas results are delayed and only indirectly reflect ventilation, so they cannot confirm where the tube is.
Auscultation is unreliable: sounds from the oesophagus can be mistaken for breath sounds, especially in a noisy unit or with lung disease.
Lung sliding on ultrasound supports tracheal placement, but it depends on the operator and is a supplement to capnography, not a replacement.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has had 6 hours of constant epigastric pain radiating to her back, with vomiting. She rarely drinks alcohol. Her lipase is 2400 U/L (normal <60). Her observations are stable. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: She has typical pain and a lipase more than 3 times the upper limit, so she already meets the criteria for acute pancreatitis. The next step is to find the cause. Every patient needs an abdominal ultrasound to look for gallstones, which are the commonest cause, especially in someone who rarely drinks, and finding them changes management (early cholecystectomy, and ERCP if needed).
notes: Contrast CT is not needed early when the diagnosis is already clear; it is kept for diagnostic doubt or for deterioration after about 72 hours to look for necrosis.
MRCP is a second-line test for a suspected duct stone or an unclear cause after an ultrasound has been done, not the first investigation.
ERCP is an invasive treatment for cholangitis or a persisting duct stone, not a first-line test to find the cause.
Amylase adds nothing once the lipase is raised, because lipase is more specific and stays raised for longer.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back. CT aortogram shows an ascending aortic dissection without pericardial effusion. BP 172/98 mmHg, heart rate 108/min. Which drug should be given first?
questions.why: He has a hypertensive, tachycardic type A dissection with no tamponade, so anti-impulse therapy should start while he waits for urgent surgery. An IV beta blocker such as esmolol comes first, aiming for a heart rate of about 60/min and a systolic BP of 100 to 120 mmHg. A vasodilator is added only once beta blockade is in place.
notes: Starting a vasodilator before beta blockade causes reflex tachycardia, which increases aortic wall stress and can extend the dissection.
Hydralazine is a direct vasodilator that causes reflex tachycardia, and it is not used first in acute dissection.
Antiplatelet therapy is contraindicated in aortic dissection because it raises the risk of bleeding and rupture before surgery.
Anticoagulation is contraindicated in aortic dissection because it can worsen bleeding into the false lumen and the pericardium.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with asthma has been wheezing for two hours since mowing. He speaks in short phrases, uses accessory muscles and has SpO2 92% on room air. No stridor or rash. Most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.why: He can speak only in short phrases, is using accessory muscles and has an SpO2 of 90 to 94%, so this is severe acute asthma without life-threatening features. Under the Australian Asthma Handbook, start repeated salbutamol (12 puffs by spacer or nebulised) with ipratropium every 20 minutes for the first hour. Also give titrated oxygen (target 93 to 95%) and oral prednisolone within the hour.
notes: IV magnesium is kept for patients who do not respond to the first hour of bronchodilators or who have life-threatening asthma, so it is not the first step.
Aminophylline has a narrow therapeutic margin, adds toxicity and adds little to inhaled bronchodilators, so it is not routine treatment.
IM adrenaline treats anaphylaxis, but he has a clear asthma trigger and no stridor, rash or hypotension.
NIV is not first-line treatment in acute asthma, and he is alert with no exhaustion or hypercapnia that would call for ventilatory support.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman discharged last week after cholecystectomy has fever, purulent sputum and left pleuritic pain. X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation. Wells score 3; D-dimer 0.62 mg/L FEU. Most appropriate next step regarding PE?
questions.why: A Wells score of 4 or less means PE is unlikely. Her age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off is 0.72 mg/L FEU (age × 0.01 for people over 50), so a D-dimer of 0.62 is negative. Together these exclude PE, and the consolidation gives a clear alternative diagnosis.
notes: CTPA is for patients where PE is likely, or unlikely with a positive D-dimer; neither applies here, so it would add radiation and contrast for no benefit.
A V/Q scan is an alternative to CTPA when imaging is needed, but imaging is not needed after a negative age-adjusted D-dimer, and consolidation makes a V/Q scan hard to read.
Leg ultrasound is used when there are signs of DVT or when lung imaging cannot be done; it is not needed once PE has been excluded.
Repeating the D-dimer adds nothing because this result is already negative; infection and recent surgery would only push the D-dimer up.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old boy with bronchiolitis is on 1 L/min nasal oxygen, SpO2 94%. In a feeding trial he takes 35 mL of his usual 150 mL; no wet nappy for 8 hours. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: The feeding trial shows he takes about a quarter of his usual feed and has had no urine output, so oral hydration is not enough. Under the RCH bronchiolitis guideline, nasogastric feeds are the first choice when oral intake is inadequate. Start at 2/3 maintenance because of the risk of increased ADH secretion.
notes: Smaller, more frequent bottle feeds still add to his work of breathing, and they will not make up an intake this low in an infant who is already passing no urine.
Isotonic IV fluid with glucose is kept for when nasogastric feeds fail or are unsafe; it is not the first choice.
His SpO2 is 94% on low-flow oxygen, so hypoxaemia and work of breathing are not getting worse and high flow is not needed.
Nebulised hypertonic saline does not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis and does nothing for his poor intake.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden severe periumbilical pain for 4 hours. Her abdomen is soft and minimally tender. Serum lactate is 6.8 mmol/L. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: A markedly raised lactate with pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen in a patient with atrial fibrillation points to embolic acute mesenteric ischaemia from bowel hypoperfusion. A normal lactate does not rule it out, but a high one here needs urgent CT angiography and an early surgical or vascular review.
notes: Perforation causes peritonism with a rigid, board-like abdomen, not a soft, minimally tender one.
Pancreatitis usually gives epigastric pain radiating to the back, diagnosed by raised lipase, and has no link to AF.
A ruptured aneurysm usually presents with back or flank pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass, not isolated pain with a high lactate.
Diverticulitis gives localised left iliac fossa tenderness and fever, developing over days rather than suddenly.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash. He is haemodynamically stable, has blood at the urethral meatus and cannot pass urine. Pelvic X-ray shows bilateral pubic rami fractures. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Blood at the meatus, urinary retention and an anterior pelvic ring fracture point strongly to a posterior urethral injury. A retrograde urethrogram should be done before anyone tries to pass a urethral catheter, because a blind attempt can turn a partial tear into a complete one. If the urethra is disrupted, the bladder is drained with a suprapubic catheter.
notes: A CT cystogram looks for bladder rupture and needs a catheter in the bladder, which should not be passed until the urethra is shown to be intact.
An ultrasound of the renal tract can show a full bladder but cannot show the urethra, so it cannot confirm or rule out a urethral tear.
An intravenous pyelogram is an outdated test of the kidneys and ureters and does not show the urethra.
Flexible cystoscopy is not the first test in a male trauma patient, as it is invasive and can make a partial urethral tear worse; in males, a retrograde urethrogram comes first.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has fever and painful swelling under his tongue and jaw four days after a lower molar toothache. Floor of mouth is raised and firm; he is drooling. Most immediate life-threatening complication?
questions.why: This is Ludwig angina, a cellulitis spreading through the submandibular and sublingual spaces on both sides, usually from a lower molar infection. It pushes the tongue up and back, so the most immediate threat is upper airway obstruction. Management starts with securing the airway early in an experienced setting, followed by IV antibiotics and surgical drainage.
notes: Mediastinitis can follow spread down the neck spaces, but it develops later than airway compromise.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis usually follows maxillary or mid-face infection, not a lower molar.
Osteomyelitis of the jaw is a slower, local complication and not an immediate threat to life.
Erosion of the carotid artery is a rare, late complication of deep neck space infection.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man at a dye-manufacturing plant develops headache and slate-grey cyanosis after an aniline spill. SpO2 is 85% on 15 L/min oxygen; arterial PO2 is 410 mmHg. Most likely explanation for these results?
questions.why: Low pulse oximetry readings that stay around 85% despite a very high arterial PO2 (a saturation gap), together with cyanosis after aniline exposure, point to methaemoglobinaemia. Confirm it with co-oximetry on a blood gas. If the patient has symptoms or a high methaemoglobin level, give methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) after checking toxicology advice.
notes: Pulse oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin, so in carbon monoxide poisoning SpO2 looks falsely normal, not low, and the patient is not cyanosed.
Cyanide stops cells from using oxygen but leaves haemoglobin saturation normal, so it would not cause cyanosis or a low SpO2.
Pulmonary oedema causes hypoxaemia, so arterial PO2 would be low rather than 410 mmHg.
Alveolar hypoventilation lowers arterial PO2 and raises PCO2, which does not fit a PaO2 of 410 mmHg on oxygen.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman becomes confused and falls, three weeks after starting sertraline for depression. She is clinically euvolaemic. Serum sodium is 121 mmol/L; urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg. Most likely cause of hyponatraemia?
questions.why: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with urine that is not maximally dilute (osmolality above 100 mOsm/kg) points to SIADH. Starting an SSRI is a common cause in older people, especially in the first few weeks. Management is to cease the sertraline and restrict fluids, with careful sodium monitoring.
notes: In primary polydipsia the urine is maximally dilute (osmolality below 100 mOsm/kg), not 480 mOsm/kg.
She is clinically euvolaemic, and nothing in the history suggests losses from the gut, kidneys or skin.
Primary adrenal insufficiency usually causes hypovolaemia, hypotension and hyperkalaemia, and nothing here suggests it.
Hypothyroidism only rarely causes hyponatraemia, and only when it is severe and has clinical features, which are absent here.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash. He is distressed, BP 78/40 mmHg, SpO2 84%, with absent left breath sounds, hyperresonance and distended neck veins. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Hypotension, hypoxia, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on one side, and raised JVP after trauma mean a tension pneumothorax. This is a clinical diagnosis and needs immediate decompression (needle at the 4th/5th intercostal space just in front of the midaxillary line, or finger thoracostomy), then an intercostal catheter. Per EMST/ATLS, you do not wait for imaging.
notes: Waiting for a chest X-ray to confirm a clinical diagnosis delays treatment and risks cardiac arrest.
A FAST scan looks for blood in the abdomen and pericardium, but hyperresonance with absent breath sounds points to a tension pneumothorax, which needs decompression first.
Tamponade also causes distended neck veins and hypotension, but it would not cause one-sided absent breath sounds or hyperresonance.
Positive-pressure ventilation before decompression makes the tension pneumothorax worse and can bring on arrest.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to a general practice 5 weeks before a 7-week trip through rural Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos for travel advice. The trip includes village homestays, forest trekking and nights in open huts. She feels well. She has a new sexual partner and uses condoms inconsistently. Her last menstrual period began 3 weeks ago and was normal. She is unsure whether she could be pregnant. She takes no medicines and has no allergies. She had chickenpox at age 6, and her mother remembers it clearly. Her Australian Immunisation Register statement shows a complete childhood schedule, including one measles-mumps-rubella dose at 12 months, a 3-dose school hepatitis B course and dTpa at age 15. Temperature is 36.6 °C, blood pressure 114/72 mmHg, pulse 70/min and respiratory rate 14/min. Examination is normal. Today the doctor plans to give a second measles-mumps-rubella dose, live attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine, combined hepatitis A-typhoid vaccine and dTpa, and to prescribe doxycycline for malaria prophylaxis. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation before vaccination today?
questions.why: The plan includes two live vaccines: measles-mumps-rubella and live attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine (Imojev). The Australian Immunisation Handbook says live vaccines should not be given in pregnancy. She has had unprotected sex, is in the second half of her cycle and cannot rule out pregnancy, so a urine beta-hCG test is needed before vaccination today. If the test is negative, the live vaccines can be given on the same day. She should be told to avoid pregnancy for 28 days afterwards. If she is pregnant, the live vaccines are deferred, and an inactivated Japanese encephalitis vaccine and a different malaria plan are considered. Doxycycline is also avoided in pregnancy, so the result affects her antimalarial too. Measles serology is not needed: adults born in or after 1966 with one documented dose should simply get the second dose. Hepatitis A serology before vaccination is only for people born before 1950, people who spent their childhood in endemic areas, or people with a history of jaundice. G6PD testing is needed before primaquine or tafenoquine, not doxycycline.
notes: Adults born in or after 1966 with one documented MMR dose should get a second dose without serology, so this test would not change management.
Hepatitis A serology before vaccination is only for people born before 1950, people who spent their childhood in an endemic country, or people with a history of jaundice, and she is none of these.
G6PD testing is needed before primaquine or tafenoquine because of the risk of haemolysis, not before doxycycline prophylaxis.
Testing hepatitis B antibodies after a completed adolescent course is not routinely recommended in an immunocompetent traveller, and the result would not affect today's vaccines.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 24 hours of crampy, diffuse abdominal pain, profuse watery diarrhoea without blood, and repeated vomiting. Two days ago she looked after her grandson, who goes to childcare and had diarrhoea. Her husband started vomiting this morning. She has not travelled, taken antibiotics or been in hospital recently. She has type 2 diabetes and hypertension, and she is an ex-smoker. Her medicines are metformin, ramipril and omeprazole. Temperature is 37.8 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg lying, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Her abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding and hyperactive bowel sounds. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Creatinine is 131 µmol/L (baseline 72), potassium 3.4 mmol/L, venous lactate 1.5 mmol/L (reference below 2.0) and CRP 28 mg/L. She is given an intravenous crystalloid bolus, her metformin and ramipril are withheld, and she is to be admitted under contact precautions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Faecal microscopy for ova and parasites
questions.why: This woman has acute infectious diarrhoea. The likely cause is norovirus: she had sudden vomiting and watery diarrhoea two days after contact with a child who had diarrhoea, and another person in her household is now ill. She also has hypovolaemia and a prerenal acute kidney injury. Most people with acute gastroenteritis do not need a stool test. Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) recommends one in specific situations: severe illness, admission to hospital, bloody diarrhoea, immunocompromise, recent antibiotic use, symptoms lasting more than 7 days, or a suspected outbreak. She is being admitted with significant dehydration and an AKI, and her household cluster fits an outbreak. A faecal multiplex PCR is the most useful test. It detects norovirus and the common bacterial causes (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella) in one sample. The result confirms the cause, guides contact precautions and bed placement on the ward, and shows whether antibiotics are needed. CT mesenteric angiography is not indicated.
notes: Her soft abdomen, normal lactate, sinus rhythm and pain that matches the examination make mesenteric ischaemia unlikely, and contrast adds risk while she has an AKI.
She has had no recent antibiotics or hospital stay and a contact is also ill, so a test that looks only for C. difficile is too narrow.
Testing for ova and parasites is for travellers, people with diarrhoea lasting more than 7 days or immunocompromised people, and she is none of these.
With a low-grade temperature and no sepsis or immunocompromise, blood cultures are unlikely to be positive, and they would not detect the likely viral cause.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner with 4 months of loose, pale stools that are hard to flush, three to four times a day. She also has bloating, tiredness and has lost 4 kg. She has had no rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, fever or recent travel. She has Hashimoto thyroiditis treated with levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily, and her brother has type 1 diabetes. She eats a normal diet that includes bread and pasta. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse is 84/min and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Her body mass index is 19 kg/m². She has conjunctival pallor. Her abdomen is soft, mildly distended and nontender. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115–165) MCV 75 fL (80–100) Ferritin 5 µg/L (30–300) Serum folate 4.8 nmol/L (>7) Vitamin B12 310 pmol/L (150–700) CRP 3 mg/L (<5) TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.5–4.0) Tissue transglutaminase IgA 180 U/mL (<20) Endomysial antibody IgA: positive Total IgA 2.0 g/L (0.7–4.0) Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: This woman most likely has coeliac disease. She has steatorrhoea, weight loss, iron and folate deficiency with a normal B12 (pointing to the proximal small bowel), and a personal and family history of autoimmune disease. Her tTG-IgA is strongly positive, her EMA is positive and her total IgA is normal. Australian guidance (GESA, Coeliac Australia, eTG) says adults need small-bowel histology to confirm the diagnosis before starting a gluten-free diet. The test is gastroscopy with multiple duodenal biopsies: at least four from the second part of the duodenum and one or two from the bulb. These are taken while she is still eating gluten, and the aim is to show villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis. The no-biopsy approach used in some children is not used for Australian adults. A biopsy also gives a baseline and checks for other pathology. HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genotyping is mainly useful for ruling the disease out: about a third of the population carries these alleles, so a positive result cannot confirm coeliac disease. A gluten challenge is only needed if a patient has already cut out gluten, and she is eating a normal gluten-containing diet.
notes: HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing has a high negative predictive value but is common in the general population, so a positive result cannot confirm coeliac disease.
Colonoscopy with ileal biopsies looks for Crohn's disease or microscopic colitis, and it does not sample the duodenum, where coeliac disease shows.
A gluten challenge is only needed for patients who have already stopped gluten, and she is eating a normal gluten-containing diet.
Faecal elastase tests for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and cannot confirm coeliac disease, which her serology already strongly suggests.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man who has sex with men has fever, sore throat, a maculopapular truncal rash and cervical lymphadenopathy, three weeks after condomless receptive anal sex. Most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.why: A mononucleosis-like illness with rash 2 to 4 weeks after a high-risk exposure suggests primary HIV infection (seroconversion). The first test, per ASHM guidance, is a fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody immunoassay: it picks up p24 antigen before antibodies appear, so it shortens the window period. If it is reactive or unclear, supplementary testing and HIV RNA confirm the diagnosis.
notes: Point-of-care antibody tests are less sensitive in early infection because antibodies may not have formed yet, so a negative result could falsely reassure.
A CD4 count stages and monitors known HIV but cannot diagnose infection, and it may be normal or only briefly low in acute HIV.
A monospot tests for EBV infectious mononucleosis, but this exposure history calls for HIV testing first, and EBV does not explain the risk.
Western blot is a later supplementary test that is often negative or indeterminate during seroconversion, so it is not the first investigation.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with polycystic kidney disease has a sudden severe headache that peaked within a minute while lifting weights. She is drowsy, GCS 14, with neck stiffness. Most appropriate first investigation?
questions.why: A thunderclap headache in a patient with ADPKD (a risk factor for berry aneurysm) is a subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. A non-contrast CT brain is the first test: it is highly sensitive early on, and it also shows hydrocephalus or a mass before any LP is considered. Her reduced GCS means she needs urgent imaging, and the Ottawa SAH rule cannot be used.
notes: Lumbar puncture is only for a suspected SAH with a negative CT, and it should not be done first when the GCS is reduced, because hydrocephalus or a mass has not been excluded.
MRI is slower, less available and harder to do safely in a drowsy patient who is getting worse, and it is not the first-line test for suspected SAH.
Catheter angiography is invasive and is used to define or treat an aneurysm once SAH is confirmed, not as the first test.
A CT venogram looks for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, which is less likely here, and it comes after a non-contrast CT rather than replacing it.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man ventilated in ICU for pneumococcal pneumonia has bilateral infiltrates. Despite tidal volume 6 mL/kg and PEEP 14 cmH2O, his PaO2/FiO2 ratio is 90 mmHg. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 below 100 mmHg) despite lung-protective ventilation. Early prone positioning for at least 12 to 16 hours a day lowers mortality when PaO2/FiO2 is below 150 mmHg (PROSEVA), and ANZICS practice uses it before rescue therapies.
notes: Inhaled nitric oxide improves oxygenation only for a short time, does not lower mortality and is not routine therapy.
Venovenous ECMO is a rescue therapy for hypoxaemia that persists after proning and other optimisation have been tried.
High-frequency oscillation gave no benefit and possible harm in trials (OSCAR, OSCILLATE), so it is not recommended.
Intravenous furosemide can support conservative fluid management, but it does not treat severe hypoxaemia, and nothing here suggests fluid overload.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 2 days of sharp central chest pain. The pain is worse when she lies flat or breathes in, and it eases when she sits forward. She had a sore throat and runny nose a week ago. She has no medical history, takes no regular medicines and weighs 62 kg. Her temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 99% on room air. A scratchy friction rub is heard at the left sternal edge while she holds her breath. An ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression. High-sensitivity troponin I is 4 ng/L at 0 hours and 4 ng/L at 2 hours (women's 99th percentile, under 16). CRP is 38 mg/L (under 5). A chest X-ray is normal, and a bedside echocardiogram shows no pericardial effusion. She is to be discharged on ibuprofen 600 mg orally 8-hourly. Along with the ibuprofen, which of the following is most likely to lower her risk of the most common complication of this condition?
options: Prednisolone 50 mg orally once daily for 5 days
Colchicine 500 micrograms orally once daily for 3 months
Esomeprazole 20 mg orally once daily while on ibuprofen
Colchicine 500 micrograms orally once daily for 1 week
Metoprolol 25 mg orally twice daily for 3 months
questions.why: This woman has low-risk acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis. She has typical pain, a friction rub and typical ECG changes. Her troponin is normal, she has no effusion, her temperature is below 38 °C and the onset was acute, so she can be treated as an outpatient. The most common complication is recurrence, which happens after about 15 to 30% of first episodes. Tamponade and constriction are rare after idiopathic pericarditis. Adding colchicine to an NSAID speeds symptom relief and roughly halves recurrence (ICAP trial). eTG and the 2025 ESC guidelines recommend a 3-month course, dosed by weight: 500 micrograms once daily under 70 kg and twice daily from 70 kg. At 62 kg, she needs the once-daily dose. Ibuprofen is tapered once pain and CRP settle, and she should have gastroprotection. She should also be told to avoid strenuous exercise until symptoms resolve and CRP returns to normal.
notes: First-line corticosteroids increase the risk of recurrent pericarditis, so they are used only when NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated or have failed, or when there is a specific indication.
A proton pump inhibitor is appropriate gastroprotection with high-dose NSAIDs, but it prevents drug-induced gastrointestinal injury and has no effect on recurrent pericarditis.
One week of colchicine is too short to reduce recurrence, because the evidence-based course for a first episode is 3 months.
Beta-blockers have no role in preventing recurrent pericarditis, and her mild tachycardia reflects inflammation and pain rather than a rhythm or ischaemic problem needing rate control.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman sees her GP before starting weekly methotrexate for seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis. Her urine beta-hCG is negative. She has a 3-year-old son and hopes to conceive within two years. Most important counselling point?
questions.why: Methotrexate is teratogenic and can cause miscarriage, so a woman who may become pregnant needs reliable contraception throughout treatment. Any pregnancy should be planned with her rheumatologist, who will stop methotrexate at least 3 months before conception (Australian Rheumatology Association advice) and switch her to a drug that is safe in pregnancy, such as hydroxychloroquine or sulfasalazine.
notes: Methotrexate for RA is taken once a week; taking it daily is a known cause of fatal toxicity.
Inactivated vaccines such as the influenza vaccine are safe and recommended on methotrexate; only live vaccines need care.
Folic acid should be taken weekly, on a different day from methotrexate, to reduce side effects, so it should not be stopped.
Stopping only after a positive pregnancy test is too late: the drug must be stopped at least 3 months before she tries to conceive.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has a PSA of 8.1 ng/mL and a PI-RADS 4 lesion. Transperineal biopsy shows adenocarcinoma: about 80% Gleason pattern 4 and 20% pattern 3. Which ISUP Grade Group is this?
questions.why: The biopsy Gleason score is the most common pattern plus the next most common one. Here that gives 4+3=7, which is ISUP Grade Group 3. Because pattern 4 is the main pattern, this is unfavourable intermediate-risk disease, worse than 3+4.
notes: Grade Group 1 means Gleason 3+3=6, with no pattern 4 at all, but this tumour is mostly pattern 4.
Grade Group 2 means Gleason 3+4=7, where pattern 3 is the main pattern, but here pattern 4 is the main pattern.
Grade Group 4 means Gleason score 8 (4+4, 3+5 or 5+3), and this biopsy has no pattern 5 and is not entirely pattern 4.
Grade Group 5 means Gleason score 9 to 10, which needs pattern 5, and none is reported here.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old concreter presents to the emergency department 10 minutes after wet cement splashed into his right eye. The eye is painful, red and watering. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Wet cement is strongly alkaline. Alkali eye injury is an emergency because it keeps penetrating and damaging the eye until it is washed out. Start copious irrigation straight away (with topical anaesthetic if needed) and continue until the conjunctival pH is neutral (7.0 to 7.5); only then examine the eye and refer.
notes: Chemical injury is the one exception where irrigation comes before visual acuity testing, because every minute of delay adds to corneal damage.
Fluorescein staining shows the extent of epithelial damage, but it is done after irrigation, not before.
Topical antibiotics may be used later for epithelial defects, but they do nothing to neutralise the alkali or stop the injury.
Urgent ophthalmology review is needed, but irrigation must start first and keep going while the referral is arranged.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man has sudden severe retrosternal pain after forceful vomiting following heavy drinking. Heart rate is 118/min, ECG is normal and there is crepitus over the neck. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Chest pain after forceful vomiting, with subcutaneous emphysema in the neck, points to Boerhaave syndrome, which is spontaneous oesophageal rupture. CT of the chest with water-soluble oral contrast is the preferred test. It confirms a contrast leak and also shows pneumomediastinum, effusion and collections, which helps plan urgent surgery.
notes: Barium leaking into the mediastinum causes severe inflammatory mediastinitis, so water-soluble contrast is used instead when perforation is suspected.
Endoscopy with air insufflation can make the tear bigger and worsen pneumomediastinum, so it is not the first test for suspected perforation.
A CT pulmonary angiogram looks for pulmonary embolism and does not use oral contrast to show an oesophageal leak.
Echocardiography looks at the heart and pericardium and cannot show an oesophageal tear or mediastinal contamination.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man is admitted to the rheumatology ward with 3 weeks of painful, swollen hands and 2 hours of morning stiffness each day. He was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis 9 years ago at an interstate hospital, and his records from there cannot be obtained. He stopped methotrexate 5 months ago when he moved and has taken no regular medicines since. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day. Temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 86/min, and blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg. Both wrists and the second to fourth MCP and PIP joints are warm and boggy, and the DIP joints are spared. He has fixed ulnar deviation, swan neck deformities and firm nodules over both elbows. Haemoglobin is 118 g/L (130 to 180), CRP 46 mg/L (less than 5), ALT 24 U/L (less than 40), and creatinine 82 µmol/L (60 to 110). Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are strongly positive. A chest X-ray taken in the emergency department overnight is clear. The team plans a short course of prednisolone and to restart methotrexate. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate before methotrexate is restarted?
questions.why: This man has a flare of established seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis after 5 months off methotrexate. The diagnosis is already settled: he has symmetrical synovitis that spares the DIP joints, fixed deformities, rheumatoid nodules, raised CRP, and strongly positive RF and anti-CCP. The question to answer now is whether it is safe to restart treatment. Australian guidance (eTG Rheumatology and the Australian Rheumatology Association's methotrexate information) says that before starting methotrexate you need a FBC, LFT, UEC, a baseline chest X-ray, and serology for hepatitis B and C. Methotrexate can cause liver injury, and immunosuppression (especially with prednisolone added) can reactivate hepatitis B. His FBC, LFT, creatinine and chest X-ray have already been done. His earlier screening cannot be found and he smokes, so hepatitis B and C serology is the one essential test still missing. It also tells you whether he needs hepatitis B vaccination or antiviral prophylaxis.
notes: A repeat hand X-ray would show how far the damage has progressed, but it does not affect whether methotrexate can be started safely and does not show current disease activity.
Wrist aspiration is for suspected septic arthritis, and this man is afebrile with a symmetrical polyarthritis and no single joint out of proportion to the others.
Serum urate does not help here: the nodules are firm and rubbery, he has never had an acute attack, and strongly positive anti-CCP already confirms rheumatoid arthritis.
An ANA titre looks for lupus, but fixed erosive deformities with strongly positive anti-CCP point to rheumatoid arthritis, not the reversible Jaccoud's arthropathy of SLE.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with newly confirmed HIV-1 infection has baseline serology: hepatitis B surface antigen negative, core antibody negative, surface antibody below 10 mIU/mL. What does this serology indicate?
questions.why: Negative surface antigen and core antibody mean he has never been infected, and a surface antibody below 10 mIU/mL means he is not immune. He is susceptible and should be vaccinated against hepatitis B. Under the Australian Immunisation Handbook, people with HIV may need a higher-dose or extended schedule, with surface antibody checked afterwards.
notes: Chronic hepatitis B needs a positive surface antigen (and core antibody), and both are negative here.
Resolved past infection leaves a positive core antibody, usually with surface antibody of 10 mIU/mL or more, and neither is present.
Vaccine-induced immunity shows as surface antibody of 10 mIU/mL or more with a negative core antibody, and his surface antibody is below 10.
Occult hepatitis B means detectable HBV DNA without surface antigen, usually with a positive core antibody, and his core antibody is negative.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman in the birth suite loses 900 mL after vaginal birth, passing clots; pulse 104 bpm. Her fundus firms with massage and oxytocin, then repeatedly softens. Perineum intact; placenta unexamined. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: If the uterus firms with treatment but keeps relaxing, retained placental tissue (Tissue) is likely. The quickest way to confirm it is to check the placenta and membranes for a missing cotyledon or a ragged defect on the maternal surface. Queensland Clinical Guidelines and RANZCOG list this as a routine step when assessing the four Ts in primary PPH.
notes: Ultrasound can show retained products, but it takes longer and is less reliable straight after birth, so it does not replace first checking the delivered placenta.
Coagulation studies are sent as part of PPH bloods, but she is forming clots and her uterus firms with treatment, so a clotting problem is not the likely cause.
A speculum examination looks for genital tract trauma, but the perineum is intact and a fundus that keeps softening points to the uterus as the source.
A full blood count measures blood loss and how much replacement she needs, but it does not identify why she is bleeding.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner with a 3-month history of tiredness, bloating, and loose, pale, offensive stools that are hard to flush. She has lost 4 kg without trying. She has Hashimoto thyroiditis treated with levothyroxine, and her sister has type 1 diabetes. She eats a normal mixed diet and rarely drinks alcohol. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 84/min and blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. She has conjunctival pallor. Her abdomen is soft, mildly distended and nontender. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 106 g/L (115–160) MCV 75 fL (80–100) Ferritin 7 microgram/L (30–300) Serum folate 5.0 nmol/L (above 7.0) TSH 2.1 mU/L (0.5–4.0) CRP 3 mg/L (below 5) Tissue transglutaminase IgA 96 U/mL (below 20) Total IgA 2.1 g/L (0.7–4.0) Faecal elastase 380 microgram/g (above 200) Stool microscopy, culture and multiplex PCR: no pathogens detected Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Strict gluten-free diet, then repeat serology in 3 months
Pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals
Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies while on her current diet
questions.why: She has malabsorption (steatorrhoea, weight loss, iron and folate deficiency). She also has autoimmune risk factors and a strongly positive tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA, so the serology result can be trusted. This picture is highly likely to be coeliac disease. Coeliac Australia, GESA and eTG advise that adults have the diagnosis confirmed by gastroscopy with multiple duodenal biopsies (including the duodenal bulb) while still eating gluten, to show villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytosis. A biopsy-confirmed diagnosis supports a lifelong gluten-free diet with a dietitian, replacement of iron, folate and vitamin D, bone health assessment, and screening of first-degree relatives. Starting a gluten-free diet before the biopsy can heal the mucosa and make the serology and histology falsely normal. HLA typing is useful only for ruling coeliac disease out. A normal faecal elastase and CRP make pancreatic insufficiency and Crohn disease unlikely.
notes: Removing gluten before the biopsy can heal the mucosa and normalise the serology, which leaves the diagnosis unconfirmed and would need a later gluten challenge.
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing has a high negative predictive value but is present in about a third of the population, so a positive result cannot confirm coeliac disease.
Her normal CRP, lack of blood in the stool and strongly positive tTG-IgA point to coeliac disease rather than ileal Crohn disease, so ileocolonoscopy is not the first investigation.
A normal faecal elastase of 380 microgram/g rules against exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, so enzyme replacement would not treat the cause of her steatorrhoea.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old man has had three falls in a month, each on getting out of bed, preceded by light-headedness. He started tamsulosin two weeks ago. Neurological examination is normal. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Falls with light-headedness on standing, soon after starting an alpha-blocker, point to orthostatic hypotension. Lying and standing blood pressure is a simple bedside test that confirms it: a drop of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing. It should be done first in any multifactorial falls assessment.
notes: A Holter monitor looks for arrhythmia, which is less likely when symptoms only come on standing and the start fits a new alpha-blocker.
With no head injury, no focal signs and a normal neurological examination, CT brain does not explain the falls and should not be the first test.
An echocardiogram looks for structural heart disease such as aortic stenosis, but there is no murmur or exertional syncope to suggest this.
Tilt-table testing is a specialist test for when the diagnosis is still unclear, after simple orthostatic measurements have been done.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman on apixaban for atrial fibrillation has a right subdural haematoma on CT. Her last dose was five hours ago. INR is 1.1 and APTT 31 seconds. Best interpretation of the coagulation results?
questions.why: The INR and APTT pick up apixaban poorly, so normal values do not rule out a clinically important anticoagulant effect. Her last dose was 5 hours ago, which is close to peak level. With an intracranial haemorrhage this means she still needs reversal, such as Prothrombinex-VF or andexanet alfa according to local protocol, plus haematology advice. An apixaban-calibrated anti-Xa level would be needed to measure the drug, and it is not available here.
notes: Apixaban has a half-life of about 12 hours, so it cannot have cleared 5 hours after a dose, and normal clotting tests cannot show that it has.
Reversal for intracranial haemorrhage depends on the timing of the last dose, not on the INR or APTT, so she still needs it.
The INR and APTT cannot measure apixaban levels, and normal values give no sign of an excess.
A consumptive coagulopathy would prolong the INR and APTT, and both are normal.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old man comes to his general practitioner for a cardiovascular risk assessment. He feels well and says his blood pressure "always jumps" at the doctor's. He takes no regular medicines, vapes nicotine daily and drinks four coffees a day. He is seated and has rested for 5 minutes, and a correctly sized cuff is used. His blood pressure is 152/94 mmHg and then 148/92 mmHg in the right arm, and 150/92 mmHg in the left arm. His pulse is 74/min. His BMI is 29 kg/m2. His fundi, heart sounds and peripheral pulses are normal. He brings a list of 9 home readings from the past 12 days. He took them on a wrist monitor he bought online, one reading each evening after dinner and coffee. They average 126/79 mmHg. A 12-lead ECG is normal. Serum potassium is 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), eGFR is above 90 mL/min/1.73 m2 and the urine albumin to creatinine ratio is 1.0 mg/mmol (below 2.5). Which of the following best describes the significance of his home readings?
options: They demonstrate a normal nocturnal dipping pattern
They are inadequate to confirm or exclude hypertension
questions.why: His repeated clinic readings of 148 to 152/92 to 94 mmHg are in the grade 1 range. He has no end-organ damage (normal fundi, ECG, eGFR and urine albumin), so the Heart Foundation guideline says to confirm the diagnosis with out-of-office measurement before labelling or treating him. A home average below 135/85 mmHg would usually point to white coat hypertension, but only if it comes from a valid protocol. That protocol is a validated upper-arm device with a correctly sized cuff, two seated readings one minute apart every morning and evening for 7 days, discarding day 1 and averaging the rest. His readings fail it. The wrist device is not validated, he took single evening readings only, he took them after caffeine, and he has too few readings. They can neither confirm nor exclude hypertension. The next step is 24-hour ambulatory monitoring or a correctly done home protocol. A diagnosis of white coat hypertension cannot rest on invalid home data. Sustained hypertension is not confirmed because the out-of-office data are unreliable and, as recorded, normal. Masked hypertension is the reverse pattern: normal in the clinic and raised outside it.
notes: White coat hypertension can only be diagnosed from a valid out-of-office measurement, and these single, post-caffeine evening readings on an unvalidated wrist device are not one.
Sustained hypertension needs a valid out-of-office average of at least 135/85 mmHg, and his recorded average is normal, though unreliable.
Masked hypertension means normal clinic but raised out-of-office readings, which is the opposite of his pattern.
Nocturnal dipping can only be judged from ambulatory readings taken during sleep, not from evening home readings taken while awake.

questions.stem: A 20-month-old girl had a 2-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home with fever of 38.9 °C and coryza. One hour later she is alert with no meningism and a normal neurological examination. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is a simple febrile seizure: generalised, under 15 minutes, full recovery within 1 hour, and a clear viral source. The RCH guideline advises no routine investigations. The next step is to reassure the parents, teach seizure first aid and when to return, and discharge her.
notes: An EEG does not predict recurrence or later epilepsy after a simple febrile seizure, so it is not indicated.
A lumbar puncture is for meningism, ongoing drowsiness, or a very young or unwell child, and she is alert with no meningism.
Neuroimaging is not indicated after a simple febrile seizure with full recovery and a normal neurological examination.
Antipyretics are for comfort only and do not prevent febrile seizures from recurring.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 3 hours of worsening breathlessness and chest tightness that began after he mowed his lawn. He has asthma and uses budesonide-formoterol only when he has symptoms. He has never been admitted to intensive care. On arrival, he could speak only 3 to 4 words at a time and was using his accessory muscles. Over the past hour, he has had oxygen titrated to his saturation, salbutamol 12 puffs and ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer every 20 minutes, and prednisolone 50 mg orally. He is now alert but still speaks in short phrases and has a tracheal tug. Temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 124/min, respiratory rate 30/min, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg and SpO2 93% on oxygen 2 L/min by nasal prongs. He has widespread expiratory wheeze with good bilateral air entry and a central trachea. There is no rash or lip swelling. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.47 (7.32 to 7.43) and pCO2 32 mmHg (38 to 50). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: This man still has severe acute asthma after a full first hour of treatment. He speaks only in short phrases, has a tracheal tug and a respiratory rate of 30/min, and needs oxygen to keep his SpO2 at 93%. He has no life-threatening features: he is alert, air entry is good, and his pCO2 is low rather than normal or rising. He has already had the right first-line treatment from the Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG: titrated oxygen, repeated salbutamol with ipratropium, and oral prednisolone within the first hour. When severe asthma does not respond to this, the next step is magnesium sulfate 10 mmol given intravenously over 20 minutes. He should also have continued bronchodilators and an early senior or ICU review. Aminophylline is not recommended because it adds no benefit to inhaled bronchodilators and has a narrow therapeutic index with arrhythmia and seizure risk. Intravenous hydrocortisone works no better than oral prednisolone, which he has already taken and can swallow. Intramuscular adrenaline is for anaphylaxis, and he has no rash, angioedema or hypotension; adrenaline in asthma is kept for life-threatening attacks that fail all other treatment.
notes: Aminophylline is not recommended in acute asthma because it adds no benefit over inhaled bronchodilators and causes arrhythmias, vomiting and seizures.
Intravenous hydrocortisone works no better than the oral prednisolone he has already taken and can swallow, so giving it adds nothing.
Intramuscular adrenaline treats anaphylaxis, and he has a clear asthma trigger with no rash, lip swelling or hypotension.
Montelukast is a maintenance controller with no role in treating a severe acute exacerbation.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman taking rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation has had four days of worsening headache after tripping and hitting her forehead a week ago. GCS is 14. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: An older anticoagulated patient with a progressive headache after minor head trauma and a reduced GCS needs an urgent non-contrast CT brain to look for a subdural haematoma. NSW head injury guidance says every anticoagulated patient with a head injury needs CT. It is fast, widely available and sensitive for acute blood, and the result guides reversal and neurosurgical referral.
notes: MRI is slower and less available, it is unsafe to send a patient with a falling GCS for it, and contrast adds nothing in looking for acute blood.
Lumbar puncture does not image a subdural collection, and it is dangerous with possible mass effect and an anticoagulant on board.
A skull X-ray may show a fracture but cannot show intracranial blood, so a normal film would give false reassurance.
ESR and CRP help screen for giant cell arteritis, but the head trauma, anticoagulant and falling GCS point to a bleed, which must be imaged first.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 30 minutes of sudden, fast, regular palpitations that began while she was sitting at rest. Her first ECG showed a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 150/min. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre reverted it to sinus rhythm. On further questioning, she reports 4 months of 5 kg weight loss, heat intolerance, loose stools and feeling on edge. She has no past medical history and takes no medicines. After reversion, her pulse is 98/min and regular, blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 16/min, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air and temperature is 37.3 °C. She has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands and a diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre with no palpable nodules. There is no proptosis. A repeat 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with a normal PR interval and no delta waves. Blood results: TSH <0.01 mIU/L (0.4–4.0), free T4 32 pmol/L (10–25), free T3 11.5 pmol/L (3.5–6.5), beta-hCG negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause of her hyperthyroidism?
questions.why: She had an SVT (probably AVNRT) set off by thyrotoxicosis. A suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and free T3 means primary hyperthyroidism. In a young woman with 4 months of symptoms and a diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre with no nodules, Graves' disease is the most likely cause. Therapeutic Guidelines (Endocrinology) recommend TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) as the first test to confirm Graves' disease. The test is highly sensitive and specific, cheap, carries no radiation, and the level helps predict relapse after antithyroid drugs. A positive TRAb confirms the diagnosis, so no imaging is needed and an antithyroid drug can be started with endocrinology input. Thyroid scintigraphy is kept for when TRAb is negative or the cause is unclear, for example a nodular gland or possible thyroiditis. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are not specific, ultrasound does not tell the causes apart, and fine-needle aspiration is only for suspicious nodules.
notes: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are found in both Graves' disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis, and in many healthy people, so a positive result does not confirm the cause.
Scintigraphy is a second-line test, used when TRAb is negative or a nodular gland or thyroiditis is suspected, and it means a radiation dose that this diffuse goitre does not need.
Ultrasound shows the size and structure of the gland but does not reliably tell Graves' disease from other causes, and it is mainly used when nodules are felt, which she does not have.
Fine-needle aspiration checks thyroid nodules for cancer, so it has no role in finding the cause of hyperthyroidism in a smooth goitre with no nodules.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old unvaccinated man sees his GP with jaundice after week-long malaise, four weeks after Vietnam travel with a hepatitis A-infected companion. Tender hepatomegaly; ALT 1240 IU/L, ALP 150 U/L. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: He is an unvaccinated traveller with a known hepatitis A contact, an incubation period that fits, a prodrome, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and a hepatocellular pattern of liver tests, so acute hepatitis A is most likely. The CDNA national guideline (SoNG) confirms acute infection with a positive HAV IgM, which is present at symptom onset and lasts for about 3 to 6 months.
notes: Total anti-HAV is mostly IgG, so it is also positive after past infection or vaccination and cannot show that the infection is acute.
HAV RNA testing is not routine, and the viraemia may be waning by the time jaundice appears, so it is less reliable than IgM.
Hepatitis E is also spread by the enteric route in Asia, but his contact with a confirmed hepatitis A case makes hepatitis A far more likely.
Malaria causes mainly unconjugated, haemolytic jaundice with fever, not an ALT rise to over 30 times normal after a contact with hepatitis A.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is reviewed on the cardiology ward of a metropolitan hospital before discharge. He was admitted 5 days ago with 3 months of worsening exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea and ankle swelling, 18 months after an anterior STEMI treated with PCI. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and knee osteoarthritis. With IV furosemide he has diuresed 6 kg and now walks the ward corridor without breathlessness. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. His discharge medicines are oral furosemide 40 mg mane, bisoprolol 2.5 mg, sacubitril/valsartan 24/26 mg twice a day, spironolactone 12.5 mg, dapagliflozin 10 mg, aspirin, atorvastatin and metformin. Temperature is 36.6 °C, pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, respirations 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. The JVP is not raised and there is no pitting oedema. Serum sodium is 137 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.2) and creatinine 104 µmol/L (60–110). Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to give him before discharge?
options: Weigh himself each morning and book a GP review if he gains more than 2 kg in 2 days
Limit his fluid intake to 1 litre per day whatever his thirst or sodium level
Rest at home and avoid walking until his cardiology review in 6 weeks
Use a potassium-based salt substitute to cut the sodium in his cooking
Stop his bisoprolol if he feels more tired during the next few weeks
questions.why: This man has HFrEF from an ischaemic cardiomyopathy and has just been discharged after his first decompensation. His biggest near-term risk is fluid building up again and bringing him back to hospital. Weight gain from fluid usually shows up before breathlessness or visible oedema. The Heart Foundation/CSANZ guidelines and eTG recommend that he weighs himself every morning, on the same scales, after voiding and before breakfast. He should see his GP promptly if he gains more than 2 kg over 2 days or if his swelling or breathlessness gets worse. He should call 000 for chest pain or severe breathlessness. Self-monitoring like this, as part of a heart failure disease-management program, lowers readmission and death. A strict 1 L fluid limit is not routine; restriction to about 1.5 L/day is kept for severe congestion or hyponatraemia, and his sodium is normal. Supervised exercise and cardiac rehabilitation are recommended in stable HFrEF, so bed rest is wrong. Potassium-based salt substitutes risk hyperkalaemia in a patient on an ARNI plus an MRA whose potassium is already 4.8 mmol/L.
notes: Routine strict fluid restriction is not recommended; about 1.5 L/day is kept for severe congestion or hyponatraemia, and his sodium is normal.
Regular exercise and cardiac rehabilitation improve symptoms and lower hospitalisation in stable HFrEF, so avoiding walking is harmful.
Potassium chloride salt substitutes can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia in a patient on sacubitril/valsartan and spironolactone whose potassium is already high-normal.
Fatigue early in beta-blocker treatment is common and usually short-lived, and stopping it removes a proven mortality benefit and can bring on ischaemia or arrhythmia.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with a previous anterior myocardial infarction has two months of exertional breathlessness, orthopnoea and ankle oedema. NT-proBNP is 4100 ng/L; chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly and small bilateral effusions. Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: A raised NT-proBNP with typical symptoms and X-ray signs makes heart failure very likely. The Australian (NHFA/CSANZ) heart failure guidelines recommend a transthoracic echocardiogram to confirm it, show the ejection fraction and structural cause, and guide treatment. Small bilateral effusions with heart failure are usually transudates and do not need to be tapped at first.
notes: Coronary angiography looks for ischaemia to treat after heart failure is confirmed, but it does not confirm the diagnosis itself.
CT pulmonary angiography is for suspected PE, which does not fit gradual orthopnoea, symmetrical oedema and cardiomegaly.
Small bilateral effusions with cardiac failure are usually transudates that settle with diuresis, so routine aspiration is not needed.
Spirometry assesses airflow obstruction such as COPD and cannot confirm or describe heart failure.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man, intubated in the emergency department, has return of circulation after a 12-minute ventricular fibrillation arrest. Venous gas: pH 7.10, pCO2 60 mmHg, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, lactate 9.0 mmol/L. Best interpretation of the gas?
questions.why: The pCO2 is high and the bicarbonate is low, so both are pushing the pH down. This is a mixed acidosis: respiratory from hypoventilation during the arrest, and lactic from hypoperfusion. Both are expected after cardiac arrest and are treated with ventilation to normocapnia and restoring perfusion, not with bicarbonate.
notes: Respiratory compensation would lower the pCO2 to about 33 mmHg (Winters' formula), not raise it to 60.
A pure acute respiratory acidosis would raise the bicarbonate slightly (to about 26), not leave it low with a lactate of 9.0.
A respiratory alkalosis needs a low pCO2, but here it is raised at 60 mmHg.
Compensation for a respiratory acidosis raises the bicarbonate, and the pH would not be as low as 7.10.
