questions.stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the emergency department 90 minutes after sudden onset of sharp right-sided pain and breathlessness. Both started while he was sitting at his desk at work. The pain is worse with deep breaths and has not eased with rest. He has no cough, fever, haemoptysis, leg swelling, recent travel or trauma. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and takes no medicines. He is 191 cm tall and weighs 68 kg. His temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 22/min, blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He speaks in full sentences. The trachea is central and the jugular venous pressure is not raised. Over the right hemithorax, expansion is reduced, the percussion note is hyper-resonant and breath sounds are reduced. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 104/min with no ST-segment or T-wave changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: This tall, thin young man who smokes has sudden one-sided pleuritic pain and breathlessness. He has reduced expansion, a hyper-resonant percussion note and reduced breath sounds on the right, so the most likely diagnosis is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and needs decompression straight away, before any imaging. Here there are no features of tension: his blood pressure is normal, the trachea is central and the JVP is not raised. That means there is time to confirm the diagnosis. The first-line test is a standard erect posteroanterior chest radiograph taken in inspiration (BTS 2023, used in Australian EDs). It shows the visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it, lets you measure the size of the pneumothorax (2 cm or more at the hilum is large) and shows any mediastinal shift. Together with his symptoms, this guides the choice between observation, needle aspiration, an ambulatory device or a drain. CT is kept for unclear or complex cases.
notes: An arterial blood gas does not confirm or size a pneumothorax, and with an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air it is not needed to assess his oxygenation.
CT pulmonary angiography involves radiation and contrast and looks for pulmonary embolism, which is unlikely here with no risk factors and clear one-sided signs of air in the pleural space.
Expiratory films are no longer recommended because they add little to detection over a standard inspiratory film and can make the size of the pneumothorax harder to judge.
A D-dimer is non-specific, does not confirm a pneumothorax, and should not come before imaging when the examination already points strongly to another diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of 10 weeks of crampy right lower abdominal pain and four to six loose stools a day. Some stools are streaked by blood, and they wake him from sleep. He has lost 4 kg without trying and has had occasional night sweats. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and has taken ibuprofen most days for the pain. He has not travelled and has had no antibiotics in the past 3 months. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 92/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. He is tender in the right iliac fossa, where there is vague fullness but no guarding. A soft perianal skin tag is present. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (130–180), CRP 42 mg/L (<5) and albumin 31 g/L (35–50). Faecal calprotectin is 640 µg/g (<50). Stool bacterial and parasite PCR, culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin are negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: This young man most likely has ileocolonic Crohn's disease. The clues are a chronic history (over 6 weeks) of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea with blood, weight loss, low-grade fever, a perianal skin tag, smoking, raised inflammatory markers, low albumin and a very high faecal calprotectin, with negative stool tests for infection. Under GESA and eTG guidance, diagnosis needs ileocolonoscopy, meaning colonoscopy that passes into the terminal ileum, with biopsies from the ileum and from each colonic segment, including normal-looking areas. This shows how far the disease extends and whether there are skip lesions or rectal sparing. Histology can show patchy transmural-type inflammation and non-caseating granulomas, and it can exclude intestinal tuberculosis, infection and malignancy. Small-bowel imaging is added after the diagnosis to stage the disease, not to make it. He should also stop ibuprofen and get urgent referral to gastroenterology.
notes: Flexible sigmoidoscopy only reaches the distal colon, so it would miss ileocaecal disease, and the rectum and sigmoid are often spared in Crohn's disease.
MR enterography is useful for staging small-bowel extent, strictures and fistulae once the diagnosis is made, but it gives no tissue and cannot confirm the diagnosis.
Capsule endoscopy takes no biopsies and is not a first-line test, and an ileocaecal mass or stricture puts him at risk of the capsule getting stuck.
ASCA and ANCA serology has low sensitivity and specificity, so it cannot confirm or exclude Crohn's disease, and guidelines do not recommend it for diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 21-day-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents on the advice of their general practitioner because of jaundice. Her skin has been yellow since day 4, her stools have been pale grey for the past 9 days, and her urine stains the nappy dark. The GP took a capillary blood sample this morning, and the heel site oozed for 20 minutes. She was born at term at home after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her parents declined all newborn injections. She is exclusively breastfed and has regained her birth weight. Temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 148/min and respirations 38/min. She is alert and jaundiced, with a soft, flat fontanelle. The liver is firm, 3 cm below the right costal margin. There is no bruising and no petechiae. Results: total bilirubin 186 µmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 121 µmol/L (less than 25), INR 3.6 (0.9 to 1.2), APTT 66 s (25 to 38), platelets 305 x 10^9/L and haemoglobin 131 g/L. Cranial ultrasound shows no haemorrhage. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Phytomenadione 1 mg by slow intravenous injection
questions.why: This infant has conjugated (cholestatic) jaundice with pale stools, dark urine and a firm liver, which should be treated as biliary atresia until it is ruled out. She also has late vitamin K deficiency bleeding. She never had prophylaxis, she is exclusively breastfed, and cholestasis stops her absorbing fat-soluble vitamins. Her INR and APTT are prolonged, her platelets are normal, and the heel site oozed. This may be a warning bleed before an intracranial haemorrhage. Australian guidance (NHMRC, RCH jaundice in early infancy) says to give vitamin K 1 mg straight away, without waiting for further results. In hospital it is given by slow IV injection, which works within hours and avoids a haematoma from an IM injection while clotting is deranged. Repeat the INR afterwards. The urgent cholestasis work-up and referral to the liver service go ahead at the same time. Plasma products are kept for active serious bleeding, and the cranial ultrasound shows no haemorrhage.
notes: Oral vitamin K is poorly and unpredictably absorbed when there is cholestasis and fat malabsorption, so it is not acceptable for treating a deficiency.
Fresh frozen plasma is kept for active life-threatening bleeding or intracranial haemorrhage, and neither is present here, so vitamin K alone is the right treatment.
Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and does nothing for conjugated jaundice or the coagulopathy, which is the immediate danger.
Ursodeoxycholic acid may be used later in some cholestatic conditions, but it does not correct the prolonged INR and it does not treat the bleeding risk.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man on a ward is given double his prescribed enoxaparin dose through a charting error. After review he is haemodynamically stable, with no bleeding, and monitoring is arranged. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Under the Australian Open Disclosure Framework, once the patient's immediate safety is secured, the next step is to tell the patient promptly, apologise, explain what happened and what will be done about it. The error should also be recorded in an incident report, but this does not replace disclosure.
notes: Waiting until discharge breaks the requirement for timely disclosure and leaves him unaware of a risk while he is still being monitored.
He has decision-making capacity, so he has the right to hear first, and telling family without his consent breaches confidentiality.
A single system-based charting error with no impairment or misconduct does not meet the threshold for a mandatory notification to AHPRA.
Disclosure is required for any adverse event, and an incident that could still cause harm must be disclosed now, not only once harm appears.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with breathlessness and wheeze that began 6 hours ago, two days into a head cold. She has had asthma since childhood and uses only a salbutamol reliever. When she arrived 70 minutes ago, she could speak only in phrases and was using her accessory muscles. Since then she has had salbutamol 12 puffs and ipratropium 8 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes for three doses, prednisolone 50 mg orally, and oxygen by nasal prongs. She is alert but still speaks in phrases and uses her accessory muscles. Temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 118/min, respirations 28/min, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg and SpO2 94% on 2 L/min oxygen. There is widespread expiratory wheeze with equal air entry on both sides, and no rash or lip swelling. Venous blood gas: pH 7.44, pCO2 36 mmHg (reference 41–51), lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation, with no pneumothorax or consolidation. Salbutamol is being continued. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: This is severe acute asthma (she speaks only in phrases and uses her accessory muscles) that has not responded well to an hour of standard treatment. She has had repeated salbutamol and ipratropium by spacer, oral prednisolone within the first hour, and oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 92–96%. The Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG advise adding IV magnesium sulfate (10 mmol over 20 minutes in adults) for severe or life-threatening asthma that responds poorly to the first bronchodilators. Salbutamol continues alongside it. She has no life-threatening features: she is alert, her SpO2 is 90% or above, her pCO2 is low rather than normal or rising, and her chest is not silent. So she does not yet need intubation, but she needs senior review and close monitoring. Aminophylline is not recommended in Australian guidelines because it adds little to standard treatment and causes arrhythmias, vomiting and seizures. IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or impending arrest, and she has no urticaria, angioedema or hypotension. IV hydrocortisone adds nothing when oral prednisolone has been given and can be swallowed.
notes: Aminophylline is not recommended in Australian guidelines: it gives little extra bronchodilation and has a narrow therapeutic index, with a risk of arrhythmias and seizures.
IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or near-arrest, and she has no urticaria, angioedema, stridor or hypotension.
She has already had oral prednisolone and can swallow; IV corticosteroid is no more effective and is only needed when oral intake is not possible.
A viral cold triggered this attack, and with no fever, purulent sputum or consolidation there is no indication for antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old woman with COPD on home oxygen and paroxysmal AF has worsening breathlessness, purulent sputum and fever 38.1 °C. ECG: regular rhythm, 110/min, P wave before each QRS. Most likely rhythm?
questions.why: A regular rhythm at 110/min with a normal P wave before every QRS is sinus tachycardia. In this patient it fits fever, hypoxaemia and an infective COPD exacerbation, so her known AF is not what is driving the breathlessness.
notes: A P wave before every QRS, a regular rhythm and a rate just over 100/min define sinus tachycardia, which fits fever and an exacerbation.
Atrial flutter shows sawtooth flutter waves, and with 2:1 block the rate is usually about 150/min, not 110/min.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is linked to COPD, but it is irregular and has at least three different P-wave shapes.
AV nodal reentry usually runs at 140 to 250/min, and the P waves are hidden or retrograde rather than upright before each QRS.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain through to his back. CT shows an ascending aortic intimal flap. His BP falls to 80/50 mmHg with distended neck veins and pulsus paradoxus. Most likely cause of his hypotension?
questions.why: A Stanford type A dissection can rupture backwards into the pericardium, and the resulting haemopericardium is a leading cause of death. Hypotension with a raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus means tamponade. Treat it by resuscitating and taking him straight to theatre for cardiothoracic surgery, and do not give a beta blocker or try to lower his BP.
notes: Acute aortic regurgitation causes hypotension with pulmonary oedema and an early diastolic murmur, not pulsus paradoxus.
Tension pneumothorax needs a pleural air leak, which a dissection does not cause, and it would give absent breath sounds on one side and a shifted trachea.
Right ventricular infarction can give a raised JVP and hypotension, but pulsus paradoxus points to pericardial compression, and dissecting into the right coronary is less common.
A haemothorax from rupture causes hypovolaemic shock with collapsed neck veins, not distended ones.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has had purulent vaginal discharge for 4 days. Examination shows vulvovaginitis only. Vaginal swab culture grows Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and repeat testing confirms it. What does this result most likely indicate?
questions.why: Outside the neonatal period, confirmed gonorrhoea in a prepubertal child is diagnostic of sexual contact and should be treated as sexual abuse. In Australia this triggers mandatory reporting to child protection and referral to a specialist child protection unit, and the specimens must be handled as forensic evidence.
notes: Perinatal infection shows up in the first weeks of life as ophthalmia or vaginitis, not at age 6.
N. gonorrhoeae dies quickly outside the body, so fomite spread is not an accepted explanation in a child.
Culture plus confirmatory repeat testing excludes a contaminated or false-positive specimen.
N. gonorrhoeae is never normal flora; finding it always means infection.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents 30 hours after condomless receptive anal sex with a casual male partner of unknown HIV status. Blood for baseline HIV testing has been taken. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Under ASHM national PEP guidelines, PEP is recommended after condomless receptive anal sex with a male partner of unknown HIV status. It should be started as soon as possible and within 72 hours of the exposure. Take baseline bloods first, but do not wait for the results before giving the first dose.
notes: Waiting for the baseline result delays PEP, which works better the sooner it starts. The baseline test only shows whether he already had HIV before this exposure.
Event-driven PrEP is taken 2 to 24 hours before sex to prevent infection. It is not the regimen for an exposure that has already happened, although he should be offered PrEP after he finishes PEP.
Repeat serology at follow-up is part of care, but on its own it misses the chance to prevent infection while he is still inside the PEP window.
Reassurance alone is wrong because this is the highest-risk sexual exposure, and the guidelines recommend PEP for it.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman sees her general practitioner because she has not opened her bowels for 6 days. Nine days ago she had an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendicectomy. She went home on oxycodone 5 mg up to four times daily, which she still takes three times a day. She was given no bowel medicine. Her last stools were small and hard. She had to strain, passing them caused sharp anal pain, and there was bright red blood on the toilet paper. She is passing flatus and has no vomiting or abdominal pain. She takes ferrous sulfate for iron deficiency. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 78/min and blood pressure 120/78 mm Hg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and bowel sounds are normal. Anal inspection shows a posterior midline fissure. Digital rectal examination finds hard stool and no mass. Haemoglobin is 124 g/L (115–165), ferritin 20 µg/L (30–300), corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10–2.60) and TSH 1.4 mIU/L (0.5–4.0). The opioid will be weaned and simple analgesia started. Which of the following is the most appropriate laxative treatment?
questions.why: This woman has opioid-induced constipation, made worse by oral iron and less activity after surgery. Passing hard stool has caused an acute anal fissure. Postoperative ileus and obstruction are unlikely: she is passing flatus, has no pain or vomiting, and her abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds. Opioids slow gut transit and make stools dry and hard. eTG recommends a regular stimulant laxative (such as senna) combined with an osmotic laxative (such as macrogol) for opioid-induced constipation, continued while she takes the opioid. Treatment should then be stepped down. Softening the stool is also the main treatment for the fissure: it stops the repeated tearing that keeps the fissure from healing and that would push it toward becoming chronic. Fibre, warm baths and simple analgesia help as well, and topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem can be added if the fissure does not heal. Bulk-forming agents add volume without improving the slowed transit, and can make symptoms worse. Peripherally acting opioid antagonists are used only when standard laxatives have failed. Softeners alone and as-needed rectal treatment are not enough for ongoing opioid use.
notes: Bulk-forming laxatives are not recommended in opioid-induced constipation because they add bulk to slowed bowel and can worsen bloating and impaction.
Peripherally acting opioid antagonists are kept for constipation that has not responded to standard laxatives, which she has not yet tried.
A stool softener on its own does not overcome the slowed transit caused by opioids and is not effective enough as the only treatment.
As-needed suppositories are a rescue measure, not maintenance therapy, and inserting them through a painful acute fissure is poorly tolerated.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presents to his GP with 14 hours of periumbilical pain, anorexia and vomiting. Temperature is 38.3 °C, heart rate 112/min, with rebound tenderness at McBurney's point. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Periumbilical pain with anorexia, vomiting, fever, tachycardia and localised peritonism at McBurney's point points to acute appendicitis, which needs same-day referral to ED for surgical review. The GP should phone a handover, keep him nil by mouth, give analgesia (it does not mask the diagnosis) and arrange safe transport.
notes: Imaging is arranged in hospital as part of surgical assessment; ordering it as an outpatient delays treatment and raises the risk of perforation.
Non-operative treatment of appendicitis uses IV antibiotics in hospital after imaging, and oral antibiotics in general practice are not appropriate with peritonism.
Fever, tachycardia and rebound tenderness show established inflammation, and waiting 24 hours risks perforation and peritonitis.
Outpatient ultrasound delays definitive care and cannot reliably exclude appendicitis in an adult man with peritonism.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man admitted with an NSTEMI is on cardiac telemetry awaiting coronary angiography. He takes indapamide. His potassium is 3.2 mmol/L and magnesium 0.61 mmol/L. Telemetry shows frequent ventricular ectopics. Most appropriate preventive step?
questions.why: In acute coronary ischaemia, low potassium and magnesium (here caused by the thiazide-like diuretic) make ventricular fibrillation more likely. Replacing them, aiming for potassium of at least 4.0 mmol/L and magnesium of at least 1.0 mmol/L, is the simple, reversible step that lowers this risk while he waits for revascularisation. Ventricular ectopics alone are not treated with prophylactic antiarrhythmics.
notes: Prophylactic amiodarone in ACS has not been shown to improve survival, and it leaves the electrolyte trigger untreated.
Prophylactic lignocaine after myocardial infarction is not recommended because it has been linked to higher mortality.
A wearable defibrillator is not used in the early inpatient phase before revascularisation, and it prevents nothing.
Temporary pacing is for symptomatic bradycardia or high-grade AV block, and he has neither.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a pelvic ring fracture on trauma CT after a motorcycle crash. He is haemodynamically stable, with blood at the urethral meatus and inability to void. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A pelvic fracture with blood at the meatus and inability to void suggests a posterior urethral injury. A retrograde urethrogram should be done to confirm it before any attempt at urethral catheterisation, because a blind catheter can turn a partial tear into a complete one. If the urethra is disrupted, the bladder is drained with a suprapubic catheter.
notes: A retrograde CT cystogram needs a urethral catheter to fill the bladder, so the urethra must be cleared first.
An intravenous urogram looks at the kidneys and ureters and does not show the urethra well.
Renal tract ultrasound cannot reliably show a urethral tear and would not change management here.
A urine dipstick only detects haematuria, which does not tell you where the bleeding is, and he cannot void anyway.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back and a brief blackout. BP is 150/88 mmHg in the left arm, 118/72 mmHg in the right. Most likely cause of the BP difference?
questions.why: A sudden tearing pain that goes through to the back, with syncope, points to a type A aortic dissection. Here the right arm reads 32 mmHg lower than the left. The flap has most likely spread into the brachiocephalic (innominate) trunk and is cutting off blood flow to the right subclavian artery. An arm-to-arm systolic difference of more than 20 mmHg is a sign that a branch artery is being underperfused (malperfusion).
notes: A flap in the left subclavian artery would lower the pressure in the left arm, but here the left arm reads higher.
Atheroma narrows an artery slowly over years, so it cannot explain a new arm difference that appeared with this sudden tearing pain.
Coarctation is present from birth and mainly causes a difference between arm and leg pressures, not a new right-sided drop with tearing pain.
Aortic regurgitation widens the pulse pressure equally in both arms, so it cannot cause a difference between them.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman has guarding and shoulder-tip pain 3 hours after hysteroscopy and curettage. After 1 L crystalloid, BP rises from 86/50 to 94/56 mmHg; haemoglobin 95 g/L (pre-operatively 131). Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She is still shocked after 1 L of crystalloid, and her haemoglobin has fallen by 36 g/L with peritonism. Together these mean she is still bleeding inside the abdomen, most likely from a uterine perforation. Under the National Blood Authority critical bleeding guideline she needs blood now, with the massive transfusion protocol if needed, while the senior gynaecologist and theatre are called urgently for surgical control.
notes: Wrong: more crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and red cells, and the guideline limits it in critical bleeding once 1 L has failed to restore perfusion.
Wrong: vasopressors do not treat hypovolaemia from ongoing bleeding and can hide how much blood she has lost.
Wrong: CT is only for stable patients, and taking a shocked patient with peritonism to the scanner delays transfusion and surgery.
Wrong: early haemoglobin underestimates acute blood loss, and waiting for repeat values delays treatment in a woman who is already shocked.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 40 minutes after her horse fell on her during a trail ride, crushing the right side of her chest. She had right-sided pleuritic pain straight away and has become steadily more breathless during transport. She has no past medical history and takes only a combined oral contraceptive pill. On arrival she is agitated and can speak only in single words. Temperature is 36.4 °C, pulse 138/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, and oxygen saturation 85% on 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask. Her trachea is deviated to the left and her neck veins are distended. There is bruising and tenderness over the right lateral ribs. The right hemithorax is hyper-resonant to percussion, and breath sounds are absent on the right. Heart sounds are clearly audible. Two large-bore cannulae are in place and blood has been sent for group and hold. A mobile chest X-ray has been requested, and the radiographer will arrive in 10 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Portable chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis before any chest procedure
Subxiphoid pericardiocentesis guided by bedside ultrasound
Rapid sequence intubation followed by positive-pressure ventilation
Needle decompression at the fifth intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line
Intravenous bolus of 1 L warmed crystalloid over 15 minutes
questions.why: This woman has a right tension pneumothorax after blunt chest trauma, with obstructive shock. She has hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the injured side, and a hyper-resonant hemithorax with absent breath sounds. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. ATLS (11th edition) and eTG advise treating it as soon as it is recognised, without waiting for imaging. In adults, the preferred site for needle decompression is the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, because the chest wall is thinner there and the catheter is more likely to reach the pleura than at the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line. Finger thoracostomy at the same site is an acceptable alternative. After decompression, an intercostal catheter is placed in the safe triangle and connected to an underwater seal. A chest X-ray should be done only after that.
notes: Wrong: tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically, and waiting 10 minutes for a film in a hypotensive, hypoxic patient risks cardiac arrest.

Wrong: tamponade is unlikely because her trachea is deviated, one side of her chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds, and her heart sounds are clear, so the chest needs decompressing rather than the pericardium.
Wrong: positive-pressure ventilation forces more air into the pleural space and can quickly worsen a tension pneumothorax and cause arrest if the chest has not been decompressed first.
Wrong: her shock is obstructive, not caused by blood loss, so fluid will not restore venous return while the tension pneumothorax is untreated, and giving it delays the treatment that saves her life.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a painless 2.5 cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe. TSH is 0.05 mIU/L (reference 0.4 to 4.0) and free T4 is high-normal. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A thyroid nodule with a suppressed TSH suggests an autonomously functioning (toxic) nodule. The next step is thyroid scintigraphy to check whether the nodule is hot. Hot nodules are rarely malignant, so they usually do not need FNA. Cold or indeterminate nodules then need ultrasound-guided FNA.
notes: A suppressed TSH means you first need to know the nodule's function, and a technetium scan shows whether it is hot (autonomous) or cold.
Contrast CT does not show the nodule's function, and the iodine load can worsen hyperthyroidism and delay radioiodine treatment.
Calcitonin screens for medullary carcinoma and does not explain a suppressed TSH, so it is not the decisive next test.
Core biopsy is more invasive than FNA and is not a first-line test for a thyroid nodule, especially one that may be hot.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman is in recovery 2 hours after hysteroscopy and curettage. She has guarding, BP 84/50 mmHg despite crystalloid and 2 units of red cells, and fat in the curettings. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Fat in the curettings means uterine perforation until proven otherwise. She is still in shock and has peritonism despite fluid and blood, so she needs emergency laparoscopy or laparotomy to stop the bleeding and look for bowel, bladder or vessel injury. CT is only for stable patients, when the senior gynaecologist asks for it.
notes: Hysteroscopy only shows the inside of the uterus, so it cannot treat bleeding inside the abdomen or show injury to the bowel or vessels.
CT is for stable patients, and sending an unstable patient to the scanner delays the surgery that will stop the bleeding.
She is still bleeding and has already been given blood, so more crystalloid will dilute her blood and cannot replace stopping the bleeding.
Watching her haemoglobin is not safe while she is in shock, and haemoglobin falls later than the real blood loss.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is reviewed on the medical ward on day 3 of treatment for herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis, confirmed by CSF PCR. She has rheumatoid arthritis, and her weekly methotrexate has been withheld since admission. She weighs 70 kg and is receiving aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. She is still drowsy and has been drinking little. Her maintenance drip was taken down yesterday when the cannula tissued, and it was not restarted. Her urine output over the past 12 hours is 250 mL. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 98/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Her mucous membranes are dry, and there is no new focal neurological deficit. Serum creatinine is 164 µmol/L (72 µmol/L on admission; reference 45–90), urea 11.8 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L and potassium 4.6 mmol/L. Urine microscopy shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Stop the antiviral and start oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily
Stop the antiviral and start intravenous foscarnet
Continue the current regimen and add intravenous furosemide 40 mg
Arrange urgent haemodialysis through a temporary vascular catheter
Start isotonic crystalloid and reduce antiviral dosing to match renal function
questions.why: This patient has acute kidney injury from aciclovir crystal nephropathy. Aciclovir is cleared by the kidneys and is poorly soluble in urine, so high-dose IV therapy in a dehydrated patient lets crystals form in the renal tubules. This is the main complication to prevent during treatment of HSV encephalitis, and it is why eTG advises keeping the patient well hydrated and monitoring renal function throughout. Her intake is poor, her drip has been stopped, she is oliguric with dry mucous membranes, her creatinine has more than doubled and her urine shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals. The right step is to restart isotonic IV fluids and adjust the aciclovir dose to her estimated creatinine clearance. Her Cockcroft-Gault clearance is about 30 mL/min, which calls for 10 mg/kg every 12 hours. IV therapy should continue for the full course, at least 14 to 21 days in an immunosuppressed patient, because stopping or under-treating HSV encephalitis carries high mortality and neurological morbidity. The injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment. Methotrexate should stay withheld, because it is also cleared by the kidneys and would add toxicity.
notes: Wrong: oral valaciclovir is not recommended for acute HSV encephalitis while the patient is drowsy and still in the IV phase, and it is converted to aciclovir, so it would not prevent crystal formation.
Wrong: foscarnet is reserved for aciclovir-resistant HSV and is more nephrotoxic, so it would make her kidney injury worse.
Wrong: furosemide would deepen her volume depletion and does nothing to clear crystals, and keeping full-dose aciclovir at this clearance would cause further accumulation and toxicity.
Wrong: she has no indication for urgent dialysis (no hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemic complications), and this injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at a travel clinic needs a second MMR dose and live Japanese encephalitis vaccine for rural Laos. Her period is 10 days late, with nausea; condom use is inconsistent. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Live vaccines such as MMR and live attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine are contraindicated in pregnancy. Her period is late, she has nausea and her contraception is unreliable, so a urine pregnancy test must be done before vaccinating. If it is negative, she can be vaccinated and should avoid pregnancy for 28 days afterwards.
notes: Measles serology is not needed before a catch-up MMR dose, because adults born in 1966 or later need 2 documented doses whatever their serology shows.
A pelvic ultrasound is not the first-line test for possible early pregnancy and would be negative before about 5 weeks' gestation, so hCG comes first.
A full blood count does not affect whether she can have live vaccines and is not part of routine pre-travel screening.

Hepatitis A serology before vaccination is only considered for people likely to have past infection, such as older adults or people raised in endemic areas, and it does not address the pregnancy risk.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman on day 8 of prophylactic enoxaparin after hip replacement has a swollen left calf. Platelets have fallen from 280 to 95 ×10^9/L; PF4 antibody assay is pending. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: She has a high 4Ts score for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: a platelet fall of more than 50%, starting on days 5 to 10, with new thrombosis. All heparin must be stopped straight away and a full-dose non-heparin anticoagulant started (fondaparinux, argatroban, danaparoid, or a DOAC such as rivaroxaban), without waiting for the antibody result.
notes: Unfractionated heparin causes HIT even more often than enoxaparin and would make the thrombosis worse.
In HIT the main risk is clotting, not bleeding, so platelet transfusion may add to thrombosis and is not indicated without bleeding.
Starting warfarin during acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene from protein C depletion, so it waits until platelets recover and is overlapped with a non-heparin anticoagulant.
With a high clinical probability and active thrombosis, heparin must be stopped while the assay is awaited, not continued.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has biopsy-confirmed coeliac disease and started a gluten-free diet three weeks ago. Intensely itchy, grouped, excoriated vesicles on both elbows are disturbing his sleep. G6PD activity is normal. Most appropriate treatment for the rash?
questions.why: This is dermatitis herpetiformis. A gluten-free diet takes months to clear it, so dapsone, usually started by a dermatologist, is the drug of choice to control the itch quickly. G6PD must be checked before starting it and the blood count monitored during treatment.
notes: Systemic corticosteroids work poorly in dermatitis herpetiformis and carry significant adverse effects, so they are not recommended.
Antihistamines do little for the itch of dermatitis herpetiformis because the itch is not driven by histamine but by IgA immune complexes in the skin.
The rash is called herpetiform because of how the blisters cluster, not because of any viral cause, so an antiviral has no role.
Topical calcineurin inhibitors are used for atopic dermatitis and do not control the IgA-mediated blistering of dermatitis herpetiformis.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy has a splenic laceration after a bike crash. Pulse is 160/min, blood pressure 70/40 mm Hg despite fluid boluses. His Jehovah's Witness parents refuse transfusion. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: In every Australian state, legislation lets doctors give a blood transfusion to a child without parental consent when it is needed urgently to prevent death or serious harm. This child is in haemorrhagic shock that has not responded to fluids, so the child's best interests come before the parents' religious refusal. Transfuse now and document the reasons clearly, ideally with a second senior doctor agreeing where local policy asks for this.
notes: A court order is the right route for non-urgent treatment the parents refuse, but waiting for one here would put the child's life at risk.
An ethics committee can advise on hard cases, but it cannot authorise treatment and would delay care in an emergency.
Giving more crystalloid alone goes along with the parents' refusal, but it will not replace lost red cells and makes coagulopathy worse in ongoing bleeding.
A child protection report may follow, but it does not authorise or deliver the emergency treatment this child needs right now.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops rapidly enlarging anterior neck swelling and stridor four hours after total thyroidectomy. Her oxygen saturation is 89% on 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Rapid neck swelling with stridor and low oxygen saturation after thyroidectomy is a compressive haematoma that threatens the airway. The first step is to open the wound at the bedside straight away, cutting the skin sutures and the strap muscle sutures and evacuating the clot (the SCOOP approach), without waiting to move her. Formal haemostasis in theatre follows once the airway is decompressed.
notes: CT imaging wastes critical time and takes an unstable airway out of a safe area when the diagnosis is already clinically obvious.
Nebulised adrenaline reduces swelling of the airway lining but does nothing about an expanding haematoma pressing on the airway from outside.
Intubating while the haematoma is still in place is likely to fail because laryngeal oedema distorts the anatomy, so decompression comes first.
Transfer to theatre delays decompression while she is deteriorating; theatre is for definitive haemostasis after the wound has been opened at the bedside.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman on apixaban fell and hit her head four days ago. Apixaban has been reversed. CT: 12 mm acute right subdural haematoma, 7 mm midline shift. GCS 14. Most appropriate definitive management?
questions.why: An acute subdural haematoma more than 10 mm thick or with more than 5 mm of midline shift needs surgical evacuation, whatever the GCS. After reversal of the anticoagulant, a rural ED should arrange urgent neurosurgical referral and retrieval for craniotomy.
notes: Waiting for a repeat scan is only for small subdurals without significant shift, and here it would delay surgery while the mass effect gets worse.
Corticosteroids have no role in acute subdural haematoma or traumatic brain injury and do not relieve the mass effect.
Tranexamic acid may limit further bleeding, but it does nothing to remove a collection that is already causing midline shift.
Mannitol only buys time if herniation is imminent and does not treat the haematoma itself.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 11 pm by his mother with noisy breathing. He has had a runny nose and fever for 2 days, and this evening developed a barking cough and a hoarse cry. He is fully immunised and has no medical history. He weighs 12 kg. On arrival he was agitated, with stridor at rest, marked sternal and subcostal recession, and SpO2 91% in room air. He was given nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 (5 mL undiluted) and oral dexamethasone 7.2 mg (0.6 mg/kg), with oxygen held near his face. Sixty minutes later he is sitting on his mother's lap and playing. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 132/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and SpO2 97% in room air. He has an occasional barking cough, no stridor at rest and no chest wall recession. His mother would like to take him home now because his older sister is home alone with a neighbour. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge home now with written advice on when to return
Obtain a lateral neck X-ray before deciding on discharge
Give a second nebulised adrenaline treatment before discharge
Observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline treatment
Arrange admission to intensive care for elective intubation
questions.why: This child had severe croup: stridor at rest, a marked increase in work of breathing, agitation and hypoxaemia. Nebulised adrenaline works within minutes but wears off within about 2 hours. Dexamethasone takes several hours to reach full effect, so the obstruction can come back once the adrenaline wears off. The RCH Croup CPG says to observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose. Discharge is appropriate only if there is still no stridor at rest at that point, with clear safety-netting advice. The improvement at 60 minutes is likely the adrenaline effect and is not proof that the illness is settling. A mild tachycardia is expected after adrenaline. Discharging now risks the obstruction returning at home in the middle of the night. A lateral neck X-ray is not needed in typical croup, would not change management and could upset the child. Giving more adrenaline to a child with no stridor at rest has no benefit, and it would only restart the observation period. Intubation is for impending airway failure, such as exhaustion, ongoing hypoxaemia or repeated adrenaline needs, and this child has responded well.
notes: Correct: the adrenaline effect lasts only about 2 hours, before the steroid has fully taken effect, so the RCH advises observing for at least 3 hours after the last dose and discharging only if there is still no stridor at rest.
Wrong: croup is a clinical diagnosis and this course is typical, so imaging would not change management and upsetting the child can worsen obstruction.
Wrong: adrenaline is given for severe obstruction such as stridor at rest with marked work of breathing, and has no preventive role in a child who has none.
Wrong: intubation is kept for a tiring child, ongoing hypoxaemia or repeated adrenaline needs, none of which this improving child has.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from a general practice. He has had 14 hours of worsening generalised headache, fever and photophobia. Five days ago he came back from a week in a crowded backpacker hostel. The general practitioner gave benzylpenicillin 2.4 g intramuscularly 4 hours ago, before transfer. He takes no medicines, and his vaccination history is unknown. His temperature is 38.8 °C, pulse 116/min, respirations 22/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. He is alert and oriented (GCS 15). He has neck stiffness, with no focal neurological signs, papilloedema or rash. Two sets of blood cultures were taken on arrival. Lumbar puncture fluid analysis shows: Appearance: turbid Neutrophils: 2900 x10^6/L (reference 0) Lymphocytes: 40 x10^6/L (reference less than 5) Protein: 1.3 g/L (reference 0.15 to 0.45) Glucose: 1.1 mmol/L (paired serum glucose 5.6 mmol/L) Gram stain: neutrophils seen, no organisms seen Which of the following investigations is most likely to identify the causative organism?
options: Bacterial culture of the CSF sample
Bacterial PCR on the CSF sample
Repeat blood cultures from two sites
Viral PCR panel on the CSF sample
questions.why: This young adult has fever, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness after crowded living. His lumbar puncture fluid shows a marked neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis, high protein and a CSF-to-serum glucose ratio of about 0.2 (below 0.4). These findings mean bacterial meningitis, most likely meningococcal. He correctly had parenteral benzylpenicillin in general practice before transfer. However, that dose sterilises the CSF and blood within hours, which explains why the Gram stain shows no organisms and why culture yield will be low. Nucleic acid testing (PCR) for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae on the CSF does not need live bacteria. It stays positive for days after antibiotics have started. eTG and the CDNA invasive meningococcal disease guidelines recommend it, and it is the test most likely to confirm the organism (and give the serogroup for public health) in a pretreated patient. Culture of the CSF should still be sent, because it gives antibiotic susceptibilities, but it is less likely to grow anything. Repeat blood cultures taken even later after antibiotics will give an even lower yield.
notes: Correct: PCR detects bacterial DNA even after antibiotics have killed the organisms, so it is the most sensitive way to confirm N. meningitidis (and its serogroup) in pretreated meningitis.
Blood cultures taken even longer after the antibiotic dose are less likely to grow anything than the sets already taken on arrival.
A positive throat culture shows only nasopharyngeal carriage, which is common in young adults, so it supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm invasive disease.
A neutrophilic CSF with high protein and a glucose ratio below 0.4 points to a bacterial cause, not a viral one, so a viral panel will not identify this organism.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with severe pneumonia is drowsy and tiring. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.12, PaCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 16 mmol/L, lactate 6 mmol/L. Which acid-base disorder is present?
questions.why: The low bicarbonate and high lactate show a metabolic (lactic) acidosis. Winter's formula predicts a PaCO2 of 1.5 x 16 + 8 = 32 ± 2 mmHg, so a PaCO2 of 52 mmHg means there is also a respiratory acidosis. This means he is tiring and heading towards respiratory failure, so he needs urgent ventilatory support.
notes: Compensation would bring the PaCO2 down to about 32 mmHg, not up to 52 mmHg, and the pH is far from normal.
In a pure acute respiratory acidosis the HCO3 would rise slightly to about 26 mmol/L, not fall to 16 mmol/L, and the lactate would not be high.
Chronic respiratory acidosis gives a clearly raised HCO3 from renal compensation, but here the HCO3 is low.
A respiratory alkalosis would need a PaCO2 below the predicted 30-34 mmHg, but here the PaCO2 is raised.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man on apixaban hit his head in a fall four days ago. Now drowsy, GCS 13; CT shows a left subdural haematoma with 9 mm midline shift. Which complication is he most at risk of?
questions.why: An expanding anticoagulant-associated subdural haematoma with more than 5 mm of midline shift and a falling GCS puts him at immediate risk of transtentorial (uncal) herniation. Look for a dilated pupil on the same side as the bleed and a Cushing response (bradycardia with rising BP), which are late signs. This is why urgent reversal, neurosurgical referral and early retrieval matter.
notes: Seizures can occur with a subdural haematoma, but they are less common and less immediately fatal than herniation from a mass that is already shifting the midline.
A supratentorial convexity subdural rarely blocks CSF flow, so obstructive hydrocephalus is not the main danger here.
SIADH can follow intracranial haemorrhage, but it develops over days and does not explain the early fall in conscious level.
Thrombosis after reversal or after stopping anticoagulation in AF is a real but later and lower risk than herniation.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a fusiform, flexed index finger two days after a thorn prick, with flexor sheath tenderness and pain on passive extension. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This finger shows Kanavel's signs: fusiform swelling, a flexed resting posture, pain on passive extension and tenderness along the flexor sheath. These mean infective flexor tenosynovitis. It needs urgent referral to the hand surgeons for washout of the sheath in theatre, plus IV antibiotics that cover Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci (for example flucloxacillin or cefazolin, per eTG), to prevent tendon necrosis, adhesions and spread into the deep spaces of the hand.
notes: Oral antibiotics with delayed review undertreat a closed-space infection, and the tendon can be lost within hours to days.
A bedside incision cannot properly irrigate the whole sheath and risks damaging the tendon and the nerves and vessels of the finger.
The diagnosis is clinical, and imaging must not delay referral and treatment.
Splinting and elevation help but are not enough without antibiotics and surgical drainage.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old woman fractures her hip in a fall at her nursing home and dies of hospital-acquired pneumonia four days later. Her treating doctor is confident of the medical cause. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: In every Australian state and territory, a death caused directly or indirectly by an injury or accident must be reported to the coroner, even when the final cause is natural, like pneumonia. The fall started the chain of events that led to her death, so the doctor must not certify it and should report it to the coroner.
notes: A doctor cannot sign a death certificate for a reportable death, even when sure of the medical cause; the coroner decides how to proceed.
A hospital (non-coronial) autopsy cannot replace a coronial report, and the coroner decides whether a post-mortem is needed.
The body must not be released before the coroner decides, because the coroner may need to keep it for investigation.
A report to the aged care regulator does not meet the legal duty to report the death to the coroner, and is not the first step.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man in ICU with septic acute kidney injury has serum potassium 7.6 mmol/L. ECG shows broad QRS complexes and absent P waves. Most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.why: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, such as broad QRS and loss of P waves, can progress to a sine-wave rhythm or cardiac arrest. Give IV calcium first: it stabilises the heart muscle within minutes, although it does not lower the potassium. Then move potassium into cells and start definitive removal.
notes: Insulin with dextrose moves potassium into cells but takes 15 to 30 minutes to work and does not protect the heart straight away, so it comes after calcium.
Salbutamol helps insulin move potassium into cells, but it is slower and less reliable, and it does not protect the heart.
Bicarbonate lowers potassium only a little and is mainly used when there is severe metabolic acidosis; it is not the first step for ECG changes.
Dialysis removes potassium for good, but it takes time to set up, so calcium must be given first to protect the heart.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old female medical student finished a three-dose hepatitis B vaccine course six weeks ago, before surgical placement. Anti-HBs is 4 mIU/mL; HBsAg and anti-HBc are negative. What does this result indicate?
questions.why: An anti-HBs level below 10 mIU/mL measured 4 to 8 weeks after a full course means she did not respond to the vaccine. Negative HBsAg and anti-HBc rule out current or past infection. Under the Australian Immunisation Handbook she needs more vaccine doses and a repeat anti-HBs test, and until then any blood exposure must be managed as if she is not immune.
notes: Chronic hepatitis B needs a positive HBsAg, and hers is negative.
Protection needs anti-HBs of at least 10 mIU/mL, and hers is 4 mIU/mL.
Resolved past infection shows a positive anti-HBc, and hers is negative.
Occult infection is HBsAg-negative but usually anti-HBc-positive with detectable HBV DNA, and nothing here suggests it.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner 6 weeks after she was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis. Before the diagnosis she had 10 weeks of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea and left-sided abdominal cramps. Stool pathogen tests were negative. Ileocolonoscopy found continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 30 cm and a normal proximal colon and terminal ileum. Biopsies showed crypt distortion with no granulomas and no dysplasia. She now takes oral mesalazine and mesalazine enemas. She has 1 to 2 formed stools a day with no blood. She has never smoked. Her mother was diagnosed with bowel cancer at age 62. No other relatives have had bowel cancer. Temperature is 36.7°C, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg and pulse 72/min. Her abdomen is soft and not tender. Haemoglobin is 129 g/L (115–165), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), ALP 74 U/L (30–110) and GGT 18 U/L (<40). She asks how her bowel cancer risk will be checked. Which of the following is the most appropriate surveillance plan for this patient?
options: Colonoscopy from 8 years after disease onset
Faecal immunochemical test every 2 years from age 45
CT colonography every 5 years starting now
questions.why: Ulcerative colitis that reaches beyond the rectum raises the risk of colorectal cancer. Her colitis runs from the rectum to 30 cm, so it is left-sided (Montreal E2) and not proctitis alone. The risk depends on how long she has had colitis, how much colon is involved and how much inflammation there is. Cancer Council Australia and GESA recommend a first colonoscopy about 8 years after symptoms began. This colonoscopy restages the disease and uses chromoendoscopy or multiple biopsies to look for dysplasia. After that, the interval (1, 3 or 5 years) is set by risk factors such as ongoing inflammation, strictures, past dysplasia, PSC and family history. Her mother's cancer at 62 may shorten later intervals, but it does not change the start point. Population or family-history screening does not apply to her, because her colitis is the bigger risk and needs colonoscopy with targeted biopsies. Annual colonoscopy straight away is only for coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.
notes: Colonoscopy every 5 years from 45 is family-history screening for a first-degree relative diagnosed under 55, which does not fit her history and starts too late for her colitis risk.
Two-yearly faecal immunochemical tests are average-risk population screening, and they cannot detect flat colitis-associated dysplasia or tell it apart from inflammatory bleeding.
Annual colonoscopy from diagnosis is for patients who also have primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.
CT colonography cannot take biopsies or show flat dysplasia, so it is not used for surveillance in inflammatory bowel disease.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to her back. BP is 84/50 mmHg. CT aortogram shows an ascending aortic intimal flap with haemopericardium. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is a Stanford type A aortic dissection with haemopericardium and shock. It is a surgical emergency, so call cardiothoracic surgery at once, resuscitate, and take her straight to theatre for open repair of the ascending aorta. Do not try to lower her blood pressure.
notes: Wrong: beta blockade is anti-impulse therapy for a hypertensive patient, and it is avoided in hypotension and tamponade because it worsens shock.

Wrong: tamponade from a dissection is treated by surgical repair. Pericardiocentesis can speed up bleeding and cause collapse, and is kept only for controlled small-volume drainage when theatre is not available.
Wrong: anticoagulation is contraindicated in acute aortic dissection because it makes bleeding and rupture worse.
Wrong: endovascular stent grafting is used for complicated type B (descending) dissection, not as standard treatment of the ascending aorta.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a headache that has got steadily worse over 6 hours. The headache is generalised and throbbing, and he has fever, rigors, vomiting and pain when looking at lights. He has no history of headaches, head injury or seizures, and he takes no medicines. His temperature is 39.3 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is alert and oriented, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15. Neck flexion is painful and restricted. Fundoscopy shows sharp optic disc margins. Cranial nerve and limb examinations are normal, and there is no rash. Blood cultures are taken, and he is given dexamethasone 10 mg IV and ceftriaxone 2 g IV. Laboratory studies show: White cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) Platelets 245 x10^9/L (150 to 400) INR 1.0 (0.9 to 1.2) C-reactive protein 210 mg/L (less than 5) Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: This man has fever, a headache that built up over hours, photophobia and neck stiffness, so he has bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. The right first steps have been taken: blood cultures, then dexamethasone and ceftriaxone without waiting for any test. Lumbar puncture is the next investigation. CSF cell count, protein, glucose ratio, Gram stain, culture with susceptibilities and PCR confirm the diagnosis, identify the organism and guide how antibiotics are narrowed and how long they are given. Under eTG, CT before LP is needed only if there is a contraindication: reduced or falling GCS, focal neurological signs, a recent seizure, papilloedema or immunocompromise. He has none of these. His platelets and INR are normal, so it is safe to go straight to LP. Organisms can often still be found in CSF in the first hours after antibiotics, and cell count, protein and glucose changes last longer, so LP should be done promptly and not put off.
notes: Correct: with GCS 15, no focal signs, no seizure, no papilloedema and normal platelets and coagulation, LP is safe without imaging, and CSF analysis is the test that confirms bacterial meningitis and identifies the organism.
MRI with contrast can show meningeal enhancement or complications, but it is slow, hard to get in the ED and does not identify the organism or confirm bacterial meningitis.
CT angiography looks for an aneurysm in subarachnoid haemorrhage, which is unlikely here because the headache built up over 6 hours with high fever and was not a thunderclap onset.
Blood meningococcal PCR is a useful extra test, especially after antibiotics, but it detects only one organism and does not replace CSF analysis as the test that confirms meningitis.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man from the Philippines has 8 weeks of productive cough, night sweats and 6 kg weight loss. Chest X-ray shows left upper lobe cavitation. Test most likely to confirm diagnosis?
questions.why: A chronic productive cough with night sweats, weight loss, birth in a high-TB country and upper lobe cavitation points to active pulmonary TB. The diagnosis is confirmed by three sputum samples sent for AFB microscopy, mycobacterial culture and NAAT. NAAT gives a fast result and detects rifampicin resistance, and culture provides full drug susceptibility testing.
notes: An IGRA detects immune sensitisation to TB, not active disease, so it cannot confirm active TB and may be negative in active TB.
A tuberculin skin test cannot tell latent infection from active disease and is less specific after BCG vaccination, which is common in people born in the Philippines.
CT shows the extent of disease in more detail but cannot identify the organism, so it does not confirm TB.
Bronchoscopy is kept for patients who cannot produce sputum or whose sputum is negative, and this man has a productive cough.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with 3 days of cough productive of green sputum, fevers, and left-sided chest pain that is worse on inspiration. Six days ago she was discharged from hospital after a 4-day admission to investigate syncope. On the ward she walked daily and received prophylactic enoxaparin. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine and has never smoked. She has no haemoptysis and no history of venous thromboembolism or cancer. Her temperature is 38.5 °C, pulse 106/min, respirations 24/min, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, and SpO2 93% on room air. There is dullness and bronchial breathing at the left base. Both calves are soft and nontender, and there is no leg swelling. A chest X-ray shows new consolidation in the left lower lobe. Results: white cell count 15.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), CRP 151 mg/L (less than 5), urea 7.9 mmol/L (2.5 to 7.5), D-dimer 0.63 mg/L FEU (less than 0.50). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating her for pulmonary embolism?
questions.why: Start by working out her pre-test probability. Her Wells score is 1.5: she gets 1.5 for a heart rate over 100/min and nothing else. She was not immobilised, because she walked daily on the ward and had prophylactic enoxaparin. She had no surgery, her calves are normal, she has no haemoptysis, no past VTE and no cancer, and pneumonia explains her illness better than PE does. A Wells score of 4 or less means PE is unlikely, so a D-dimer is the right test to rule it out. In patients over 50, the D-dimer cut-off is age-adjusted: age x 0.01 mg/L FEU, which is 0.71 mg/L for a 71-year-old. Her D-dimer of 0.63 mg/L is above the standard laboratory limit of 0.50 but below her age-adjusted cut-off. This is a negative result, and with low pre-test probability it excludes PE (eTG Cardiovascular; ADJUST-PE). She needs no further tests for PE. The next step is to manage the left lower lobe pneumonia, which began soon after a hospital stay. CT pulmonary angiography is wrong because it is only needed if PE is likely (Wells over 4) or the D-dimer is above the age-adjusted cut-off.
notes: CT pulmonary angiography is wrong because it is only needed when PE is likely (Wells over 4) or the D-dimer is above the age-adjusted cut-off of 0.71 mg/L, and neither applies to her.

A V/Q scan is wrong because it is an alternative to CTPA for patients who cannot have contrast, and with a low Wells score and a D-dimer below the age-adjusted cut-off she does not need imaging for PE.
Compression ultrasound of both legs is wrong because her calves are normal with no swelling, and a negative D-dimer with low pre-test probability has already excluded thromboembolism.
Repeating the D-dimer is wrong because the first result is already negative using the correct cut-off, so a repeat adds nothing and delays treatment of her pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a 3-month non-healing ulcer with raised, everted edges. It arose within a scar from a childhood flame burn to his thigh. The scar had been stable for 50 years. Most likely malignancy?
questions.why: A Marjolin ulcer is a cancer that grows in a chronic wound or an old burn scar, usually decades after the injury, and it is most often squamous cell carcinoma. Any non-healing ulcer in an old scar needs a biopsy to rule out SCC. These tumours spread to lymph nodes more aggressively than ordinary cutaneous SCC.
notes: BCC can occasionally arise in a burn scar, but it is much less common than SCC there and usually looks pearly with a rolled edge rather than everted.
Melanoma rarely arises in burn scars, and this lesion shows no pigment or change in a pre-existing mole.
Merkel cell carcinoma is a fast-growing red nodule on sun-damaged skin, not a slowly developing ulcer in a chronic scar.
DFSP is a slow-growing firm plaque on the trunk of young adults and is not linked to chronic burn scars.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old Aboriginal man with type 2 diabetes attends his annual health check. eGFR is 82 mL/min/1.73 m². His urine albumin:creatinine ratio is 14 mg/mmol on two separate samples taken over three months. What do these results show?
questions.why: A urine ACR that stays between 2.5 and 25 mg/mmol in a man (Kidney Health Australia; KDIGO A2 is 3 to 30) is moderately increased albuminuria, also called microalbuminuria. With an eGFR of 82, this means stage 2 chronic kidney disease, most likely early diabetic kidney disease. This group is at high risk, so he needs an ACE inhibitor or ARB and tight control of blood pressure, glucose and cardiovascular risk.
notes: Wrong: severely increased albuminuria in a man is an ACR above 25 mg/mmol (KDIGO above 30), and 14 is below that.
Wrong: normal albumin excretion in a man is an ACR below 2.5 mg/mmol, so 14 mg/mmol is clearly abnormal.
Wrong: nephrotic-range loss means an ACR of roughly 220 mg/mmol or more, far above 14 mg/mmol.
Wrong: a transient rise after exercise would not stay high on two separate samples taken months apart.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the emergency department 2 hours after he was punched in the face outside a hotel. He says both sides of his nose are blocked and his nose is painful. He had a nosebleed that stopped on its own after 10 minutes. He has no clear fluid running from his nose, no double vision and no headache. He takes no regular medicines and has no allergies. His temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 88/min, blood pressure 128/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The nasal bridge is swollen and bent to the left. After phenylephrine–lidocaine spray, anterior rhinoscopy shows a smooth, red-purple swelling on both sides of the septum that blocks both nostrils. The swelling has not shrunk and feels soft and fluctuant when pressed with a cotton bud. Eye movements are full, cheek sensation is normal and his bite is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Same-day incision and drainage with bilateral nasal packing
Closed reduction of the nasal bones in 7 days
Oral amoxicillin–clavulanate with review in 48 hours
Silver nitrate cautery to the anterior septum
CT of the facial bones before specialist review
questions.why: This man has a bilateral nasal septal haematoma. After a blow to the nose he has blockage on both sides, and on both sides of the septum there is a smooth, red-purple, fluctuant swelling that does not shrink with a decongestant. Septal cartilage has no blood supply of its own and gets its nutrients from the overlying mucoperichondrium. Blood collecting under the perichondrium lifts it off the cartilage. Within about 24 to 72 hours this can cause cartilage necrosis and infection. The results are a septal abscess, which can spread to the cavernous sinus or the meninges, a septal perforation and a saddle nose deformity. Bilateral haematomas carry the highest risk. The aim is to prevent these complications, so the haematoma must be drained the same day, by ENT or by a trained emergency doctor: incise and drain each side, then use bilateral packing or septal splints to stop it filling again. He should also have antibiotics that cover Staphylococcus aureus (as advised in Therapeutic Guidelines) and early ENT follow-up. The displaced nasal fractures can be reduced later, once the swelling settles.
notes: Delayed closed reduction is right for the displaced nasal bone fracture on its own, but a 7-day wait would let the septal cartilage die and become infected.
Antibiotics are added after drainage, but on their own they cannot remove the blood starving the cartilage, so the necrosis and abscess risk stays.
Cautery treats bleeding from vessels in Little's area; it does nothing for a blood collection under the perichondrium, and his nosebleed has already stopped.
This is a clinical diagnosis, he has no features of a naso-orbito-ethmoid, orbital or other facial fracture, and waiting for imaging delays drainage that should not be delayed.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to a general practice in July because of a dry cough that started suddenly 3 days ago. She also has fevers, muscle aches, fatigue, a sore throat and a blocked nose. Two colleagues at the café where she works have had similar symptoms this week. She has no breathlessness or chest pain. She has no history of serious illness, takes no medicines, is not pregnant and did not have an influenza vaccine this year. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily. Her temperature is 38.2 °C, pulse 96/min, respiratory rate 16/min, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She is alert and talking in full sentences. The pharynx is mildly red without exudate. The chest is clear to auscultation. A multiplex nasopharyngeal PCR swab shows: influenza A RNA detected; influenza B RNA not detected; SARS-CoV-2 RNA not detected; respiratory syncytial virus RNA not detected; Bordetella pertussis DNA not detected. Based on these results, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days
Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days
Paracetamol, fluids and rest, avoiding contact with others until well
Chest X-ray within the next 24 hours
Repeat SARS-CoV-2 rapid antigen test in 48 hours
questions.why: The PCR confirms influenza A and rules out SARS-CoV-2, RSV and pertussis. Her observations show fever and a high-normal heart rate, but her respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and blood pressure are normal, she is alert and her chest is clear. Together these results mean uncomplicated influenza in a healthy adult. She has no complications and no risk factors for severe disease (she is not pregnant, not immunocompromised and has no chronic heart or lung disease). The right management is symptom relief with paracetamol, fluids and rest. She should stay away from work and other people until she is well, and use cough etiquette and hand hygiene. She should also be offered next season's influenza vaccine and brief smoking cessation advice, and told to seek urgent care if she becomes breathless at rest, gets chest pain or confusion, or gets worse again after improving. eTG keeps oseltamivir for severe illness or people at higher risk. In healthy adults it only modestly shortens symptoms, and only when started within 48 hours of onset. She is at day 3. Antibiotics do not help a viral infection when there is no sign of bacterial pneumonia.
notes: Wrong: oseltamivir is for severe illness or higher-risk patients, and she is a healthy, non-pregnant adult at day 3, past the 48-hour window where it helps a little.
Wrong: the illness is confirmed viral, with a clear chest and normal saturation, so there is no sign of bacterial pneumonia that would justify antibiotics.
Wrong: a clear chest, normal respiratory rate and 98% saturation on room air give no sign of pneumonia, so imaging would not change management.
Wrong: a negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR is more sensitive than a rapid antigen test, and influenza A already explains her illness, so retesting adds nothing.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is in the terminal phase, unresponsive, with noisy gurgling breathing. He appears comfortable; repositioning has not helped and his family is distressed. Most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: This is noisy breathing from respiratory secretions in a dying patient. Repositioning has not helped, so eTG Palliative Care recommends a subcutaneous anticholinergic such as hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg. Explaining to the family that the noise is not distressing him is also part of care. Anticholinergics reduce new secretions but do not clear secretions that are already there, so start early.
notes: The secretions sit in the pharynx and airway, not as pulmonary oedema, so a diuretic will not help and IV access burdens a dying patient.
Midazolam treats terminal agitation or distress, and he looks comfortable, so it does nothing for the secretions.
Morphine relieves breathlessness or pain, neither of which he has, and it does not reduce secretions.
Deep suction is distressing, can stimulate more secretions and is not recommended; only gentle oral suction is sometimes used.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 8 hours of constant, severe epigastric pain that radiates to her back, with repeated vomiting. The pain began 2 hours after a large evening meal. She drinks 2 standard drinks on weekends and does not smoke. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Her BMI is 34 kg/m2. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rigidity and no jaundice. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST changes. Results: lipase 2400 U/L (reference <60), white cell count 13.2 x10^9/L, CRP 40 mg/L, total bilirubin 22 µmol/L (<20), ALT 186 U/L (<35), ALP 140 U/L (30–110), corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.8 mmol/L and creatinine 78 µmol/L. IV fluids and titrated opioid analgesia have been started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the pancreas
questions.why: She already meets 2 of the 3 criteria for acute pancreatitis: typical epigastric pain going through to the back, and a lipase more than 3 times the upper limit. The diagnosis is made, so the next step is to find the cause. Gallstones cause about half of all cases. An early ALT above about 150 U/L strongly suggests a biliary cause, and her obesity and diabetes add to the risk. Her calcium and triglycerides are normal and she drinks little alcohol. Australian guidance (eTG) and international guidance say every patient with acute pancreatitis should have a transabdominal ultrasound on admission to look for gallstones and a dilated bile duct. This is because a gallstone cause changes management: ERCP if there is cholangitis or a persisting duct stone, and cholecystectomy in the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis. The test is quick, cheap, uses no radiation and can be done at the bedside. Early contrast CT does not help when the diagnosis is already clear. ERCP is for cholangitis or a proven obstruction that persists. MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound are second-line tests for when the ultrasound is unclear or no cause is found. Amylase adds nothing once the lipase is raised.
notes: Contrast CT is for when the diagnosis is uncertain, or for looking for necrosis if she deteriorates after 72 hours; the diagnosis is already made, and CT in the first days underestimates necrosis and is poor at showing gallstones.
ERCP is invasive, carries a risk of making pancreatitis worse, and in the early phase is only for cholangitis or a proven persisting bile duct obstruction, neither of which has been shown here.
MRCP is a second-line test for suspected duct stones when the ultrasound is unclear or the liver tests stay abnormal; it should not come before the first-line ultrasound.
Amylase is less specific than lipase and clears sooner, so it adds nothing to a lipase already more than 30 times the upper limit and does not show the cause.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man has had painful swelling of both wrists and MCP joints for 3 months, with 90 minutes of morning stiffness. His DIP joints are spared, and his skin and nails are normal. Which blood test best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.why: He has symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis of the wrists and MCPs with long morning stiffness and spared DIPs, which points to rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-CCP antibodies are about 95% specific for RA, so they are the best test to confirm it. A strongly positive result also predicts erosive disease.
notes: Rheumatoid factor is sensitive but not specific, because it is also positive in infection, Sjögren's, older people and other connective tissue diseases.
ANA is used to screen for SLE, and his history has no lupus features; ANA is also often positive in RA, so it cannot confirm it.
HLA-B27 is linked with spondyloarthritis, which usually causes axial or asymmetrical large-joint disease rather than symmetrical small-joint synovitis.
Serum urate does not confirm gout, which usually causes acute attacks in single joints, and urate is often normal during an attack.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has four months of bloating, pale loose stools and fatigue. Ferritin is 8 microgram/L; tTG-IgA is 96 U/mL with normal total IgA. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: He has malabsorption, iron deficiency and a strongly positive tTG-IgA with normal total IgA. In Australian adults, coeliac disease must be confirmed with duodenal biopsies at gastroscopy while the patient is still eating gluten. The gluten-free diet starts only after the diagnosis is confirmed.
notes: Starting a gluten-free diet before biopsy can heal the villi and make the histology falsely normal, so the diagnosis can no longer be confirmed.
Waiting to repeat strongly positive serology delays the diagnosis and adds nothing, because the result is already reliable with a normal total IgA.
HLA typing is mainly useful for ruling coeliac disease out because of its high negative predictive value; a positive result cannot confirm the diagnosis.
Colonoscopy looks at the colon and terminal ileum, not the proximal small bowel where coeliac disease causes damage, so it is not the next step here.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with newly confirmed HIV-1 infection has a CD4 count of 480 cells/µL and osteoporosis on DXA. His doctor plans dolutegravir, abacavir and lamivudine rather than tenofovir. Most appropriate test before starting?
questions.why: ASHM guidelines say to screen for HLA-B*5701 before starting abacavir. Carriers have a high risk of a hypersensitivity reaction that can be fatal, so a positive result rules the drug out. A negative result makes abacavir a safe choice for a patient who needs to avoid tenofovir because of bone disease.
notes: HLA-B*1502 predicts Stevens-Johnson syndrome with carbamazepine in people of Asian ancestry, not abacavir hypersensitivity.
TPMT activity guides the dose of azathioprine or mercaptopurine and has no role before antiretroviral therapy.
G6PD deficiency matters for drugs such as dapsone or primaquine, not for this regimen.
A co-receptor tropism assay is needed only before maraviroc, which is not part of this regimen.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has a 9 mm pigmented lesion on his back that has grown over three months. Dermoscopy shows irregular borders and variegated colour. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A changing pigmented lesion with irregular borders and variegated colour is suspicious for melanoma. Australian melanoma guidelines recommend complete excisional biopsy with 2 mm margins, which confirms the diagnosis and gives an accurate Breslow thickness. The definitive margins and the need for sentinel node biopsy are then decided from that thickness.
notes: A shave biopsy can cut through the base of the lesion, so the Breslow thickness cannot be measured and staging is wrong.
A punch biopsy samples only part of a lesion this size, so it can miss the deepest or most atypical area and under-stage or miss the melanoma.
Wide local excision before a tissue diagnosis has no Breslow thickness to set the margins and can disrupt lymphatic drainage needed for sentinel node mapping.
Short-term digital monitoring is for flat lesions with low suspicion, not a lesion already growing with features of melanoma.
