questions.stem: A 62-year-old female smoker with type 2 diabetes presents to vascular clinic with 3 weeks of forefoot rest pain eased by dependency. No pedal pulses, dry gangrene of three toes, ABI 0.28. Most likely cause of death within 5 years?
questions.why: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia is a marker of widespread atherosclerosis. Up to half of patients die within 5 years, mostly from coronary and cerebrovascular events. That is why an antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, BP and glucose control and stopping smoking are part of her treatment, alongside revascularisation.
notes: Dry gangrene can become wet and cause sepsis, but this is a threat to the limb and a less common cause of death than coronary events.
She is less mobile, but PE causes far fewer deaths in PAD than heart attack or stroke.
Smoking raises her risk of lung cancer, but over 5 years her risk of dying from heart disease is much higher.
Aortic aneurysm is linked to PAD, but rupture causes only a small share of deaths, and fewer in women.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man reports three spontaneous hours-long attacks of spinning vertigo with left tinnitus. Left audiometry: air and bone thresholds 45 dB at 250–500 Hz, normal from 2000 Hz. Right ear normal. What does audiometry show?
questions.why: Air and bone thresholds are equal, so there is no air-bone gap and the loss is sensorineural. It affects only 250–500 Hz and recovers by 2000 Hz, so it is a low-frequency loss. A documented one-sided low-frequency sensorineural loss with spontaneous attacks of vertigo lasting hours meets the Bárány criteria for Ménière's disease, and because the loss is asymmetric he also needs ENT referral.
notes: A conductive loss needs bone conduction better than air conduction (an air-bone gap), and here the two thresholds are equal.
The thresholds are normal from 2000 Hz upward, so the high frequencies are spared; a high-frequency loss suggests presbycusis or a vestibular schwannoma.
A mixed loss needs both raised bone thresholds and an air-bone gap, and there is no gap here.
Noise-induced loss causes a dip around 4000 Hz, but here the loss is at 250–500 Hz and the high frequencies are normal.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man who works as a mechanic sees his general practitioner because of tiredness for 4 months. He drinks about 4 L of water a day. He gets up three times a night to pass urine, even when he avoids drinks in the evening. He has gained 15 kg over 2 years and has not lost weight recently. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and takes no other medicines. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. His father has type 2 diabetes. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 138/86 mm Hg and respiratory rate 14/min. His BMI is 36 kg/m². He has velvety, darkened skin in both axillae and looks well hydrated. Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+, ketones negative, protein negative and specific gravity 1.025. A random fingerprick reading on the practice meter is 15.2 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: This man has the typical symptoms of hyperglycaemia: thirst, polyuria and nocturia that continues when he drinks less in the evening. He also has metabolic risk factors: obesity, acanthosis nigricans, hypertension, smoking and a family history of type 2 diabetes. His urine is concentrated and full of glucose, and he has no ketones, which points to type 2 diabetes. A fingerprick meter reading is not enough to diagnose diabetes, so the RACGP handbook and eTG require a laboratory test. HbA1c is the most appropriate test. A level of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more diagnoses diabetes, he does not need to fast for it, and Medicare funds it for diagnosis. Because he has symptoms, one abnormal laboratory result is enough and no repeat test on another day is needed. A fasting or random venous plasma glucose would also be acceptable, but neither is among the options. An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for equivocal results or pregnancy. The water deprivation test, GAD antibodies and C-peptide do not confirm that he has diabetes.
notes: An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for equivocal fasting (5.5 to 6.9 mmol/L) or random (5.5 to 11.0 mmol/L) glucose results or for pregnancy, and it is unnecessary and burdensome in a patient with symptoms and marked hyperglycaemia.

A water deprivation test looks for diabetes insipidus, but his urine is concentrated (specific gravity 1.025) and full of glucose, which shows an osmotic diuresis, and fluid restriction could make his dehydration worse.

GAD antibodies help classify suspected type 1 diabetes or latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (for example in a lean patient with weight loss or ketosis), but they do not confirm that diabetes is present.
C-peptide measures how much insulin the pancreas can still make and helps classify the type of diabetes, but it does not diagnose diabetes and can be misleadingly low during hyperglycaemia.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man who has sex with men has a 10-day painless, indurated penile ulcer. Syphilis EIA and TPPA are positive; RPR is 1:32. No drug allergies. Most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: A painless indurated chancre with positive treponemal tests and a reactive RPR means primary syphilis. Under the Australian STI Management Guidelines and eTG, the treatment is a single dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 million units IM. Syphilis must also be notified, sexual contacts traced, and HIV and other STIs tested for.
notes: A single dose of ceftriaxone treats gonorrhoea but is not enough to treat syphilis.
Azithromycin is not recommended for syphilis because macrolide resistance in Treponema pallidum is widespread.
Doxycycline is only the alternative for penicillin allergy, and it needs 14 days for early syphilis, not 7.
Valaciclovir treats genital herpes, which causes painful multiple ulcers and negative treponemal serology.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to a general practice because of recurrent headaches over the past 3 months. She has had four attacks. Each begins with shimmering zigzag lights in one half of her vision that spread slowly over 20 minutes and then clear completely. Within 30 minutes, a throbbing one-sided headache follows, with nausea and sensitivity to light and noise, and lasts about 18 hours. The side varies between attacks, and she is well in between. Her mother has a similar history. She uses a copper intrauterine device, takes ibuprofen during attacks and takes no regular medicines. She is worried that she has a brain tumour. Her temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 76/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. There is no neck stiffness. A full neurological examination is normal, including fundoscopy, which shows sharp discs and spontaneous venous pulsations. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: MRI of the brain with gadolinium
questions.why: This woman has recurrent, stereotyped attacks that meet ICHD-3 criteria for migraine with aura. The aura is a positive visual disturbance that spreads gradually over more than 5 minutes, lasts under 60 minutes, resolves fully and is followed within an hour by a throbbing, unilateral headache with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia. The side varies, she is well between attacks, she has a family history, and her neurological examination and fundi are normal. Migraine is a clinical diagnosis. eTG (Neurology) states that a typical history with a normal examination and no red flags needs no neuroimaging. The most useful next investigation is a diary she keeps from now on, recording when each attack happens, the aura, how long it lasts, triggers, acute medicine days and menstrual timing. The diary confirms the stereotyped pattern and flags any change that would point to a secondary cause. It also counts medicine days to detect medication overuse and gives the attack frequency needed to decide on preventive treatment. Reassure her and explain why she does not need a scan, rather than ordering imaging to ease her worry.
notes: MRI is kept for red flags such as an atypical or prolonged aura, a changed pattern, abnormal examination findings or papilloedema, none of which she has, so a scan would not change management.

Non-contrast CT is used for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage or acute intracranial pathology, but her headaches build up gradually after an aura in a recurrent pattern, and she would receive radiation for no diagnostic benefit.

CT venography is used when cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is suspected, for example with a persistent progressive headache, papilloedema or a prothrombotic risk such as oestrogen use, but she has discrete attacks, normal fundi and a non-hormonal contraceptive.

Electroencephalography is used to investigate seizures, and occipital seizures cause brief coloured circular images lasting seconds to a few minutes, not the slowly spreading zigzag aura followed by migraine headache that she describes.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man who drinks heavily presents with two weeks of increasing abdominal distension. Serum albumin is 28 g/L. Ascitic fluid albumin is 7 g/L and total protein 8 g/L. What does this ascitic result indicate?
questions.why: The serum-ascites albumin gradient is 28 − 7 = 21 g/L. A gradient of 11 g/L or more indicates portal hypertensive ascites, which in a heavy drinker is most likely from alcohol-related cirrhosis. Ascitic protein below 10 g/L also puts him at high risk of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
notes: Peritoneal malignancy gives a SAAG below 11 g/L, usually with high ascitic protein.
Tuberculous peritonitis gives a low SAAG with high protein and a lymphocyte-rich fluid.
Nephrotic syndrome gives a SAAG below 11 g/L, because the ascites comes from hypoalbuminaemia, not portal hypertension.
Pancreatic ascites gives a low SAAG with a very high ascitic amylase.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man who smokes has 5 months of worsening breathlessness. Erect chest X-ray shows a dense right opacity with a concave meniscus reaching the 2nd rib. The trachea is deviated left. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: A dense opacity with a concave meniscus that pushes the trachea and mediastinum to the other side is a large pleural effusion: the fluid takes up space. Anything that causes volume loss on the right, such as collapse or pneumonectomy, would pull the trachea towards the opacity instead. In a heavy smoker, this calls for ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration and a CT to look for malignancy.
notes: Collapse causes volume loss, so the trachea would be pulled towards the right, not pushed away to the left.
Consolidation does not change lung volume, so the trachea would stay central. It usually shows air bronchograms rather than a meniscus.
After a pneumonectomy the mediastinum moves towards the empty hemithorax, so the trachea would shift right.
A raised hemidiaphragm keeps its domed outline, has no meniscus, does not reach the 2nd rib and does not push the trachea away.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner for her annual diabetes review. She has had type 2 diabetes for 14 years. Over the past 4 months, small print has become harder to read with her right eye, even with new reading glasses. She also has hypertension and dyslipidaemia. Her medicines are metformin 1 g twice daily, modified-release gliclazide 60 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Her last eye examination was 2 years ago. Blood pressure is 144/86 mmHg and pulse is 76/min. Visual acuity is 6/18 in the right eye and 6/9 in the left, and the right eye does not improve with a pinhole. Both lenses are clear. Good-quality non-mydriatic retinal photographs show microaneurysms and dot and blot haemorrhages in both eyes, and a ring of hard exudates within one disc diameter of the right fovea. There are no new vessels and no venous beading. HbA1c is 8.8% (73 mmol/mol). Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause of the reduced vision in her right eye?
questions.why: She has non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes. In the right eye she has hard exudates near the fovea and slowly worsening central vision that a pinhole does not correct, so a refractive error is not the cause. This pattern points to diabetic macular oedema, which causes most vision loss in diabetes and can occur at any stage of retinopathy. Retinal photographs are two-dimensional and cannot show retinal thickening, so they cannot confirm or exclude macular oedema. The NHMRC diabetic retinopathy guideline and the RACGP handbook advise referral to an ophthalmologist. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the non-invasive test that confirms the diagnosis. It measures central retinal thickness, shows intraretinal and subretinal fluid, and is used to decide on and monitor anti-VEGF treatment. Fluorescein angiography is an invasive second-line test. Ultrasound is only needed when the fundus cannot be seen. Visual field testing and repeat photographs cannot assess retinal thickness.
notes: Fluorescein angiography is invasive, carries a risk of dye reactions, and is kept for assessing ischaemia or new vessels or for planning laser, so it is not the first test to confirm macular oedema.
B-scan ultrasound is used when the view of the retina is blocked, for example by vitreous haemorrhage or dense cataract, but her lenses are clear and the fundus can be seen.
Automated perimetry tests peripheral visual fields for glaucoma or neurological disease, and it cannot show the structural macular changes behind her central blur.
Repeat photographs after dilation give a better view but are still two-dimensional, so they cannot measure retinal thickness or reliably exclude macular oedema.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman, para 3, is in the birth suite 40 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth of twins at 37 weeks' gestation. The placenta is complete and there are no genital tract tears. She keeps bleeding despite intramuscular oxytocin, an oxytocin infusion, intramuscular ergometrine, intramuscular carboprost, an indwelling urinary catheter and bimanual compression. She has been given intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g. The weighed blood loss is 2,000 mL and the blood contains clots. She has no history of a bleeding disorder and takes no regular medicines. Her temperature is 36.3 °C, pulse is 130/min, blood pressure is 86/48 mm Hg, respirations are 26/min and SpO2 is 96% on 6 L/min of oxygen. The fundus is intermittently soft. Two 16-gauge cannulas are in place, the massive transfusion protocol has been activated, O-negative red cells are running and theatre is being prepared. Point-of-care haemoglobin is 82 g/L (reference 115–160 g/L). Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to guide further blood component replacement?
questions.why: This woman has a major primary postpartum haemorrhage (2,000 mL and still bleeding) from uterine atony. Her risk factors are twins, which overdistend the uterus, and multiparity. Large blood loss leads to dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy, which makes the bleeding worse. In obstetric haemorrhage, fibrinogen is the first clotting factor to fall to a critical level. It falls well before the platelet count or the clotting times change. A fibrinogen level below 2 g/L is the best early lab predictor of progression to severe PPH. RANZCOG, the Queensland Clinical Guidelines and the National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Module 5 all advise measuring it (Clauss fibrinogen, or FIBTEM on viscoelastic testing where available) and repeating it often. Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is given to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L. The fact that she is forming clots does not rule out a falling fibrinogen. D-dimer is normally raised in pregnancy and after birth, so it does not help guide replacement. APTT and PT stay normal until late in obstetric haemorrhage, so they are poor early guides.
notes: D-dimer is normally raised in pregnancy and the puerperium, so it cannot reliably detect coagulopathy or guide what to give.
The APTT stays normal until late in obstetric haemorrhage, so it misses the early fall in fibrinogen that drives ongoing bleeding.
The platelet count usually falls only after very large losses or with abruption or HELLP, so it is a late and poor guide here.
Haemoglobin lags behind acute blood loss and only measures red cells, so it cannot guide replacement of clotting factors.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man attends a hospital pre-admission clinic before a planned colonoscopy. He has had 2 years of intermittent loose stools, crampy right iliac fossa pain, recurrent mouth ulcers and an unintentional 6 kg weight loss. He sometimes wakes at night to open his bowels. His GP started ferrous sulfate tablets 3 weeks ago. He eats a normal diet that includes bread and pasta and takes no other medicines. His temperature is 37.2 °C, pulse 88/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and respiratory rate 14/min. His conjunctivae are pale, and he has mild right iliac fossa tenderness with no palpable mass. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (135–175) MCV 76 fL (80–100) Platelets 448 x10^9/L (150–400) Ferritin 16 µg/L (30–500) Transferrin saturation 8% (20–50) CRP 28 mg/L (less than 5) Albumin 31 g/L (35–50) Vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (150–700) Faecal calprotectin 520 µg/g (less than 50) Which of the following best explains this patient's blood count findings?
options: Anaemia of inflammation with replete iron stores
Vitamin B12 deficiency from terminal ileal disease
Absolute iron deficiency with coexisting inflammation
Folate deficiency from small bowel malabsorption
questions.why: This man probably has ileocolonic Crohn's disease. His raised CRP, platelets and calprotectin and his low albumin show active inflammation, and he has a microcytic anaemia (Hb 118 g/L, MCV 76 fL). Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so inflammation pushes it up. A ferritin of 16 µg/L despite a CRP of 28 mg/L, and despite 3 weeks of oral iron, therefore confirms that his iron stores are truly empty. In active IBD, a ferritin below 100 µg/L already suggests iron deficiency, and below 30 µg/L confirms it. A transferrin saturation of 8% supports this. The likely causes are blood loss from ulcerated mucosa and poor absorption. What this means for him: he needs his iron replaced, and IV iron (for example ferric carboxymaltose) is preferred because oral iron is poorly absorbed and poorly tolerated in active IBD. He should also stop the oral iron 5 to 7 days before colonoscopy. Anaemia of inflammation alone would give a normal or high ferritin. B12 deficiency and folate deficiency both cause a large-cell (macrocytic) anaemia, and his B12 is normal. Thalassaemia trait does not cause a low ferritin or a low transferrin saturation.
notes: Wrong: anaemia of inflammation alone gives a normal or raised ferritin, but his ferritin of 16 µg/L is low even though inflammation should be pushing it up.
Wrong: terminal ileal disease can cause B12 deficiency, but that gives a macrocytic anaemia, and his B12 of 380 pmol/L is normal.
Wrong: thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis with normal or high iron stores, so it would not explain a ferritin of 16 µg/L and a transferrin saturation of 8%.
Wrong: folate deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia, not a microcytic one with an MCV of 76 fL and low iron studies.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of difficulty swallowing for 10 weeks. Bread and meat feel as if they stick behind his lower sternum a few seconds after he swallows. He now cuts food into small pieces but drinks fluids easily. He has no choking, coughing, nasal regurgitation or hoarseness. He has lost 6 kg without trying and feels tired. He has had heartburn for about 20 years and treats it on and off using over-the-counter antacids. He smoked 30 pack-years until 5 years ago. He takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 84/min, blood pressure 136/82 mm Hg and BMI 34 kg/m². He has conjunctival pallor. The abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Haemoglobin is 116 g/L (reference 130–180), mean corpuscular volume 76 fL (80–100) and ferritin 10 µg/L (30–500). Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: He has progressive dysphagia to solids only, with food sticking after the swallow. This suggests a mechanical oesophageal obstruction. He also has alarm features: weight loss, fatigue and iron deficiency anaemia. His risk factors for distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma are long-standing untreated reflux (a possible Barrett's oesophagus), obesity and a smoking history. The Australian optimal care pathway for oesophagogastric cancer recommends urgent gastroscopy, ideally within 2 weeks, for dysphagia with alarm features. Gastroscopy shows the mucosa directly and allows biopsies, which give the tissue diagnosis needed to confirm cancer, and it can also find Barrett's mucosa or a benign peptic stricture. A barium swallow cannot provide tissue and would delay the endoscopy he needs anyway. CT is used for staging once a cancer is proven by biopsy. Manometry is for suspected motility disorders, and only after endoscopy has ruled out an obstruction. Testing for Helicobacter pylori does not investigate dysphagia and is not appropriate when there are alarm features.
notes: A barium swallow cannot take tissue for diagnosis, and any abnormality would still need endoscopy, so it delays the diagnosis.
CT is used to stage an oesophageal cancer after biopsy has confirmed it, and it cannot provide tissue for diagnosis.
Manometry assesses motility disorders such as achalasia, which cause dysphagia to solids and liquids, and should only be done after endoscopy rules out a mechanical cause.
A urea breath test looks for Helicobacter pylori in uncomplicated dyspepsia and does not investigate dysphagia with alarm features.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has had confusion, polyuria and constipation for three days. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her corrected calcium is 3.6 mmol/L. Most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.why: This is severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia of malignancy, and the patient is dehydrated from polyuria. The first step is IV rehydration with 0.9% sodium chloride, which restores volume and increases calcium excretion by the kidneys. An IV bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid is given once she is rehydrated (eTG).
notes: Zoledronic acid is the right second step, but it takes 2 to 4 days to work and can harm the kidneys if given before rehydration.
Furosemide worsens dehydration and is now used only for fluid overload once the patient has been rehydrated.
Denosumab is kept for hypercalcaemia that does not respond to bisphosphonates or for severe renal impairment, not for first treatment.
Steroids help mainly in hypercalcaemia driven by calcitriol (lymphoma, granulomatous disease), not in bone metastases from breast cancer.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 8 days of fever, malaise and anorexia, followed by a right upper quadrant ache and dark urine. He returned 16 days ago from 6 weeks volunteering in a rural village in Papua New Guinea, where he drank untreated water and was often bitten by mosquitoes. He had no pre-travel vaccines, took no chemoprophylaxis and takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 38.3 °C, pulse 102/min, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and SpO2 98% on room air. He is alert and his sclerae are mildly icteric. The liver edge is tender 2 cm below the costal margin and the spleen is not palpable. Results: ALT 2460 U/L (<35), ALP 155 U/L (30–110), bilirubin 46 µmol/L (<20), INR 1.1 and platelets 198 x10^9/L. Hepatitis A IgM is detected. A rapid Plasmodium antigen test is negative and one blood film shows no parasites. Ultrasound shows a thick-walled gallbladder with no stones and a common bile duct of normal calibre. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Repeat malaria microscopy in 12 to 24 hours
questions.why: This unvaccinated traveller has acute hepatitis A. He has a hepatocellular pattern of liver injury (ALT in the thousands with ALP only slightly raised), a positive hepatitis A IgM, and an incubation period that fits. His synthetic function is preserved (INR 1.1). However, he has a fever after travel to a highly malaria-endemic area with mosquito exposure and no prophylaxis, so malaria has to be actively excluded, even though another diagnosis has been found. Co-infection is possible, and missing falciparum malaria can be fatal. One negative rapid antigen test and one negative film set do not exclude malaria. Australian guidance (eTG and the laboratory recommendations) is to repeat thick and thin films every 12 to 24 hours until three sets are negative. A thickened gallbladder wall without stones, without a sonographic Murphy's sign and without duct dilatation is a common finding in acute hepatitis and needs no further biliary imaging. The diagnosis is already confirmed, so no further serology or tissue is needed.
notes: A HIDA scan looks for acalculous or calculous cholecystitis, but gallbladder wall thickening without stones or ductal dilatation is an expected reactive finding in acute viral hepatitis.
MRCP looks for biliary obstruction, which is unlikely with a normal-calibre common bile duct and a hepatocellular rather than cholestatic pattern of liver tests.
Hepatitis A IgG shows past infection or immunity and adds nothing once IgM has already confirmed acute infection.
Liver biopsy is invasive and not needed when serology has confirmed acute hepatitis A and the INR shows preserved synthetic function.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has fever and 30 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain. Ultrasound confirms calculous cholecystitis; common bile duct 5 mm. ALP 480 U/L, bilirubin 24 µmol/L. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: A blocked cystic duct alone usually causes only mild LFT changes. An ALP more than 4 times the upper limit means a common bile duct stone is possible, even though the bilirubin is only slightly raised and the duct is not dilated, because partial obstruction often looks like this. This puts her at intermediate risk, so she needs non-invasive duct imaging with MRCP (or endoscopic ultrasound) before cholecystectomy.
notes: ERCP carries a risk of pancreatitis and bleeding, so it is kept for a confirmed duct stone or cholangitis, and neither has been shown here.
Ultrasound has already confirmed cholecystitis, and a HIDA scan cannot reliably show stones in the common bile duct.
CT misses many bile duct stones and adds radiation without answering the question.
Repeat ultrasound sees the distal common bile duct poorly and is no better at finding a stone than the first scan.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has 6 weeks of burning epigastric pain waking him at night. He takes no medications and has no weight loss, vomiting or melaena. Haemoglobin is 146 g/L. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: This young man has dyspepsia that sounds like a duodenal ulcer, takes no NSAIDs and has no ALARM features. eTG recommends a test-and-treat approach in this case: a non-invasive test for current H. pylori infection, either a urea breath test or a faecal antigen test, done when he has been off PPIs and antibiotics.
notes: Gastroscopy is kept for patients with ALARM features, older patients with new symptoms, or symptoms that persist after test and treat, and he has none of these.
Serology stays positive after the infection has been cleared, so it cannot show current infection and is not recommended.
Ultrasound looks for gallstones, but burning nocturnal pain without colic or right upper quadrant features does not point to biliary disease.
Lipase is for acute pancreatitis, which would cause severe constant pain going through to the back, not weeks of intermittent burning nocturnal pain.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has full-thickness circumferential burns of the left forearm after a house fire. Six hours into resuscitation, his hand is cool and pale with no radial Doppler signal. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Full-thickness burn eschar is stiff and does not stretch. As the tissue swells during fluid resuscitation, a circumferential eschar acts like a tourniquet and cuts off blood flow to the hand. Loss of distal perfusion is a clinical diagnosis, and Australian burns guidelines (ANZBA EMSB) call for urgent escharotomy to release the eschar and restore circulation.
notes: Fasciotomy is kept for compartment syndrome that persists after escharotomy, or for electrical or crush injury, so it is not the first step here.
Elevation helps reduce swelling but cannot release a constricting eschar once the pulse is lost.
Cutting back fluids risks under-resuscitation and shock; the fluid rate should be guided by urine output, not by limb swelling.
Imaging delays a decision that should be made at the bedside on clinical grounds, and the limb is at risk of irreversible ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has two weeks of worsening thoracic back pain and new bilateral leg weakness. Reflexes are brisk in both legs. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: New back pain, leg weakness and upper motor neuron signs in a patient with known cancer suggest malignant spinal cord compression. This needs an urgent whole spine MRI, ideally within 24 hours, along with high-dose dexamethasone. The whole spine is imaged because about a third of patients have compression at more than one level.
notes: Plain X-rays cannot show the spinal cord or epidural disease and miss many metastases, so a normal film would not rule out compression.
A bone scan can show bone metastases but not compression of the cord or the epidural space, so it does not guide urgent treatment.
PSA reflects overall disease burden but cannot confirm or locate cord compression, and checking it would only delay definitive imaging.
CT shows less soft tissue and cord detail than MRI and is kept for patients who cannot have MRI; imaging only the thoracic spine would also miss lesions at other levels.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with diabetes has 40 minutes of central chest pain at rest despite aspirin, sublingual and intravenous GTN, and morphine. ECG shows no ST elevation; first troponin is normal. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Ongoing ischaemic pain that does not respond to nitrates and opioid makes this suspected NSTEACS very high risk under the Heart Foundation/CSANZ guideline, even with a normal ECG and a normal first troponin. Very high-risk patients need invasive coronary angiography within 2 hours, so cardiology should be contacted now.
notes: Thrombolysis is only for STEMI and does not help in non-ST-elevation ACS.
Serial troponins are still needed, but waiting for them delays angiography, which very high-risk features require now.
CT coronary angiography is for low to intermediate risk stable patients, not for ongoing ischaemia, and it cannot open a blocked artery.
Stress testing is unsafe during ongoing pain and is only for low-risk patients once ACS has been ruled out.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever and new confusion. After IV fluids and antibiotics, BP is 94/60 mmHg. Ultrasound: dilated common bile duct, distal stone. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Jaundice, pain, fever, confusion and hypotension make up Reynolds' pentad. This is severe acute cholangitis from an obstructing common bile duct stone. Once sepsis resuscitation and IV antibiotics have started, he needs urgent biliary drainage by ERCP for source control, with cholecystectomy planned after he recovers.
notes: Emergency cholecystectomy in a septic, unstable patient does not clear the duct stone; it is done after he has recovered.
MRCP only images the duct, which ultrasound has already shown is blocked, and it would delay drainage.
Cholecystostomy drains the gallbladder, not the obstructed common bile duct, so it is used for high-risk acute cholecystitis.
Antibiotics alone leave the duct obstructed, and organ dysfunction in severe cholangitis means he needs urgent drainage.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man comes to his general practitioner because of episodes of a racing, irregular heartbeat. Over the past 6 weeks he has had four episodes. Each started suddenly at rest, lasted 1 to 3 hours and stopped on its own. He has had no chest pain, breathlessness or fainting. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and takes perindopril and metformin. He drinks about four standard drinks of alcohol a day and has never smoked. He arrived during an episode. A 12-lead ECG then showed an irregularly irregular, narrow-complex rhythm at 104/min with no P waves. Two hours later his pulse is 74/min and regular, blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg and SpO2 is 98% on room air. Heart sounds are normal with no murmurs. Haemoglobin is 142 g/L, creatinine 86 µmol/L (eGFR 79 mL/min/1.73 m^2), potassium 4.3 mmol/L and TSH 1.8 mIU/L. A repeat ECG shows sinus rhythm. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to start today?
questions.why: This man has paroxysmal atrial fibrillation: sudden irregular palpitations that stop on their own, an ECG during an episode showing AF, and sinus rhythm afterwards. His CHA2DS2-VA score is 3 (age 65 to 74, hypertension, diabetes). Stroke risk in paroxysmal AF is about the same as in persistent AF, so the score, not the pattern of episodes, decides anticoagulation. The 2018 NHFA/CSANZ Australian AF guidelines and eTG recommend oral anticoagulation for a CHA2DS2-VA score of 2 or more. They prefer a DOAC such as apixaban over warfarin in non-valvular AF because it causes less intracranial bleeding and needs no INR monitoring. His renal function is normal, so no dose reduction is needed. His alcohol intake raises his bleeding risk. It should be addressed as part of AF risk factor management, not used as a reason to withhold anticoagulation. Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF. Digoxin is a rate-control drug for persistent AF and does nothing for a patient now in sinus rhythm. Flecainide should not be started before structural and ischaemic heart disease have been excluded.
notes: Aspirin gives little or no stroke protection in AF and still carries a bleeding risk, so Australian guidelines advise against it.
Digoxin only slows the ventricular rate in sustained AF, gives no stroke protection and has no role while he is in sinus rhythm.
Flecainide for rhythm control should wait until an echocardiogram and ischaemia assessment have excluded structural heart disease, and it does not reduce stroke risk.
Warfarin works but is second line to a DOAC in non-valvular AF because it causes more intracranial haemorrhage and needs INR monitoring.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to a general practice because his partner noticed 2 days ago that his eyes were yellow. Ten days ago he developed nausea, anorexia, fevers and right upper quadrant discomfort. These have mostly settled, and his urine is dark. He returned 5 weeks ago from 3 weeks in Bali, where he ate at street stalls and had unprotected sex with two new partners. He takes no medicines and is not sure which vaccines he had as a child. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse is 78/min and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. He has scleral icterus and mild right upper quadrant tenderness. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease and no asterixis. Investigations show: ALT 1450 U/L (less than 40) AST 720 U/L (less than 40) ALP 150 U/L (30 to 110) Total bilirubin 52 µmol/L (less than 20), conjugated 38 µmol/L INR 1.0 (0.9 to 1.2) Hepatitis A IgM: detected Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg): not detected Hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc), total: not detected Hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs): 2 mIU/mL (protective level 10 or more) Hepatitis C antibody: not detected Which of the following best describes his hepatitis B status?
questions.why: This man has acute hepatitis A: a hepatocellular pattern (ALT more than 15 times the upper limit and higher than AST, with only a mildly raised ALP), mostly conjugated bilirubin, a normal INR and a positive hepatitis A IgM. Separately, his hepatitis B results have to be read one marker at a time. A negative HBsAg means he has no current hepatitis B infection, acute or chronic. A negative total anti-HBc means he has never been infected, and it also rules out the core window period, because anti-HBc is the marker present in that window. An anti-HBs of 2 mIU/mL is below the protective level of 10 mIU/mL, so he has no serological immunity. He is therefore susceptible and not infected. The Australian Immunisation Handbook advises checking the Australian Immunisation Register and giving a hepatitis B vaccine course if he has no documented primary course. His last sexual exposure was only about 5 to 6 weeks ago, which is still within the hepatitis B incubation period, so HBsAg and anti-HBc should be repeated at about 3 months, along with HIV, syphilis and hepatitis C serology.
notes: Wrong: chronic hepatitis B needs a positive HBsAg for more than 6 months, and his HBsAg is not detected.
Wrong: resolved past infection shows a positive anti-HBc, usually with anti-HBs, but his anti-HBc is not detected.
Wrong: immunity from vaccination needs an anti-HBs of 10 mIU/mL or more with a negative anti-HBc, and his anti-HBs is only 2 mIU/mL.
Wrong: in the core window period HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBc (IgM) is positive, and his anti-HBc is negative.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with COPD and a large right pleural effusion has ultrasound-guided therapeutic aspiration. After 2.2 L is removed, he develops a cough, frothy sputum and right-sided crackles, with SpO2 85%. Most likely complication?
questions.why: If a lung that has been collapsed for a long time re-expands quickly, it can develop pulmonary oedema on the same side. This causes a cough, frothy sputum, crackles and hypoxia. To lower this risk, remove no more than about 1.5 L at one time, and stop if he develops a cough or chest tightness.
notes: A pneumothorax would give reduced breath sounds and a hyper-resonant chest, not crackles and frothy sputum, and tension would add low blood pressure and a shifted trachea.
A haemothorax would show as fluid building up again with dullness and low blood pressure, not as crackles and frothy sputum.
A vasovagal reaction causes a slow heart rate, low blood pressure and fainting, without crackles or a big fall in SpO2.
Hypercapnia from oxygen in COPD causes drowsiness and a rising pCO2, not frothy sputum and crackles on one side straight after drainage.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old medical student gets a needlestick injury while taking blood from a patient known to be HBsAg positive. She is fully vaccinated against hepatitis B. Her anti-HBs today is 150 mIU/mL. Most appropriate HBV management?
questions.why: An anti-HBs level of 10 mIU/mL or more shows that a vaccinated person is immune. Under the Australian Immunisation Handbook, a known responder exposed to an HBsAg-positive source needs no hepatitis B prophylaxis. She should still do first aid, report the incident and follow the HIV and HCV exposure pathway.
notes: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin is for unvaccinated people or known non-responders, and she is protected.
A booster is for vaccinated people whose anti-HBs is below 10 mIU/mL, which is not the case here.
HBIG plus a booster is for people whose immunity is unknown or inadequate after exposure, not for a proven responder.
Repeating the whole course is for non-responders and adds nothing for someone with protective antibody levels.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy fell off his scooter 15 minutes ago. His upper permanent central incisor was knocked out whole; he holds it by the crown. He is otherwise uninjured. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: An avulsed permanent tooth should be replanted as soon as possible, ideally within minutes, because periodontal ligament cells die quickly once the tooth is out of the mouth, especially if it is kept dry. Hold it by the crown, rinse it briefly in milk or saline if it is dirty, push it back into the socket, have the child bite on gauze, then arrange urgent dental splinting.
notes: Milk is only a holding medium for when immediate replantation is not possible, and the delay worsens the outcome.
Scrubbing the root destroys the periodontal ligament cells needed for reattachment; a dirty tooth only needs a brief rinse.
Discarding is right for an avulsed primary tooth, but this is a permanent incisor that can be saved.
Waiting until tomorrow means a long dry time and ligament death, so replantation will almost certainly fail.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman attends pre-admission clinic with a penicillin allergy label. At age 8 she developed a non-itchy maculopapular rash on day 5 of amoxicillin, without blistering or mucosal involvement. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: This is a low-risk history (PEN-FAST under 3): a benign, delayed maculopapular rash in childhood more than 5 years ago, with no severe cutaneous or mucosal features. Australian antibiotic allergy guidance (ASCIA, AusPAAS) supports delabelling with a direct oral amoxicillin challenge under observation, without skin testing first.
notes: Skin testing is kept for higher-risk immediate reactions, and its poor negative predictive value adds little in a low-risk history.
Serum specific IgE has low sensitivity and is not recommended to rule out penicillin allergy.
Keeping the label leads to broader-spectrum antibiotics, more resistance and worse surgical prophylaxis, with no benefit in a low-risk history.
Desensitisation is for confirmed IgE-mediated allergy when penicillin is essential, not for delabelling a probable non-allergy.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has dysuria and urethral discharge. First-pass urine NAAT is positive for Mycoplasma genitalium, with a macrolide resistance mutation detected. Gonorrhoea and chlamydia NAATs are negative. After doxycycline, which antibiotic is most appropriate?
questions.why: The resistance result shows macrolide-resistant M. genitalium. Australian STI guidelines recommend resistance-guided therapy: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, then moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for 7 days. A test of cure is done 14 to 21 days after treatment ends.
notes: Azithromycin is the follow-on drug only for macrolide-sensitive infection, so it will likely fail here and select further resistance.
Ceftriaxone treats gonorrhoea, which is negative, and has no activity against M. genitalium.
Metronidazole treats trichomonas and bacterial vaginosis and does not work against M. genitalium.
Pristinamycin is kept for infection that fails or resists both macrolides and fluoroquinolones, so it is not used first.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man cut his palm on a broken beer glass 2 hours ago. The 1.5 cm wound has stopped bleeding, but gripping causes sharp localised pain. Tendon and nerve function are intact. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Sharp pain on gripping after a glass injury suggests a retained foreign body. Most glass fragments over about 2 mm show up on plain film, so a plain X-ray is the first-line test for any glass wound where a foreign body is suspected. It should be done before the wound is explored and closed.
notes: Ultrasound is best for radiolucent foreign bodies such as wood or plastic, and is used if the X-ray is negative but suspicion remains.
CT exposes the patient to more radiation and costs more, and it is kept for complex or deep foreign bodies after a plain film.
MRI is slow and costly, and is not a first-line test for a suspected glass foreign body.
A fresh, clean 2-hour-old wound has no signs of infection, so a swab would not change management or find a foreign body.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy has wheeze and breathlessness overnight after 3 days of coryza. He has bilateral expiratory wheeze, equal air entry and SpO2 95% on room air, improving with salbutamol. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: This is a moderate episode of viral-induced (preschool) wheeze. The diagnosis is clinical, and RCH and Queensland guidelines advise against routine X-ray, bloods or blood gas. Severity is graded at the bedside and treatment is salbutamol by spacer.
notes: A chest X-ray is not routine with bilateral wheeze, equal air entry and no focal signs, and it does not change management.
A blood gas is kept for severe or life-threatening episodes that are not responding to treatment, which does not fit an alert child with SpO2 95%.
A full blood count does not help diagnose or grade viral wheeze and is not recommended.
Spirometry cannot be done reliably under about 6 years and is not used in an acute episode.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with hypertension has worsening breathlessness. ECG: sinus 102/min, S V1 plus R V5 40 mm, downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T-wave inversion in V5-V6, unchanged from six months ago. Best explanation of the ST changes?
questions.why: She meets voltage criteria for LVH, and the lateral downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T-wave inversion is the typical strain pattern. It is unchanged from her ECG six months ago and fits long-standing hypertension. This makes a new ischaemic change unlikely, although a troponin is still needed.
notes: Acute ischaemia would show new or changing ST-T changes, but these are unchanged from six months ago and come with LVH voltage.
Digoxin causes scooped ST depression in many leads with a short QT, not changes confined to the lateral leads alongside LVH voltage.
Hypokalaemia causes flattened T waves, prominent U waves and a long QT, not lateral strain alongside LVH voltage.
Left bundle branch block needs a QRS of at least 120 ms with a broad notched R in V6, which is not described here.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man comes to a sexual health clinic in Melbourne with his regular male partner, aged 32, to discuss results. Last week the patient was diagnosed with HIV-1 infection after a reactive screening immunoassay was confirmed on Western blot. He has no other illness and takes no medicines. He starts daily antiretroviral therapy today. The couple have had condomless anal sex about weekly for 2 years, most recently 5 days ago. The partner says he dislikes condoms and will not use them reliably. The partner is well, has had no fever, rash or sore throat, and has a temperature of 36.7 °C and a normal examination. The patient's CD4 count is 480 cells/µL (reference 500–1500) and his HIV-1 viral load is 64,000 copies/mL. The partner's results today: HIV-1/2 antigen and antibody immunoassay non-reactive; hepatitis B surface antigen negative; hepatitis B surface antibody 120 mIU/mL; creatinine 79 µmol/L; eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m². Which of the following is the most appropriate measure to prevent HIV transmission to the partner?
options: Daily oral tenofovir disoproxil–emtricitabine for the partner until viral suppression is sustained
A 28-day course of three-drug post-exposure prophylaxis for the partner
Condomless sex resumed once the patient's first follow-up viral load is undetectable
Suppressive valaciclovir for the patient to reduce genital mucosal viral shedding
Three-monthly HIV testing of the partner with no antiretroviral medicine
questions.why: The partner is HIV negative, will not use condoms reliably, and is having regular condomless anal sex with a man whose viral load is high (64,000 copies/mL) and who only starts ART today. He is at high ongoing risk and meets ASHM criteria for PrEP. Australia's PBS subsidises PrEP. His kidney function is normal and he is immune to hepatitis B, so he can start daily tenofovir disoproxil–emtricitabine today. He needs a repeat HIV test at about 4 weeks because his last exposure was 5 days ago, which is still inside the window period of the fourth-generation test. Under U=U, sexual transmission is prevented only once the patient's viral load has been undetectable for at least 6 months. PrEP should continue until then and can be reviewed after that. Post-exposure prophylaxis is not appropriate because the last exposure was more than 72 hours ago. Stopping protection at the first undetectable result is too early. Valaciclovir does not lower HIV transmission. Testing alone gives no protection.
notes: Wrong: PEP must start within 72 hours of exposure and his last exposure was 5 days ago; it also does not cover ongoing exposures, which is what PrEP is for.
Wrong: U=U applies only after the viral load has stayed undetectable for at least 6 months, so a single first undetectable result is not enough to prevent sexual transmission.
Wrong: trials of herpes suppression with aciclovir or valaciclovir did not reduce HIV transmission to partners, and there is no evidence that this patient has HSV.
Wrong: regular testing picks up infection after it has happened but does nothing to stop it during high-risk ongoing exposure.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman is on the orthopaedic ward 6 days after an elective left total knee replacement. This afternoon she suddenly became short of breath and developed sharp left-sided chest pain that is worse on inspiration. Her left calf has been aching and swollen since yesterday. She has hypertension treated with perindopril. Since surgery she has had subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin 40 mg each evening, and the last dose was 18 hours ago. She weighs 74 kg. Her temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 114/min, blood pressure 136/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Her left calf measures 3 cm more around than the right. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Haemoglobin is 115 g/L, platelets 245 x10^9/L, creatinine 72 µmol/L (eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m2) and high-sensitivity troponin T 8 ng/L (reference <14). CT pulmonary angiography shows segmental filling defects in both lower lobes. The right-to-left ventricular diameter ratio is 0.8. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Switch to enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily
Inferior vena cava filter insertion today
Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily added to current prophylaxis
Warfarin 5 mg orally daily without heparin cover
questions.why: This woman has an acute pulmonary embolism caused by surgery, with a left calf DVT as the likely source. She is haemodynamically stable: her blood pressure is normal, her troponin is normal and her right ventricle is not dilated (RV:LV ratio below 1.0). That makes her non-high-risk. eTG recommends immediate therapeutic anticoagulation for stable PE. In a patient 6 days after surgery, a short-acting injectable drug is the sensible choice. Stop the prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin and replace it with therapeutic enoxaparin, 1 mg/kg (about 75 mg) subcutaneously every 12 hours. Give the first dose now, because the last prophylactic dose was 18 hours ago. Do not give both. Her eGFR is normal, so she needs no renal dose change. Agree the bleeding risk with the surgical team. Later she can move to a DOAC or warfarin, and a provoked PE is treated for 3 months. Prophylaxis lowers the risk of VTE but does not remove it, so PE can still occur while she is on it. Thrombolysis is for PE with shock. A filter is only for patients who cannot be anticoagulated. Warfarin started alone is unsafe.
notes: Thrombolysis is for high-risk PE with sustained low blood pressure or shock, and knee replacement 6 days ago is a strong contraindication because of the bleeding risk.
An inferior vena cava filter is only for patients with acute VTE who cannot be anticoagulated, and this patient has no contraindication to anticoagulation.
Giving a therapeutic dose on top of the prophylactic dose doubles up the heparin and raises the risk of bleeding with no extra benefit, so the prophylactic dose must be stopped.
Warfarin takes several days to work and can cause a temporary prothrombotic state at the start, so it must overlap with a parenteral anticoagulant until the INR is in range.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends the high-risk foot clinic with a painful right fifth-toe ulcer without surrounding erythema. Pedal pulses absent. ABI is 1.42; toe pressure 22 mmHg. Most likely interpretation?
questions.why: In diabetes, calcification of the tibial artery walls can make the ankle arteries impossible to compress, so an ABI above 1.3 gives a falsely high reading and cannot be trusted. Digital arteries are usually spared, so the toe pressure of 22 mmHg (below 30 mmHg) with a foot ulcer shows severe ischaemia. This is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and needs urgent vascular imaging (Diabetes Feet Australia 2021).
notes: An ABI above 1.3 means the arteries cannot be compressed, not that perfusion is normal, and the toe pressure and absent pulses show ischaemia.
A toe pressure of 22 mmHg with tissue loss means severe ischaemia, not mild disease, whatever the ABI reading.
Infection does not raise the ABI or lower the toe pressure, and nothing here suggests infection.
Venous disease causes shallow ulcers in the gaiter area with normal pulses, not a painful toe ulcer with a low toe pressure.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote Northern Territory community has a 2-day sore throat, fever of 38.4 °C and red, swollen tonsils. He has no allergies. Most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: An Aboriginal child in a remote Northern Territory community is at high risk of acute rheumatic fever. Under the RHD Australia guideline and eTG, a sore throat in this group should be treated straight away as group A streptococcal pharyngitis. A single dose of IM benzathine benzylpenicillin is preferred because it treats the infection in one dose and does not depend on finishing a course.
notes: Wrong: in a high-risk population, a sore throat without antibiotics can lead to acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease.
Wrong: a swab can be taken, but in high-risk groups antibiotics should not wait for the result.
Wrong: azithromycin is kept for severe (immediate) penicillin allergy, and this child has no allergies.
Wrong: oral penicillin must be given for 10 days to eradicate the streptococcus, so a 5-day course is too short.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with new HIV, viral load 120,000 copies/mL, starts ART. His HIV-negative partner asks when condomless sex will not transmit HIV. When is transmission prevented?
questions.why: Under Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U), there is effectively no sexual transmission once the viral load has stayed below 200 copies/mL for at least 6 months on ART. Until then, the partner needs other protection, such as PrEP or condoms. Viral load, not CD4 count, is the measure of how infectious he is.
notes: Taking ART for a set time does not prove suppression, and at 4 weeks the viral load is often still detectable.
CD4 count shows immune recovery, not how infectious he is, and suppression can happen at any CD4 level.
One undetectable result is not enough; U=U needs suppression sustained for 6 months.
A viral load of thousands of copies/mL can still transmit HIV; U=U applies only below 200 copies/mL, held for 6 months.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with polycystic kidney disease has a sudden severe headache. Her GCS is 15 and BP 148/88 mmHg. CT shows subarachnoid blood, and CT angiography shows an anterior communicating artery aneurysm. Which drug should be started now?
questions.why: This is aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. eTG recommends starting oral nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days as soon as possible, because it reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia and improves outcome. The patient also needs urgent neurosurgical referral so the aneurysm can be secured.
notes: Tranexamic acid lowers the rebleeding rate, but it does not improve functional outcome and it raises the risk of thrombosis, so it is not routine.
Corticosteroids give no proven benefit in aneurysmal SAH and cause hyperglycaemia.
Routine seizure prophylaxis is not recommended when she has had no seizure.
Her BP of 148/88 mmHg is already below the usual target of systolic under 160 mmHg before the aneurysm is secured, so she needs no antihypertensive.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female registrar who has no regular doctor asks you, a fellow junior doctor, to prescribe temazepam so she can sleep between night shifts. Most appropriate response?
questions.why: The Medical Board of Australia's Code of Conduct says doctors should have their own GP and should not prescribe informally for colleagues, especially drugs of dependence. Informal prescribing skips a proper assessment and puts both doctors at risk. The safest response is to point her to independent care, such as a GP or a doctors' health service.
notes: Prescribing a drug of dependence for a colleague without a proper consultation or records is unprofessional, even if the supply is small.
Swapping to a lower-risk drug is still informal prescribing for a colleague without an independent assessment.
Nothing suggests impairment that puts the public at substantial risk, so the threshold for a mandatory notification is not met.
Taking ward stock for a staff member is drug diversion and is both illegal and a professional misconduct issue.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man sees his general practitioner on the afternoon after his first half marathon (21 km). His longest previous run was 10 km, three weeks ago. Over the final 6 km he became gradually more short of breath, slowed to a walk, and felt back to normal within 15 minutes of finishing. He had no chest pain, palpitations, light-headedness, syncope, wheeze, cough, throat tightness or haemoptysis. He has no history of asthma or atopy, and no recent surgery, travel or immobilisation. He takes no medicines and does not smoke. No family member has died suddenly of a cardiac cause. He is 183 cm tall and weighs 75 kg. Temperature is 36.6 °C, pulse 64/min and regular, respirations 14/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, and SpO2 99% on room air. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable, with no calf swelling or tenderness. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with no abnormalities. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.85 (LLN 0.72) and FEV1 101% predicted, with a change of +100 mL (2%) after salbutamol. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Salbutamol inhaler, two puffs 15 minutes before each run
Mannitol bronchial provocation test in a respiratory laboratory
Serum D-dimer measurement to exclude pulmonary embolism
Transthoracic echocardiogram to look for cardiomyopathy
Reassurance, a slower mileage build-up and return precautions
questions.why: This fit young man more than doubled his longest run. His breathlessness came on gradually late in the race, eased when he walked and settled within 15 minutes. He had no red-flag symptoms, and his observations, examination, ECG and spirometry are all normal. This is physiological breathlessness from running beyond his current fitness. The right management is to explain this and reassure him, advise a gradual increase in distance, and safety-net: he should return urgently if he gets chest pain, syncope, palpitations, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or wheeze, or if the breathlessness keeps happening at distances he is used to. He does not need more tests or treatment. He is PERC negative with a low pretest probability, so the eTG advises no D-dimer. Nothing in his history suggests exercise-induced bronchoconstriction or structural heart disease. The Australian Asthma Handbook advises against starting an inhaler on suspicion alone. A bronchial provocation test is kept for people whose symptoms suggest exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
notes: Wrong: he has no wheeze, cough, chest tightness or atopy, and Australian guidance advises against starting a reliever for presumed exercise-induced bronchoconstriction without objective testing.
Wrong: provocation testing is used when symptoms suggest exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, which he does not have, so it would not change management.
Wrong: he has a low pretest probability and meets every PERC criterion, so a D-dimer is not indicated and could give a false positive that leads to unnecessary CTPA.
Wrong: he has no exertional chest pain, syncope, palpitations, murmur, family history of sudden death or ECG abnormality, so echocardiography is not indicated.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman born in Cambodia has newly diagnosed hepatitis C cirrhosis. Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg not detected, core antibody (total) not detected, surface antibody 120 mIU/mL. What does this serology show?
questions.why: Surface antibody alone, with no surface antigen and no core antibody, means immunity from vaccination. The vaccine contains only surface antigen, so it never produces core antibody. She needs no hepatitis B vaccine, though in cirrhosis her hepatitis A immunity should still be checked.
notes: Natural infection that has resolved leaves core antibody, which is not detected here.
Chronic infection needs HBsAg to persist for more than 6 months, and HBsAg is negative here.
Acute infection shows HBsAg and core IgM antibody, and neither is present here.
A surface antibody level of 120 mIU/mL is well above the protective level of 10 mIU/mL, so she is immune.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community has had a discharging left ear for 8 weeks. Otoscopy shows pus and a central tympanic membrane perforation. He is afebrile. Most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Ear discharge through a perforated tympanic membrane for more than 6 weeks is chronic suppurative otitis media, which is common in Aboriginal children in remote communities. The Australian otitis media guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and eTG recommend cleaning the ear (dry mopping) plus topical ciprofloxacin 0.3% drops twice daily until the ear has been dry for at least 3 days. Hearing should be assessed and the child followed up.
notes: Oral antibiotics penetrate the middle ear poorly in chronic suppurative otitis media and work less well than topical quinolone drops, so they are not first line.
Aminoglyoside drops can damage the inner ear when the tympanic membrane is perforated, so ciprofloxacin is preferred.
Leaving chronic suppurative otitis media untreated risks permanent conductive hearing loss, developmental delay and complications such as mastoiditis.
Surgical repair is only considered after medical treatment fails and the ear is dry, so it is not the first step.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back. Blood pressure is 170/95 mmHg in the right arm and 135/80 mmHg in the left. ECG is normal. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: Sudden tearing pain radiating to the back, with a blood pressure difference of more than 20 mmHg between the arms, strongly suggests acute aortic dissection. In a stable patient, ECG-gated CT angiography of the whole aorta is the test of choice to confirm it and to tell type A from type B, which decides whether he needs emergency surgery. This matches eTG and Australian emergency guidelines.
notes: CT pulmonary angiography looks for pulmonary embolism, and its contrast timing is not set up to image the aorta, so a dissection can be missed.
Invasive coronary angiography is for acute coronary syndrome, but the ECG is normal, and passing a catheter through a dissected aorta is risky and delays diagnosis.
Transthoracic echocardiography can show an ascending aortic flap or a pericardial effusion, but it cannot reliably exclude dissection or image the descending aorta.
Serial troponin measurement looks for myocardial infarction, is often normal in dissection, and waiting for repeat results delays an urgent diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman has 8 months of mechanical hand pain, 15 minutes' morning stiffness and hard DIP swellings. CRP 3 mg/L, ESR 12 mm/h, RF and anti-CCP negative. Best interpretation of these results?
questions.why: Osteoarthritis is diagnosed clinically. CRP, ESR, RF and anti-CCP are ordered to exclude inflammatory arthritis, not to prove osteoarthritis. Her normal markers and negative serology make an inflammatory cause less likely and fit her clinical picture of nodal osteoarthritis.
notes: Osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis, and normal bloods do not confirm it; they only make other causes less likely.
Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis would still usually show synovitis, stiffness lasting over 30 to 60 minutes and raised CRP or ESR, and it typically spares the DIPs.
Negative serology alone does not point to psoriatic arthritis, which needs features such as psoriasis, nail changes, dactylitis or erosions on X-ray.
Polymyalgia rheumatica causes shoulder and hip girdle stiffness with raised ESR and CRP, not normal markers with small-joint hand pain.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with eczema has eaten peanut butter several times a week with no symptoms. Skin prick testing ordered by his GP shows a 7 mm wheal to peanut. What does this result indicate?
questions.why: A positive skin prick test shows only that peanut-specific IgE is present (sensitisation). It must be read alongside the clinical history. This boy regularly eats peanut with no reaction, so he does not have clinical allergy and should keep eating peanut, in line with ASCIA guidance, rather than being told to avoid it.
notes: Diagnosing IgE-mediated allergy needs both sensitisation and typical reactions after eating, and he has repeatedly eaten peanut with no symptoms.
Non-IgE food allergy is not detected by skin prick testing, and he has no delayed gastrointestinal symptoms.
Antihistamines suppress the wheal and cause false-negative results, so they cannot explain a positive one.
Resolved allergy means there were earlier reactions, but he has never reacted to peanut.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old woman fell onto her left side at home and cannot bear weight. Hip rotation is painful; the leg is not shortened. Hip and pelvic X-rays show no fracture. Most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: An older person who cannot bear weight after a fall may have an occult hip fracture even when the X-rays are normal. Under the ANZ Hip Fracture Guideline, MRI is the test to get now, with CT if MRI is not available within 24 hours, so that surgery is not delayed.
notes: Waiting to repeat the X-ray delays diagnosis and surgery, which raises the risk of fracture displacement, immobility complications and death.
A bone scan is less specific and may not turn positive for 48 to 72 hours in older patients, so it is only a back-up when MRI cannot be done.
Ultrasound can show a joint effusion but cannot reliably show or rule out a fracture of the femoral neck.
A DEXA scan measures bone density to guide long-term osteoporosis treatment but cannot diagnose an acute fracture.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of 6 months of numbness and intermittent shooting pain in both feet. He feels unsteady when he walks to the bathroom at night. He has no back pain and no bladder or bowel symptoms. He has had type 2 diabetes for 8 years and has taken metformin 1 g twice daily the whole time, along with ramipril. He drinks two standard drinks a week and eats a mixed diet. His blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Pinprick and 10 g monofilament sensation are reduced symmetrically to the mid-shins. Vibration sense is absent at both great toes. Ankle reflexes are absent, knee reflexes are normal and plantar responses are flexor. Power and tone are normal. Romberg test is positive. Pedal pulses are palpable. Investigations: HbA1c 8.4% (target 7.0% or less), haemoglobin 141 g/L, MCV 92 fL (80 to 100), eGFR 74 mL/min/1.73 m2 and TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.5 to 4.0). Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Nerve conduction studies of the legs
questions.why: This man has a typical distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy. The loss is length-dependent and stocking-shaped, he has lost protective sensation and vibration sense, his ankle reflexes are absent while his knee reflexes are kept, and he has sensory ataxia. This fits poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. Before calling it diabetic neuropathy, the treatable mimics need to be excluded. His TSH and eGFR are normal and he drinks little, so the main mimic left is vitamin B12 deficiency. Metformin reduces B12 absorption, and he has taken it for 8 years. A normal MCV does not exclude B12 deficiency, because neuropathy can come before anaemia or macrocytosis. Australian guidance (eTG Diabetes and the RACGP type 2 diabetes handbook) recommends checking B12 in people on long-term metformin, especially when neuropathy appears. Diabetic neuropathy is a clinical diagnosis, so nerve conduction studies, imaging, CSF analysis and biopsy are only needed for atypical features. These include asymmetry, rapid progression, marked weakness, early involvement of the hands, or upper motor neuron or sphincter signs.
notes: Wrong: nerve conduction studies are kept for atypical features, such as asymmetry, rapid progression or prominent weakness, and they would not separate diabetic from B12-related neuropathy.
Wrong: he has no back pain, sphincter symptoms, saddle anaesthesia, upper motor neuron signs or dermatomal pattern, so imaging the spine is not indicated.

Wrong: CSF protein is used when chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is suspected, which presents with proximal and distal weakness and loss of all reflexes, not a purely distal sensory picture.
Wrong: nerve biopsy is invasive and is kept for suspected vasculitic or infiltrative neuropathy, which would present with asymmetric or rapidly progressive deficits.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with a COPD exacerbation is given 15 L/min oxygen by non-rebreather mask. An hour later she is drowsy, with SpO2 99%, pH 7.21 and PaCO2 84 mmHg. Most likely cause?
questions.why: In a CO2 retainer, uncontrolled high-flow oxygen worsens V/Q mismatch, increases dead space and reduces the Haldane effect, so it causes acute hypercapnic acidosis and drowsiness. The TSANZ guideline sets the SpO2 target at 88 to 92% and recommends air-driven nebulisers or a spacer. If acidosis persists despite this, NIV is indicated.
notes: A massive PE would cause hypoxaemia, usually with hypocapnia from hyperventilation, not SpO2 99% with a PaCO2 of 84 mmHg.
A tension pneumothorax would cause falling saturations and haemodynamic collapse, not saturations of 99%.
A stroke does not explain an acute respiratory acidosis that started straight after high-flow oxygen.
Hypoglycaemia causes drowsiness, but it does not raise PaCO2 or cause respiratory acidosis.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man is reviewed before discharge after a painless maroon rectal bleed that stopped spontaneously. Colonoscopy shows sigmoid diverticula only. He takes ibuprofen daily for knee osteoarthritis. Which advice most reduces his risk of rebleeding?
questions.why: Diverticular bleeding usually stops by itself but often recurs, and NSAIDs are the main risk factor you can change, so he should stop ibuprofen and use paracetamol instead. A high-fibre diet with good fluid intake and treatment of constipation are also advised.
notes: A proton pump inhibitor protects the upper GI tract but does not protect against NSAID-related bleeding in the colon.
Avoiding nuts, seeds and popcorn is an outdated myth with no evidence that it lowers the risk of bleeding or diverticulitis.
A low-residue diet worsens constipation, whereas a high-fibre diet is recommended for diverticular disease.
Tranexamic acid has no proven benefit in GI bleeding, adds clot risk, and is not used long term to prevent recurrence.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has had three spontaneous attacks of rotatory vertigo over 4 months, each lasting 3 to 6 hours, with fluctuating left-ear fullness and tinnitus. Audiometry shows left low-frequency sensorineural loss. Which drug is most appropriate for her acute attacks?
questions.why: Her history meets the criteria for definite Ménière's disease: two or more spontaneous attacks of vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, a documented low-frequency sensorineural loss, and fluctuating symptoms in the same ear. eTG advises a short course of a vestibular suppressant antiemetic such as prochlorperazine for acute attacks, along with ENT referral and advice to cut down on salt, caffeine and alcohol.
notes: Betahistine is sometimes used to try to prevent attacks, with weak evidence, and it does not relieve an attack in progress.
A thiazide diuretic is a possible preventive treatment started by a specialist, and it does nothing for acute vertigo.
Intratympanic gentamicin destroys vestibular function and is kept for ENT management of disabling attacks that have not responded to other treatment.
Oral corticosteroids are used for sudden sensorineural hearing loss, not as routine treatment of Ménière's vertigo attacks.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 18 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain that began after a takeaway dinner. The pain radiates to her right shoulder, and she has vomited four times. She has had three shorter, similar episodes over the past 6 months. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill and drinks alcohol occasionally. Her temperature is 38.4 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg and respiratory rate 18/min. She is not jaundiced and is alert. Her right upper quadrant is tender, and Murphy's sign is positive. Blood tests show: white cell count 14.9 x10^9/L (4.0–11.0), CRP 128 mg/L (<5), total bilirubin 15 µmol/L (<20), ALP 131 U/L (30–110), GGT 52 U/L (<38), ALT 44 U/L (<35), lipase 40 U/L (<60) and serum beta-hCG <2 IU/L. Ultrasound shows multiple gallstones, a gallbladder wall of 7 mm with pericholecystic fluid, and a common bile duct of 4 mm with no duct stone seen. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of her liver function results?
options: Biliary obstruction, warranting urgent ERCP to clear the duct
Reactive cholestatic change, making choledocholithiasis unlikely
Hepatocellular injury, suggesting a superimposed acute viral hepatitis
Early cholangitis, warranting urgent biliary decompression
Alcohol-related injury, suggested by the elevated GGT level
questions.why: She has acute calculous cholecystitis. She has constant right upper quadrant pain for more than a few hours, fever, a positive Murphy's sign, a raised white cell count and CRP, and an ultrasound showing gallstones, a thickened wall and pericholecystic fluid. Her ALP, GGT and ALT are all less than 1.5 times the upper limit of normal. Her bilirubin is normal and her common bile duct is not dilated (4 mm) with no duct stone seen. Small rises in ALP, GGT and ALT are common in cholecystitis. Inflammation next to the liver and the bile ducts causes them, not a blocked common bile duct. With a normal bilirubin, a normal duct calibre and no stone seen, her risk of a common bile duct stone is low. She does not need a preoperative MRCP or ERCP and can go to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with IV antibiotics as eTG recommends. A raised bilirubin, a dilated duct or a duct stone would change this. With fever, they would point to cholangitis. Option A is wrong because a blocked duct would normally raise the bilirubin and widen the duct, and she has neither.
notes: A blocked common bile duct would normally raise the bilirubin and dilate the duct, but her bilirubin is 15 µmol/L and her duct is 4 mm, so ERCP is not indicated.
Acute viral hepatitis causes a large ALT rise, often in the hundreds or thousands, but her ALT is only 44 U/L with a mildly cholestatic pattern, and the ultrasound explains her symptoms.
Cholangitis needs fever plus evidence of a blocked duct, such as jaundice, a raised bilirubin or a dilated duct, and she has none of these, so urgent decompression is not needed.
A small GGT rise alongside a raised ALP fits reactive cholestasis, and she rarely drinks, so alcohol does not explain these results.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman, a primary school teacher, comes to the rheumatology outpatient clinic to discuss treatment of rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 2 weeks ago. She has had 4 months of pain and swelling in both hands, wrists and forefeet, with 2 hours of morning stiffness. She has a 3-year-old daughter. She stopped her combined oral contraceptive pill 2 months ago, is trying to conceive and does not want to use contraception or delay pregnancy. Her only medicine is naproxen 500 mg twice daily. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 78/min and blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg. She has soft synovial swelling of both wrists and the 2nd to 4th MCP and PIP joints, and the DIP joints are spared. CRP is 31 mg/L (reference below 5), rheumatoid factor 88 IU/mL (below 20) and anti-CCP 240 U/mL (below 7). Hepatitis B and C serology is negative, ALT is 22 U/L, eGFR is above 90 mL/min/1.73 m² and urine beta-hCG is negative. A hand X-ray shows periarticular osteopenia and a marginal erosion at the right 2nd MCP joint. Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-modifying drug to start?
questions.why: She has early, seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis with poor prognostic features, so she needs a DMARD started now to prevent more joint damage. The most important risk in her case is the drug harming a pregnancy, because she is trying to conceive and will not use contraception. Under eTG and Australian Rheumatology Association guidance, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine are the conventional synthetic DMARDs that can be used before conception and through pregnancy. Sulfasalazine is started at a low dose and increased to 1 g twice daily. It is a folate antagonist, so she should also take high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) before conception. It can be combined with hydroxychloroquine and short-term low-dose prednisolone if needed. She should plan her pregnancy with the rheumatologist and stop naproxen while trying to conceive. Leflunomide and methotrexate are teratogenic and need reliable contraception. Mycophenolate and tofacitinib are also unsuitable.
notes: Leflunomide is teratogenic and its active metabolite stays in the body for up to 2 years, so a woman trying to conceive would need a washout with cholestyramine; it is contraindicated for her.

Methotrexate is usually the first-line DMARD, but it is teratogenic and abortifacient, so it needs reliable contraception and must be stopped before conception; it is contraindicated while she is actively trying to conceive.
Mycophenolate is a strong teratogen that causes miscarriage and malformations, and it is not a standard DMARD for rheumatoid arthritis.
Tofacitinib is a JAK inhibitor that should be avoided around conception and in pregnancy, and in Australia it is reserved for disease that has not responded to conventional synthetic DMARDs.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman sees her general practitioner with 3 months of palpitations, heat intolerance and 6 kg of unintentional weight loss. She is not breathless and has no chest pain. She has no past medical history, takes no medicines or supplements, and has a contraceptive implant. Temperature is 37.0 °C, pulse 110/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 126/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
