She is alert and has a fine tremor, warm moist hands, and bilateral lid retraction and mild proptosis, with normal visual acuity, colour vision and eye movements. There is a diffuse, smooth, non-tender goitre with a bruit. There are no signs of heart failure. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 110/min with narrow QRS complexes. TSH is <0.01 mIU/L (0.4–4.0), free T4 48 pmol/L (10–20), free T3 18.5 pmol/L (3.5–6.5) and TSH receptor antibodies 12.4 IU/L (<1.8). Full blood count, liver function tests and serum beta-hCG are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: She has Graves' disease, shown by suppressed TSH, high free T4 and T3, strongly positive TRAb, a diffuse goitre with a bruit and orbitopathy. It is complicated by thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation. She is haemodynamically stable, afebrile and alert, with no heart failure, so she does not have thyroid storm and can be managed as an outpatient. eTG recommends a non-selective beta blocker such as propranolol to control the heart rate and adrenergic symptoms. It also recommends a thionamide, with carbimazole first-line outside the first trimester, to make her euthyroid. Baseline FBC and LFTs are normal and she is not pregnant. Thyrotoxic AF usually reverts to sinus rhythm once she is euthyroid. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 0, so anticoagulation is not indicated. She must be told to stop carbimazole and have a same-day FBC if she gets a sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers. Amiodarone is wrong because its iodine load worsens thyrotoxicosis, and she does not need anticoagulation. Digoxin works poorly in a hyperadrenergic state, and propylthiouracil is kept for the first trimester or thyroid storm because it can damage the liver.
notes: Amiodarone's iodine load can worsen thyrotoxicosis, and with a CHA2DS2-VA score of 0 she does not need anticoagulation.
Digoxin controls the rate poorly in a hyperadrenergic thyrotoxic state, and propylthiouracil is kept for the first trimester of pregnancy or thyroid storm because it can cause severe liver injury.
Radioiodine is not first-line treatment for a new, uncontrolled presentation and can worsen her active Graves' orbitopathy, especially before she is euthyroid.
Cardioversion in a patient who is still thyrotoxic often fails and the AF tends to come back, so it is deferred until she is euthyroid, by which time the AF usually reverts on its own.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 10 days of worsening breathlessness. It has been severe since overnight, and she has orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Six weeks ago she had an anterior myocardial infarction treated with a stent. Since then she has been taking over-the-counter naproxen for knee pain. Her pulse is 110/min and regular, blood pressure 194/102 mm Hg, respiratory rate 30/min and SpO2 87% on room air. She has a raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound and bilateral basal crackles. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia with anterior Q waves, unchanged from her discharge ECG. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar opacification and small effusions. NT-proBNP is 7900 ng/L (age-adjusted rule-in level above 900 ng/L). High-sensitivity troponin I is 38 ng/L, then 37 ng/L at 3 hours (female 99th percentile 16 ng/L). Creatinine is 142 µmol/L. After CPAP, glyceryl trinitrate and intravenous furosemide, she is comfortable on 2 L/min of oxygen by nasal prongs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.why: This woman has acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. She has orthopnoea, PND, a raised JVP, an S3, crackles, alveolar oedema with effusions on X-ray and a very high NT-proBNP. The likely cause is ischaemic left ventricular dysfunction after her recent anterior MI, made worse by NSAID-related fluid retention and hypertension. Her two troponin values are stable and barely raised, and her ECG has not changed, so this is chronic myocardial injury rather than a new infarct. The 2018 National Heart Foundation and CSANZ heart failure guideline recommends transthoracic echocardiography for every patient with suspected heart failure. Echo confirms the diagnosis and measures the LVEF, which decides between HFrEF and HFpEF and therefore which survival-improving treatments she should get. Echo also looks for mechanical complications of the recent MI (mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal defect, aneurysm, left ventricular thrombus), regional wall motion problems and valve disease. It is quick, done at the bedside and needs no contrast or radiation.
notes: Incorrect: orthopnoea, PND, an S3, alveolar oedema and an NT-proBNP of 7900 explain her hypoxia, so pulmonary embolism is unlikely and iodinated contrast with a creatinine of 142 µmol/L brings risk for no gain.
Incorrect: her troponin is flat with no new ECG change, so there is no acute coronary syndrome needing urgent angiography, and the contrast load would add to her kidney injury.
Incorrect: cardiac MRI is a second-line test for when echo images are poor or the cause is unclear, not the first test for ventricular function in an acutely unwell patient.
Incorrect: a V/Q scan tests for pulmonary embolism, which the clinical picture does not suggest, and alveolar oedema and effusions make the scan hard to interpret.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with BMI 43 kg/m2 and type 2 diabetes has 10 months of irregular, heavy bleeding. Pipelle biopsy shows endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. Main mechanism linking her obesity to this?
questions.why: Adipose tissue converts androgens (mainly androstenedione) into oestrone. With anovulation there is no progesterone to oppose it, so the endometrium is driven to hyperplasia and cancer. Hyperinsulinaemia adds to the risk by lowering SHBG and raising IGF-1, so counsel her that losing weight and taking a progestogen reduce her risk.
notes: Obesity and hyperinsulinaemia lower SHBG rather than raise it, which leaves more free oestrogen.
Obesity-related anovulation means there is no luteal progesterone, and that lack is what leaves the oestrogen unopposed.
Obesity tends to raise androgen levels, which gives more substrate for aromatisation.
Obesity and type 2 diabetes cause hyperinsulinaemia, and the raised insulin and IGF-1 promote endometrial growth.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old woman trips at home and strikes her forehead. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. She is alert, GCS 15, with a small forehead haematoma and no neurological deficit. Most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Older adults taking anticoagulants who have a head injury are at high risk of intracranial haemorrhage, even when GCS is 15 and the neurological exam is normal. Australian adult head injury guidelines, such as NSW Health's, call for a non-contrast CT brain in this situation. Reversal is used only if a bleed is confirmed.
notes: Skull X-ray cannot rule out intracranial haemorrhage and has no role in current head injury assessment.
Anticoagulant reversal is for a confirmed significant bleed, not a head injury that has not yet been imaged.
Sending her home without imaging misses a delayed or hidden intracranial haemorrhage, which is more likely with anticoagulation.
Watching her without imaging is not enough, because anticoagulated older patients can bleed without early clinical signs.

questions.stem: A calcium figure of 11 mg / dL (normal less than 10.5 mg / dL) is found in a 30-year-old patient during a routine business examination. The PTH determination was 45 pg / ml (VN 10-55 pg / ml). The story is anodyne, except for the fact that the mother and the paternal grandfather were diagnosed with hyperparathyroidism and intervened, although they remained hypercalcemic. Which test is most useful to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: Mild hypercalcaemia with an inappropriately normal PTH, a family history, and relatives who stayed hypercalcaemic after parathyroid surgery points to familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. Low urinary calcium excretion confirms it: a calcium/creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01.
notes: 25-OH vitamin D shows vitamin D stores. It does not tell FHH apart from primary hyperparathyroidism, which is the key question here.
1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D can be high or normal in both PTH-mediated states and in granulomatous disease. It does not separate FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism.
Tubular phosphate reabsorption falls under PTH action in both conditions, so it does not tell them apart. Urinary calcium excretion is what separates them.
PTHrP is used for humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy, where PTH is suppressed. Here PTH is not suppressed and the patient is a healthy 30-year-old with a family history.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 67-year-old patient on ticlopidine treatment went to the emergency department with headache, asthenia and petechiae in the lower extremities. In the analytical sample hemoglobin 8.2 g / dl, VCM 100 fl, platelets 25000 / ul and leukocytes 7500 / ul with normal formula. The number of reticulocytes is high and in the blood smear numerous schistocytes are observed. The coagulation studies (APTT, TP and Fibrinogen) are normal. In the biochemistry highlights LDH 2700 IU / l and bilirubin 2.6 mg / dl. What is the most likely diagnosis of the patient?
questions.why: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, high LDH, high reticulocytes, raised bilirubin) plus severe thrombocytopenia and normal clotting tests means TTP. Ticlopidine is a classic cause of TTP. Remember that clotting tests are normal in TTP and abnormal in DIC.
notes: Immune thrombocytopenia causes isolated thrombocytopenia. It does not cause schistocytes, haemolysis or a very high LDH.
Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia with low reticulocytes. Here the white count is normal and reticulocytes are high, which shows peripheral destruction.
Simple drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia lowers platelets only. The schistocytic haemolytic anaemia points to ticlopidine-associated TTP.
DIC would prolong the APTT and PT and consume fibrinogen. All of these are normal here.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 19-year-old girl with no medical history of interest, except for a self-limiting flu-like illness 3 weeks before, who went to the Emergency Department for petechiae and spontaneously occurring bruising. On physical examination, the patient is in good general condition, afebrile, normotensive and oriented in time and space. Petechiae disseminated by EEII and small abdomen and ecchymoses are observed in decubitus areas. No enlarged adenopathy or splenomegaly. The analysis carried out offers the following findings: Hb 12.6 g / dL, Leukocytes 5,500 / mm3, platelets 7000 / mm3. The study of the peripheral blood smear offers a normal erythrocyte morphology, normal differential leukocyte count and the platelet count is concordant with the autoanalyzer figure without observing plaque aggregates. Biochemistry, proteinogram, beta 2 microglobulin and normal LDH. What do you think is the most appropriate initial treatment of the following?
options: Cyclophosphamide in pulses of 4 days every 21 days.
Prednisone at 1 mg / day for 2-3 weeks.
questions.why: A young woman after a viral illness with isolated, confirmed severe thrombocytopenia, a normal smear and no organomegaly has primary immune thrombocytopenia. First-line treatment is corticosteroids. The intended dose is prednisone 1 mg/kg/day ("1 mg/day" is a typo); in Australia prednisolone is used.
notes: Transfused platelets are destroyed quickly in ITP. Transfusion is kept for life-threatening bleeding, alongside steroids and IVIG, and this patient is stable with only skin bleeding.
Rituximab is a second-line option for ITP that persists or comes back after steroids. It is not the first treatment.
Cyclophosphamide is a later-line immunosuppressant for refractory ITP and is never used first.
Plasma exchange treats TTP. There are no schistocytes and LDH is normal, so TTP is excluded.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man consulted for fever and malaise. In the clinical history, homosexual relationships were collected for 4 months with a new partner. 2 months before the current consultation, she had an ulcerous lesion on the glans, painless, with bilateral inguinal adenopathies, all self-limiting. Serological studies are requested with the following results: HIV negative, RPR 1/320, TPHA 1/128. What treatment would you indicate in this patient?
options: Intravenous penicillin G, 24 MU every day for 14 days.
Penicillin Benzatine 2.4 MU intramuscular, three doses in three consecutive weeks.
Ceftriaxone 2 grams intramuscular in a single dose.
Penicillin Benzatine 2.4 MU intramuscular in a single dose.
questions.why: A painless chancre with inguinal nodes two months ago, followed by fever and malaise with high-titre RPR and TPHA, is early (secondary) syphilis. A single dose of benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM is curative. In Australia this is Bicillin L-A 1.8 g (2.4 MU) IM once.
notes: Reactive treponemal and non-treponemal tests with a high RPR titre mean active syphilis, which must be treated. Partners also need tracing.
High-dose IV penicillin G for 10 to 14 days is for neurosyphilis or ocular syphilis. There are no neurological or eye features here.
Three weekly doses are for late latent syphilis, latent syphilis of unknown duration, or tertiary syphilis. This infection began within the last few months.
A single dose of ceftriaxone treats gonorrhoea, not syphilis. Ceftriaxone is only an alternative for syphilis, given as repeated doses.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man diagnosed with diabetes mellitus type 2 came to our clinic. He reported fever of 40ºC with chills and shivering, arthromyalgia and headache, which is why he started treatment with paracetamol. The painting began 24 hours before his return to Spain. After 3 days, he presented with a generalized maculo-papular rash that progressed to the formation of more intense petechiae in the lower limbs. It provides analytics where leukopenia stands out with 3,200 / mm3 and platelets 91,000 / mm3 and mild elevation of aminotransferases. Thickness, peripheral blood smear, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and malaria antigen are negative. What is the most likely suspected diagnosis?
questions.why: Sudden high fever with myalgia and headache in a returning traveller, then a maculopapular rash turning petechial around day 3 to 5, with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and mildly raised transaminases, after malaria has been excluded, is classic dengue.
notes: Coronavirus infections mainly cause respiratory illness. They do not give a petechial rash with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia after travel.
Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus spreads from rodents and causes a febrile illness with aseptic meningitis. It does not cause a haemorrhagic rash or thrombocytopenia.
Chikungunya looks similar, but its hallmark is severe and often lasting polyarthralgia or arthritis. Marked thrombocytopenia and petechiae favour dengue.
St Louis encephalitis is a flavivirus infection that causes encephalitis in older adults. There is no altered consciousness here, and it does not cause a petechial rash.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy referred to a health center referring to a 39-degree fever of 48 hours of evolution with a sore throat. The family doctor consults the history of the patient where it does not cost any previous illness. The patient did not report cough and the examination performed by his family doctor reveals the presence of bilateral whitish tonsillar exudate and anterior cervical adenopathies enlarged and painful on palpation. What would be the treatment of choice for this patient?
questions.why: Fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes and no cough give a full Centor score, so group A streptococcal pharyngitis is likely. Narrow-spectrum penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days is the treatment of choice. Australian guidelines also use phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days.
notes: GAS is always sensitive to penicillin. Adding clavulanate only widens the spectrum and raises side effects with no benefit.
Doxycycline is unreliable against group A streptococcus and is not used for streptococcal pharyngitis.
Ciprofloxacin has poor activity against streptococci and is not suitable for tonsillitis.
Metronidazole covers anaerobes and protozoa, not group A streptococcus.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man consulted for dyspnea and hemoptysis. Blood tests have creatinine 7 mg / dl, urea 250 mg / dl and anti-MBG (anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies) positive high titer. A renal biopsy was performed, showing crescents in 75% of the glomeruli, and in the immunofluorescence a linear Ig deposition pattern appeared. Which of the following is the correct answer?
options: It is an Ig A Nephropathy with acute renal failure.
The performance of plasmapheresis would be indicated.
Mycophenolate mofetil is the initial treatment of choice.
Glomerular involvement is caused by the presence of circulating immune complexes.
questions.why: Pulmonary haemorrhage, rapidly progressive renal failure with crescents, high-titre anti-GBM antibodies and linear IgG deposits mean anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease. Treatment is plasma exchange plus corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide. Pulmonary haemorrhage is an indication for plasma exchange whatever the renal prognosis.
notes: IgA nephropathy shows mesangial granular IgA deposits and anti-GBM is negative. Here immunofluorescence is linear and anti-GBM is strongly positive.
Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome with subepithelial granular IgG deposits. It does not cause crescentic failure with hemoptysis and linear staining.
Mycophenolate is not induction therapy for anti-GBM disease. The standard is plasma exchange, steroids and cyclophosphamide.
The linear pattern shows antibodies binding directly to the basement membrane (type II hypersensitivity). Immune complexes give a granular pattern.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 26-year-old patient with no prior medical-surgical history came to the emergency room for dyspnea of ​​15 days of evolution. No findings of interest were detected on the physical examination except a nodule of hard consistency in the left testicle. A chest x-ray is performed, showing multiple pulmonary nodules in "balloon release". His analytical highlights a B-hCG of 30,000 mIU / ml. What do you think is the most probable origin of the pathology of this picture?
questions.why: A young man with a testicular mass, very high beta-hCG and multiple cannonball lung metastases with early blood-borne spread most likely has choriocarcinoma. It is a trophoblastic germ cell tumour that makes large amounts of hCG and spreads early through the blood.
notes: Seminoma can raise beta-hCG only modestly, through syncytiotrophoblast cells. It usually spreads to retroperitoneal nodes first, not to many lung nodules with hCG this high.
Renal angiomyolipoma is a benign tumour linked with tuberous sclerosis. It does not cause a testicular mass, hCG elevation or lung metastases.
Wilms tumour is a kidney tumour of young children. It is not a testicular cancer in a 26-year-old and does not make hCG.
Testicular lymphoma affects older men, usually over 60, and does not produce beta-hCG.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: Before a 49-year-old man, asymptomatic, with a family history of a father who died of prostate cancer, a PSA (Specific Prostate Antigen) of 5.9 ng / ml was identified in a routine company control, with a PSA ratio free / Total PSA of 11% and that in a digital rectal examination there is an increase in consistency in the right prostatic lobe, what is the following clinical indication?
options: Ask the patient to perform a transrectal ultrasound and prostate biopsy.
Start treatment with 5 alpha reductase inhibitors to halve PSA levels.
Start combined treatment of LHRH analogues and antiandrogens.
questions.why: A PSA of 5.9 ng/mL with a low free/total ratio (11%), a firm right lobe on DRE and a father with prostate cancer make cancer likely, and only a biopsy can confirm it. In Australia, multiparametric MRI usually comes first to target the biopsy, often done by the transperineal route.
notes: Abdominopelvic CT is for staging and is only considered after a biopsy confirms cancer. Even then it is reserved for higher-risk disease, so it is premature here.
5-alpha reductase inhibitors lower PSA and would hide a likely cancer. They are a treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia, not a response to a suspicious DRE.
Androgen deprivation is for confirmed, usually advanced or high-risk, prostate cancer. It is never started without a tissue diagnosis.
A bone scan stages confirmed high-risk disease. It is not indicated before histology, and an asymptomatic man with a PSA under 10 has a low chance of bone metastases.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 55-year-old asthmatic patient goes to the ER with an exacerbation. One hour after the administration of supplemental oxygen and two nebulizations of salbutamol the patient does not improve. On examination, he breathed at 42 rpm with supraclavicular drainage and presented disseminated inspiratory and expiratory wheezing. The peak flow has dropped from 310 to 220 L / min. A gasometry extracted with oxygen at 28% shows a pO2 of 54 mmHg and a pCO2 of 35 mmHg. Which of the following attitudes seems LESS indicated?
options: Nebulize ipratropium bromide together with salbutamol every 20 minutes.
questions.why: This is a severe exacerbation: RR 42, accessory muscle use, PaO2 54 on 28% O2. A normal pCO2 in a tachypnoeic asthmatic means he is tiring. NIV has weak evidence in asthma and can delay intubation, so it is the least indicated step. The Australian Asthma Handbook likewise does not recommend routine NIV.
notes: He is hypoxaemic at 54 mmHg on 28% oxygen, so titrating oxygen up to an adequate saturation is clearly indicated (Australian target SpO2 93-95%).
Early systemic corticosteroids are standard in any moderate-severe exacerbation; IV methylprednisolone is appropriate, though Australian practice often uses IV hydrocortisone or oral prednisolone.
Adding ipratropium to repeated salbutamol nebulisation improves outcomes in severe exacerbations and is recommended when there is a poor response to beta-agonist alone.
IV magnesium sulfate is recommended for severe or life-threatening asthma that does not respond to initial bronchodilators, as in this patient.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of pancreatic cancer undergoing chemotherapy. Emergency consultation for pain and edema of the entire lower limb from the groin. Which diagnostic test is more cost-effective to confirm the diagnostic suspicion?
questions.why: Pain and swelling of the whole leg from the groin in a patient with active cancer on chemotherapy gives a high pretest probability of proximal DVT. Venous compression Doppler ultrasound is accurate, non-invasive and cheap, so it is the most cost-effective confirmatory test.
notes: D-dimer only helps to exclude DVT when probability is low and is often raised in cancer, so it cannot confirm the diagnosis in this high-probability patient.
MR venography is accurate but expensive and less available. It is reserved for pelvic or iliac clots that ultrasound cannot show.
Contrast phlebography is the historical gold standard but is invasive and needs contrast, so it is not cost-effective as first-line confirmation.
CT venography adds radiation, contrast and cost, and it is not the first-line test for suspected lower-limb DVT.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: After a traffic accident, a 38-year-old patient enters the ICU in a coma. After several days the patient does not improve neurologically and CT shows hemorrhagic punctate lesions in the corpus callosum and cortico-subcortical union. What is your diagnosis?
questions.why: Coma after high-speed acceleration-deceleration trauma that does not match the initial CT, plus small punctate haemorrhages in the corpus callosum and at the grey-white junction, is typical of diffuse axonal injury. Corpus callosum involvement means severe (higher grade) injury.
notes: An acute subdural haematoma shows on CT as a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection, not as punctate lesions deep in the white matter.
TTP is a haematological disorder with thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolysis, and it does not explain traumatic coma with this CT pattern.
Haemorrhagic contusions are focal cortical lesions, typically frontal and temporal poles (coup-contrecoup). They do not involve the corpus callosum.
Hypoxic-ischaemic injury affects watershed cortex, basal ganglia and hippocampi diffusely after hypoxia or arrest. It does not produce punctate callosal haemorrhages.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man consulted for cognitive deterioration, slowness and awkwardness of movements, of eight months of evolution. The family reported that the patient had visual hallucinations, so his Primary Care physician prescribed low doses of risperidone, with a significant worsening of motor status. In view of these data, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Dementia with early parkinsonism and visual hallucinations, then marked motor worsening on a low-dose antipsychotic, is classic dementia with Lewy bodies. Severe sensitivity to neuroleptics is a supportive feature, so avoid typical antipsychotics and use even risperidone with great caution.
notes: Alzheimer disease begins with memory loss, and early parkinsonism, early hallucinations and severe neuroleptic sensitivity are not typical of it.
Frontotemporal dementia presents with behavioural or language change, and prominent visual hallucinations with early parkinsonism are not typical of it.
Vascular dementia usually progresses stepwise with focal signs and vascular risk factors, and severe neuroleptic sensitivity is not one of its features.
Sporadic CJD progresses over weeks with myoclonus and ataxia. Eight months of slow decline with neuroleptic sensitivity fits Lewy body disease much better.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man is admitted with a sudden picture of aphasia and right hemiparesis. As background highlights, hypertension, well controlled diet and cognitive impairment in the last year under study by his neurologist. Emergency cranial CT demonstrates a left frontal lobar hematoma without contrast enhancement. What is the most likely cause of the hematoma?
options: Arteriovenous malformation masked by the acute hematoma.
Vasculitis isolated from the nervous system.
questions.why: A lobar (cortico-subcortical) haemorrhage in an 80-year-old with progressive cognitive impairment strongly suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Remember: hypertension causes deep bleeds (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum), while amyloid angiopathy causes lobar bleeds in the elderly.
notes: AVMs cause lobar haemorrhage mainly in young patients. They would not explain an 80-year-old's background cognitive decline.
Hypertensive haemorrhages are typically deep, and this patient's blood pressure is well controlled, so a lobar bleed points elsewhere.
Isolated CNS vasculitis is rare and presents with headache, multifocal ischaemic events and encephalopathy rather than a single lobar haematoma.
A bleeding tumour is possible, but the absence of contrast enhancement and the history of cognitive decline favour amyloid angiopathy.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presents, for a few months, without previous trauma, lumbar pain, difficulty walking, loss of strength and paresthesias in lower limbs, having to stop a few meters after starting it. The patient is increasingly inclining the trunk forward. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: An older patient with back pain, leg weakness and paraesthesia that come on after walking a short distance (neurogenic claudication), and who leans forward for relief because flexion widens the canal, has lumbar spinal canal stenosis.
notes: An osteoporotic vertebral fracture causes sudden localised back pain, often after minor strain. It does not cause walking-related leg symptoms relieved by flexion.
A central L5-S1 herniation is acute, with radicular pain or cauda equina features. It is not a gradual walking-induced claudication relieved by leaning forward.
Spondylodiscitis causes constant, inflammatory, night-time back pain with fever or raised inflammatory markers, not neurogenic claudication.
Degenerative scoliosis can coexist with stenosis and cause back pain, but the claudication pattern relieved by forward flexion is the hallmark of canal stenosis itself.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 80-year-old woman who consults for presenting, for 1 month, progressive increase of the abdominal perimeter. During the previous 4-5 months note asthenia, anorexia and weight loss not specified. On physical examination, tension ascites and malleolar edema are seen, with no other relevant signs. Ultrasonography and CT scan of the abdomen demonstrate the presence of ascites, of homogeneous density, without appreciating peritoneal implants or abdominal or pelvic masses. Liver, pancreas, adrenal glands, spleen and kidneys without significant findings. Paracentesis is performed through a thick needle, obtaining a somewhat yellowish, dense and gelatinous fluid with difficulty. What is the most likely etiology?
options: Hydropic decompensation secondary to liver cirrhosis.
Chylose ascites due to non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.
questions.why: Thick, yellowish, gelatinous fluid that is hard to aspirate is mucinous ascites (pseudomyxoma peritonei). This comes from a mucin-producing adenocarcinoma, usually appendiceal or ovarian, spreading through the peritoneum. Small implants are often missed on imaging. Remember: gelatinous ascites means mucinous adenocarcinoma.
notes: Cirrhotic ascites is thin, clear and straw-coloured, and the liver and spleen are normal on imaging here, so there is no sign of portal hypertension.
Chylous ascites is milky white and high in triglycerides, not gelatinous, and imaging shows no lymphadenopathy or masses to suggest lymphoma.
Tuberculous ascites is a clear or turbid exudate high in lymphocytes and ADA, often with fever. It is not thick, mucoid fluid that is hard to aspirate.
Constrictive pericarditis gives thin, high-protein ascites (SAAG of 1.1 or more) with a raised JVP and hepatic congestion, and none of these fits gelatinous fluid with a normal liver.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 0 months previously healthy with acute gastroenteritis of one day of evolution and signs of mild dehydration, without blood or mucus in the stool and without oral intolerance. What is the initial choice treatment in our environment?
options: Intravenous rehydration, absolute diet 8 hours and start feeding with astringent diet.
Rehydration with low osmolality oral rehydration solution (sodium 60-75 mEq / L) and continue with your usual diet.
Rehydration with low osmolality oral rehydration solution (sodium 60-75 mEq / L), maintain regular feeding and oral amoxicillin for 10 days.
Rehydration with low osmolality oral rehydration solution (sodium 60-75 mEq / L) and start feeding with lactose-free formula.
Rehydration with low osmolality oral rehydration solution (sodium 60-75 mEq / L), maintain regular feeding and loperamide 7 days.
questions.why: Mild dehydration from viral gastroenteritis in a child who tolerates fluids is treated with a low-osmolality oral rehydration solution and early return to the usual diet. Early feeding shortens the illness and improves nutrition. Australian guidelines say the same, using ORS products such as Gastrolyte.
notes: IV fluids are for severe dehydration or when oral or nasogastric rehydration fails, and fasting and restrictive astringent diets are outdated and not helpful.
Antibiotics are not indicated for presumed viral gastroenteritis without blood or mucus in an otherwise healthy child.
Lactose-free formula is not needed routinely. Consider it only if diarrhoea persists with proven secondary lactose intolerance.
Loperamide is contraindicated in young children because of the risk of ileus and CNS toxicity, and it does not treat the dehydration.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy comes to the Health Center who, 5 minutes earlier, begins with angioedema on his face, conjunctivitis, nasal congestion and hoarseness, coinciding with the intake of a spoonful of yogurt that was mistakenly given him at school. Among the background is diagnosed with cow's milk protein allergy. The examination revealed mild hypotension, heart rate 110 beats / min, Sat O2 93%, pale and somewhat sweaty, with disseminated wheezing. What is the first treatment of choice?
questions.why: Allergen exposure followed by skin and mucosal signs plus airway involvement (hoarseness, wheeze, SpO2 93%) and hypotension is anaphylaxis. First-line treatment is 1:1000 adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg IM into the anterolateral thigh, as ASCIA guidelines also recommend.
notes: Inducing vomiting is not recommended. It delays adrenaline and risks aspiration in a child with airway compromise.
Subcutaneous adrenaline is absorbed more slowly and less reliably than IM, so it is no longer advised for anaphylaxis.
Corticosteroids work too slowly to treat acute anaphylaxis and do not replace adrenaline. At most they are an adjunct.
Nebulised salbutamol can help residual bronchospasm after adrenaline, but it does nothing for the hypotension or the upper airway oedema.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman asks for preconceptional advice. The patient reports that she underwent cervical conization due to a high-grade intraepithelial lesion (H-SIL) and that she subsequently suffered three miscarriages between 20 and 22 weeks of gestation. He does not have living children. On all three occasions he went to the Emergency Department with a sensation of weight in the hypogastrium and there it was found that he arrived with a dilatation of 8 cm and with prominent amniotic membranes. I had never felt contractions. What advice would you give for the next pregnancy?
options: I would recommend prophylaxis with atosiban orally throughout the pregnancy.
It would offer lung maturation with corticosteroids from 19-20 weeks of gestation.
I would recommend performing a cervical cerclage programmed from the 14th week of gestation.
I would advise you not to try more pregnancies because of the high risk of recurrence.
I would recommend resorting to assisted reproduction techniques.
questions.why: Repeated painless second-trimester losses with advanced dilation and bulging membranes, and no contractions, after a conization point to cervical insufficiency. A history-indicated cerclage at about 12-14 weeks is the recommended prevention.
notes: Atosiban is an IV tocolytic for active preterm labour. It is not given orally and is not used as prophylaxis, and these losses happened without contractions.
Steroids at 19-20 weeks come before viability and would not prevent painless cervical dilation, so they would not save the pregnancy.
Cervical insufficiency can be treated and cerclage gives good outcomes, so advising against further pregnancy is inappropriate.
She has no fertility problem, since she conceives easily. Her problem is keeping the pregnancy, so assisted reproduction adds nothing.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 16-year-old woman consulted for primary amenorrhea. It presents a normal female development of secondary sexual characteristics. The levels of estradiol and testosterone are normal. In the gynecological examination, agenesis of the vagina is appreciated. Ultrasound is performed and there is absence of uterus. The ovaries are normal ultrasound. No left kidney is seen. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.why: Primary amenorrhoea with normal female secondary sexual characteristics, normal ovaries and hormones, an absent vagina and uterus, and unilateral renal agenesis is Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome. It is Müllerian agenesis in a 46,XX female, and renal anomalies often go with it.
notes: Androgen insensitivity (Morris syndrome) gives a blind vagina and no uterus, but there are testes instead of ovaries, testosterone is in the male range, and pubic hair is scant.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes virilisation and high androgens, and the uterus and vagina are present.
PCOS causes oligo-amenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism, and the uterus and vagina are normal.
Kallmann syndrome is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia, so oestradiol is low, puberty is absent, and the uterus is present.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 50-year-old woman who for 1 month has a depressed mood, anhedonia, memory loss, easy crying, loss of energy, sense of worthlessness and guilt, marked weight loss and early awakening, as well as inability to perform their tasks usual at home. In separation proceedings for 3 months. Point out the most appropriate diagnosis:
questions.why: She has well over five depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, guilt, weight loss, early waking, low energy, poor concentration) lasting more than two weeks with marked impairment. That meets major depressive episode criteria. A recent stressor does not change the diagnosis once full criteria are met.
notes: Dysthymia needs chronic, milder symptoms lasting at least two years, not one month of severe symptoms.
Pseudodementia is cognitive impairment caused by depression. Memory loss here is one symptom inside a full depressive syndrome, which is the main diagnosis.
Adjustment disorder applies only when symptoms after a stressor do not meet criteria for another disorder such as major depression.
Minor depression means fewer than five symptoms, but she has many more, with severe functional impairment.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: Adolescent of 16 years who consults for primary amenorrhea. He does not have medical-surgical history of interest. On physical examination, we found female secondary sex characteristics, female external genitalia, with stage III-IV breast development, scanty pubic and axillary hair. He presents a stature in the 90th percentile for his age. The plain radiograph reveals a bone age of 15.8 years. The analytical study reveals an estradiol of 50 pg / ml, and high gonadotropins. Which of the following clinical entities would be compatible with the diagnosis?
questions.why: A tall person with a female phenotype, good breast development, scant pubic and axillary hair, primary amenorrhoea and high gonadotropins has complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY). Testes make testosterone, which is converted to oestradiol and drives breast growth. Androgen-dependent hair does not develop because the androgen receptor does not work.
notes: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) gives a male phenotype with small testes and gynaecomastia, not female external genitalia and primary amenorrhoea.
Kallmann syndrome is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia, so gonadotropins would be low and breast development absent or poor.
Constitutional delay gives low gonadotropins and a delayed bone age with little pubertal development. Here bone age matches chronological age and gonadotropins are high.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a 46,XX patient causes virilisation with abundant androgen-dependent hair and short adult height, the opposite of scant hair and tall stature.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and moderate heart failure attended the clinic due to a persistent and dry cough that started as a sensation of itching in the throat. In the analytical hyperkalemia is observed. What is the drug suspected of causing the clinical and analytical alteration of the patient?
questions.why: ACE inhibitors such as enalapril cause a dry, tickly cough because bradykinin builds up, and they cause hyperkalaemia because they reduce aldosterone. Cough plus high potassium in a patient with hypertension and heart failure points to this class.
notes: Thiazides cause hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia, and do not cause cough.
Beta-blockers may cause bronchospasm in susceptible people but not a dry tickly cough, and they do not typically cause clinically important hyperkalaemia.
Loop diuretics such as furosemide cause hypokalaemia and do not cause cough.
Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia, headache and a lupus-like syndrome, not cough or hyperkalaemia.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of a heart murmur detected in the pediatric age. Enter the Emergency Department for symptoms of palpitations, easy fatigue and malignant edema. Physical examination reveals absence of cyanosis. Oxygen Saturation by pulse oximeter 97%. TA: 120/80 mm Hg. Irregular heart rate at 100 bpm. Systolic ejection murmur (2/6) in pulmonary focus. 2nd R unfolded, wide and fixed. No death rattles. Slight hepatomegaly (2-3 cm). Slight malleolar edema. ECG: complete arrhythmia due to atrial fibrillation at 100 bpm. AQRS: + 120º. Conduction disorder of the right branch of the bundle of His. What is your diagnostic orientation?
questions.why: A wide, fixed split second heart sound is the hallmark of atrial septal defect. Add a pulmonary flow murmur, right axis deviation, RBBB, and adult-onset AF with right heart failure, and this is a secundum ASD presenting in middle age.
notes: VSD gives a holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border, and fixed splitting of the second sound is not typical.
Aortic stenosis gives an ejection murmur at the aortic area radiating to the carotids, with a soft or paradoxically split second sound and left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG.
Mitral stenosis causes AF but gives a diastolic rumble with an opening snap at the apex, not fixed splitting.
A patent ductus gives a continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle and wide pulse pressure, not fixed splitting of the second sound.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 52-year-old patient who reported dyspnea of ​​medium effort for 6 months. He has not presented angina or syncopes. The physical examination and diagnostic tests show the existence of an average aortic transvalvular gradient of 55 mmHg and a calculated area of ​​0.7 cm2. Ejection fraction of 65%. The treatment that should be indicated to this patient is:
options: Diuretics and more frequent controls by a specialist.
In case of increasing dyspnea on exertion, a percutaneous dilatation of the aortic valve with a balloon catheter should be performed.
Replacement of the aortic valve with a prosthesis / bioprosthesis.
Replacement of the aortic valve by a homograft.
questions.why: Mean gradient over 40 mmHg and valve area under 1 cm2 mean severe aortic stenosis, and exertional dyspnoea means it is symptomatic. Severe symptomatic AS needs valve replacement whatever the EF. At 52 with no high-risk features, surgical AVR is standard, and Australian practice is the same.
notes: Medical therapy does not change the prognosis of severe symptomatic AS, and diuretics can drop preload dangerously; delaying intervention once symptoms start increases mortality.
Balloon valvuloplasty gives only short-lived benefit with early restenosis, so it is used as a bridge or palliation, not as definitive treatment for a fit 52-year-old.
Homografts are mainly used in special cases such as aortic root endocarditis; they are not the standard replacement for isolated degenerative or calcific AS.
TAVI is used mainly in older or higher surgical-risk patients; a fit 52-year-old is better treated with surgical AVR, given long-term durability.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man underwent a truncal vagotomy and antrectomy with Billroth II reconstruction, for suffering from a chronic peptic ulcer disease with pylorus-duodenal stenosis. Six weeks after the surgery, he reported that shortly after (less than half an hour) of the ingestions he presented with a nauseating state, asthenia and sweating, dizziness and abdominal cramps, usually accompanied by diarrheal descent. Which of the following is the most appropriate attitude for its initial management?
options: Apply treatment with a somatostatin analog (octeotide).
Perform a test treatment with a benzodiazepine.
Perform the search for a probable neuroendocrine tumor (eg, carcinoid).
Indicate surgical treatment to perform an anti-peristaltic gastro-jejunostomy in Roux-en-Y.
questions.why: Symptoms within 30 minutes of eating after vagotomy and Billroth II are early dumping syndrome, caused by rapid hyperosmolar emptying into the jejunum. First-line treatment is diet: small frequent meals, few simple sugars, liquids taken apart from solids, and lying down after meals.
notes: Octreotide works but is kept for dumping that does not respond to dietary changes, not used as first-line.
Benzodiazepines do nothing for the physiology of dumping; the symptoms come from fluid shifts and vasoactive peptides, not anxiety.
The timing just after gastric surgery and the link to meals clearly point to dumping, so searching for a carcinoid or other NET is not justified.
Revision to a Roux-en-Y is only for severe dumping that has failed both diet and drug treatment, not for initial management at six weeks.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man, the father of a celiac son, with iron deficiency anemia and a recent increase in the rhythm of deposition, has been determined to have a negative HLA-DQ2 and HLADQ8 allele. Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate in this case?
options: Upper digestive endoscopy with taking of duodenal biopsies.
Evaluate the response to a gluten-free diet.
questions.why: Negative HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 almost rules out coeliac disease because the negative predictive value is close to 100%. In a 55-year-old, iron deficiency anaemia with a new change in bowel habit points to colorectal cancer, so colonoscopy is the test. In Australian practice, bidirectional endoscopy (gastroscopy plus colonoscopy) is usual for iron deficiency anaemia.
notes: Coeliac serology adds nothing once HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 are negative, because coeliac disease is then almost excluded.
Duodenal biopsy for coeliac disease is not justified after negative HLA typing, and on its own it would miss the colorectal cancer suggested by anaemia plus a change in bowel habit.
The D-xylose test is an outdated screen for malabsorption and cannot assess for colorectal neoplasia.
A gluten-free diet trial is not a valid diagnostic test, and it would delay investigation of a likely colorectal cancer.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman attended the emergency department for asthenia, anorexia, weight loss, jaundice, fever and abdominal pain. It does not refer to recent history of blood transfusion, risky sexual contacts or addiction to parenteral drugs. Usual consumption of 60 grams of alcohol per day during the last five years, consumption that has increased during the previous month due to family problems. Temperature 38.5ºC, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. Physical examination shows temporo-spatial disorientation, malnutrition, asterixis, jaundice and painful hepatomegaly. No ascites or peritoneal irritation data. Laboratory tests include leukocytes 15,000 / microliter with 90% polymorphonuclear cells, red blood cells 3 million / mm3, hemoglobin 10 g / dl, mean corpuscular volume 115 fl, bilirubin 15 mg / dl direct predominance, AST (GOT) 300 IU / L, ALT (GPT) 120 IU / L, GGT 635 IU / L, prolongation of prothrombin time greater than 50%. What is the most likely diagnosis of the condition presented by the patient?
questions.why: Heavy drinking that recently increased, followed by fever, painful hepatomegaly, marked jaundice, neutrophilia, an AST:ALT ratio above 2 with AST under 400, very high GGT, macrocytosis, coagulopathy and encephalopathy, is severe alcoholic hepatitis. Assess severity with the Maddrey discriminant function (severe if 32 or more) or MELD.
notes: A liver abscess causes fever and right upper quadrant pain, but deep jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy and an alcoholic AST:ALT pattern point to diffuse hepatocellular injury, not a focal lesion.
Acute cholecystitis gives right upper quadrant pain with a Murphy sign, and usually no or only mild jaundice. It does not cause encephalopathy, coagulopathy or macrocytosis.
Cholangitis gives fever, jaundice and pain with a cholestatic pattern from biliary obstruction. The alcohol history, AST:ALT above 2 and liver failure point to alcoholic hepatitis.
Acute pancreatitis presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and raised lipase. It would not explain painful hepatomegaly, bilirubin of 15 mg/dL and liver failure.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy, an athlete with no history of interest, goes to the doctor for occasional conjunctival jaundice. Denies drug intake and abdominal pain. In the analyzes performed, normal ALT, AST, GGT, and FA were observed, with total bilirubin of 3.2 mgr / dl and direct bilirubin of 0.4 mgr / dl. It does not have anemia and the liver is ecographically normal. What is your diagnosis?
questions.why: A healthy young man has episodic jaundice with isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, normal liver enzymes, no anaemia (so no haemolysis) and a normal liver on ultrasound. This is Gilbert syndrome, caused by reduced UGT1A1 activity. Episodes are often brought on by fasting, exercise or illness.
notes: Rotor syndrome causes conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia, but here direct bilirubin is only 0.4 of 3.2 mg/dL.
Choledocholithiasis causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with raised ALP and GGT, a dilated bile duct and often pain, and none of these is present.
Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, whereas this patient's raised bilirubin is mostly unconjugated.
Acute hepatitis would raise ALT and AST, usually markedly, along with mixed hyperbilirubinaemia. Here the transaminases are normal.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman came to the consultation sent from Surgery with the diagnosis of a neuroendocrine tumor diagnosed after partial pancreatectomy due to a 2-cm tumor in the tail of the pancreas. The tumor had been detected by chance on an abdominal CT scan requested to complete the study of a simple liver cyst. Interrogating the patient, the background is irregular rules, being in amenorrhea for 6 months, and repetitive colic of recurrence from the age of 20 for those who have required lithotripsy on several occasions. In addition, he has a family history of renoureteral colic. What is your diagnostic suspicion?
options: A multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 or Wermer syndrome.
A multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 A or Sipple syndrome.
questions.why: A pancreatic NET, recurrent kidney stones from a young age (primary hyperparathyroidism), amenorrhoea (likely prolactinoma) and a family history of stones make the 3 Ps of MEN1: parathyroid, pancreas and pituitary.
notes: MEN2A combines medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism; it does not include pancreatic NETs or pituitary tumours.
MEN2B causes medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas and a marfanoid build, but not hyperparathyroidism or pancreatic NETs.
Somatostatinoma causes gallstones, diabetes and steatorrhoea; it does not explain lifelong kidney stones, amenorrhoea or the family history.
An ectopic PTH-secreting NET is very rare and would not explain stones since age 20, the family history of stones or the amenorrhoea.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man who underwent cardiac catheterization with revascularization of the right coronary artery 3 weeks ago and consulted for nausea and vomiting of 3 days of evolution. It presents arterial pressure of 185/85 mm Hg and purple lesions on the toes of both feet. In the analytical, urea 230 mg / dL and creatinine 5.8 mg / dL were observed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 78-year-old man with poorly controlled rheumatoid arthritis (RA). A history of 2 admissions for heart failure and atrial fibrillation in the last 6 months. In current treatment with infliximab, prednisone, furosemide, enalapril, carvedilol and acenocoumarol. Enter again for biventricular heart failure clinic. The ECG showed atrial fibrillation at 102 bpm and advanced left bundle branch block. An echocardiogram shows biatrial dilation, thickening of the left ventricular wall with ejection fraction of 45% and restrictive pattern. The analytical highlights: Hb 10 gr / dL, creatinine 2.1 mg / dL (FG 20 mL / min), CRP 124 mg / L, rheumatoid factor 240 U / L, BNP 980 ng / L, proteinuria 4.8 g / 24h. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Long-standing uncontrolled RA with a very high CRP, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and a thick-walled restrictive heart with conduction disease point to one systemic infiltrative process: secondary AA amyloidosis.
notes: Cardiorenal syndrome type 2 is CKD caused by chronic heart failure; it does not explain nephrotic proteinuria or a thick-walled restrictive ventricle.
Giant cell myocarditis is a fulminant illness of younger patients with ventricular arrhythmias; it does not cause a restrictive thick-walled picture with nephrotic syndrome.
Anti-TNF drugs can worsen heart failure, but they do not cause wall thickening, restrictive filling or nephrotic proteinuria.
Membranous nephropathy in RA, usually from gold or penicillamine, could explain the proteinuria but not the restrictive infiltrative cardiomyopathy.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man goes to the emergency department for inflammation of the right knee of about 24 hours of evolution. The patient does not report previous trauma and is the first episode of arthritis that presents. A the anamnesis directed that 4 weeks ago he returned from a trip to Morocco and that being there he presented chills and diarrhea that subsided after a week. The examination also revealed inflammation of the right Achilles tendon. What is the attitude to follow?
options: It is a spondyloarthropathy, start treatment with methotrexate.
Immobilize the knee with a bandage for 15 days and give non-steroidal anti-inflammatories.
Practice an arthrocentesis to perform culture, analysis of microcrystals and cellular counting of the synovial fluid.
It is a gouty arthritis, I would start treatment with allopurinol.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman consulted for the appearance of maculo-papular lesions in the upper limbs without other symptoms. The biopsy of one of them demonstrates the presence of noncaseating granulomas. Blood tests are normal except for an elevation of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels. On chest radiography, bilateral hilar adenopathies are detected. Which of the following considers the most appropriate attitude?
questions.why: This is stage I sarcoidosis (bilateral hilar lymph nodes, noncaseating granulomas, raised ACE) with mild skin lesions and no symptoms. It often resolves on its own, so treatment is not needed yet. Workup should continue: lung function tests, eye exam, ECG, and serum and urine calcium.
notes: Oral corticosteroids are kept for symptomatic or progressive lung disease, or for heart, eye, nerve or high-calcium involvement, none of which is present.
Hydroxychloroquine can treat troublesome skin sarcoid, but these minor symptom-free lesions do not need systemic therapy.
Azathioprine is a second-line steroid-sparing drug for chronic disease that needs treatment, not for symptom-free stage I sarcoidosis.
Leflunomide is a second-line steroid-sparing drug kept for refractory or steroid-dependent sarcoidosis, which is not the case here.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 23-year-old boy, who makes a jump while playing basketball, falls on his right lower limb with his knee in hyperextension, applying a sharp turn to his knee while keeping his foot fixed on the ground. The patient, perceives a snap and sharp pain in his knee, unable to continue playing. Note feeling of instability when performing the support of said extremity. On clinical examination, intense articular effusion is seen, so arthrocentesis is performed, which shows an important acute hemarthrosis without the presence of droplets of fat supernatanting in the extracted fluid. The mobility of the knee is free and the Lachman maneuver is positive. What is the diagnostic suspicion?
options: Break in cube handle of the inner meniscus.
Isolated rupture of the lateral collateral ligament.
Fracture by tearing of the anterior tibial spine.
Unicondylar fracture of the medial condyle.
Rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament
questions.why: A twisting injury with a pop, instability, rapid bloody effusion and a positive Lachman test means ACL rupture. No fat droplets in the aspirated blood argues against a fracture. The ACL is the most common cause of acute traumatic haemarthrosis.
notes: A bucket-handle meniscal tear typically causes mechanical locking and a block to extension, but knee movement here is free and Lachman is positive.
The LCL lies outside the joint, so an isolated tear causes varus laxity without a large haemarthrosis or a positive Lachman.
A tibial spine avulsion is a bone injury, so fat droplets would appear in the haemarthrosis, and it is mostly seen in children.
A condylar fracture is usually high-energy and gives a haemarthrosis with fat droplets, which were absent.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 60-year-old patient who came to the hospital's emergency department due to a left chest pain, cough and yellowish sputum, a temperature of 38.7ºC, a sensation of shortness of breath. Artificial saturation of 02 80%. Hemogram leukocytes 12000 / uL with 86% polymorphonuclear cells. Chest x-ray: alveolar infiltrate on the left base with air bronchogram. On suspicion of pneumonia, pneumococcal Ag is made in urine, which is positive and sputum culture is sent to the Microbiology service. Which empirical antibiotic treatment of the indicated ones is more correct in expectation of microbiological results?
questions.why: This is pneumococcal pneumonia with hypoxaemia (SpO2 80%) needing admission, and ceftriaxone reliably covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, including strains with reduced penicillin sensitivity. In Australia, eTG uses benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline for moderate CAP, and ceftriaxone plus azithromycin for severe CAP.
notes: Ceftazidime has weak activity against pneumococcus. It is an antipseudomonal drug and not a choice for typical CAP.
Pneumococcal macrolide resistance is high, so a macrolide alone is inadequate for a hypoxaemic inpatient.
Azithromycin alone carries the same pneumococcal resistance problem and is not enough for hospitalised pneumonia with severe hypoxaemia.
Doxycycline alone suits mild outpatient CAP, not a hypoxaemic patient needing admission with confirmed pneumococcus.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 28-year-old Caucasian woman, Nulípara, attends an annual gynecological examination and requests the possibility of reducing the risk of ovarian cancer given that her mother died of this neoplasm at 64 years of age. In the detailed questioning, no other family history of ovarian or breast cancer is identified. Which of the following strategies is the most appropriate to reduce the risk of ovarian cancer in this patient?
options: Continuous daily administration of aspirin at low dose.
Advise her to use artificial lactation if she is pregnant.
questions.why: One first-degree relative with ovarian cancer at 64 and no other family history means only modestly raised risk, with no indication for surgery. Combined oral contraceptives cut ovarian cancer risk by about half with long-term use, and they are reversible.
notes: Tubal occlusion does lower ovarian cancer risk, but permanent sterilisation is inappropriate for a 28-year-old woman with no children.
Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy is for proven BRCA or Lynch carriers once childbearing is complete, not for one late-onset case in the family.
Evidence that aspirin reduces ovarian cancer risk is weak and inconsistent, so it is not the recommended strategy.
Breastfeeding lowers ovarian cancer risk, so advising formula feeding would remove a protective factor rather than reduce risk.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A pregnant woman of 31 weeks goes to the emergency department referring loss of fluid through the vagina. Objective speculum exploration of clear fluid through the external cervical os. It is apyletic. The cardiotocographic record does not reveal contractions and the fetal heart rate is normal. The ultrasound scan reveals no malformations and the cervix is ​​not shortened. What therapeutic combination would it indicate?
questions.why: This is preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 31 weeks, with no fever, no contractions and a normal CTG. Manage expectantly: corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation and antibiotics to prolong latency. Tocolysis is pointless when there are no contractions. In Australia this means betamethasone plus erythromycin.
notes: Tocolytics are not indicated because there are no contractions, and in PPROM they add no benefit while possibly masking infection.
Tocolysis has no role without contractions, and leaving out corticosteroids at 31 weeks forgoes the main proven fetal benefit.
Tocolytics are not needed without contractions, and leaving out antibiotics loses the latency and infection benefit shown in PPROM.
Induction with oxytocin is for PPROM near term (around 34 weeks or later) or for chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise, and none of these is present at 31 weeks.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the emergency room due to abdominal pain and scarce vaginal blood loss. It refers to an amenorrhea of ​​7 weeks. You perform a pregnancy test, with a positive result. What is the next step?
options: Recommend home rest and repeat the pregnancy test in a week.
Evacuate the uterus by curettage by aspiration.
Standard progesterone micronized vaginally until week 14 of gestation.
Evacuate the uterus by intravaginal administration of prostaglandins.
questions.why: With a positive test, pain and spotting at 7 weeks, the first priority is to find where the pregnancy is and whether it is viable. Transvaginal ultrasound, usually alongside a quantitative beta-hCG, tells an intrauterine pregnancy (threatened, incomplete or missed miscarriage) apart from an ectopic before any treatment is chosen.
notes: Sending her home to rest and repeat the test in a week risks missing an ectopic pregnancy that could rupture, and rest does not change the course of a miscarriage.
Uterine evacuation before ultrasound could end a viable pregnancy and would miss an ectopic, so the diagnosis has to come first.
Progesterone could only be considered once ultrasound confirms a viable intrauterine pregnancy, and it is not the first step.
Medical evacuation with prostaglandins needs a confirmed nonviable intrauterine pregnancy, and giving it blind could harm a viable pregnancy or miss an ectopic.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: He is presented with a cohort study involving 1000 female smokers and 2000 non-smoking women of the same age. If, after 5 years, 30 smokers and 20 nonsmoking women have experienced a stroke, what would be the relative risk and the attributable risk?
options: Relative risk = 3, attributable risk = 10 out of every 1000.
Relative risk = 3, attributable risk = 20 out of every 1000.
Relative risk = 1.5, attributable risk = 10 out of every 1000.
Relative risk = 1.5, attributable risk = 30 out of 1000.
Relative risk = 10 out of 1000, attributable risk = 3.
questions.why: Risk in smokers is 30/1000 (3%) and in non-smokers 20/2000 (1%). Relative risk is 3%/1% = 3. Attributable risk is the risk difference, 3% − 1% = 2%, or 20 per 1000. Always divide events by each group's own denominator before you compare.
notes: The relative risk of 3 is right, but 10 per 1000 is the non-smokers' risk (20/2000), not the difference between the groups.
A relative risk of 1.5 comes from comparing raw counts (30 vs 20) without dividing by the unequal group sizes of 1000 and 2000.
This repeats the 1.5 error from raw counts and also gives the smokers' total risk (30/1000) instead of the excess risk.
This swaps the two measures: relative risk is a ratio with no units, and attributable risk is a rate difference.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A study has been carried out to determine the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) associated with the use of different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). For this purpose, 2,777 patients with UGIB and 5,532 patients matched with the previous ones were included by age and month of admission or consultation, in the same hospitals, but for reasons that had nothing to do with the use of NSAIDs. The comparative risk of suffering a UGIB associated with previous exposure to different NSAIDs was calculated. What kind of study is it?
questions.why: Subjects were chosen by outcome: patients with UGIB (cases) and matched patients without it (controls). Their past NSAID exposure was then compared, which is the definition of a case-control study. The usual effect measure is the odds ratio.
notes: A cohort study picks people by exposure (NSAID users and non-users) and follows them for the outcome, but here people were picked because they had or did not have bleeding.
A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at one point in time in a population sample, without choosing people by outcome or matching controls.
An experimental study needs the investigator to assign NSAID exposure, which did not happen here because exposure was observed retrospectively.
An ecological study compares groups or populations rather than individuals, but here exposure and outcome were recorded for individual patients.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A study is carried out to investigate the association between factor X and disease Z. To do this, 120 subjects with the disease and 420 controls (without the disease) are matched by age and sex. In both groups it is found that 20 subjects were exposed to factor X. What is the odds ratio (OR) between factor X and disease Z?
questions.why: Cases: 20 exposed and 100 unexposed. Controls: 20 exposed and 400 unexposed. OR = (20×400)/(100×20) = 4. The same number of exposed people in each group does not mean OR = 1, because the groups are different sizes.
notes: OR = 1 is the trap of comparing only the equal exposed counts (20 and 20) and ignoring that the groups have 120 and 420 people.
OR = 2 does not come from the 2×2 table. The correct cross-product is (20×400)/(100×20) = 4.
OR = 6 does not match the data. The odds of exposure are 20/100 in cases and 20/400 in controls, a ratio of 4.
OR = 8 overestimates the association. The cross-product ratio of this table is 4.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: In a cohort study, the population treated with an anticoagulant drug had an incidence of severe hemorrhage of 3%, while in the untreated population the incidence of severe bleeding was 1%, with the NNH ("Number Needed to Harm") of 50. What is the correct interpretation of this data?
options: In the group treated with the anticoagulant 50 people presented a severe hemorrhage.
In the group treated with anticoagulant there were 50 cases of severe hemorrhage more than in the untreated group.
The risk of severe hemorrhage in those treated with the anticoagulant was 50 times higher than in those not treated.
It was necessary to treat 50 people with the anticoagulant to produce 1 case of severe hemorrhage attributable to the drug.
Of every 100 patients treated with the anticoagulant, 50 had a severe hemorrhage.
questions.why: NNH is the reciprocal of the absolute risk increase: 1/(0.03 - 0.01) = 1/0.02 = 50. So 50 patients must be treated for one extra severe haemorrhage attributable to the anticoagulant. Remember that NNT and NNH are always 1 divided by an absolute risk difference.
notes: The NNH is not a count of bleeding cases. The treated group had an incidence of 3%, not 50 cases.
The NNH is not an absolute excess of cases. The excess risk was 2 percentage points, not 50 extra cases.
The relative risk is 3%/1% = 3, not 50. NNH is based on absolute difference, not relative risk.
An incidence of 3% means 3 per 100 treated patients bled, not 50 per 100.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman enters the Short Stay Medical Unit due to a clinical picture that began with an episode of syncope and then presented feeling of dizziness and dyspnea. On physical examination, she is sweaty, afebrile at 126 beats per minute and at 30 breaths per minute, with a blood pressure of 88/46 and an oxygen saturation of 85% while breathing room air. Cardiac auscultation shows tachycardia without murmurs or gallop and pulmonary auscultation is clean. Which, among the following, seems the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute cerebrovascular accident of posterior territory.
Acute pulmonary edema secondary to atrial flutter.
questions.why: She had sudden syncope, then dyspnoea, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension and marked hypoxaemia (saturation 85%), yet her lungs are clear and there are no murmurs or gallop. Hypoxic shock with clear lungs points to massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism.
notes: A posterior circulation stroke would cause neurological deficits. It would not explain severe hypoxaemia, tachypnoea and shock with clear lungs.
An acute coronary syndrome severe enough to cause shock would usually cause chest pain and pulmonary congestion or a gallop. None of these is present.
Hypovolaemic shock would not cause marked hypoxaemia and tachypnoea with clear lungs, and there is no source of fluid or blood loss.
Acute pulmonary oedema would cause crackles on auscultation, and her lungs are clear.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman consulted for hemoptotic expectoration. In the two previous months she had low-grade fever, asthenia, anorexia and unquantified weight loss. In the cytological analysis of sputum, hemosiderophages were observed and in the chest radiograph bilateral alveolar infiltrates were observed. Analytically it stood out: Hb 8.2gr / dL, PO2: 58mmHg, creatinine: 5mg / dL, urine: proteinuria +++ microhematuria, cylinders, hematics. ANCAp (antibodies against the cytoplasm of perinuclear neutrophils): positive: anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies: negative. Antinuclear antibodies: negative. The most likely diagnosis would be:
options: Systemic lupus erythematosus with severe renal involvement.
questions.why: She has a pulmonary-renal syndrome: alveolar haemorrhage with haemosiderophages, plus rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with red cell casts. Positive p-ANCA (MPO) with negative anti-GBM and ANA points to microscopic polyangiitis, a small-vessel vasculitis with pauci-immune necrotising glomerulonephritis.
notes: Idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis mainly affects children, does not involve the kidneys and is ANCA negative.
Goodpasture syndrome causes a pulmonary-renal picture but needs positive anti-GBM antibodies, which are negative here.
Lupus nephritis with lung haemorrhage would almost always come with positive ANA, which is negative here.
Classical polyarteritis nodosa affects medium-sized arteries, spares the lungs and glomeruli, and is typically ANCA negative.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman came to the emergency room referring to pain in the right groin and vomiting for about 6 hours. On examination, a hard consistency tumor is palpable just below the line joining the anterosuperior iliac spine and the pubis (which corresponds to the location of the inguinal ligament).
