Most likely, it is one:
questions.why: A hard, tender groin mass below the inguinal ligament with vomiting in an elderly woman suggests an incarcerated femoral hernia. Femoral hernias lie below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, are most common in older women, and often strangulate because the femoral ring is narrow.
notes: A direct inguinal hernia lies above the inguinal ligament, in Hesselbach's triangle, and rarely incarcerates.
A Spigelian hernia occurs higher on the anterior abdominal wall, along the semilunar line, not below the inguinal ligament.
An indirect inguinal hernia comes out above the inguinal ligament through the deep ring and the inguinal canal.
An obturator hernia is rarely palpable. It usually presents as bowel obstruction with medial thigh pain (Howship-Romberg sign) in thin elderly women.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man, previously diagnosed with liver cirrhosis of alcoholic etiology, is brought to the Emergency Department due to an increase in the abdominal perimeter and temporo-spatial disorientation. On physical examination, there is evidence of ascites and "flapping tremor" or asterixis. Which of the following explorations should be done as a matter of urgency?
options: A cranial computed tomography to rule out a cerebrovascular accident.
An abdominal ultrasound to confirm the presence of ascites.
An exploratory paracentesis to rule out a spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
An electroencephalogram to confirm the existence of hepatic encephalopathy.
An abdominal computed tomography to rule out a hepatocellular carcinoma.
questions.why: A cirrhotic with ascites and new hepatic encephalopathy needs a precipitant found, and SBP is a common one that is easy to miss. Diagnostic paracentesis (neutrophils over 250/mm3) is mandatory urgently in any cirrhotic admitted with ascites, especially with decompensation.
notes: Asterixis with confusion in known cirrhosis points to hepatic encephalopathy, not stroke; CT is kept for focal signs, head trauma or failure to improve.
Ascites is already obvious on examination, so ultrasound adds nothing urgent and does not identify the cause of the decompensation.
Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis; an EEG is not needed and would delay finding and treating the trigger.
HCC can cause decompensation, but imaging for it is not urgent; ruling out infection such as SBP comes first.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman came to the emergency room due to shivering, fever of 39ºC, pain in the right hypochondrium, jaundice and vomiting. The scan reveals TA 100/50 mmHg. FC 110 lpm. Prostration and pain on palpation in the right quadrant, with positive Murphy. The analytical sample shows leukocytosis with left deviation and abdominal ultrasound, cholelithiasis, choledocholithiasis and dilation of the extrahepatic bile duct. Empirical treatment is started with antibiotic and fluid therapy. What is the most effective procedure to perform next?
options: Maintain antibiotic treatment and support measures with posterior regulated cholecystectomy.
Placement of an external biliary drainage.
Urgent cholecystectomy with cannulation of the common bile duct.
questions.why: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain (Charcot triad) with choledocholithiasis, a dilated duct, tachycardia and borderline BP mean acute cholangitis. Antibiotics alone are not enough. Urgent biliary drainage is needed, and ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is first line.
notes: Antibiotics and support with delayed cholecystectomy might suit simple biliary colic or mild cholecystitis, but obstructive cholangitis needs the bile duct drained.
Cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder but does not clear the obstructed common bile duct, which is causing the sepsis.
Percutaneous transhepatic drainage is the fallback when ERCP fails or is not possible; it is not first choice.
Emergency open surgery with duct exploration in a septic patient carries much higher morbidity and mortality than endoscopic drainage.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman, diagnosed with diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypertension, consults for palpitations of weeks of evolution. Provides an electrocardiogram performed a week ago in which he is in atrial fibrillation with an average ventricular rate of 70 beats / min. In the physical examination and in a new electrocardiogram performed in consultation is in sinus rhythm. Is it necessary to anticoagulate it chronically?
options: It is not necessary to anticoagulate because it has a paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and is not currently in atrial fibrillation.
It is not necessary to anticoagulate because it is less than 75 years old and has not had a previous stroke.
You must be chronically anticoagulated because you have a CHADS of 2 and a CHADS-VASc of 3.
Anticoagulation is not necessary, but antiaggregation with acetylsalicylic acid may be prescribed.
Must be anticoagulated only with subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin when in atrial fibrillation.
questions.why: Stroke risk in AF depends on risk factors, not on whether the AF is paroxysmal or persistent. Hypertension, diabetes and female sex give CHADS2 2 and CHA2DS2-VASc 3, so she needs long-term anticoagulation. Australian guidance uses CHA2DS2-VA (no sex point), which still scores 2, and prefers a DOAC.
notes: Paroxysmal AF carries roughly the same stroke risk as persistent AF, so being in sinus rhythm today does not remove the need to anticoagulate.
Age 75 or over and prior stroke are only some of the risk factors; her hypertension and diabetes alone are enough to justify anticoagulation.
Aspirin gives little stroke protection in AF and still causes bleeding, so it is not an acceptable substitute when risk scores call for anticoagulation.
Anticoagulating only during AF episodes does not work, because paroxysms are often silent; long-term oral anticoagulation is needed, not intermittent LMWH.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with no history of interest or cardiovascular risk factors. Clinic of dyspnea when climbing a floor of stairs of 1 month of evolution. Consultation due to sudden syncope preceded by exertion. Family history of death not explained abruptly in his brother. On physical examination, a more audible rumen systolic murmur with aortic focus is highlighted. The electrocardiogram performed in the consultation shows a sinus rhythm with a compatible pattern of left ventricular hypertrophy. An echocardiogram was performed to document an important asymmetric hypertrophy of the interventricular septum with a subvalvular dynamic gradient of 70 mmHg with moderate secondary mitral regurgitation and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. Which therapeutic option is the LESS indicated?
questions.why: In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (LVOT gradient 70 mmHg), positive inotropes such as digoxin increase contractility and worsen the dynamic obstruction. Digoxin is contraindicated, while drugs that lower contractility or heart rate are the treatment of choice.
notes: Beta-blockers are first-line in symptomatic obstructive HCM: they lower contractility and heart rate and reduce the gradient.
Verapamil or diltiazem are the alternative when beta-blockers fail or are not tolerated, because they improve relaxation and reduce obstruction.
Unexplained exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death are major risk factors, so an ICD is indicated for primary prevention.
A resting gradient of 50 mmHg or more with symptoms is an indication for septal myectomy if drugs fail, so it is reasonable here.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man, smoker and diabetic, is brought to the Emergency Department for presenting an oppressive, deep-throating sweat for about an hour. In the ECG performed, sinus rhythm was observed at 80 bpm and a complete block of the left branch. What should our attitude be?
options: Perform an analytical determination of troponin and wait for its result to confirm the presence of an acute myocardial infarction.
Treat the patient as if it were an infarction with ST-segment elevation, proposing a reperfusion therapy as early as possible.
To implant a transcutaneous pacemaker before the possibility of developing a more advanced block.
Perform an urgent CT to rule out the presence of an acute pulmonary embolism.
As it could be an acute pericarditis, we will administer NSAIDs.
questions.why: Ongoing ischaemic chest pain with LBBB, especially if new or of unknown duration, is treated as a STEMI equivalent because LBBB hides ST changes. Arrange reperfusion promptly and do not wait for troponin; Sgarbossa criteria help, but suspected ischaemia with LBBB still means primary PCI.
notes: Waiting for troponin delays reperfusion in a possible occlusion MI, and every minute of delay means more myocardium lost.
Isolated LBBB in sinus rhythm at 80 bpm is not an indication for pacing; reperfusion takes priority.
Oppressive chest pain with sweating in a diabetic smoker points to ACS, not PE, and CT pulmonary angiography would delay reperfusion.
Pericarditis gives pleuritic, positional pain with diffuse ST elevation, not LBBB; giving NSAIDs would miss an infarction.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: Man of 55 years, obese, dyslipidemic and active smoker. In study for refractory hypertension without evidence of cardiac or renal damage so far. He refers to morning headache with daytime hypersomnia. ABPM was performed (ambulatory blood pressure monitoring 24 hours) and arterial hypertension was confirmed despite 3 drugs, one of them diuretic, with higher nighttime blood pressures than daytime blood pressure. What diagnostic test would you request next with your clinical suspicion?
questions.why: Resistant hypertension in an obese smoker with morning headache, daytime sleepiness and a non-dipping or reverse-dipping pattern on ABPM points to obstructive sleep apnoea. Overnight polysomnography is the test to confirm it. OSA is the most common secondary cause of resistant hypertension.
notes: Phaeochromocytoma causes episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations, not daytime sleepiness with nocturnal hypertension in an obese patient.
Primary aldosteronism should be screened for in resistant hypertension, but the morning headache, sleepiness and nocturnal pattern point first to sleep apnoea.
Doppler for renal artery stenosis would fit sudden worsening of hypertension or renal deterioration, neither of which is described here.
CT of the aorta looks for coarctation, which fits a young patient with arm-leg blood pressure difference or weak femoral pulses, not this picture.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea and a non-productive cough several years old. In chest X-ray, pleural plaques are seen in the mediastinal and diaphragmatic pleura. On CT, these plaques are confirmed, also appreciating the presence of reticulonodulillar involvement predominantly in lower fields. Among the following, what attitude would you recommend in the first place?
options: Request blood tests to rule out eosinophilia.
questions.why: Pleural plaques are almost pathognomonic of asbestos exposure, and with them, basal-predominant reticular interstitial disease suggests asbestosis. The first step is a detailed occupational history, because the diagnosis rests on documented exposure plus compatible imaging, usually without biopsy.
notes: Smoking history is relevant to overall lung risk, but smoking does not cause pleural plaques, so it does not explain the defining finding.
Eosinophilia points to eosinophilic lung disease or parasites and has nothing to do with pleural plaques and basal fibrosis.
Lung function tests measure severity but do not identify the cause; finding out about exposure comes first.
Biopsy is invasive and usually not needed when exposure history and imaging are typical of asbestosis.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 50-year-old man, mechanic, consulted for a two-year evolution of difficulty in handling the right hand and a feeling of stiffness in the arm. His wife notices his expressionless face and reports that he has very vivid nightmares that wake him up agitated. During the examination, rigidity was observed in the right limbs and slow walking without right arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Asymmetric onset of rigidity and bradykinesia, reduced arm swing and hypomimia, plus vivid dream-enacting nightmares (REM sleep behaviour disorder, a prodromal synucleinopathy feature), make idiopathic Parkinson's disease the most likely diagnosis.
notes: A lacunar infarct starts suddenly with hemiparesis or sensory loss; it does not cause slowly progressive rigidity, hypomimia and REM sleep behaviour disorder.
ALS causes weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs (fasciculations, hyperreflexia), not extrapyramidal rigidity and bradykinesia.
A cervical plexopathy would cause weakness, sensory loss and pain in a root or plexus distribution, not parkinsonism with hypomimia.
Corticobasal degeneration is asymmetric but has cortical signs such as apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss and myoclonus; REM sleep behaviour disorder points to a synucleinopathy.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient who went to the emergency room for general malaise, headache and progressive tiredness in recent weeks. On physical examination, a slight icteric dye of the skin and mucous membranes was detected and a 2-cm splenomegaly was felt under the costal margin. The analytical presents hemoglobin 8.6 g / dL, VCM 100 fL. The number of reticulocytes is high and anisopoikilocytosis is observed in the blood smear. In the biochemistry highlights LDH 1300 IU / L, bilirubin 2.2 mg / dL and undetectable haptoglobin. Which test is the most appropriate to guide the diagnosis of the patient?
options: Determination of iron, cobalamin and folic acid.
questions.why: The stem shows haemolysis: anaemia, high reticulocytes, raised LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, undetectable haptoglobin and splenomegaly. The next step is the direct Coombs (antiglobulin) test, which separates immune from non-immune haemolysis. Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is the classic cause in an adult.
notes: Faecal occult blood investigates GI blood loss, which gives a low reticulocyte, iron-deficient microcytic picture, not high LDH and absent haptoglobin.
Haematinics fit hypoproliferative anaemia. The high reticulocyte count shows the marrow is responding, and the MCV of 100 fits reticulocytosis rather than B12/folate deficiency.
Ultrasound would only confirm splenomegaly, which is already palpable. It does not tell you the cause of the haemolysis.
Bone marrow aspirate is not needed when peripheral markers clearly show peripheral destruction with an appropriate reticulocyte response.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 35-year-old woman on hormonal treatment for infertility. He went to the emergency department due to constitutional syndrome and paresthesias in the left side of the body. In blood tests, Hb 7.5 g / dL, reticulocytes 10% (0.52%), platelets 5,000 / uL, normal leukocytes, LDH 1,200 IU / L, direct negative Coombs test, undetectable haptoglobin are detected. Morphology of peripheral blood with abundant schistocytes. Normal coagulation tests. What is the diagnostic suspicion and the most appropriate treatment?
options: Von Willebrand disease. Administration of desmopressin.
Thrombocytopenic purpura. Start steroids and platelet transfusion.
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Treatment with plasmapheresis.
questions.why: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, high LDH, absent haptoglobin, negative Coombs) with severe thrombocytopenia, neurological signs and normal coagulation is TTP. TTP is an emergency. Treat urgently with plasma exchange, usually with steroids; caplacizumab is now often added.
notes: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia gives a positive direct Coombs test and spherocytes, not schistocytes. It also does not explain platelets of 5,000.
Von Willebrand disease is a bleeding disorder. It does not cause haemolysis, schistocytes or neurological deficits, and desmopressin has no role here.
Immune thrombocytopenia does not cause schistocytic haemolysis. Platelet transfusion is relatively contraindicated in TTP because it may worsen thrombosis.
Evans syndrome is AIHA plus ITP, so the Coombs test would be positive and the smear would not show prominent schistocytes.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man should undergo cataract extraction surgery. He has a mitral mechanical prosthesis for 10 years and is being treated with acenocoumarol. The electrocardiogram shows a sinus rhythm. Which of the following recommendations do you find most appropriate?
options: Perform eye surgery without stopping acenocoumarol.
Suspend acenocoumarol 5 days before surgery and restart it the day after it.
Suspend acenocoumarol 5 days before surgery, start low molecular weight heparin 3 days before surgery and suspend it 24 hours before surgery.
Suspend acenocoumarol 1 day before the intervention and use fresh frozen plasma during it.
Suspend acenocoumarol 1 day before the intervention and give vitamin K just before it.
questions.why: Cataract surgery carries very low bleeding risk, so vitamin K antagonists should continue, keeping the INR in the therapeutic range. Interrupting anticoagulation with a mechanical mitral valve risks valve thrombosis. In Australia warfarin is the VKA used rather than acenocoumarol, but the principle is the same.
notes: Stopping the VKA with no bridging leaves a mechanical mitral valve unprotected for days, which is a high thrombotic risk, and it is unnecessary for a low-bleeding-risk procedure.
Interruption with LMWH bridging is meant for high-bleeding-risk surgery. It exposes the patient to needless thrombotic and bleeding risk for cataract surgery.
Fresh frozen plasma reversal is for urgent surgery or major bleeding. Neither applies to an elective, low-risk eye procedure.
Vitamin K reversal makes later re-anticoagulation difficult and puts the mechanical valve at risk. It is not indicated for cataract surgery.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital for pulmonary embolism confirmed by angio-CT. He has no history of recent surgery, trauma or travel. He refers to Raynaud's phenomenon for 2 years, and the previous year he had an abortion at 12 weeks of gestation. He has no family history of venous thromboembolic disease. The activated partial thromboplastin time is 56 sg (normal 25-35 sg) and the platelet count is 120000 / uL. Which of the following diagnostic tests would help you most in the diagnosis?
questions.why: An unprovoked PE in a young woman with a prolonged aPTT that does not explain bleeding, mild thrombocytopenia, pregnancy loss and Raynaud's (possible SLE) strongly suggests antiphospholipid syndrome. Lupus anticoagulant explains the prolonged aPTT and is one of the defining laboratory tests.
notes: Antithrombin deficiency causes venous thrombosis but does not prolong the aPTT or cause thrombocytopenia, and there is no family history.
Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia, but it does not prolong the aPTT, lower platelets or fit Raynaud's.
Protein C deficiency does not explain the prolonged aPTT, the thrombocytopenia or the autoimmune features.
Protein S deficiency does not explain the prolonged aPTT and low platelets that together point to antiphospholipid antibodies.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with no personal or family history of interest, who enters Neurosurgery due to a cranial fracture due to a motorcycle accident. Three days later it begins abruptly with polyuria, polydipsia and intense thirst both during the day and at night. In the study conducted, a urinary volume of 7 liters with urinary osmolarity of 190 mOsm / L (90-1200) and plasma osmolarity of 292 mOsm / L (275-295) was observed. The plasma Na is 143 mmol / L. A water restriction test is performed and after checking that there is no increase in urinary osmolarity, a dose of 2 micrograms of desmopressin subcutaneously is administered. The posterior urinary osmolality is 410 mOsm / kg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Polyuria with dilute urine after head trauma, no concentration during water deprivation, and a rise in urine osmolality of more than 50% (190 to 410) after desmopressin show ADH deficiency with intact renal response. This is central diabetes insipidus, now also called AVP deficiency.
notes: Primary polydipsia gives low-normal plasma osmolality and sodium and concentrates urine with water deprivation. Here plasma osmolality is high-normal and the urine does not concentrate.
Acute adrenal insufficiency presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia, not high-volume dilute polyuria that corrects with desmopressin.
SIADH causes hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine and low urine output, which is the opposite of this picture.
Nephrogenic DI would show little or no rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin. The large response here shows the kidneys respond to ADH.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with a loss of 6 kg in the last 4 months, asthenia and anorexia. Amenorrhea for 2 months. The hormonal results indicate a basal cortisol serum concentration of 108 nmol / l (baseline normal value 115-550) and 123 nmol / l after stimulation with ACTH. The baseline plasma concentration of ACTH is 48 pmol / l (normal value: 2-12). What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Tertiary adrenal insufficiency due to hypothalamic lesion.
More tests should be done since the diagnosis is inconclusive.
questions.why: Low basal cortisol that does not rise after ACTH stimulation, with markedly raised plasma ACTH, means the adrenal glands themselves have failed. That is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's), here with weight loss, asthenia and anorexia.
notes: Secondary adrenal insufficiency has low or inappropriately normal ACTH. The ACTH here is four times the upper limit.
Hypothalamic (tertiary) insufficiency also gives low ACTH, so it cannot explain a markedly raised ACTH.
A corticotropinoma raises ACTH but drives cortisol excess (Cushing's disease), not low cortisol with a flat response to stimulation.
The results are conclusive: low cortisol, no response to ACTH and high ACTH together confirm primary adrenal failure.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man consulted for edema in lower limbs of 3 weeks of evolution. In blood analysis, creatinine 1.3 mg / dL, total cholesterol 270 mg / dL and albumin 2.4 g / dL. In the urine sediment, it presents 15-20 red cells per field and in urine of 24 hours proteinuria is detected 3.7 g / day. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: A middle-aged adult with nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia, oedema) and near-normal creatinine most likely has membranous nephropathy, the commonest primary cause in non-diabetic adults. Microscopic haematuria can occur. Check anti-PLA2R antibodies and look for secondary causes such as malignancy.
notes: Minimal change disease is the main cause in children and is rare in a 47-year-old, and haematuria is uncommon.
FSGS is a common cause of adult nephrotic syndrome, especially in Black patients and with obesity or HIV, but it is less likely than membranous at this age.
MPGN type I usually gives a mixed nephritic-nephrotic picture with low complement and is often linked to hepatitis C; this stem is mainly nephrotic.
Mesangial proliferative GN, such as IgA nephropathy, usually shows haematuria with less proteinuria and rarely causes full nephrotic syndrome.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 46-year-old male injecting drug user who presented to the emergency room with fever with chills, mental confusion, diffuse myalgias and intense pain in the left hand of 24 hours of evolution without clear local phlogotic signs. It does not refer any traumatic antecedent. The examination highlights: temperature 38.9ºC, 120 beats per minute, respiratory rate 30 / min, blood pressure 90/54 mm Hg. In the laboratory, a leukocytosis with left deviation stands out (25,000 leukocytes / mm3, 80% neutrophils); increase in creatinine (1.6 mg / dL) and CK (138 U / L). Among the following, what is the most likely diagnosis ?:
questions.why: In an injecting drug user, severe limb pain out of proportion to minimal skin signs with septic shock, confusion and kidney injury suggests necrotising fasciitis with streptococcal toxic shock. It needs urgent surgical debridement and antibiotics, including clindamycin.
notes: Clostridial gas gangrene usually follows trauma or deep wounds and gives crepitus and marked myonecrosis with very high CK. The CK here is normal.
Mycobacterial skin infection is indolent and develops over weeks. It does not cause hyperacute septic shock within 24 hours.
Erysipelas causes a sharply demarcated, raised, red plaque. The absence of obvious skin changes despite severe pain and shock argues against it.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 32-year-old male from Cameroon consulted for fever cough and pain in the left hemithorax of 1 month of evolution. He took amoxicillin-clavulanate for 1 week without improvement of symptoms. An analysis is carried out with a leukocyte count of 8000 / microL and a hemoglobin of 12.8 g / dL. The chest radiograph shows a loculated left pleural effusion occupying a third of the hemithorax. A thoracentesis shows a yellowish fluid with the following characteristics: red blood cells 2000 / μL, leukocytes 2500 / μL with 90% lymphocytes, proteins 4.9 g / dL, lactate dehydrogenase 550 U / L, glucose 67 mg / dL and absence of cells malignancies in the cytological study. Which of the following tests would be most useful in diagnosing the cause of the pleural effusion?
options: Measurement of the pH of the pleural fluid.
Measurement of adenosine deaminase from pleural fluid.
questions.why: A lymphocytic exudate (90% lymphocytes, high protein and LDH) that is not malignant, in a young man from a high-TB country who did not respond to antibiotics, points to tuberculous pleuritis. A high pleural fluid ADA has high sensitivity and specificity for this.
notes: CT shows the anatomy, such as loculation and the pleura, but cannot confirm tuberculosis as the cause.
Pleural pH helps decide whether a parapneumonic effusion needs drainage, but it does not identify tuberculosis in a lymphocytic exudate.
A tuberculin test only shows infection, not disease, and is often negative in TB pleuritis. A positive result is also common in people from endemic areas.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman, non-smoker, previously diagnosed with atopic rhinitis, presented for a two-month period consisting of cough and intermittent sibilants predominantly nocturnal. Normal chest x-ray. Spirometry within normality with negative bronchodilator test. Which of the following tests would you request next?
questions.why: Night-time cough and wheeze in an atopic patient suggest asthma, but spirometry and the bronchodilator test are normal. The next step is a bronchial challenge such as methacholine to show airway hyperresponsiveness, which has a high negative predictive value.
notes: Sinus X-ray is of little value and would not confirm or exclude asthma as the cause of the wheeze.
With a normal chest X-ray and a typical asthma picture, CT adds radiation without answering the question.
A skin prick test shows allergic sensitisation, which is already likely given her atopic rhinitis, but it does not confirm asthma.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man presents a picture of arthritis of the metacarpophalangeal of both hands and a right pleuritis. On examination, bilateral malar erythema was observed. Positive antinuclear antibodies are detected (titre 1/640), with native anti-DNA antibodies also positive; Anti-Sm negative. What would be the initial treatment of choice for this patient?
options: The picture will probably be self-limiting and does not require treatment.
questions.why: This is SLE with mild-to-moderate disease: arthritis, serositis and malar rash, with no kidney or CNS involvement. First-line treatment is NSAIDs plus an antimalarial (hydroxychloroquine, the standard in Australia), with low-dose steroids only if needed.
notes: High-dose glucocorticoids are kept for severe organ-threatening lupus such as nephritis or CNS disease, which this patient does not have.
Mycophenolate is induction therapy for lupus nephritis or severe disease and is not needed for joints, skin and pleura alone.
Active SLE with high-titre anti-dsDNA needs treatment, and hydroxychloroquine is advised for almost every patient to reduce flares and damage.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 70-year-old woman with a history of anorexia, weight loss, discomfort in the musculature and proximal joints plus pain in the temporo-mandibular region who goes to the emergency department for loss of unilateral vision (hand movement), sudden and painless onset (afferent pupillary defect). What test would you request in the first place for diagnostic purposes?
questions.why: An older woman with polymyalgia symptoms, jaw claudication and sudden painless monocular loss with an afferent pupillary defect has giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise. ESR/CRP is the quick first test. In Australia, start high-dose steroids straight away and confirm with temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy.
notes: Lumbar puncture has no role here: there are no meningeal signs, no fever and nothing to suggest raised intracranial pressure, and it would not show arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy.
MR angiography may show large-vessel involvement but is not the first test; a cheap, fast inflammatory marker supports the diagnosis while urgent steroids are started.
Carotid ultrasound looks for embolic amaurosis or retinal artery occlusion, but polymyalgia, weight loss and jaw claudication in a 70-year-old point to giant cell arteritis, not atheroma.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: Attended a scheduled review, a 50-year-old man diagnosed with polyangiitis with granulomatosis 10 years previously and without treatment for 5 years is asymptomatic. Chest x-ray, blood analysis and urine sediment are normal except for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) positive to title 1/320, with antiproteinase 3 specificity, which had previously been negativized. What is the most advisable therapeutic attitude?
questions.why: A rising ANCA titre alone, with no clinical, radiological, blood or urine signs of activity, does not justify immunosuppression. It predicts relapse poorly, so the right approach is closer monitoring.
notes: Steroids for an isolated serological change in an asymptomatic patient expose him to toxicity without proven benefit.
Cyclophosphamide is induction therapy for active severe GPA and is not justified without disease activity.
Mycophenolate is not indicated for an isolated ANCA rise with no clinical relapse.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman was referred to the gynecology office for evaluation, referring to dyspareunia for about 8 months, along with occasional dyschezia and rectal bleeding coinciding with menstruation for 3-4 months. It also refers to dysmenorrhea for years that controls well with Ibuprofen. She has been trying to get pregnant about 16 months without having achieved it yet. In the gynecological examination, only pain is seen when pressing the posterior vaginal cul-de-sac. What proof do you think would allow you to reach the diagnosis of certainty of your pathology?
questions.why: Dyspareunia, cyclical dyschezia and rectal bleeding, dysmenorrhoea, infertility and a tender posterior fornix suggest deep endometriosis. Laparoscopy with biopsy and histology gives the definitive diagnosis. Current Australian and ESHRE guidance also accepts expert ultrasound or MRI to make the diagnosis without surgery.
notes: Transvaginal ultrasound is a good first-line test for endometriomas and deep nodules, but it depends on the operator and misses superficial peritoneal disease, so it cannot give a certain diagnosis.
MRI helps map deep rectovaginal or bowel disease before surgery, but it is not the test that confirms the diagnosis by histology.
Colonoscopy usually looks normal because the endometriosis invades the bowel from the outside (serosa) inward, so it rarely shows lesions and cannot confirm the diagnosis.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man came to his office to evaluate a cholecystectomy program by laparoscopy. He has a history of hypertension in treatment for 10 years. Denies heart or lung disease. No chest pain She has an active life and daily goes to the gym where she alternates swimming and walking the treadmill for at least an hour. Usual treatment: nebivolol 5 mg every 24 hours and hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily. Physical examination: weight 73 kgs; size 179 cms; blood pressure 138/80 mmHg; heart rate 60 beats / minute. No murmurs are heard. Which of the following is the most appropriate preoperative approach?
options: Perform a scintigraphy with thallium and dipyridamole.
questions.why: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is low-to-intermediate risk, and he has excellent functional capacity (more than 4 METs) with no cardiac symptoms. No stress testing or imaging is needed, but a baseline ECG is reasonable given his age and hypertension.
notes: Stress testing does not change management when functional capacity is above 4 METs and there are no symptoms.
Echocardiography is only indicated for murmurs, dyspnoea or suspected heart failure, and none is present here.
Pharmacological perfusion imaging is for patients with poor or unknown functional capacity before higher-risk surgery.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: An 88-year-old man comes to the clinic because he has fallen 3 times in the last 6 months. None of the falls was accompanied by "dizziness" or syncope. A fall occurred while walking through the garden, in the other stumbled inside the house. His medical history includes high blood pressure without postural changes in blood pressure, gout, osteoarthritis and depression. Take 5 medicines regularly. Which of the following is most likely to contribute to falls in this patient?
questions.why: SSRIs such as paroxetine are among the strongest drug risk factors for falls in older people, through sedation, slowed reactions, impaired balance and hyponatraemia. Paroxetine is also anticholinergic. The stem points away from the antihypertensives by stating there are no postural blood pressure changes and no dizziness.
notes: Allopurinol does not affect balance, alertness or blood pressure, so it is not a recognised fall-risk drug.
Thiazides can cause falls through orthostatic hypotension or hyponatraemia, but the stem specifically says there is no postural drop and no dizziness.
ACE inhibitors cause falls mainly through hypotension, which the stem excludes by documenting no postural change and no presyncope.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes treated with oral antidiabetic agents, HBP in treatment with beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors, and congestive heart failure grade 1 of NYHA, with a LVEF of 48%, and currently asymptomatic. Functional state: ECOG 0. History of 2 years of evolution of small lumps in the neck. Cervical adenopathy biopsy: grade 2 follicular lymphoma. Extension study: Hb 12 gr / dL, Leucocytes 6,900 / microL (Neutrophils 60%, Lymphocytes 27%, Monocytes 6%, Eosinophils 4%, Basophils 4%) Platelets 220,000 / microL. MO: infiltrated by follicular lymphoma. Creatinine 1.5 mg / dL, LDH 235 U / L, Beta2 microglobulin 2.1 microg / mL. TAC: adenopathies less than 3 cm in cervical, axillary, retroperitoneal, iliac and inguinal territories; Normal liver and spleen. Which of the following treatments is the most appropriate?
options: Do not try and watch (wait and see).
questions.why: This is a grade 2 follicular lymphoma with low tumour burden: she has no symptoms, normal blood counts and LDH, nodes under 3 cm, no splenomegaly and a low beta2-microglobulin, so she meets no GELF criteria. Asymptomatic low-burden indolent lymphoma is watched without treatment, because treating early does not improve survival.
notes: R-CHOP is used for follicular lymphoma that needs treatment or has transformed, and it brings anthracycline toxicity in a woman with heart failure. She has no indication for treatment.
R-CVP is a choice once follicular lymphoma meets criteria for treatment, but her disease is asymptomatic and low burden, so it is not indicated yet.
Rituximab-bendamustine is a standard first-line regimen once treatment criteria are met, but her low-burden asymptomatic disease does not yet need treatment.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 57-year-old patient diagnosed with stage T3N1M0 colon adenocarcinoma. He was treated with resection followed by postoperative FOLFOX chemotherapy (fluorouracil, leucovorin and oxaliplatin) for six months. In a routine control, two years later, elevation of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was detected at 30 ng / mL (previous to less than 2 ng / mL). He has no symptoms, the physical examination is bland, the chest radiograph is normal. On CT, a mass of 3 cm is seen in the right hepatic lobe, which is captured in PET. No other alterations were observed in CT or PET. What attitude seems more correct?
options: Chemotherapy with FOLFIRI (fluorouracil, leucovorin and irinotecan) plus bevacizumab.
Evaluation by resection surgery of the hepatic lesion.
questions.why: He has a single 3 cm liver metastasis with no other disease on CT and PET. Isolated metachronous colorectal liver metastases should be assessed for resection first, because surgery offers a chance of long-term cure.
notes: FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab is used for unresectable metastatic disease, or as conversion therapy. It is not first-line for a single resectable liver lesion.
Single-agent capecitabine is a palliative or low-intensity option and would give up the chance of cure in a fit patient with one resectable metastasis.
Liver radiotherapy, such as SBRT, is reserved for patients who cannot have surgery. Resection remains the standard of care for a single resectable metastasis.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: An epidemiological study tried to correlate the consumption of processed meat "per capita" in different countries in 2012 with the incidence of colon cancer registered in that same year in those countries. What kind of study is it?
questions.why: Both exposure (per-capita meat consumption) and outcome (colon cancer incidence) were measured at the level of whole countries, not individuals. A study whose unit of analysis is a population group is ecological, and its conclusions are open to the ecological fallacy.
notes: A case series describes individual patients who share a condition and has no comparison of exposure across populations.
A case-cohort study samples individuals from a defined cohort and compares cases with a subcohort. Here no individual-level data were collected.
A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome in individuals at one point in time. This study used aggregate country-level data.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: We selected a random sample among patients who come for flu vaccination during the annual campaign in a health center. It is recorded in selected patients if they are using lipid-lowering drugs and if they are diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, among other data. It is obtained that diabetes mellitus is more frequent among patients taking lipid-lowering drugs than among those who do not take them. Which of the following corresponds to the design of this study?
questions.why: A random sample of patients was assessed once, recording current lipid-lowering drug use and diabetes status at the same time, with no follow-up and no selection by outcome. That is a cross-sectional (prevalence) study, which shows association but not which came first.
notes: A case-control study selects participants by outcome (diabetes or no diabetes) and then looks back at exposure. Here the sample was random and not chosen by outcome.
A prospective cohort study follows people grouped by exposure over time to see who develops the outcome. Here both were recorded at a single point.
A randomised trial assigns the intervention. In this study drug use was only observed.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: Gustavo goes to the Emergency Department with skin lesions and general malaise of several days of evolution. It has psoriasiform lesions on the trunk with affectation of palms and plants. It also presents a nonsuppurative asymmetric joint inflammation and bilateral ocular redness as well as erosions in the glans. In the following anamnesis, Gustavo recognizes a risky sexual contact 20 days before. What is your diagnosis?
questions.why: Asymmetric oligoarthritis, conjunctivitis, circinate balanitis and psoriasiform palmoplantar lesions (keratoderma blennorrhagicum) after a sexual exposure 20 days earlier make up the classic picture of Reiter syndrome. This is now called reactive arthritis, usually triggered by Chlamydia.
notes: Acute HIV causes a mononucleosis-like illness with a maculopapular rash, but not this combination of conjunctivitis, balanitis, asymmetric arthritis and keratoderma.
Secondary syphilis also affects the palms and soles, but it usually appears 4 to 10 weeks after exposure and does not explain conjunctivitis with asymmetric oligoarthritis.
Erythema multiforme causes target lesions and mucosal erosions, often after HSV or drugs, but not psoriasiform palmoplantar plaques or inflammatory arthritis.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 84-year-old woman who came for loss of vision in the left eye of 4 days of evolution accompanied by metamorphopsias. The macula shows abundant hard exudates, two small deep hemorrhages and a localized detachment of the neurosensory retina. In the contralateral eye presents abundant soft drusen. Given this scenario, which of the following diagnoses do you think is most likely?
options: Macular Degeneration Associated with Age (DMAE) Exudative.
Obstruction of the central artery of the retina.
questions.why: An elderly woman has subacute vision loss with metamorphopsia, and the macula shows exudates, deep haemorrhages and neurosensory detachment, all signs of choroidal neovascularisation. Soft drusen in the other eye confirm the underlying AMD. Neovascular (wet) AMD is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections.
notes: Posterior vitreous detachment causes floaters and flashes, not metamorphopsia, macular exudates, haemorrhages or subretinal fluid.
Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless profound vision loss with a pale retina and a cherry-red spot, not exudates and neurosensory detachment.
NAION causes sudden vision loss with a swollen optic disc and altitudinal field loss. The macula is not affected and metamorphopsia does not occur.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: In a colon cancer screening program, a 52-year-old patient undergoes a colonoscopy. The entire colon is normal in appearance, except for the finding of a 2 cm pedicled sigmoid polyp that is removed with a diathermy loop. The anatomopathological result indicates that there is carcinoma "in situ" limited to the head of the polyp. He has a thoracoabdominal CT reported as normal. Indicate what would be the correct conduct to follow:
options: Segmental resection of the affected colon.
Local resection of the base of the polyp.
questions.why: Carcinoma in situ (Tis) confined to the head of a pedunculated polyp that has been completely removed carries almost no risk of lymph node spread. Polypectomy is therefore curative and only colonoscopic surveillance is needed.
notes: Segmental colectomy is for invasive cancer with high-risk features such as stalk or margin involvement, lymphovascular invasion or poor differentiation, none of which apply here.
Further local excision of the base is only needed if margins are involved or excision was incomplete, but here the in situ disease is confined to the head.
Oncological resection with lymphadenectomy is for invasive carcinoma with risk of nodal spread, but in situ disease cannot metastasise.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman presented with chronic watery diarrhea of ​​4 months evolution. In the endoscopy, the mucosa did not show relevant aspects. In particular, no ulcers or friable areas were observed. A transverse colon biopsy was performed. In the histopathological study, a thickened area was recognized below the surface coating epithelium, which was more evident by Masson's trichrome technique and involved epithelial atrophy and denudation. There was also a clear increase in the density of intraepithelial lymphocytes. Is the diagnosis of the intestinal lesion?
questions.why: Chronic watery diarrhoea with normal-looking mucosa points to microscopic colitis. A thickened subepithelial band that stains with Masson trichrome (collagen, over 10 µm), with surface epithelial damage and more intraepithelial lymphocytes, defines collagenous colitis.
notes: Ulcerative colitis would show continuous friable or ulcerated mucosa on endoscopy, with crypt distortion and crypt abscesses, not a subepithelial collagen band.
Pseudomembranous colitis shows yellow-white plaques on endoscopy and 'volcano' exudates of fibrin and neutrophils on histology, usually after antibiotics.
Fibrosing Crohn's causes transmural fibrosis with strictures and often ulcers or granulomas, not a thin subepithelial collagen layer under normal-looking mucosa.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man reported a history of 3 weeks of evolution with progressive, moderately painful skin lesions on his left arm. It had started as an erythematous lesion on his left thumb. It had reddish streaks visible as connecting lines between the lesions. The patient did not present fever or other general symptoms. He had been working in his garden but could not remember having any injuries. The etiological diagnosis was made by culture of a skin biopsy. What is the most likely causative agent of this process?
questions.why: A lesion that starts on a digit after gardening and then spreads as nodules up the arm along the lymphatics, with no fever, is sporotrichoid lymphocutaneous spread. Sporothrix schenckii from soil or plants is the classic cause, and it is confirmed by culture of a biopsy.
notes: Microsporum gypseum (a soil dermatophyte) causes a superficial annular, scaly tinea, not nodules spreading along lymphatics over weeks.
Staphylococcus aureus lymphangitis comes on acutely over hours to days, usually with fever and pus, not as a slow 3-week chain of nodules.
Mycobacterium marinum also spreads in a sporotrichoid pattern, but it follows fish tank or water exposure, not gardening.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman came to the hospital for 2 hours of oppressive chest pain. The blood pressure is 68/32 mm Hg, the heart rate is 124 beats / min, the respiratory rate is 32 breaths / min, the oxygen saturation is 91% with 50% oxygen. Pulmonary auscultation showed bilateral crepitations. An ECG is performed showing a subepicardial lesion on the anterior side, with a mirror image on the inferior face. The chest radiograph shows a bilateral alveolar pattern. What is your therapeutic decision?
questions.why: This is an anterior STEMI with cardiogenic shock (BP 68/32) and pulmonary oedema. Urgent primary PCI to restore blood flow is the treatment that improves survival in shock, and it is preferred over fibrinolysis.
notes: Nitrates are contraindicated with a systolic pressure this low because they worsen the hypotension.
Fibrinolysis works less well in cardiogenic shock and is only a fallback if timely PCI is not available.
Furosemide does not treat the cause, and it can worsen hypotension in shock; it is not the key decision here.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A young 18-year-old with a history of asthma, allergy to pollens, mites and cat hair, goes to urgency referring to sensation of food detention at retrosternal level with a practically inability to swallow his own saliva. Refer to similar episodes on other occasions that have spontaneously subsided in a few minutes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: A young atopic patient (asthma, multiple allergies) with repeated, self-resolving food bolus impactions fits eosinophilic esophagitis. It is the leading cause of food impaction in young adults, and the diagnosis needs biopsies showing at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field.
notes: Barrett's esophagus causes no symptoms of its own. It follows long-standing reflux in older patients and does not cause episodes of bolus impaction.
A Schatzki ring causes intermittent 'steakhouse' impaction, but usually in people over 40, and it has no link to atopy.
Infectious esophagitis causes painful swallowing in immunocompromised patients, not recurrent food impaction in an atopic young person.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man, diagnosed with liver cirrhosis and an active drinker, was admitted due to progressive abdominal distension with diffuse discomfort, of two weeks evolution. It does not refer fever or other symptoms. The exploration highlights changing dullness to abdominal percussion, with absence of edema. A diagnostic paracentesis is performed, finding a slightly cloudy liquid, with 2,300 cells / mL, of which 30% are lymphocytes, 60% polymorphonuclear and 10% red blood cells. What is the first therapeutic measure that would prompt this patient immediately?
options: Treatment with a third generation cephalosporin.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman came to the clinic with anxiety, loss of about 6 kg of weight and sensation of "nervousness" in the last three months. Physical examination revealed tachycardia, hyperreflexia and absence of goiter. In the analytical carried out, TSH values ​​are <0.01 microU / mL, T4 is elevated and thyroglobulin levels are lowered. When a scan is performed, an absence of uptake is detected in the thyroid region. What do you think is the most likely diagnosis ?:
questions.why: Thyrotoxicosis with suppressed TSH, no uptake on the scan and no goitre points to exogenous thyroxine. Low thyroglobulin is the decisive finding, because taking thyroxine suppresses the gland's own thyroglobulin output.
notes: Graves' disease shows diffuse high uptake on the scan and usually a goitre, with normal or raised thyroglobulin.
Struma ovarii shows little uptake in the neck but uptake in the pelvis, and thyroglobulin is raised because the ovarian tissue makes hormone.
Subacute thyroiditis has low uptake but a tender gland and a high ESR, and thyroglobulin is raised as follicles break down.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man consulted for intense polyuria and polydipsia and involuntary loss of 10 kg of weight and was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus by a plasma glycemia of 322 mg / dL and a glycosylated hemoglobin of 9.8%. Your doctor gives you dietary recommendations, the convenience of physical exercise, and starts treatment with metformin 850 mg / 12 hours and glimepiride 6 mg / day. In the following weeks the glycemic controls are progressively reduced. At 4 months the glycemia is 94 mg / dL and the HbA1c is 5.9%. The patient complains of frequent episodes of dizziness, epigastric pain, blurred vision, sweating and tremor, which improve eating something and that occur especially at the end of the morning and at the end of the afternoon. What modification would you propose in your treatment?
options: Check the distribution of carbohydrates in your diet.
Replace metformin with a DPP4 inhibitor.
questions.why: The episodes are hypoglycaemia (adrenergic and neuroglycopenic symptoms relieved by eating), and HbA1c 5.9% means he is over-treated. Sulfonylureas such as glimepiride release insulin whatever the glucose level and cause hypoglycaemia. Metformin does not, so the sulfonylurea is the drug to stop.
notes: Diet changes will not fix hypoglycaemia caused by a high-dose sulfonylurea when HbA1c is already 5.9%. The cause is the drug, not how carbohydrate is spread through the day.
Metformin on its own almost never causes hypoglycaemia and is the first-line drug to keep. Stopping it would remove the safest agent and leave the one causing the problem.
DPP-4 inhibitors and metformin carry little risk of hypoglycaemia, so this swap does nothing about the cause. Glimepiride would still be driving the episodes.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: We refer from ophthalmology to a 31-year-old man who consulted for vision loss and progressive headache. On physical examination, a temporal hemianopsia was observed and in pituitary magnetic resonance a tumor measuring 35 x 30 x 20 mm compressed the chiasm and cavernous sinus. The results of the functional study are cortisol 14 microg / dL, TSH 1.4 microU / mL, T4L 1.2 ng / dL, prolactin 480 microg / L (vn <15), testosterone 160 ng / dL (vn 300-1200) , FSH 1,2 U / L (vn 5-15) and LH 2 U / L (vn 3-15). What is the initial therapeutic approach ?:
options: Treatment of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with testosterone.
questions.why: Prolactin of 480 µg/L with a 35 mm adenoma is a macroprolactinoma. Dopamine agonists are first-line even when there is chiasmal compression and a visual field defect, because they usually shrink the tumour and restore vision quickly. Cabergoline is the preferred agent in Australia.
notes: Surgery is kept for resistance to or intolerance of dopamine agonists, apoplexy, or a non-prolactin-secreting tumour. Visual loss from a prolactinoma does not by itself call for surgery first.
Radiotherapy is a third-line option for tumours that resist both medical and surgical treatment. It acts slowly and causes hypopituitarism.
His hypogonadotropic hypogonadism comes from high prolactin suppressing GnRH. It often recovers once prolactin falls, so testosterone is not the first step.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic valve disease, who requires mitral valve replacement by a mechanical prosthesis. The initial postoperative evolution is favorable. However, after starting treatment with acenocoumarol develops a pattern of skin necrosis affecting the abdominal region and extremities. Which of the following alterations would justify this table?
questions.why: Skin necrosis that starts soon after a vitamin K antagonist is begun points to protein C deficiency. Protein C has a short half-life and falls before factors II and X, so a transient prothrombotic state causes microvascular thrombosis. In Australia warfarin, not acenocoumarol, is the usual vitamin K antagonist.
notes: Antithrombin deficiency causes venous thrombosis and heparin resistance, not necrosis triggered by starting a vitamin K antagonist, because antithrombin levels do not depend on vitamin K.
Factor V Leiden is the commonest inherited cause of venous thromboembolism, but it is not linked to necrosis after starting a coumarin, because it does not create the early protein C drop.
Hyperhomocysteinaemia raises arterial and venous thrombotic risk, but it has nothing to do with vitamin K and does not explain necrosis timed to coumarin initiation.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: One of the following pathogens transmitted by ticks can be confused with malaria, given the clinical characteristics with which it usually occurs, which includes fever and hemolysis, as well as its appearance in the microscopic study of blood smears stained with Giemsa. Which of the following corresponds to the pathogen described?
questions.why: Babesia is a tick-borne protozoan that infects red cells. It causes fever and haemolysis, and on Giemsa smear its ring forms (sometimes tetrads, the Maltese cross) look like Plasmodium falciparum. It is the tick-borne infection most easily mistaken for malaria.
notes: Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease, with erythema migrans, arthritis and neurological features. It does not cause haemolysis or intra-erythrocytic forms.
Francisella tularensis causes ulceroglandular or pneumonic tularaemia. It is not a red-cell parasite and does not look like malaria on a smear.
Rickettsia conorii causes Mediterranean spotted fever, with fever, rash and an eschar (tache noire). It lives in endothelial cells, not red cells.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: In a phase III study aimed at confirming the bacteriological efficacy of a new antibiotic for the treatment of patients with severe acute pyelonephritis, which of the following clinical trial designs do you consider most appropriate ?:
options: Parallel, randomized, double blind, controlled with another antibiotic.
Crossed, open, controlled with another antibiotic.
Crossed, randomized, double blind, placebo controlled.
questions.why: Severe acute pyelonephritis needs effective treatment, so a placebo control is unethical and the new drug must be compared with a standard antibiotic. Randomisation and double blinding cut bias. A parallel design suits an acute illness that is cured, because crossover is impossible.
notes: Giving placebo for severe pyelonephritis would be unethical. Open-label, unrandomised allocation would also introduce bias.
Crossover designs need a stable, chronic condition that returns to baseline between periods. An acute infection that is cured cannot be crossed over, and open-label adds bias.
This combines two problems: placebo in a serious infection is unethical, and a crossover design does not suit an acute illness that is cured.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: It is desired to know the degree of association that exists between the metabolic syndrome and the vitamin D deficit in the general population. To do this, a sample of a health center is selected from among patients older than 18 years of age, they are scheduled and at the visit a clinical examination is performed to determine if they meet the metabolic syndrome criteria and blood is drawn to measure the concentrations Serum levels of 25 hidoxivitamin D. What is the design of this study ?:
questions.why: Exposure (vitamin D level) and outcome (metabolic syndrome) are both measured once, at the same visit, in a sample of the population. That is a cross-sectional design. It estimates prevalence and association but cannot show which came first.
notes: A prospective cohort would follow people grouped by vitamin D status over time to see who develops metabolic syndrome, but here there is a single visit with no follow-up.
A case-control study would choose people by outcome (with and without metabolic syndrome) and then look back at exposure, whereas here unselected adults are sampled and both are measured together.
A case-crossover study compares a transient exposure just before an acute event with earlier control periods in the same person, so it does not fit a chronic condition measured once.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: Which of the following types of study would be the one of choice to study the association between the appearance of a very rare and delayed serious adverse reaction, and the consumption of a certain drug?
options: Clinical trial with the suspect medication.
questions.why: For a very rare outcome with a long latency, a case-control study is the design of choice. It starts from the people who already have the reaction and compares their past drug exposure with controls, which is efficient when there are few events.
notes: Clinical trials are too small and too short to detect a very rare, delayed adverse reaction, and deliberately exposing people to a suspected harm is unethical.
A prevalence study measures exposure and outcome at one point in time. It would capture too few cases of a rare event and cannot show which came first.
An ecological study uses group-level data, so it cannot link drug exposure to the reaction in individuals and is prone to the ecological fallacy.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: In a cohort study comparing a group of subjects with hypertension and a group of subjects with normal blood pressure, an annual incidence of acute myocardial infarction of 15 per thousand and 5 per thousand, respectively, is obtained. Assuming there are no biases or confounding factors, what would be the risk of acute myocardial infarction attributable to hypertension among hypertensive subjects ?:
questions.why: The risk attributable to exposure among the exposed is the risk difference: incidence in the exposed minus incidence in the unexposed. Here that is 15 − 5 = 10 per 1000 per year.
notes: 20 per 1000 comes from adding the two incidences together, which has no epidemiological meaning.
15 per 1000 is the total incidence in hypertensive people. It includes the baseline risk that is not due to hypertension.
3 is the relative risk (15/5). It is a ratio with no units, not an excess incidence per 1000 per year.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 72-year-old patient was seen in the ER one month earlier due to accidental fall and knee trauma. Check again for bilateral lumbar pain and dark urine for a week. BACKGROUND: HTA, non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, obesity and gonarthrosis. Continue treatment with enalapril / hydrochlorothiazide 20 / 12.5 mg / day, naproxen on demand, atorvastatin 20 mg / day and metformin 850 mg / day. In the emergency analysis, the following stand out: moderate microcytic anemia, uric acid 9.5 mg / dL; CPK 45 U / L; creatinine 1.9 mg / dL; urea 75 mg / dL; Na 138 mEq / L; K 5.6 mEq / L. In urine: microhematuria ++, proteinuria - and very abundant desquamative cells. No bacteria are observed. In the previous visit to the Emergency Room 1 month ago, all the parameters were normal. An urgent ultrasound is reported as possible bilateral papillary necrosis. What could be the current picture?
options: Acute renal failure due to enalapril.
questions.why: His tests were normal a month ago. Since the knee injury he has likely been taking more naproxen, and now he has kidney failure, hematuria without proteinuria, sloughed papillary cells and papillary necrosis on ultrasound. NSAIDs cause papillary necrosis, and risk is higher with diabetes, an ACE inhibitor plus a diuretic, and older age.
notes: He had been on enalapril long term with normal kidney function, and an ACE inhibitor alone would not cause papillary necrosis or shed papillary cells.
Diabetic nephropathy progresses over years with proteinuria, but here proteinuria is negative and kidney function was normal a month ago.
A CPK of 45 U/L is normal, which rules out rhabdomyolysis, and rhabdomyolysis would not cause papillary necrosis.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy goes to the neurologist, referring in the previous months to morning jolts in both arms without affecting the level of consciousness. In addition, their parents report episodes of disconnection with a fixed gaze and oral automatisms practically every day. In the previous days, he presented a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in a context of sleep deprivation and alcohol intake. There is a family history of a similar process. Which of the following processes would you suspect in the first place?
options: Epilepsy of the mesial temporal lobe.
questions.why: A teenager with morning jerks in both arms while fully conscious, daily absences and a tonic-clonic seizure after sleep loss and alcohol, plus a family history, has juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. This is a genetic generalised epilepsy, and these triggers are typical of it.
notes: Lennox-Gastaut starts in early childhood with tonic seizures, intellectual disability and slow spike-wave on EEG, none of which fits a 15-year-old with this history.
Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy causes focal seizures with automatisms but not morning myoclonic jerks in both arms, and it is not usually triggered by sleep loss in a family pattern.
Alcohol here is only a trigger: months of morning myoclonus and daily absences plus a family history point to an underlying epilepsy, not a drug effect.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman has been diagnosed by ultrasound with an intramural uterine myoma of 4 cm. Has two children. Her menstruations are of type 4-5 / 28-30, of a somewhat abundant amount, without clots and without pain. It does not have other symptoms. What would you recommend?
options: Treatment with Gn-RH analogues for 6 months.
questions.why: A 4 cm intramural fibroid in a woman with completed family, only mildly heavy periods and no other symptoms needs no treatment. Monitor it with a repeat ultrasound. Treatment is for fibroids causing significant symptoms, anaemia, infertility or rapid growth.
notes: Myomectomy is for symptomatic fibroids or fibroids affecting fertility, and this woman is basically asymptomatic and has completed her family.
Hysterectomy is major surgery and far too much for a small fibroid that is causing almost no symptoms.
GnRH analogues work only temporarily, cause menopausal side effects and are mainly used before surgery, so they have no role in an asymptomatic fibroid.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman who comes to the clinic for 5 days of abundant rules for 2 years. His last rule was 8 days ago. In the initial assessment and when performing a vaginal ultrasound, a rounded, well-defined, homogenous and hypoechoic formation of 25 mm is evidenced in the endometrial cavity. What would be the pattern to follow?
options: Establish treatment with oral estrogengestergens and clinical follow-up.
Establish treatment with tranexamic acid in menses and clinical follow-up.
questions.why: The ultrasound shows a 25 mm well-defined lesion inside the uterine cavity, most likely a submucosal fibroid or polyp, causing heavy periods. Hysteroscopy lets you see the lesion, biopsy it and remove it in the same procedure, so it is the standard approach for a focal lesion in the cavity.
notes: A blind endometrial aspirate can miss a focal lesion and does not treat it, and endometrial cancer risk is low at 31.
The combined pill may reduce bleeding but leaves a structural lesion undiagnosed and untreated.
Tranexamic acid only controls symptoms and does nothing to diagnose or remove the lesion causing the bleeding.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 32-week-old minor who goes to the emergency room for vaginal bleeding. Although she does not provide any report of control of her pregnancy, she refers the antecedent of a previous delivery by caesarean section. Upon speculum examination, red blood is seen through the external cervical os. The patient does not report abdominal pain. The cardiotocographic record confirms the absence of contractions and the normality of the fetal heart rate. The blood count is normal. What is the next step?
options: Finish the pregnancy through an emergency caesarean section.
Finish the pregnancy by inducing labor.
Perform an artificial rupture of membranes.
questions.why: Painless bright red bleeding at 32 weeks in a woman with a previous caesarean, with mother and fetus both stable, suggests placenta praevia. Locate the placenta by ultrasound first. Transvaginal ultrasound is safe and more accurate than transabdominal, whereas a digital exam is avoided.
notes: An emergency caesarean is only needed for heavy bleeding, maternal instability or fetal distress, and here mother and fetus are both stable.
Induction of labour is contraindicated if placenta praevia has not been excluded, and the baby is preterm at 32 weeks.
Artificial rupture of membranes is contraindicated with possible placenta praevia and is not appropriate in a stable preterm pregnancy.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 48 year old woman In a mammographic screening study, a group of suspicious microcalcifications was detected in the upper external quadrant of the right breast. Percutaneous biopsy assisted by vacuum in a prone table. The anatomopathological diagnosis is of G II intraductal carcinoma. You propose a surgical exeresis of the lesion with radiological marking (harpoon). The anatomopathological study of the surgical piece reports infiltrating ductal carcinoma of 6 mm (RE ++ 100%, RP ++ 100%, Ki-67 10%, Her-2 negative) associated with intraductal component. Free surgical edges. You report the result to the patient. What would you propose?
options: Selective biopsy of sentinel lymph node.
questions.why: The excision showed a 6 mm invasive ductal carcinoma, so the axilla now has to be staged. In a clinically node-negative axilla this is done by sentinel lymph node biopsy. Margins are clear, and adjuvant radiotherapy and endocrine therapy are planned once nodal status is known.
notes: Radiotherapy plus endocrine therapy will probably be needed after breast-conserving surgery, but the invasive disease has not been staged, so the axilla must be assessed first.
Mastectomy is not needed for a small, completely excised tumour, and axillary dissection is not done in a clinically node-negative axilla before a sentinel node result.
Chemotherapy is not indicated before staging, and this small luminal A–like tumour (strongly ER/PR positive, Ki-67 10%, HER2 negative) is unlikely to need it.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy attended consultation due to fatigability and progressive effort dyspnea. At birth, he had discovered a heart murmur, but he did not go for check-ups. On physical examination, the face and hands are pink, while the lower extremities are cyanotic. What anomaly would explain these findings?
options: Ventricular septal defect with pulmonary hypertension.
Persistent ductus arteriosus with Eisenmenger syndrome.
questions.why: Cyanosis in the legs but pink face and hands is differential cyanosis. It occurs when a patent ductus reverses (Eisenmenger) and sends deoxygenated blood into the aorta beyond the arm and head arteries. The long-standing murmur fits an untreated PDA.
notes: Tetralogy of Fallot causes cyanosis of the whole body, not just the lower limbs.
Eisenmenger from a VSD mixes blood inside the heart, so cyanosis affects the whole body equally.
Coarctation causes a blood pressure and pulse difference between arms and legs, not lower-limb cyanosis in a 9-year-old.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019
