questions.stem: A 2-month-old girl who was referred to the pediatric urology clinic due to grade-III bilateral vesicoureteral reflux. Background: prenatal diagnosis of bilateral pyelic ectasia. Acute pyelonephritis, one month after diagnostic cystourethrography. Of the following options, what would be the most advisable indication?
options: Do nothing; since the reflux can disappear spontaneously.
Request renal scintigraphy (DMSA) and perform a monthly urine culture.
Antibiotic prophylaxis with amoxicillin and request renal scintigraphy (DMSA).
questions.why: A young infant with bilateral grade III reflux who has had pyelonephritis is at risk of repeat infection and kidney scarring. Give continuous antibiotic prophylaxis and do a DMSA scan to look for scarring. Australian practice usually uses trimethoprim or cefalexin for prophylaxis.
notes: Reflux may resolve over time, but after pyelonephritis with bilateral grade III reflux, doing nothing risks repeat infection and scarring.
Endoscopic correction is not first line at 2 months and is kept for breakthrough infections despite prophylaxis or persistent high-grade reflux.
Routine monthly urine cultures without prophylaxis do not prevent repeat pyelonephritis and are not recommended in a child without symptoms.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 60-year-old diabetic patient. Hospital admission 2 weeks ago due to hyperosmolar decompensation. Consult the Emergency Department for pain and swelling in the right knee. Physical examination: Tº 37.2ºC, heart rate 100 beats / minute, respiratory rate 18 / minute, signs of arthritis in the referred joints. Analytical: blood count with 18,000 leukocytes / mm3, uric acid 8.11 mg / dL, creatinine 1.4 mg / dL. Synovial fluid: 20,000 leukocytes / mm3 with 85% polynuclear, no microcrystals are observed and the gram stain does not show germs. What would be the most correct attitude?
options: Practice intra-articular infiltration with triamcinolone of the affected joint.
Start outpatient treatment with amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid and assess the response in a week.
Indicate admission and immediate parenteral antibiotic treatment until the result of the culture.
Treatment with corticoids at low doses and allopurinol.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man consulted for the appearance of red and painful nodules in both lower limbs at the pretibial level of 2 weeks of evolution. In addition, the patient reports that for a few months and recurrently has oral ulcers and ulcers at the genital level. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Recurrent oral ulcers plus genital ulcers with erythema nodosum-like lesions point to Behçet syndrome. Recurrent oral aphthae are the essential criterion, and genital ulcers, skin lesions, eye and pathergy findings support it.
notes: Sarcoidosis causes erythema nodosum but not recurrent oral and genital ulceration.
Dermatomyositis presents with proximal weakness, heliotrope rash and Gottron papules, not mucosal ulcers or nodules.
SLE can cause oral ulcers, but recurrent genital ulcers with erythema nodosum are typical of Behçet, and lupus is far more common in women.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: Serves a 32-year-old man, computer specialist, who consults for lumbar pain and asymmetric gluteus, predominantly nocturnal, inflammation of the toes, negative rheumatoid factor and C-reactive protein higher than 20mg / dL. What is the most correct attitude?
options: By age and sex, it is likely that it is gout and would start treatment with allopurinol and colchicine.
I will ask about a family history of psoriasis and would request HLA-B27, it is likely to suffer from a type of spondyloarthritis.
The type of pain in the spine guides the diagnosis to a herniated disc. I refer the patient to Neurosurgery.
I would start treatment with methotrexate that is effective for spinal pain and inflammation of toes.
questions.why: A young man with inflammatory nocturnal low back and buttock pain, dactylitis ('sausage toes'), seronegativity and raised CRP has spondyloarthritis. Ask about psoriasis (psoriatic arthritis) and check HLA-B27.
notes: Gout does not cause inflammatory nocturnal back and buttock pain, and allopurinol is not started without a confirmed diagnosis or during acute inflammation.
Disc herniation gives mechanical pain that eases with rest, not nocturnal inflammatory pain with dactylitis and high CRP; surgical referral is not indicated.
Methotrexate does not work for axial disease; NSAIDs come first, then biologics for axial spondyloarthritis, and the diagnosis must be confirmed first.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient with a history of gout and chronic use of corticosteroids. He is brought to the emergency room due to inability to ambulate due to knee extension deficit. Radiology shows a low patellar height in relation to the contralateral knee. What is the diagnostic suspicion?
questions.why: Loss of active knee extension with a low-lying patella (patella baja) means quadriceps tendon rupture, because the patella is no longer pulled up. Gout and chronic steroids are classic risk factors in older patients.
notes: Osteonecrosis causes knee pain but leaves the extensor mechanism intact, so it does not cause patella baja or loss of extension.
Gouty arthritis gives a hot, swollen, painful joint but does not change patellar height or abolish active extension.
Patellar tendon rupture also abolishes extension, but the patella rides high (patella alta); it is more typical in younger patients.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 59-year-old man, active smoker, with a history of hypertension, dyslipidemia and alcoholism. It refers to progressive picture in the last 2 years of difficulty climbing stairs with weakness in lower and upper limbs that fluctuates during the day and improves slightly with sustained exercise. Occasionally he has presented episodes of diplopia. Lately persistent dry cough has been added. As part of the study an electromyogram is performed that shows incremental increases in muscle action potential in response to repetitive nerve stimulation. A chest CT scan shows subcarinal lymphadenopathy and a 3.1 cm nodule in the left lower lobe. These findings are consistent with primary pulmonary neoplasia. What is the diagnosis of the associated picture?
questions.why: Proximal weakness that improves with sustained exercise, increments on repetitive nerve stimulation, and a smoker's lung mass (likely small cell carcinoma) mean Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, caused by antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.
notes: Paraneoplastic neuropathy (e.g. anti-Hu sensory neuronopathy) causes sensory loss and does not produce an incremental response or improve with exercise.
Polymyositis causes fixed proximal weakness with raised CK; it does not fluctuate, cause diplopia or give an increment on repetitive stimulation.
Alcoholic myopathy does not fluctuate, improve with effort or show increments on repetitive stimulation.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A medicalized ambulance is mobilized to care for a young man who is traumatized by a traffic accident. On physical examination, right anisocoria with arreactive mydriatic pupil, coma with 4 points on the Glasgow coma scale (eye response 1, motor response 2, verbal response 1), blood pressure 180/100 mmHg, heart rate 56 beats per minute , respiratory rate 8 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry 90% breathing room air. What should be the first action of the out-of-hospital emergency team?
options: Channel a peripheral venous line and administer intravenous mannitol.
Endotracheal intubation with control of the cervical spine.
Oxygen therapy with ventimask-type mask and immediate transfer to a hospital with a neurosurgeon on duty.
questions.why: GCS 4 (8 or below), hypoventilation, hypoxaemia and signs of herniation (blown pupil, Cushing triad) mean the airway comes first. Secure it with endotracheal intubation while protecting the cervical spine, as in any major trauma.
notes: A laryngeal mask is a rescue airway; it does not give a definitive protected airway or allow controlled ventilation in severe TBI.
Mannitol may follow for herniation, but airway and breathing come first, and hypoxia and hypercapnia make intracranial hypertension worse.
A Venturi mask does not protect the airway or fix hypoventilation in a comatose patient breathing 8 times a minute.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man who consulted urgently for colicky pain located in the left iliac fossa, with some irradiation towards the scrotum. He has not had similar episodes. In the laboratory, serum creatinine is 0.9 mg / dL, leukocytes 6.700 / mm3 and the leukocyte formula is normal. In the urinary sediment there are 12-15 red blood cells / field and the pH of the urine is 6. He has no fever and his body mass index (BMI) is 25.5 kg / m2. Which imaging test is the most sensitive to make the diagnosis?
questions.why: Renal colic with microscopic haematuria is best confirmed by non-contrast helical CT, the most sensitive and specific test for stones of any composition, including radiolucent uric acid stones.
notes: A plain abdominal X-ray misses radiolucent stones (e.g. uric acid) and small or overlying stones, so its sensitivity is low.
Ultrasound avoids radiation and shows hydronephrosis, but it is poor for ureteric stones, so it is less sensitive than CT.
Intravenous urography is outdated, needs contrast, and has been replaced by non-contrast CT because it is less sensitive.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl who presented with asthenia, abdominal pain and gross hematuria with dark urine without voiding symptoms. He has been receiving treatment with amoxicillin for 3 days for acute pharyngotonsillitis. The family reports two similar previous self-limited episodes coinciding with gastroenteritis and otitis media respectively. What is your diagnosis of suspicion ?:
questions.why: Macroscopic haematuria at the same time as a mucosal infection (pharyngitis, gastroenteritis, otitis), recurring and self-limited, is typical of IgA nephropathy (synpharyngitic haematuria). Post-streptococcal GN has a 1 to 3 week latency and does not recur.
notes: Membranoproliferative GN usually presents with nephritic or nephrotic syndrome and persistently low complement, not recurrent self-limited haematuria with each infection.
X-linked Alport syndrome typically affects boys with persistent haematuria, sensorineural deafness and eye changes; the episodes are not tied to infection.
Post-infectious GN follows infection after a latent period of 1 to 3 weeks and does not usually recur; haematuria starting during the infection argues against it.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman, with no relevant medical history, presented six months ago with dyspnea of ​​effort that has progressively increased. At auscultation showed basal crackles. The chest radiograph showed bilateral basal densities. Open lung biopsy was performed. In the histopathological study, a complex, heterogeneous lesion was observed, with altered areas that alternated with others preserved, with fibrosis of the alveolar septa and development of marked fibroblastic foci and pneumocytic type 2 hyperplasia. The affectation was fundamentally subpleural. Is the diagnosis of the lung injury?
questions.why: Patchy, heterogeneous involvement with fibrotic areas alternating with preserved lung, prominent fibroblastic foci and a subpleural, basal predominance is the textbook histological pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia. Temporal and spatial heterogeneity with fibroblastic foci is the key point to remember.
notes: Langerhans cell histiocytosis affects young smokers, favours the upper lobes, and shows peribronchiolar stellate nodules with Langerhans cells, not basal subpleural fibrosis with fibroblastic foci.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis) shows bronchiolocentric lymphocytic inflammation with poorly formed granulomas, often worst in the upper and mid zones, and needs an antigen exposure, which this stem does not mention.
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis fills the alveoli with PAS-positive lipoproteinaceous material while the architecture stays preserved; it does not cause septal fibrosis or fibroblastic foci.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: There is a genetic polymorphism of the enzyme thiopurine methyltransferase that is associated with a high risk of severe hematological toxicity when one of the following drugs is administered to homozygous individuals. What is the drug?
questions.why: Thiopurine methyltransferase inactivates azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine. Homozygous-deficient patients build up toxic thioguanine nucleotides and develop severe myelosuppression. TPMT activity or genotype is checked before starting a thiopurine.
notes: Warfarin sensitivity is linked to CYP2C9 and VKORC1 polymorphisms, not TPMT, and the main risk is bleeding rather than marrow toxicity.
Isoniazid toxicity is linked to slow N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) acetylator status and causes neuropathy and hepatotoxicity, not TPMT-related cytopenias.
Prolonged apnoea after succinylcholine comes from pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) deficiency, not TPMT.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: When does the coronary blood flow of the left ventricle reach its maximum value?
options: At the beginning of isovolumetric systole.
When the aortic pressure is maximum.
When the aortic blood flow is maximum.
questions.why: In systole the contracting left ventricular wall compresses the intramyocardial vessels, so left coronary flow is mostly diastolic. Flow peaks in early diastole, when the myocardium relaxes and aortic pressure is still high.
notes: In isovolumetric contraction, wall tension rises sharply and squeezes the intramural vessels, so left coronary flow falls to its lowest point and may even reverse briefly.
Aortic pressure peaks in mid-systole, when myocardial compression is limiting flow, so the high driving pressure does not produce maximal left coronary flow.
Aortic flow peaks during early ejection, while the ventricle is contracting and restricting its own coronary perfusion.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: 80 year old patient from a nursing home. Presents sepsis of urinary origin that does not respond to empiric treatment with ceftriaxone. In the blood cultures and urocultures, E. coli resistant to cephalosporins grows. The laboratory informs us that it is a strain that produces beta-lactamases with an extended spectrum. Which antibiotic, among the following, should be used?
questions.why: Carbapenems are the treatment of choice for serious infections such as bacteraemia caused by ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, which the MERINO trial supported. Ertapenem is suitable for a stable patient, and in Australia meropenem is often preferred if the patient is critically ill.
notes: ESBL enzymes are poorly reliably inhibited by clavulanate in serious infections, and amoxicillin-clavulanate is not adequate for ESBL bacteraemia.
Piperacillin-tazobactam was inferior to meropenem for ESBL E. coli bloodstream infection in the MERINO trial, so it is not the best choice for sepsis.
ESBL strains often carry fluoroquinolone resistance too, so ciprofloxacin is unreliable as empirical treatment for sepsis before susceptibility results are known.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with no history of interest is diagnosed with high blood pressure a year ago. He continues treatment with amlodipine 10 mg (1-0-0) and losartan / hydrochlorothiazide 100/25 mg (1-0-0), and performs a low sodium diet, with good adherence. Despite this, it has figures of PA 168/92 mmHg. What is the next step to make?
options: Increase the dose of any of the ones you are taking.
Conduct a study to rule out secondary arterial hypertension.
questions.why: BP stays high despite full doses of three drugs, one of them a diuretic, and good adherence. The first step is ambulatory BP monitoring to rule out pseudo-resistance (white-coat effect) before confirming true resistant hypertension. Australian guidance agrees.
notes: Adding a fourth drug such as spironolactone is right for true resistant hypertension, but this must be confirmed with out-of-office readings first.
All three drugs are already at full dose (amlodipine 10 mg, losartan 100 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg), so increasing a dose is not possible or useful.
Testing for secondary causes is done once resistant hypertension is confirmed, and ABPM comes first to exclude white-coat hypertension.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient, with a 15-year history of ulcerative colitis, presented in a control colonoscopy a rectal cancer eight cm from the anal margin and moderate activity of his colitis, especially on the left side of the colon. It is staged as T2N0M0 after performing image tests. What is the correct intervention for your treatment?
options: Pantoctocolectomy with ileoanal reservoir and protection ileostomy.
Anterior resection of rectum with protective lateral ileostomy.
External radiotherapy, and if there is good response, do a local surgery and maintain medical treatment of your inflammatory bowel disease.
questions.why: Cancer arising in long-standing ulcerative colitis, with colitis still active, means the whole colonic mucosa is at risk of further cancers. Restorative proctocolectomy with an ileal pouch and a defunctioning ileostomy treats the cancer and the disease together. Low-risk T2N0 disease does not need neoadjuvant therapy.
notes: Anterior resection would leave diseased, actively inflamed colon at high risk of synchronous or metachronous cancer, so it suits only sporadic rectal cancer.
A tumour 8 cm from the anal verge allows sphincter preservation, and abdominoperineal resection still leaves the colitic colon in place.
Organ-preserving radiotherapy with local excision is not appropriate in UC, where the remaining mucosa keeps its cancer risk, and pelvic radiation harms a later pouch.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation who was followed in the endocrinology clinic by a multinodular goiter (BMN) with multiple nodules in both lobes between 2.5 and 3 cm, none with malignancy characteristics in the imaging tests. . In the last review for 6 months refers to dysphagia for solids. In the analytical one it presents a TSH of 0.001 uU / mL (0.47-4.68) and T4-free of 1.62 ng / mL (0.78-2.19). On follow-up ultrasound, a large BMN with intrathoracic component and multiple nodules is described, one of which presents an increase in size from 3 to 4.4 cm with respect to the previous control of a year ago. Aspiration aspiration of said nodule is requested, being the result of cytology compatible with colloid goitre (benign cytology). What is the most correct attitude to follow?
options: Annual follow-up with thyroid ultrasound and thyroid function analytics.
questions.why: This is a large multinodular goitre with a retrosternal part, compressive dysphagia, subclinical hyperthyroidism (suppressed TSH, normal free T4) and a growing nodule. Total thyroidectomy relieves compression, cures the hyperthyroidism and removes the risk of a false-negative biopsy. Compressive or intrathoracic goitre is a surgical problem.
notes: Watching is not enough once there are compressive symptoms, intrathoracic extension, a growing nodule and suppressed TSH in a patient with atrial fibrillation.
Radioiodine shrinks a large multinodular goitre only partly and slowly, and can cause swelling in an already compressive retrosternal goitre, so it is for patients unfit for surgery.
Antithyroid drugs would control the subclinical hyperthyroidism but do nothing for the size of the goitre or the dysphagia, and toxic nodular goitre relapses when they stop.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man referred from the digestive consultation. He is diagnosed with hypergastrinemia secondary to pancreatic islet cell tumor and has detected a calcium level of 12.3 mg / dL (normal 8.5-10.5). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: A young patient with a gastrin-secreting pancreatic islet tumour (gastrinoma) and hypercalcaemia from primary hyperparathyroidism fits MEN1 (the three Ps: parathyroid, pancreas, pituitary). The MEN1 gene encodes menin.
notes: McCune-Albright syndrome combines polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait macules and precocious puberty from a GNAS mutation, not gastrinoma with hyperparathyroidism.
Carney complex involves cardiac myxomas, spotty skin pigmentation and primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, not pancreatic gastrinoma.
Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 causes hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcaemia), mucocutaneous candidiasis and Addison disease, which is the opposite of this picture.
questions.credit: HEAD-QA (Vilares and Gómez-Rodríguez, ACL 2019): Spanish MIR exam question, Ministerio de Sanidad, as translated by the dataset's authors; documents last updated 14 January 2019

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of itchy, watery eyes for the past week. He has also been sneezing multiple times a day during this period. He had a similar episode 1 year ago around springtime. He has iron deficiency anemia and ankylosing spondylitis. Current medications include ferrous sulfate, artificial tear drops, and indomethacin. He works as an elementary school teacher. His vital signs are within normal limits. Visual acuity is 20/20 without correction. Physical examination shows bilateral conjunctival injection with watery discharge. The pupils are 3 mm, equal, and reactive to light. Examination of the anterior chamber of the eye is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Itchy, watery eyes with sneezing that recur each spring, and normal acuity, pupils and anterior chamber, point to seasonal allergic conjunctivitis. First-line treatment is a topical antihistamine/mast cell stabiliser such as ketotifen.
notes: Erythromycin ointment treats bacterial conjunctivitis, which gives purulent discharge rather than itch, watery discharge and sneezing.
Warm compresses are for blepharitis, chalazion or meibomian gland dysfunction. Cool compresses may ease allergic symptoms, but they do not treat the allergy.
A topical corticosteroid can raise intraocular pressure and cause cataract. It is kept for severe allergic eye disease that does not respond to first-line drugs, under ophthalmology care.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of acute chest pain. He has hypertension and asthma. Current medications include atorvastatin, lisinopril, and an albuterol inhaler. He appears pale and diaphoretic. His pulse is 114/min and blood pressure is 130/88 mm Hg. An ECG shows ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, and aVF. Laboratory studies show an increased serum troponin T concentration. The patient is treated for acute coronary syndrome and undergoes percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty. At the time of discharge, echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 58%. In addition to aspirin, which of the following drugs should be added to this patient's medication regimen?
questions.why: After acute coronary syndrome treated with PCI, the patient needs dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, usually for 12 months. In Australian ACS guidelines, ticagrelor or prasugrel is generally preferred over clopidogrel unless bleeding risk or contraindications apply.
notes: Short-acting dihydropyridines such as nifedipine cause reflex tachycardia and are linked to worse outcomes after ACS. They play no part in secondary prevention here.
Enoxaparin is used acutely around the ACS and PCI. It is not continued as a discharge medication.
Spironolactone is indicated after MI when LVEF is 40% or less with heart failure or diabetes. This patient's EF of 58% is preserved.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of tingling pain in the sole of his right foot when he raises it above chest level during exercises. He reports that he started exercising regularly 2 months ago and that his right calf cramps when he uses the incline feature on the treadmill, forcing him to take frequent breaks. The pain completely disappears after resting for a few minutes. He has an 8-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 34 years. His only medication is metformin. His pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 170/92 mm Hg. Straight leg raise test elicits pallor and tingling pain in the right foot. There is no pain in the back. His muscle strength is normal. Femoral pulses are palpable; right pedal pulses are absent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute thrombosis of right popliteal vein
questions.why: Calf claudication with palpable femoral pulses but absent pedal pulses places the stenosis below the femoral artery and above the calf, in the femoropopliteal segment. Pallor and pain on raising the leg (positive Buerger elevation sign) confirm arterial insufficiency in a smoker with diabetes.
notes: Popliteal vein thrombosis causes constant calf swelling and pain. It does not cause exertional cramping that settles with rest, pallor on elevation, or absent pulses.
Lumbar spinal stenosis causes back and leg pain that comes on with standing and eases with flexion, and pulses are normal. Here there is no back pain and pedal pulses are absent.
Aortoiliac disease causes buttock and thigh claudication, weak femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction (Leriche syndrome). This patient's femoral pulses are palpable.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents to his physician with progressive fatigue and new onset muscle cramps. He has had no recent changes to his medication regimen, which includes hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, and amlodipine. His temperature is 98.0°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 174/111 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, respirations are 12/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The patient's cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams are unremarkable. Laboratory values are ordered as seen below. Serum: Na+: 138 mEq/L Cl-: 100 mEq/L K+: 3.3 mEq/L HCO3-: 33 mEq/L BUN: 20 mg/dL Glucose: 129 mg/dL What is the most likely underlying etiology of this patient's hypertension?
questions.why: Hypertension resistant to three drugs, together with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis (HCO3 33) despite an ACE inhibitor that should raise potassium, points to primary hyperaldosteronism. Screen with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio.
notes: A phaeochromocytoma causes episodic headache, sweating and palpitations with labile blood pressure, not hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis as the main finding; his pulse is 70.
Cortisol excess can cause hypokalaemia and hypertension, but there are no Cushingoid features, and glucose of 129 alone does not suggest it.
Renal artery stenosis causes secondary hyperaldosteronism, but he has no bruit, no flash pulmonary oedema and a normal BUN; primary aldosteronism is the more common cause of this picture.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old male newborn is brought to the hospital because of poor weight gain since birth. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation via normal vaginal delivery. He weighed 3005 g (6 lb, 10 oz) at birth and currently weighs 2835 g (6 lb, 4 oz). He has been latching on and breastfeeding well since birth. His mother has a history of Graves' disease and underwent near-total thyroidectomy in the second trimester of her pregnancy after her symptoms could not be controlled with antithyroid drugs. She is currently receiving L-thyroxine therapy. The patient's temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 176/min, and respirations are 42/min. He appears irritable. Examination shows a diaphoretic infant with a paucity of subcutaneous fat. There is swelling of the neck at the midline. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Transplacental passage of thyroid peroxidase antibodies
Transplacental passage of TSH receptor antibodies
questions.why: Fever, tachycardia, irritability, sweating, poor weight gain and a goitre point to neonatal thyrotoxicosis. Maternal TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies cross the placenta and stay in her circulation after thyroidectomy, even though she now needs thyroxine.
notes: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies do not stimulate the thyroid. They do not cause neonatal hyperthyroidism or goitre.
Congenital viral infection gives TORCH features such as rash, hepatosplenomegaly or microcephaly. It does not cause a hyperthyroid picture with goitre.
Neonatal opioid withdrawal causes irritability and sweating, usually starting within the first few days. It does not cause a goitre, and nothing in the history suggests maternal opioid use.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man comes to the physician because of pruritus and a hypopigmented rash on his upper body for 5 days. He first noticed the symptoms after returning from a business trip last week in the Bahamas. While he was there, he visited a couple of beaches and went hiking with some coworkers. The rash initially started as a single lesion on his upper back but since then has extended to his shoulders. He has a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus controlled with an insulin pump. He works as an office manager and has no known exposure to melanocytotoxic chemicals. He has been sexually active with three female partners over the past year and uses condoms inconsistently. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 80 kg (176 lb); BMI is 23.9 kg/m2. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. A photograph of the rash is shown. One month ago, his hemoglobin A1C was 7.8%. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.why: An itchy, hypopigmented rash on the upper trunk after heat, humidity and sweating is pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia). KOH preparation confirms it by showing short hyphae and yeast cells, the 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance.
notes: Wood lamp may show yellow-green fluorescence, which supports the diagnosis, but it is often negative and is not confirmatory.
Malassezia is lipophilic and needs special media to grow. Culture is not used to diagnose pityriasis versicolor.
Skin biopsy is invasive and unnecessary when a bedside KOH scraping makes the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 62-year old female comes to the physician because of vaginal spotting and urinary urgency for the past 4 days. She has had no fever, abdominal pain, or diarrhea. Menopause occurred at 52 years of age. Her last Pap smear 1 year ago was normal. She has hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and diabetes. Medications include atorvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide, metformin, and aspirin. She is sexually active with her husband. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 95/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 155/65 mm Hg. Pelvic exam demonstrates a 4 x 3 cm firm, immobile erythematous mass on the right inner vaginal wall. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: A firm, fixed vaginal wall mass with postmenopausal bleeding must be treated as possible vaginal cancer. A visible lesion needs tissue diagnosis by biopsy.
notes: Cytology is a screening test and is not used to assess a visible mass. In Australia the Pap smear has also been replaced by HPV-based cervical screening.
Incision and drainage suits a fluctuant, tender abscess or cyst. A firm, immobile mass in a postmenopausal woman needs malignancy excluded first.
Gonorrhoea and chlamydia testing does not explain a firm fixed mass. The urgency is more likely from mass effect on the urethra or bladder.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has been unable to conceive for 3 years. Analysis of her husband's semen has shown normal sperm counts during this time. The patient also reports episodic pelvic and back pain accompanied by painful diarrhea for 5 years. She has about one such episode on average per month for 4–6 days. She has taken ibuprofen for the pain, which has provided some relief. Menses have occurred at regular 29-day intervals since menarche at the age of 14 years and last for 7 days. She is sexually active with her husband and does not use contraception. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic and bimanual examinations are normal; rectal examination is unremarkable. A hysterosalpingogram 6 months prior showed normal results. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's symptoms?
options: Loss of fallopian tube function following infection
Smooth muscle tumor arising from the myometrium
Endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity
Increased secretion of androgens and luteinizing hormone
questions.why: Infertility, recurrent pelvic pain and painful bowel movements around menstruation (dyschezia), with a partner of normal fertility and a normal HSG, suggest endometriosis: endometrial tissue outside the uterus. A normal pelvic examination does not exclude it, and laparoscopy confirms it.
notes: Tubal damage after infection would usually show on the hysterosalpingogram, which was normal, and would not explain cyclic dyschezia.
Fibroids cause heavy menstrual bleeding and an enlarged, irregular uterus on bimanual examination; her examination was normal.
Raised androgens and LH (PCOS) cause irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism, but her cycles are regular at 29 days and there is no hirsutism or acne.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after being involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which she was a restrained passenger. On arrival, she is lethargic and incoherent. She has severe facial lacerations and is in respiratory distress. Her pulse is 130/min, respirations are 29/min, and blood pressure is 90/58 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 70%. Examination shows multiple facial lacerations. There is dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds over the left lung base. Abdominal examination shows diffuse tenderness with no guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds are normal. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Her hemoglobin concentration is 12.1 g/dL. An x-ray of the chest shows a fractured left second rib, depression of the left mainstem bronchus, deviation of the nasogastric tube to the right, and a widened mediastinum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: A high-speed deceleration injury plus a widened mediastinum, NG tube pushed to the right, a depressed left mainstem bronchus and an upper rib fracture is the classic x-ray picture of traumatic aortic rupture. Blood around the rupture causes the left haemothorax and hypotension. Confirm with CT angiography.
notes: Diaphragmatic rupture shows bowel or the NG tube in the left chest and a raised or blurred hemidiaphragm, not a widened mediastinum with the bronchus pushed down.
Bronchial rupture causes pneumothorax with a persistent air leak, pneumomediastinum and the fallen lung sign; it does not explain a widened mediastinum or the NG tube shifted right.
Tension pneumothorax gives hyperresonance and a mediastinal shift away from the affected side, not dullness at the base; it is treated on clinical signs without waiting for an x-ray.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with severe knee, hip, and groin pain. The patient has a past medical history notable only for obesity and asthma. His temperature is 98°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 124/65 mmHg, pulse is 128/min, respirations are 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical exam is notable for an inability of the patient to bear weight on his left leg and limited range of motion of the left hip. Which of the following is the best management for this patient?
options: Immobilization of the hip in a Pavlik harness
Surgical pinning of the femoral head
questions.why: An obese adolescent with hip, groin or knee pain, limited hip movement and inability to bear weight has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis until proven otherwise. An unstable slip needs urgent surgical in situ screw fixation of the epiphysis, with no weight bearing beforehand, to prevent further slip and avascular necrosis.
notes: Casting and crutches do not stabilise the physis, and the slip can progress, so this is not definitive treatment for SCFE.
A Pavlik harness treats developmental dysplasia of the hip in infants under about 6 months, not an adolescent with a slipped epiphysis.
Observation suits transient synovitis or early Legg-Calve-Perthes disease; leaving SCFE untreated risks further slip and avascular necrosis.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to a pediatrician by his parents for evaluation of frequent bed wetting during the night. A detailed history reveals that there has been no history of urinary incontinence during the day since the boy was 4 years of age, but that he has never been dry at night continuously for 1 week. There is no history of urinary tract infections, urgency, frequency, or hesitancy. On physical examination, the boy’s vital signs are stable. His neurologic and abdominal examinations are completely normal. His laboratory investigations are as follows: Urine-specific gravity (first-morning sample) 1.035 Urine red blood cells Absent Urine pus cells Absent Urine culture Negative Which of the following is the next step in the management of this patient?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine
Reassuring the parents and use of an enuresis alarm
questions.why: This is primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis: dry by day, never dry at night, normal examination, normal urinalysis and culture, and well-concentrated morning urine. Management starts with reassurance and an enuresis alarm, which has the best long-term cure rate. Desmopressin is the other first-line option.
notes: Spinal MRI is for suspected occult spinal dysraphism, such as abnormal neurological signs, daytime symptoms or a sacral skin lesion, and none of these is present.
Oxybutynin is for overactive bladder with daytime urgency or frequency; it is not first-line for monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis.
Imipramine works but is third-line because of cardiotoxicity and danger in overdose, so it is kept for cases where alarm and desmopressin have failed.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl comes to the physician with her father for evaluation of her short stature. She feels well overall, but is concerned because all of her friends are taller than her. Her birth weight was normal. Her father reports he had a short stature during his teenage years; he is currently 177 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall. She is at the 2ndpercentile for height and 35th percentile for weight. Breast development is Tanner stage 2. Pubic and axillary hair is absent. An x-ray of the left hand and wrist shows a bone age of 11 years. Which of the following is the most appropriate next best step in management?
questions.why: Delayed bone age (11 years at age 14), puberty that has begun (Tanner 2 breasts), normal birth weight and a father who was short as a teenager all point to constitutional delay of growth and puberty. Reassurance and follow-up is the right step.
notes: A pelvic ultrasound would be used for primary amenorrhoea or suspected gonadal dysgenesis, but she has begun puberty and has no Turner features.
DHEA is measured for premature adrenarche or androgen excess, which does not fit delayed growth with absent pubic hair in a constitutionally delayed girl.
Brain MRI is for suspected pituitary or hypothalamic disease, such as headaches, visual field loss or stalled puberty, and none of these is present.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with dry cough, shortness of breath, and low-grade fever that began 6 days ago. He also reports that he has had 3 episodes of watery diarrhea per day for the last 2 days. He appears slightly pale. His temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 65/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 140/78 mm Hg. Diffuse crackles are heard over bibasilar lung fields. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL Leukocyte count 16,000/mm3 Platelet count 150,000/mm3 Serum Na+ 131 mEq/L Cl- 102 mEq/L K+ 4.7 mEq/L HCO3- 26 mEq/L Urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL An x-ray of the chest shows patchy infiltrates in both lungs. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?"
questions.why: Atypical pneumonia with diarrhoea, hyponatraemia and relative bradycardia for the fever suggests Legionella. It needs a respiratory fluoroquinolone or a macrolide. In Australia, guidelines prefer IV azithromycin for suspected Legionella, with ciprofloxacin or moxifloxacin as alternatives.
notes: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole is first-line for Pneumocystis pneumonia, which needs an immunocompromised host; it is not reliable against Legionella.
Amoxicillin covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, but beta-lactams do not reach intracellular organisms such as Legionella.
Rifampin is not used alone because resistance develops quickly; at most it is an add-on in severe Legionella, never monotherapy.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a generalized rash for 3 days. During this period, he has had severe itching and was not able to sleep well. He has also had fever, headache, and some muscle pain. Five days ago, he had a runny nose which subsided with over-the-counter medications. He returned from a camping trip 1 week ago. He attends a daycare center. The patient is at the 55th percentile for height and at the 50th percentile for weight. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.7°F), pulse is 97/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Examination of the skin shows several macules, papules, and crusted lesions over his face, trunk, and extremities. There are a few fluid-filled vesicles over his abdomen and back. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: An itchy generalised rash with lesions at different stages at once (macules, papules, vesicles and crusts) on the face, trunk and limbs, after a mild prodrome in a child at daycare, is varicella.
notes: Measles gives a non-itchy maculopapular rash spreading from the head down, with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots, not vesicles and crusts.
Poison ivy (urushiol) dermatitis forms linear vesicles on exposed skin where the plant touched; it does not cause fever, headache, myalgia or a truncal rash.
Rubella causes a mild pink maculopapular rash spreading from the face down, with postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy, not vesicles; there is no lymphadenopathy here.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with fever, weakness, and decreased responsiveness. He is diagnosed with urosepsis based on urinalysis and culture and started on ceftriaxone and intravenous fluids. By hospital day 3, he is clinically improving. During the evening, the patient becomes irritable. He is talking to someone despite nobody being present in the room. He is easily agitated and attempts to strike a nurse with a remote control to his TV. Subsequently, the patient keeps getting out of bed and trying to walk away despite being a fall risk. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: Acute fluctuating confusion with hallucinations in an older inpatient with sepsis is delirium. Treat the cause and use non-drug measures first. When agitation endangers the patient or staff, a low-dose antipsychotic is preferred; in Australia, haloperidol or risperidone are often used.
notes: Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and can cause or worsen delirium in older people (Beers criteria).
Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam worsen delirium and increase falls in older people; they are kept for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
Physical restraints increase agitation, injury and delirium; they are a last resort, not the next step when safer drug options exist.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man is brought to the physician by his daughter because of increasing forgetfulness over the past 5 weeks. He had been living independently but came to live with his daughter temporarily after he complained that he was unable to perform some of his daily activities. He has left the front door wide open and tap water running on multiple occasions. He does not sleep well and wakes up 6–7 times during the night. He does not leave his room and rarely makes conversation with his daughter. He says that he used to enjoy playing the piano but has not played for several months. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine. Vital signs are within normal limits. Mental status examination shows orientation to person, place, and time and psychomotor retardation. He has a blunted affect. Short- and long-term memory is impaired. Attention and concentration are impaired. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Serum concentration of electrolytes, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and vitamin B12 are within the reference range. He is very concerned about his memory lapses. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.why: Subacute memory and concentration problems with anhedonia, poor sleep, withdrawal, psychomotor slowing and blunted affect, in a patient worried about his own memory, suggest pseudodementia (depression). The deficits improve once the depression is treated, so an SSRI is appropriate.
notes: Aspirin is for vascular disease, but vascular dementia would usually show stepwise decline and focal neurological signs, which are absent here.
A VP shunt treats normal pressure hydrocephalus, which presents with gait disturbance and urinary incontinence alongside dementia, and neither is described.
Memantine is for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease, which develops over years with little insight, not over 5 weeks with prominent depressive symptoms.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 18-month-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents for evaluation of an abdominal mass noticed a few days ago. He appears markedly pale and lethargic. Examination shows a 6-cm, nonmobile mass in the left upper quadrant that crosses the midline. 24-hour urine collection shows elevated homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid. Further evaluation including biopsy confirms the diagnosis of intermediate-risk neuroblastoma. The physician recommends the established standard treatment, which is initiation of neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgical resection, if possible. After a thorough discussion of the risks and benefits of chemotherapy, the likelihood of unresectability without neoadjuvant treatment, and the prognosis without it, the patient's parents steadily refuse chemotherapy because they do not want their son to suffer the side effects. They prefer to take their son home for supportive care only. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the physician?
options: Help the parents to arrange supportive care at home
Refer the patient to another oncologist
Recommend for parents to take 2 weeks to think about decision
Seek a court order for neoadjuvant chemotherapy
questions.why: Intermediate-risk neuroblastoma has a good chance of cure with standard treatment, and refusing it puts the child at serious risk. Parents cannot refuse life-saving treatment for a minor, so the physician should seek a court order. In Australia, this means a Supreme Court (parens patriae) or child protection application.
notes: Arranging home supportive care would accept a refusal that leaves the child with a likely fatal but treatable cancer, so it fails the physician's duty to the child.
Another oncologist would recommend the same standard treatment, so referral delays care without changing anything.
The parents have already refused after a full discussion, and a 2-week delay in a growing malignancy risks making the tumour unresectable.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old college student presents to the clinic with a history of intermittent chest discomfort. He reports that, about once per month for the past 8 or 9 months, he's had episodes of "feeling like my chest is going to explode." During these episodes, he also feels shortness of breath, feels shakiness throughout his arms and legs, and sweats so heavily that he needs to change his shirt. He is unsure of any clear precipitating factors but thinks they may occur more often around important exams or when big school projects are due. He shares that, as these episodes continue to recur, he has had mounting anxiety about having one when he is in class or at a restaurant. As a result, he is leaving the house less and less. He has no past medical history; the physical exam is unremarkable. Which of the following is the best medication for the long-term management of this patient's condition?
questions.why: He has recurrent unexpected panic attacks, worry about having more, and avoidance of public places. This is panic disorder with agoraphobia. An SSRI such as citalopram is the first-line long-term medication, usually combined with CBT, which matches Australian guidance.
notes: Lithium is a mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder and has no role in panic disorder.
Propranolol can blunt the physical symptoms of performance anxiety, but it does not prevent panic attacks or treat agoraphobic avoidance over the long term.
Quetiapine is an antipsychotic with metabolic side effects and is not a recommended long-term treatment for panic disorder.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old primigravid woman at 12 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of vaginal bleeding and dull suprapubic pain for 3 hours. She has had spotting during the last 3 days. Her medications include folic acid and a multivitamin. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 89/65 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a dilated cervical os and a uterus consistent in size with an 11-week gestation. Ultrasonography shows an embryo of 4 cm in crown-rump length and no fetal cardiac activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: A dilated os with a nonviable embryo means an inevitable or incomplete miscarriage. Her tachycardia and hypotension show haemodynamic instability. An unstable patient needs urgent surgical evacuation of the uterus (D&C, called suction curettage in Australia), not medical or expectant management.
notes: Misoprostol is an option for a stable patient with miscarriage, but it works slowly and unpredictably and is not suitable when she is hypotensive and bleeding.
Methotrexate treats a stable ectopic pregnancy, but this is an intrauterine embryo with a dilated os.
Bed rest does not prevent or treat miscarriage, and it does nothing for a nonviable pregnancy with haemodynamic compromise.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician because of episodic pelvic pain radiating to her back and thighs for 4 months. The pain occurs a few hours before her menstrual period and lasts for 2 days. She has been taking ibuprofen, which has provided some relief. Menses have occurred at regular 28-day intervals since menarche at the age of 12 years and last for 5 to 6 days. She is sexually active with two male partners and uses condoms inconsistently. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
options: Endometrial sloughing and uterine contractions mediated by prostaglandin
Ascending infection of the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, or surrounding tissue
Hormone-sensitive smooth muscle tumor of the myometrium
questions.why: Her pain starts with menses in a regular cycle a few years after menarche, the exam is normal, and NSAIDs help. This is primary dysmenorrhoea, caused by prostaglandin-driven uterine contractions and ischaemia during endometrial shedding.
notes: PID would cause fever, cervical motion tenderness or discharge and pain not tied to the cycle, and her exam is normal despite her risk factors.
An ovarian cyst does not reliably cause pain that recurs with every period, and adnexal findings would be expected.
Fibroids are rare in adolescents and usually cause heavy bleeding and an enlarged uterus, which she does not have.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of abdominal bloating and increased frequency of stools. He describes the stools as bulky, foul-smelling, and difficult to flush. He also has a 4-month history of recurrent dull upper abdominal pain that usually lasts for a few days, worsens after meals, and is not relieved with antacids. He has had a 10-kg (22-lb) weight loss in the past 4 months. He has no personal or family history of serious illness. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 37 years. He has a 12-year history of drinking 6 to 8 beers daily. He is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 52 kg (115 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m2. His vital signs are within normal limits. Abdominal examination shows mild epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds are normal. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
questions.why: Years of heavy drinking with recurrent postprandial epigastric pain, steatorrhoea and weight loss suggest chronic pancreatitis, while smoking and weight loss also raise concern for pancreatic cancer. Contrast CT is the first-line test: it shows calcifications, duct changes and any mass.
notes: Endoscopic ultrasound is more invasive and is used when CT is equivocal or a mass needs biopsy, not as the first test.
Ultrasound often shows the pancreas poorly because of bowel gas and is less sensitive for calcifications and masses.
Upper endoscopy looks at the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum, but steatorrhoea and weight loss point to the pancreas, which endoscopy cannot assess.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man arrives to his primary care physician to discuss his fear of flying. The patient reports that he has had a fear of flying since being a teenager. He went on a family vacation 15 years ago, and during the flight there was turbulence and a “rough landing”. Since then he has avoided flying. He did not go to his cousin’s wedding because it was out of the country. He also was unable to visit his grandmother for her 80th birthday. The last time his job asked him to meet a client out of state, he drove 18 hours instead of flying. Two years ago he promised his fiancé they could fly to Florida. Upon arrival at the airport, he began to feel dizzy, lightheaded, and refused to go through security. During the clinic visit, the patient appears anxious and distressed. He recognizes that his fear is irrational. He is upset that it is affecting his relationship with his wife. Additionally, his current job may soon require employees in his sales position to fly to meet potential clients. He is embarrassed to have a conversation with his manager about his fear of flying. Which of the following is the best therapy for the patient’s condition?
questions.why: He has a long-standing, irrational fear of flying that causes avoidance and impairs his life. This is a specific phobia. CBT with exposure therapy is the treatment of choice and gives lasting benefit.
notes: A benzodiazepine may be used occasionally before an unavoidable flight, but it does not treat the phobia and can cause dependence.
SSRIs are first line for generalised and social anxiety disorders, but they are not effective first-line treatment for specific phobia.
Psychodynamic therapy is not an evidence-based first-line treatment for specific phobia compared with exposure-based CBT.

questions.stem: Twelve hours after admission to the hospital because of a high-grade fever for 3 days, a 15-year-old boy has shortness of breath. During this period, he has had generalized malaise and a cough productive of moderate amounts of green sputum. For the past 10 days, he has had fever, a sore throat, and generalized aches; these symptoms initially improved, but worsened again over the past 5 days. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 109/min, respirations are 27/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. There are decreased breath sounds and crackles heard over the upper right lung field. His hemoglobin concentration is 13.3 g/dL, leukocyte count is 15,000/mm3, and platelet count is 289,000/mm3. An x-ray of the chest shows a right upper-lobe infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.why: A viral illness that improved and then worsened, followed by high fever, purulent sputum, leucocytosis and a lobar infiltrate, fits a secondary bacterial pneumonia. S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of typical lobar community-acquired pneumonia, including after influenza.
notes: Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia, with dry cough, a gradual onset and patchy interstitial infiltrates, rather than purulent sputum and lobar consolidation.
Chlamydophila causes a mild atypical pneumonia, often with hoarseness and a dry cough, not acute lobar pneumonia with green sputum.
H. influenzae can cause pneumonia, usually in COPD or older patients, but it is much less common than pneumococcus in an otherwise healthy teenager.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the physician because she feels depressed, has difficulty sleeping, has a poor appetite, and has had a problem concentrating for the past 3 months. During this time, she has also has had low energy and has lost interest in playing the guitar. During high school, the patient went through similar episodes of low mood and poor sleep. At that time, she would repeatedly engage in binge eating and purging behavior, for which she was referred to therapy. There is no evidence of suicidal ideation. Her physician offers to prescribe a medication for her current symptoms. Treatment with which of the following drugs should be avoided in this patient?
questions.why: Her history of bulimia (binge eating and purging) is a contraindication to bupropion, which lowers the seizure threshold, especially with electrolyte disturbance. In Australia, bupropion is approved only for smoking cessation, not depression.
notes: Citalopram is a reasonable first-line SSRI for major depression and is not contraindicated by a history of eating disorder.
Fluoxetine is safe here and is actually the SSRI approved for bulimia nervosa.
Trazodone does not carry the seizure risk of bupropion and can help her insomnia, so it does not need to be avoided.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with altered mental status. The patient is in acute distress and cannot provide history due to disorientation. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.6°F), blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg, pulse is 103/min, respiratory rate is 22/min, and BMI is 20 kg/m2. On examination, his sclera and skin are icteric. On abdominal examination, the patient moans with deep palpation to his right upper quadrant. Laboratory test Complete blood count Hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL MCV 88 fl Leukocytes 16,500/mm3 Platelets 170,000/mm3 Basic metabolic panel Serum Na+ 147 mEq/L Serum K+ 3.8 mEq/L Serum Cl- 106 mEq/L Serum HCO3- 25 mEq/L BUN 30 mg/dL Serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL Liver function test Total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL AST 50 U/L ALT 65 U/L ALP 180 U/L The patient is treated urgently with intravenous fluid, dopamine, and broad spectrum antibiotics. The patient’s blood pressure improves to 101/70 mm Hg. On ultrasound of the abdomen, the common bile duct is dilated. What is the best next step in the management of this patient?
questions.why: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain plus hypotension and confusion (Reynolds pentad), with a dilated common bile duct, is acute suppurative cholangitis. Once resuscitated and on antibiotics, he needs urgent biliary drainage, and ERCP is first line. In Australia, noradrenaline rather than dopamine is the usual first vasopressor.
notes: MRCP only images the duct and cannot drain it; ultrasound has already shown obstruction, so MRCP would just delay decompression in a septic patient.
Percutaneous transhepatic drainage is the fallback when ERCP fails, is unavailable, or anatomy is altered; it is not the first choice here.
CT adds little once ultrasound shows a dilated duct in clinical cholangitis, and it delays the drainage this patient needs.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old African-American woman presents to the emergency room with hip pain. She has a past medical history significant for sarcoidosis which was recently diagnosed 6 months ago and is currently being treated. She reports that the pain started 2 weeks ago and is localized to the left hip and groin. The pain has been getting progressively more intense. Her temperature is 98.1°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg, pulse is 80/min, respirations are 13/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam is notable for pain with manipulation without restriction of range of motion of the hip. Which of the following is the most sensitive test for this condition?
questions.why: A patient with sarcoidosis on treatment is presumably taking corticosteroids, and new groin pain with preserved hip range of motion suggests early avascular necrosis of the femoral head. MRI is the most sensitive test and shows marrow oedema before any change appears on X-ray.
notes: Plain X-rays are often normal early in avascular necrosis and only show sclerosis, crescent sign or collapse later, so they are a poor test for sensitivity.
A bone scan can pick up avascular necrosis but is less sensitive and less specific than MRI, and it has largely been replaced by MRI.
Ultrasound can show a hip effusion but cannot assess the bone marrow, so it cannot diagnose avascular necrosis.

questions.stem: A 6-day-old male newborn is brought to the physician because he has become increasingly irritable and restless over the past 2 days. During this period, he has had 12 bowel movements. He feeds 10 to 12 times a day. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation and weighed 1800 g (3 lb 15 oz); he currently weighs 1700 g (3 lb 12 oz). His mother has Graves' disease and received propylthiouracil during the last trimester of pregnancy. She has a history of intravenous heroin use. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 180/min, and respirations are 50/min. Examination shows mild diaphoresis and a firm 2-cm midline neck swelling. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.why: The mother has Graves' disease, so her TSH-receptor antibodies cross the placenta and can cause neonatal thyrotoxicosis. It often appears around day 5-7, once the PTU has cleared from the baby. Here it shows as tachycardia, irritability, frequent stools, weight loss and goitre. Treat with a thionamide plus a beta-blocker. Australian practice may use carbimazole, which is converted to methimazole.
notes: Iodide can be added for a severe thyroid storm, but only after a thionamide has been started; on its own it is not the first-line step.
Naloxone reverses acute opioid toxicity, which causes depressed breathing. Heroin withdrawal causes irritability and loose stools but not a goitre, and naloxone would make withdrawal worse.
Calcium gluconate treats neonatal hypocalcaemia, which causes jitteriness or seizures. It does not explain the goitre, the very fast heart rate or the maternal Graves' history.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of an increasing sensation of fullness in the upper left side of his abdomen. He complains of increasing fatigue and dyspnea. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 90/min, respiratory rate is 18/min, and blood pressure is 125/70 mm Hg. His conjunctivae are pale. The examination of the heart and lungs shows no abnormalities. The splenic margin is palpable 8 cm (3.1 in) below the costal margin. No abnormal lymph nodes are found. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 8 g/dL Mean corpuscular volume 90 μm3 Leukocyte count 3,000/mm3 Platelet count 85,000/mm3 Peripheral blood smear shows small lymphocytes with cell membrane projections. Bone marrow aspiration is unsuccessful. Cell immunophenotyping is positive for CD25. Which of the following is the most effective pharmacotherapy at this time?
questions.why: Massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, a dry tap on marrow aspiration, lymphocytes with hair-like projections and CD25 positivity point to hairy cell leukaemia. The purine analogue cladribine is first line and gives durable complete remissions in most patients.
notes: Fludarabine is a purine analogue with some activity in hairy cell leukaemia, but it is less effective than cladribine and is mainly used for CLL.
Corticosteroids do not treat hairy cell leukaemia and would make the infection risk from neutropenia worse.
Thalidomide is used for multiple myeloma and has no role in hairy cell leukaemia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old primigravid woman at 22 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department by her husband for lethargy, nausea, and vomiting for 4 days. This morning she became drowsy. She returned from a business trip to Sudan 3 weeks ago. She denies eating any seafood while traveling. Medications include iron supplements and a multivitamin. Her immunizations are up-to-date and she has never received blood products. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. She is oriented to person and place. Examination shows jaundice and mild asterixis. Pelvic examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 22-week gestation. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL Prothrombin time 18 sec (INR=2.0) Serum Total bilirubin 4.4 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase 398 U/L AST 4,702 U/L ALT 3,551 U/L Lactate dehydrogenase 3,412 U/L Anti-nuclear antibody negative Anti-smooth muscle antibody negative Anti-CMV antibody negative Anti-EBV nuclear antigen antibody negative An ELISA for HIV is negative. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?"
questions.why: She is pregnant, recently returned from Sudan where hepatitis E is endemic, and has acute hepatitis with liver failure (encephalopathy, INR 2.0). This picture points to hepatitis E, which is spread by the faecal-oral route and is fulminant in pregnancy, especially in the third trimester. Anti-HEV IgM confirms acute infection.
notes: Her immunisations are up to date, so she is protected against hepatitis B. The travel history and pregnancy point to HEV, not HBV.
Anti-HAV IgG shows past infection or vaccination, not acute illness. Acute hepatitis A would need IgM, and she is immunised anyway.
She has no risk factors for HCV such as blood products or injecting drugs, HCV rarely causes acute fulminant hepatitis, and IgG does not show acute infection.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of worsening shortness of breath for 6 hours. For the past 5 days, he has had intermittent stabbing pain in the middle of his chest that worsens with lying down or taking deep breaths. He has also had a runny nose and a dry cough for the past 2 weeks. He has hypercholesterolemia and hypertension. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 34 years. His current medications include atorvastatin, enalapril, and hydrochlorothiazide. He appears pale and sweaty. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 105/min, and respirations are 25/min. Blood pressure is 107/72 mm Hg during expiration and 86/65 mm Hg during inspiration. Examination shows jugular venous distention and pitting edema below the knees. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?
options: Dilation of the atria and ventricles
Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space
questions.why: After a viral illness he has pleuritic chest pain that changes with position (pericarditis). He now has hypotension, raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus, with a systolic drop of 21 mmHg on inspiration. That is cardiac tamponade from a pericardial effusion.
notes: Dilated cardiomyopathy causes heart failure with a displaced apex and an S3, not positional pleuritic pain or a large pulsus paradoxus.
Myocardial infarction causes pressure-like chest pain that does not change with posture, and on its own it does not give pulsus paradoxus after a viral prodrome.
Constrictive pericarditis develops over months and typically shows Kussmaul's sign and a pericardial knock, not acute pulsus paradoxus within days of acute pericarditis.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old boy is brought to the physician with a 3-day history of fever and cough. His mother reports that he has had multiple episodes of loose stools over the past 3 months. He has been treated for otitis media 4 times and bronchiolitis 3 times since birth. He was born at 37 weeks' gestation, and the neonatal period was uncomplicated. He is at the 10th percentile for height and 3rd percentile for weight. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 126/min, and respirations are 35/min. Examination shows an erythematous scaly rash over his trunk and extremities. The white patches on the tongue and buccal mucosa bleed when scraped. Inspiratory crackles are heard in the right lung base. An X-ray of the chest shows an infiltrate in the right lower lobe and an absent thymic shadow. Which of the following is the most likely definitive treatment for this patient’s condition?
questions.why: An infant with chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive, recurrent infections, oral thrush and an absent thymic shadow has severe combined immunodeficiency. The rash may be graft-versus-host disease from maternal T cells. The definitive cure for SCID is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
notes: IVIG replaces antibodies and is a supportive bridge, but it does not restore T-cell function, so it cannot cure SCID.
Leucovorin is used for folate antagonist toxicity or certain folate disorders. It does not correct a combined T- and B-cell defect.
Thymic transplantation is used for complete DiGeorge syndrome. That would also feature hypocalcaemia, heart defects and facial features, and most SCID is a stem-cell defect, not a thymic one.

questions.stem: A six-year-old boy with a history of asthma currently uses an albuterol inhaler as needed to manage his asthma symptoms. His mother brings him into your office because she feels she has had to increase the patient’s use of his inhaler to four times per week for the past month. She also reports that he has woken up three times during the night from his symptoms this month. The boy reports that he is upset because he can’t always keep up with his friends in the playground. His past medical history is significant for allergic rhinitis. The patient’s temperature is 98°F (36.6°C), blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 88/min, and respirations are 18/min with an oxygen saturation of 98% O2 on room air. Auscultation of his lungs reveals bilateral late expiratory wheezes. What changes should be made to his current asthma treatment regimen?
questions.why: Using a reliever more than twice a week and waking at night several times a month means persistent (not intermittent) asthma, so he needs a daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid. In Australia, children aged 6 to 11 are likewise stepped up to regular low-dose ICS.
notes: Needing a reliever four times a week, waking at night and having limited activity show poorly controlled persistent asthma, so continuing SABA alone is not adequate.
A LABA must never be used as monotherapy in asthma because of increased risk of severe exacerbation and death; it is only added to an ICS at a higher step.
Zileuton is a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor that is not first-line, needs liver monitoring and is not approved for a 6-year-old; it is also not available in Australia.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl presents to her pediatrician with intensely pruritic lesions over her buttocks, as shown. These lesions occur intermittently but have worsened over time. Her medical history is remarkable for iron deficiency, for which she is on ferrous sulfate. The patient has also experienced intermittent episodes of mild diarrhea, previously diagnosed as lactose intolerance. Her height is at the 30th percentile and weight is at the 25th percentile for age and sex. An immunoglobulin A (IgA) tissue transglutaminase titer is 5 times the upper limit of normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.why: Intensely itchy grouped vesicles on the buttocks are dermatitis herpetiformis. Together with iron deficiency, chronic diarrhoea, short stature and a raised IgA tTG, this points to coeliac disease, where IgA antibodies against epidermal transglutaminase are deposited in the dermal papillae.
notes: Crohn's disease can cause iron deficiency and poor growth, but its skin signs are erythema nodosum or pyoderma gangrenosum, and it does not raise IgA tTG or cause dermatitis herpetiformis.
CVID causes low immunoglobulins and recurrent sinopulmonary infections; she has a high IgA tTG, and a true IgA deficiency would make that test falsely low.
HSP causes palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs with abdominal pain, arthritis and nephritis; the lesions are not intensely itchy and tTG is not raised.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of diarrhea, moderate abdominal pain, and weakness. Her symptoms began on the return flight from a 2-week yoga retreat in India, where she stayed at a resort. She was mildly nauseous as she boarded the flight, and diarrhea followed immediately after eating the in-flight meal. Since then, she has had up to five watery stools daily. She has a 1-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease and is allergic to shellfish. Her only medication is ranitidine. She appears lethargic. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 115/72 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows diffuse tenderness with no guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. Which of the following is the most likely pathogen?
questions.why: Watery diarrhoea and cramps starting 1 to 3 days after a stay in India, with no fever and no blood, is classic traveller's diarrhoea, and ETEC is the most common cause. Acid suppression with ranitidine also raises the risk. (Ranitidine has been withdrawn in Australia.)
notes: Giardia has a longer incubation period of 1 to 2 weeks and causes greasy, foul-smelling stools with bloating, not acute watery diarrhoea beginning on the trip home.
Shigella causes fever and bloody, mucoid stools with tenesmus, but she has no fever and her stools are watery.
Staphylococcal food poisoning comes 1 to 6 hours after the meal, mostly as vomiting, and settles within a day; her nausea started before the meal and she has been unwell for 3 days.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of painful enlarging bruises and skin ulceration over his thighs and external genitalia. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus, mitral regurgitation, and atrial fibrillation. Three days ago, he was started on treatment with warfarin. His only other medications are metformin and lisinopril. His temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F), pulse is 108/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 155/89 mm Hg. Examination of the skin shows large purpura, hemorrhagic bullae, and areas of skin necrosis over his anterior legs, gluteal region, and penis. This patient is most likely to benefit from treatment with which of the following?
questions.why: Painful purpura, haemorrhagic bullae and necrosis in fatty areas (thighs, buttocks, penis) a few days after starting warfarin point to warfarin-induced skin necrosis. Protein C falls faster than the clotting factors and causes a temporary hypercoagulable state. Treat by stopping warfarin, giving vitamin K and heparin, and replacing protein C.
notes: Hyperbaric oxygen is used for necrotising soft tissue infection or carbon monoxide poisoning; it does not correct the protein C deficiency that causes this necrosis.
Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor used for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; this patient has had no heparin and his problem is caused by warfarin.
