options: Attempt to identify the father's physician and work with that physician to obtain chromosome studies on the father
Contact the father by telephone and arrange for him to give a blood sample at a local hospital
Document your attempts to work with the mother but proceed no further, since you have no physician-patient relationship with the father
Help the mother deal with her anger and educate her regarding the potential benefit to her son and others if the father's chromosome studies are done
questions.why: The mother is your patient's guardian and the only legitimate route to the father. The best first step is to address her anger and explain how knowing the father's carrier status helps her son (recurrence risk, prognosis) and the father's relatives. Confidentiality and consent mean you work through the family, not around them.
notes: Going to the father's physician behind the mother's back breaches confidentiality about the child, and you have not yet tried to get the mother on side.
Phoning the father directly discloses the child's genetic information without the guardian's consent and skips the step of working with the mother.
Giving up too early leaves the child and family without useful information; you should first try to engage and educate the mother.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the office because of urticaria. This is her first episode of urticaria and it has occurred and then resolved several times in the past week. The history and physical examination disclose no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
questions.why: Acute urticaria (under 6 weeks) in a patient with a normal history and examination is usually self-limited and idiopathic or due to a viral trigger. No investigations are needed, so treat the symptoms with a non-sedating H1 antihistamine.
notes: Serum IgE is nonspecific and does not change management of a first, self-limited episode with no abnormal findings.
An eosinophil count adds nothing when history and examination are normal and there are no clues to parasitic or systemic disease.
Specialist referral is for chronic urticaria or features of anaphylaxis, not a first, brief episode that has settled.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 7-month history of leg weakness and dry eyes and mouth. He also has had a 10.4-kg (23-lb) weight loss over the past 4 months despite no change in appetite. He has smoked one and a half packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years. He drinks 4 oz of alcohol daily. He has peptic ulcer disease and emphysema. Medications include cimetidine, theophylline, and low-dose prednisone. Examination shows mild ptosis. He has a barrelshaped chest. Breath sounds are distant. There is moderate weakness of proximal muscles of the lower extremities. Reflexes are absent. He has difficulty rising from a chair. Sensory examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray shows a hyperinflated chest and a 3 x 4-cm mass in the right hilum. His neurologic findings are most likely due to a lesion involving which of the following?
questions.why: A heavy smoker with a hilar mass (probable small cell carcinoma), proximal leg weakness, absent reflexes, mild ptosis, and dry mouth and eyes has Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release.
notes: Myopathy causes proximal weakness, but reflexes are usually kept and it does not explain the autonomic dry mouth and eyes or the ptosis.
The dryness is autonomic, but the underlying problem is reduced presynaptic acetylcholine release at both nicotinic and muscarinic synapses, not a primary parasympathetic lesion.
Peripheral neuropathy would usually cause distal weakness with sensory loss, but sensation here is normal.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because he has been tired and irritable for the past 3 months. He is a high school freshman and a member of the track team. He reports that his symptoms began shortly after starting spring training. He practices sprints 5 nights a week and runs 2 to 5 miles several days a week in addition to leg training with weights. He admits to being tired and says the training is becoming more intense and that he is a little concerned about his ability to continue on the team. His appetite has been unchanged. Medical history is unremarkable and he takes no medications. He has been your patient for the past 3 years. He seems more sullen than you remember from previous visits. You ask his mother to leave the examining room while you complete the physical examination. After she leaves the room, he admits that he is worried about some lumps in his groin. It is most appropriate to obtain additional history regarding which of the following?
questions.why: A teenager who tells you about groin lumps only after his mother leaves suggests inguinal lymphadenopathy that could come from a sexually transmitted infection. A confidential sexual history (HEADSS approach) is the key next step.
notes: Systemic symptoms matter, but the private disclosure of groin lumps points first to a sexual history to look for an STI.
He seems sullen, but mood questions do not explain or address the groin lumps he raised in private.
School performance is part of a psychosocial screen, but it does not help you assess new inguinal lumps.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old primigravid woman comes for her initial prenatal visit at 16 weeks' gestation. She is not sure about the date of her last menstrual period but says that the pregnancy probably occurred immediately after she stopped taking oral contraceptives 5 months ago. Maternal serum α-fetoprotein (MSAFP) concentration is increased to 3 multiples of the median. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Triple screening for MSAFP, serum β-hCG, and serum estriol concentrations
Amniocentesis for measurement of α-fetoprotein concentration
questions.why: A raised MSAFP should first be followed by ultrasound. The commonest cause is wrong dating, and her dates are uncertain here. Ultrasound also detects multiple pregnancy, fetal death, and neural tube or abdominal wall defects.
notes: Repeating MSAFP delays diagnosis and does not resolve uncertain dates or detect structural defects.
Triple screening is mainly for aneuploidy risk; it adds little once MSAFP is already clearly raised and the dating is uncertain.
Amniocentesis is invasive and only considered if ultrasound confirms the dates and shows no explanation; it is not the first step.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an 8-week history of difficulty sleeping, fatigue, and muscle tension. During this period, she also has had memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and has been reprimanded at work for arriving late. Over the past 2 weeks, she has had three episodes of palpitations and shortness of breath that have awakened her from sleep. Her pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 110/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Mental status examination shows a depressed mood and constricted affect. She says that she is no longer interested in activities that she used to enjoy. She has suicidal ideation without a plan. Her hemoglobin concentration is 11 g/dL, and serum ferritin concentration is 140 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in treatment?
questions.why: She has major depression with anxiety features and probable nocturnal panic attacks: low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and concentration, and suicidal ideation without a plan. An SSRI such as paroxetine is first-line. Her ferritin is normal, so iron deficiency is not the cause.
notes: Her memory lapses come from depression (pseudodementia), not Alzheimer disease, so a cholinesterase inhibitor is not indicated.
A ferritin of 140 ng/mL rules out iron deficiency, so iron would not help her mild anaemia or her mood.
Ginkgo has no proven benefit for depression or cognition and would delay effective treatment.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with paranoid schizophrenia is transferred to the emergency department from the residential facility where he lives 2 hours after having swallowed a nail. The patient says he does not have any symptoms. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable. His only current medication is haloperidol. The patient is not in acute distress. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Mental status examination discloses a flat affect, distractibility, and derailment of thoughts. X-ray of the abdomen is obtained and shows a 4-cm nail in the left upper quadrant. No free air is visible. After admitting the patient to the hospital, which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Administration of ipecac to induce vomiting and expectoration of the nail
Observation to allow passage of the nail via normal peristalsis
Open laparotomy and removal of the nail through a gastrotomy incision
Removal of the nail through endoscopic esophagogastroscopy
questions.why: A sharp, long object (a 4 cm nail) that is still in the stomach, within reach of the scope, should be removed endoscopically. Once it passes the pylorus it can perforate the bowel. The rule to remember: remove sharp objects and objects longer than about 5-6 cm before they leave the stomach.
notes: Ipecac is no longer recommended, and forcing a sharp object back up by vomiting risks injury to the oesophagus and aspiration.
Waiting for it to pass suits small blunt objects, but a sharp nail carries a high risk of perforating the bowel as it moves through.
There is no free air and the patient is stable, so surgery is not needed while a less invasive endoscopic removal is possible.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he had an episode of chest pain radiating to his jaw while shoveling snow. His pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows an S4. While undergoing an ECG, the patient says that he feels the chest pain returning. The most appropriate immediate treatment is a drug with which of the following mechanisms of action?
questions.why: Exertional chest pain radiating to the jaw, now recurring, is suspected acute coronary syndrome. Immediate relief comes from a nitrate such as sublingual GTN, which releases nitric oxide, raises cGMP and causes venodilation, lowering preload and myocardial oxygen demand.
notes: Drugs that raise cAMP, such as dobutamine or milrinone, increase myocardial contractility and oxygen demand, which would worsen ischaemia.
Potassium channel blockers such as amiodarone are class III antiarrhythmics; he is in sinus rhythm at 80/min and has no arrhythmia to treat.
Sodium channel blockers such as lidocaine are class I antiarrhythmics; they do not relieve ischaemic chest pain and are not used routinely in ACS.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man in general practice. Age 75 with asbestos exposure in the late 1960s and 1970s, progressive dry cough and exertional breathlessness, 6 kg weight loss, hoarseness, dull upper right chest pain, right apical dullness and a 6 cm right apical mass on the chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Primary lung carcinoma of the right superior sulcus
questions.why: Primary lung carcinoma of the right superior sulcus fits: age 75 with asbestos exposure in the late 1960s and 1970s, progressive dry cough and exertional breathlessness, 6 kg weight loss, hoarseness, dull upper right chest pain, right apical dullness and a 6 cm right apical mass on the chest X-ray. A cough lasting more than 3 weeks with weight loss, hoarseness, chest pain or breathlessness in an older adult needs a chest X-ray. A suspicious film needs an urgent CT and specialist referral, with the patient seen within 2 weeks.
notes: The X-ray shows a discrete apical mass with no pleural effusion, plaques or pleural thickening.
No fevers, night sweats, travel or TB contact, and the lesion is a solid mass without cavitation.
No clubbing, no fine crackles, no reticular change on the X-ray, and it does not explain the mass.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman in general practice. Two spontaneous attacks of spinning vertigo lasting about 8 hours, fluctuating right hearing loss with tinnitus and fullness, a documented right low-frequency sensorineural loss, and a normal examination between attacks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ménière's disease of the right ear
questions.why: Ménière's disease of the right ear fits: two spontaneous attacks of spinning vertigo lasting about 8 hours, fluctuating right hearing loss with tinnitus and fullness, a documented right low-frequency sensorineural loss, and a normal examination between attacks. Clarify what “dizzy” means first. True vertigo is vestibular, and its timing and triggers (seconds and positional, hours and spontaneous, or days and continuous) narrow the cause.
notes: The symptoms are episodic and the loss is low-frequency, with good word recognition, present acoustic reflexes and normal cranial nerves V and VII.
The attacks lasted 8 hours each with full recovery, there are no neurological symptoms, the examination is normal and the ear symptoms point to the inner ear.
No headache, aura or light or noise sensitivity, and she has a documented one-sided low-frequency sensorineural loss.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman in general practice. Diffuse smooth goitre with a bruit, exophthalmos and lid retraction, weight loss, tremor, warm moist hands, AF, suppressed TSH with high free T4 and T3, and positive TRAb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Graves' disease fits: diffuse smooth goitre with a bruit, exophthalmos and lid retraction, weight loss, tremor, warm moist hands, AF, suppressed TSH with high free T4 and T3, and positive TRAb. Examine thyroid status as well as the gland: hands, tremor, reflexes, eyes from the front, side and above, the neck with a swallow and tongue protrusion, palpation from behind, percussion of the manubrium, a bruit, and the legs.
notes: Afebrile (37.0 °C), alert and oriented, no vomiting, only mildly increased bowel frequency, no heart failure, haemodynamically stable. A Burch–Wartofsky score may reach the mid-20s to 30s from the AF and restlessness alone, but clinically she is compensated. Admit if fever, confusion, vomiting, worsening tachycardia or heart failure develop.
She is 32, the gland is smooth and diffuse with no nodules, she has eye signs, and TRAb is positive.
There is no solitary nodule, both lobes are enlarged, and TRAb is positive.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman in the emergency department. Colicky periumbilical pain, faeculent vomiting, no stool or flatus, distension, tinkling bowel sounds, previous laparoscopy, and a CT transition point under the right iliac fossa port site with no mass or hernia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Adhesive small bowel obstruction fits: colicky periumbilical pain, faeculent vomiting, no stool or flatus, distension, tinkling bowel sounds, previous laparoscopy, and a CT transition point under the right iliac fossa port site with no mass or hernia. Colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation (no stool or flatus) are the cardinal features of bowel obstruction. Always ask specifically about flatus and previous surgery.
notes: Lactate is normal, bowel wall enhancement is normal, the SMA and SMV are patent, she has no AF and the pain is colicky, not constant.
She had only one episode of diarrhoea and nothing since, she is afebrile, and the colon is collapsed on CT with no wall thickening.
Vomiting began within hours of the pain, and CT shows a collapsed colon with the transition point in the small bowel.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman in the emergency department. Sharp retrosternal pleuritic pain that is worse lying down and better sitting forward, a friction rub, widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression, a febrile son 10 days ago, temperature 37.8 °C and CRP 46. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: ST-elevation myocardial infarction or other acute coronary syndrome
questions.why: Acute pericarditis fits: sharp retrosternal pleuritic pain that is worse lying down and better sitting forward, a friction rub, widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression, a febrile son 10 days ago, temperature 37.8 °C and CRP 46. Pericarditis pain is sharp, pleuritic and positional: worse lying flat and eased by sitting forward. Acute pericarditis needs 2 of 4 criteria: typical pain, a friction rub, typical ECG changes and a pericardial effusion.
notes: She is 34 with no cardiovascular risk factors, the pain is sharp, pleuritic and positional, the ST elevation spans limb and chest leads without fitting one coronary territory, with PR depression and no Q waves, and hs-troponin is normal at 0 and 2 hours.
The pain is not tearing and does not go to the back, BP is equal in both arms, and the mediastinum is not widened on the chest X-ray.
She has no breathlessness, haemoptysis, calf symptoms, previous clot, immobility or oestrogen, SpO2 is 99%, Wells is 1.5 and the D-dimer is normal.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman in general practice. Rusty productive cough, fever, left pleuritic pain and breathlessness after a cold with sick contacts, left basal dullness with bronchial breathing, neutrophilia with CRP 148, and left lower lobe consolidation with a small effusion on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Community-acquired pneumonia of the left lower lobe
Acute bronchitis or viral lower respiratory tract infection
questions.why: Community-acquired pneumonia of the left lower lobe fits: rusty productive cough, fever, left pleuritic pain and breathlessness after a cold with sick contacts, left basal dullness with bronchial breathing, neutrophilia with CRP 148, and left lower lobe consolidation with a small effusion on X-ray. A productive cough with rusty sputum, fever, pleuritic pain and focal chest signs after a viral illness is community-acquired pneumonia until proven otherwise; Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause.
notes: No travel, immobility, surgery or calf symptoms; purulent rusty sputum after a viral illness, a neutrophilia and lobar consolidation.
Lifelong non-smoker, no weight or appetite loss, no haemoptysis, no lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hilar abnormality on the X-ray.
Focal bronchial breathing and dullness at the left base, CRP 148, and consolidation on the X-ray.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman in general practice. Six-week progressive productive cough with 5 days of haemoptysis, low-grade fever, fatigue, breathlessness and 5 kg weight loss; born in and travels annually to Cambodia; right upper zone crackles and right upper lobe opacification. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Pulmonary tuberculosis fits: six-week progressive productive cough with 5 days of haemoptysis, low-grade fever, fatigue, breathlessness and 5 kg weight loss; born in and travels annually to Cambodia; right upper zone crackles and right upper lobe opacification. A cough lasting more than 3 weeks with haemoptysis, fever and weight loss in someone born in or travelling to a country with high TB rates is pulmonary TB until proven otherwise.
notes: Aged 26 with only 1.5 pack-years and a 6-week history, no clubbing or lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hilar enlargement on the X-ray.
Gradual productive cough with fever, no pleuritic pain, no immobility or calf signs, SpO2 97% and a normal heart rate.
No diabetes, heavy alcohol use or kidney disease; sputum culture with the lab alerted to Burkholderia will help exclude it.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man in general practice. Constant dull periumbilical pain for 12 hours with nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever, pain on coughing and movement, and right iliac fossa tenderness with rebound and a positive Rovsing's sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Acute appendicitis fits: constant dull periumbilical pain for 12 hours with nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever, pain on coughing and movement, and right iliac fossa tenderness with rebound and a positive Rovsing's sign. Early appendicitis causes vague, constant periumbilical pain (visceral afferents) that later localises to the right iliac fossa as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.
notes: Lower abdominal and periumbilical rather than epigastric pain, no back radiation, and no gallstones.
No distension, bowel sounds present, and no previous abdominal surgery.
No weight loss, fatigue, diarrhoea or blood in the stool, and only a 12-hour history.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman in general practice. Two months of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea with blood, weight loss, perianal inflammation with skin tags, clubbing, a smoker, calprotectin 820, and cobblestoning with skip lesions and granulomas at colonoscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Crohn's disease fits: two months of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea with blood, weight loss, perianal inflammation with skin tags, clubbing, a smoker, calprotectin 820, and cobblestoning with skip lesions and granulomas at colonoscopy. Chronic diarrhoea with blood, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss or fever is organic until proven otherwise; ask about each directly, along with NSAIDs, smoking and a family history of IBD.
notes: The granulomas are non-caseating, the acid-fast bacilli stain is negative, and she has no TB risk factors.
Right iliac fossa pain, perianal skin tags, terminal ileal disease, skip lesions with rectal sparing, and granulomas on biopsy.
Symptoms for 2 months with no travel, antibiotics or sick contacts, and negative stool PCR, culture and C. difficile toxin.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man in the emergency department. About 4 beers a night with 12 last night, constant epigastric pain through to the back eased by leaning forward, lipase 1850 U/L, a bulky pancreas with peripancreatic fluid on ultrasound, no gallstones and an isolated raised GGT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ruptured or leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm
questions.why: Acute alcohol-related pancreatitis fits: about 4 beers a night with 12 last night, constant epigastric pain through to the back eased by leaning forward, lipase 1850 U/L, a bulky pancreas with peripancreatic fluid on ultrasound, no gallstones and an isolated raised GGT. Acute pancreatitis needs 2 of 3 criteria: typical epigastric pain through to the back, lipase more than 3 times the upper limit, and characteristic imaging. The height of the lipase does not reflect severity.
notes: No NSAIDs or previous indigestion, no rigidity or rebound, and the lipase is more than 30 times the upper limit.
The pain is not tearing, BP is normal and equal in both arms, there is no pulsatile mass, the aorta measures 2.0 cm on ultrasound, and (partly) at 56 he is below the usual risk age.
No chest pain or breathlessness, the pain is positional, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST or T wave changes.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman in the emergency department. Constant right upper quadrant pain for about 20 hours after a rich meal, radiating to the shoulder tip, with fever, chills, vomiting, earlier postprandial episodes, a positive Murphy's sign, WCC 15.8, CRP 142 and an ultrasound showing a 6 mm wall, pericholecystic fluid and an impacted neck stone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Acute calculous cholecystitis fits: constant right upper quadrant pain for about 20 hours after a rich meal, radiating to the shoulder tip, with fever, chills, vomiting, earlier postprandial episodes, a positive Murphy's sign, WCC 15.8, CRP 142 and an ultrasound showing a 6 mm wall, pericholecystic fluid and an impacted neck stone. Biliary colic settles within a few hours. Constant RUQ pain lasting longer, with fever, Murphy's sign and raised WCC and CRP, is acute cholecystitis.
notes: No jaundice or confusion, bilirubin 16, common bile duct 4 mm with no duct stone, normal BP and lactate.
Pain maximal in the RUQ with only mild epigastric tenderness, no reflux or melaena, no rigidity or generalised peritonism, and the ultrasound shows a clear biliary cause.
She takes the pill daily, had a normal period 2 weeks ago, has no bleeding or faintness, a normal BP and a serum beta-hCG below 2 IU/L.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman in the emergency department. She has 4 weeks of burning retrosternal pain that is worse lying down and after meals, with acid regurgitation, no exertional features, a normal ECG and negative serial troponin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute coronary syndrome or unstable angina
questions.why: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease fits: she has 4 weeks of burning retrosternal pain that is worse lying down and after meals, with acid regurgitation, no exertional features, a normal ECG and negative serial troponin. In ED chest pain, rule out ACS before settling on reflux: a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, then serial high-sensitivity troponin on a validated assay-specific 0/1 h or 0/2 h pathway. A normal ECG alone does not exclude ACS.
notes: The pain is burning, positional and related to meals, never exertional and has no associated features, and her ECG during pain and her troponin at 0 and 2 hours are normal.
She has no anaemia, haematemesis, hoarseness or palpable lymph nodes, and she is 45 and a non-smoker.
The pain is retrosternal rather than epigastric, with no bloating, early satiety, NSAID use or bleeding, and her Hb is normal.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man in general practice. Twelve weeks of pale floating loose stools with weight loss, fatigue and bloating, an itchy blistering rash on both knees, family type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease, iron and folate deficiency, and strongly positive tTG-IgA and EMA with normal total IgA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Crohn's disease of the small bowel
questions.why: Coeliac disease fits: twelve weeks of pale floating loose stools with weight loss, fatigue and bloating, an itchy blistering rash on both knees, family type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease, iron and folate deficiency, and strongly positive tTG-IgA and EMA with normal total IgA. In chronic diarrhoea, ask what the stool looks like: pale, floating stools suggest fat malabsorption, and weight loss, steatorrhoea or anaemia are red flags that rule out a label of IBS until they are explained.
notes: No blood, abdominal pain, mouth ulcers or perianal disease, a normal CRP, and serology and a rash that point to coeliac disease.
No heat intolerance, palpitations or tremor, no goitre, and a normal TSH and free T4.
No travel, untreated water, sick contacts or fever.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman in general practice. Jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, confusion and hypotension with known gallstones, a cholestatic LFT pattern and a dilated duct with a distal stone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pancreatic head carcinoma causing malignant biliary obstruction
questions.why: Severe acute cholangitis fits: jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, confusion and hypotension with known gallstones, a cholestatic LFT pattern and a dilated duct with a distal stone. Charcot's triad (jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever) suggests acute cholangitis. Adding confusion and hypotension makes Reynolds' pentad, which marks sepsis with organ dysfunction and hypoperfusion and needs urgent drainage of the bile duct.
notes: No weight loss or steatorrhoea, acute febrile onset, a stone seen in the duct, and no distal duct stricture or mass effect on the ERCP cholangiogram.
Normal lipase and no peripancreatic fluid on ultrasound.
Murphy's sign negative, no gallbladder wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid, and conjugated jaundice with a dilated common bile duct.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man in general practice. Four months of daily burning retrosternal pain after dinner, worse lying down and with spicy food, with an acid taste in the throat, a night cough and a normal ECG and bloods. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease fits: four months of daily burning retrosternal pain after dinner, worse lying down and with spicy food, with an acid taste in the throat, a night cough and a normal ECG and bloods. Burning retrosternal pain after meals, worse lying down, with an acid taste and a night cough, is typical of GORD, which is a clinical diagnosis.
notes: No dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting or anaemia, and a short 4-month history.
Burning pain that lasts about 30 minutes whatever he does and is not relieved by rest, is not brought on by tennis, is worse lying down with an acid taste, and a normal ECG.
No epigastric tenderness, no NSAID or aspirin use, and a normal haemoglobin and ferritin.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman in the emergency department. Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after 3 days of a swollen, tender right calf, a long-haul flight 4 days ago, oestrogen HRT, limited mobility and smoking, with sinus tachycardia and bilateral filling defects on CTPA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Acute pulmonary embolism fits: sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after 3 days of a swollen, tender right calf, a long-haul flight 4 days ago, oestrogen HRT, limited mobility and smoking, with sinus tachycardia and bilateral filling defects on CTPA. Ask every patient with pleuritic chest pain or breathlessness about VTE risk factors (travel, oestrogen, immobility, surgery, cancer, previous VTE, smoking), and examine both legs.
notes: The pain is sharp and pleuritic with no radiation, nausea or sweating, and the ECG and hs-troponin are normal.
No tearing pain or radiation to the back, no syncope or hypertension, equal arm BPs, and a normal-calibre aorta with no flap on CT.
No chest trauma or lung disease, the trachea is central, percussion and breath sounds are normal, and CT shows no pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man in the emergency department. A 64-year-old with a new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, worsening right visual loss with RAPD and a pale swollen disc, a tender pulseless right temporal artery, ESR 86 and CRP 78. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Giant cell arteritis fits: a 64-year-old with a new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, worsening right visual loss with RAPD and a pale swollen disc, a tender pulseless right temporal artery, ESR 86 and CRP 78. A new headache in anyone over 50 is giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise. Always ask about scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms and polymyalgia rheumatica.
notes: The onset was gradual, not thunderclap, and he has no meningism, vomiting or focal signs.

The headache is not worse in the morning or on lying or straining, he has no weight loss or behaviour change, and the disc swelling is in one eye with a field defect and RAPD rather than bilateral papilloedema.
The disc is pale (chalky) rather than hyperaemic, and he has headache, jaw claudication, an abnormal temporal artery and ESR 86 with CRP 78.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man in general practice. Sudden single hot, swollen knee with an effusion, pain on any movement, unable to bear weight, fever with rigors and tachycardia, a dirty nail puncture 2 days earlier, diabetes and pre-existing OA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Septic prepatellar or superficial infrapatellar bursitis
Septic arthritis of the left knee
questions.why: Septic arthritis of the left knee fits: sudden single hot, swollen knee with an effusion, pain on any movement, unable to bear weight, fever with rigors and tachycardia, a dirty nail puncture 2 days earlier, diabetes and pre-existing OA. An acute, single hot, swollen joint with fever is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. The knee is involved in about half of cases.
notes: Against gout: no previous attacks, no tophi, no diuretics, normal first MTPs. Pseudogout (CPPD) is common in an OA knee at 70 and cannot be excluded clinically; only crystals on aspiration distinguish it, and crystals do not exclude coexisting infection. The nail puncture and rigors favour infection.
A true joint effusion with tenderness all around the joint, pain on any movement and no separate swelling in front of the patella.
Married and monogamous for 45 years, with no discharge, dysuria, rash or tenosynovitis.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man in general practice. Sharp pain with every bowel motion lasting hours since a hard stool, small bright red bleeding, constipation, a posterior midline tear with clean edges and no sentinel tag, and too tender for a DRE. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Acute primary anal fissure fits: sharp pain with every bowel motion lasting hours since a hard stool, small bright red bleeding, constipation, a posterior midline tear with clean edges and no sentinel tag, and too tender for a DRE. Anal fissure pain is sharp during a bowel motion and lasts minutes to hours afterwards, often with a small amount of bright red blood on the paper, after a hard stool.
notes: Pain is episodic rather than constant and throbbing, he is afebrile, and there is no swelling, fluctuance, discharge or external opening.
Single posterior midline fissure; one long-term partner, no anal sex or STI symptoms; no diarrhoea, weight loss, abdominal pain or extraintestinal features.
Short history with bleeding on the paper explained by the fissure, no change in bowel habit, weight loss or family history.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman in clinic. Three months of symmetrical synovitis of the wrists, MCPs and PIPs with DIP sparing, tender MTPs, 90 minutes of morning stiffness, raised CRP and ESR, positive RF and anti-CCP, and marginal erosions with periarticular osteopenia on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Early seropositive erosive rheumatoid arthritis fits: three months of symmetrical synovitis of the wrists, MCPs and PIPs with DIP sparing, tender MTPs, 90 minutes of morning stiffness, raised CRP and ESR, positive RF and anti-CCP, and marginal erosions with periarticular osteopenia on X-ray. Examine the hands in order: prepare (consent, exposure above the elbows, pillow, ask about pain), general inspection, look at the backs and palms, elbows, feel each joint group, move with special tests and function, then the feet and the systemic features.
notes: No psoriasis, nail pitting, onycholysis or dactylitis, the DIPs are spared, there is no periostitis or pencil-in-cup change, and anti-CCP is strongly positive.
No rash, photosensitivity, mouth ulcers, alopecia or Raynaud's, ANA is negative, and the X-ray shows erosions, which SLE arthritis does not cause.
It has lasted 3 months rather than a few weeks, there is no rash in her or her contacts, and she has erosions and a strongly positive anti-CCP.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man in general practice. Prodrome of nausea, chills, anorexia and right upper quadrant discomfort then jaundice, 4 to 7 weeks after eating street food in Thailand and Vietnam with no travel vaccines, with hepatocellular LFTs and a positive hepatitis A IgM. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Paracetamol or other drug-induced liver injury
questions.why: Acute hepatitis A infection fits: prodrome of nausea, chills, anorexia and right upper quadrant discomfort then jaundice, 4 to 7 weeks after eating street food in Thailand and Vietnam with no travel vaccines, with hepatocellular LFTs and a positive hepatitis A IgM. Classify jaundice as pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic using the urine and stool colour, itch, and the LFT pattern (transaminases versus ALP and GGT, conjugated versus unconjugated bilirubin).
notes: HBsAg and anti-HBc are both negative.
Only occasional doses within the recommended amount, a normal INR, and a positive hepatitis A IgM.
Hepatitis E IgM not detected, and hepatitis A IgM is positive.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man in general practice. Right neck pain radiating to the thumb with paraesthesia, weakness of shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and wrist extension, reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, pain reproduced by neck extension, and concordant right C4-5 and C5-6 foraminal stenosis on MRI. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Right C5 and C6 radiculopathy fits: right neck pain radiating to the thumb with paraesthesia, weakness of shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and wrist extension, reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, pain reproduced by neck extension, and concordant right C4-5 and C5-6 foraminal stenosis on MRI. Examine the upper limbs in a fixed order, comparing sides at every step: inspection, tone, pronator drift, power, reflexes, coordination, then sensation. Isolate each movement and use reinforcement before calling a reflex absent.
notes: No hand clumsiness, gait change or bladder symptoms, normal tone, no Hoffmann's sign or inverted supinator reflex, normal lower limbs and a normal cord on MRI.

The weakness is never sudden in onset; it comes only when he loads the arm and settles with rest, with no face, speech or leg involvement, and there is a fixed lower motor neuron deficit with radicular pain.

Pain and sensory symptoms, no fasciculations, no upper motor neuron signs anywhere (normal tone, no Hoffmann's sign, normal lower limbs), a deficit confined to two roots and concordant root compression on MRI.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman in general practice. Five to six months of new constipation at 62 with straining, tenesmus, blood mixed with the stool, fatigue, iron deficiency anaemia, a brother diagnosed at 48 and smoking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Upper gastrointestinal source of iron deficiency
questions.why: Colorectal cancer fits: five to six months of new constipation at 62 with straining, tenesmus, blood mixed with the stool, fatigue, iron deficiency anaemia, a brother diagnosed at 48 and smoking. A new, persistent change in bowel habit at an older age, especially with rectal bleeding, tenesmus or anaemia, is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise, even when there is a benign explanation such as previous haemorrhoids.
notes: No dyspepsia, weight loss or melaena, and the visible blood and change in bowel habit point to the colon.
Blood is mixed through the stool rather than on the paper, there are no haemorrhoids on rectal examination or proctoscopy, and haemorrhoids do not explain the change in habit.

Diverticulosis is usually silent and does not cause a progressive change in habit or chronic iron deficiency; no LIF pain or fever to suggest diverticulitis; diverticular bleeding is usually sudden, painless and large.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man in general practice. Strictly left orbital pain at 10/10, lasting 2 to 3 hours, at the same time almost daily for 2 months and waking him, with same-sided tearing, red eye, rhinorrhoea and partial Horner's, restlessness, an earlier bout a year ago with 8 pain-free months, a father with similar headaches, and a normal examination and MRI. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Space-occupying lesion or raised intracranial pressure
questions.why: Cluster headache fits: strictly left orbital pain at 10/10, lasting 2 to 3 hours, at the same time almost daily for 2 months and waking him, with same-sided tearing, red eye, rhinorrhoea and partial Horner's, restlessness, an earlier bout a year ago with 8 pain-free months, a father with similar headaches, and a normal examination and MRI. Strictly one-sided orbital pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes, at the same time each day, with tearing, a red eye, a runny or blocked nose on the same side and restlessness, is cluster headache. Patients with migraine lie still, while patients with cluster headache pace.
notes: Daily recurrent attacks that build over minutes and resolve completely, with no thunderclap onset, meningism or neurological deficit, and a normal MRI with no blood on SWI.
Fixed-time attacks with complete resolution, no vomiting, positional or Valsalva features or progression, no papilloedema or focal signs, and a normal MRI with contrast.
Recurrent stereotyped attacks over months with full resolution; Horner's resolves between attacks; no neck pain, trauma or focal deficit.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man in general practice. Painless bright red blood on the paper after wiping, fullness after defaecation, chronic constipation and a low-fibre diet, with bleeding internal cushions and no prolapse on proctoscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Internal haemorrhoids fits: painless bright red blood on the paper after wiping, fullness after defaecation, chronic constipation and a low-fibre diet, with bleeding internal cushions and no prolapse on proctoscopy. Painless bright red blood on the toilet paper after wiping, not mixed with the stool, points to an anal canal source, most often internal haemorrhoids.
notes: No change in bowel habit, weight loss, abdominal pain or anaemia symptoms, with a normal haemoglobin and ferritin.
Normal digital rectal examination and normal lower rectal mucosa on proctoscopy, with no tenesmus.
Painless bleeding with no pain on defaecation, and no fissure on inspection or proctoscopy.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman in general practice. Pale foul-smelling diarrhoea, bloating, 3 kg weight loss, grouped vesicles on both extensor knees, a mother with Graves' and a twin with type 1 diabetes, and tTG-IgA 128 U/mL with normal total IgA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Coeliac disease fits: pale foul-smelling diarrhoea, bloating, 3 kg weight loss, grouped vesicles on both extensor knees, a mother with Graves' and a twin with type 1 diabetes, and tTG-IgA 128 U/mL with normal total IgA. Do not accept 'stress' for new fatigue with diarrhoea and weight loss: screen every system, and ask specifically about the stool, the skin and the periods.
notes: No blood or mucus, no mouth ulcers, normal CRP and ESR, and serology strongly positive for coeliac; faecal calprotectin, or ileocolonoscopy (with terminal ileal biopsy), with MR enterography or capsule endoscopy if needed, if duodenal histology is not typical.
Heavy periods do not explain the steatorrhoea, weight loss, low folate and vitamin D, or the strongly positive coeliac serology.
Her faecal elastase is normal at 410 and her pain does not radiate to the back.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man in the emergency department. Sudden maximal tearing central pain through to the back with syncope in a hypertensive smoker, a weak right radial with a 32 mmHg arm BP difference, an aortic regurgitation murmur, very raised D-dimer and a CT flap from the ascending aorta. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection
questions.why: Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection fits: sudden maximal tearing central pain through to the back with syncope in a hypertensive smoker, a weak right radial with a 32 mmHg arm BP difference, an aortic regurgitation murmur, very raised D-dimer and a CT flap from the ascending aorta. Sudden, maximal, tearing chest pain radiating to the back, especially with syncope, is aortic dissection until proven otherwise; descending dissection may give interscapular pain and some patients present with syncope alone.
notes: The pain is tearing and goes to the back rather than crushing to the jaw or arm, the ECG shows no ST elevation and is unchanged from 2024, and the small troponin rise can be explained by demand or coronary involvement by the dissection.
He has no calf symptoms, travel, immobility, previous clot or cancer, and the arm BP difference, murmur and CT findings explain everything.
There was no trauma, the pain is not pleuritic, the chest is resonant with equal breath sounds, and CT shows no pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man in general practice. Worsening left calf claudication, night rest pain eased by hanging the foot down, a punched-out pale ulcer on a bony prominence, absent left popliteal and pedal pulses, Buerger's angle 20 degrees, ABI 0.56 and toe pressure 24 mmHg in a smoker with diabetes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Infected diabetes-related foot ulcer or osteomyelitis
questions.why: Arterial ulcer fits: worsening left calf claudication, night rest pain eased by hanging the foot down, a punched-out pale ulcer on a bony prominence, absent left popliteal and pedal pulses, Buerger's angle 20 degrees, ABI 0.56 and toe pressure 24 mmHg in a smoker with diabetes. Ask about rest pain: night pain in the forefoot eased by hanging the foot down, with an ulcer, means chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and needs urgent vascular referral.
notes: No cellulitis, pus or odour, afebrile, probe to bone negative, and normal WCC and CRP.
Gradual worsening over a year, no sudden pain, coldness, numbness or weakness, and sensation and movement are normal.
The ulcer is painful, not on the sole, has no callus, and monofilament and vibration sensation are intact.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man in the emergency department. A 75-year-old with lifelong constipation and a low-fibre diet who suddenly passed a large volume of painless dark red blood with clots, has a normal anorectal examination and CRP, and whose colonoscopy shows extensive sigmoid and descending diverticula with no other source. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Diverticular bleeding fits: a 75-year-old with lifelong constipation and a low-fibre diet who suddenly passed a large volume of painless dark red blood with clots, has a normal anorectal examination and CRP, and whose colonoscopy shows extensive sigmoid and descending diverticula with no other source. Diverticular bleeding is sudden, painless and often large-volume, bright red or maroon with clots, in an older patient with constipation or a low-fibre diet. It usually stops by itself but can recur.
notes: No change in bowel habit, weight loss or tiredness, no rectal mass, normal MCV and ferritin, and no tumour or polyp on a complete colonoscopy (a negative screening FOBT 2 years ago gives little reassurance in a symptomatic patient).
No vascular lesions were seen on a complete colonoscopy and diverticula explain the bleed.
No lump, itch or prolapse, the blood was dark with clots and mixed with stool rather than on the paper, and no haemorrhoids on inspection or retroflexion.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman in the emergency department. One day of fever with worsening confusion, personality change and right arm weakness in an immunosuppressed woman with past cold sores, left temporal hypodensity on CT and HSV-1 PCR detected in a lymphocytic CSF. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis fits: one day of fever with worsening confusion, personality change and right arm weakness in an immunosuppressed woman with past cold sores, left temporal hypodensity on CT and HSV-1 PCR detected in a lymphocytic CSF. Fever with an altered mental state, personality change or focal signs is encephalitis until proven otherwise. Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly at once, without waiting for CT, LP or PCR.
notes: She has no headache, neck stiffness, photophobia or rash, and her CSF has a normal glucose, no organisms and a lymphocytic pattern.
She has no swinging fevers, seizures or ear, sinus or dental source, and CT shows no mass or collection.
She has fever and a progressive course over a day, no facial droop or dysarthria, an inflammatory CSF and a CT change outside a single arterial territory.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man on the ward. He woke with a congruous, macula-sparing left homonymous hemianopia and no other deficit; MRI shows an acute right calcarine infarct with a P2 occlusion; the ECG shows AF; and he had a transient left-sided visual episode 2 months ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Right posterior cerebral artery territory ischaemic stroke
Intracerebral haemorrhage in the right occipital lobe
Right middle cerebral artery territory infarct involving the optic
questions.why: Right posterior cerebral artery territory ischaemic stroke fits: he woke with a congruous, macula-sparing left homonymous hemianopia and no other deficit; MRI shows an acute right calcarine infarct with a P2 occlusion; the ECG shows AF; and he had a transient left-sided visual episode 2 months ago. Localise a field defect: one eye only is in front of the chiasm, bitemporal is the chiasm, and homonymous is behind the chiasm on the opposite side.
notes: No haemorrhage on the ED CT or on MRI susceptibility imaging.
The onset was sudden, on waking, and the MRI shows diffusion restriction in an arterial territory with an occluded P2 and no mass effect.
No face or arm weakness, sensory loss or neglect; the macula is spared; and the MRI shows the MCA territory and optic radiations are normal.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man in the emergency department. A thunderclap worst-ever headache while jogging, a sentinel headache 2 weeks ago, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, GCS 13 and subhyaloid (Terson) haemorrhages in a man with ADPKD and hypertension, with basal cistern blood and a 7 mm ACom aneurysm on CT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage fits: a thunderclap worst-ever headache while jogging, a sentinel headache 2 weeks ago, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, GCS 13 and subhyaloid (Terson) haemorrhages in a man with ADPKD and hypertension, with basal cistern blood and a 7 mm ACom aneurysm on CT. A thunderclap headache, maximal within seconds to a minute, is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Always ask about an earlier 'warning' headache, which is often mistaken for migraine.
notes: He has no focal deficit, and the CT shows no parenchymal haematoma.
The onset was sudden rather than over hours, he is afebrile at 37.3 °C, and he has no rash or infective symptoms.
He had no head injury or fall, and the CT shows no extra-axial collection.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man in the emergency department. Two hours of central pressure to the left arm and jaw on exertion with breathlessness, sweating and nausea, multiple risk factors, new ST depression in V4 to V6, I and aVL and hs-troponin T rising from 62 to 148 ng/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction fits: two hours of central pressure to the left arm and jaw on exertion with breathlessness, sweating and nausea, multiple risk factors, new ST depression in V4 to V6, I and aVL and hs-troponin T rising from 62 to 148 ng/L. Central pressure radiating to the arm and jaw, brought on by exertion and not relieved by rest, with breathlessness, sweating and nausea in a man with many risk factors is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise; get an ECG within 10 minutes.
notes: The pain built over minutes as a pressure, is not tearing and does not go to the back, the arm BPs are equal and the mediastinum is not widened.
No pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf swelling, immobility, surgery, travel or previous clot, and the ECG and troponin pattern fit coronary ischaemia.
The pain was not sudden or one-sided, breath sounds and percussion are equal, and the chest X-ray shows no pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man in the emergency department. Sudden left leg weakness and sensory loss with urinary incontinence, sparing the face and arm, still present at 2 hours after two 10-minute TIAs, in AF with missed apixaban doses, with a right A2 occlusion and ACA perfusion deficit on CT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Spinal cord or cauda equina compression
questions.why: Acute ischaemic stroke fits: sudden left leg weakness and sensory loss with urinary incontinence, sparing the face and arm, still present at 2 hours after two 10-minute TIAs, in AF with missed apixaban doses, with a right A2 occlusion and ACA perfusion deficit on CT. A sudden focal deficit still present after an hour, with ischaemia on imaging, is a stroke, not a TIA. Earlier brief episodes in the same territory were TIAs and are warnings that need same-day assessment.
notes: No headache, vomiting or drowsiness, and the non-contrast CT shows no haemorrhage.
He ate breakfast, has no adrenergic symptoms, and his bedside glucose is 8.4 mmol/L.
Only one leg is affected, with no back or radicular pain, intact saddle sensation, no retention on bladder scan, no sensory level, and an upgoing plantar with a vascular cause shown on CT.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man in general practice. A daily bilateral pressing headache of 5 to 6/10 that builds through the day, not worse with cycling, with neck and shoulder stiffness, tender pericranial muscles, thesis stress and long desk hours, and a normal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Tension-type headache fits: a daily bilateral pressing headache of 5 to 6/10 that builds through the day, not worse with cycling, with neck and shoulder stiffness, tender pericranial muscles, thesis stress and long desk hours, and a normal examination. Separate primary from secondary headache by grouping your red flag questions by diagnosis: SAH (thunderclap onset), meningitis (fever, rash, neck stiffness), raised pressure or tumour (progressive, worst on waking, worse with coughing or straining, vomiting), stroke or TIA, and head injury.
notes: Six weeks of daily headache in someone who is well, afebrile, with no rash, photophobia or meningism and full passive neck flexion.
Never on waking, not worse with coughing, straining or lying down, no vomiting, sharp discs with venous pulsations and a normal neurological examination.
The pain is bilateral, pressing and moderate, not throbbing, with no nausea, light or noise sensitivity or aura, and it is not worsened by activity.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man in general practice. Sudden-onset, self-terminating, fast irregular palpitations now daily, an irregularly irregular pulse with a pulse deficit, an ECG with no P waves, a regular pulse after the episode stopped, and heavy alcohol, smoking, hypertension, OSA and obesity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation fits: sudden-onset, self-terminating, fast irregular palpitations now daily, an irregularly irregular pulse with a pulse deficit, an ECG with no P waves, a regular pulse after the episode stopped, and heavy alcohol, smoking, hypertension, OSA and obesity. Ask the patient to tap out the palpitations: fast and irregular points to AF, fast and regular to SVT or VT, and a missed beat to ectopics.
notes: Narrow QRS complexes, no chest pain, breathlessness or fainting, and no ischaemic change on the ECG.
Sustained fast episodes lasting minutes to hours, and the ECG shows a continuous irregular rhythm without P waves rather than isolated early beats.
The rhythm he taps and the ECG are irregularly irregular, with no regular flutter waves.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man in the emergency department. Known COPD in a heavy current smoker, with breathlessness worse since last night, wheeze, a new yellow sputum, feeling hot, partial relief from the paramedics' bronchodilator, widespread wheeze, raised WCC and CRP, and hyperinflation with no consolidation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute heart failure or acute coronary syndrome
questions.why: Infective exacerbation fits: known COPD in a heavy current smoker, with breathlessness worse since last night, wheeze, a new yellow sputum, feeling hot, partial relief from the paramedics' bronchodilator, widespread wheeze, raised WCC and CRP, and hyperinflation with no consolidation. In a person with COPD, more breathlessness with wheeze and a change in sputum colour or volume is an exacerbation until proven otherwise; actively exclude pneumonia, pneumothorax, PE and cardiac causes in the history, the examination and the X-ray.
notes: No pleuritic pain, symmetrical expansion and breath sounds, trachea central, and no pneumothorax on X-ray.
Already anticoagulated with apixaban, no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, immobility or calf swelling, and a clear infective, wheezy picture.

Tightness is respiratory in character (not crushing, no radiation), ECG sinus tachycardia with no acute change, first hs-troponin below the 99th percentile (repeat pending), no orthopnoea or oedema, JVP not raised, and no oedema on CXR.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman in general practice. 50 pack-years, progressive exertional breathlessness, chronic white productive cough, wheeze, flare-ups with colds, hyperinflation with wheeze, and post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50 with FEV1 58% predicted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease fits: 50 pack-years, progressive exertional breathlessness, chronic white productive cough, wheeze, flare-ups with colds, hyperinflation with wheeze, and post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50 with FEV1 58% predicted. COPD is confirmed on spirometry by a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7; by COPD-X, an FEV1 of 40 to 59% predicted is moderate disease. A chest X-ray supports it and excludes other causes but cannot diagnose it.
notes: No weight loss, appetite change, night sweats, haemoptysis, hoarseness or lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hilar enlargement on the chest X-ray.
The tightness comes with wheeze and breathlessness, is not crushing, does not radiate and has no sweating or nausea.
Productive rather than dry cough, no fine crackles or clubbing, no interstitial change on X-ray, and obstructive rather than restrictive spirometry.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman in general practice. Lower abdominal pain before bowel motions with urgency, alternating loose and hard stools, bloating, triggers of stress and dairy, gastroenteritis 6 months ago, and normal bloods, coeliac serology, calprotectin and stool tests. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Irritable bowel syndrome fits: lower abdominal pain before bowel motions with urgency, alternating loose and hard stools, bloating, triggers of stress and dairy, gastroenteritis 6 months ago, and normal bloods, coeliac serology, calprotectin and stool tests. In chronic lower GI symptoms, screen every patient for red flags: rectal bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, fever, a mass, and a family history of colorectal cancer, IBD or coeliac disease. Rectal bleeding with a change in bowel habit warrants colonoscopy even in a young adult.
notes: No blood, weight loss, night symptoms or extraintestinal features, no right iliac fossa mass, and a normal CRP and calprotectin of 28.
Aged 26 with no rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia or family history, a normal examination and a normal calprotectin.
Negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA while eating gluten, and normal ferritin and folate.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman in general practice. Months of daytime sleepiness with unrefreshing sleep, chronic heavy snoring, poor concentration, BMI 36 with a 42 cm neck and crowded oropharynx, hypertension, T2DM, smoking, evening alcohol, ESS 15, STOP-Bang 5 and OSA50 6. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Obstructive sleep apnoea fits: months of daytime sleepiness with unrefreshing sleep, chronic heavy snoring, poor concentration, BMI 36 with a 42 cm neck and crowded oropharynx, hypertension, T2DM, smoking, evening alcohol, ESS 15, STOP-Bang 5 and OSA50 6. Separate sleepiness (dozing off) from fatigue (lack of energy) early. Sleepiness points to a sleep disorder such as OSA.
notes: No weight loss, night sweats, fevers, lumps or bleeding, and a normal blood count.
No cold intolerance, constipation or skin changes, normal reflexes and a normal TSH.
Regular periods and no hot flushes or night sweats.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man in the emergency department. A minor fall hitting the right side of his head 5 days ago, then 3 days of progressive right-sided headache on apixaban, now drowsier; crescentic mixed-density right collection crossing sutures with 8 mm midline shift. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Right subdural haematoma fits: a minor fall hitting the right side of his head 5 days ago, then 3 days of progressive right-sided headache on apixaban, now drowsier; crescentic mixed-density right collection crossing sutures with 8 mm midline shift. In every older person with a new or progressive headache, ask directly about falls or head injury and about anticoagulants. A trivial knock days earlier, with no loss of consciousness, is the typical story for a subdural haematoma.
notes: No loss of consciousness or lucid interval, no skull fracture, and the collection is crescentic and crosses the suture lines.
Gradual onset over days with no thunderclap, no neck stiffness or photophobia, and no subarachnoid blood on CT.
Clear history of head trauma, no morning or postural features or weight loss, and no mass on CT.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man in the emergency department. Fever, chills and constant diffuse abdominal pain since yesterday with ascites growing over 2 weeks, in untreated alcohol-related cirrhosis with ongoing drinking, and an ascitic neutrophil count of 1295 x10^6/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis fits: fever, chills and constant diffuse abdominal pain since yesterday with ascites growing over 2 weeks, in untreated alcohol-related cirrhosis with ongoing drinking, and an ascitic neutrophil count of 1295 x10^6/L. Fever, abdominal pain, worsening ascites, encephalopathy, AKI or a GI bleed in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites call for a diagnostic ascitic tap. SBP can be painless.
notes: Gradual onset, no guarding or rigidity, no previous surgery, ascitic protein 9 g/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L and LDH below the serum limit, and no organisms on Gram stain.
It does not explain the fever, rigors, WCC 13.8 or the ascitic neutrophil count.
The pain is generalised, not epigastric through to the back, there is no vomiting, and lipase is 40 U/L.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man in clinic. Crampy right iliac fossa pain, diarrhoea, mouth ulcers and 6 kg weight loss, with terminal ileal linear ulcers, cobblestoning, skip lesions, rectal sparing and a non-caseating granuloma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Colorectal cancer or small bowel lymphoma
questions.why: Ileocolonic Crohn's disease fits: crampy right iliac fossa pain, diarrhoea, mouth ulcers and 6 kg weight loss, with terminal ileal linear ulcers, cobblestoning, skip lesions, rectal sparing and a non-caseating granuloma. Structure a procedure explanation with IPBRAD: indication, procedure (before, during, after), benefits, risks including the risk of not having it, alternatives, and documentation. Find out what the patient knows first and check understanding throughout.
notes: Born in Australia with no travel or TB contact, non-caseating granuloma with no acid-fast bacilli, and a negative stool pathogen PCR.
Aged 25, no palpable mass, no mass at colonoscopy and no dysplasia or malignancy on biopsy.
No rectal bleeding, terminal ileal disease, skip lesions, a normal rectum and granulomas on histology.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman in the emergency department. Four months of exertional dyspnoea, 2-pillow orthopnoea, PND and ankle swelling a year after an anterior STEMI, with a raised JVP, S3, bibasal crackles, oedema, cardiomegaly and congestion on CXR and an NT-proBNP of 4850. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute coronary syndrome precipitating heart failure
questions.why: Decompensated biventricular heart failure fits: four months of exertional dyspnoea, 2-pillow orthopnoea, PND and ankle swelling a year after an anterior STEMI, with a raised JVP, S3, bibasal crackles, oedema, cardiomegaly and congestion on CXR and an NT-proBNP of 4850. Quantify breathlessness against the patient's baseline (distance, stairs or activities) and ask specifically about orthopnoea (number of pillows), PND and ankle swelling.
notes: No chest pain, a gradual 4-month course, a flat troponin (24 then 25) and an ECG unchanged from 12 months ago.
No weight loss, haemoptysis or hoarseness, and no mass or nodule on CXR.
No cough, sputum or wheeze, orthopnoea and PND with oedema, and no hyperinflation on CXR.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man in general practice. Eight years of type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.9% from metformin non-adherence, gradual symmetrical stocking sensory loss to mid-shin, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg and loss of protective sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Spinal cord or cauda equina compression
questions.why: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy fits: eight years of type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.9% from metformin non-adherence, gradual symmetrical stocking sensory loss to mid-shin, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg and loss of protective sensation. Glove-and-stocking sensory loss points to a length-dependent peripheral neuropathy, a dermatomal pattern to a root or cord lesion, and a single nerve territory to a nerve compression or injury.
notes: Against cord compression: no upper motor neuron signs (flexor plantars, no clonus, normal tone, knee reflexes not brisk) and no sensory level; against cauda equina: no back pain, no sphincter or saddle symptoms, and a gradual symmetrical stocking pattern rather than a saddle or radicular one.
He rarely takes the metformin, he is not vegetarian or vegan, and his B12, folate and MCV are normal.
He drinks only an occasional can of beer on weekends, and his GGT, LFTs and MCV are normal.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man in the emergency department. Five months of progressive breathlessness with 20 kg weight loss, night sweats, blood-tinged sputum, a hoarse voice, clubbing, a hard right supraclavicular node and 50 pack-years, with a large unilateral right effusion on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Malignant right pleural effusion fits: five months of progressive breathlessness with 20 kg weight loss, night sweats, blood-tinged sputum, a hoarse voice, clubbing, a hard right supraclavicular node and 50 pack-years, with a large unilateral right effusion on X-ray. In a smoker with progressive breathlessness, ask directly about weight loss, haemoptysis, hoarseness and night sweats, and quantify smoking in pack-years (20 a day for 50 years is 50 pack-years).
notes: The 5-month gradual course, no pleuritic pain or sick contacts, and a normal white cell count.
Haemoptysis, a hoarse voice and a supraclavicular node point more to a primary lung cancer.
Born in Australia with no TB travel, contacts or past TB, and the smoking history and node make cancer more likely.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman in the emergency department. Three weeks of constant burning forefoot pain that is worse lying flat and eased by hanging the leg, after years of claudication, with gangrene of three toes, absent right popliteal and pedal pulses, right ABI 0.28 and heavy cardiovascular risk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia of the right leg
questions.why: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia of the right leg fits: three weeks of constant burning forefoot pain that is worse lying flat and eased by hanging the leg, after years of claudication, with gangrene of three toes, absent right popliteal and pedal pulses, right ABI 0.28 and heavy cardiovascular risk. Ischaemic rest pain is constant forefoot and toe pain, worse lying flat or at night and eased by hanging the leg down. Present for more than 2 weeks, or with gangrene or an ulcer, it defines chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.
notes: She has no new numbness or weakness, power is 5/5 and her rhythm is regular, with a stable 3-week course.
Her calves are soft, non-tender and equal with no warmth or swelling, and the pain is in the toes and eased by dependency.
The current pain is constant at rest and there is tissue loss, so she has moved beyond claudication.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man on the ward. Day 5 after major orthopaedic surgery with little mobilisation, sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, HR 124, SpO2 92%, a swollen red right calf, Wells 9, and bilateral lower lobe emboli on CTPA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Acute pulmonary embolism fits: day 5 after major orthopaedic surgery with little mobilisation, sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, HR 124, SpO2 92%, a swollen red right calf, Wells 9, and bilateral lower lobe emboli on CTPA. Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after major orthopaedic surgery is PE until proven otherwise: always examine both legs for a DVT.
notes: Sharp right-sided pleuritic pain without radiation, sweating or nausea, no ischaemic change on the ECG, and two normal troponins.
Pain is not tearing and does not go to the back, BP is equal in both arms, and the aorta is normal on CT.
No cough or sputum, a clear chest on examination and no consolidation on CT.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man in the emergency department. Breathlessness and sharp left pleuritic pain straight after a fall onto the left side, with tracheal deviation to the right, distended neck veins, left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds, tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia, and complete left lung collapse with mediastinal shift on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Left tension pneumothorax fits: breathlessness and sharp left pleuritic pain straight after a fall onto the left side, with tracheal deviation to the right, distended neck veins, left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds, tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia, and complete left lung collapse with mediastinal shift on X-ray. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: breathlessness, hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and hyper-resonance with reduced or absent breath sounds. Decompress before imaging.
notes: Heart sounds are not muffled, the trachea is deviated, and the left chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds on one side; a normal cardiac silhouette does not exclude acute tamponade, so eFAST is still needed.
The left chest is hyper-resonant rather than dull, the X-ray shows no effusion or fluid level, the neck veins are distended rather than flat, and the Hb is normal.
No leg swelling, immobility, travel or previous clots, and the trauma and one-sided signs explain the picture.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man in the emergency department. He shared needles 2 months ago, had a prodrome of fever, arthralgia, urticaria and malaise, now has jaundice with dark urine and pale stools and a tender smooth liver, with ALT 1635 and HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc and HBeAg positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Paracetamol or other drug-induced liver injury
questions.why: Acute hepatitis B infection fits: he shared needles 2 months ago, had a prodrome of fever, arthralgia, urticaria and malaise, now has jaundice with dark urine and pale stools and a tender smooth liver, with ALT 1635 and HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc and HBeAg positive. Viral hepatitis has a prodrome (anorexia, malaise, fever, RUQ pain; urticaria and arthralgia especially in hepatitis B), then an icteric phase with dark urine, pale stools, itch and jaundice.
notes: No rigors, haemodynamically stable, normal WCC with only a mild CRP rise, transaminase rise far greater than the ALP rise, a viral prodrome, and no duct dilatation or stones on ultrasound.
He denies any paracetamol, overdose, other medicines or supplements, and the paracetamol level is undetectable.
The HCV antibody is negative, although this can be falsely reassuring in the window period, and the hepatitis B serology already explains the illness.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman in general practice. Returned from Thailand a month ago after eating street food without pre-travel vaccination, with a 2-week prodrome, then jaundice, a hepatocellular picture and a positive HAV IgM. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Acute hepatitis A infection fits: returned from Thailand a month ago after eating street food without pre-travel vaccination, with a 2-week prodrome, then jaundice, a hepatocellular picture and a positive HAV IgM. Dark urine and pale stools mean conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Always ask the 4 Ps (pee, poo, pruritus, pain) in jaundice.
notes: No gallstones or bile duct dilatation on ultrasound, ALT far higher than ALP, and a normal white cell count.
Normal haemoglobin and platelets, and a positive HAV IgM explains the picture.
Constant pain not related to food, no history of gallstones, and no stones or duct dilatation on ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman in the emergency department. RUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad), pale stools, dark urine and itch, cholestatic LFTs with WCC 17.8 and CRP 186, and an 11 mm common bile duct with a distal stone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Acute ascending cholangitis fits: rUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad), pale stools, dark urine and itch, cholestatic LFTs with WCC 17.8 and CRP 186, and an 11 mm common bile duct with a distal stone. RUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad) is acute cholangitis until proven otherwise. Confusion and hypotension (Reynolds' pentad) mean severe disease.
notes: Lipase 42 is normal, the pain does not go through to the back, and the visualised pancreas is normal.
She is jaundiced with obstructive features, Murphy's sign is negative, and the gallbladder wall is thin with no pericholecystic fluid.
No IV drugs, travel or unsafe sex, the LFTs are cholestatic with ALP and GGT raised more than ALT, and the bile ducts are dilated.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man in the emergency department. Two days of worsening headache with fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia and positive Kernig's sign in a man on prednisolone, with turbid neutrophilic CSF, high protein and a low glucose ratio. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Bacterial meningitis fits: two days of worsening headache with fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia and positive Kernig's sign in a man on prednisolone, with turbid neutrophilic CSF, high protein and a low glucose ratio. Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean meningitis until proven otherwise. Always ask about and look for a non-blanching rash.
notes: He is oriented with GCS 15, intact attention, no drowsiness, behaviour change, seizures or focal signs.
It was not a thunderclap or worst-ever, with no collapse, and has built over 2 days with fever; the CT is normal and the CSF has minimal red cells.
His CSF is turbid with neutrophils, a high protein and a low glucose, and he has a CRP of 214 with a raised lactate.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman in general practice. Fever of 39 °C, a worsening generalised headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and a positive Kernig's sign in an 18-year-old after a crowded festival with a shared tent and uncertain meningococcal vaccination; the CSF is neutrophilic with a low glucose, Gram-negative diplococci and a positive N. meningitidis PCR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Bacterial meningitis fits: fever of 39 °C, a worsening generalised headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and a positive Kernig's sign in an 18-year-old after a crowded festival with a shared tent and uncertain meningococcal vaccination; the CSF is neutrophilic with a low glucose, Gram-negative diplococci and a positive N. meningitidis PCR. Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. Ask about and look for a rash, but its absence does not exclude meningococcal disease.
notes: She is alert and oriented (GCS 15) with no seizures, behaviour change or focal signs, and the CSF is neutrophilic with organisms seen.
The headache built up over hours, she has a fever and a coryzal prodrome, and the CSF has no xanthochromia and only 5 red cells.
The CSF has 8500 neutrophils, a protein of 1.1 g/L, a glucose ratio of 0.24 and Gram-negative diplococci.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman in general practice. Five stereotyped attacks of severe, one-sided throbbing headache lasting 6 to 7 hours, with light and noise sensitivity and nausea, each preceded by about 20 minutes of fully reversible visual aura, with a normal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Migraine fits: five stereotyped attacks of severe, one-sided throbbing headache lasting 6 to 7 hours, with light and noise sensitivity and nausea, each preceded by about 20 minutes of fully reversible visual aura, with a normal examination. Ask how fast the headache started and whether it matches previous attacks. A gradual, stereotyped headache with a normal examination and no red flags (SNOOP) needs no imaging.
notes: The onset was gradual, it is the same as four previous attacks, and the neurological examination and fundi are normal.
She is afebrile, with no neck stiffness, negative Kernig's sign and no rash.
The visual symptoms are positive (dots, jumbled lines), spread gradually, resolve fully and are followed by headache, with no weakness, numbness or speech change and a normal examination.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man in general practice. Two months of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with LIF pain, weight loss, fatigue and erythema nodosum, and continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 25 cm with crypt distortion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Ulcerative colitis fits: two months of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with LIF pain, weight loss, fatigue and erythema nodosum, and continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 25 cm with crypt distortion. Chronic bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with weight loss in a young adult is inflammatory bowel disease until proven otherwise; IBS cannot be diagnosed with blood, weight loss, nocturnal stools or a raised calprotectin.
notes: Age 25, and colonoscopy found no mass, with no dysplasia on biopsy.
Continuous inflammation from the rectum, normal terminal ileum, inflammation confined to the mucosa, no granulomas and no perianal disease.
No travel, sick contacts or antibiotics, a 2-month course, and negative stool PCR, culture, C. difficile and parasite tests.

questions.stem: Dorothy, 71, is in ED resus with 2 mm ST elevation in V2 to V5, sepsis from a right lower lobe pneumonia, and a husband who died 4 days ago. She asks: "My daughter says people die of a broken heart. Is that what this is?" Which reply is best?
options: Yes, grief can cause broken heart syndrome, and it usually recovers fully with rest.
Likely a heart attack and chest infection; an urgent angiogram will check the arteries
No, that's a myth; this is your chest infection, and antibiotics should settle it.
We can't tell until a heart scan tomorrow, so tonight we'll treat the chest infection.
notes: Takotsubo can't be diagnosed until angiography shows no culprit lesion, so telling her it is broken heart syndrome is wrong and may lead her to refuse urgent reperfusion.
This dismisses her concern and ignores the anterior STEMI, which needs emergency angiography, not just antibiotics.
An echo can't exclude ACS, and putting reperfusion off until tomorrow misses the 90-minute target from first medical contact.
