Raising the arm narrows the costoclavicular space. That is why arm elevation brings on thoracic outlet symptoms rather than relieving them.
Resting the hand on the head does not meaningfully flex the neck. His cord is also normal, so canal space is not the cause of his pain.
questions.why: This is the shoulder abduction relief sign. Raising the arm shortens the path from the foramen to the limb, which reduces traction and tension on the compressed nerve root and so eases radicular pain. It points to radiculopathy rather than a shoulder problem.

questions.stem: Mr Pascoe, 63, has an MRI of his cervical spine for right arm radicular pain. It reports severe narrowing of the right intervertebral foramen at C5-6, between the C5 and C6 vertebrae. Which nerve root leaves the spinal canal through this foramen?
options: C5 root, since cervical roots exit below the pedicle of their numbered vertebra
C6 root, since cervical roots exit above the pedicle of their numbered vertebra
C7 root, since the root passes the disc and exits at the foramen one level down
C4 root, since roots exit one level above the cord segment they arise from
notes: Exiting below the numbered vertebra is the thoracic and lumbar pattern. The C5 root exits at C4-5, which is where his moderate stenosis is.
A root that passes the disc and exits a level lower is how a lumbar disc affects the traversing root. A foraminal lesion in the neck compresses the root that exits at that level.
Roots are named for the foramen they exit through, not for a mismatch with cord segments. The C4 root exits at C3-4.
questions.why: There are 8 cervical roots but only 7 cervical vertebrae. Each cervical root exits above the vertebra of the same number, so the C6 root leaves at C5-6 and C8 leaves at C7-T1. From T1 downwards, roots exit below their vertebra.

questions.stem: Jane, 62, sees you at the GP with 5 to 6 months of new constipation, straining, blood mixed through her stool and tiredness. Her brother was diagnosed with bowel cancer at 48. She says, "I was hoping to get one of those bowel test kits." What is the best response?
options: Give her the kit today and refer for colonoscopy only if the result is positive
Say it is likely her haemorrhoids again and give the kit for peace of mind
Explain the kit is for people without symptoms and she needs a colonoscopy
Give her the kit and suggest she repeats it in two years if it is negative
notes: Waiting for an FOBT result delays a colonoscopy she needs now, and a false negative could stop the referral altogether.
Blood mixed through the stool and a change in habit are not explained by haemorrhoids, and an FOBT does not suit a patient with symptoms.
This applies the screening interval to a patient with symptoms; she needs a diagnostic test now, not routine screening.
questions.why: An FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms. A patient with symptoms (change in habit, blood mixed in the stool) needs a diagnostic colonoscopy, because a negative FOBT does not rule out cancer and would falsely reassure her.

questions.stem: Jane's bloods show Hb 108 g/L, MCV 76 fL and ferritin 8 µg/L. TSH, calcium and kidney function are normal. You are referring her for an urgent colonoscopy. Which further investigation should also be arranged for her iron deficiency anaemia?
options: Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies, together with coeliac serology
Serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level to screen for cancer
CT colonography to image the whole colon and look for any extracolonic pathology
Faecal calprotectin to look for bowel inflammation
notes: CEA is too insensitive and nonspecific to diagnose cancer; it is used for staging and follow-up once cancer is confirmed.
CT colonography repeats the colonoscopy, cannot take biopsies and does not look at the upper GI tract.
Calprotectin helps tell IBD from IBS in diarrhoea; it does not look for an upper GI source of iron loss.
questions.why: Iron deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman needs both ends of the gut looked at: colonoscopy plus gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies, and coeliac serology. This finds upper GI cancer, peptic ulcer or coeliac disease, and two lesions can occur together.

questions.stem: Jane, 62, with iron deficiency anaemia (ferritin 8 µg/L), is started on oral ferrous sulfate while she waits for endoscopy. She is advised to take it on alternate days rather than twice daily. What is the main reason alternate-day dosing can improve absorption?
options: Daily iron fully saturates transferrin, so the surplus iron is then excreted in the bile
Iron is absorbed in the terminal ileum, which needs 48 hours between doses
Daily dosing suppresses erythropoietin, so less iron is taken up by marrow
Each dose raises hepcidin for about a day, blocking ferroportin in enterocytes
notes: Her transferrin saturation is 5%, far from saturated, and the body has no regulated way to excrete excess iron in bile.
Non-haem iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, not the terminal ileum.
Oral iron does not suppress erythropoietin; the limit on the dose schedule is gut absorption, not uptake by the marrow.
questions.why: An oral iron dose raises hepcidin for about 24 hours. Hepcidin breaks down ferroportin, the channel that moves iron out of duodenal enterocytes, so a dose taken the next day is poorly absorbed. Spacing doses avoids this and causes fewer GI side effects.

questions.stem: Jane's colonoscopy shows a tumour at the rectosigmoid junction, above the dentate line. Biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma, and the surgeon plans a resection with its regional lymph nodes. To which lymph nodes does this tumour first drain?
options: Superficial inguinal nodes in the femoral triangle
Nodes along the superior rectal vessels to the inferior mesenteric nodes
Internal iliac nodes along the middle rectal vessels and then the common iliac chain
Superior mesenteric nodes at the root of the small bowel mesentery
notes: Superficial inguinal nodes drain the anal canal below the dentate line, not a tumour at the rectosigmoid.
Drainage to the internal iliac nodes along the middle rectal vessels is mainly from the lower rectum, not the rectosigmoid junction.
Superior mesenteric nodes drain the midgut up to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon, not the hindgut.
questions.why: Lymph from the sigmoid and upper rectum drains alongside the superior rectal and inferior mesenteric vessels to the inferior mesenteric nodes. This is why the resection includes a high tie of the inferior mesenteric artery with its mesentery.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, has 3 months of fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation, with a resting heart rate of 56. In the examination you tell the examiner you will look for the reflex sign of hypothyroidism. Which technique best shows it?
options: Knee jerk with Jendrassik reinforcement, looking for a brisk, wide-amplitude response
Plantar response with a blunt stimulus, looking for an upgoing great toe
Ankle jerk with her kneeling on a chair, watching for a slow relaxation phase
Biceps jerk with her arm relaxed, looking for spread to finger flexion
notes: Brisk, wide-amplitude reflexes suggest hyperthyroidism or an upper motor neurone lesion, and reinforcement only helps when a reflex is hard to get.
An upgoing plantar is an upper motor neurone sign and plays no part in hypothyroidism.
Spread of a reflex to nearby muscles is an upper motor neurone sign; it does not show the delayed relaxation seen in hypothyroidism.
questions.why: Hypothyroidism slows the relaxation phase of the reflex (it is 'hung up'), not the contraction. The ankle jerk with the patient kneeling on a chair, feet hanging free, shows this best.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, of average build with no heart disease, has TSH 52 mIU/L, free T4 4.3 pmol/L and strongly positive anti-TPO antibodies. Her sodium and potassium are normal, and she has no pigmentation, postural drop or hypos. Which treatment plan is best?
options: Levothyroxine about 100 micrograms daily before breakfast; recheck TSH in 6 to 8 weeks
Levothyroxine 25 micrograms daily, increasing by 25 micrograms monthly on free T4 alone
Liothyronine 20 micrograms twice daily; recheck free T3 and TSH in 2 weeks
Levothyroxine about 100 micrograms daily with breakfast; recheck TSH in 2 weeks
notes: Starting low and titrating slowly is for older patients or those with ischaemic heart disease; here it just delays recovery, and TSH, not free T4 alone, guides the dose.
Liothyronine is not first-line replacement: its short half-life gives swings in T3, and levothyroxine is the standard treatment.
Food reduces levothyroxine absorption, and TSH has not reached steady state at 2 weeks, so the result would mislead dosing.
questions.why: A young patient without heart disease can start the full replacement dose of levothyroxine, about 1.6 micrograms/kg (around 100 micrograms), on an empty stomach. TSH takes about 6 weeks to settle, so check it 6 to 8 weeks after each dose change.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, has Hashimoto thyroiditis and an anaemia with Hb 104 g/L and MCV 118 fL. Her B12 and folate results are pending. A colleague suggests starting folic acid now to save time. Why is giving folic acid alone risky if she turns out to be B12 deficient?
options: It corrects the anaemia while B12-dependent nerve damage keeps progressing
It competes with B12 for uptake in the terminal ileum, worsening the deficiency
It drives such rapid red cell production that it causes severe hypokalaemia
It stimulates parietal cell autoantibodies and speeds up the atrophic gastritis
notes: Folate is absorbed in the proximal small bowel by a different mechanism, and it does not block uptake of the B12-intrinsic factor complex.
Hypokalaemia can occur when severe megaloblastic anaemia is treated, but it is not why folate alone is avoided. The worry is irreversible nerve damage.
Folic acid has no effect on the autoimmune process in pernicious anaemia.
questions.why: Folate can bypass the methylfolate trap and restore DNA synthesis, so the blood count improves. It cannot replace B12's role with methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in making myelin, so subacute combined degeneration progresses without being noticed.

questions.stem: Jenny, 34, has type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto thyroiditis and a macrocytic anaemia (MCV 118 fL). Pernicious anaemia is suspected. In this condition, autoimmune gastritis destroys the cells that make intrinsic factor. Which part of the gut is mainly affected?
options: Gastric antrum, where the gastrin-secreting G cells lie
Proximal duodenum, where B12 is transferred onto intrinsic factor
Terminal ileum, where the B12-intrinsic factor complex is absorbed
Gastric body and fundus, where the parietal cells lie
notes: The antrum is typically spared in autoimmune gastritis. Its G cells overproduce gastrin in response to the low acid.
B12 does bind intrinsic factor in the duodenum, but the intrinsic factor is made in the stomach. The duodenum is not the autoimmune target.
The terminal ileum is where B12 is absorbed, and it is affected in Crohn disease or resection. It is not the site of the lesion in pernicious anaemia.
questions.why: Parietal cells, which secrete acid and intrinsic factor, sit in the oxyntic mucosa of the gastric body and fundus. Autoimmune gastritis attacks this area and spares the antrum, so gastrin rises as acid output falls.

questions.stem: Abdul, 30, is in your GP room mid-attack with 10/10 strictly left orbital pain for 2 hours, rocking in his chair. His history fits cluster headache. You now tell the examiner what you are examining. Which examination step is most likely to show a sign that supports this diagnosis?
options: Fundoscopy of both eyes looking for papilloedema
Palpation of both temporal arteries for tenderness, nodularity and reduced pulse
Comparing pupil size and eyelid height on both sides in dim light
Passive neck flexion looking for meningism
notes: Fundoscopy is an essential red-flag screen for raised intracranial pressure, but here it is expected to be normal and does not support cluster headache.
Temporal artery palpation screens for giant cell arteritis, which is very unlikely at 30 and would not support cluster headache.
Checking for meningism screens for subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis. It is expected to be negative and gives no positive support for cluster headache.
questions.why: During an attack many patients have a partial Horner's on the side of the pain (miosis and mild ptosis), so compare the two pupils and lids. The difference shows best in dim light, because the small pupil fails to dilate.

questions.stem: Abdul, 30, has episodic cluster headache with a normal ECG and normal MRI brain. He comes to the GP clinic 15 minutes into a typical left orbital attack and wants relief now. Which acute treatment is most appropriate?
options: Oxygen 2 L/min via nasal prongs for 15 minutes
Oral sumatriptan 50 mg at onset, repeated after 2 hours if needed up to 200 mg daily
100% oxygen at 12 to 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask for 15 minutes
Oral ibuprofen 400 mg with paracetamol 1 g
notes: Low-flow oxygen through nasal prongs doesn't deliver a high enough concentration to abort a cluster attack.
Oral triptans are absorbed too slowly to help a cluster attack. The subcutaneous (6 mg) or intranasal route is needed.
Simple oral analgesics don't work for cluster attacks, and Abdul has already found paracetamol useless.
questions.why: High-flow 100% oxygen at 12 to 15 L/min through a non-rebreather for 15 minutes aborts many cluster attacks. Subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg is the other first-line option. Oral drugs act too slowly for attacks that peak quickly.

questions.stem: During his attacks, Abdul, 30, has a watering red left eye and a runny, blocked left nostril, on the same side as his left orbital pain. What mechanism best explains these features?
options: Trigeminal-autonomic reflex driving parasympathetic outflow via the facial nerve
Sympathetic overactivity arising from the superior cervical ganglion on the left side
Passive fluid leak from venous congestion of the left cavernous sinus
Mast cell histamine release in the left nasal and conjunctival mucosa
notes: Tearing and nasal secretion are parasympathetic functions. In cluster headache the sympathetic supply is actually underactive, which is why a partial Horner's syndrome appears.
Venous congestion of the cavernous sinus doesn't explain active glandular secretion, and Abdul's MRI showed normal cavernous sinuses.
Histamine release from mast cells is the mechanism of allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. It doesn't explain strictly one-sided features tied to a pain attack.
questions.why: Pain input from the trigeminal nerve activates the superior salivatory nucleus. Parasympathetic fibres then travel via the facial nerve (greater petrosal nerve) and pterygopalatine ganglion to the lacrimal gland and nasal mucosa, causing tearing, redness and rhinorrhoea on the same side.

questions.stem: During an attack, Abdul, 30, has mild drooping of his left upper eyelid and a small left pupil. Both resolve once the attack settles. This is a partial Horner's syndrome. Loss of sympathetic supply to which muscle causes the mild ptosis?
notes: The levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the oculomotor nerve. Paralysis of it causes marked or complete ptosis, not the mild droop of Horner's.
The orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids and is supplied by the facial nerve. Weakness of it causes incomplete eye closure, not ptosis.
The inferior tarsal muscle helps hold down the lower lid. Losing its supply slightly raises the lower lid, so it doesn't cause the upper lid droop.
questions.why: The superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle is smooth muscle with a sympathetic supply. It adds a few millimetres of upper lid elevation, so sympathetic loss gives only mild ptosis. Complete ptosis points to the levator and the oculomotor nerve.

questions.stem: Peter, 42, has 2 days of painless bright red blood on the toilet paper. Partway through your history he asks: "Could this be bowel cancer? My dad died of cancer." You have established that his father died of testicular cancer at 56 and that no one in the family has had bowel cancer or polyps. What is the best response?
options: Reassure him it is almost certainly haemorrhoids, so no further tests will be needed
Tell him his father's cancer puts him at high risk, so he needs urgent screening
Acknowledge his worry, say his dad's cancer doesn't raise his risk, explain the checks
Offer a home iFOBT kit today so he knows quickly whether a cancer is present in his bowel
notes: This is false reassurance: haemorrhoids found on proctoscopy don't clear the bowel above, and an adult with new rectal bleeding should still have a colonoscopy.
Testicular cancer is not linked to colorectal cancer risk, so this is wrong and needlessly alarming.
The iFOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms; he already has visible bleeding, and a negative result would not exclude cancer.
questions.why: Address the worry honestly: testicular cancer in a father does not raise his colorectal cancer risk. But new rectal bleeding still needs examination and colonoscopy, so explain the plan instead of offering blanket reassurance.

questions.stem: Peter, 42, has had about 4 days of painless bright red blood on the paper. Proctoscopy shows grade I internal haemorrhoids with fresh blood at 3 o'clock and normal lower rectal mucosa. Hb 151 g/L, ferritin 142 µg/L, CRP 2 mg/L. No change in bowel habit, no weight loss and no family history of bowel cancer. Alongside fibre, fluids and psyllium, what investigation should the GP arrange?
options: Colonoscopy referral to gastroenterology or colorectal surgery
iFOBT now, with colonoscopy referral only if it is positive
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to look for a colonic mass
No further tests unless bleeding persists after 6 months of fibre
notes: An iFOBT is for screening people without symptoms; with visible bleeding a positive result is expected and a negative one does not exclude a lesion.
CT is not the first-line test for the colonic mucosa; it can miss polyps and small cancers, and it cannot take a biopsy.
Waiting months before investigating new rectal bleeding risks delaying the diagnosis of a polyp or cancer above the reach of the proctoscope.
questions.why: A proctoscope sees only the anal canal and lower rectum, and finding haemorrhoids does not prove they are the only cause. Adults with new rectal bleeding, including those under 50, should be referred for colonoscopy.

questions.stem: Peter, 42, has had intermittent constipation for years and eats a low-fibre diet at work. Proctoscopy shows congested internal vascular cushions at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock that bleed but do not prolapse on straining. Which mechanism best explains how his haemorrhoids developed?
options: Portal hypertension opening portosystemic anastomoses in the anal canal over time
A tear in the anoderm from hard stool, with internal sphincter spasm
Obstruction and infection of anal glands in the intersphincteric space
Straining and hard stool engorging the cushions and stretching their supports
notes: Portal hypertension causes anorectal varices, a different condition, and Peter has no features of liver disease.
This is the mechanism of an anal fissure, which is painful and was not seen on proctoscopy.
This is how a perianal abscess and fistula form, which cause pain, swelling or discharge, not painless bleeding.
questions.why: Haemorrhoids are normal anal vascular cushions. Straining and hard stool slow venous outflow, engorge the cushions and push them down, which weakens the supporting connective tissue. The congested cushions then bleed and, in later grades, prolapse.

questions.stem: Peter's proctoscopy shows bleeding internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line, and his bleeding is painless. By contrast, an anal fissure or thrombosed external haemorrhoid below the dentate line is very painful. Which nerve carries pain sensation from the anal canal below the dentate line?
options: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4 parasympathetic)
Inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve)
Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1 to L2)
notes: Pelvic splanchnic nerves give visceral (autonomic) supply above the dentate line, where sharp somatic pain is not felt.
Sympathetic fibres from the inferior hypogastric plexus supply the rectum and upper anal canal, not the somatically sensitive anoderm.
The genitofemoral nerve supplies the scrotum and upper anterior thigh, not the anal canal.
questions.why: Below the dentate line the anoderm has somatic innervation from the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4), so lesions there hurt. Above it, the supply is visceral and autonomic and does not sense somatic pain, which is why internal haemorrhoids are painless.

questions.stem: Evelyn, 16, tells you in the ED, "I just can't stop throwing up. I think I've got gastro." She is breathing deeply and quickly but is alert. You have a few minutes of focused history. Which question is most likely to uncover the underlying diagnosis?
options: Have you had any diarrhoea, and has anyone at home or school been sick recently?
Is the pain worse if I press on the lower right side of your tummy?
Have you been thirstier, or weeing more often, over the last few weeks?
Have you had any headache, or any trouble with your vision?
notes: Worth asking to test her gastro theory, but a negative answer only makes gastro less likely. It does not point to the actual cause.
Screens for appendicitis, which doesn't fit her mild generalised soreness and wouldn't explain the deep, fast breathing.
Screens for raised intracranial pressure as a cause of vomiting, but it doesn't target the osmotic symptoms that point to DKA.
questions.why: Adolescents rarely mention polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia or weight loss unless asked. Vomiting plus these osmotic symptoms means DKA until proven otherwise, so check a bedside glucose and ketones early.

questions.stem: Evelyn, 16, weighs about 52 kg and has severe DKA (glucose 38.2 mmol/L, pH 7.05, HCO3 4, ketones 6.0, K 5.3). Her 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus has been given, and deficit fluids with potassium are running. Which insulin plan is most appropriate?
options: IV insulin bolus 0.1 units/kg, then an infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h started straight away
IV infusion 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, started about 1 h after fluids, no bolus
Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin 0.1 units/kg every 2 hours
IV infusion 0.1 units/kg/h, stopped once glucose falls below 15 mmol/L
notes: An insulin bolus is not recommended in paediatric DKA. It increases the risk of hypokalaemia and of rapid osmotic shifts.
Subcutaneous insulin is not appropriate in severe DKA with dehydration. Absorption is unreliable and the dose can't be adjusted hour by hour.
Insulin is needed until the ketosis clears. When glucose falls below about 15 mmol/L you add 5% glucose to the fluids and keep the insulin running.
questions.why: Paediatric DKA guidelines (RCH, ISPAD) use an IV insulin infusion of 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, started about an hour after fluids, with no bolus. A bolus speeds the falls in glucose, osmolality and potassium and may add to the risk of cerebral oedema.

questions.stem: Evelyn, 16, has severe DKA after 3 weeks of osmotic diuresis and a day of vomiting, yet her serum potassium is 5.3 mmol/L. Her normal ECG is a baseline before insulin starts. Which mechanism mainly explains why her serum potassium will fall quickly once the insulin infusion starts?
options: Insulin stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase, moving K+ into muscle and liver cells
Insulin raises aldosterone, increasing K+ secretion in the collecting duct
Insulin increases albumin binding of K+, lowering the free plasma fraction
Insulin blocks proximal tubular K+ reabsorption, causing a kaliuresis
notes: Insulin doesn't act mainly through aldosterone. The fall in K+ is a shift into cells, not a sudden rise in renal loss.
Potassium isn't meaningfully protein-bound. Albumin binding matters for calcium, not potassium.
Insulin doesn't block proximal tubular K+ handling. The fast fall comes from K+ moving into cells, not from urinary loss.
questions.why: Without insulin, and with acidosis, potassium shifts out of cells, so the serum level looks normal or high even though total body potassium is depleted. Insulin switches on Na+/K+-ATPase and drives K+ back into cells, so serum K can fall fast. That is why potassium goes into the fluids once K is below 5.5.

questions.stem: Six hours into DKA treatment, Evelyn, 16, complains of a worsening headache and becomes drowsy. Her heart rate falls to 58 and her BP rises. Her right pupil is now dilated and reacts sluggishly to light. Compression of which structure best explains the pupil sign?
options: Right abducens nerve, stretched over the petrous temporal apex during downward shift
Right cervical sympathetic chain, within the carotid sheath
Left optic tract, near the lateral geniculate body
Right oculomotor nerve, compressed by the uncus at the tentorial edge
notes: Abducens stretch is a false localising sign. It causes lateral rectus weakness with a convergent squint, not a dilated pupil.
Loss of sympathetic supply causes Horner's syndrome, with a small pupil (miosis) and ptosis, not a dilated one.
An optic tract lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, not a unilateral dilated, sluggish pupil.
questions.why: Cerebral oedema can push the medial temporal lobe (uncus) through the tentorial notch, compressing the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve. Its parasympathetic pupillary fibres run on the outside of the nerve, so a dilated, sluggish pupil appears early. This is an emergency: give mannitol or hypertonic saline at once.

questions.stem: You are examining the feet of Jack, 57, at his annual diabetes review in general practice. He reports a year of numb toes, "like I'm wearing socks". You now test protective sensation with a 10 g monofilament at standard sites on each foot. Which technique is correct?
options: Press firmly over any callus, as these sites carry the highest plantar pressure
Apply perpendicular until it bends, hold 1 to 2 seconds, eyes closed
Drag the filament lightly along the sole and ask whether he feels it scratch
Demonstrate on his toe first, then test each site while he watches the filament
notes: Callus dampens sensation and gives a false negative, so test next to callus, scar or ulcer and never over it.
Dragging tests a different stimulus with no set force, so the result cannot be read as loss of protective sensation.
Show him the feel on a sensate area such as the hand, not the foot being tested, and keep his eyes closed so he cannot guess from sight.
questions.why: The 10 g monofilament is pressed at right angles until it buckles, which delivers a fixed 10 g force. It is held about 1 to 2 seconds while the patient's eyes are closed, after a demonstration on the hand or sternum. If he cannot feel it, he has lost protective sensation.

questions.stem: Jack, 57, takes metformin XR 2 g and glargine 30 units nightly, injected into the same thigh site, which has lipohypertrophy. HbA1c is 9.4% (79 mmol/mol), eGFR 76 and uACR 6.8 mg/mmol. He has had two mild hypos when he skipped lunch. Along with fixing his injection technique, which is the best glucose-lowering change to make now?
options: Add gliclazide MR 30 mg orally once daily with breakfast
Add empagliflozin 10 mg orally once daily
Add sitagliptin 100 mg orally once daily
Increase glargine to 36 units subcutaneously at night
notes: A sulfonylurea on top of insulin makes hypos more likely in a man who already has them, and it does not protect the kidneys or heart.
A DPP-4 inhibitor lowers HbA1c only modestly and has no proven kidney or cardiovascular benefit, so it is not preferred with albuminuria.
Raising the dose while he injects into lipohypertrophy and is already having hypos risks severe hypos once he moves to healthy skin.
questions.why: With albuminuria (early diabetic kidney disease) and high cardiovascular risk, an SGLT2 inhibitor is preferred because it protects the kidneys and heart independently of glucose lowering. Consider reducing glargine and give sick-day advice (ketoacidosis risk).

questions.stem: Jack, 57, has type 2 diabetes with an eGFR of 76 and a uACR of 6.8 mg/mmol. You start an SGLT2 inhibitor, partly to slow his kidney disease, and warn him that his eGFR may dip a little at first. By what mechanism does this drug lower intraglomerular pressure?
options: It dilates the efferent arteriole, blocking angiotensin II action at its receptor site
It lowers glucose, reducing glycation of the glomerular basement membrane
It raises macula densa sodium delivery, causing afferent arteriolar constriction
It blocks aldosterone in the collecting duct, reducing sodium reabsorption
notes: Efferent arteriolar dilation is how ACE inhibitors and ARBs such as his perindopril work, not SGLT2 inhibitors.
The kidney benefit appears quickly and does not depend on glucose lowering, so long-term glycation is not the main mechanism.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone or finerenone work this way; SGLT2 inhibitors act in the proximal tubule.
questions.why: In diabetes, increased proximal sodium-glucose reabsorption means less sodium reaches the macula densa, so the afferent arteriole dilates and the glomerulus hyperfilters. SGLT2 blockade restores tubuloglomerular feedback, which constricts the afferent arteriole and lowers glomerular pressure.

questions.stem: Jack, 57, smokes, has diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and has stocking sensory loss in both feet. During his foot examination you assess for peripheral arterial disease and go to palpate the dorsalis pedis pulse. Where on the foot is this pulse best felt?
options: Behind the medial malleolus, between it and the calcaneal tendon
On the dorsum of the foot, just medial to the extensor hallucis longus tendon at midfoot
In front of the lateral malleolus, over the sinus tarsi
On the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon
notes: That is where you feel the posterior tibial pulse, the other foot pulse to check in this examination.
The artery runs lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, not medial to it.
Nothing large enough to palpate runs over the sinus tarsi; the dorsalis pedis is on the dorsum, well medial to this.
questions.why: The dorsalis pedis artery continues from the anterior tibial artery and runs on the dorsum just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, towards the proximal first intermetatarsal space. Ask the patient to extend the big toe to find the tendon.

questions.stem: Rachel, a 28-year-old lawyer seen in general practice, has had 2 months of fatigue, pale foul-smelling diarrhoea, 3 kg of unintended weight loss and an itchy rash on both knees. Near the end of the history she asks, 'Could this all just be stress?' You have not yet examined her or ordered any tests. What is the best response?
options: "It's probably burnout. Take two weeks off work and we'll see if things settle by then."
"Stress may play a part, but weight loss, pale stools and a rash need checking first."
"This isn't stress. I'm fairly sure you have coeliac disease."
"A psychologist referral would help us deal with the stress side first."
notes: Putting new fatigue with steatorrhoea and weight loss down to burnout misses an organic cause and gives false reassurance.
Naming a diagnosis before any examination or results is premature, and it may be wrong or frighten her.
Sending her for psychological care before investigating red-flag physical symptoms delays the diagnosis.
questions.why: Acknowledge her idea, then explain why it doesn't fit. Weight loss, steatorrhoea and a new rash are red flags for an organic cause, so they need examination and tests before anyone puts fatigue down to stress.

questions.stem: Rachel, 28, has steatorrhoea, weight loss and a vesicular rash on her extensor knees. tTG-IgA is 128 U/mL (upper limit 7), total IgA is normal and DGP-IgG is positive. She is still eating gluten. In Australian adult practice, what is the next step to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies (including bulb) while still eating gluten
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping, then start a gluten-free diet if either allele is present
Start a gluten-free diet now and confirm with a falling tTG-IgA at 6 months
Ileocolonoscopy with terminal ileal biopsies, followed by MR enterography
notes: HLA typing is useful when results are equivocal or the patient is already gluten-free. A negative result excludes coeliac disease, but a positive one cannot diagnose it, because about a third of the population carry these alleles.
Australian guidance does not accept a no-biopsy diagnosis in adults, and starting the diet first would make a later biopsy unreliable.
This is the workup for small-bowel Crohn's disease. It is kept for when duodenal histology is not typical, not used as the first step when coeliac serology is strongly positive.
questions.why: In Australian adults, coeliac disease is confirmed by duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytes, even when serology is very high. Take several D2 biopsies plus bulb biopsies while the patient is still eating gluten.

questions.stem: Rachel's duodenal biopsy is expected to show villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Her tTG-IgA is 128 U/mL. Which mechanism best explains how dietary gluten damages her small bowel mucosa?
options: IgE on mucosal mast cells binds wheat protein, causing degranulation and mucosal oedema
Lack of a brush-border peptidase lets undigested gluten injure enterocytes directly
Anti-gliadin IgA activates complement, causing vasculitis of the villous capillaries
tTG deamidates gliadin; HLA-DQ2/DQ8 presents it to CD4 T cells, injuring mucosa
notes: This describes IgE-mediated wheat allergy, which causes acute urticaria or anaphylaxis and does not cause villous atrophy.
Coeliac disease is not an enzyme deficiency. Gluten resists digestion in everyone, and the damage depends on an immune response restricted by HLA-DQ2/DQ8.
The antibodies are markers of the disease. The mucosal damage is driven by T cells, not by complement-mediated vasculitis.
questions.why: Coeliac disease is a T-cell-mediated enteropathy. Tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin peptides, which then bind HLA-DQ2/DQ8 strongly and activate gluten-specific CD4 T cells, causing villous atrophy. tTG is also the autoantigen behind the tTG-IgA test.

questions.stem: Rachel, 28, with probable coeliac disease, has a ferritin of 6 microgram/L and a low folate, but her vitamin B12 is normal. Which part of the gut is the main site of iron and folate absorption, explaining this pattern of deficiency?
notes: Gastric acid helps keep iron soluble, and the stomach makes intrinsic factor for B12, but neither iron nor folate is absorbed to a significant degree in the stomach.
The terminal ileum is where B12 and bile salts are absorbed. Disease there would lower B12, which is normal in Rachel.
The colon absorbs water and electrolytes, not iron or folate.
questions.why: Iron (via DMT1 on duodenal enterocytes) and folate are absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Coeliac disease affects this part most, so iron and folate fall while B12, absorbed in the terminal ileum, is often spared.

questions.stem: Giuseppe, 66, is in the ED with sudden tearing central chest pain going through to his back, and a brief blackout. You move on to a focused examination and tell the examiner each step. Which bedside step most directly checks whether a dissection has spread into the aortic arch branches?
options: Listen for a pericardial friction rub with him leaning forward
Feel for radio-femoral delay between the right radial and femoral pulses
Compare both radial pulses and measure the BP in both arms
Press on the sternum and costochondral joints for reproducible tenderness
notes: A rub is a sign of pericarditis and tells you nothing about blood flow in the arch branches.
Radio-femoral delay is the classic sign of coarctation. It compares an arm with a leg, so it cannot pick up a difference between the two arms.
Chest wall tenderness is a cluster question for musculoskeletal pain. It does not test for dissection, and finding it would not rule dissection out.
questions.why: A pulse deficit, or a systolic difference of more than 20 mmHg between the arms, shows the flap has involved the arch branches. It is a high-risk examination feature in the ADD-RS, so every patient with suspected dissection needs pulses and BP checked in both arms.

questions.stem: At 10:24 Giuseppe, 66, feels faint: BP 96/60 in the left arm, HR 112, CRT 4 s. Bedside echo shows a moderate pericardial effusion with early right atrial collapse, a dilated aortic root with a possible flap, and aortic regurgitation. The cardiothoracic registrar is aware. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Start an IV esmolol infusion aiming for a heart rate of about 60/min
Withhold BP-lowering drugs, give small fluid or blood boluses, expedite theatre
Drain the pericardial effusion to dryness by ED pericardiocentesis, then reassess BP
Give a rapid 2 L crystalloid bolus to bring the systolic BP above 140 mmHg
notes: Beta blockade removes the compensatory tachycardia in tamponade and can cause collapse, and he already has first-degree AV block on verapamil.
Draining a haemopericardium to dryness can raise aortic pressure and cause catastrophic re-bleeding. Only controlled, small-volume drainage is used, and only if he arrests or cannot reach theatre.
Pushing the systolic BP high with large volumes raises wall stress and the risk of rupture. The aim is permissive, low-volume resuscitation.
questions.why: Hypotension in type A dissection points to tamponade, rupture or acute aortic regurgitation. Stop anti-impulse therapy, give only enough fluid or blood to keep him perfused and conscious, and get him to surgery, because surgery is what treats the haemopericardium.

questions.stem: On arrival Giuseppe, 66, had a BP of 150/88 and a HR of 98. If he had stayed hypertensive with his dissection, anti-impulse therapy would start with an IV beta blocker and add a vasodilator only afterwards. What is the main physiological reason for this order?
options: A vasodilator alone lowers coronary perfusion pressure and causes myocardial ischaemia
Beta blockade prevents the cyanide toxicity caused by sodium nitroprusside
A vasodilator alone constricts the false lumen and stops branch vessel blood flow
A vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia, raising dP/dt and aortic wall stress
notes: Lowering BP in a controlled way to a systolic of 100 to 120 mmHg does not usually cause ischaemia. The order of the drugs is about the reflex response, not coronary perfusion.
Cyanide toxicity depends on the dose and duration of nitroprusside. Beta blockers do not prevent it.
Vasodilators do not constrict the false lumen. Branch malperfusion comes from the flap, not from the choice of drug.
questions.why: A fall in BP from a vasodilator triggers a baroreflex sympathetic surge, which raises the heart rate and the force of ventricular ejection (dP/dt). That increases shear stress on the torn aortic wall and can extend the flap. Beta blockade first blunts this response, with a target HR of about 60 and a systolic BP of 100 to 120 mmHg.

questions.stem: Giuseppe, 66, has a weak right radial pulse and a right arm systolic BP 32 mmHg lower than the left. His CT aortogram shows a flap that starts in the ascending aorta and extends into an arch branch, narrowing it with false lumen. Involvement of which artery best explains his right arm findings?
notes: The left subclavian artery supplies the left arm, so narrowing it would make the left arm read lower, not the right.
The right common carotid artery supplies the head and neck, not the arm. Its involvement would cause stroke symptoms, not a weak radial pulse.
The right vertebral artery branches off the subclavian and supplies the brain, so it does not carry blood to the arm.
questions.why: The brachiocephalic trunk is the first branch of the arch and divides into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries. Narrowing it lowers flow to the right arm, so the BP should be monitored in the left arm or through a left radial arterial line.

questions.stem: Markus Ore, 66, is in hospital with unstable angina. Before he goes home you give him his chest pain action plan for his GTN spray (400 micrograms). He asks: if the pain comes on at home and he has stopped, rested and used his spray, at what point should he call 000?
options: After three GTN doses taken 5 minutes apart have not relieved the pain
If the pain continues for 30 minutes despite resting and using GTN
If the pain is severe, is getting worse or has lasted 10 minutes
Only if he is also sweaty, breathless or feeling faint with the pain
notes: This is the older plan; waiting through three doses (about 15 minutes) delays reperfusion, and the current plan calls 000 at 10 minutes.
Thirty minutes of ongoing ischaemic pain is far too long to wait; heart muscle is being lost, and today's presentation began like this.
Many patients with MI have no associated symptoms, so waiting for them before calling an ambulance would delay care.
questions.why: The Heart Foundation action plan says stop and rest, use GTN, repeat after 5 minutes, and call 000 if the pain is severe, getting worse or has lasted 10 minutes. He should not drive or be driven to hospital.

questions.stem: At 10:40 Markus, 66, still has 6/10 central chest pain despite sublingual GTN and IV opioid, and an IV GTN infusion is starting. He has had aspirin. His repeat ECG shows no ST deviation, and his hs-troponin I at 40 minutes was 4 ng/L. What is the most appropriate plan for coronary assessment?
options: Repeat hs-troponin at 2 hours, then CT coronary angiography if it stays normal
Invasive coronary angiography within 2 hours, arranged with cardiology now
Admit for invasive angiography within 24 hours if the repeat troponin rises
Thrombolysis with tenecteplase now, as his pain is not responding to nitrates
notes: CT coronary angiography is for low to intermediate risk patients whose pain has settled, not for someone with ongoing ischaemic pain despite treatment.
The 24-hour timeline is for high-risk patients whose pain has settled; ongoing pain despite treatment needs angiography within 2 hours, without waiting for the troponin.
Fibrinolysis is only for STEMI. In NSTEACS it gives no benefit and adds bleeding risk, and his ECG shows no ST elevation.
questions.why: Ongoing ischaemic pain despite nitrates and opioid puts him in the very high-risk NSTEACS group, which needs invasive angiography within 2 hours whatever the troponin shows. Very high-risk features override a normal early troponin.

questions.stem: Markus, 66, has had stable exertional angina for 5 years. Over 3 weeks it has become crescendo, and today he has had over 30 minutes of crushing rest pain with a normal ECG and a normal early hs-troponin. Which process best explains the change from stable to unstable angina?
options: Plaque rupture or erosion with a non-occlusive, platelet-rich thrombus
Slow growth of a fixed fibrous plaque with no thrombus on its surface
Complete thrombotic occlusion of an epicardial artery with transmural necrosis
Higher myocardial oxygen demand from left ventricular hypertrophy
notes: A fixed plaque with no thrombus causes stable angina at a predictable workload; it does not explain sudden prolonged rest pain.
Complete occlusion with transmural infarction is the mechanism of STEMI, and that would show ST elevation and a rising troponin.
His ECG shows no LVH by voltage criteria, and higher demand alone does not explain an abrupt change to rest pain.
questions.why: In unstable angina an unstable plaque ruptures or erodes and a partly occlusive platelet-rich thrombus forms, so blood flow falls at rest without necrosis yet. This is why antiplatelets and anticoagulants are central to treatment.

questions.stem: Markus, 66, has ongoing ischaemic chest pain, but his 12-lead ECG recorded during pain shows no ST deviation. The examiner asks why you would also record posterior leads V7 to V9. Ischaemia in the territory of which artery is most often missed on the standard 12-lead ECG?
options: Left anterior descending artery (anterior wall and septum)
Right coronary artery (inferior wall and right ventricle)
Left main coronary artery (most of the left ventricle)
Left circumflex artery (lateral and posterior walls)
notes: LAD territory sits right under V1 to V4, so ischaemia there is usually well seen on the standard ECG.
RCA ischaemia usually shows in the inferior leads II, III and aVF, and right-sided leads can show the right ventricle.
Left main ischaemia usually gives widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR, so it is rarely silent.
questions.why: The circumflex supplies the lateral and posterior left ventricle, which the standard leads cover poorly, so circumflex ischaemia is often electrically silent. Posterior leads V7 to V9 (posterior axillary line, scapular line, paraspinal at the V6 level) help to show it.

questions.stem: Mary, 26, is in your GP clinic with 2 days of constant left calf pain and swelling. She takes the combined pill. While examining her, you tell the examiner you will check for calf swelling, which is one of the Wells score criteria. How should you measure it?
options: Measure both calves 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity and compare the two
Measure the left calf at its widest point and compare it with the expected norm
Measure both legs 10 cm above the medial malleolus and compare the two
Measure both thighs 15 cm above the upper pole of the patella and compare
notes: Wells compares one leg with the patient's other leg, not with a population norm, and the 'widest point' is a different spot on each leg, so the two measurements can't be compared.
This measures the lower leg near the ankle, not the calf. Ankle oedema is assessed as pitting oedema, which is a separate Wells item.
Thigh swelling isn't the calf criterion. 'Entire leg swollen' is a separate Wells item, and Mary's thighs were equal.
questions.why: In the Wells score, calf swelling counts only if the symptomatic calf is more than 3 cm bigger than the other leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity on both sides. Mary's 3.5 cm difference scores 1 point.

questions.stem: Mary, 26, has an ultrasound-confirmed acute left popliteal DVT that extends into her calf veins. She has no features of PE, her observations are normal, she is not pregnant, and her FBC, clotting and renal and liver function are normal (CrCl about 145 mL/min). You plan to treat her as an outpatient. Which anticoagulant regimen should she start today?
options: Rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily with food from day 1, continued for at least 3 months
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily from day 1, continued for 3 months
Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily with food for 21 days, then 20 mg daily with food
Warfarin 5 mg daily alone, adjusted to keep the INR between 2 and 3
notes: This is the maintenance dose. If you skip the 21-day loading phase at 15 mg twice daily, the dose is too low in the early weeks, when the risk of recurrence is highest.
This is apixaban's maintenance dose. Initial treatment needs 10 mg twice daily for 7 days first.
Warfarin alone isn't used to start treatment. It takes days to work and can briefly make clotting more likely, so it needs heparin overlap until the INR is 2 to 3.
questions.why: Acute VTE treated with a DOAC needs a higher-dose loading phase first. For rivaroxaban this is 15 mg twice daily for 21 days, then 20 mg daily, taken with food. Treat for 3 months for a provoked DVT, then review.

questions.stem: Mary, 26, has taken a combined oestrogen-containing oral contraceptive pill for 8 years and now has an acute left popliteal DVT. She has no personal or family history of VTE. By which mechanism does the oestrogen in her pill mainly raise her risk of venous thrombosis?
options: It raises the platelet count by stimulating hepatic thrombopoietin release
It damages the venous endothelium directly, exposing subendothelial collagen to platelets
It inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, which lowers protein C activity
It raises hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and lowers natural anticoagulants
notes: The combined pill does not cause a clinically meaningful thrombocytosis, and Mary's platelet count is normal.
Direct injury to the vessel wall is the endothelial part of Virchow's triad, as seen in trauma or surgery. It is not how oestrogen causes thrombosis.
Inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase is how warfarin works. Oestrogen does not do this.
questions.why: Oestrogen acts on the liver. It increases production of procoagulant factors (fibrinogen and factors II, VII, VIII and X) and reduces protein S and antithrombin, which causes acquired resistance to activated protein C. This makes the blood more likely to clot, the hypercoagulability part of Virchow's triad.

questions.stem: Mary's ultrasound shows occlusive thrombus in her left popliteal vein, while the femoral and common femoral veins above it are compressible and clot-free. You explain that the clot stops at the popliteal vein, before the vein continues as the femoral vein. At which landmark does the popliteal vein become the femoral vein?
options: The lower border of the popliteus muscle
The saphenous opening of the fascia lata
The adductor hiatus in adductor magnus
notes: This is where the popliteal vein begins: the anterior and posterior tibial veins join here. It isn't where the popliteal vein ends.
Here the common femoral vein becomes the external iliac vein, which is much higher than the popliteal–femoral junction.
Here the great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein, in the upper thigh. It isn't where the popliteal vein ends.
questions.why: The popliteal vein passes upwards through the adductor hiatus, a gap in the adductor magnus tendon, and from there it is called the femoral vein. Clot in the popliteal vein or above it counts as a proximal DVT.

questions.stem: You are taking consent from Michael, 38, for laparoscopic appendicectomy for CT-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis. When you get to alternatives, he asks: "Could I just have antibiotics instead of the operation?" What is the most accurate thing to tell him?
options: No, antibiotics don't treat appendicitis, so an operation is the only option
Yes, antibiotics cure it for good in almost everyone, so surgery is optional
Most settle at first, but about 3 in 10 need the operation within a year
Most settle, and only about 1 in 20 ever need the operation later
notes: Antibiotics alone are an evidence-based alternative for uncomplicated appendicitis, so you must offer it as an alternative for valid consent.
Overstates the benefit: around 3 in 10 need surgery within a year and more later, so antibiotics are not a reliable cure.
Understates the failure rate by about six times. Trials show close to 30% go on to appendicectomy within the first year.
questions.why: Antibiotics alone are a real option for uncomplicated appendicitis, but about 3 in 10 patients need appendicectomy within the first year (APPAC 27% at 1 year, CODA 29% by 90 days), and more by 5 years. Surgery is still recommended, and the choice is his.

questions.stem: It is 18:00. Michael, 38, has CT-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis diagnosed last night and is now on tomorrow morning's list, about 34 hours after diagnosis. All his observations are in the white zone and only paracetamol is charted. What is the best next step?
options: Call registrar to flag delay, ask about tonight's list and start IV antibiotics
Change nothing: he is stable, so wait for the morning list on paracetamol only
Call a rapid response because he may have a perforated appendix with sepsis tonight
Request a repeat CT abdomen tonight to look for perforation before theatre
notes: Stable obs do not make an untreated delay of more than 24 hours acceptable. He needs empirical IV antibiotics and the delay escalated.
No yellow or red zone criteria are met, so a rapid response is not triggered. He shows no clinical sign of perforation or sepsis.
Last night's CT already showed uncomplicated appendicitis. With him clinically stable, repeat imaging adds radiation and delay without changing management.
questions.why: A short delay (up to about 24 hours) is acceptable for uncomplicated appendicitis. Beyond that, flag it to the registrar to get him on tonight's list or first on the morning list, and start empirical IV antibiotics per eTG.

questions.stem: Michael, 38, describes pain that started as a dull, poorly localised ache around his umbilicus and hours later became sharp and settled in the right iliac fossa. What best explains why the early pain was felt around the umbilicus?
options: Somatic fibres from inflamed parietal peritoneum lying over the appendix
Vagal afferents from the appendix projecting directly to the periumbilical skin
Hindgut visceral afferents entering the spinal cord at the L1 segment
Midgut visceral afferents entering the cord at T10, referred to that dermatome
notes: This explains the later, sharp, well-localised RIF pain, not the early vague periumbilical ache.
Visceral pain afferents travel with sympathetic nerves to the spinal cord. The vagus does not supply the skin of the abdominal wall.
The appendix comes from the midgut, not the hindgut. Hindgut pain is referred to the suprapubic region.
questions.why: Stretch of the appendix (a midgut structure) is carried by visceral afferents travelling with sympathetic fibres to T10, so the pain is referred to the T10 (umbilical) dermatome. It localises to the RIF once the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum is inflamed.

questions.stem: During Michael's laparoscopic appendicectomy, the surgeon divides the mesoappendix, which carries the appendicular artery, before dividing the base of the appendix. The appendicular artery is usually a branch of which artery?
notes: The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon. It does not usually give rise to the appendicular artery.
The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon and is a long way from the appendix.
The inferior epigastric artery runs in the anterior abdominal wall. It matters for where ports are placed but does not supply the appendix.
questions.why: The appendicular artery comes off the ileocolic artery, the last branch of the superior mesenteric artery. It runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix and is divided or sealed during appendicectomy.

questions.stem: Mr Clayton, 75, is seen in general practice with a left foot ulcer. After 10 minutes supine, brachial systolic pressures are 142 mmHg (right) and 138 mmHg (left); left dorsalis pedis is 80 mmHg and left posterior tibial 74 mmHg. The examiner asks you to explain how his left ankle-brachial index is calculated. Which calculation is correct?
options: 74 ÷ 138: lower left ankle pressure ÷ left arm pressure
80 ÷ 142: higher left ankle pressure ÷ higher arm pressure
80 ÷ 138: higher left ankle pressure ÷ left brachial systolic pressure
74 ÷ 142: lower left ankle pressure ÷ higher arm pressure
notes: Using the lower ankle pressure and the arm on the same side both lower the ratio and break the standard method.
The higher brachial pressure of the two arms is used, not the arm on the same side, because the higher one best reflects central aortic pressure.
The higher of the two ankle pressures for that leg is the numerator, not the lower.
questions.why: The ABI for each leg is the higher of that leg's dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pressure divided by the higher brachial systolic pressure of the two arms. That gives 80/142 = 0.56 here, and 0.90 or below indicates peripheral arterial disease.

questions.stem: Mr Clayton, 75, smoker with type 2 diabetes, has a 6-week painful punched-out ulcer over the left first MTP joint, a month of night forefoot pain eased by hanging the foot down, absent left pedal pulses, ABI 0.56 and left toe pressure 24 mmHg. No erythema, pus or fever; CRP is normal. Nothing has changed suddenly. What is the most appropriate disposition from general practice?
options: Routine vascular outpatient referral with GP review in 3 months
Wound swab, oral cefalexin 500 mg QID for 5 days and practice nurse review in one week
Urgent vascular surgery referral to be seen within days for imaging
Same-day ED transfer for an intravenous heparin infusion
notes: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia carries a high amputation risk, so a routine referral with review months away is unsafe.
The ulcer shows no clinical signs of infection and CRP is normal, so a swab and antibiotics are not indicated and do nothing for the ischaemia.
An IV heparin infusion and same-day transfer are for acute limb ischaemia; his decline has been gradual, with normal sensation and movement.
questions.why: Rest pain or tissue loss with objectively confirmed arterial disease (toe pressure below 30 mmHg) is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia. He needs urgent vascular review within days for duplex imaging and to consider revascularisation, because the risk of amputation is high.

questions.stem: Mr Clayton, 75, has moderate left peripheral arterial disease. For a month he has woken at night with forefoot pain that eases when he hangs his foot over the side of the bed or walks around, and is worse with his leg up on a pillow. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?
options: Dependency adds hydrostatic pressure, raising foot perfusion pressure beyond the stenoses
Dependency pools venous blood in the foot, lowering tissue metabolic oxygen demand
Dependency triggers a venoarteriolar reflex that dilates the foot arterioles
Dependency increases shear stress, releasing nitric oxide that dilates the stenosed artery
notes: Venous pooling does not lower the foot's metabolic oxygen demand; the relief comes from higher arterial perfusion pressure.
The venoarteriolar reflex causes arteriolar vasoconstriction when the limb is dependent, not dilatation.
Atherosclerotic stenoses are fixed and respond little to endothelial nitric oxide; gravity, not flow-mediated dilatation, explains the relief.
questions.why: Beyond fixed stenoses the distal perfusion pressure is only just enough. Lying flat or elevating the leg removes the hydrostatic column, so flow falls below resting needs and the foot hurts. Hanging the foot down restores that pressure, which is why patients with rest pain sleep with the leg dependent or in a chair.

questions.stem: Mr Clayton, 75, has a year of left calf claudication. On examination his left femoral pulse is palpable (weaker than the right, with a bruit) but the left popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent. Disease in which artery best explains the loss of the popliteal pulse with calf claudication?
options: Internal iliac artery in the pelvis
Profunda femoris artery in the deep posterior thigh near its origin
Anterior tibial artery in the leg
Superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal
notes: Internal iliac disease causes buttock claudication and erectile dysfunction; this artery does not continue to the popliteal artery.
The profunda femoris supplies the thigh and is an important collateral route; blocking it alone would not abolish the popliteal pulse.
The anterior tibial artery arises below the popliteal artery, so disease there would leave the popliteal pulse intact.
questions.why: A palpable femoral pulse with an absent popliteal pulse puts the lesion between the two, in the superficial femoral artery. Its distal segment at the adductor canal and hiatus is the commonest site of lower-limb atherosclerosis and classically causes calf claudication.

questions.stem: You are doing a rectal examination on David, 75, in the ED for painless dark red rectal bleeding. He is in the left lateral position and the nurse is chaperoning. You have inspected the anus, asked him to strain, checked tone at rest and on squeeze, and swept the rectal wall and prostate. You now withdraw your finger. What is the next step?
options: Ask him to bear down again to check for a prolapsing internal haemorrhoid
Smear material from the glove onto an FOBT card to confirm the blood
Inspect the glove for blood, mucus and the colour of any stool
Remove your gloves, wash your hands and then tell him the findings
notes: Straining to look for prolapse belongs to inspection, before the finger goes in, and David has already done it.
FOBT is a screening test for people without symptoms. It adds nothing when the bleeding is visible, and a symptomatic patient needs colonoscopy whatever it shows.
This skips the glove inspection, and he should be cleaned and covered before you discuss the findings.
questions.why: Always look at the glove before you take it off. Fresh blood, melaena, mucus or pale stool tell you where the bleeding is coming from and what kind it is. Here it confirmed blood with no mass.

questions.stem: David, 75, is on day 2 after his colonoscopy and has had no further bleeding. HR 72, BP 118/74, no chest pain, no dyspnoea and no known cardiovascular disease. His repeat Hb is 96 g/L (baseline 141), MCV 89, ferritin 145 µg/L. What is the most appropriate plan for his haemoglobin?
options: No transfusion now; repeat FBC and transfuse only if Hb falls below 70 g/L
Transfuse 1 unit of red cells now, as he is over 65 with an Hb below 100 g/L, then recheck
Transfuse 2 units of red cells, as his Hb has fallen by more than 40 g/L
Give IV ferric carboxymaltose now, as his Hb has fallen below 100 g/L
notes: Age over 65 is not an indication. Transfusing at Hb 70–100 g/L in a stable patient with no symptoms gives no benefit and carries risks such as fluid overload.
The size of the fall is not a transfusion trigger. The decision depends on the current Hb, whether bleeding continues and his haemodynamics.
His ferritin of 145 µg/L shows his iron stores are full, so IV iron is not indicated for an acute blood loss anaemia.
questions.why: Australian Patient Blood Management guidance uses a restrictive threshold: transfuse at Hb below 70 g/L, or below 80 g/L with cardiovascular disease. A stable patient who is no longer bleeding and has Hb 96 g/L does not need red cells.

questions.stem: At 14:05, a few hours after passing a cupful of dark red blood, David, 75, has an Hb of 124 g/L against a baseline of 141 g/L. The sample is not haemolysed. Your registrar warns that this first result underestimates how much blood he has lost. Why does an early Hb underestimate an acute bleed?
options: The marrow releases reticulocytes within an hour, restoring red cell mass
Splenic contraction releases stored red cells into the circulation
Whole blood is lost, so Hb concentration falls only as fluid refills plasma
Plasma is lost faster than red cells from a bleeding vessel, concentrating blood
notes: The marrow takes days to raise its output, and the reticulocyte response peaks at about a week. It does not restore red cell mass within hours.
In humans the spleen stores very few red cells, so splenic contraction does not explain a near-normal early Hb.
Bleeding loses whole blood, not plasma first. The delay comes from the time it takes for haemodilution to happen.
questions.why: An acute bleed removes red cells and plasma in proportion, so the Hb concentration hardly changes at first. It falls over 24–72 hours as interstitial fluid shifts in, the kidneys retain fluid and IV fluids dilute the blood.

questions.stem: David's colonoscopy shows numerous sigmoid and descending colon diverticula and no other source of bleeding. You explain that diverticula bleed because of how closely they sit to the vessels in the colonic wall. Where do colonic diverticula typically form?
options: Through the taeniae coli, where the longitudinal muscle bundles are weakest and thinnest
At the antimesenteric border, between the two antimesenteric taeniae
At the rectosigmoid junction, where the taeniae spread into a continuous coat
Where vasa recta pierce the circular muscle, between mesenteric and lateral taeniae
notes: The taeniae are thick bands of longitudinal muscle. Diverticula form in the gaps between them, not through them.
The area between the two antimesenteric taeniae has no penetrating vasa recta and is largely spared.
Where the taeniae merge into a continuous longitudinal coat at the rectum, the wall is stronger. This is why rectal diverticula are rare.
questions.why: Diverticula push out through weak points where the vasa recta pass through the circular muscle. That leaves the vessel stretched over the dome of the sac, where it can rupture and cause a sudden, painless, large bleed.

questions.stem: In the ED you are taking consent from Jenny, 32, for an urgent lumbar puncture for suspected meningitis. She has a GCS of 15, sharp optic discs and no focal signs. She asks what is most likely to go wrong afterwards. Which complication should you tell her is the most common?
options: Brain herniation (coning) causing drowsiness and trouble breathing
A headache that is worse sitting or standing and eases lying flat
Bleeding around the spinal nerves causing weakness in the legs
Infection at the needle site spreading into the spine
notes: Herniation is a rare but serious risk and is very unlikely without signs of raised intracranial pressure, which Jenny does not have. Mention it, but not as the most likely problem.
A spinal haematoma is rare and is mainly a risk with anticoagulants or a bleeding disorder. Jenny has neither, and her clotting and platelets are normal.
Infection is a rare risk when aseptic technique is used and the skin is intact, as hers is. It is far less common than post-LP headache.
questions.why: Post-dural puncture headache is the most common complication of an LP. It is caused by CSF leaking through the dural hole, is typically postural (worse upright, better lying flat) and usually settles within days. Tell her about it first and say it can be treated.

questions.stem: At 11:00 the laboratory phones Jenny's CSF Gram stain through: Gram-positive diplococci. Jenny, 32, had dexamethasone 10 mg IV and ceftriaxone 2 g IV at 10:45. She is immunocompetent, not pregnant, has no allergies and has normal renal function. What is the most appropriate change to her antimicrobial therapy now?
options: Change ceftriaxone to IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly
Add IV amoxicillin 2 g 4-hourly to cover Listeria monocytogenes until cultures return
Add IV vancomycin (loading dose 25–30 mg/kg) until susceptibilities return
Add IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly to cover herpes simplex virus
notes: Switching to benzylpenicillin is only right once the isolate is shown to be susceptible. Doing it before then risks failing to treat a resistant pneumococcus.
Listeria is a Gram-positive bacillus. Empirical cover is only for people over 50, immunocompromised patients, pregnant women or people with alcohol dependence, and Jenny is none of these.
She has a bacterial CSF picture with organisms seen and no confusion, seizures or focal signs, so herpes simplex encephalitis cover is not indicated.
questions.why: Gram-positive diplococci in CSF mean Streptococcus pneumoniae, which may be resistant to penicillin or ceftriaxone. eTG advises adding vancomycin to ceftriaxone until susceptibilities are known, then narrowing treatment to fit the organism.

questions.stem: Jenny, 32, has pneumococcal meningitis. She received dexamethasone 10 mg IV straight after her LP, just before her first dose of ceftriaxone. A student asks why the steroid has to be given before or with the first antibiotic dose rather than later. What is the main mechanism behind its benefit?
options: It blunts the cytokine surge when antibiotics lyse bacteria and release cell wall products
It increases ceftriaxone penetration across the inflamed blood–brain barrier
It reduces CSF production by the choroid plexus, which stops intracranial pressure rising
It directly slows pneumococcal replication within the subarachnoid space
notes: Dexamethasone does the opposite: it makes the blood–brain barrier less leaky. This can reduce antibiotic penetration, especially of vancomycin.
Cutting CSF production is how acetazolamide works. It is not the reason dexamethasone helps in bacterial meningitis.
Corticosteroids have no antibacterial action. Their benefit comes from modifying the host's inflammatory response.
questions.why: When beta-lactams lyse bacteria, cell wall components and pneumolysin are released. These trigger TNF and IL-1 and subarachnoid inflammation, which damage the brain and cochlea. Dexamethasone given before or with the first dose damps this surge, reducing deaths and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis.

questions.stem: The ED registrar positions Jenny, 32, on her left side with her knees drawn to her chest for a lumbar puncture, aiming for the L3/4 interspace. Which surface landmark best guides her to the right level?
options: A line joining the posterior superior iliac spines (the sacral dimples)
A line joining the lower borders of the 12th ribs posteriorly
A line joining the inferior angles of the scapulae
A line joining the highest points of the iliac crests
notes: The posterior superior iliac spines lie at about S2, the level where the dural sac ends. That is too low for a standard LP.
The 12th ribs are near the T12/L1 level, which is at or above the conus medullaris. Going in there would risk injuring the spinal cord.
The inferior angles of the scapulae lie at about T7. This is a thoracic landmark and has nothing to do with lumbar puncture.
questions.why: The supracristal (Tuffier's) line joining the tops of the iliac crests crosses the L4 spinous process or the L4/5 interspace. The space just above it is L3/4. These levels are well below the conus medullaris, which ends at about L1/2 in adults, so the needle meets only nerve roots floating in CSF.

questions.stem: At 19:30 in ED, Jane (68) opens her eyes only to voice, is confused, and does not obey commands. You now need to find out whether she localises to a painful stimulus. Which stimulus should you use?
options: Fingertip pressure on the side of a finger with a pen
Trapezius pinch or supraorbital notch pressure
A loud command close to the ear with a shoulder shake
notes: Fingertip pressure is a peripheral stimulus. It tests eye opening and flexion, but she cannot localise to it because the hand being pressed is the one that would have to move.
Sternal rub is not a recommended standard stimulus: it is hard to apply consistently, causes bruising, and gives poorly reproducible responses.
A loud voice and a shoulder shake test eye opening to sound. They are not a painful stimulus and cannot test for localising.
questions.why: Localising means the hand moves to a central stimulus above the clavicle. Trapezius pinch or supraorbital pressure is the standard central stimulus. Fingertip pressure is used for eye opening and for telling flexion from extension.

questions.stem: Jane, 68, weighs 68 kg and has a creatinine of 72 µmol/L (eGFR 85). She takes weekly methotrexate and intermittent prednisolone. CSF HSV-1 PCR has just come back positive. Which antiviral regimen should she continue?
options: Aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8-hourly for at least 21 days
Aciclovir 5 mg/kg IV 8-hourly for 7 to 10 days
Aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 12-hourly for 14 days, then oral valaciclovir step-down
notes: 5 mg/kg is the dose for mucocutaneous HSV. It is too low for encephalitis, and 7 to 10 days is too short.
Oral valaciclovir does not reliably reach adequate CNS levels for acute encephalitis, and she is drowsy and vomiting. Treatment must be IV.
12-hourly dosing is a reduction for renal impairment, and her CrCl of about 70 mL/min does not need one. 14 days is also too short given her immunosuppression.
questions.why: HSV encephalitis is treated with IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for at least 14 days, extended to 21 days in immunosuppressed patients. Use her actual weight, keep her hydrated, and only reduce the dose for renal impairment.

questions.stem: Jane, 68, has HSV encephalitis and is charted aciclovir 680 mg IV 8-hourly. The ED nurse asks why you want her kept well hydrated, with her creatinine checked daily. What is the main mechanism of aciclovir kidney injury?
options: Afferent arteriolar constriction from reduced renal prostaglandins
Immune-complex glomerulonephritis from viral antigen deposition
Efferent arteriolar dilation lowering glomerular filtration pressure
Crystal precipitation in the renal tubules when urine flow is low
notes: Afferent constriction from prostaglandin inhibition is how NSAIDs injure the kidney, not aciclovir.
HSV does not cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, and this would not explain why hydration protects the kidney during aciclovir treatment.
Efferent arteriolar dilation is how ACE inhibitors and ARBs lower GFR. It has nothing to do with aciclovir.
questions.why: Aciclovir is excreted unchanged by the kidney and dissolves poorly in urine. High IV doses with low urine flow let it crystallise in the tubules and cause obstructive AKI. Hydration and slow infusion prevent this.

questions.stem: Jane, 68, with HSV-1 encephalitis, has a CT showing left anteromedial temporal hypodensity and pauses to find words. She also has right arm weakness (4/5) with pins and needles. Involvement of which area best explains her arm signs?
options: Left anteromedial temporal lobe and hippocampus
Left lateral precentral and postcentral gyri
Right lateral precentral and postcentral gyri
Left paracentral lobule on the medial surface
notes: The anteromedial temporal lobe has no primary motor or sensory cortex; it explains her memory, behaviour and language problems but not her arm signs.
A right-sided cortical lesion would affect the left arm, because the motor and sensory pathways cross.
The paracentral lobule on the medial surface represents the leg and foot, which are normal in Jane.
questions.why: The arm is represented on the lateral convexity of the primary motor (precentral) and sensory (postcentral) cortex. Corticospinal and sensory pathways cross, so right arm signs mean the left hemisphere is involved, beyond the medial temporal change seen on CT. MRI shows this spread better than CT.

questions.stem: Mr Kenneth, 78, is on the ward with a suspected stroke. He says, "It's my left eye, doctor. I keep bumping into things on that side." Acuity is 6/9 in each eye. He has not tried covering either eye. Which examination step best shows whether the problem is in his left eye or behind the optic chiasm?
options: Swinging light test, looking for a left relative afferent pupillary defect
Fundoscopy of the left eye, looking for retinal pallor, emboli or optic disc cupping
Confrontation visual fields in each eye separately, with the other eye covered
Red desaturation test, comparing colour vision in the left and right eyes
notes: The swinging light test is normal in occipital lesions because the pupil fibres leave the visual pathway before the lateral geniculate body, so a normal result cannot show a homonymous defect.
Fundoscopy looks for eye or optic nerve disease and is normal in a lesion behind the chiasm, so it cannot show the homonymous pattern of his field loss.
Red desaturation picks up optic nerve disease in one eye. Both eyes have intact central pathways, so the test would be normal and would not localise his defect.
questions.why: Testing each eye on its own shows the pattern of field loss. If the left half-field is missing in both eyes up to the vertical midline, the defect is homonymous and the lesion is behind the chiasm on the right. Patients often blame the eye on the side of the hemianopia.

questions.stem: Mr Kenneth, 78, has an acute right PCA infarct with no haemorrhage on MRI and newly found atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VA 5). Creatinine is 98 micromol/L (eGFR 63) and his FBC and coagulation are normal. He has had aspirin since ED. The stroke team is planning his long-term antithrombotic therapy. Which regimen is most appropriate?
options: Aspirin 100 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily for 21 days, then one antiplatelet alone
Apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily, stopping the aspirin once he is anticoagulated
Apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily, continuing aspirin 100 mg daily alongside it
Warfarin with enoxaparin bridging, aiming for an INR of 2.0 to 3.0
notes: Short-term dual antiplatelet therapy is for minor non-cardioembolic stroke or TIA. Antiplatelets alone do not adequately prevent stroke from AF.
He needs at least two dose-reduction criteria for 2.5 mg twice daily and has none. Adding aspirin to a DOAC raises the bleeding risk without reducing stroke.
DOACs are preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF, and heparin bridging after an acute infarct increases the risk of haemorrhagic transformation.
questions.why: A cardioembolic stroke from AF needs an oral anticoagulant, and a DOAC is preferred. He has none of the apixaban dose-reduction criteria (age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more), so he takes 5 mg twice daily. The stroke team times the start by infarct size.

questions.stem: Mr Kenneth, 78, has an acute right occipital infarct. His MR angiogram shows an abrupt right P2 occlusion with no stenosis in the neck vessels, and his ECG shows atrial fibrillation that was not present two years ago. Where did the embolus most likely form, and by what mechanism?
options: Left atrial appendage, from blood stasis after loss of coordinated atrial contraction
Left ventricle, from mural thrombus forming over a dyskinetic, ischaemic wall segment
Right atrium, with the clot crossing to the left heart through a patent foramen ovale
Carotid bifurcation, from rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with thrombus on top
notes: Left ventricular mural thrombus follows a myocardial infarction or cardiomyopathy. His ECG shows no ischaemic change and the mechanism in AF is atrial stasis.
A paradoxical embolus needs a venous clot and a shunt. Neither is suggested here, and AF itself explains a left atrial source.
His neck vessels show no stenosis, and carotid emboli usually travel to the MCA, not the PCA, which is mostly supplied by the vertebrobasilar system.
questions.why: In AF the atria quiver instead of contracting, so blood stagnates in the blind-ended left atrial appendage and thrombus forms there (Virchow's stasis). The clot can embolise into the systemic arteries, here a branch of the posterior cerebral artery.

questions.stem: Formal perimetry in Mr Kenneth, 78, shows a complete left homonymous hemianopia that is congruous between the two eyes, with sparing of the central 5 degrees. His pupils, acuity and fundi are normal, and he has no limb weakness, sensory loss or neglect. Where along the visual pathway is the lesion most likely?
options: Right optic tract, between the optic chiasm and the lateral geniculate body
Right Meyer's loop, the inferior optic radiation in the temporal lobe
Right superior optic radiation, passing deep through the parietal lobe
Right primary visual cortex, above and below the calcarine fissure
notes: Optic tract lesions give an incongruous hemianopia that splits the macula, and often a relative afferent pupillary defect, because the pupil fibres are still in the tract.
A Meyer's loop lesion gives a contralateral superior quadrantanopia, not a complete hemianopia, and usually comes with other temporal lobe signs.
