A parietal radiation lesion gives an inferior quadrantanopia that splits the macula, often with sensory loss or neglect, and he has neither.
questions.why: Homonymous defects become more congruous the further back the lesion sits, and macular sparing is typical of the occipital cortex. The occipital pole, where central vision is represented, has a collateral MCA supply in addition to the PCA, so central vision survives a PCA infarct.

questions.stem: Clark Kent, 40, is in ED. His first words are that this is the worst headache of his life. He is a bit muddled and answers short, simple questions best. Which single history question best tells you whether this is a thunderclap headache that needs urgent investigation for subarachnoid haemorrhage?
options: Where exactly in your head is the pain right now?
Did you see flashing lights or zigzags before the pain began?
How quickly did the pain reach its worst after it started?
Is the headache worse when you cough, sneeze or strain?
notes: SAH headache can be anywhere, often generalised or occipital, so the site does not separate thunderclap headache from other severe headaches.
This asks about migraine aura. Having no aura does not rule out SAH, and aura does not tell you how fast the headache came on.
Headache that is worse with coughing or straining is a feature of raised ICP or a mass lesion. It does not define a sudden-onset thunderclap headache.
questions.why: A thunderclap headache is defined by its onset: it reaches maximum intensity within seconds to a minute. Treat it as SAH until proven otherwise, whatever its site or character.

questions.stem: Clark Kent, 40, has an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage from a 7 mm ACom aneurysm with early hydrocephalus. Neurosurgery is coming to place an EVD and plan securing of the aneurysm. His coagulation is normal and his eGFR is 70. Which medication order should you chart to reduce the risk of a poor outcome from delayed cerebral ischaemia?
options: Nimodipine 60 mg orally or via NG tube every 4 hours for 21 days
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV every 8 hours until the aneurysm is secured
Dexamethasone 8 mg IV every 12 hours for 7 days
Glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to a systolic BP below 120 mmHg
notes: Antifibrinolytics reduce rebleeding but do not improve functional outcome and may increase ischaemic complications, so they are not routine.
Corticosteroids have no proven benefit in aneurysmal SAH and cause hyperglycaemia. Raised ICP here is from hydrocephalus, not vasogenic oedema.
GTN dilates cerebral vessels and can raise ICP. Pushing SBP below 120 lowers cerebral perfusion pressure; neurosurgery or ICU should set the BP target.
questions.why: Oral or NG nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days improves outcome after aneurysmal SAH by reducing delayed cerebral ischaemia. If it causes hypotension, split the dose to 30 mg 2-hourly rather than stopping it.

questions.stem: At 15:25 Clark's GCS falls from 13 to 11. His BP rises to 204/100, his HR falls to 48 and his breathing becomes irregular. CT showed early hydrocephalus. His potassium is 4.2 and his only regular medicine is amlodipine. What best explains the fall in his heart rate?
options: Hypokalaemia from repeated vomiting slowing sinoatrial node firing
Amlodipine building up with reduced kidney function and slowing AV conduction
Catecholamine-induced myocardial stunning causing complete heart block
Baroreceptors sensing the surge in BP and triggering reflex vagal slowing
notes: His potassium is normal at 4.2. Hypokalaemia tends to cause tachyarrhythmias and ectopy, not sinus bradycardia.
Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine that is cleared by the liver and does not slow the SA or AV node; it more often causes reflex tachycardia.
Neurogenic stunned myocardium in SAH causes ECG changes and LV dysfunction with hypotension, not this pattern of hypertension, bradycardia and falling GCS.
questions.why: Rising ICP lowers cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP − ICP). Brainstem ischaemia drives a sympathetic surge that raises MAP to protect perfusion, and carotid and aortic baroreceptors respond with vagal bradycardia (the Cushing response). This is why you do not chase the BP down.

questions.stem: The nurse looking after Clark, 40, who has SAH, hydrocephalus and a falling GCS, is told to report a new unilateral dilated, unreactive pupil as a sign of transtentorial (uncal) herniation. Why does this herniation dilate the pupil?
options: The expanding aneurysm presses directly on the optic chiasm
The abducens nerve is stretched over the petrous temporal apex
Sympathetic fibres on the internal carotid artery are compressed
The oculomotor nerve is compressed against the tentorial edge
notes: Pressure on the chiasm causes a bitemporal field defect, not a fixed dilated pupil. The pupil light reflex is mostly spared.
Abducens stretch from raised ICP causes a lateral rectus palsy (false localising sign), not pupil dilation.
Damage to the sympathetic fibres causes Horner's syndrome with a small (miotic) pupil, not a dilated one.
questions.why: In uncal herniation the medial temporal lobe pushes the oculomotor nerve (CN III) against the free edge of the tentorium. Its parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres run on the outside of the nerve, so they are hit first and the pupil on that side becomes fixed and dilated.

questions.stem: Bill, 70, is in the ED with 2 hours of central chest pressure, 5/10. BP 148/86, HR 94. You have screened for aortic dissection and plan to ask the nurse to give sublingual GTN. Which question must you ask Bill before the GTN is given?
options: "Have you taken Viagra, Cialis or a similar tablet in the last two days?"
"Have you ever had a stomach ulcer, black stools or vomited blood in the last year?"
"Have you ever reacted to the X-ray dye used for scans?"
"Which puffers do you use for your COPD, and how often?"
notes: Bleeding and ulcer history is the screen you do before aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors and anticoagulants. It has no bearing on GTN.
Contrast allergy matters before coronary angiography, not before sublingual GTN.
His inhalers matter if a beta blocker is being considered. They are not a contraindication to nitrates.
questions.why: PDE5 inhibitors taken with nitrates can cause severe, refractory hypotension. Before any GTN, ask about sildenafil or vardenafil (within 24 h) and tadalafil (within 48 h), and check that systolic BP is above 90.

questions.stem: Bill, 70, 92 kg, has an NSTEMI: new ST depression in V4 to V6 and hs-troponin T rising from 62 to 148 ng/L. Creatinine clearance is about 73 mL/min, with no bleeding risk. Cardiology agree to enoxaparin. Which regimen should you prescribe?
options: Enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg (about 140 mg) subcut once daily
Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg (about 90 mg) subcut once daily
notes: This is a VTE prophylaxis dose. It gives no therapeutic anticoagulation for an acute coronary syndrome.
Once-daily 1.5 mg/kg is a VTE treatment regimen. It is not the dose used in acute coronary syndrome.
Once-daily 1 mg/kg is the renally adjusted dose for CrCl below 30 mL/min. Bill's clearance is about 73.
questions.why: For NSTEACS the therapeutic enoxaparin dose is 1 mg/kg subcut 12-hourly when creatinine clearance is 30 mL/min or more. The interval only drops to once daily when CrCl is below 30.

questions.stem: Bill, 70, has ongoing ischaemic chest pain. His ECG shows new horizontal ST depression of 1.5 mm in V4 to V6 and 1 mm in I and aVL, with no ST elevation in any lead, including V1 to V3. Potassium is 4.6 mmol/L. What best explains the ST depression?
options: Transmural infarction with injury through the full wall thickness of the left ventricle
Subendocardial ischaemia in the layer furthest from epicardial supply
A reciprocal change from ST elevation in the posterior wall
Repolarisation changes caused by a raised serum potassium
notes: Transmural injury produces ST elevation, and Bill has none.
Posterior MI causes reciprocal ST depression in V1 to V3, which Bill does not have; his is in V4 to V6.
His potassium of 4.6 mmol/L is normal, and hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves, not horizontal ST depression.
questions.why: The subendocardium is at the far end of the coronary circulation and is squeezed hardest during systole, so it becomes ischaemic first. Subendocardial injury causes ST depression that does not reliably localise the culprit artery, whereas transmural injury causes ST elevation.

questions.stem: Bill, 70, describes central chest pressure radiating down the inner left arm and into his jaw. You explain to the examiner that this is referred pain from ischaemic myocardium. Which spinal cord segments receive the cardiac pain afferents that explain the arm radiation?
options: C3 to C5, via afferents travelling in the phrenic nerves
T10 to L1, via afferents travelling with the lesser and least thoracic splanchnic nerves
T1 to T4, via afferents travelling with the cardiac sympathetic nerves
Nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla, via the vagus nerve
notes: Phrenic afferents (C3 to C5) carry pain from the pericardium and diaphragm to the shoulder tip, as in pericarditis. They do not carry myocardial ischaemic pain.
T10 to L1 receive visceral afferents from the lower gut and pelvic organs. They do not explain pain in the arm.
Vagal cardiac afferents mainly carry reflex and baroreceptor information to the brainstem, not the pain that is referred to the arm.
questions.why: Cardiac pain afferents run with the sympathetic cardiac nerves to the T1 to T4 segments. There they converge with somatic afferents from the chest wall and the medial arm (T1, and T2 via the intercostobrachial nerve), so the pain is felt in those areas.

questions.stem: You are examining Adam, 74, in general practice for worsening breathlessness. On auscultation you hear a harsh ejection systolic murmur, loudest at the right 2nd intercostal space. Which next step best shows the examiner that this is aortic stenosis?
options: Roll him onto his left side and listen at the apex with the bell in held expiration
Listen at the left lower sternal edge during deep inspiration
Listen over both carotids with the diaphragm while he holds his breath
Listen in the left axilla with the diaphragm in held expiration
notes: Left lateral position with the bell at the apex brings out the low-pitched diastolic rumble of mitral stenosis.
Louder in inspiration at the left lower sternal edge points to a right-sided lesion such as tricuspid regurgitation.
Radiation to the axilla is typical of mitral regurgitation, not aortic stenosis.
questions.why: The aortic stenosis murmur radiates along the direction of flow into the carotids. Listen over the carotids with the patient holding his breath so breath sounds do not mask it.

questions.stem: Adam, 74, has exertional breathlessness, chest tightness and syncope, with orthopnoea and PND. His echo shows a calcified trileaflet aortic valve, peak velocity 4.6 m/s, mean gradient 52 mmHg, AVA 0.7 cm² and LVEF 60%. He asks how it will be fixed. What is the definitive management?
options: Optimise antihypertensives and diuretics, then repeat the echo and review in 3 to 6 months
Heart team assessment for aortic valve replacement (TAVI or SAVR) with a tissue valve
Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as the definitive treatment of the stenosis
Surgical aortic valve replacement with a mechanical valve and lifelong warfarin, INR 3.0
notes: Surveillance echo suits asymptomatic disease. Once severe aortic stenosis causes symptoms, medical therapy does not change survival.
Balloon valvuloplasty gives only short-lived benefit and restenosis is early, so it is used as a bridge or palliation, not as definitive treatment.
At 74 a tissue valve is preferred, because a mechanical valve needs lifelong warfarin and carries a higher bleeding risk in older patients.
questions.why: Severe aortic stenosis with symptoms is a Class I indication for valve replacement, because without it the outlook is poor. At 74 the heart team weighs TAVI against SAVR, and a bioprosthetic (tissue) valve is preferred.

questions.stem: Adam, 74, has severe calcific aortic stenosis. Twice in recent months, walking uphill, he became dizzy and briefly blacked out, then recovered at once. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with no heart block. What is the main mechanism of his exertional syncope?
options: Fixed outflow obstruction stops cardiac output rising as exercising muscle vasodilates
An exercise-triggered vagal surge causing bradycardia and venous pooling
Calcific emboli from the valve briefly blocking cerebral arteries
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation from left atrial stretch that reduces ventricular filling
notes: A vasovagal faint usually follows a trigger such as standing or pain and comes with a prodrome. It is not typically brought on by exertion in a patient with a fixed obstruction.
Emboli cause focal deficits that last as long as the TIA or stroke, not a global blackout with instant recovery on exertion.
He is in sinus rhythm with no palpitations. AF would also not explain a blackout brought on reliably by exertion.
questions.why: On exertion, resistance in the exercising muscles falls. The stenosed valve fixes stroke volume, so cardiac output cannot rise to match, blood pressure falls and cerebral perfusion drops.

questions.stem: Adam, 74, is told his narrowed aortic valve may be replaced 'through a tube from the groin' (transfemoral TAVI). A student is asked to palpate the femoral pulse that would be used for access. Where is the common femoral artery best palpated?
options: At the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, above the deep inguinal ring
Just lateral to the pubic tubercle, at the superficial inguinal ring
Medial to the femoral vein, deep to the lacunar ligament
At the mid-inguinal point, midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis
notes: The midpoint of the inguinal ligament (halfway from ASIS to pubic tubercle) marks the deep inguinal ring. It lies slightly lateral to the artery.
The superficial inguinal ring, beside the pubic tubercle, is where the spermatic cord leaves the canal, not where the artery runs.
The artery lies lateral to the femoral vein. The space medial to the vein, near the lacunar ligament, is the femoral canal.
questions.why: The common femoral artery is felt at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis, just below the inguinal ligament. Order from lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, then the empty space and lymphatics (NAVEL).

questions.stem: Nancy, 51, has COPD and uses home oxygen at 2 L/min. In general practice she tells you her breathlessness has been getting worse over a week. You are taking a focused history. Which question best tells you how severe this exacerbation is?
options: "How breathless do you feel right now, on a scale from 0 to 10, compared with last week?"
"Do you get more breathless when you lie flat at night?"
"What can you do now, and how much oxygen do you need, compared with usual?"
"Did the breathlessness come on suddenly, or over several days?"
notes: A 0 to 10 score is subjective and has no baseline, so it does not show how far she has dropped from her usual function.
Orthopnoea is a cluster question to screen for heart failure. It does not measure how severe the COPD exacerbation is.
Onset (sudden or gradual) helps tell PE or pneumothorax apart from an exacerbation, but it does not measure how severe her breathlessness is.
questions.why: In COPD, measure breathlessness by what the patient can do and how much oxygen they need, compared with their own baseline. Nancy now needs oxygen almost all the time and needs it to walk from her bed to the living room.

questions.stem: Nancy, 51, has an infective COPD exacerbation: purulent sputum, temperature 38.2 °C, WCC 13.4, CRP 62, and no consolidation on chest X-ray. She has a penicillin allergy (rash). Her GP starts treatment before transfer to ED. Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
options: Doxycycline 200 mg orally first dose, then 100 mg daily, 5 days in total
Moxifloxacin 400 mg orally daily for 10 days, starting once sputum culture is back
notes: Amoxicillin is a first-line choice for most patients, but Nancy has a penicillin allergy, so doxycycline is the better option.
Ciprofloxacin covers Streptococcus pneumoniae poorly and is not recommended for exacerbations treated in the community.
Moxifloxacin is kept for pneumonia in patients with severe penicillin allergy. It is not needed for this exacerbation, and 10 days is too long.
questions.why: In a COPD exacerbation with purulent sputum, eTG recommends amoxicillin or doxycycline for 5 days. With a penicillin allergy, use doxycycline: 200 mg for the first dose, then 100 mg daily, 5 days in total.

questions.stem: Nancy, 51, has severe COPD, an SpO2 of 88% on 2 L/min and a fever, and she is waiting for an ambulance. A colleague suggests a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min. You explain that oxygen should be titrated to 88 to 92%. What is the main mechanism by which high-flow oxygen causes hypercapnia in COPD?
options: Removing the hypoxic drive to breathe, sensed by the central chemoreceptors in the medulla
Reversing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which worsens ventilation-perfusion mismatch
Raising tissue metabolic rate, so more carbon dioxide is produced
Oxygen toxicity damaging type II pneumocytes, so surfactant is lost
notes: Loss of hypoxic drive plays only a small part, and that drive is sensed mainly by the peripheral (carotid body) chemoreceptors, not the central ones.
Extra oxygen does not meaningfully raise the amount of carbon dioxide the tissues produce.
Oxygen toxicity takes hours to days of very high oxygen levels to develop and does not explain carbon dioxide retention.
questions.why: High-flow oxygen reverses hypoxic vasoconstriction, so blood flows back to poorly ventilated alveoli. Dead space rises and PaCO2 goes up, with a smaller added contribution from the Haldane effect. Loss of hypoxic drive is a minor factor.

questions.stem: Nancy's chest X-ray report says she is hyperinflated, with 8 anterior ribs visible above the right hemidiaphragm in the midclavicular line. In a normal adult on a well-inspired erect PA film, the dome of the right hemidiaphragm meets about which anterior rib?
notes: Eight anterior ribs is what Nancy's film shows, and it is a sign of hyperinflation, not a normal finding.
A diaphragm this high suggests a poor inspiration, lung volume loss or diaphragm splinting, not a normal film.
Ten anterior ribs would mean severe hyperinflation. The normal figure of about 10 counts posterior ribs, not anterior ones.
questions.why: On a well-inspired PA film the right hemidiaphragm normally meets about the 6th anterior rib (roughly the 10th posterior rib). More than 6 or 7 anterior ribs above it, with flattened domes, suggests hyperinflation, as in Nancy's COPD.

questions.stem: Jeoff, 53, a dairy farmer seen in a rural GP clinic, likely has a large bowel obstruction. He had adenomas removed 5 years ago, missed his 3-year surveillance colonoscopy, and his father had colon cancer. While you explain the hospital plan he asks, "Be straight with me, Doc. Is it cancer?" What is the best response?
options: "It's very unlikely to be cancer, so try not to worry about that at all right now."
"Cancer is one possibility; the scan and camera test in hospital will tell us."
"With your history, I'm afraid this is almost certainly a bowel cancer."
"That's for the surgeons to discuss with you; I can't comment on that."
notes: This is false reassurance. With his adenomas, missed surveillance and family history, cancer is a real possibility, and his trust is lost if it turns out to be cancer.
This is premature and alarming. A diverticular stricture or a volvulus could equally cause this, and the diagnosis needs imaging.
This dodges a direct question, which leaves him anxious and damages rapport. You can be honest about the uncertainty without overstepping.
questions.why: When a patient asks directly, be honest without guessing at a diagnosis. Say that cancer is possible (along with a stricture or a twist), then explain in plain English how CT and colonoscopy will find the cause.

questions.stem: Jeoff, 53, is transferred to the regional ED with suspected large bowel obstruction: sudden left lower quadrant pain, gross tympanic distension, no flatus, late bilious vomiting and an empty rectum. He has sigmoid diverticulosis and previous adenomas. Which investigation best confirms the obstruction and identifies its level and cause?
options: Water-soluble contrast enema under fluoroscopy to show the level
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
notes: An X-ray may show dilated colon or a coffee-bean sign, but it is less sensitive and cannot reliably show the cause, ischaemia or staging.
A contrast enema can tell mechanical obstruction from pseudo-obstruction, but it has largely been replaced by CT and shows nothing outside the bowel lumen.
Endoscopy is used later to decompress a confirmed volvulus or to biopsy a lesion. Going straight to it without CT risks perforation and misses complications.
questions.why: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the key test in suspected bowel obstruction. It confirms LBO, shows the transition point and the cause (tumour, stricture or volvulus with a whirl sign), and detects ischaemia, perforation, caecal dilatation and metastases.

questions.stem: Jeoff, 53, has a suspected sigmoid large bowel obstruction. The surgical registrar warns that if his ileocaecal valve is competent, the colon becomes a closed loop and the caecum is the usual site of ischaemia and perforation. What best explains why the caecum is most at risk?
options: Its larger diameter gives the highest wall tension at a given pressure (Laplace)
It is furthest from the obstruction, so intraluminal pressure is highest there in the loop
It is a watershed zone between the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries
Its thick muscular wall contracts hardest against the obstruction and tears
notes: Pressure is roughly the same throughout a closed loop. The caecum fails because of its radius, not because it is further from the blockage.
The colonic watershed areas are the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and the rectosigmoid (Sudeck's point), not the caecum, which is supplied by the ileocolic artery.
The caecum is thin-walled, not thick, which adds to its risk. Strong muscle contraction is not the mechanism of perforation.
questions.why: By Laplace's law, wall tension is proportional to pressure times radius. In a closed loop the pressure is roughly the same throughout, so the caecum, which is the widest and thin-walled, carries the most tension. This compromises mucosal perfusion and leads to ischaemia and perforation.

questions.stem: Jeoff, 53, presents with sudden left lower quadrant pain and gross abdominal distension that developed within a day while he was milking. Sigmoid volvulus is on the differential alongside an obstructing cancer or a diverticular stricture. Which anatomical feature allows the sigmoid colon to twist on itself?
options: Retroperitoneal fixation of the sigmoid colon to the left psoas muscle
Convergence of the taeniae coli into a complete layer at the sigmoid
A long sigmoid mesocolon attached by a narrow base to the pelvic wall
A persistent mesentery holding the sigmoid close to a mobile caecum
notes: Retroperitoneal fixation would stop the bowel twisting. The descending colon is retroperitoneal and rarely volvulises, whereas the sigmoid colon has a mesentery.
The taeniae coli merge into a continuous longitudinal muscle layer at the rectosigmoid junction and rectum. This does not make the sigmoid colon mobile.
A mobile caecum on a persistent mesentery is the cause of caecal volvulus, which is a different and right-sided condition.
questions.why: The sigmoid colon is intraperitoneal and hangs on a long, mobile sigmoid mesocolon with a narrow root. It can therefore rotate around its mesenteric axis, causing a closed-loop obstruction and compromising its blood supply from the sigmoid branches of the inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: Mr Rodriguez, 65, is in ED with sudden left leg weakness and numbness. You have established he was last known well at 09:30 today and that he takes apixaban, which he often forgets. A code stroke has been called. Which further history item most directly decides whether he can have thrombolysis?
options: Whether he has had similar brief episodes of leg weakness before
When he last ate or drank anything by mouth
The exact time and date of his last apixaban dose
Whether he smokes or uses recreational drugs such as cocaine
notes: His earlier TIAs matter for the diagnosis and for urgent secondary prevention, but they do not decide whether he can be thrombolysed.
He must stay nil by mouth until a swallow screen, but the time of his last meal has no bearing on reperfusion eligibility.
Smoking and cocaine are risk factors to deal with in secondary prevention, but neither stops him having thrombolysis.
questions.why: A DOAC taken in the last 48 hours rules out thrombolysis unless a drug-specific level shows no relevant effect. So the timing of the last dose, together with the last known well time, must be pinned down early.

questions.stem: Mr Rodriguez, 65, has a right A2 occlusion and no haemorrhage on CT. Onset was 09:30 and it is now 12:00. His last apixaban dose was at 7 pm last night. INR 1.1, APTT 33 s, platelets 236. An apixaban-calibrated anti-Xa level is pending. Which statement best guides the decision on thrombolysis?
options: Thrombolyse now, as the normal INR and APTT show no significant residual apixaban effect
Withhold thrombolysis unless the apixaban anti-Xa level shows no relevant drug effect
Give idarucizumab to reverse the apixaban, then proceed with thrombolysis
Thrombolyse now, because more than 12 hours have passed since his last apixaban dose
notes: INR and APTT are not reliable for apixaban, so normal values do not show that the drug has cleared.
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only. Reversing a DOAC just so you can thrombolyse is not standard practice.
The usual cut-off is 48 hours unless a drug-specific level is reassuring. Seventeen hours after the last dose, he may still have a meaningful anticoagulant effect.
questions.why: Apixaban taken within 48 hours contraindicates thrombolysis unless a drug-calibrated anti-Xa level shows no relevant effect under the local protocol. A normal INR and APTT do not exclude a clinically important apixaban effect.

questions.stem: Mr Rodriguez, 65, has an acute right anterior cerebral artery stroke. He has wet himself twice without warning since onset. He can pass urine normally, the bladder scan shows no retention, and saddle sensation is intact. Which mechanism best explains his incontinence?
options: Detrusor areflexia with overflow from loss of sacral parasympathetic supply
Detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia from interruption of the suprasacral spinal cord pathways
Urethral sphincter weakness from loss of pudendal nerve motor supply
Loss of cortical inhibition of the pontine micturition centre (uninhibited detrusor)
notes: An areflexic bladder overflows with a large residual volume, as in cauda equina syndrome, but his bladder scan shows no retention.
Dyssynergia comes from a spinal cord lesion between the pons and the sacral cord and causes incomplete emptying. His lesion is cortical, so the pontine coordination of voiding still works.
Pudendal nerve damage causes stress incontinence, usually with saddle sensory loss. His saddle sensation is intact.
questions.why: The medial frontal and paracentral cortex, supplied by the ACA, normally keeps the pontine micturition centre in check. When this is lost, the bladder empties in full, coordinated contractions without warning, and there is no retention.

questions.stem: Mr Rodriguez, 65, has a CT angiogram showing abrupt occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery in the proximal A2 segment. Isolated ACA territory infarcts are uncommon, about 2% of ischaemic strokes. Why does an A2 occlusion cause infarction when an A1 occlusion is often tolerated?
options: A2 lies distal to the anterior communicating artery, so the other ACA cannot cross-fill
A2 lies distal to the posterior communicating artery, so PCA inflow cannot reach the A2
A2 gives off the lenticulostriate arteries, which are end arteries without collaterals
A2 has no leptomeningeal anastomoses with MCA branches, unlike the A1 segment
notes: The posterior communicating artery joins the internal carotid artery to the PCA. It is not part of the ACA's route of supply.
The lenticulostriate arteries come mainly from the M1 segment of the MCA and supply deep structures, not the medial cortex where the leg is represented.
The distal ACA cortical branches do have leptomeningeal anastomoses with the MCA and PCA. That is part of why he has salvageable penumbra on perfusion imaging.
questions.why: The anterior communicating artery joins the two A1–A2 junctions. If A1 is blocked, the other ACA can still fill the distal territory, but a blockage beyond ACom (A2) loses this protection, so the paracentral lobule infarcts.

questions.stem: Sylvie, 23, has iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 86 g/L) from heavy menstrual bleeding and is starting treatment in general practice. You are safety netting before she leaves. Which bleeding pattern should you tell her means she needs to go to the emergency department?
options: Passing clots larger than a 50-cent coin on the first day of a period
A period that lasts longer than 7 days
Soaking a pad or tampon every hour for 2 hours or more
Needing to get up overnight to change pads or tampons
notes: Large clots are a marker of heavy menstrual bleeding, which she already has, but they do not on their own mean acute, dangerous loss.
Periods longer than 7 days suggest heavy menstrual bleeding (hers last 8 days), but this is the chronic problem being treated, not an emergency.
Overnight changes help define heavy menstrual bleeding in the history, but she already does this, so it cannot be her trigger to go to ED.
questions.why: Soaking a pad or tampon every hour for 2 hours or more (or heavy bleeding with dizziness or fainting) means acute heavy loss and needs urgent review in ED. The other features show chronic heavy menstrual bleeding and are managed in general practice.

questions.stem: Sylvie, 23, has Hb 86 g/L, MCV 68 fL, ferritin 4 µg/L and a normal CRP. Resting HR is 104 with a small postural drop, but she has no chest pain, no syncope and no active heavy bleeding. She has never taken iron. Which is the most appropriate first-line iron replacement?
options: Oral iron, about 100 mg elemental iron daily or on alternate days
IV ferric carboxymaltose infusion this week, because her Hb is below 90 g/L
Red cell transfusion of 1 unit, then oral iron
notes: An Hb below 90 g/L is not on its own a reason for IV iron; it is used when oral iron fails, is not tolerated or is not absorbed, or when a rapid rise is needed.
Transfusion is not needed for a stable patient with chronic iron deficiency, and it exposes her to transfusion risks for no benefit.
IM iron is painful, can stain the skin permanently and is not recommended, now that oral and IV options are available.
questions.why: Oral iron (about 100 mg elemental daily or on alternate days, with vitamin C and away from tea, coffee and dairy) is first line in a stable patient. IV iron is kept for intolerance, failure, malabsorption or when a rapid rise is needed.

questions.stem: Sylvie, 23, with ferritin 4 µg/L, is starting oral iron. Your GP supervisor suggests she take about 100 mg elemental iron on alternate days rather than daily, saying each dose may then be absorbed better and cause fewer side effects. What is the main mechanism behind this?
options: Daily doses keep gastric pH high, so less ferric iron is reduced to ferrous iron
Iron suppresses erythropoietin, so the marrow takes up less iron on dosing days
Unabsorbed iron injures duodenal villi, and a day off lets the damaged mucosa recover
Each dose raises hepcidin, which breaks down ferroportin and cuts absorption next day
notes: Iron does not raise gastric pH; acid (helped by vitamin C) supports reduction to ferrous iron, and this does not explain the benefit of alternate days.
Iron does not suppress erythropoietin, which is driven by tissue hypoxia, and her anaemia keeps EPO high.
Iron can irritate the GI tract and cause nausea, but villous injury is not the reason alternate-day dosing improves absorption.
questions.why: An oral iron dose raises hepcidin for about 24 hours. Hepcidin binds ferroportin on enterocytes and causes it to be broken down, which blocks iron export. A dose taken the next day is therefore absorbed less well, and spacing doses lets hepcidin fall back.

questions.stem: Sylvie, 23, has heavy menstrual bleeding. Menstrual blood comes from spiral arterioles in the endometrial functional layer, fed by radial and arcuate arteries in the myometrium. Which vessel is the main arterial supply to the uterus?
options: Ovarian artery, arising directly from the abdominal aorta
Uterine artery, from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery
Internal pudendal artery, from the anterior division of the internal iliac
Uterine artery, from the posterior division of the internal iliac artery
notes: The ovarian artery joins the uterine artery near the fundus but is not the main uterine supply. It mainly supplies the ovary and tube.
The internal pudendal artery supplies the perineum and external genitalia, not the uterus.
The posterior division of the internal iliac gives parietal branches (iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal), not the visceral uterine artery.
questions.why: The uterine artery comes off the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. It crosses above the ureter ('water under the bridge') and joins the ovarian artery. This is the vessel targeted in uterine artery embolisation.

questions.stem: Skye, a 33-year-old mechanic seen in general practice for 5 months of fatigue, says he gets up 3 or 4 times a night to pass urine. You want to know whether this is true polyuria or frequent small voids from a bladder or prostate problem. Which question best tells them apart?
options: "Does it sting or burn when you pass urine?"
"Are you passing a large amount each time, or only small amounts often?"
"Do you have trouble getting started, or is the stream weak or dribbling at the end?"
"Do you get a sudden urge to go that is hard to hold on?"
notes: This screens for a UTI, but dysuria does not tell you whether the total urine volume is increased.
This screens for outlet obstruction such as prostatic enlargement, which is unlikely at 33, and it does not measure the volume passed.
Urgency suggests an overactive bladder, which causes small frequent voids. It does not show whether he is passing a large volume.
questions.why: Polyuria means a large total volume of urine, so each void is large. Frequency means small amounts passed often. Asking about the volume of each void (or using a voiding diary) separates an osmotic or DI cause from bladder, prostate or infective causes.

questions.stem: Skye, 33, has new type 2 diabetes in general practice: HbA1c 9.1% (76 mmol/mol), fasting glucose 12.4 mmol/L, urine ketones negative, eGFR over 90, uACR normal, no weight loss. Your GP supervisor will start medication today alongside lifestyle change. Which initial regimen is most appropriate?
options: Gliclazide modified release 30 mg orally each morning as the sole first-line agent
Insulin glargine 10 units subcutaneously at night until HbA1c falls below 7%
Metformin 500 mg orally once daily with the evening meal, increased gradually
Metformin 1 g orally twice daily from day one so he reaches target quickly
notes: A sulfonylurea is a second-line add-on. Used alone first line it causes weight gain and hypoglycaemia and skips metformin, which he can take.
Insulin is for catabolic features, ketosis or failure of oral agents. Skye has no weight loss, negative ketones and has not tried metformin.
Starting at the full dose makes nausea and diarrhoea much more likely and hurts adherence. Titrating slowly is standard.
questions.why: Metformin is first line for type 2 diabetes with normal renal function. Start low with food (e.g. 500 mg daily) and increase every 1 to 2 weeks to limit GI side effects, then recheck HbA1c at 3 months.

questions.stem: Skye, 33, has nocturia that persists even when he stops drinking after dinner. His fasting glucose is 12.4 mmol/L and his urine dipstick shows glucose 3+ with specific gravity 1.020. What mechanism best explains why glucose appears in his urine?
options: Insulin deficiency suppresses ADH release, so free water and glucose are lost together
Hyperglycaemia makes the collecting duct resistant to ADH, so glucose leaks into urine
Filtered glucose exceeds the maximum reabsorption of proximal tubule SGLT transporters
Hyperfiltration speeds tubular flow so glucose bypasses reabsorption in the loop of Henle
notes: Insulin does not regulate ADH release, and ADH deficiency (central DI) produces dilute urine without glucose, unlike Skye's.
Glucose does not cause collecting duct ADH resistance; nephrogenic DI gives dilute, glucose-free urine, whereas Skye's urine is concentrated.
Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, not the loop of Henle, and glycosuria comes from saturating that transport, not from faster flow.
questions.why: Glucose is normally fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by SGLT2 and SGLT1. Above about 10 mmol/L plasma glucose, the filtered load exceeds this transport maximum. The glucose left in the tubule holds water with it, causing an osmotic diuresis.

questions.stem: During Skye's focused examination (33, new type 2 diabetes, smoker), you check his peripheral pulses as part of a baseline diabetic foot assessment. Where should you palpate the dorsalis pedis artery?
options: Behind the medial malleolus, midway between it and the calcaneal tendon
Behind the lateral malleolus, alongside the fibularis longus and brevis tendons
In the first web space, between the heads of the 1st and 2nd metatarsals of the forefoot
Lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon on the proximal dorsum of the foot
notes: This is where you feel the posterior tibial artery, the other foot pulse to check in a diabetic foot assessment.
The fibular artery runs deep behind the lateral malleolus and is not normally palpable as a foot pulse.
Distally the dorsalis pedis dives between the 1st and 2nd metatarsals to join the plantar arch, so it is not reliably felt in the web space.
questions.why: The dorsalis pedis continues the anterior tibial artery. Feel for it on the proximal dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, over the tarsal bones and bases of the 1st and 2nd metatarsals.

questions.stem: James, 26, has had a daily pressing headache for 6 weeks and keeps rubbing his stiff, sore neck. He is afebrile. While examining him in general practice, you want to show the examiner you have assessed for meningism. Which examination finding best argues against meningeal irritation?
options: Tenderness on palpation of the trapezius and suboccipital muscles bilaterally
Full, painless passive neck flexion bringing the chin to the chest
Pain-free active neck rotation through a full range to both sides
Normal power, tone and reflexes in all four limbs
notes: Pericranial muscle tenderness supports tension-type headache, but finding it does not exclude meningeal irritation as well.
Meningism usually leaves rotation relatively spared, so a full range of rotation does not rule it out.
A normal limb neurological examination looks for focal deficits, not meningeal irritation.
questions.why: Meningeal irritation mainly limits and makes painful passive neck flexion, because flexion stretches the inflamed meninges. Full, painless passive flexion (with a negative Kernig's sign) separates muscular stiffness from meningism.

questions.stem: James, 26, has had a daily tension-type headache for 6 weeks while writing his thesis. He takes paracetamol about 5 days a week and adds ibuprofen once or twice a week. Ibuprofen has never made his mild asthma worse. His examination is normal. Which advice about acute analgesia is best?
options: Paracetamol 1 g or ibuprofen 400 mg early in a headache, on fewer than 10 days a month
Paracetamol 1 g four times daily, every day, until his thesis is submitted in two months
Paracetamol-codeine combination on afternoons when paracetamol alone fails
Stop all analgesics abruptly and take none until his next GP review
notes: Regular daily paracetamol means analgesic use on 15 or more days a month, which is exactly the pattern that causes medication-overuse headache.
Codeine combinations cause medication-overuse headache at 10 or more days a month, carry a risk of dependence and are not recommended for tension-type headache.
Abrupt withdrawal is the treatment for established medication-overuse headache. He does not meet the criteria (under 3 months), and he still needs effective treatment on bad days.
questions.why: Simple analgesics taken early in a headache are first line for tension-type headache. Keeping acute treatment to fewer than 10 days a month (about 2 days a week) prevents medication-overuse headache, which he is heading towards at his current frequency.

questions.stem: James, 26, has taken analgesics on about 20 to 25 days a month for 6 weeks for tension-type headache. You warn him that if this continues he will develop medication-overuse headache. Which mechanism best explains how frequent analgesic use makes headache worse?
options: Central sensitisation of trigeminal pain pathways, lowering the pain threshold
Rebound cerebral vasodilation each time a paracetamol dose wears off, within hours
Build-up of a toxic paracetamol metabolite causing low-grade encephalopathy
NSAID-induced fluid retention gradually raising intracranial pressure
notes: Rebound vasodilation has been proposed for ergotamine, not simple analgesics, and it does not explain medication-overuse headache from paracetamol.
Therapeutic doses of paracetamol do not cause encephalopathy. Its toxic metabolite NAPQI matters in overdose and harms the liver, not the brain.
Occasional ibuprofen does not raise intracranial pressure, and medication-overuse headache also happens with paracetamol alone.
questions.why: Repeated analgesic exposure is thought to change central pain processing, sensitising trigeminal nociceptive neurones and weakening descending pain inhibition. The threshold drops and headaches become more frequent.

questions.stem: On fundoscopy, James, 26, has sharp optic disc margins with spontaneous venous pulsations, which argues against raised intracranial pressure as the cause of his 6 weeks of daily headache. Which anatomical feature explains why raised intracranial pressure would cause papilloedema?
options: The optic nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure beside the cavernous sinus
The optic nerve is supplied within the orbit by the posterior cerebral artery
Optic nerve fibres are myelinated by Schwann cells, which swell under pressure
The optic nerve sheath has a subarachnoid space continuous with the intracranial one
notes: The optic nerve enters through the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.
The orbital optic nerve is supplied by branches of the ophthalmic artery (from the internal carotid), not the posterior cerebral artery.
The optic nerve is a CNS tract myelinated by oligodendrocytes, and myelin swelling is not how papilloedema develops.
questions.why: The optic nerve is wrapped in meninges, and its subarachnoid space is continuous with the intracranial one. Raised CSF pressure therefore travels along the sheath to the disc, blocking axoplasmic flow and venous return, which swells the disc and abolishes venous pulsations.

questions.stem: Brad, 64, has an anterolateral STEMI in a regional ED with no cath lab. The PCI-centre cardiologist agrees with fibrinolysis. BP is 148/88. Before tenecteplase is drawn up, you check his history once more. Which question most directly screens for an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis?
options: Have you taken sildenafil or similar erection tablets in the last 48 hours?
Have you ever had a reaction to the iodine contrast used for scans?
Have you ever had a stroke, a bleed in the brain or a recent head injury?
Do you drink alcohol most days, and how much do you have each week?
notes: PDE5 inhibitor use is a contraindication to GTN, not to fibrinolysis, so it decides whether you can give nitrates rather than whether you can give a lytic.
Contrast reactions matter for coronary angiography later. They have no bearing on whether tenecteplase is safe.
Daily alcohol is a risk factor worth addressing, but on its own it is not a contraindication to fibrinolysis.
questions.why: Any previous intracranial haemorrhage, an ischaemic stroke in the last 3 months and significant head trauma in the last 3 months are all absolute contraindications to fibrinolysis. Always screen for bleeding, stroke, recent surgery or trauma, and suspected dissection before you give a lytic.

questions.stem: Brad, 64, 92 kg, arrived 3 hours after his pain began. His ECG shows ST elevation in V2 to V5, I and aVL. He is haemodynamically stable with no contraindications to fibrinolysis. The nearest PCI centre is 3 hours away by road, and he cannot reach a cath lab within 90 minutes of first medical contact. What is the most appropriate reperfusion plan?
options: Tenecteplase in the ED within 30 minutes of arrival, then transfer for angiography
Road transfer for primary PCI, withholding the lytic to limit bleeding risk, with aspirin
Repeat troponin at 3 hours to confirm infarction before choosing reperfusion
Heparin infusion and local admission, with elective angiography next week
notes: A 3-hour transfer goes well past the 90-minute PCI target, and the delay costs more myocardium than the lytic's bleeding risk.
STEMI is diagnosed on the ECG and the clinical picture. Reperfusion never waits for a troponin result.
Anticoagulation alone does not reperfuse an occluded LAD, and delaying angiography leaves him untreated.
questions.why: When primary PCI cannot happen within 90 minutes of first medical contact and symptoms began less than 12 hours ago, give fibrinolysis within 30 minutes of arrival. Then transfer for angiography, which is rescue PCI if reperfusion fails.

questions.stem: Brad, 64, with an anterolateral STEMI, had 8/10 chest pressure. The paramedics gave him two doses of sublingual GTN 400 micrograms and his pain eased. He has no history of PDE5 inhibitor use. Which mechanism mainly explains how GTN relieves ischaemic chest pain?
options: Direct lysis of the coronary thrombus, restoring flow down the occluded artery
Slowing of the heart rate, which lengthens diastolic coronary filling time
Inhibition of platelet thromboxane A2 synthesis, so the thrombus cannot grow any further
Nitric oxide-mediated venodilation, lowering preload, wall stress and oxygen demand
notes: GTN has no fibrinolytic action. Dissolving the clot takes a plasminogen activator such as tenecteplase.
Slowing the heart rate is what beta blockers do. Nitrates tend to cause a reflex tachycardia instead.
Blocking thromboxane A2 by inhibiting COX-1 is how aspirin works, not GTN.
questions.why: GTN releases nitric oxide, which raises cGMP in vascular smooth muscle and dilates mainly the veins. Preload and ventricular wall stress fall, so myocardial oxygen demand falls. Because PDE5 inhibitors also raise cGMP, the combination can cause profound hypotension.

questions.stem: Brad, 64, has 3 hours of chest pressure radiating to his left arm and jaw. His ECG shows ST elevation in V2 to V5 and in I and aVL, reciprocal ST depression in III, and Q waves in V2 to V4. Where is the culprit coronary occlusion most likely to be?
options: Distal left anterior descending artery, beyond its diagonal branches near the apex
Proximal left anterior descending artery, before its first diagonal branch
Left circumflex artery, at the origin of its obtuse marginal branch
Right coronary artery, proximal to its acute marginal branch
notes: A distal LAD occlusion spares the diagonal branches, so you would not expect ST elevation in I and aVL.
A circumflex occlusion mainly affects the lateral or posterior leads. It would not give 3 to 4 mm of ST elevation in V2 to V4.
An RCA occlusion causes inferior ST elevation (II, III, aVF). Here III shows reciprocal depression instead.
questions.why: The LAD supplies the anterior wall (V2 to V4). Its diagonal branches supply the high lateral wall (I, aVL). Changes in both territories, with reciprocal change inferiorly, point to an occlusion in the proximal LAD, which puts a large area of myocardium at risk.

questions.stem: Frank, 66, is in your GP room with fast irregular palpitations right now. His radial pulse is irregularly irregular. The practice nurse is with you. You want to show the examiner whether he has a pulse deficit. Which technique is best?
options: Palpate both radial pulses at the same time and compare their timing
Palpate the radial and femoral pulses together and feel for any delay between them
Count the apex rate by auscultation while the radial is counted, over 60 s
Count the radial pulse for 15 seconds and multiply the result by four
notes: Comparing both radials looks for radio-radial delay (e.g. subclavian stenosis or dissection), not for beats that fail to reach the wrist.
Radio-femoral delay is a sign of coarctation of the aorta and does not compare the heart rate with the peripheral pulse rate.
>Counting for 15 seconds is unreliable in an irregular rhythm and only measures the radial rate, which undercounts the true ventricular rate in AF.
questions.why: A pulse deficit is when the apical rate is higher than the radial rate. You find it by counting both at the same time for a full minute. It is typical of AF, where some beats are too weak to reach the wrist.

questions.stem: Frank, 66, has newly diagnosed paroxysmal AF and is now back in sinus rhythm. He has hypertension but no diabetes, stroke, heart failure or vascular disease. BMI 36, eGFR 75, Hb 148, platelets and INR normal. He drinks about nine middies of full-strength beer a day. Which stroke prevention plan is best?
options: Aspirin 100 mg daily, as his AF is paroxysmal rather than persistent
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily, with support to cut down his alcohol intake
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, because heavy drinking raises bleeding risk
No anticoagulant until his alcohol intake has fallen to safe levels
notes: Aspirin does not prevent stroke well in AF and still causes bleeding, and paroxysmal AF carries a stroke risk similar to persistent AF.
Alcohol is not a criterion for reducing the apixaban dose, and the 2.5 mg dose would leave him under-protected from stroke.
You lower bleeding risk by treating modifiable factors such as alcohol and BP, not by withholding indicated anticoagulation in the meantime.
questions.why: His CHA2DS2-VA score is 2 (age 65 to 74, hypertension), so he needs oral anticoagulation, preferably a DOAC. Apixaban stays at the full 5 mg twice daily unless he meets two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or under, creatinine 133 µmol/L or over.

questions.stem: Frank's ECG during palpitations shows a fibrillatory baseline with no P waves and an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm at about 110/min. His atria are depolarising chaotically at 350 to 600/min. Which mechanism best explains this ventricular rate and rhythm?
options: The sinoatrial node fires irregularly at around 110 impulses per minute at rest
A ventricular escape focus takes over and fires at an irregular rate
The bundle of His blocks alternate atrial impulses in a fixed 2:1 ratio
The AV node is refractory after each impulse, so only some pass, at random
notes: In AF the sinoatrial node is overridden by chaotic atrial activity, which is why there are no P waves.
A ventricular escape rhythm is slow (20 to 40/min) and broad-complex, not a narrow-complex rhythm at about 110/min.
A fixed conduction ratio gives a regular ventricular rhythm, as in atrial flutter with 2:1 block, not an irregularly irregular one.
questions.why: The AV node conducts slowly and stays refractory after each impulse it passes, so it filters the chaotic atrial impulses and lets only some through, at random. That is why the narrow-complex response is irregularly irregular. Rate-control drugs such as beta-blockers work by lengthening AV nodal refractoriness.

questions.stem: Frank, 66, has paroxysmal AF without valve disease. You explain that the main danger is a clot travelling to the brain and causing a stroke. Where in the heart does this thrombus most often form?
notes: Clot from the right atrium would go to the lungs as a pulmonary embolus rather than to the brain, and the right appendage is a much less common site.
Left ventricular apical thrombus is linked to anterior myocardial infarction or cardiomyopathy, not to AF with normal ventricular function.
The coronary sinus drains venous blood into the right atrium and is not a site where clot forms in AF.
questions.why: Over 90% of thrombi in non-valvular AF form in the left atrial appendage, a blind-ended, trabeculated pouch where blood pools once the atrium stops contracting. Clot from the left heart embolises into the systemic circulation, including the brain.

questions.stem: Bernard, 67, is in ED with decompensated heart failure. He says he takes all his prescribed tablets every day. He has no chest pain, palpitations, fever or sputum. He mentions that his big toe was 'agony' a couple of weeks ago but has now settled. Which question is most likely to uncover the trigger for his decompensation?
options: "Has your GP changed the dose of any of your heart tablets or water tablets lately?"
"Did you take anything for the toe, such as tablets bought from the chemist?"
"Have you been eating more salty food or takeaway meals recently?"
"Have you been drinking more fluid than usual over the last week?"
notes: A recent dose change is worth asking about, but the gout history points to an unreported over-the-counter medicine as the more likely trigger here.
Too much salt is a common trigger, but nothing in the history points to it, while the painful toe points to self-treatment with an NSAID.
Too much fluid can cause decompensation, but the gout flare is the clue in this case, and it points to an NSAID rather than fluid intake.
questions.why: A recent gout flare in someone with heart failure should make you ask straight away about over-the-counter NSAIDs. Ibuprofen causes sodium and water retention, and taken with a diuretic and an ARB it also causes AKI (the 'triple whammy'). Patients often don't count chemist medicines as 'tablets', so ask about them directly.

questions.stem: Bernard, 67, is being admitted from ED with acute decompensated heart failure. RR 26, SpO2 91% on room air, BP 144/86, warm peripheries. Creatinine is 132 µmol/L (baseline 86). His usual diuretic is furosemide 40 mg orally each morning. Which initial diuretic order is most appropriate?
options: Furosemide 20 mg IV now, using a lower dose because of the AKI
Furosemide 40 to 80 mg IV now, repeated according to response
Furosemide 80 mg orally now, double his usual morning dose
Furosemide 250 mg IV infusion over 1 hour now, then review
notes: The congestion is driving the AKI, so it is not a reason to cut the dose. A dose below his usual one is unlikely to relieve the congestion.
When the gut wall is oedematous, oral furosemide is poorly absorbed. A patient who is hypoxic and breathless at rest needs IV treatment.
This is a high dose meant for diuretic resistance. It is excessive as a first dose and raises the risk of ototoxicity and electrolyte upset.
questions.why: In acute decompensation the IV loop diuretic dose should be at least his usual oral daily dose, up to about 2.5 times it (so 40 to 80 mg IV here). Then titrate to urine output, daily weights and daily UEC.

questions.stem: Bernard, 67, takes furosemide and candesartan for heart failure. He took ibuprofen for 5 days for gout and his creatinine is now 132 µmol/L (baseline 86). Which mechanism best explains how the ibuprofen reduced his glomerular filtration rate?
options: It blocked prostaglandin-mediated dilatation of the afferent arteriole
It blocked angiotensin II-mediated constriction of the efferent arteriole
It caused direct toxic injury to proximal tubular cells, giving ATN
It inhibited the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
notes: This is how candesartan (the ARB) contributes to the triple whammy, not how ibuprofen does.
NSAID kidney injury here is caused by changes in blood flow, not direct tubular toxicity; aminoglycosides and contrast are classic direct tubular toxins.
This is how furosemide works; ibuprofen does not act on NKCC2.
questions.why: When kidney perfusion falls, prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, which together keep glomerular pressure up. NSAIDs remove the afferent dilatation and the ARB removes the efferent constriction. Add volume loss from the diuretic and the GFR falls.

questions.stem: You examine Bernard, 67, to assess his jugular venous pressure. He is sitting at 45° with his head turned slightly to the left. Where should you look for the pulsation of the right internal jugular vein?
options: Superficial to sternocleidomastoid, crossing the muscle obliquely downwards
In the suprasternal notch, medial to the sternal head of sternocleidomastoid
In the posterior triangle, lateral to the clavicular head of sternocleidomastoid
Deep to sternocleidomastoid, between its two heads, rising towards the earlobe
notes: This is the course of the external jugular vein, which can be kinked or affected by valves and is less reliable for estimating right atrial pressure.
The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the trachea and the sternal head, not in the suprasternal notch.
The posterior triangle lies outside the line of the internal jugular vein; pulsation there is more likely the external jugular vein or the subclavian artery.
questions.why: The internal jugular vein runs deep to sternocleidomastoid. Low in the neck it lies between the sternal and clavicular heads, and it runs up towards the earlobe. It drains in a straight line, without valves, through the brachiocephalic vein and SVC into the right atrium. Measure the JVP as the vertical height above the sternal angle.

questions.stem: Sophia, 20, with known asthma, is in ED speaking 3 to 4 words at a time. Oxygen and salbutamol have been started and you have time for only a few targeted questions about her asthma history. Which question best identifies her risk of a fatal asthma attack?
options: How old were you when you were first diagnosed with asthma?
Does anyone else in your family have asthma, eczema or hay fever?
Have you ever needed intensive care or a breathing tube for asthma?
What do you think set off this attack while you were jogging in the cold this morning?
notes: Age at diagnosis has little bearing on how dangerous an acute attack is, and asking about it wastes her limited breath.
Family atopy supports the diagnosis of asthma but does not tell you how likely this attack is to be fatal.
Knowing the trigger helps later education, but it does not stratify her risk of dying from this attack.
questions.why: A previous ICU admission or intubation for asthma is the strongest predictor of a future fatal attack. Always ask about it, along with hospital admissions, courses of oral steroids, current control and whether she uses a preventer.

questions.stem: Sophia, 20, has severe acute asthma in ED: she speaks 3 to 4 words per breath, is using her accessory muscles and has an SpO2 of 92% on room air. She can use a spacer, and oxygen titrated to 93 to 95% has been started. Which salbutamol regimen should you prescribe for the first hour?
options: 12 puffs (100 microgram) by pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes
4 puffs by pMDI and spacer every 4 minutes until help arrives
2.5 mg by nebuliser every 4 hours, with puffs as needed between
IV salbutamol infusion as the first-line bronchodilator
notes: This is the community asthma first aid plan for use until an ambulance arrives, not the regimen for severe asthma in ED.
This dose is far too small and too infrequent for severe asthma, which needs repeated doses every 20 minutes in the first hour.
IV salbutamol is not first line. It is kept for refractory asthma under senior or ICU direction, because inhaled salbutamol works as well with fewer adverse effects.
questions.why: For severe acute asthma in adults, the Australian Asthma Handbook recommends salbutamol 12 puffs by pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour, or 5 mg by nebuliser if she cannot use a spacer. Give ipratropium and oral prednisolone with it.

questions.stem: Sophia's arrival ABG, taken on oxygen, showed pH 7.51 and pCO2 28 mmHg. One hour later she is still very breathless and wheezy despite treatment, and a repeat gas shows a pCO2 of 44 mmHg. What does this rise in pCO2 most likely reflect?
options: Renal bicarbonate retention correcting the earlier alkalaemia
Respiratory muscle fatigue with falling alveolar ventilation
Bronchospasm easing, so her ventilation has returned to normal
Loss of hypoxic respiratory drive caused by the extra oxygen
notes: Renal compensation takes days, and it changes bicarbonate, not pCO2. It would not raise the pCO2 within an hour.
If she were improving, her distress and wheeze would be settling. A 'normal' pCO2 in a patient who is still struggling to breathe is ominous.
Hypercapnia from oxygen happens in chronic CO2 retainers such as some people with COPD, not in a young woman with acute asthma who was hypocapnic on arrival.
questions.why: Early in acute asthma, hyperventilation drives the pCO2 down. If the pCO2 climbs back to normal while she is still distressed, she is tiring and her alveolar ventilation is failing. This is a sign of life-threatening asthma and needs senior and ICU review.

questions.stem: Sophia is sitting bolt upright, leaning forward with her hands braced on her knees (tripod position). Bracing her arms fixes her shoulder girdle. Which muscles does this position let her recruit most effectively as accessory muscles of inspiration?
notes: These are the primary muscles of inspiration. They work whatever the arm position, so they are not the accessory muscles this posture recruits.
These are muscles of forced expiration, not inspiration.
These muscles mainly elevate and rotate the scapula. They have no useful attachment to the ribs for expanding the chest.
questions.why: When the arms and scapulae are fixed, the pectoral muscles reverse their usual action. Instead of moving the arm, they pull on the ribs and sternum and lift the chest wall. This is why breathless patients brace their arms in the tripod position.

questions.stem: Shawn, 75, has COPD and is breathless in ED on 2 L/min nasal prongs. As part of your focused examination you want to check for a CO2 retention flap, because his oxygen needs careful titration. Which instruction to Shawn best elicits this sign?
options: "Hold your arms out in front, palms up, and close your eyes for me and hold still."
"Touch your nose, then my finger, as quickly as you can, a few times."
"Arms straight out, bend your wrists back, spread your fingers and hold."
"Squeeze my two fingers as hard as you can with both hands, and let go."
notes: This tests for pronator drift, a sign of an upper motor neurone lesion, not a hypercapnic flap.
Finger-nose testing looks for cerebellar ataxia and intention tremor, not asterixis.
Grip strength tests power. A flap needs a sustained posture with the wrists bent back, not a squeeze.
questions.why: A CO2 retention flap (asterixis) shows when the wrists are held dorsiflexed with the fingers spread: the sustained posture briefly lapses, giving a flapping movement. Hold the position for about 30 seconds.

questions.stem: Shawn, 75, with an infective exacerbation of COPD, has had repeated salbutamol and ipratropium, prednisolone and amoxicillin, with oxygen titrated to SpO2 88 to 92%. A repeat ABG at 1 hour shows pH 7.29 and PaCO2 66 mmHg. He is alert and can protect his airway. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start bilevel non-invasive ventilation in a monitored area
Increase the oxygen to target SpO2 94 to 98% by Hudson mask
Give an IV aminophylline loading dose over 20 minutes
Start CPAP at 10 cm H2O by full face mask
notes: More oxygen in a CO2 retainer worsens hypercapnia and acidosis. The target stays at 88 to 92%.
Aminophylline adds little benefit and has significant toxicity in COPD exacerbations. It does not replace ventilatory support for acidosis.
CPAP gives no inspiratory pressure support, so it does little to clear CO2. Bilevel NIV is the mode for hypercapnic COPD.
questions.why: Acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH below 7.35, PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) that persists despite optimal medical treatment is the indication for bilevel NIV. Inspiratory pressure support increases ventilation and clears CO2. Escalate to ICU if he deteriorates or cannot tolerate it.

questions.stem: Shawn, 75, has compensated chronic hypercapnia (PaCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 29 mmol/L). A clinician puts him on a high-flow mask. His SpO2 rises to 98% but he becomes drowsy as his PaCO2 climbs. What is the main mechanism behind this rise in PaCO2?
options: Abolition of the hypoxic drive, so central respiratory drive stops altogether
Oxygen-induced bronchospasm, which raises airway resistance and the work of breathing
Higher CO2 production as metabolic rate rises with better tissue oxygen delivery
Release of hypoxic vasoconstriction, so blood goes to poorly ventilated alveoli
notes: Minute ventilation falls only a little with oxygen and does not stop. Loss of hypoxic drive is a minor contributor, not the main mechanism.
Oxygen does not cause bronchospasm. Airway resistance in his exacerbation comes from inflammation and bronchoconstriction.
Extra oxygen does not meaningfully raise CO2 production. The problem is CO2 elimination, not production.
questions.why: High FiO2 reverses hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Blood then perfuses poorly ventilated units, which worsens V/Q mismatch and effective dead space. Together with the Haldane effect, this raises PaCO2 more than any loss of hypoxic drive does.

questions.stem: Shawn, 75, needs a repeat arterial blood gas from his right radial artery an hour after starting treatment in ED. You palpate the pulse at the wrist, just proximal to the flexor retinaculum, before inserting the needle. Where does the radial artery lie at this site?
options: Between the flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus tendons, beside the median nerve
Just lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon, over the distal radius
Just lateral to the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, beside the pisiform
Deep in the anatomical snuffbox, on the scaphoid and trapezium
notes: The median nerve lies here, so a puncture at this site risks nerve injury rather than reaching the artery.
This is where the ulnar artery and nerve lie, not the radial artery.
The radial artery does pass through the snuffbox, but that is distal to this site and is not where an ABG is usually taken.
questions.why: At the distal forearm the radial artery runs just lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon, lying on the distal radius. The bone underneath lets you compress it after the puncture. Check ulnar collateral flow (modified Allen test) first.

questions.stem: Mr Josip, 70, is in ED, sitting upright and very breathless, with a raised JVP and leg oedema. You tell the examiner you will examine both lung bases to tell pulmonary oedema apart from pleural effusion. Which group of findings at a base points to a pleural effusion?
options: Hyperresonant percussion with reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance
Fine end-inspiratory crackles that do not clear with coughing, normal percussion
Stony dull percussion with reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance
Dull percussion with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance
notes: Hyperresonance with reduced breath sounds suggests pneumothorax, not fluid.
Fine crackles that persist after coughing are the sign of interstitial or alveolar oedema in the lung tissue, not fluid in the pleural space.
Dullness with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance means consolidation, where solid lung carries sound better.
questions.why: Fluid in the pleural space gives stony dullness, and it muffles breath sounds and vocal resonance. Oedema in the lung tissue gives fine crackles instead, and in heart failure the two often occur together.

questions.stem: Mr Josip, 70, has acute pulmonary oedema in ED. He has smoked about 30 pack-years and uses tiotropium. On room air his SpO2 is 87%. His venous gas shows pH 7.31 and pCO2 56 mmHg with a normal bicarbonate. The nurse is putting oxygen back on and asks what saturation to aim for. What is the most appropriate SpO2 target?
options: 88 to 92%, titrating the oxygen up or down to stay in range
92 to 96%, titrating the oxygen up or down to stay in range
94 to 98%, titrating the oxygen up or down to stay in range
98 to 100%, using a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min
notes: 92 to 96% is the TSANZ target for most acutely ill adults, but he is at risk of hypercapnia, which calls for a lower target.
94 to 98% is the older UK target for patients without hypercapnic risk, and it is too high for a patient who is already retaining CO2.
Aiming for near-100% saturation causes hyperoxia, which can worsen hypercapnia and acidosis in a patient at risk of CO2 retention.
questions.why: TSANZ guidance sets a target of 88 to 92% for anyone at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure. A smoker on tiotropium with acute respiratory acidosis (raised pCO2, low pH) qualifies. Too much oxygen can worsen his CO2 retention, so confirm with an arterial gas.

questions.stem: Mr Josip, 70, has hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema with BP 184/100. After a further sublingual dose of glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) and the start of an IV GTN infusion, he breathes more easily within minutes and his BP falls to 170/92. What is the main mechanism of this early benefit?
options: Inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, causing natriuresis
Stimulation of cardiac beta-1 receptors, increasing contractility and stroke volume
Blockade of arteriolar L-type calcium channels, causing marked afterload reduction
Nitric oxide release raising cGMP in venous smooth muscle, venodilating to reduce preload
notes: This is how furosemide works. Its diuretic effect takes longer, and GTN does not act on the kidney.
Nitrates are not inotropes; beta-1 agonists such as dobutamine are kept for cardiogenic shock.

Nitrates do reduce afterload at higher doses, but through nitric oxide and cGMP, not calcium channel blockade. The calcium channel blocker verapamil is negatively inotropic and should be avoided in acute heart failure.
questions.why: Nitrates release nitric oxide, which raises cGMP in vascular smooth muscle. At low doses this mainly dilates veins, which lowers venous return and LV filling pressure. Pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure falls and less fluid leaks into the lung tissue. Higher doses also dilate arterioles and reduce afterload.

questions.stem: Mr Josip, 70, had an MI 12 years ago and coronary bypass surgery 10 years ago. Today's ECG shows sinus tachycardia with pathological Q waves, poor R wave progression and T wave inversion in V1 to V3, unchanged from an ECG 2 years ago. Which coronary artery was most likely occluded in his previous infarct?
options: Right coronary artery, proximal to its acute marginal branch
notes: An RCA occlusion usually causes an inferior infarct (II, III, aVF), sometimes with right ventricular or posterior involvement, not Q waves in V1 to V3.
A circumflex occlusion usually affects the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) or the posterior wall, not V1 to V3.
The posterior descending artery supplies the inferior wall and posterior septum, which show up in the inferior leads, not as anteroseptal Q waves.
questions.why: V1 to V4 look at the interventricular septum and the anterior wall, which the left anterior descending artery supplies. An old anteroseptal infarct with poor R wave progression fits an LAD occlusion. Loss of anterior myocardium is a common cause of ischaemic cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: You are teaching Phoebe, 65, newly diagnosed with COPD in general practice, to use her salbutamol metered-dose inhaler with a small-volume spacer. She has shaken the inhaler and fitted it into the spacer. What should you tell her to do next?
options: Fire two puffs into the spacer together, then breathe in slowly through the mouthpiece
Seal your lips on the mouthpiece, fire one puff, then breathe normally four times
Fire one puff into the spacer, wait about 30 seconds, then take one deep breath in
Breathe in fast and hard through the mouthpiece while firing one puff into the spacer
notes: Firing several puffs at once makes the aerosol clump and stick to the spacer walls, so less drug gets to the lungs.
Waiting before inhaling lets the aerosol settle out on the spacer walls, so she should breathe in straight after firing.
A fast, forceful breath is the technique for a dry powder inhaler. With a spacer, slow or tidal breathing gets the most drug into the lungs.
questions.why: With a spacer, fire one puff at a time with the lips sealed, then either tidal-breathe about four times or take one slow deep breath and hold it for about 10 seconds. Shake the inhaler and repeat for each puff, and check technique at every visit.

questions.stem: Phoebe, 65, has moderate COPD (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50, FEV1 58% predicted) with breathlessness that stops her daily walks. Her blood eosinophils are 0.20 × 10^9/L. You have prescribed salbutamol as needed via a spacer. Which regular maintenance treatment should you start now in general practice?
options: Fluticasone propionate inhaler on its own, twice daily
notes: An inhaled corticosteroid on its own is not recommended in COPD. It raises the risk of pneumonia and does not give the bronchodilation she needs.
Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist used in asthma and has no established role in COPD.
Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index and many interactions, and is kept for later when inhaled therapy is not enough.
questions.why: COPD-X recommends a long-acting bronchodilator, usually a LAMA such as tiotropium, when breathlessness persists despite a reliever. Step up to LAMA/LABA if she stays breathless, and add an inhaled corticosteroid only for repeated flare-ups.

questions.stem: Phoebe, 65, a current smoker with 50 pack-years, has a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC of 0.50 with no significant bronchodilator response. Her chest X-ray shows hyperinflation, flattened hemidiaphragms and upper zone hyperlucency. What mechanism best explains the air trapping in her emphysema?
options: Reduced lung compliance stops the lungs emptying fully at end expiration, so gas stays
Reversible bronchial smooth muscle spasm narrows the large central airways
Loss of elastic recoil removes radial traction, so small airways collapse on expiry
Surfactant deficiency causes alveolar collapse that traps gas behind it
notes: Emphysema increases lung compliance. Reduced compliance is the restrictive picture seen in pulmonary fibrosis.
A reversible spasm would give a significant bronchodilator response, and her FEV1 rose by only 60 mL (5%).
Surfactant deficiency causes alveolar collapse with low lung volumes, as in neonatal respiratory distress, not hyperinflation.
questions.why: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, which reduces elastic recoil (the force that drives expiration) and removes the tethering that holds small airways open. The airways collapse early in expiration and trap air. Compliance is increased, not reduced.

questions.stem: You start Phoebe, 65, with moderate COPD, on an inhaled long-acting muscarinic antagonist. It works by blocking the acetylcholine that drives resting bronchomotor tone, the main reversible part of airway narrowing in COPD. The postganglionic fibres releasing this acetylcholine come from preganglionic fibres carried in which nerve?
notes: The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) is motor to the diaphragm and does not supply bronchial smooth muscle.
The intercostal nerves are somatic nerves to the chest wall muscles and skin, not autonomic nerves to the airways.
Sympathetic fibres from T1 to T4 cause bronchodilation, and they are not cholinergic, so a LAMA does not act on them.
questions.why: Parasympathetic supply to the bronchi runs in the vagus nerve (CN X) to the pulmonary plexus. Postganglionic fibres release acetylcholine onto M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle and glands, causing bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion, and this is what LAMAs block.

questions.stem: Jessica, 26, is back at the GP for her results. Her bloods, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin and stool tests are all normal. You explain that irritable bowel syndrome is the likely diagnosis. She looks upset and asks, "So is this all in my head?" What is the best response?
options: No. Your symptoms are real; gut and brain signal abnormally, and stress can worsen it
Your tests are all normal, so there is nothing physically wrong with your bowel right now
Stress is the main cause, so seeing a psychologist is the key treatment for you
We can't be sure what it is until a colonoscopy has ruled out something serious
notes: Saying 'nothing is wrong' dismisses real symptoms, makes her feel disbelieved and does nothing to build trust in the diagnosis.
Stress makes it worse but does not fully explain it, and psychological therapy is one part of management, not the whole treatment.
She has no red flags and a normal calprotectin, so colonoscopy is not indicated, and suggesting it adds to her fear of cancer.
questions.why: IBS should be explained as a positive diagnosis: a real, common disorder of gut-brain interaction (visceral hypersensitivity, altered motility) that stress can worsen, and that does not damage the bowel or cause cancer.

questions.stem: Jessica, 26, has 2 months of crampy lower abdominal pain, alternating loose and hard stools, and bloating. She has no rectal bleeding, weight loss or night symptoms, and no family history. FBC, ferritin, CRP and coeliac serology are normal, stool PCR is negative, and faecal calprotectin is 28 µg/g. What is the most appropriate next step in general practice?
options: Refer for colonoscopy to exclude microscopic colitis and early IBD, with biopsies
Repeat faecal calprotectin in 6 weeks before making any diagnosis
No colonoscopy; working IBS diagnosis with GP review in 4 to 6 weeks
Request CT abdomen and pelvis to exclude a structural cause
notes: Colonoscopy is for red flags or a raised calprotectin. Microscopic colitis mostly affects older people, and she has neither.
A repeat test is for a borderline or raised result. 28 µg/g is clearly normal, and holding back the diagnosis delays treatment.
CT adds radiation and finds incidental lesions without a clinical question to answer; her examination and tests do not suggest a structural cause.
questions.why: A calprotectin below 50 µg/g in a young adult with no red flags makes IBD unlikely and means no colonoscopy is needed. Make a positive working IBS diagnosis, start treatment and review in 4 to 6 weeks to confirm it.
