questions.stem: Jessica, 26, says her bloating, wind and loose stools are worse after a lot of dairy. She drinks milk-based bubble tea most days. She has a history of bee sting anaphylaxis. What mechanism best explains why dairy brings on her symptoms?
options: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the gut mucosa in response to cow's milk protein
Low brush-border lactase: lactose reaches colon, draws in water and is fermented to gas
Deficient pancreatic lactase secretion leaves lactose undigested in the small bowel lumen
Milk fat triggers excess bile acid release, which stimulates colonic water secretion
notes: IgE cow's milk allergy causes rapid urticaria, vomiting or anaphylaxis, not dose-related bloating. Her bee sting allergy does not make it likely.
Lactase is not a pancreatic enzyme; it sits on the small bowel brush border, so pancreatic insufficiency does not cause lactose intolerance.
Bile acid diarrhoea follows ileal disease or cholecystectomy and does not explain sugar fermentation, gas or the link with dose of milk.
questions.why: Lactase is a brush-border enzyme of small bowel enterocytes. When it is low, undigested lactose pulls water into the lumen (osmotic diarrhoea), and colonic bacteria ferment it to hydrogen, CO2 and short-chain fatty acids, which causes bloating and wind.

questions.stem: Jessica, 26, cannot pinpoint her crampy pain and gestures vaguely around her umbilicus and lower abdomen. Pain from distension of midgut-derived bowel (distal duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon) is usually referred to which region?
options: Epigastrium, via visceral afferents entering the cord at about T6 to T8
Suprapubic region, via visceral afferents entering the cord at about T12 to L1
Perineum, via visceral afferents travelling with pelvic splanchnics at S2 to S4
Periumbilical region, via visceral afferents entering the cord at about T10
notes: Epigastric referral is for foregut structures such as the stomach, proximal duodenum, liver and gallbladder.
Suprapubic (hypogastric) referral is for hindgut structures from the distal transverse colon to the upper rectum, not the midgut.
Pelvic splanchnic afferents carry pain from the lower rectum and pelvic organs, not from distension of midgut bowel.
questions.why: Visceral afferents travel with sympathetic fibres to the cord segments that supplied the embryonic gut tube, bilaterally and across several levels, so pain is vague and midline. Midgut pain is referred to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus.

questions.stem: Mr Reid, 68, sees you in general practice. His opening line: "I've had a bad cough in the past few days and have been coughing up stuff recently." You have characterised the cough and the yellow, offensive sputum. Which single question is most likely to change both the organisms you need to cover and his venous thromboembolism risk?
options: Have you been working with potting mix or doing gardening recently?
Have you been in hospital or a nursing home in the past few months?
Have you been in contact with anyone known to have COVID-19?
Have you noticed any pain or swelling in either of your calves?
notes: Potting mix exposure points to Legionella (atypical) cover but tells you nothing about his VTE risk.
COVID contact changes viral testing and infection control but does not change his thromboembolic risk.
Calf symptoms are a sign of DVT, not a risk factor, and asking about them tells you nothing about which organisms to cover.
questions.why: A recent admission (his was 8 to 4 days ago) points to possible hospital-acquired organisms such as Gram-negative bacilli and Staphylococcus aureus, and it is a major risk factor for PE. In this case it only comes out if you ask for it.

questions.stem: Mr Reid, 68, has right lower lobe consolidation on X-ray, 4 days after discharge from hospital where he walked daily and had prophylactic enoxaparin. His Wells score is 1.5 (only HR over 100 scores). His D-dimer is 0.58 mg/L FEU, against a laboratory cut-off of 0.50. What is the most appropriate next step regarding pulmonary embolism?
options: Request a CTPA because the D-dimer is above the laboratory cut-off
Start therapeutic enoxaparin while a CTPA is being arranged
Request bilateral lower limb venous duplex ultrasound
No PE imaging, as the D-dimer is below his age-adjusted cut-off
notes: Using the unadjusted cut-off in a patient over 50 loses specificity and would expose him to an unnecessary CTPA and contrast.
Empirical anticoagulation is only for patients with a high probability of PE awaiting imaging. PE has been excluded here, and anticoagulating him would add bleeding risk for no benefit.
He has no leg symptoms and PE is already excluded, so a duplex scan would not change management.
questions.why: When PE is unlikely (Wells 4 or less), a D-dimer below the age-adjusted cut-off (age × 0.01 mg/L FEU over 50, here 0.68) excludes PE. Using the age-adjusted cut-off avoids unnecessary CTPAs in older patients.

questions.stem: Mr Reid, 68, has dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms. His RR is 26, and his SpO2 has fallen from 94% to 91% on room air over the day. Which mechanism mainly accounts for his hypoxaemia?
options: Alveolar hypoventilation raising alveolar PCO2 and lowering alveolar PO2
Increased dead space from ventilated alveoli that are no longer perfused
Shunt, as blood keeps perfusing alveoli filled with inflammatory exudate
Diffusion limitation across a thickened alveolar-capillary membrane
notes: He is tachypnoeic, so his overall ventilation is increased and his PaCO2 will be normal or low, not raised.
Dead space (ventilated but unperfused alveoli) is the typical defect in PE, not in consolidation, where the alveoli are perfused but not ventilated.
Diffusion limitation is the main problem in interstitial lung disease and matters most on exertion. Exudate-filled alveoli are not ventilated at all.
questions.why: In consolidation the alveoli are filled with exudate but still perfused, so deoxygenated blood passes through without gas exchange (shunt, the extreme of low V/Q). Hypoxic vasoconstriction only partly offsets this, and true shunt responds poorly to supplemental oxygen.

questions.stem: Mr Reid's chest X-ray (PA and lateral) shows new right-sided airspace opacification with air bronchograms. The right hemidiaphragm outline is lost but the right heart border is preserved, so the radiologist places it in the lower lobe. Consolidation of which part of the lung would have obscured the right heart border?
options: Right lower lobe, posterior basal segment
notes: The anterior segment of the upper lobe lies above the horizontal fissure and borders the ascending aorta and SVC region, not the right heart border.
The superior segment of the lower lobe lies posteriorly at about the level of the hilum. It does not touch the right heart border.
The posterior basal segment sits posteriorly on the diaphragm. Its consolidation obscures the hemidiaphragm, which is the pattern seen here.
questions.why: The medial segment of the right middle lobe lies against the right atrium. When it consolidates, the right heart border is lost (silhouette sign). The lower lobe lies posteriorly on the diaphragm, so its consolidation hides the hemidiaphragm instead.

questions.stem: Wendy, 35, had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 8 days ago. She has not opened her bowels for 5 days, feels bloated and says her tummy looks bigger. You are taking her history in general practice. Which single question best helps tell simple constipation apart from postoperative ileus or bowel obstruction?
options: Have you noticed any bright red blood on the toilet paper?
Does your tummy feel bloated or look bigger than usual?
Are you still passing wind from your back passage?
How much water and fibre are you having each day?
notes: Rectal bleeding points to a fissure or a colorectal cause, but it does not help separate constipation from ileus or obstruction.
Bloating and distension occur in both constipation and obstruction, so the answer does not tell them apart (and she has already told you this).
Fluid and fibre intake help explain why she is constipated, but they do not exclude an obstructed or paralysed bowel after surgery.
questions.why: Passing flatus means the bowel is not completely obstructed and is moving, which argues against ileus or adhesive obstruction. After abdominal surgery, always ask about flatus, pain and vomiting before calling it simple constipation.

questions.stem: Wendy, 35, takes oxycodone 5 mg up to 4 times a day and daily oral iron after her cholecystectomy. She has hard pebbly stools, a loaded rectum and an acute anal fissure, with no features of obstruction. You plan to wean the oxycodone and start regular paracetamol. Which laxative regimen is most appropriate?
options: Psyllium 1 sachet twice daily, taken with extra water and a high-fibre diet
Macrogol 1 sachet once or twice daily plus senna 2 tablets at night
Docusate 120 mg twice daily as the only laxative, continued while on oxycodone
Subcutaneous methylnaltrexone 12 mg every second day, with no other laxative
notes: Bulk-forming laxatives are not recommended in opioid-induced constipation. They can make the stool harder or cause impaction when gut motility is slowed.
A stool softener used alone is weak and is not adequate for opioid-induced constipation; it does not overcome the slowed peristalsis.
Peripheral opioid antagonists are kept for constipation that fails standard laxatives, mostly in palliative care. They are not first line in a short opioid course.
questions.why: Opioid-induced constipation is treated with a regular osmotic and/or stimulant laxative, usually both (e.g. macrogol plus senna), adjusted to give a soft stool. The softer stool also lets her fissure heal.

questions.stem: Wendy, 35, has been taking oxycodone every day since her laparoscopic cholecystectomy 8 days ago. She now has hard, pellet-like stools that she has to strain to pass. Which mechanism best explains how the opioid causes her constipation?
options: Reduced bile acid delivery to the colon after cholecystectomy, which slows colonic transit
Muscarinic receptor blockade reducing parasympathetic drive to the colon and gut wall
A mainly central effect on transit that wears off as tolerance develops
Gut mu-receptor activation reduces propulsion and secretion, so more water is absorbed
notes: After cholecystectomy more bile acid reaches the colon, not less, and it tends to cause diarrhoea rather than constipation.
This is how anticholinergic drugs cause constipation. Opioids act through mu-opioid receptors.
Opioid constipation is mainly a peripheral enteric effect, and tolerance to it barely develops, which is why a laxative is needed for the whole course.
questions.why: Opioids act on mu receptors in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. Propulsive peristalsis falls, non-propulsive tone rises, secretion falls and transit slows, so more water is absorbed and the stool becomes hard. Little tolerance develops to this gut effect.

questions.stem: Anal inspection with a chaperone shows that Wendy, 35, has a posterior midline fissure in the anoderm below the dentate line. Passing a stool is very painful for her, and the DRE is uncomfortable. Which nerve carries the pain from this fissure?
options: Inferior rectal (anal) nerve, a branch of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4)
Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) via the inferior hypogastric plexus
Ilioinguinal nerve (L1), supplying skin of the anterior perineum
Sympathetic fibres from the sacral trunk via the superior rectal plexus
notes: Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry visceral afferents from above the dentate line. That mucosa is relatively insensitive to cutting or tearing.
The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the anterior labia or scrotum and the medial thigh, not the anal canal.
Sympathetic and visceral fibres serve the rectum and the upper anal canal. They do not carry the sharp somatic pain of a fissure below the dentate line.
questions.why: Below the dentate line the anal canal has somatic sensory supply from the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve, so fissures there are sharply painful. Above the line the supply is visceral, so internal haemorrhoids are usually painless.

questions.stem: Martha, 48, a laboratory scientist, tells you at her GP visit that she has felt "so awfully tired" for several months and it is getting worse. You want to work out early whether this is sleepiness or fatigue. Which question does this best?
options: "Do you feel weak or short of breath when you climb stairs or carry heavy shopping?"
"How many hours of sleep do you usually get each night, including weekends?"
"Do you nod off when you sit still, such as watching TV or reading?"
"Have you lost interest in the things you used to enjoy, or felt low most days?"
notes: This screens for anaemia or heart and lung disease, which cause fatigue or breathlessness. It does not tell you whether she actually falls asleep.
Hours of sleep are part of the sleep history, but Martha sleeps about 7 hours and still dozes, so the answer does not separate sleepiness from fatigue.
This screens for anhedonia in depression, which is one of the differentials. It does not tell you whether her tiredness means dozing off.
questions.why: Sleepiness means dozing off when inactive, and it points to a sleep disorder such as OSA. Fatigue is a lack of energy without falling asleep. Patients use "tired" for both, so ask directly whether they nod off.

questions.stem: Martha, 48, comes back to the GP. ESS 15, STOP-Bang 5, OSA50 6, BMI 36, neck 42 cm. FBC, iron studies and TSH are normal. After long days she sometimes feels drowsy driving home. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm and grade the likely diagnosis?
options: Request an unattended home sleep study directly, marked urgent for drowsy driving
Start auto-titrating CPAP now and review her sleepiness score and usage in four weeks
Arrange overnight pulse oximetry and refer only if significant desaturations are recorded
Refer to ENT for assessment for upper airway surgery before any sleep study is arranged
notes: CPAP is first line for moderate to severe OSA, but only once a sleep study has confirmed and graded it. Starting it on questionnaire scores alone is premature.
Oximetry alone cannot reliably diagnose or grade OSA, because it gives no AHI and misses hypopnoeas with arousals. A normal result would not rule OSA out.
Surgery is an alternative for selected patients after the diagnosis is confirmed and CPAP has failed. It is not how OSA is diagnosed.
questions.why: Her scores meet the MBS criteria for a GP to request a home sleep study directly: ESS 8 or more plus STOP-Bang 4 or more or OSA50 5 or more. Polysomnography confirms OSA and grades it by AHI. Drowsy driving makes it urgent.

questions.stem: Martha, 48, has probable obstructive sleep apnoea and drinks one or two glasses of wine before bed most nights "to help me sleep". You advise her to stop drinking in the evening. By what main mechanism does alcohol before bed make her OSA worse?
options: Bronchospasm narrows her lower airways while she is asleep
Brainstem respiratory drive stops, so she makes no effort to breathe
Nasal congestion forces her to breathe through her mouth
Pharyngeal dilator tone falls, so her narrow upper airway collapses
notes: OSA is a collapse of the upper airway (the pharynx), not narrowing of the lower airways. Bronchospasm is the mechanism in asthma.
Loss of respiratory drive with no effort to breathe is central sleep apnoea. In OSA she keeps trying to breathe against a closed airway.
Alcohol can congest the nose a little, but that is minor. The main effect is relaxation of the pharyngeal muscles and a higher threshold for waking.
questions.why: During sleep the pharyngeal dilator muscles (mainly genioglossus) lose the drive they have when awake. Alcohol reduces their tone further and raises the arousal threshold, so her already crowded oropharynx collapses more often and for longer.

questions.stem: Martha, 48, has a BMI of 36 and a crowded oropharynx. In OSA, the genioglossus loses tone during sleep, so the base of the tongue falls back against the posterior pharyngeal wall. Which nerve supplies this muscle?
options: Vagus nerve via the pharyngeal plexus (CN X)
Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3)
notes: CN IX gives taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue, and its only motor supply is stylopharyngeus. It does not supply genioglossus.
The pharyngeal plexus of CN X supplies the pharyngeal constrictors, most of the soft palate and palatoglossus, but not genioglossus.
CN V3 supplies the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric, plus general sensation to the anterior tongue. It does not supply the tongue muscles.
questions.why: The hypoglossal nerve supplies all the intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus, including genioglossus, the main airway dilator that pulls the tongue forward. Hypoglossal nerve stimulation is an option for selected patients who cannot tolerate CPAP.

questions.stem: Harold Brennan, 72, comes to a rural ED with a headache. It came on gradually 3 days ago, is dull, worse on the right and getting steadily worse. He takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation and is alert and oriented. What is the most important question to ask him next?
options: "Is the headache worse in the morning, or when you cough or strain?"
"Have you noticed any pain in your jaw when you chew?"
"Have you had any falls or knocks to your head in the past few weeks?"
"Do you see flashing lights or zigzag lines before the headache starts?"
notes: Raised intracranial pressure features are worth screening for, but the more urgent question is a head injury, which points straight to a subdural bleed in an anticoagulated man.
Jaw claudication screens for giant cell arteritis, which matters over 50, but a missed head injury on apixaban is far more dangerous and more likely here.
Aura points to migraine, and a first migraine at 72 is unlikely. This question will not pick up the dangerous cause in an anticoagulated man.
questions.why: In any older person on an anticoagulant with a new, progressive headache, ask directly about falls or head injury. Patients often play down a trivial knock days earlier, and that knock is the typical story for a subdural haematoma.

questions.stem: Harold, 72, has a 15 mm right subdural haematoma with 8 mm midline shift, and his GCS has fallen to 14. His last apixaban dose was at 08:00 today. CrCl is about 70 mL/min and INR is 1.2. Neurosurgical retrieval is being arranged. What is the most appropriate way to reverse his anticoagulation in this rural ED?
options: Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg IV, with haematology advice
Vitamin K (phytomenadione) 10 mg IV, repeated after 6 hours if the INR rises again
Idarucizumab 5 g IV, given as two 2.5 g infusions within 15 minutes of each other
Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg IV, followed by cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen is low
notes: Vitamin K reverses warfarin by restoring synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors. It has no effect on apixaban, which inhibits factor Xa directly.
Idarucizumab is a specific antidote for dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. It does not bind apixaban.
FFP does not reliably reverse apixaban, takes time to thaw and needs a large volume. Concentrated factor replacement with Prothrombinex-VF is preferred.
questions.why: For a life-threatening bleed on a factor Xa inhibitor, give prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF about 50 units/kg IV, or as per local protocol) now, with haematology advice. Use andexanet alfa where it is available and local protocol allows.

questions.stem: Harold, 72, takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily. His last dose was at 08:00 and his CrCl is about 70 mL/min. Bloods at 13:25 show an INR of 1.2 and an APTT of 33 s. A colleague says the anticoagulant has probably worn off. Why do these results not exclude an apixaban effect?
options: Apixaban inhibits thrombin directly, an effect that the INR and APTT do not measure well
Apixaban blocks platelet aggregation, which standard clotting times do not reflect
Apixaban lowers vitamin K-dependent factors only after several days of regular use
INR and APTT are insensitive to direct factor Xa inhibition at therapeutic levels
notes: Direct thrombin inhibition is how dabigatran works. Apixaban inhibits factor Xa.
Apixaban is an anticoagulant, not an antiplatelet agent. It acts on factor Xa in the coagulation cascade, not on platelet aggregation.
This describes warfarin. Apixaban works within hours of a dose and does not affect synthesis of clotting factors.
questions.why: Apixaban is a direct, reversible factor Xa inhibitor. Routine PT/INR and APTT reagents respond poorly to it, so they can be near normal at therapeutic levels. Only an apixaban-calibrated anti-Xa assay measures it, so judge the effect from the time of the last dose (half-life about 12 h) and renal function.

questions.stem: Harold, 72, fell 5 days ago and knocked the right side of his head. CT shows a crescent-shaped right subdural collection that crosses the suture lines, with no skull fracture. In older people, cerebral atrophy makes this kind of bleed more likely after a trivial knock. Which vessels are the most likely source?
options: Branches of the middle meningeal artery running in grooves on the inner skull
Bridging cortical veins crossing the subdural space to the dural venous sinuses
Saccular aneurysm of an artery in the subarachnoid space at the circle of Willis
Lenticulostriate perforating arteries supplying the basal ganglia and capsule
notes: Middle meningeal artery injury, usually with a temporal bone fracture, causes an extradural haematoma. That is lentiform and limited by the sutures, because the dura is firmly attached to them.
A ruptured berry aneurysm causes subarachnoid haemorrhage with a thunderclap onset and blood in the sulci and cisterns, not a crescentic subdural collection.
Lenticulostriate artery rupture causes a deep intracerebral haemorrhage, usually from hypertension, not an extra-axial collection after trauma.
questions.why: Subdural haematoma is venous blood between the dura and the arachnoid, from torn bridging veins draining the cortex into the dural sinuses such as the superior sagittal sinus. Atrophy stretches these veins, so minor trauma can tear them. The bleed spreads along the convexity across sutures but is limited by the falx.

questions.stem: Jake Morrison, 78, has come to a Williamstown GP with more than a month of yellow eyes. His wife has been giving him carrot juice, and he asks, "Is it the carrot juice?" His palms look faintly yellow. Which examination step best tells carotenaemia apart from true jaundice?
options: Inspect the palms and soles for yellow discolouration in daylight, comparing both sides
Inspect the sclera in natural light with the lower lid gently pulled down
Press on the nail bed and watch the colour as it blanches and refills over several seconds
Look for yellow discolouration of the nasolabial folds and forehead under room light
notes: Palms and soles turn yellow in both carotenaemia and jaundice, so yellow palms cannot separate the two.
Capillary refill tests peripheral perfusion and tells you nothing about what is causing the yellow colour.
Carotene tends to collect in the nasolabial folds and forehead, but jaundice also yellows the skin, so this sign does not separate them.
questions.why: Carotene builds up in the outer layer of the skin but spares the sclera. Bilirubin binds to the elastin of the sclera, so scleral icterus seen in natural light means true hyperbilirubinaemia rather than carotenaemia.

questions.stem: Jake, 78, has obstructive jaundice. His pancreatic-protocol CT shows a 32 mm hypoattenuating pancreatic head mass with a double duct sign, no vascular involvement and no metastases. The hepatobiliary MDT wants a tissue diagnosis. Which is the preferred way to get it?
options: Percutaneous CT-guided core biopsy of the pancreatic head mass
ERCP with brush cytology of the distal common bile duct
Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy of the mass
Diagnostic laparoscopy with biopsy of the pancreatic head
notes: A percutaneous biopsy risks seeding tumour along the needle tract and peritoneum in potentially curable disease, so it is kept for unresectable cases where EUS is not possible.
Brush cytology at ERCP has low sensitivity for pancreatic cancer. ERCP is used mainly for biliary drainage, not for diagnosis.
Laparoscopy is invasive and is used selectively for staging, to look for occult peritoneal disease, not as the first-line way to get tissue.
questions.why: EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy is the preferred way to get tissue from a pancreatic mass. It gives a high diagnostic yield, adds local staging, and avoids seeding tumour along a percutaneous tract in disease that may be resectable.

questions.stem: Jake, 78, has a pancreatic head mass blocking his common bile duct. Bilirubin is 186 µmol/L (mostly conjugated), ALP is 612 U/L, albumin is 32 g/L and INR is 1.4. He takes no anticoagulant. What is the most likely mechanism of his raised INR?
options: Bile salts cannot reach the gut to form micelles, so vitamin K is poorly absorbed
Hepatic synthesis of clotting factors has failed from established hepatic cirrhosis
Clotting factors are being consumed by tumour-driven chronic intravascular coagulation
Conjugated bilirubin directly inhibits gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors in liver
notes: Nothing suggests cirrhosis (no stigmata, mildly low albumin, a cholestatic pattern). An INR that corrects with parenteral vitamin K points to malabsorption, not synthetic failure.
Nothing points to DIC: he is well and afebrile, and there is no thrombocytopenia or bleeding. DIC would also not explain an isolated mild INR rise.
Bilirubin does not inhibit the vitamin K-dependent carboxylase. The defect is a lack of vitamin K itself.
questions.why: Vitamin K is fat-soluble and needs bile salt micelles to be absorbed. Biliary obstruction therefore depletes factors II, VII, IX and X. This corrects with parenteral phytomenadione, which matters before EUS, ERCP or surgery.

questions.stem: Jake's CT shows a pancreatic head mass with abrupt cut-off of both a dilated common bile duct (14 mm) and a dilated main pancreatic duct (6 mm): the double duct sign. Where do these two ducts normally join and drain, explaining why one head mass blocks both?
options: First (superior) part of the duodenum, beside the gastroduodenal artery
Third (horizontal) part of the duodenum, passing beneath the SMA
Duodenojejunal flexure, at the suspensory ligament of the duodenum
Second (descending) part of the duodenum, at the major duodenal papilla
notes: The gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum, but the ducts do not drain there.
The third part of the duodenum crosses beneath the SMA (where SMA syndrome happens); no ducts drain into it.
The duodenojejunal flexure is where the duodenum meets the jejunum, well away from where the ducts drain.
questions.why: The distal common bile duct runs behind or through the pancreatic head and joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla. This opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum, so a head mass can block both ducts at once.

questions.stem: Frank, 76, is on an ED trolley after a 30-second blackout with no warning. On examination his radial pulse is regular, large-volume and 34/min. Before you see the ECG, you want bedside evidence of AV dissociation. Which examination step should you tell the examiner you are doing next?
options: Lie and then stand him to measure postural blood pressure over 3 minutes
Perform right carotid sinus massage while watching the cardiac monitor
Inspect the JVP at 45 degrees for intermittent cannon a waves
Auscultate for an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
notes: Postural BP looks for orthostatic hypotension, not AV dissociation, and standing a patient with a pulse of 34 risks another collapse, so it is deferred.
Carotid sinus massage increases vagal tone and could cause asystole in a patient who already has severe bradycardia and pauses.
An ejection systolic murmur suggests aortic stenosis as a cause of exertional syncope, but it says nothing about whether the atria and ventricles are dissociated.
questions.why: In AV dissociation the right atrium sometimes contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, which produces irregular cannon a waves in the JVP. A first heart sound that varies in loudness is the matching sign on auscultation.

questions.stem: At 11:00, Frank, 76, has a 4-second pause on the monitor with light-headedness, and his systolic BP falls to 94. His ECG shows complete heart block with a broad escape at 30/min. Pacing pads are on and IV access is in. Electrolytes are normal. He took metoprolol 50 mg at 7 am. Which drug should be given first?
options: Atropine 0.6 mg IV, repeated as needed to a maximum of 3 mg
Glucagon 5 mg IV bolus to reverse the beta-blockade
Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 10 minutes
Adrenaline 1 mg IV bolus, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes
notes: Glucagon is for beta-blocker overdose. Frank is on a therapeutic dose, and his block is below the AV node, so beta-blockade does not explain it.
IV calcium treats hyperkalaemia or calcium channel blocker toxicity. His potassium and calcium are normal.
A 1 mg IV adrenaline bolus is the cardiac arrest dose. A patient who has a pulse needs a titrated adrenaline infusion, and only if atropine fails.
questions.why: Under ANZCOR, symptomatic bradycardia with adverse features (syncope, pauses, hypotension) is treated first with atropine 0.5 to 0.6 mg IV, repeated up to 3 mg. If that fails, the next steps are an isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion or transcutaneous pacing.

questions.stem: Frank, 76, has complete heart block on his ECG. P waves at 84/min are dissociated from a regular escape rhythm at 32/min, and the QRS is 150 ms with RBBB morphology and left axis deviation. The registrar says atropine may not lift his rate much. What is the main reason for this?
options: Atropine is broken down quickly by plasma cholinesterase in older adults
Beta blockade from metoprolol stops atropine acting at muscarinic receptors
The escape focus depends on sympathetic tone, which atropine reduces
The block is in the His-Purkinje system, which has little vagal innervation
notes: Atropine is cleared mostly by the liver and kidneys, not plasma cholinesterase, and a short duration would not explain the lack of any response.
Atropine acts on muscarinic receptors whether or not beta receptors are blocked, so metoprolol does not stop it binding.
Atropine is antimuscarinic and does not reduce sympathetic tone. If anything, it lets sympathetic tone act unopposed.
questions.why: Atropine blocks vagal (muscarinic) input, which mainly affects the SA and AV nodes. A broad escape means the block and the escape focus are below the node, where vagal tone has little effect, so atropine often fails.

questions.stem: The cardiology registrar asks whether Frank, 76, could be having an inferior MI. She points out that inferior infarction usually causes block at the AV node itself with a narrow escape, rather than the broad escape Frank has. Which artery most commonly supplies the AV node?
options: Left anterior descending artery via its septal perforator branches
Right coronary artery via the AV nodal branch at the crux
Left circumflex artery via its obtuse marginal branches
Left main coronary artery via the ramus intermedius
notes: The septal perforators of the LAD supply the bundle branches. An anterior MI therefore causes block below the node with a broad escape, not AV nodal block.
In left-dominant hearts the circumflex can supply the AV node, but through its terminal posterior branch at the crux, not through the obtuse marginals, which supply the lateral wall.
The left main divides into the LAD and circumflex, and the ramus intermedius supplies the lateral wall, not the AV node.
questions.why: In most people the circulation is right-dominant, and the AV nodal artery comes off the RCA at the crux of the heart. That is why an inferior (RCA) MI usually causes AV nodal block, which is often transient and has a narrow escape.

questions.stem: You are examining Roger, 45, in ED. His abdomen is distended. Standing on his right, you percuss from the umbilicus out to the left flank and find dullness in the flank. What is the correct next step to show shifting dullness?
options: Roll him onto his left side, then re-percuss the same spot straight away and compare notes
Keep a finger on the dull spot, roll him onto his right side, wait, then re-percuss
Have him press a hand along the midline, tap one flank, and feel for a thrill
Sit him upright and percuss down from the costal margin for a fluid level
notes: Lying on the left side keeps the fluid in the left flank, so the spot stays dull and the test cannot show anything; you also need to wait for the fluid to move.
This is the fluid thrill test. It is a different and less sensitive sign that is usually positive only with large, tense ascites, so it is not the next step in shifting dullness.
Sitting him up and looking for a fluid level is not a recognised bedside test for ascites, and it does not show fluid moving with a change in position.
questions.why: Mark where the dullness starts, roll the patient towards you so that flank is uppermost, wait about 30 seconds for the fluid to move, then percuss again. If ascites is present, the spot that was dull is now resonant.

questions.stem: Roger, 45, weighs about 73 kg. His ascitic neutrophil count is 1295 x10^6/L and his creatinine has risen from 72 to 118 µmol/L. IV antibiotics are running in ED. Apart from the antibiotics, which treatment most reduces his risk of hepatorenal syndrome and death?
options: 20% albumin IV, 8 g for every litre of ascites drained at paracentesis
Terlipressin 1 mg IV 6-hourly with 20% albumin 20 to 40 g daily
20% albumin 1.5 g/kg IV within 6 hours, then 1 g/kg IV on day 3
Oral spironolactone 100 mg and furosemide 40 mg daily
notes: This is the albumin dose given to prevent circulatory dysfunction after large-volume paracentesis. It is not the regimen for SBP, and Roger had only a 40 mL diagnostic tap.
Terlipressin with albumin treats established hepatorenal syndrome-AKI once other causes are excluded. It is not the first-line preventive treatment in SBP and needs specialist input.
Diuretics should be withheld in SBP with AKI and falling blood pressure, because they reduce renal perfusion further and can bring on hepatorenal syndrome.
questions.why: In SBP, IV albumin 1.5 g/kg within 6 hours of diagnosis and 1 g/kg on day 3, given with antibiotics, lowers the rates of hepatorenal syndrome and death. For Roger the first dose is about 110 g.

questions.stem: Roger, 45, has SBP on a background of decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis. His systolic BP is falling and his creatinine has risen from 72 to 118 µmol/L. He is given IV albumin to prevent hepatorenal syndrome. Which mechanism is the albumin mainly countering?
options: Splanchnic vasodilatation lowers effective arterial volume, so renal vessels constrict
Bacteria from the ascites seed the kidneys and cause acute tubular necrosis within days
Tense ascites raises intra-abdominal pressure and compresses the renal arteries and veins
Raised bilirubin forms bile casts that block the renal tubules
notes: Hepatorenal syndrome is a functional, haemodynamic renal failure. The tubules are structurally normal and the kidneys are not infected.
Very tense ascites can impair renal venous outflow, but this is not the mechanism of hepatorenal syndrome in SBP, and albumin would not relieve compression.
Bile cast nephropathy happens at much higher bilirubin levels, usually above about 340 µmol/L. Roger's is 86, and albumin does not prevent cast formation.
questions.why: Infection makes the splanchnic vasodilatation of portal hypertension worse, so effective arterial blood volume falls. RAAS, the sympathetic system and ADH are activated, the renal arteries constrict and GFR falls. Albumin expands the circulating volume and has anti-inflammatory effects.

questions.stem: Roger, 45, has cirrhosis with ascites. The ED registrar does a diagnostic tap under ultrasound in the left iliac fossa, about 3 cm superomedial to the anterior superior iliac spine and lateral to the rectus sheath. Which artery is this site mainly chosen to avoid?
notes: The external iliac artery lies deep in the pelvis and passes under the inguinal ligament. It is well below and away from a correctly placed iliac fossa paracentesis needle.
This small superficial branch runs in subcutaneous tissue towards the ASIS. It is not the vessel the landmark is chosen to avoid.
This artery runs deep along the inguinal ligament and the iliac crest. The paracentesis landmark is defined by staying lateral to the rectus, which protects the inferior epigastric artery.
questions.why: The inferior epigastric artery runs upward deep to the rectus abdominis, inside the rectus sheath. Putting the needle lateral to the rectus sheath avoids it. Damaging it can cause a large abdominal wall haematoma, especially when platelets are low and the INR is high, as in Roger.

questions.stem: In the pre-admission clinic you are explaining Samuel's colonoscopy. He will have propofol sedation given by an anaesthetist. He says it is tax time, and asks whether he can drive himself home afterwards and get back to the office that afternoon. His partner Jess could collect him. What is the best advice?
options: He may drive once he is alert in recovery, usually 1 to 2 hours after the procedure ends
He can take a taxi home on his own and work from home that afternoon
Jess takes him home; no driving, alcohol, big decisions or legal documents for 24 hours
Jess takes him home, but he can go back to work that afternoon if he feels well
notes: Feeling alert in recovery does not mean the sedation has worn off, and driving is not allowed for 24 hours after sedation.
Going home alone in a taxi is not safe: a responsible adult needs to take him home, and work decisions should wait 24 hours.
Being driven home is right, but going back to work the same afternoon means making important decisions while still affected by sedation.
questions.why: Sedation dulls judgement and reaction time for longer than the patient feels it does. A responsible adult must take him home, ideally stay overnight, and he should not drive, drink alcohol, operate machinery, make important decisions or sign legal documents for 24 hours.

questions.stem: Samuel, 25, has ileocolonic Crohn's disease confirmed at colonoscopy: terminal ileal ulcers, a mildly narrowed ileocaecal valve and patchy right colonic ulcers. He is well enough to be managed as an outpatient. The gastroenterologist rates the activity as mild to moderate ileocaecal disease. Which treatment is first-line to induce remission?
options: Oral mesalazine 4 g daily in divided doses for 8 weeks, then reassess
Oral azathioprine 2.5 mg/kg daily as monotherapy, reviewed at 12 weeks
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly as an inpatient, then switch to oral prednisolone
Oral budesonide 9 mg daily for about 8 weeks, then taper
notes: Mesalazine has little effect in Crohn's disease and is not recommended to induce remission, unlike in ulcerative colitis.
Thiopurines take about 3 months to work, so they are used for steroid-sparing maintenance, not on their own to induce remission.
IV corticosteroids are for acute severe disease needing admission, which a stable outpatient with mild to moderate disease does not have.
questions.why: Controlled-release budesonide releases the drug in the ileum and right colon. Most of it is broken down on first pass through the liver, so it has fewer systemic steroid effects. It is first-line induction for mild to moderate ileocaecal Crohn's disease, and is tapered once he responds.

questions.stem: Samuel, 25, with active Crohn's disease (CRP 28), has Hb 118 g/L, MCV 76 fL, ferritin 16 µg/L and transferrin saturation 8% despite 3 weeks of oral iron. The gastroenterologist plans IV iron instead. Which mechanism best explains why oral iron works poorly while his bowel is inflamed?
options: Inflammation lowers hepcidin, so stored iron leaks from macrophages and is lost
The terminal ileum is the main site of iron absorption and it is ulcerated
Inflammation lowers gastric acid, so dietary ferric iron is not reduced to ferrous
IL-6 raises hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin and blocks enterocyte iron export
notes: Inflammation raises hepcidin rather than lowering it, and the effect is to trap iron in macrophages, not to release it.
Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. The terminal ileum is where vitamin B12 and bile salts are absorbed.
Gastric acid is not the main problem in Crohn's disease, and Ferro-Grad is already ferrous iron, so no reduction step is needed.
questions.why: Inflammatory cytokines, mainly IL-6, make the liver produce more hepcidin. Hepcidin breaks down ferroportin, so iron stays trapped in enterocytes and macrophages and oral iron is poorly absorbed. This is why IV iron is preferred in active IBD.

questions.stem: Samuel's colonoscopy shows Crohn's disease in the distal 10 cm of the terminal ileum, with an ulcerated, mildly narrowed ileocaecal valve. If the narrowing progresses, he may later need an ileocaecal resection. Which artery is the main blood supply to this segment?
options: Middle colic artery, from the superior mesenteric artery
Ileocolic artery, from the superior mesenteric artery
Right colic artery, from the inferior mesenteric artery
Ileal arteries, from the coeliac trunk
notes: The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon, not the terminal ileum or caecum.
The right colic artery comes from the superior mesenteric artery, not the inferior mesenteric artery, and it supplies the ascending colon rather than the ileocaecal region.
Ileal arteries come from the superior mesenteric artery. The coeliac trunk supplies foregut structures such as the stomach, liver and proximal duodenum.
questions.why: The ileocolic artery is the last branch on the right side of the superior mesenteric artery. It supplies the terminal ileum, the caecum and the appendix, and it is the vessel ligated in an ileocaecal resection.

questions.stem: Sophia Greenwood, 69, is in an ED bay with 4 months of worsening breathlessness, 2-pillow orthopnoea, PND and swollen ankles. She had an anterior STEMI a year ago. You now examine her neck veins. How should you position her and measure the jugular venous pressure?
options: Lie her flat, then measure the height of the pulsation above the clavicle
Sit her at 90°, then measure the external jugular vein's height below the earlobe in cm
Recline at 45°, head turned slightly left; measure vertical height above sternal angle
Recline at 45°, then measure the distance along the neck from the suprasternal notch
notes: Lying her flat would make her more breathless, and the clavicle is not the reference point; the sternal angle is used because it sits about 5 cm above the right atrium.
The external jugular can be kinked or affected by valves, so it is less reliable, and the earlobe is not a reference point for measuring the JVP.
The JVP is a vertical height measured from the sternal angle. A distance along the slope of the neck from the suprasternal notch overestimates it and has no reference range.
questions.why: The JVP is the vertical height of the right internal jugular pulsation above the sternal angle, with the patient at about 45° and the head turned slightly to the left. Normal is up to 3 to 4 cm. Sophia's is raised by 5 cm, which shows systemic venous congestion.

questions.stem: Sophia, 69, has decompensated heart failure in the ED: RR 28, SpO2 92% on room air, BP 144/84, bibasal crackles, oedema to mid-shins and pulmonary oedema on CXR. She has never taken a diuretic. Creatinine is 98 umol/L (eGFR 52). The nurse asks you for a drug, dose and route to treat her congestion now. Which order is most appropriate?
notes: Bowel wall oedema makes oral absorption unreliable and slower, so for acute pulmonary oedema the IV route is used.
A beta-blocker should not be started while she is congested and decompensated. It is started at a low dose once she is euvolaemic and stable, if the echo shows HFrEF.
>Spironolactone is a weak diuretic with a slow onset. It is a long-term prognostic drug for HFrEF once she is stable and her potassium and renal function allow, not treatment for acute congestion.
questions.why: In acute congestion, a patient who has never had a diuretic is given IV furosemide 20 to 40 mg. Then reassess breathing and urine output, and monitor fluid balance, daily weights and UEC with K and Mg.

questions.stem: Sophia, 69, has heart failure after an anterior STEMI. She needs two extra pillows at night. In ED she slid down the trolley, and her RR rose from 26 to 28 and her SpO2 fell from 93% to 92%. What is the main mechanism of her worse breathlessness when she lies flat?
options: The abdominal contents push the diaphragm up and splint the lung bases
Lying flat lowers cardiac output by reducing venous return to the heart
Lying flat abolishes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and worsens V/Q matching
Blood shifts from legs and gut to the chest, raising pulmonary venous pressure
notes: The diaphragm does rise slightly when supine, but the main problem in orthopnoea is pulmonary venous congestion. Diaphragm splinting is the mechanism in ascites or obesity.
Lying flat increases venous return rather than reducing it. The problem is a failing ventricle that cannot handle the extra preload, not a fall in output from too little filling.
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is not abolished by posture, and V/Q mismatch does not explain why a raised preload brings on breathlessness in heart failure.
questions.why: Lying flat moves blood from the legs and gut into the chest and increases venous return. A failing left ventricle cannot handle the extra preload, so left atrial and pulmonary capillary pressures rise and fluid leaks into the lung interstitium. Overnight reabsorption of leg oedema adds to this and causes PND.

questions.stem: Sophia, 69, had a STEMI treated with a stent 12 months ago. Today's ECG shows sinus tachycardia with pathological Q waves in V1 to V4, poor R wave progression and shallow T inversion in V2 to V4, all unchanged from her post-PCI ECG. Which coronary artery was most likely occluded in her previous infarct?
options: Right coronary artery, proximal to the acute marginal branch
Left circumflex artery, including the obtuse marginal branches
Posterior descending artery, arising from a dominant right coronary
notes: Occlusion of the right coronary artery usually gives an inferior infarct, with changes in II, III and aVF. It may also involve the RV or the posterior wall.
The left circumflex supplies the lateral wall. Its infarcts show in I, aVL and V5 to V6, or as posterior changes, not in V1 to V4.
The posterior descending artery supplies the inferior wall and the posterior third of the septum. Its infarcts show inferiorly, not as anterior Q waves in V1 to V4.
questions.why: V1 to V4 cover the septum and anterior wall of the LV, which the left anterior descending artery supplies. Losing this large area of muscle is a common cause of ischaemic cardiomyopathy and HFrEF.

questions.stem: James, 62, is in ED after vomiting bright red blood with clots twice this morning, and he has had a black, sticky bowel motion. He drinks heavily. In your focused history you want to judge how likely a Mallory-Weiss tear is as the source. Which question is most useful?
options: Have you taken any anti-inflammatory tablets such as ibuprofen recently?
Have you had burning pain in the upper middle part of your tummy?
Were you retching or vomiting before any blood came up?
Have your bowel motions been black, sticky or very smelly?
notes: NSAID use is a risk factor for peptic ulcer, not a Mallory-Weiss tear, so this question helps assess a different differential.
Epigastric burning pain points towards peptic ulcer disease or gastritis rather than a tear caused by retching.
Melaena confirms an upper GI source with significant bleeding, but it does not tell a Mallory-Weiss tear apart from varices or an ulcer.
questions.why: A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction caused by forceful retching or vomiting, so blood that appears only after repeated non-bloody retching suggests one. James's blood came up on its own, which argues against it.

questions.stem: James, 62, has a suspected variceal bleed in alcohol-related cirrhosis: HR 130, BP 92/56, INR 1.8, albumin 27 g/L and moderate ascites. He is nil by mouth, terlipressin has been charted and endoscopy is being arranged. Which antibiotic regimen should you start in the emergency department?
options: Amoxicillin with clavulanate 875/125 mg orally twice daily
notes: Oral norfloxacin is an older regimen used mainly for long-term SBP prophylaxis. It is unsuitable for a shocked, vomiting, nil-by-mouth patient, and ceftriaxone works better in advanced cirrhosis.
Metronidazole covers anaerobes but misses the enteric Gram-negative bacilli that cause most infections after a variceal bleed.
An oral agent is inappropriate while he is nil by mouth and actively vomiting blood, and it is not the recommended prophylaxis in acute variceal bleeding.
questions.why: In cirrhosis with GI bleeding, prophylactic antibiotics reduce bacterial infections (including SBP), rebleeding and death. eTG recommends ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, started before endoscopy, for up to 7 days.

questions.stem: James, 62, has suspected oesophageal variceal haemorrhage from alcohol-related cirrhosis with portal hypertension. Before endoscopy he is given terlipressin 2 mg IV. By what mechanism does terlipressin reduce bleeding from his varices?
options: V2 receptor water reabsorption expands plasma volume and supports blood pressure
Contraction of the lower oesophageal sphincter mechanically compresses the varices
Relaxation of hepatic stellate cells lowers intrahepatic vascular resistance
V1-mediated splanchnic arteriolar constriction reduces portal venous inflow
notes: Terlipressin's V2 effect causes free water retention and hyponatraemia (watch his sodium of 131), but this does not stop the bleeding. Volume expansion would actually raise portal pressure.
Terlipressin has no useful effect on the lower oesophageal sphincter, and sphincter tone does not control variceal bleeding.
Terlipressin acts on inflow to the portal system, not on intrahepatic resistance. Lowering sinusoidal resistance is the target of other agents, not vasopressin analogues.
questions.why: Terlipressin is a vasopressin analogue that constricts splanchnic arterioles through V1 receptors. This cuts blood flow into the portal system, lowering portal pressure and variceal wall tension so the bleeding slows.

questions.stem: James, 62, has cirrhosis with portal hypertension on ultrasound and is bleeding from suspected oesophageal varices. Varices in the lower oesophagus form where portal venous blood is diverted into the systemic circulation. Which veins make up this portosystemic anastomosis?
options: Superior rectal veins and middle and inferior rectal veins
Left gastric vein and oesophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
Paraumbilical veins and superficial epigastric veins of the abdominal wall
Splenic vein and left renal vein via retroperitoneal collaterals
notes: The rectal anastomosis is a real portosystemic site, but it produces anorectal varices, not oesophageal ones.
Paraumbilical-to-abdominal wall collaterals produce caput medusae on the anterior abdominal wall, not oesophageal varices.
A splenorenal collateral is a retroperitoneal shunt that can form spontaneously, but it lies away from the oesophagus and does not form oesophageal varices.
questions.why: In the lower oesophagus, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vein (portal) join oesophageal veins that drain to the azygos system (systemic). Raised portal pressure dilates these submucosal veins into varices.

questions.stem: You are examining the feet of Patrick, 63, who has type 2 diabetes and 6 months of numbness in both feet. Shoes and socks are off and there is mild callus under both first metatarsal heads. You are about to test protective sensation with a 10 g monofilament. Which technique is correct?
options: Drag it along the sole from heel to toe and ask when he first feels it
Press it on the callus under the first metatarsal head, where ulcers most often form
Press perpendicular until it buckles for about 2 s, eyes closed, avoiding callus
Press it until the skin blanches, with his eyes open so he can watch each touch
notes: Dragging tests light touch moving across the skin, not a fixed 10 g pressure, so it does not assess protective sensation.
Callus dulls sensation and gives a false absent response, so test next to it, never on it.
>10 g and blanching are not the end point, and with his eyes open he can see when he is touched, which defeats the test.
questions.why: The monofilament is pressed at right angles to the skin until it bends (which delivers 10 g) for about 2 seconds, with the patient's eyes closed, at the plantar forefoot sites and hallux. Avoid callus, scar and ulcers, because thick skin can make sensation seem absent when it is not.

questions.stem: Patrick, 63, has type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.9% (74 mmol/mol) and eGFR 72. He admits he rarely takes his immediate-release metformin because it gives him diarrhoea. He has never tried any other formulation or strategy. What is the most appropriate change to his glucose-lowering treatment now?
options: Stop metformin and start an SGLT2 inhibitor such as empagliflozin on its own
Change to metformin XR 500 mg once daily with the evening meal, titrating slowly
Stop metformin and start gliclazide MR 30 mg once daily with breakfast
Start insulin glargine 10 units at night and keep metformin for when he can manage
notes: Stopping metformin is premature because he has not tried the measures that usually make it tolerable. An SGLT2 inhibitor is normally added to metformin, not used instead of it.
A sulfonylurea risks hypoglycaemia and weight gain, which is a bad choice in a man who is already unsteady and at risk of falls, and metformin has not yet failed.
Insulin is not needed for an asymptomatic HbA1c of 8.9% when oral treatment has never been taken properly.
questions.why: Metformin is first line, and gut intolerance is often managed by taking it with food, starting low and titrating slowly, or switching to the extended-release form. Try this before giving up on it. Add a second agent (an SGLT2 inhibitor is favoured if the albuminuria is confirmed) if HbA1c is still above target at 3 months.

questions.stem: Patrick, 63, has diabetic peripheral neuropathy and feels unsteady in the dark. He stands steadily with his feet together and eyes open, but sways and nearly falls when he closes his eyes. He has no postural drop and his power is near normal. What is the mechanism of this positive Romberg test?
options: Loss of joint position input from large myelinated sensory fibres, made up for by vision
Cerebellar vermis dysfunction that impairs coordination of the trunk muscles during stance
Postural hypotension from autonomic neuropathy that reduces cerebral perfusion on standing
Weakness of the ankle dorsiflexors from loss of distal motor axons
notes: Cerebellar ataxia makes the patient unsteady even with the eyes open, so Romberg is not positive in the true sense.
He has no postural drop, and hypotension would not depend on whether his eyes are open or closed.
Motor weakness causes the same unsteadiness whether or not he can see, and his power is near normal.
questions.why: Balance depends on vision, vestibular input and proprioception. When large-fibre neuropathy removes joint position sense from the feet, vision makes up for it, so balance fails only when the eyes close or it is dark. This is sensory ataxia.

questions.stem: Examining Patrick, 63, who has diabetic peripheral neuropathy, you find both ankle reflexes absent even with reinforcement, while both knee reflexes are present. Losing the ankle jerk first fits a length-dependent neuropathy. Which spinal root and peripheral nerve carry the ankle reflex arc?
options: L3 and L4 roots via the femoral nerve
L5 root via the common fibular nerve
S2 to S4 roots via the pudendal nerve
S1 root via the tibial nerve
notes: L3 and L4 through the femoral nerve carry the knee jerk, which is preserved here.
The common fibular nerve supplies the anterior and lateral leg compartments. L5 has no reliable routine reflex and does not carry the ankle jerk.
S2 to S4 through the pudendal nerve serve the anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes and saddle sensation, not the ankle jerk.
questions.why: The ankle jerk is an S1 reflex carried in the sciatic nerve and then its tibial branch to gastrocnemius and soleus. It is the longest reflex arc in the body, so it is lost before the knee jerk (L3 to L4, femoral nerve) in a length-dependent neuropathy.

questions.stem: Charlie, a 34-year-old builder, has PCR-confirmed uncomplicated influenza A with a clear chest and SpO2 97% on room air. You are safety netting before he goes home from the GP clinic. Which new symptom should you tell him means calling 000, not booking a GP review?
options: A dry cough that is still there two weeks from now
Getting better, then a new fever with coloured phlegm that lasts more than two days
Breathlessness while resting, or struggling to breathe
A fever around 38 °C that is still there on day five
notes: A cough and tiredness lasting 1 to 2 weeks or more after influenza is expected, so this needs reassurance or routine review, not an ambulance.
Getting better and then worse again suggests secondary bacterial pneumonia, which needs same-day GP or ED review, not necessarily a 000 call.
A fever that lasts longer than expected deserves GP review, but on its own, without respiratory distress or confusion, it is not an emergency.
questions.why: Breathlessness at rest suggests hypoxia from influenza pneumonia or another serious complication, so he needs an ambulance. Breathlessness at rest, chest pain, blue lips, confusion or drowsiness mean 000. Getting worse again after improving means same-day review.

questions.stem: Charlie, 34, is a previously well smoker with 3 days of fever and dry cough. Influenza A is detected on PCR. T 38.0 °C, HR 94, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, chest clear. He lives with well adult housemates. What is the most appropriate treatment in general practice?
options: Supportive care only, with no antiviral or antibiotic
Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily for 5 days, with rest, fluids and paracetamol
Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily for 5 days, with supportive care
Supportive care, plus oseltamivir 75 mg orally daily as prophylaxis for housemates
notes: He is beyond 48 hours from onset, not severely unwell and not in a higher-risk group, so oseltamivir would add little apart from adverse effects.
This is a viral illness with a clear chest and normal observations. There is no evidence of bacterial pneumonia, so antibiotics would not help.
Post-exposure prophylaxis is for high-risk contacts, such as unvaccinated people with risk factors or residents of aged-care outbreaks, not healthy adult housemates.
questions.why: This is uncomplicated influenza in a healthy adult more than 48 hours from onset, so eTG advises supportive care alone. Oseltamivir is reserved for severe illness, people at higher risk of complications, or (if considered at all in healthy adults) the first 48 hours.

questions.stem: Charlie, 34, asks why he can't have the flu tablet his friend got. His supervising GP explains that, in healthy adults, oseltamivir helps only if started within 48 hours of symptom onset. Which mechanism of action best explains this time window?
options: Blocks haemagglutinin binding to sialic acid, stopping the virus entering cells
Inhibits neuraminidase, stopping release of new virions from infected cells
Blocks the M2 ion channel, stopping uncoating of the virus inside the cell
Inhibits viral RNA polymerase, stopping replication of the viral genome
notes: Haemagglutinin-mediated attachment is the target of vaccine-induced neutralising antibodies, not oseltamivir.
M2 blockade is how amantadine works. It is not used, because circulating influenza A is resistant and it has no effect on influenza B.
Oseltamivir does not act on the polymerase complex. Baloxavir is the drug that targets the polymerase complex, through its cap-dependent endonuclease.
questions.why: Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase, the enzyme that cleaves sialic acid so that progeny virions can leave the infected cell. It limits spread to new cells, which matters only while viral replication is peaking in the first 1 to 2 days.

questions.stem: The practice nurse is collecting Charlie's nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory PCR. He is seated with his head tilted slightly back. To reach the posterior nasopharynx safely, in which direction should the swab be advanced through the nostril?
options: Upwards towards the bridge of the nose, following the line of the nasal bones
Upwards and laterally into the middle meatus beneath the middle concha
Upwards along the nasal septum towards the roof of the nasal cavity
Straight back along the nasal floor, parallel to the hard palate
notes: Angling upwards along the nasal bones aims at the roof of the nasal cavity, so the swab misses the nasopharynx and is more painful.
The middle meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses. It is not the nasopharynx, and probing it is uncomfortable.
The roof of the nasal cavity is the thin cribriform plate of the ethmoid. Aiming there risks injury and does not sample the nasopharynx.
questions.why: The nasal floor runs horizontally back to the nasopharynx. Advance the swab parallel to the hard palate, at right angles to the face, to a depth of about the distance from the nostril to the tragus of the ear.

questions.stem: Linda Faulker, 69, is improving in ED with presumed norovirus gastroenteritis, caught after changing her 3-year-old grandson's diarrhoeal nappies. Before discharge she asks when it is safe to prepare food for others and look after the grandchildren again. What is the best advice to give her?
options: Once she has had 24 hours without any diarrhoea or vomiting and is eating normally
Once a stool PCR confirms that norovirus is no longer present
Once 48 hours have passed since her last diarrhoea or vomiting
Once a full 7 days have passed since her symptoms first began
notes: 24 hours is too short for norovirus; she can still pass it on, and the standard exclusion period is 48 hours after symptoms stop.
Clearance stool testing is not used for norovirus, as PCR can stay positive for weeks; return is based on time since symptoms stopped.
A fixed 7 days from onset has no basis; exclusion is counted from when symptoms stop, and 48 hours is enough.
questions.why: Norovirus is still shed and spreads easily after symptoms settle, so Australian exclusion advice (food handling, caring for children) is 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting. Pair this with soap-and-water hand washing, because alcohol rub works poorly against norovirus.

questions.stem: Linda, 69, with gastroenteritis, had lying BP 96/58 and HR 124 (usual BP 140/80). After a first 500 mL crystalloid bolus she is lying flat with HR 128, BP 94/54, CRT 3 s and little urine. VBG shows a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, K 3.3, lactate 1.6. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give a further 500 mL Hartmann's bolus, then reassess HR, BP and urine output
Start maintenance fluid with 20 mmol KCl at 80 mL/h and review in 4 hours
Give 1 L of 4% albumin over 30 minutes, then recheck lactate, HR, BP and urine output
Start a peripheral noradrenaline infusion aiming for a MAP of 65 mmHg
notes: Maintenance rates will not correct the deficit in a patient who is still hypovolaemic, and potassium should go in once she is passing urine and resuscitated.
Albumin has no advantage over crystalloid for resuscitating fluid lost to gastroenteritis, and it costs more.
Vasopressors are for hypotension that persists after adequate fluid; she has had only 500 mL despite ongoing large losses.
questions.why: Values still in the yellow zone after one bolus mean she is still hypovolaemic and needs more crystalloid boluses, each followed by reassessment. A balanced fluid such as Hartmann's avoids making her hyperchloraemic acidosis worse.

questions.stem: Linda, 69, takes captopril 50 mg twice daily and has been taking ibuprofen. After 8 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea her creatinine is 128 µmol/L (baseline 70) and her urea is disproportionately raised. By what mechanism does captopril lower her GFR when she is hypovolaemic?
options: Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilation
Loss of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction
Direct toxicity to proximal tubular cells causing tubular necrosis
Bradykinin build-up causing afferent arteriolar constriction
notes: This is how ibuprofen contributes, by blocking afferent prostaglandin vasodilation, not how captopril does.
ACE inhibitors cause a haemodynamic (prerenal) fall in GFR, not direct tubular toxicity; a raised urea:creatinine ratio fits a prerenal cause.
Bradykinin is a vasodilator; its build-up with ACE inhibitors causes cough and angioedema, not afferent constriction.
questions.why: When renal perfusion falls, angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole to keep glomerular pressure up. An ACE inhibitor removes this, so GFR falls. NSAIDs block afferent prostaglandin vasodilation, which is why the two together with dehydration cause prerenal AKI.

questions.stem: Linda, 69, is a hypertensive, diabetic ex-smoker who woke with sudden diffuse abdominal pain. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm, but the registrar wants mesenteric ischaemia kept in mind. If an embolus, for example from AF, caused it, which artery would it most likely lodge in, and why?
options: Coeliac trunk, as it is the first and shortest anterior branch of the abdominal aorta
Inferior mesenteric artery, as its narrow lumen readily traps emboli
Marginal artery at the splenic flexure, as it is a watershed end vessel
Superior mesenteric artery, as it leaves the aorta at an acute, oblique angle
notes: The coeliac trunk is short and has a rich collateral supply; it is rarely the site of embolic occlusion.
The IMA's small calibre and sharp take-off actually make embolism there uncommon, and IMA territory has good collaterals.
Watershed areas such as the splenic flexure are typical of low-flow (non-occlusive) ischaemia, not embolic occlusion.
questions.why: The SMA arises from the aorta at about L1, at a narrow angle and almost in line with aortic flow, so emboli pass into it easily. They usually lodge a few centimetres beyond its origin, near the middle colic branch, causing small bowel ischaemia.

questions.stem: You are examining Sam, 72, in the ED. His right mid and lower zones are stony dull to percussion and breath sounds there are absent. You tell the examiner which further test you will do over the dull area. Which finding would best support a pleural effusion rather than consolidation?
options: Bronchial breath sounds with whispering pectoriloquy over the dull area
Increased tactile vocal fremitus over the dull area
Reduced vocal resonance over the dull area
Trachea deviated towards the side of the dullness
notes: Bronchial breathing and whispering pectoriloquy point to consolidation. Over an effusion you may hear bronchial breathing only in a thin band just above the fluid level.
Tactile fremitus is increased over consolidation but reduced over fluid, which blocks the vibration reaching the chest wall.
A trachea pulled towards the dull side suggests lobar collapse or pneumonectomy. A large effusion like Sam's pushes the trachea away.
questions.why: Fluid between the pleural layers dampens transmitted sound, so vocal resonance and fremitus are reduced over an effusion. Consolidated lung conducts sound better, so they are increased. A large effusion pushes the trachea away from its side.

questions.stem: Sam, 72, has a large right pleural effusion up to the 2nd anterior rib, normal clotting and no anticoagulants. The registrar does an ultrasound-guided diagnostic and therapeutic pleural aspiration after consent. How much fluid should be removed at this first aspiration?
options: No more than 500 mL, to limit the risk of pneumothorax and bleeding at the puncture site
No more than about 1.5 L, stopping earlier if he gets cough or chest tightness
About 3 L, because the effusion reaches the 2nd anterior rib
Drain to dryness, so the CT can show the underlying lung clearly
notes: 500 mL is too cautious for a large symptomatic effusion and gives less relief than needed. Pneumothorax risk depends on technique and ultrasound guidance, not this volume limit.
Removing 3 L at once greatly raises the risk of re-expansion pulmonary oedema, however big the effusion.
Draining to dryness risks re-expansion oedema, and CT is better done with some fluid in place so the pleura can be assessed.
questions.why: Remove no more than about 1.5 L at one time, and stop sooner if cough, chest tightness or pain develops. Draining more quickly risks re-expansion pulmonary oedema. Contrast CT is ideally done before full drainage.

questions.stem: Sam, 72, has COPD and SpO2 92% on room air. The nurse asks why you won't just put him on 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask. In a patient with COPD, what is the main mechanism by which high-concentration oxygen raises the PaCO2?
options: Suppression of hypoxic ventilatory drive from the peripheral chemoreceptors
Oxygen toxicity damaging the alveoli and reducing CO2 diffusion
Greater haemoglobin affinity for CO2 as haemoglobin becomes fully saturated
Release of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening V/Q mismatch
notes: Loss of hypoxic drive is the classic explanation, but minute ventilation barely falls. It is a minor contributor, not the main mechanism.
Oxygen toxicity needs prolonged exposure to a very high FiO2 and does not cause the rapid rise in CO2 seen in COPD.
This reverses the Haldane effect: oxygenated haemoglobin binds less CO2, so more CO2 is released into the plasma and PaCO2 rises.
questions.why: High FiO2 removes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, so blood flows to poorly ventilated alveoli. This increases physiological dead space and V/Q mismatch. The Haldane effect adds to it, and loss of hypoxic drive matters much less. This is why the TSANZ target is 88 to 92%.

questions.stem: The registrar is preparing an ultrasound-guided aspiration of Sam's large right pleural effusion through a lateral intercostal space. You are asked where the needle should pass in relation to the ribs to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle. Where should it go?
options: Just above the upper border of the rib below the chosen space
Just below the lower border of the rib above the chosen space
Midway between the two ribs, whatever the site of entry
Onto the rib first, then walked off its lower edge
notes: This is where the bundle runs, in the costal groove under the rib above, so it risks bleeding from the intercostal artery and nerve injury.
Collateral branches run along the upper border of the rib below, and near the spine the main vessels may cross mid-space. The safe line is just above the lower rib.
Walking off the lower edge of a rib puts the needle straight into the costal groove and the neurovascular bundle.
questions.why: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN, top to bottom) run in the costal groove on the inferior border of each rib. Inserting the needle just over the superior border of the rib below avoids them. Posteriorly, near the spine, the vessels are tortuous and less protected.

questions.stem: You are the ED intern seeing Jeff, 35, who has severe acute asthma after exposure to a cat and pollen. Salbutamol via spacer and oxygen have been started and the senior is on the way. You now have time for a few targeted questions. Which question best identifies his risk of a fatal asthma attack?
options: "How old were you when first diagnosed with asthma, and who made the diagnosis?"
"Does anyone in your family have asthma, eczema or hayfever?"
"Have you ever needed intensive care or a breathing tube for asthma?"
"Does exercise or cold air tend to make your breathing worse?"
notes: Age at diagnosis helps confirm asthma but does not predict whether an attack will be fatal.
Family history and atopy support the diagnosis of asthma but do not grade the risk of this attack.
Exercise and cold air are triggers. Knowing about them helps long-term control but does not show the risk of a fatal attack.
questions.why: Previous ICU admission or intubation is the strongest marker of risk of a fatal attack. Ask it of every person with asthma, along with admissions, oral steroid courses, reliever use, preventer use and whether they have a written action plan.

questions.stem: Jeff, 35, cannot finish sentences. RR 28, SpO2 92% on room air, HR 116. He took 2 puffs of his own salbutamol an hour ago with little benefit and can use a spacer. The ED nurse asks, "How much salbutamol, and how?" What do you prescribe?
options: 4 puffs via pMDI and spacer, repeated every 4 hours as needed
12 puffs via pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour
2.5 mg nebulised once, then review the response in 4 hours
IV salbutamol infusion at 5 microgram/minute as first-line therapy
notes: 4 puffs every 4 hours is a dose for mild exacerbations or maintenance, far too little for a man who cannot finish sentences.
A single 2.5 mg nebule followed by a 4-hour wait is too small a dose and too long an interval for severe asthma, which needs repeated doses in the first hour.
IV salbutamol is not first-line. Inhaled salbutamol works as well with fewer adverse effects, and IV is kept for senior or ICU use in refractory cases.
questions.why: In severe acute asthma in adults, the Australian Asthma Handbook advises salbutamol 100 microgram x 12 puffs via pMDI and spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour. Use 5 mg nebulised, driven by oxygen, if he cannot use a spacer. Then reassess and give it again as needed.

questions.stem: Jeff's first venous gas, taken on room air, showed pH 7.46 and pCO2 33 mmHg. An hour later he is still wheezy and breathless with RR 30, now looks tired, and his repeat venous pCO2 is 44 mmHg. What best explains the rise in his pCO2?
options: Renal compensation for the earlier respiratory alkalosis, with bicarbonate retention
Better ventilation-perfusion matching after bronchodilator treatment
Extra CO2 production from salbutamol-related lactic acidosis
Falling alveolar ventilation as tiring muscles fail against air trapping
notes: Renal compensation for respiratory alkalosis excretes bicarbonate over days. It does not raise pCO2, which is set by alveolar ventilation.
Better ventilation-perfusion matching would improve gas exchange and come with clinical improvement, not a rising pCO2 in a tiring patient.
Salbutamol can cause lactic acidosis, but the normal response is to breathe harder and lower pCO2, so a rising pCO2 still points to failing ventilation.
questions.why: Early in acute asthma, hypoxaemia and stimulation of airway receptors drive hyperventilation, so pCO2 should be low. A normal or rising pCO2 in a patient who is still breathless means alveolar ventilation is failing from exhaustion and severe obstruction. This is a life-threatening feature that needs ICU review.

questions.stem: Examining Jeff, 35, in the ED, you see him sitting forward with his hands on his knees. Muscles at the side of his neck tighten with every breath in, and you report accessory muscle use. Which muscles, running from the cervical vertebrae to the first and second ribs, are lifting his upper rib cage?
options: Upper fibres of trapezius, from the occiput and nuchal ligament to the clavicle
notes: The infrahyoid muscles attach to the hyoid, thyroid cartilage, sternum and scapula. They depress the hyoid and larynx and do not insert on the ribs.
Platysma is a thin superficial muscle of facial expression (facial nerve) in the subcutaneous tissue. It does not attach to the ribs or lift the rib cage.
Upper trapezius attaches to the clavicle and scapula and elevates the shoulder girdle. It does not run from the cervical vertebrae to the first and second ribs.
questions.why: The scalenes arise from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae. Anterior and middle scalene insert on the first rib and posterior scalene on the second. With sternocleidomastoid, they are the main accessory muscles of inspiration recruited in severe airflow obstruction.

questions.stem: Leticia, 35, has returned from India 3 weeks ago with fever, RUQ ache, dark urine and pale stools. You are in the ED examining her abdomen and want to find the edge of a possibly enlarged, tender liver. How should you palpate for the liver edge?
options: Start just below the right costal margin and press deeply as she breathes out
Start in the epigastrium and move laterally along the costal margin as she breathes out
Start in the right iliac fossa and move up towards the costal margin as she breathes in
Start in the left upper quadrant and sweep across to the right as she breathes in
notes: If you start at the costal margin, your hand can already be over a large liver and you will miss its edge. The liver also comes down on inspiration, not expiration.
The liver moves down on inspiration, so palpating as she breathes out works against you. Starting in the epigastrium also misses a liver edge lying low in the right flank.
This is the route for the spleen, which enlarges from the left upper quadrant towards the right iliac fossa. It is not how you look for the liver edge.
questions.why: Start low in the right iliac fossa so you do not miss a large liver. Then advance your hand towards the costal margin a little with each breath, feeling for the edge to hit your fingers as the diaphragm pushes the liver down on inspiration.

questions.stem: Leticia, 35, was in rural India with no malaria prophylaxis and few mosquito nets. Her temperature is 38.1 °C. Hepatitis A IgM is detected. Her first malaria antigen test and thick and thin films are negative. Platelets are normal. What should be done next about malaria?
options: No further testing, as the confirmed hepatitis A explains her fever
Repeat thick and thin films with antigen 12 to 24 hours apart until 3 sets are negative
Start empirical artemether-lumefantrine now and repeat films only if she remains febrile
Send malaria serology at her 2-week follow-up appointment
notes: Having one diagnosis does not rule out another. She has unprotected exposure in an area with P. falciparum and P. vivax, and a single negative set is not enough.
Antimalarials are given for a confirmed diagnosis. Empirical treatment is only for severe illness when testing is unavailable, and she is stable with tests under way.
Serology shows past exposure, not current infection, and waiting 2 weeks could miss falciparum malaria, which can kill within days.
questions.why: One negative set does not exclude malaria in a febrile traveller. Repeat films and antigen testing 12 to 24 hours apart until 3 sets are negative, even when another diagnosis has been confirmed.
