questions.stem: Leticia, 35, has acute hepatitis A with ALT 2840 U/L. Her INR is 1.1 and albumin 39 g/L. The registrar says the INR, not the albumin, is the result to watch for early liver failure. What is the main physiological reason?
options: Albumin is lost in the vomitus, so its level reflects losses rather than synthesis
The INR measures how bilirubin impairs platelet function in hepatitis
Albumin falls only once fibrosis develops, so it stays normal for weeks in acute illness
Factor VII has a half-life of about 6 hours, so the INR rises within a day of failure
notes: Vomitus contains very little protein, so vomiting does not lower serum albumin to any useful degree.
The INR is a measure of the prothrombin time, which reflects clotting factor activity. It has nothing to do with platelet function.
Albumin can fall in acute illness too, but slowly because of its long half-life. The issue is timing, not whether fibrosis is present.
questions.why: The liver makes the clotting factors, and factor VII has a half-life of about 6 hours, so the INR rises quickly when synthesis fails. Albumin's half-life is about 3 weeks, so it stays normal early. Judge severity by INR, glucose and mental state.

questions.stem: Leticia, 35, has fever and right upper quadrant pain after travel, and cholecystitis is on your differential. You test for Murphy's sign by pressing over the gallbladder fundus while she breathes in. Where is the surface marking of the gallbladder fundus?
options: Tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, at the lateral edge of rectus
Tip of the right 11th rib in the midaxillary line, below the lower costal margin
In the midline just below the xiphisternum
Right renal angle, below the 12th rib posteriorly
notes: The 11th rib tip in the midaxillary line overlies the lateral liver and hepatic flexure, too far lateral and posterior for the gallbladder fundus.
The area below the xiphisternum is the epigastrium, overlying the stomach and left lobe of the liver. Tenderness here suggests peptic disease or pancreatitis.
The renal angle is where you check for kidney tenderness, as in pyelonephritis. The gallbladder lies in front, not at the back.
questions.why: The gallbladder fundus lies at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where the linea semilunaris (lateral edge of rectus abdominis) meets the costal margin. If she stops breathing in when you press there, Murphy's sign is positive.

questions.stem: Phillip, 75, collapsed in the ED waiting area. CPR is in progress, pads are on, and the first rhythm check shows VF. Using COACHED, you charge the defibrillator during compressions, then deliver a single shock once everyone is clear. What do you direct the team to do immediately after the shock?
options: Check the carotid pulse for up to 10 seconds, then resume CPR if absent
Watch the monitor for an organised rhythm before restarting compressions
Resume compressions straight away for 2 minutes, then check the rhythm
Give adrenaline 1 mg IV, then restart compressions once it is flushed
notes: A pulse check straight after the shock delays compressions; check the pulse only if the 2-minute rhythm check shows an organised rhythm.
Pausing to watch the monitor interrupts CPR; even if a rhythm appears after a shock, it rarely perfuses at first, so compressions continue.
ANZCOR gives adrenaline after the second shock, not the first, and drugs are given during CPR, never as a reason to delay restarting compressions.
questions.why: ANZCOR: after each shock, restart CPR straight away for 2 minutes without a pulse or rhythm check, because the heart is rarely perfusing just after a shock and pauses in CPR lower survival. Check the rhythm only at the end of each 2-minute loop.

questions.stem: Phillip, 75, had a VF arrest in the ED of a hospital that has a cath lab, with ROSC at 10:18. His ECG at 10:22 shows ST elevation in V2 to V4, I, aVL, V5 and V6 with reciprocal depression in III and aVF. He is GCS 3 and ventilated by bag-valve-mask, BP 96/60. What is the most appropriate reperfusion plan?
options: Immediate coronary angiography with primary PCI
IV tenecteplase in ED, then transfer for angiography
CT brain first, then angiography if there is no bleed
Defer angiography until his GCS improves in ICU
notes: Fibrinolysis is only for when timely PCI is not available. Here the lab is on site, and lysis after CPR carries extra bleeding risk.
A witnessed VF arrest with a clear STEMI has an obvious cause. Routine CT brain first only delays reperfusion.
A low GCS soon after ROSC does not predict outcome. Prognosis is judged at 72 hours or later, and delaying PCI makes the infarct bigger.
questions.why: When the ECG shows STEMI after ROSC and a cath lab is on site, the patient goes for immediate angiography and primary PCI, whatever his conscious state. Do not wait for the troponin or for him to wake up.

questions.stem: Before his arrest, Phillip, 75, had been breathless since early morning. At triage his RR was 24 and his SpO2 93% on room air. After ROSC he has fine crackles at both lung bases, and his ECG shows an evolving anterolateral STEMI. Which mechanism best explains his crackles and hypoxia?
options: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from albumin moving into the interstitium
Increased capillary permeability from inflammatory alveolar injury
Raised systemic venous pressure from right ventricular failure
Raised LV filling pressure transmitted back to the pulmonary capillaries
notes: Low oncotic pressure (e.g. nephrotic syndrome or liver failure) is not the problem in an acute MI, and his oedema is pulmonary rather than generalised.
A permeability (non-cardiogenic) leak is the mechanism in ARDS or sepsis, not in an acute anterior infarct with LV failure.
Right ventricular failure raises the JVP and causes peripheral oedema, not alveolar oedema; his infarct is in the LV territory.
questions.why: Infarcted LV myocardium contracts poorly, so LV end-diastolic and left atrial pressures rise. This pressure is transmitted back to the pulmonary capillaries, and the raised hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid into the interstitium and alveoli, which causes the crackles and V/Q mismatch (cardiogenic pulmonary oedema).

questions.stem: Phillip, 75, has ST elevation in V2 to V4 and also in I and aVL after his VF arrest. Angiography shows a single occlusion in the left anterior descending artery. Which branch, beyond the occlusion, supplies the high lateral wall shown by I and aVL, which is why the occlusion is judged to be proximal?
options: First diagonal branch of the LAD
First septal perforator of the LAD
Obtuse marginal branch of the circumflex
notes: The septal perforators supply the interventricular septum (seen in V1 and V2), not the high lateral wall seen in I and aVL.
The obtuse marginal arises from the circumflex, so it lies outside the LAD and would not be affected by an LAD occlusion.
The posterior descending artery usually arises from the RCA and supplies the inferior wall and posterior septum (II, III, aVF), not the lateral wall.
questions.why: Diagonal branches of the LAD supply the anterolateral and high lateral LV wall, which leads I and aVL show. ST elevation in I and aVL alongside V2 to V4 therefore places the LAD occlusion proximal to the first diagonal.

questions.stem: Andre, 65, has CT-confirmed acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis. The report shows no discrete mass but says an underlying neoplasm cannot be excluded in the thickened segment. A colleague of his recently had bowel cancer. He asks you, 'Is it cancer, Doc?' Which response best answers him?
options: No, the CT was clear, so cancer is ruled out and you won't need any more tests
We'll do a colonoscopy tomorrow while you're still in hospital so we can check properly
No sign of it on the scan, but swelling can hide one, so a camera test in about 6 weeks
Restart the bowel screening poo test after you go home and we'll go from there
notes: This gives false reassurance: wall thickening can hide a tumour, so luminal assessment is still needed after the episode.
Colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis is contraindicated because insufflation can perforate the inflamed bowel.
A faecal occult blood test is a screening tool for people without symptoms and does not replace direct imaging of the lumen in a man with a thickened sigmoid segment.
questions.why: CT cannot exclude cancer in an inflamed, thickened segment. Arrange a colonoscopy (or CT colonography) about 6 weeks after recovery, and tell him honestly that this is the plan.

questions.stem: Andre, 65, is on day 3 of IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole for CT-confirmed uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis. He is still febrile at 38.4 °C, his LIF pain is no better and his CRP has risen from 128 to 190. He is haemodynamically stable and the tenderness is still localised. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent colonoscopy to look directly at the inflamed sigmoid segment
Repeat CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast to look for an abscess
Emergency laparotomy and Hartmann's procedure today
Switch to oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and plan discharge
notes: Colonoscopy is contraindicated in acute diverticulitis because of the risk of perforation, and it would not show an extraluminal collection.
Emergency surgery is for perforation with purulent or faecal peritonitis or for uncontrolled sepsis. A stable patient with localised signs needs imaging first.
Fever and a rising CRP mean he is not responding. Stepping down to oral antibiotics and discharging him would miss a developing complication.
questions.why: If diverticulitis is not improving after 48 to 72 hours of treatment, repeat the CT to look for a complication such as a pericolic or pelvic abscess. An abscess may need percutaneous drainage.

questions.stem: Andre, 65, eats a low-fibre diet ('meat and three veg, white bread'). His CT shows multiple diverticula in the sigmoid and distal descending colon, one of which is now inflamed. Which mechanism best explains how these diverticula formed?
options: High segmental pressure pushes mucosa and submucosa through vasa recta entry points
Congenital weakness produces outpouchings that include every layer of the colonic wall
Inferior mesenteric artery ischaemia thins the wall so it balloons outward
Chronic mucosal inflammation from bile acids erodes through the muscularis propria
notes: That describes a true diverticulum, such as Meckel's. Colonic diverticula are acquired and contain no muscle layer.
Ischaemia causes ischaemic colitis, not diverticula. The vessels matter only because the points where they enter the wall are weak.
Diverticula form through mechanical herniation, not erosion from inflammation. Inflammation comes later, as diverticulitis.
questions.why: Colonic diverticula are pulsion pseudodiverticula. High intraluminal pressure, which is greatest in the narrow sigmoid and made worse by low-fibre stool, pushes mucosa and submucosa through gaps in the circular muscle where the vasa recta penetrate.

questions.stem: Andre, 65, has sigmoid diverticulitis. His pain is now constant and sharply localised to the left iliac fossa, worse with coughing and with every bump in the car, and he has rebound tenderness there. Early colonic pain is usually vague and felt in the midline. Which nerves carry this localised pain?
options: Visceral afferents running with sympathetic fibres back to the L1 to L2 cord segments
Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4) carrying afferents from the sigmoid wall
Genitofemoral nerve (L1 to L2) irritated where it runs on psoas major
Somatic nerves of the parietal peritoneum, from lower thoracic and L1 spinal nerves
notes: Hindgut visceral afferents give poorly localised, dull pain referred to the hypogastrium, not sharp LIF pain with rebound.
Pelvic splanchnic afferents are visceral too. They carry stretch and pain from the distal colon that is poorly localised.
Genitofemoral irritation would cause pain in the groin or thigh. The psoas sign tests for retroperitoneal inflammation, not localised LIF peritonism.
questions.why: Once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, pain travels in the somatic nerves that supply the overlying abdominal wall (lower intercostal, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal). That is why it is sharply localised and made worse by movement.

questions.stem: You are giving Samantha, 65, her biopsy result in general practice. After a warning shot you tell her in plain words that the biopsy shows cancer in the lower part of her food pipe. She goes quiet and looks down at her hands. What is the best thing to do next?
options: Explain the PET-CT and the treatment the team is likely to offer her
Pause, allow silence, then acknowledge how she is feeling
Reassure her that most oesophageal cancers are curable with surgery
Give her a written leaflet and book a follow-up visit to discuss it
notes: Moving straight to the plan while she is in shock overloads her, and she will not take it in; strategy comes after acknowledging emotion.
This is false reassurance: staging is not complete, and oesophageal cancer often cannot be cured even when it is locoregional.
Ending the conversation as soon as she reacts leaves her alone with the news; she needs support and a plan now, with follow-up added on top.
questions.why: After the news is given, the next step is to stop talking, allow silence and respond to emotion (e.g. 'This is a lot to take in'). She cannot take in information until her emotional response has been acknowledged (SPIKES: Emotions before Strategy).

questions.stem: At the results visit, Samantha, 65, still takes naproxen 500 mg twice daily for knee osteoarthritis. Bloods show Hb 112 g/L and ferritin 12 µg/L, and gastroscopy found an ulcerated, friable distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Her renal and liver tests are normal. What is the best change to her knee analgesia?
options: Continue naproxen and increase pantoprazole to 40 mg twice daily
Change naproxen to celecoxib 100 mg twice daily and continue pantoprazole
Stop naproxen; give regular paracetamol 1 g four times daily, liquid or dispersible
Stop naproxen; start regular oral oxycodone 5 mg four times daily, reviewed at one week
notes: A higher PPI dose does not remove the antiplatelet and mucosal effects of naproxen on a friable, bleeding tumour.
COX-2 selective drugs still carry GI and cardiovascular risk and are not a good choice with active GI blood loss and an ulcerated cancer.
Regular opioids are not first-line for osteoarthritis, and they add constipation, sedation and falls risk; try paracetamol first.
questions.why: NSAIDs add to bleeding from an ulcerated tumour and make iron deficiency worse, so stop naproxen. Regular paracetamol (max 4 g/day) is first-line for osteoarthritis, and a liquid or dispersible form is easier to swallow past a stricture.

questions.stem: Samantha, 65, has had reflux for 15 years. Her gastroscopy shows a C4M6 segment of salmon-coloured mucosa above the gastro-oesophageal junction, and biopsy shows intestinal metaplasia with high-grade dysplasia. Which cellular change defines Barrett's oesophagus?
options: Stratified squamous epithelium replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Columnar epithelium of the lower oesophagus replaced by stratified squamous cells
Basal cell hyperplasia and elongated papillae within intact squamous epithelium
Loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons in the lower oesophageal sphincter wall
notes: This has the direction backwards: the normal oesophagus is squamous, and in Barrett's it becomes columnar.
These are the features of reflux oesophagitis in squamous mucosa, not metaplasia to a columnar lining.
This is the lesion in achalasia, a motility disorder; it is not a change in the epithelium.
questions.why: Repeated injury from acid and bile causes metaplasia: the normal stratified squamous lining is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells. This can progress through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: While examining Samantha, 65, who has a suspected distal oesophageal cancer, you palpate the cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes. Enlargement of which node is classically linked to lymphatic spread from the stomach and gastro-oesophageal junction?
notes: The right supraclavicular nodes drain the right lung and mediastinum through the right lymphatic duct, not abdominal lymph through the thoracic duct.
The jugulodigastric node drains the tonsils and pharynx; it is not on the drainage path from the distal oesophagus or stomach.
Submandibular nodes drain the face, lips, tongue and floor of the mouth, not the gut below the diaphragm.
questions.why: Lymph from the abdomen and lower oesophagus drains through the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct, which empties at the left venous angle (where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet). Tumour spread along this route enlarges the left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node, also called Troisier's sign.

questions.stem: Petunia, 62, has had constant right forefoot pain for 3 weeks that eases when she hangs the leg down. In the ED you do Buerger's test: she lies flat while you raise both legs, then she sits up with her legs over the side of the trolley. Which finding shows severe ischaemia of the right leg?
options: Right foot stays pink at 90° and its veins refill within 10 seconds when hung down
Right foot goes pale below 20° of elevation, then turns dusky red when hung down
Right foot turns blue when raised, and the blue colour fades once it is hung down
Right foot goes pale only at 80°, and its colour returns within 10 seconds when hung down
notes: This is a normal result: a well-perfused foot stays pink at full elevation and its veins refill quickly when it hangs down.
An ischaemic foot goes pale (not blue) when raised and turns red when it hangs down. Blue on raising that fades on hanging down is the reverse of the expected pattern.
Going pale only near 90° and recovering colour quickly is at most mild disease. It does not fit an ABI of 0.28 with rest pain.
questions.why: A Buerger's angle (the elevation at which the foot goes pale) below 20°, followed by dusky red reactive hyperaemia (dependent rubor) when the leg hangs down, means severe ischaemia. A well-perfused leg stays pink at 90°.

questions.stem: Petunia, 62, is waiting in a rural ED for transfer to the tertiary vascular unit. Her right foot has dry black gangrene of the first three toes with a sharp line of demarcation, and no redness, pus or moist tissue. WCC is normal and CRP is 12. What is the most appropriate care of her foot while she waits?
options: Raise the right leg on pillows to reduce swelling and ease her pain
Start IV flucloxacillin to stop the dry gangrene from becoming wet
Keep the leg hanging down, apply a dry non-adherent dressing and offload the heel
Debride the black toes at the bedside so the tissue underneath can be assessed today
notes: Raising the leg lowers perfusion pressure to an already critically ischaemic foot and makes her rest pain worse.
There is no clinical or laboratory sign of infection, so antibiotics are not indicated. The foot should be watched for any change to wet gangrene.
Debriding non-viable tissue in an unrevascularised foot can create a wound that will not heal. Decisions about debridement and amputation belong to the vascular team after they have imaged her.
questions.why: In CLTI, letting the leg hang down helps the little perfusion she has. Dry gangrene should be kept dry and protected under a non-adherent dressing, with the heels offloaded to prevent pressure ulcers. Leave debridement to the vascular team.

questions.stem: Petunia, 62, has severe right leg arterial disease (ABI 0.28). She sleeps half sitting up with her right leg over the edge of the bed. Her forefoot pain gets worse within a minute of lying flat and eases when she hangs the leg down. What best explains this pattern?
options: Hanging the leg drains venous blood from the toes and lowers their tissue pressure
Lying flat triggers sympathetic vasoconstriction of her collateral arteries
Hanging the leg compresses sensory nerves and damps the ischaemic pain signals
Gravity adds hydrostatic pressure and raises perfusion pressure beyond the block
notes: Venous congestion builds up when the leg hangs down; it does not fall. A lower venous pressure is not why the ischaemic toes feel better.
Lying flat does not cause collateral arteries to clamp down. The vessels beyond the blockage are already maximally dilated, and the problem is a lack of driving pressure.
Hanging the leg does not compress any nerve. The relief comes from better perfusion, not from blocking pain signals.
questions.why: Beyond a severe blockage, the arterial pressure reaching the foot is very low. When the leg hangs down, the weight of the column of blood (hydrostatic pressure) adds to that pressure and improves blood flow to the toes. When she lies flat she loses that help, and at night cardiac output also falls.

questions.stem: The ED registrar is measuring Petunia's right ankle pressures with a handheld Doppler and has already found the dorsalis pedis signal. Petunia is 62 and has suspected chronic limb-threatening ischaemia. Where should the probe go next to find the posterior tibial artery?
options: On the top of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon
Behind the lateral malleolus, midway between it and the calcaneal tendon
In front of the medial malleolus, next to the tibialis anterior tendon
Behind the medial malleolus, midway between it and the calcaneal tendon
notes: This is where the dorsalis pedis artery is found, which has already been measured.
Behind the lateral malleolus lie the sural nerve and small saphenous vein. The posterior tibial artery does not run there.
The great saphenous vein runs in front of the medial malleolus. A venous signal there would give a misleading result.
questions.why: The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus in the tarsal tunnel, under the flexor retinaculum. It lies with the tibial nerve between the flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus tendons, about midway between the malleolus and the calcaneal tendon.

questions.stem: You are examining Mr Loh, 47, on the orthopaedic ward, day 5 after surgery for a right neck of femur fracture. He has sudden pleuritic chest pain, and his right calf has been sore, red and swollen since early this morning. You want to record the calf swelling objectively, as the Wells DVT criteria define it. How should you measure it?
options: Measure both ankles at the malleoli; any difference of more than 1 cm counts
Measure the right thigh 15 cm above the patella and compare with the admission measure
Measure both calves 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity; a difference over 3 cm counts
Dorsiflex the right foot with the knee extended and record any calf pain (Homans sign)
notes: Ankle swelling at the malleoli is not the validated measure. A 1 cm cut-off is too sensitive and picks up normal post-operative oedema.
The thigh is swollen after hip surgery anyway, and a single-leg measure compared over time is not the Wells criterion. The calf is where his symptoms are.
Homans sign is unreliable, has poor sensitivity and specificity, and is not part of any validated score. It should not be used to document a DVT.
questions.why: Calf swelling in the Wells criteria is measured on both legs 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity, and it counts when the affected calf is more than 3 cm bigger. Always examine and compare both legs when you suspect PE.

questions.stem: Mr Loh, 47, weighs 98 kg and is day 5 after hip fracture surgery. He has been on prophylactic enoxaparin. CTPA shows bilateral lower lobe PE with no RV strain. BP is 128/78 and SpO2 is 94% on 2 L/min. Creatinine is 84, platelets 298 and Hb 118. The orthopaedic consultant agrees the bleeding risk is acceptable. Which anticoagulation plan is best?
options: Stop prophylactic enoxaparin; start enoxaparin 100 mg SC 12-hourly
Continue enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily and add enoxaparin 100 mg SC 12-hourly
Give alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours, then start an unfractionated heparin infusion
Withhold all anticoagulation and arrange an inferior vena cava filter
notes: Adding a therapeutic dose on top of the prophylactic dose doubles up the anticoagulation and raises the risk of bleeding, especially at a fresh surgical site.
Thrombolysis is for PE with shock. He is normotensive with no RV strain, and major surgery 5 days ago is a contraindication.
An IVC filter is only for patients who cannot be anticoagulated. His surgical team has agreed that anticoagulation is safe.
questions.why: A stable PE is treated with therapeutic anticoagulation: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC 12-hourly (about 100 mg for 98 kg, normal renal function). This replaces the prophylactic dose; it is not added to it. A PE provoked by surgery is treated for 3 months.

questions.stem: Mr Loh, 47, day 5 after hip surgery, has bilateral lower lobe PE on CTPA. He is breathing 28 times a minute with SpO2 91% on room air, and his RV is not dilated. A blood gas would be expected to show hypoxaemia with a low PaCO2. What is the main mechanism of his hypoxaemia?
options: Global alveolar hypoventilation from splinting of the chest by pleuritic pain
Thickening of the alveolar-capillary membrane that limits oxygen diffusion
Right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale from high right atrial pressure
V/Q mismatch, as blood is diverted to the lung regions that are still perfused
notes: Global hypoventilation would raise PaCO2. He is tachypnoeic and is expected to have a low PaCO2, so this cannot explain his hypoxaemia.
A diffusion defect happens in interstitial lung disease, not in acute vascular obstruction. His alveolar membrane is normal.
Shunting through a PFO needs raised right heart pressures, as in massive PE. His RV is not dilated and he has no strain.
questions.why: In PE, emboli create dead space and push the cardiac output through the remaining lung, which then has a low V/Q ratio with a short transit time. This lowers PaO2. Hyperventilation clears CO2, so PaCO2 is usually low.

questions.stem: Mr Loh, 47, day 5 after hip surgery, points to his right lower posterolateral chest. The pain is sharp, well localised and worse on deep inspiration. CTPA shows a small peripheral right lower lobe infarct with a small effusion. Which nerves carry this pain?
options: Vagal afferents from the visceral pleura over the infarcted lobe
Intercostal nerves supplying the costal parietal pleura
The phrenic nerve supplying the central diaphragmatic pleura
Cardiac sympathetic afferents entering the T1 to T4 cord segments
notes: The visceral pleura has only autonomic supply and is insensitive to pain. It cannot produce sharp, localised pleuritic pain.
Phrenic nerve pain from the central diaphragmatic pleura is referred to the shoulder tip (C3 to C5), not the lower posterolateral chest wall.
Cardiac visceral afferents produce diffuse central pain, like the pain of ACS, and it is poorly localised. It does not change with breathing.
questions.why: The costal parietal pleura is supplied by somatic intercostal nerves. This is why inflammation over a peripheral infarct gives sharp pain that is well localised and pleuritic. The visceral pleura has no somatic pain fibres.

questions.stem: You are examining Bob, 20, in ED after a fall onto his left side while mountain biking. He is sitting up and breathless, BP 88/60, HR 134, and his neck veins are distended. Which examination step best tells a tension pneumothorax from cardiac tamponade at the bedside?
options: Listen for muffled heart sounds over the praecordium
Check for a pulsus paradoxus with the BP cuff
Percuss and auscultate both hemithoraces, comparing left with right
Assess the jugular venous pressure at 45 degrees, measured from the sternal angle
notes: Heart sounds are hard to judge in a noisy resus bay, and muffling is an unreliable sign that does not localise anything to one hemithorax.
Pulsus paradoxus can occur in both tamponade and tension pneumothorax, and it takes too long to measure in a shocked patient.
The JVP is raised in both conditions so it does not separate them, and Bob is worse lying flat.
questions.why: Distended neck veins with hypotension after chest trauma can mean tension or tamponade. One-sided hyper-resonance with reduced or absent breath sounds, plus tracheal deviation, points to tension. In tamponade the chest is resonant and breath sounds are equal on both sides.

questions.stem: Bob, 20, has a left tension pneumothorax after a bike fall. Needle decompression at the left 4th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line, releases a rush of air. On high-flow oxygen his BP comes up to 112/70 and SpO2 to 96%. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the chest X-ray in 4 hours and remove the cannula if the lung remains fully up
Insert a left intercostal catheter in the safe triangle on an underwater seal
Aspirate through the cannula and discharge him if the lung re-expands
Arrange a CT chest to define the air leak before any further intervention
notes: Leaving only a cannula risks the tension coming back, and a traumatic pneumothorax that has already caused tension needs a drain, not watchful waiting.
Aspiration and discharge are for selected primary spontaneous pneumothoraces, not a traumatic tension pneumothorax with shock.
CT does not replace treatment. Definitive drainage should not be delayed for imaging in a patient who has just come out of obstructive shock.
questions.why: Needle decompression only buys time. The cannula can kink, dislodge or block, and tension can come back. A traumatic tension pneumothorax needs a definitive intercostal catheter in the 4th or 5th space in the safe triangle, attached to an underwater seal drain.

questions.stem: Bob, 20, fell onto his left side mountain biking. Within an hour he has a BP of 88/60, HR 134, distended neck veins and a trachea deviated to the right. His Hb is 148. What is the main mechanism of his hypotension?
options: Blood loss into the left pleural space causing a large fall in circulating volume
Hypoxic depression of left ventricular contractility
Loss of sympathetic tone causing widespread vasodilation
Raised intrathoracic pressure compressing the venae cavae, cutting venous return
notes: Haemorrhagic shock gives flat neck veins and a dull hemithorax, and his chest is hyper-resonant with no effusion on the X-ray.
His hypoxia is moderate (SpO2 91%). The main problem is a lack of venous filling, not a failing pump.
Neurogenic shock follows spinal cord injury and causes bradycardia with warm peripheries. Bob is tachycardic, with no neck injury or neurological deficit.
questions.why: A one-way valve traps air in the pleural space with each breath, and intrathoracic pressure rises. The mediastinum shifts, the venae cavae are compressed and kinked, and preload falls, so cardiac output drops. This is obstructive shock, which is why the neck veins are distended.

questions.stem: During Bob's left chest decompression, the registrar advances the needle just over the upper border of the 5th rib, anterior to the mid-axillary line. This technique avoids the main intercostal neurovascular bundle. Where does that bundle lie?
options: Lower border of the rib above, between internal and innermost intercostals
Upper border of the rib below, between the external and internal intercostal muscles
Lower border of the rib above, superficial to the external intercostal
Midway across the space, just deep to the parietal pleura
notes: Going over the upper border of the rib below is the safe route. The main bundle is not there, and it lies deep to the internal intercostal, not between the external and internal.
The bundle is in the costal groove, but it lies deep to both the external and internal intercostals, not superficial to them.
The bundle runs in the costal groove of the rib above, not across the middle of the space, and it lies outside the endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura.
questions.why: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN, top to bottom) run in the costal groove along the inferior border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Going in just over the top of the rib below keeps the needle or drain away from them.

questions.stem: Wesley, 3, is going home after his viral-induced wheeze has settled. He has his own salbutamol puffer, a spacer and a mask. His mother Kate says she has only ever sprayed her daughter's puffer straight into his mouth. You are showing her how to use the spacer. Which instruction is correct?
options: Fire all the puffs into the spacer, then let him breathe through the mask for 1-2 minutes
Fire one puff, then ask him to take one deep breath and hold it for 10 seconds
Shake before each puff, seal the mask, fire one puff, then let him take 4 normal breaths
Fire one puff, then take the mask off as soon as he has taken a single breath
notes: Firing several puffs into the spacer at once makes the aerosol stick together and settle on the spacer wall, so much less of the drug is inhaled.
A deep breath and a 10-second breath-hold is the mouthpiece technique for older children; a 3-year-old cannot do it reliably, so tidal breathing through a mask is used.
One breath does not clear the spacer, so much of each puff is lost; about 4 tidal breaths are needed for each puff.
questions.why: In a preschool child the mask must seal over the nose and mouth. Shake the puffer, fire one puff at a time and let him take about 4 normal (tidal) breaths after each puff, then repeat until the full dose is given.

questions.stem: Wesley, 3, 15 kg, is in ED with viral-induced wheeze. Twenty minutes after his first dose of salbutamol (6 puffs by spacer and mask) he has RR 40, SpO2 95% on room air and HR 156. He is alert, with mild subcostal recession and an ongoing wheeze. The registrar is in resus. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat salbutamol 6 puffs by spacer and mask, reassessing 20 minutes after each dose
Add ipratropium 4 puffs by spacer to the next salbutamol dose and repeat each 20 minutes
Give oral prednisolone 15 mg now and continue salbutamol every 3 hours on the ward
Start nasal prong oxygen to keep SpO2 at 96% or above, then repeat the salbutamol dose
notes: Ipratropium is added in the first hour only for a severe episode or a poor response to salbutamol. Wesley has a moderate episode and is improving.
Oral prednisolone isn't routine in preschool viral wheeze. It is reserved for severe episodes, a poor response or admission. Wesley isn't stable on 3-hourly salbutamol yet.
Oxygen is only needed if SpO2 falls below 92%, and then the aim is to keep it at 92% or above. At 95% on room air, Wesley doesn't need oxygen.
questions.why: In a moderate episode that is improving, the first-line treatment is salbutamol 6 puffs by spacer (dose for under 6 years), repeated every 20 minutes for up to 3 doses in the first hour, with a reassessment after each dose. Then space the doses out as he responds.

questions.stem: Wesley, 3, has had a cold for 2 days and now makes a high-pitched whistling noise mainly when he breathes out. You hear bilateral wheeze on auscultation. His mother asks why the noise comes on the out-breath rather than the in-breath. Which mechanism best explains an expiratory wheeze?
options: Extrathoracic airways collapse as pressure inside them falls below atmospheric pressure
Airway smooth muscle contracts only during expiration, narrowing the bronchi each breath
Fluid and exudate in the alveoli pop open and shut at the end of each expiration
Rising pleural pressure in expiration compresses narrowed intrathoracic airways further
notes: This describes extrathoracic (upper) airway collapse during inspiration, which causes inspiratory stridor, as in croup. It doesn't cause an expiratory wheeze.
Bronchospasm doesn't switch on and off with each breath. It is sustained, and it is the changing pleural pressure that makes the narrowing worse in expiration.
Alveolar fluid gives crackles, not a musical wheeze, and suggests pneumonia. Wesley has no focal crackles.
questions.why: During expiration, pleural pressure rises and squeezes the intrathoracic airways, which are already narrowed by viral inflammation. Air moving fast through these narrowed airways makes the walls oscillate, which produces the wheeze. A child's small airways make this worse.

questions.stem: Wesley, 3, has access to his older sister's Lego. His story fits viral wheeze, but you still ask about a sudden choking episode. If a small Lego piece had passed his larynx, where would it most likely lodge, and why?
options: Left main bronchus, because it is longer and leaves the trachea at a steeper angle
Right main bronchus, because it is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left
Left lower lobe bronchus, because the aortic arch pushes the left bronchus vertical
Right upper lobe bronchus, because it is the first branch and points straight upward
notes: The left main bronchus is longer, but it leaves the trachea at a more horizontal angle because it has to pass under the aortic arch. That makes it the less likely side.
The aortic arch arches over the left main bronchus and makes it run more horizontally, not more vertically. The left bronchial tree is not the usual site.
The right upper lobe bronchus runs upward and outward, against gravity and the direction of airflow. Objects more often lodge in the right main bronchus, bronchus intermedius or lower lobe bronchus.
questions.why: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and closer to the line of the trachea than the left, so inhaled foreign bodies usually go to the right. Suspect one if there was a sudden choking episode or the chest signs are one-sided.

questions.stem: Sam, 73, is sitting bolt upright on an ED trolley. His RR is 34 and SpO2 86% on room air, and he says, "Don't lie me down, I can't breathe flat." You now want to examine his neck veins. How should you assess his jugular venous pressure?
options: Lie him flat briefly so the neck veins fill, then measure from the sternal angle
Assess him sitting upright; a venous pulsation above the clavicle means a raised JVP
Skip the JVP and use ankle oedema as the marker of right-sided filling pressure
Recline him to 45° for a minute, because the JVP is only reliably measured at that angle
notes: Lying him flat will make his orthopnoea and hypoxaemia worse. Also, the neck veins fill when lying flat even when the JVP is normal, so the finding tells you little.
Ankle oedema is a late and insensitive sign, and Sam has not noticed any swelling. Skipping the JVP misses a key sign of congestion.
45° is only a convenient angle and is not needed for a valid reading. Reclining a patient in respiratory distress adds risk and gains nothing.
questions.why: The sternal angle stays about 5 cm above the right atrium in any position, so you can assess the JVP with him sitting at 90°. If a venous pulsation is visible above the clavicle while he is fully upright, his JVP is clearly raised. Never lie an orthopnoeic patient flat.

questions.stem: Sam, 73, has hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema a month after an anterior MI. On oxygen his SpO2 is 92%, but he is still very breathless, with BP 212/112 and HR 114. He takes no PDE5 inhibitor, and CPAP is being set up. Which drug treatment should you start now?
options: IV morphine 2.5 mg, repeated every 5 min, to reduce preload and relieve his air hunger
IV metoprolol 5 mg, repeated, to slow the tachycardia and lower his BP
Sublingual GTN 400 microgram spray every 5 min while systolic BP stays above 100 mmHg
Oral amlodipine 10 mg to bring his blood pressure down over the next few hours
notes: Morphine is no longer routinely recommended in APO. It causes respiratory depression and vomiting and is linked to worse outcomes, including more need for ventilation.
His sinus tachycardia is compensating for a failing ventricle. Giving an IV beta-blocker during acute decompensation can tip him into cardiogenic shock.
Oral amlodipine acts slowly and does not reduce preload. It has no role in the emergency management of acute pulmonary oedema.
questions.why: Nitrates dilate veins, which lowers preload, and at higher doses dilate arteries, which lowers afterload. This gives rapid relief in hypertensive APO. Repeat sublingual GTN, then start an IV infusion titrated to response, and hold it if systolic BP falls below 100 mmHg or if a PDE5 inhibitor has been taken.

questions.stem: Sam, 73, on perindopril after an anterior MI, took regular ibuprofen for 2 weeks for back pain. His creatinine rose from 95 to 150 µmol/L and he developed acute pulmonary oedema. Which mechanism best explains how the ibuprofen contributed?
options: Blocking renal prostaglandins, constricting afferent arterioles and retaining Na+
Blocking cardiac L-type calcium channels, reducing contractility over several days
Blocking angiotensin II action at the efferent arteriole, lowering glomerular pressure
Activating PPAR-gamma in the collecting duct, increasing sodium reabsorption
notes: Negative inotropy through calcium channel blockade is how verapamil and diltiazem worsen heart failure, not how NSAIDs do.
Loss of angiotensin II tone at the efferent arteriole is the effect of his perindopril, not of ibuprofen.
PPAR-gamma activation causing fluid retention is the mechanism of glitazones such as pioglitazone.
questions.why: Prostaglandins keep the afferent arteriole dilated and promote sodium excretion when the kidney is underperfused. NSAIDs block them, so GFR falls (worse with an ACE inhibitor, which dilates the efferent arteriole) and the body retains salt and water. That fluid load overwhelmed his failing ventricle.

questions.stem: Sam, 73, had an MI treated with a coronary stent a month ago and now has heart failure. Today's ECG is unchanged from his discharge ECG. It shows Q waves in V1 to V3, poor R wave progression and T wave inversion in V1 to V4. Occlusion of which artery most likely caused this infarct?
options: Right coronary artery, occluded in its proximal segment
Left circumflex artery, occluded at its proximal segment
Posterior descending artery, occluded near its origin
notes: The right coronary artery usually supplies the inferior wall, so its infarcts show changes in II, III and aVF, not the anterior chest leads.
The circumflex supplies the lateral wall, so its infarcts show changes in I, aVL, V5 and V6, or posterior changes. They do not cause anterior Q waves.
The posterior descending artery supplies the inferior wall and the posterior part of the septum. Its occlusion causes inferior or posterior changes, not Q waves in V1 to V3.
questions.why: Leads V1 to V4 look at the septum and anterior wall, which the left anterior descending artery supplies. An anterior infarct damages a large area of left ventricular muscle, so it commonly leads to reduced ejection fraction and heart failure.

questions.stem: Sally, 47, is lying still on the ED trolley. She has had constant right upper quadrant pain for 26 hours and is febrile. You are examining her abdomen and want to elicit Murphy's sign, telling the examiner what you are doing. How do you perform the manoeuvre?
options: Press deeply in the right upper quadrant, then let go quickly and watch for pain
Press in the left iliac fossa and ask whether she feels pain referred to the right side
Press under right costal margin at the midclavicular line as she inhales deeply
Lay a hand over the lower right ribs and strike it firmly with the other fist
notes: This is rebound tenderness, a general sign of peritoneal irritation; it does not test the gallbladder's descent on inspiration and is needlessly painful.
This is Rovsing's sign for appendicitis, and Sally has already had an appendicectomy.
Fist percussion tests renal angle or liver tenderness; it does not look for the catch in inspiration that defines Murphy's sign.
questions.why: Murphy's sign: fingers under the right costal margin at the midclavicular line (gallbladder fundus), then deep inspiration. It is positive if she stops breathing in because of pain as the inflamed gallbladder descends onto your fingers. Repeat it on the left, where it should be negative.

questions.stem: Sally, 47, has acute calculous cholecystitis on ultrasound. T 38.9 °C, HR 108, BP 122/74, normal lactate and renal function, no known drug allergies, BMI 32. Blood cultures have been taken and she is being admitted under general surgery. Which empirical antibiotic regimen does eTG recommend now?
options: Amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4 to 7 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally 12-hourly, then discharge to clinic
Vancomycin 25 mg/kg IV loading dose plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly
Meropenem 1 g IV 8-hourly as monotherapy until the culture results return
notes: A febrile, tachycardic patient with acute cholecystitis needs admission, IV antibiotics and early cholecystectomy. This is not a discharge diagnosis.
Vancomycin targets Gram-positive organisms such as MRSA. It misses the Gram-negative enteric organisms that cause biliary infection, so it is not indicated here.
Meropenem is kept for known or suspected resistant organisms such as ESBL producers. Using it first line in community-acquired mild cholecystitis promotes resistance.
questions.why: For acute cholecystitis eTG recommends IV amoxicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4 to 7 mg/kg (adjusted body weight if obese), with later doses timed by renal function. Ceftriaxone is the alternative if gentamicin is contraindicated.

questions.stem: Sally, 47, says her pain began about 3 hours after a big fatty barbecue lunch. Over the past year she has had milder episodes in the same place after meals. Ultrasound now shows a 15 mm stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. Which mechanism best explains why fatty meals bring on her pain?
options: Secretin from duodenal S cells makes the gallbladder contract against the impacted stone
Gastrin from antral G cells makes the gallbladder contract against the impacted stone
Motilin from duodenal M cells makes the gallbladder contract against the impacted stone
Cholecystokinin from duodenal I cells makes the gallbladder contract against the stone
notes: Secretin is released in response to duodenal acid and mainly drives bicarbonate-rich pancreatic and biliary ductal secretion, not gallbladder contraction after fat.
Gastrin is released by peptides and gastric distension and mainly stimulates gastric acid secretion; it is not the main trigger for gallbladder contraction after fat.
Motilin drives the migrating motor complex in the fasting state; it is not released by a fatty meal.
questions.why: Fat and amino acids in the duodenum release cholecystokinin from I cells. CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, so the gallbladder squeezes against a stone blocking its neck or the cystic duct, which causes pain.

questions.stem: When asked directly, Sally, 47, says she also has pain at the tip of her right shoulder. Ultrasound shows a distended, inflamed gallbladder with a rim of pericholecystic fluid, and she has a positive Murphy's sign. Which nerve pathway best explains the shoulder-tip pain?
options: Greater splanchnic nerve (T5 to T9) carrying visceral afferents from the gallbladder
Phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) from irritated diaphragmatic peritoneum, sharing C4 skin
Right vagus nerve carrying afferent fibres from the inflamed gallbladder wall
Lower intercostal nerves (T7 to T11) supplying the parietal peritoneum of the RUQ
notes: Splanchnic visceral afferents cause the vague epigastric or RUQ pain of biliary colic, sometimes felt near the inferior angle of the scapula, but not at the shoulder tip.
Vagal afferents mainly carry non-painful sensation and reflexes such as nausea; they do not cause referred somatic pain at the shoulder.
Intercostal nerves supply the anterior abdominal parietal peritoneum and cause localised RUQ tenderness (as in Murphy's sign), not pain referred to the shoulder.
questions.why: Inflammation spreading to the peritoneum under the diaphragm irritates phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) sensory fibres. The brain refers this pain to the shoulder tip, whose skin is supplied by the same segments (C3 to C4, supraclavicular nerves).

questions.stem: Jaden, 45, is in a rural ED with 3 days of colicky central abdominal pain and bilious vomiting. She tells you she has not opened her bowels for 3 days. Which question best shows whether she has absolute constipation, which points to mechanical bowel obstruction?
options: Have you tried any laxatives or enemas for this, and did they help at all?
Was your last bowel motion hard or painful to pass, and was there any blood?
Have you been able to pass any wind from your back passage?
How often do you normally open your bowels each day, and has that changed lately?
notes: Her laxative use is worth knowing, but a laxative failing does not tell you whether gas can still get past a blockage.
A hard last stool fits simple constipation and says nothing about whether the bowel is completely blocked.
Her usual bowel habit gives you a baseline, but it cannot tell you whether gas is getting through now.
questions.why: Absolute constipation means no stool and no flatus. Not passing wind is what separates complete obstruction from simple constipation, and patients rarely mention it unless you ask directly.

questions.stem: Jaden, 45, has adhesive small bowel obstruction in a rural ED. She is nil by mouth, her creatinine is 102 umol/L (baseline 64) and she takes venlafaxine 75 mg daily. Her colicky pain is 8/10. Which analgesic is the most appropriate first choice?
options: IV morphine in small increments (e.g. 2.5 mg), titrated to effect
IV tramadol 100 mg slowly over 5 minutes, repeated after 30 minutes if needed
IM pethidine 50 mg into the thigh, repeated every 3 hours as needed
Oral ibuprofen 400 mg with oral paracetamol 1 g, repeated every 6 hours as needed
notes: Tramadol is serotonergic, so combining it with venlafaxine risks serotonin toxicity. It also lowers the seizure threshold.
Pethidine is serotonergic, which is a risk with venlafaxine. Its metabolite norpethidine builds up in AKI and causes neurotoxicity, and IM absorption is unreliable.
She is nil by mouth and vomiting, so she cannot take oral drugs. NSAIDs would also worsen her prerenal AKI.
questions.why: Small IV doses of morphine, titrated against her pain and sedation, give fast and controllable relief. It is safe with venlafaxine, and giving it does not mask the signs of peritonism.

questions.stem: Jaden, 45, has vomited bile for 3 days from a small bowel obstruction. Venous gas: pH 7.46, HCO3 31 mmol/L. K 3.3 mmol/L, Cl 94 mmol/L, creatinine 102 umol/L (baseline 64), Hb up from 128 to 146 g/L. What is the main mechanism of her hypokalaemia?
options: Direct loss of potassium-rich fluid in the vomitus over three days of vomiting
Shift of potassium into cells driven by the alkalosis and raised bicarbonate
Reduced dietary potassium intake while unable to eat or drink for three days
Aldosterone-driven renal potassium excretion from volume depletion
notes: Vomited gastric and upper small bowel fluid contains little potassium (about 5–15 mmol/L), so direct loss accounts for only a small part of the deficit.
Alkalosis does push some potassium into cells, but only a small amount, and it does not explain a true loss of body potassium.
Three days without food lowers intake a little, but the kidneys normally conserve potassium, so this alone would not cause much hypokalaemia.
questions.why: Losing fluid activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Aldosterone makes the distal nephron reabsorb sodium in exchange for K+ and H+, so most of the potassium is lost in the urine, which also worsens the alkalosis.

questions.stem: You are examining the hernial orifices of Jaden, 45, who has small bowel obstruction. You know that femoral hernias are easily missed in women and often present with obstruction. Where does the neck of a femoral hernia lie on examination?
options: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle, at the superficial inguinal ring
Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, medial to the femoral vein
Above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, at the deep inguinal ring
Below the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery pulse
notes: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle is where an inguinal hernia comes out through the superficial ring.
The deep inguinal ring sits above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament. Indirect inguinal hernias enter the canal there, not femoral hernias.
Lateral to the femoral artery is the femoral nerve. The femoral canal is on the medial side of the femoral vein.
questions.why: A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal, the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, just medial to the femoral vein. Its neck therefore sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. The canal is narrow and rigid, so these hernias are prone to strangulation.

questions.stem: Andrew, 40, is in ED with jaundice, dark urine and right upper quadrant pain. He was irritable after a long wait but has settled. When you ask whether he has ever used drugs or needles, he snaps, "What's that got to do with anything?" What is the best thing to say next?
options: "It's a routine question on our form, so I need an answer from you before we move on."
"Some liver infections spread by shared needles. I ask everyone, and it's confidential."
"That's fine, it's probably not relevant, so we'll skip it and focus on the pain first."
"Your blood tests will show any drugs anyway, so it's better to be upfront with me now."
notes: Pointing to a form gives no clinical reason for the question and feels bureaucratic, so a defensive patient is likely to stay curt or lie.
Dropping the question misses the key risk factor for viral hepatitis; you should explain why it matters, not give up on it.
This is coercive and misleading (a routine LFT panel doesn't screen for drugs), and it damages trust just when you need him to tell you more.
questions.why: Explaining why the question matters, saying you ask everyone and promising confidentiality keeps it non-judgemental, and patients disclose more that way. Here it uncovers the needle sharing 2 months ago that explains his hepatitis B.

questions.stem: Andrew, 40, has acute hepatitis B in ED: bilirubin 185 µmol/L, ALT 1635 U/L, INR 1.0, albumin 38 g/L, and he is alert with no asterixis. Gastroenterology plans early outpatient review if he stays well. Which blood test best tracks whether his liver's synthetic function is starting to fail over the coming days?
options: Serum albumin level measured daily over the next week
ALT trend measured daily over the next week
notes: Albumin has a half-life of about 3 weeks, so it falls too slowly to pick up acute liver failure early.
ALT measures how much liver is being damaged, not how well it is working, and a falling ALT can mean either recovery or massive loss of liver cells.
Bilirubin shows the degree of jaundice and cholestasis, but it can stay high in an uncomplicated recovery and is not a direct measure of synthetic function.
questions.why: Clotting factors (especially factor VII, half-life about 6 hours) turn over fast, so a rising INR is the earliest blood marker of failing synthetic function. Along with glucose and conscious state, it defines acute liver failure.

questions.stem: Andrew, 40, has acute icteric hepatitis B with bilirubin 185 µmol/L and a hepatocellular pattern of LFTs. For the past week his urine has been dark like tea and his stools pale. His haemoglobin and haemolysis index are normal. What best explains his dark urine?
options: Unconjugated bilirubin from haemolysis being filtered at the glomerulus and excreted
Excess urobilinogen absorbed from the gut and excreted by the kidneys
Concentrated urine from poor oral intake and fever-related fluid loss
Conjugated bilirubin, which is water-soluble, refluxing into blood and filtered
notes: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and is not filtered, so it never darkens urine, and he has no evidence of haemolysis.
Urobilinogen is colourless, and with pale stools less bilirubin is reaching the gut, so urobilinogen production falls rather than rises.
Mild dehydration makes urine more concentrated but does not make it tea-coloured, and it doesn't explain the pale stools that come with it.
questions.why: Damaged hepatocytes fail to excrete conjugated bilirubin into bile, so it leaks back into the blood. It is water-soluble and not tightly bound to albumin, so the kidneys filter it and the urine turns dark. Less bilirubin reaches the gut, so less stercobilin is made and the stools turn pale.

questions.stem: You are examining Andrew, 40, an ED patient with fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. You want to elicit Murphy's sign to look for acute cholecystitis. Where on the abdominal wall does the gallbladder fundus lie, which is where you place your fingers?
options: Right costal margin at the midclavicular line, tip of the ninth costal cartilage
Right fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, level with the nipple in men
Angle between the twelfth rib and the lateral border of erector spinae
Just below the xiphisternum in the midline
notes: The fifth intercostal space marks roughly the upper border of the liver, which you find by percussion, not the gallbladder.
This is the renal angle, used to check for renal tenderness in pyelonephritis, not the gallbladder.
The subxiphoid epigastrium overlies the stomach and pancreas, not the gallbladder fundus.
questions.why: The gallbladder fundus lies where the right midclavicular line (or the lateral edge of rectus) meets the costal margin, at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage. When the patient breathes in, an inflamed gallbladder descends onto the examining fingers and the breath catches.

questions.stem: Bruce, 74, is in ED with an upper GI bleed, probably from a peptic ulcer. He takes ibuprofen 400 mg TDS for hip and knee osteoarthritis and aspirin 100 mg daily since a stroke in 2013. He asks, "Can I keep taking my tablets?" Which explanation is best?
options: Stop both the ibuprofen and the aspirin for good, as together they caused the ulcer
Keep the ibuprofen, as long as you take the esomeprazole every day from now on
Stop the ibuprofen for good; aspirin may pause briefly but restarts within days
Change the ibuprofen to celecoxib and stop the aspirin until the ulcer has fully healed
notes: Stopping aspirin indefinitely leaves him without secondary stroke prevention, and his risk of a thrombotic event outweighs the risk of a rebleed once he is on a PPI.
A PPI lowers the risk but does not make continued NSAID use safe after a major ulcer bleed. The NSAID should be stopped and paracetamol used instead.
A COX-2 inhibitor still carries a risk of ulcer bleeding, and withholding aspirin for weeks until healing delays secondary stroke prevention without need.
questions.why: After an ulcer bleed the NSAID is stopped for good. Aspirin for secondary prevention after stroke is kept going or paused only briefly, then restarted within days once the bleeding is controlled, as agreed with gastroenterology, alongside a daily PPI.

questions.stem: Bruce, 74, has haematemesis and melaena. HR 116, SBP 106, Hb 84 g/L, platelets 268, INR 1.1, normal albumin and bilirubin, and only one spider naevus. The bleed is presumed non-variceal and endoscopy is planned within 24 hours. Which drug should you start now in the ED?
options: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g IV over 8 hours
Pantoprazole 80 mg IV, then an IV PPI continued until endoscopy
Terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 hours until the bleeding is controlled
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as prophylaxis against bacterial infection
notes: Tranexamic acid is not recommended in GI bleeding: HALT-IT showed no reduction in mortality and an increase in venous thromboembolic events.
Terlipressin is a splanchnic vasoconstrictor used for suspected variceal bleeding. Bruce has no evidence of portal hypertension.
Prophylactic antibiotics are given in variceal bleeding in cirrhosis to reduce infection and rebleeding. They are not indicated in a non-variceal bleed.
questions.why: In a presumed non-variceal upper GI bleed, give a high-dose IV PPI (e.g. pantoprazole 80 mg IV) before endoscopy. Raising gastric pH helps keep the clot stable and reduces the high-risk stigmata that need endoscopic treatment.

questions.stem: Bruce, 74, with haematemesis and 2 weeks of melaena, has a urea of 16.8 mmol/L (baseline 6.2) while his creatinine is 102 µmol/L (baseline 88). Apart from reduced renal perfusion, what mechanism best explains why the urea has risen much more than the creatinine?
options: Acute tubular necrosis from NSAIDs reducing tubular secretion of urea over several days
Catabolic stress response breaking down skeletal muscle protein to urea
Reduced hepatic urea production from alcohol-related liver injury
Blood protein digested in the gut, absorbed, then converted to urea by the liver
notes: Acute tubular necrosis would raise creatinine substantially, and urea is filtered and reabsorbed rather than secreted. His creatinine has barely moved.
Stress catabolism adds little in a few hours and cannot explain a near-threefold rise. It is also not specific to an upper GI source.
Liver injury reduces urea synthesis, so it would lower urea, not raise it. Bruce's liver function is also essentially normal.
questions.why: Blood from an upper GI source is digested in the small bowel as a protein meal. The amino acids are deaminated and the liver converts the nitrogen into urea, so urea rises out of proportion to creatinine. Hypovolaemia adds a prerenal component.

questions.stem: At gastroscopy, Bruce, 74, is found to have a deep ulcer on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum (duodenal bulb), with a visible vessel at its base. Erosion of which artery most likely caused his major haemorrhage?
notes: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach and bleeds from lesser-curve gastric ulcers, not from duodenal bulb ulcers.
The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas behind the stomach and can be eroded by posterior gastric ulcers, not by duodenal bulb ulcers.
The superior mesenteric artery passes in front of the third part of the duodenum, well away from the duodenal bulb.
questions.why: The gastroduodenal artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery, runs immediately behind the first part of the duodenum. Posterior duodenal bulb ulcers erode into it and cause brisk, life-threatening bleeding. Anterior ulcers are more likely to perforate.

questions.stem: Sanjana, 30, is jaundiced after a trip to Thailand. As part of your focused GP examination you tell the examiner you will look for hepatic encephalopathy by checking for asterixis. How should you elicit this sign?
options: Arms outstretched, palms up, eyes closed; watch about 30 seconds for slow downward drift
Arms outstretched, palms down, paper on the fingers; watch for a fine tremor
Arms outstretched, wrists dorsiflexed, fingers spread; watch about 30 seconds for a flap
Repeated finger-to-nose testing with eyes open; watch for a tremor near the target
notes: This tests for pronator drift, a sign of an upper motor neurone lesion, not of metabolic encephalopathy.
A sheet of paper shows a fine postural tremor, as in thyrotoxicosis or sympathomimetic use, not the coarse flap of asterixis.
Finger-to-nose testing shows a cerebellar intention tremor. It does not show the lapses in posture that produce asterixis.
questions.why: Asterixis is a negative myoclonus. Sustained wrist extension briefly lapses, so the hands flap. Hold the arms out with wrists cocked back and fingers spread for about 15 to 30 seconds. In hepatitis A it is a sign of encephalopathy and means hospital.

questions.stem: Sanjana, 30, has acute hepatitis A and is being managed at home. Four days later she comes back to the GP for repeat bloods. She is fully oriented and managing small meals. Which new result would most warrant urgent referral to ED or hepatology?
options: INR 1.6, with albumin unchanged at 44 g/L
ALT risen to 1250 U/L, with INR 1.1
Bilirubin risen to 120 µmol/L, with INR 1.1
ALP risen to 260 U/L, with GGT 110 U/L
notes: Transaminase levels reflect active hepatocyte injury, not prognosis. With a normal INR and normal mental state she can still be managed at home with close review.
A rising bilirubin with preserved synthetic function and a clear mental state is common in the icteric phase. It calls for close follow-up, not urgent transfer.
A rising ALP and GGT reflects the cholestatic phase of hepatitis A. It does not mean liver failure while the INR stays normal.
questions.why: INR and mental state are the markers of evolving acute liver failure. In acute hepatitis A, an INR of 1.5 or more needs urgent hospital or hepatology assessment. The size of the transaminase rise does not predict prognosis.

questions.stem: Sanjana, 30, has acute hepatitis A with a bilirubin of 88 µmol/L, 66 of it conjugated. She reports dark urine and pale stools. What is the best explanation for these two symptoms?
options: Unconjugated bilirubin spills into urine, and less is turned into urobilinogen in the gut
Haemolysis raises urobilinogen, which darkens the urine while the stools stay pale
Bile salts build up and darken the urine, while their loss from the gut bleaches stool
Water-soluble conjugated bilirubin enters urine, and less reaches gut as stercobilin
notes: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and is not water-soluble, so it is not filtered into the urine (acholuric jaundice).
Haemolysis causes unconjugated jaundice with normal or dark stools. Her haemoglobin is normal and most of her bilirubin is conjugated.
Retained bile salts cause itch, but bile salts do not colour the urine. Stool colour comes from stercobilin, a bilirubin product.
questions.why: In hepatitis, conjugated bilirubin leaks back into the blood instead of draining into bile. It is water-soluble, so the kidneys filter it and the urine darkens. Less bilirubin reaches the gut to become stercobilin, so the stools go pale.

questions.stem: Sanjana, 30, has fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Cholangitis and cholecystitis are on your differential. You tell the examiner you will test for Murphy's sign. Where do you place your fingers to press over the gallbladder fundus?
options: Right fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line
Tip of the right ninth costal cartilage, at the lateral edge of rectus abdominis
Two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine
Right renal angle, between the twelfth rib and the erector spinae
notes: The fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line is roughly the upper border of liver dullness on percussion. It is not the surface marking of the gallbladder.
This is McBurney's point, the surface marking of the appendix base, and is used when assessing for appendicitis.
The renal angle is where you test for kidney tenderness, as in pyelonephritis. It is posterior and well away from the gallbladder.
questions.why: The gallbladder fundus lies at the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage. This is where the lateral border of rectus abdominis (linea semilunaris) meets the costal margin, on the transpyloric plane. Press there while the patient breathes in.

questions.stem: In a rural ED you are examining Marge, 28, who has crampy right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors and jaundice. You tell the examiner you will now test for Murphy's sign. How do you elicit it?
options: Press deeply in the right upper quadrant, release quickly and watch for pain on release
Press in the left iliac fossa and watch for pain felt in the right upper quadrant
Rest fingers under the right costal margin, then ask her to take a deep breath in
Strike a fist placed over the right lower ribs and watch for a wince of pain
notes: This tests rebound tenderness, a sign of peritonism. It is not specific to the gallbladder and is unkind to a patient already in severe pain.
This is Rovsing's sign, used for appendicitis, and she has already had her appendix out.
This is percussion tenderness over the liver (or a renal punch if done at the loin). It does not test whether the gallbladder catches on inspiration.
questions.why: Place your fingers below the right costal margin at the midclavicular line and ask her to breathe in deeply. The sign is positive if she stops breathing in because the inflamed gallbladder hits your hand, and the same manoeuvre on the left side does not hurt.

questions.stem: Marge, 28, has acute cholangitis from a distal common bile duct stone in a rural ED: T 39.1 °C, HR 124, SBP 98, lactate 2.6, creatinine normal, no drug allergies (shellfish only). Blood cultures have just been taken. Per eTG, which empirical antibiotic regimen should be started now?
options: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 4-hourly plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly
Amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 7 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Flucloxacillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 7 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Amoxicillin+clavulanate 875+125 mg orally 12-hourly, review in 24 hours
notes: This regimen has no reliable cover for the gram-negative enteric bacilli that cause most cholangitis. Anaerobic cover is not routinely needed unless she has had a biliary-enteric anastomosis.
Flucloxacillin targets staphylococci and does not cover enterococci, a key biliary pathogen. It is the wrong beta-lactam for this infection.
She is septic with rigors, tachycardia and a falling blood pressure, so she needs IV antibiotics now. Oral therapy is only for step-down once she has improved.
questions.why: eTG first line for biliary sepsis is amoxicillin (covers enterococci) plus gentamicin (covers gram-negative enteric bacilli such as E. coli and Klebsiella). Give it within 60 minutes, then set the gentamicin interval by renal function.

questions.stem: Marge, 28, has a 9 mm stone obstructing the distal common bile duct. For two days her stools have been pale and her urine dark. Her bilirubin is 68 µmol/L, of which 54 is conjugated, with ALP and GGT raised more than the transaminases. What best explains her dark urine?
options: Retained bile salts spill into the blood and are excreted in the urine
Unconjugated bilirubin from red cell breakdown is filtered by the kidneys into the urine
Extra urobilinogen reabsorbed from the gut is excreted by the kidneys
Conjugated bilirubin refluxes into the blood and, being water-soluble, is filtered
notes: Retained bile salts cause her itch, but they do not colour the urine.
Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and is not filtered, so pre-hepatic jaundice gives normal-coloured urine. Her bilirubin is mostly conjugated.
Urobilinogen is made by gut bacteria from bilirubin that reaches the bowel. A blocked duct reduces urobilinogen, it does not increase it.
questions.why: In post-hepatic obstruction, conjugated (glucuronidated, water-soluble) bilirubin backs up into the blood and is filtered at the glomerulus, which darkens the urine. Bile cannot reach the gut, so no stercobilin forms and the stools are pale.

questions.stem: Marge, 28, has a 9 mm stone in the distal common bile duct and is transferred for ERCP. The endoscopist passes a side-viewing duodenoscope to cannulate the bile duct at its opening and perform a sphincterotomy. Where does the common bile duct open into the gut?
options: Major duodenal papilla, posteromedial wall of the second part of the duodenum
Minor duodenal papilla, proximal to the major papilla in the second part of the duodenum
Posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum, just distal to the pylorus
Medial wall of the third part, behind the superior mesenteric vessels
notes: The minor papilla drains the accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini), not the bile duct. Cannulating it would not reach the stone.
The common bile duct runs behind the first part of the duodenum but does not open there. It continues behind the pancreatic head to the second part.
The third part crosses behind the superior mesenteric vessels and receives no duct. Duodenal compression here is the SMA syndrome.
questions.why: The common bile duct joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater). This opens through the sphincter of Oddi at the major duodenal papilla, about halfway down the descending (second) part of the duodenum. That is why a stone here can also cause gallstone pancreatitis.

questions.stem: Sasha, 15, is on the ward recovering from DKA and is now alert. Her mother has told you that Sasha's sister says she has been skipping insulin to lose weight. You want to explore this and her wider wellbeing before discharge planning. What is the best way to start this conversation?
options: See Sasha alone, explain confidentiality and its limits, then do a HEEADSSS assessment
Interview Sasha with her mother present so that the history can be corroborated by both
Open by asking Sasha directly why she has been skipping her insulin to lose weight
Give her a written eating disorder questionnaire to fill in before any interview
notes: With her mother present, Sasha is less likely to talk openly about weight, mood, alcohol or conflict at home, so parents should be asked to step out for part of the consultation.
Opening with a confronting, blaming question about the sister's report before building rapport and covering confidentiality is likely to make her defensive and shut the conversation down.
A screening tool can help later, but it does not replace a confidential face-to-face psychosocial assessment, and handing it over before any interview damages rapport.
questions.why: Adolescents disclose sensitive issues such as disordered eating, mood, alcohol and self-harm much more readily when seen alone, after being told what stays confidential and when you would have to share (risk of serious harm). HEEADSSS gives a structured, non-judgemental way into these topics.

questions.stem: Sasha, 15, has moderate DKA (pH 7.25, HCO3 9 mmol/L, glucose 22 mmol/L, K 4.5 mmol/L) and a GCS of 13. She is not shocked and is passing urine. Rehydration with 0.9% sodium chloride and added potassium has just been started in ED. Following the RCH guideline, how should her insulin be started?
options: IV bolus of 0.1 units/kg, then an infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h started straight away in ED
Subcutaneous NovoMix at her usual dose now, then recheck ketones in 2 hours
IV infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, starting about 1 hour after fluids, with no bolus
IV infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h, started only once the glucose has fallen below 15
notes: An insulin bolus is not used in children with DKA. It drops glucose and osmolality too fast and raises the risk of cerebral oedema and hypokalaemia.
Subcutaneous premixed insulin is absorbed unpredictably in a dehydrated, acidotic child and will not reliably switch off ketogenesis. DKA needs an IV infusion.
Insulin is what clears the ketoacidosis, so it must not wait for the glucose to fall. When the BGL drops below 15, glucose is added to the fluids and the insulin continues.
questions.why: In paediatric DKA, give an IV insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h about 1 hour after fluids have started, with no bolus. A bolus and early insulin cause a rapid fall in osmolality and are linked to cerebral oedema. Add glucose to the fluids once the BGL is below 15 instead of stopping the insulin.

questions.stem: Sasha, 15, with DKA has a plasma potassium of 4.5 mmol/L before treatment. The registrar warns that it will fall once the insulin infusion starts, even though her total-body potassium is already low from vomiting and polyuria. What is the main mechanism of this fall in plasma potassium?
options: Insulin inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase, so potassium leaks out of cells and into the urine
Insulin stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase, shifting potassium from the plasma into cells
Insulin increases aldosterone release, so the kidney secretes more potassium
Saline dilutes plasma potassium, with no real shift of potassium into cells
notes: This is the wrong direction. Insulin stimulates the pump and moves potassium into cells. It does not make it leak out.
Insulin does not meaningfully raise aldosterone. The early fall in potassium happens because potassium moves into cells, not because more is lost through the kidney.
Dilution adds a little, but the main and fastest cause is insulin-driven uptake of potassium into cells. That is why the fall comes when insulin starts.
questions.why: Lack of insulin and high osmolality shift potassium out of cells, while osmotic diuresis and vomiting lose it, so the plasma level looks normal despite a total-body deficit. Insulin switches on Na+/K+-ATPase and drives potassium back into cells. That is why potassium goes into the fluids once K is below 5.5 and she is passing urine.

questions.stem: Six hours into DKA treatment, the nurse calls you about Sasha, 15. She has a new headache, her GCS has fallen to 10, her HR is 58 and her right pupil is dilated and sluggish. You suspect cerebral oedema with transtentorial herniation. Compression of which structure best explains the change in her pupil?
options: Right optic nerve compressed in the optic canal by raised intracranial pressure
Right abducens nerve stretched over the petrous apex of the temporal bone
Right cervical sympathetic chain compressed by displacement of the brainstem
Right oculomotor nerve compressed at the tentorial edge by the herniating uncus
notes: Optic nerve damage causes visual loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect, with both pupils equal in size. It does not cause a single dilated pupil.
Stretching of the abducens nerve is a false localising sign of raised ICP. It weakens the lateral rectus (abduction deficit) and does not change pupil size.
Damage to the sympathetic chain causes Horner syndrome, with a small pupil (miosis) and ptosis, not a dilated one.
questions.why: In uncal (transtentorial) herniation, the medial temporal lobe presses the oculomotor nerve against the tentorial edge. Its parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres run on the outside of the nerve, so a dilated, sluggish pupil on the same side is an early sign. Neuro obs must include the pupils.

questions.stem: Code Blue on a ward. Collin, 64, collapsed after chest pain. There is no danger. He does not respond to voice or a trapezius squeeze, and you have sent Sam for the defibrillator. After a head tilt and chin lift you see slow, noisy gasps every few seconds and no other movement. Sam says, "He's still breathing!" What is your next step?
options: Feel for a carotid pulse for up to 10 seconds before deciding on CPR
Start chest compressions at 30:2, 100 to 120 a minute, straight away
Roll him into the recovery position and monitor him until the team arrives
Give two rescue breaths by bag-valve-mask, then reassess his breathing
notes: Pulse checks are unreliable, even for skilled staff, and must not delay compressions once he is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
The recovery position is for an unresponsive person who is breathing normally. Agonal gasps mean cardiac arrest, so turning him over only delays CPR.
Adult BLS under ANZCOR starts with compressions. Giving breaths first delays the perfusion that matters most in a witnessed VF arrest.
questions.why: Under ANZCOR, a person who is unresponsive and not breathing normally needs CPR. Slow, noisy agonal gasps are not normal breathing, so start compressions at once (30:2, a third of chest depth, 100 to 120 a minute).
