questions.stem: It is 10:47. Collin, 64, with an evolving NSTEMI, is in VF on a regional ward. He has had two 200 J biphasic shocks (10:44 and 10:46), CPR is continuing and IV access is in. VBG: pH 7.07, pCO2 64 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L, K 3.2 mmol/L. The registrar asks what drug to give now, in this cycle. Which drug do you give?
notes: Amiodarone 300 mg is given after the third shock, not the second. It is the next drug if he is still in VF at the next rhythm check.
Acidosis during an arrest is expected and is treated with good CPR and ventilation. Bicarbonate is reserved for hyperkalaemia or tricyclic overdose and adds CO2.
Lidocaine is only an alternative if amiodarone is not available. Like amiodarone, it is not given until after the third shock.
questions.why: In the ANZCOR shockable arm, adrenaline 1 mg IV goes after the second shock and then every second cycle (about every 4 minutes). Amiodarone 300 mg follows the third shock.

questions.stem: Collin, 64, takes indapamide. Before his VF arrest his potassium had fallen from 3.6 to 3.3 and then 3.2 mmol/L, and his magnesium was 0.62 mmol/L, neither yet replaced. By what main mechanism does hypokalaemia make the ventricular myocardium more prone to arrhythmia?
options: Lower K+ conductance delays repolarisation, triggering early afterdepolarisations
The resting membrane depolarises, inactivating Na+ channels and slowing conduction
Extracellular calcium falls, shortening the plateau phase and the refractory period
Sinoatrial automaticity is suppressed, so ventricular escape rhythms take over
notes: Depolarisation of the resting membrane with Na+ channel inactivation and slowed conduction is the mechanism of hyperkalaemia, not hypokalaemia.
Hypokalaemia does not lower calcium, and it prolongs repolarisation rather than shortening it. A shorter plateau is not how it causes VF.
Hypokalaemia increases ectopic automaticity and triggered activity. It does not cause VF by suppressing the sinus node and unmasking escape rhythms.
questions.why: Low extracellular K+ reduces the conductance of the repolarising K+ currents (IKr, IK1). This prolongs the action potential and QT and promotes afterdepolarisations and triggered activity. Low Mg adds to this and makes K+ harder to replace.

questions.stem: Kate arrives with the defibrillator for Collin, 64, who is in cardiac arrest on the ward. With compressions continuing, you place the first pad to the right of the upper sternum, just below the right clavicle. Where should the second (apical) pad go so that the current passes through the ventricular mass?
options: Left midclavicular line, 2nd intercostal space, just below the left clavicle
Left sternal edge, 4th intercostal space, overlying the right ventricle
Left midclavicular line, 5th intercostal space, directly over the left nipple in men
Left mid-axillary line, at the level of the V6 electrode (5th intercostal space)
notes: This sits over the base of the heart and the great vessels, so the current between the two pads largely misses the ventricles.
A pad this medial puts the pads too close together. Current shunts across the anterior chest wall and little of it reaches the left ventricle.
This is too medial, and breast tissue raises impedance. A common error is putting the apical pad too far forward; it belongs in the mid-axillary line.
questions.why: For anterolateral placement, the apical pad goes in the left mid-axillary line at the V6 level. The current between the two pads then crosses the bulk of the ventricles, which sit to the left and lie low in the chest.

questions.stem: Ned, 32, is in ED with 2 days of worsening headache, fever, vomiting, photophobia and a stiff neck. He is on prednisolone. You tell the examiner you will test for Kernig's sign. Which manoeuvre do you perform, and what counts as a positive result?
options: Flex the neck passively; positive if the hips and knees flex involuntarily
Raise the straight leg with knee extended; positive if pain shoots down the leg
Flex hip and knee to 90°, then extend the knee; positive if pain and resistance
Turn the head side to side 2 to 3 times a second; positive if the headache worsens
notes: This is Brudzinski's neck sign, a different sign of meningism.
This is the straight leg raise (Lasègue's sign), which tests for lumbosacral nerve root irritation, for example from a disc prolapse.
This is jolt accentuation of headache, a separate bedside test for meningism.
questions.why: For Kernig's sign, flex the hip and knee to 90° and then try to straighten the knee. Pain or resistance from stretched, inflamed meninges is positive. The sign is specific but insensitive, so a negative result never rules out meningitis.

questions.stem: Ned, 32, has bacterial meningitis on CSF. He has been on oral prednisolone for a month. He reports a non-severe rash with penicillin as a child. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly and dexamethasone have been given. Which antibiotic should you add to cover Listeria monocytogenes?
options: IV trimethoprim+sulfamethoxazole, with infectious diseases advice
Vancomycin IV, dosed to target trough levels
notes: Benzylpenicillin is the usual Listeria cover, but empirical penicillin is avoided while he carries a penicillin allergy label that has not been assessed.
Vancomycin is added for resistant pneumococcus. It is not reliable treatment for Listeria meningitis.
Azithromycin does not cover Listeria meningitis and does not reach adequate CSF levels for this purpose.
questions.why: Cephalosporins do not cover Listeria. His corticosteroids put him at risk, so he needs added cover. With a penicillin allergy label, avoid benzylpenicillin empirically and use IV trimethoprim+sulfamethoxazole with ID input. Refer him for allergy delabelling later.

questions.stem: In ED, Ned, 32, with suspected bacterial meningitis, has blood cultures taken, and dexamethasone 10 mg IV is given just before his first dose of ceftriaxone 2 g IV. A student asks why the steroid has to be given before or with the first antibiotic dose, not hours later. What is the best explanation?
options: It improves antibiotic penetration across the inflamed meninges into the CSF early on
It replaces cortisol, because a month of prednisolone has suppressed his adrenals
It lowers intracranial pressure by reducing CSF production at the choroid plexus
It blunts the cytokine surge triggered when the first antibiotic dose lyses bacteria
notes: Dexamethasone reduces meningeal inflammation, which actually lowers antibiotic penetration. This is why it matters when vancomycin is used.
Adrenal suppression is a real concern for Ned and may need stress-dose cover, but it is not why dexamethasone has to be timed with the first antibiotic.
Reducing CSF production is how acetazolamide works. Dexamethasone's benefit in meningitis is anti-inflammatory.
questions.why: Antibiotics that kill bacteria release cell wall components that drive a burst of cytokines and subarachnoid inflammation. Dexamethasone given before or with the first dose blunts this burst, which lowers the rate of hearing loss and neurological sequelae (and deaths in pneumococcal meningitis).

questions.stem: The ED registrar does Ned's lumbar puncture in the left lateral position after a normal CT brain. She palpates the line joining the highest points of the iliac crests to choose her level. Which level does she target, and why is it safe in an adult?
options: L3–4 or L4–5 interspace; the conus medullaris ends at about L1–L2
T12–L1 interspace; the spinal cord ends at about T10 in most adults
L1–L2 interspace; the spinal cord ends at about L3
L5–S1 interspace; the dural sac ends at about L5
notes: The adult cord does not end at T10, and a T12–L1 puncture would risk hitting the conus.
The intercristal line marks L4, not L1–L2, and the adult cord ends at about L1–L2, not L3.
The dural sac ends at about S2, not L5. Low lumbar interspaces above S1 are the usual targets.
questions.why: The intercristal (Tuffier's) line crosses the L4 spinous process or the L4–5 interspace. The adult cord ends at about L1–L2, so a needle at L3–4 or L4–5 enters the lumbar cistern among cauda equina roots, below the cord.

questions.stem: Molly, 18, is seen in general practice with fever, a worsening generalised headache, photophobia and a stiff neck. She is alert. You lie her flat on the couch to test for Kernig's sign and tell the examiner what you are doing. Which manoeuvre tests Kernig's sign correctly?
options: Passively flex her neck and watch for involuntary flexion of her hips and knees
Raise her leg with the knee straight and note the angle at which pain begins
Flex her hip and knee to 90 degrees, then try to straighten the knee
Ask her to turn her head side to side quickly and note if the headache worsens
notes: This is Brudzinski's neck sign, a different sign of meningism.
This is the straight leg raise (Lasègue's test) for lumbosacral nerve root irritation, such as a disc prolapse, not Kernig's sign.
This is jolt accentuation of headache, a separate bedside test for meningism, not Kernig's sign.
questions.why: For Kernig's sign, flex the hip and knee to 90 degrees, then extend the knee. Pain or resistance in the back or hamstrings is positive, because stretching the lumbosacral roots pulls on the inflamed meninges. A negative sign does not exclude meningitis.

questions.stem: Molly, 18, is in a general practice with fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. Repeat observations: T 39.3 °C, HR 130, RR 26, BP 108/66, SpO2 97%, alert. She has no rash and no known allergies. An ambulance has been called via 000. What is the most appropriate next step while you wait?
options: Take two sets of blood cultures and leave the antibiotic for the ED to give
Give benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV or IM now and record the dose and time
Give oral amoxicillin 1 g now so that absorption begins before transfer
Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV now and leave the antibiotic for the ED to give
notes: Blood cultures are taken only if they cause no delay. Holding the antibiotic until the ED is a dangerous delay in suspected meningococcal disease.
Oral antibiotics are absorbed unreliably, do not reach adequate CSF levels and have no role in suspected bacterial meningitis.
Dexamethasone is an add-on given with or before the first antibiotic dose in hospital. Giving it without the antibiotic leaves the infection untreated.
questions.why: Suspected meningococcal disease outside hospital needs a parenteral antibiotic straight away: benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV or IM (eTG adult dose), or ceftriaxone 2 g IV or IM. Do not delay it for cultures or transfer, and send the drug, dose and time with her.

questions.stem: Molly, 18, had a lumbar puncture in the ED for suspected meningitis. Her CSF is turbid, with neutrophils 8500 x10^6/L, protein 1.1 g/L and glucose 1.2 mmol/L. Her paired serum glucose is 5.0 mmol/L (ratio 0.24). Which mechanism best explains her low CSF glucose?
options: Serum glucose falls in sepsis and the CSF passively equilibrates with it over hours
Increased CSF production by the inflamed choroid plexus dilutes the glucose
Cytokines trigger local insulin release that drives glucose into neurons
Bacteria and neutrophils use up glucose, and its carrier transport into CSF fails
notes: Her serum glucose is normal at 5.0 mmol/L. The very low ratio of 0.24 shows the problem is in the CSF, not in the blood.
The high opening pressure in meningitis comes mainly from impaired CSF absorption and cerebral oedema, not from extra CSF production diluting glucose.
No insulin is made in the CNS that could explain this. The fall comes from consumption and impaired transport.
questions.why: Glucose normally enters the CSF by GLUT1-facilitated transport and sits at about 60% of serum. In bacterial meningitis, impaired transport plus glycolysis by neutrophils, bacteria and inflamed brain lowers it. A CSF:serum ratio below 0.4 points to a bacterial cause.

questions.stem: In the ED, Molly, 18, has a lumbar puncture lying on her side. The registrar finds the level by feeling for the line joining the highest points of the iliac crests, then inserts the needle at the L3/4 interspace. Why is this interspace a safe site in an adult?
options: The conus medullaris ends at about L1–L2, so only cauda equina roots lie below
The dural sac ends at about L3, so CSF pools in a large cistern at L3/4
The conus medullaris ends at about L4, so the needle passes just below its tip
The filum terminale ends at L3, so the sac below it holds no neural tissue
notes: The dural sac continues to about S2, not L3. The lumbar cistern runs from the conus down to S2.
The conus lies at L1–L2 in adults. A cord ending at L4 would make L3/4 dangerous.
The filum terminale runs to the coccyx, and the cauda equina roots fill the sac below the conus.
questions.why: In adults the spinal cord ends at about L1–L2. Below this the lumbar cistern holds only the floating cauda equina roots, which move away from the needle. The intercristal (Tuffier's) line crosses the L4 spinous process or L4/5, so L3/4 and L4/5 are both safe.

questions.stem: Helen, 24, has migraine with aura. Before each attack she gets about 20 minutes of jumbled lines and bright dots, and then the headache starts. Her GP is prescribing sumatriptan 50 mg for severe attacks. What is the best instruction to give her about when to take it?
options: As soon as the visual symptoms begin, well before any headache has started
At the start of the headache, once the visual symptoms have passed
Only once paracetamol has failed to help within 4 hours
Every morning during exam weeks to stop attacks starting
notes: Taking a triptan during the aura does not stop the headache developing, and it may not work as well. The dose should wait until the pain starts.
Waiting hours for simple analgesia to fail lets the attack become established. A triptan works best taken early in the headache, and it can be used first-line for severe attacks.
Triptans are acute treatments, not preventives. Taking them daily risks medication-overuse headache. Prevention uses drugs such as propranolol, amitriptyline or pizotifen.
questions.why: Triptans work best when taken early in the headache phase. Taken during the aura, they do not prevent the headache and work less well. So tell her to take it as soon as the pain begins, once the aura has finished.

questions.stem: Helen, 24, has migraine with typical visual aura. She has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill correctly for 3 years. She does not smoke, her repeat BP is 124/78, and her urine hCG is negative. She wants to stay on reliable contraception. What is the best plan for her contraception?
options: Continue the combined pill unchanged, as she is young, normotensive and a non-smoker
Change to a lower-dose combined pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinylestradiol
Stop the combined pill and start a progestogen-only method today, with no gap
Take the combined pill continuously, skipping the hormone-free week
notes: Aura alone makes the combined pill UKMEC 4, whatever her age, BP or smoking status. Her other low-risk features do not make it safe.
Any dose of oestrogen is contraindicated in migraine with aura. A lower-dose ethinylestradiol pill still carries the added stroke risk.
Continuous dosing is sometimes used for menstrual migraine without aura. She is still taking oestrogen, so it remains contraindicated.
questions.why: Migraine with aura at any age is an absolute contraindication to oestrogen-containing contraception (UKMEC 4) because of the risk of ischaemic stroke. Switch her straight to a progestogen-only method (implant, LNG-IUD, POP or injection) or a copper IUD, with no gap in protection.

questions.stem: Helen, 24, describes bright dots and jumbled lines that start in one part of her vision. They spread slowly over about 20 minutes and then go completely before her throbbing headache begins. Which mechanism best explains this slowly spreading visual aura?
options: A slow wave of neuronal depolarisation spreading across the occipital cortex
Transient spasm of the cerebral arteries causing focal occipital lobe ischaemia
Small emboli passing through the retinal artery and briefly blocking flow
Trigeminal nerve fibres releasing CGRP around the meningeal blood vessels
notes: The old vascular theory has been replaced. The reduced blood flow during aura follows the neuronal wave and stays above ischaemic thresholds, and ischaemia gives negative, not spreading positive, symptoms.
Retinal emboli cause sudden, monocular, negative loss of vision (amaurosis fugax). They do not cause positive phenomena that spread slowly across the visual field.
Activation of trigeminal fibres with CGRP release explains the headache pain (the target of triptans and CGRP drugs), not the visual aura.
questions.why: Aura is caused by cortical spreading depression: a wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation that moves across the visual cortex at about 2 to 5 mm/min, followed by a period of suppressed activity. Its slow speed explains why symptoms spread over 5 minutes or more and are positive at first.

questions.stem: Helen, 24, has throbbing migraine pain over her left forehead. The pain comes from activated sensory fibres supplying the supratentorial dura and the large blood vessels inside it. Which nerve carries these fibres and explains why the pain is felt in the forehead?
options: Greater occipital nerve, from the dorsal ramus of C2
Meningeal branch of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X)
Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1)
notes: The greater occipital nerve supplies the back of the scalp, and C2 contributes to the posterior fossa dura. Pain from these sources is felt at the back of the head, not the forehead.
The facial nerve is mainly a motor nerve to the muscles of facial expression. It carries no meaningful sensory supply to the supratentorial dura.
Meningeal branches of the vagus supply the dura of the posterior fossa. Pain from there is referred to the ear and the back of the head, not the forehead.
questions.why: The supratentorial dura and large intracranial vessels are supplied mainly by V1 (the trigeminovascular system). Pain from them is therefore referred to the V1 dermatome: the forehead, the area around the eye and the front of the scalp.

questions.stem: Andy, 25, has just been diagnosed with ulcerative proctosigmoiditis and is starting mesalazine under shared care. You are finishing the GP consultation with safety-netting advice. Which instruction about when to go to the emergency department is most appropriate?
options: Go to ED today if new tender red lumps appear on your shins or forearms
Go to ED today if your stools are still loose after 3 days of starting regular mesalazine
Go to ED today if you notice any mucus or streaks of blood in your stool
Go to ED today if 6+ bloody stools a day with fever, racing heart or a swollen tummy
notes: New erythema nodosum needs a same-day or early GP or specialist review, not an ED visit.
Mesalazine takes 2 to 4 weeks to work, so loose stools at 3 days are expected and should be reviewed at the planned follow-up.
He already has blood and mucus at this mild to moderate stage, so this would send him to ED every day without picking out severe disease.
questions.why: Six or more bloody stools a day with systemic signs (fever, tachycardia, abdominal distension or severe pain) suggests acute severe colitis or toxic megacolon. This needs same-day admission for IV corticosteroids and surgical review.

questions.stem: Andy, 25, returns to his GP. Colonoscopy shows ulcerative colitis running continuously from the anal verge to 25 cm (proctosigmoiditis). He has 4 to 5 bloody stools a day. Temp 36.8 °C, HR 82, Hb 124 g/L, ESR 28 mm/h. Stool pathogens are negative. What is the best first-line treatment?
options: Oral prednisolone 40 mg each morning, then weaned gradually over 8 weeks
Mesalazine 1 g suppository at night, used alone
Rectal mesalazine enema or foam at night plus oral mesalazine daily
Hospital admission for IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly
notes: Steroids are second line, added if there is no response to mesalazine. They are not the first choice in mild to moderate disease because of their adverse effects.
A suppository only reaches the rectum (about 15 cm), but his disease extends to 25 cm, and rectal therapy alone is less effective than combining it with oral mesalazine.
He doesn't meet the criteria for acute severe UC (6 or more bloody stools a day plus fever, HR above 90, Hb below 105 or ESR above 30), so he can be managed as an outpatient.
questions.why: Mild to moderate distal UC is treated first with a rectal 5-ASA plus oral mesalazine, and the combination works better than either alone. An enema or foam is needed to reach the sigmoid. A corticosteroid is added only if there is no response.

questions.stem: Andy, 25, has 2 months of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea. His stool tests for pathogens are negative, and his faecal calprotectin is 720 µg/g (normal below 50). Colonoscopy later confirms ulcerative colitis. What is the main source of the raised faecal calprotectin?
options: Neutrophils migrating into the inflamed mucosa and shedding into the lumen
Haemoglobin from mucosal bleeding into the lumen, broken down by colonic bacteria
Increased turnover and shedding of normal colonic epithelial cells
Plasma proteins leaking across the damaged mucosa into the lumen
notes: Calprotectin is not a breakdown product of haemoglobin. Blood in the stool is detected by faecal occult blood or immunochemical (FIT) tests, which measure something different.
Epithelial cells are not the main source. Calprotectin comes mainly from neutrophils, so it rises with inflammatory cell infiltration, not with cell turnover.
Calprotectin is not a plasma protein lost through a leaky mucosa. It is released locally by neutrophils within the gut wall and lumen.
questions.why: Calprotectin is a calcium- and zinc-binding protein found mainly in the cytosol of neutrophils. When neutrophils infiltrate inflamed bowel mucosa and pass into the lumen, faecal levels rise, so it is a marker of mucosal inflammation that separates IBD from functional disorders such as IBS.

questions.stem: Andy's colonoscopy report describes continuous inflammation from the anal verge to 25 cm, crossing the rectosigmoid junction. On a teaching ward round, you are asked about the gross anatomy of this region. Which anatomical feature marks where the sigmoid colon ends and the rectum begins?
options: Dentate line, where rectal columnar epithelium meets squamous epithelium
Peritoneal reflection forming the rectovesical pouch
Puborectalis sling forming the anorectal angle
Taeniae coli spreading out into a continuous longitudinal muscle coat
notes: The dentate line lies in the anal canal and marks the junction of endoderm and ectoderm. It is well below the start of the rectum.
The peritoneal reflection lies at the junction of the middle and lower thirds of the rectum, not where the rectum begins.
Puborectalis forms the anorectal junction at the lower end of the rectum, not the upper end where it meets the sigmoid colon.
questions.why: At the rectosigmoid junction (about S3, where the sigmoid mesocolon ends), the three taeniae coli spread out to form a continuous outer longitudinal muscle layer. The rectum therefore has no taeniae, haustra, appendices epiploicae or mesentery.

questions.stem: A stonemason cutting engineered stone inhales fine dust. Which inhaled agent, found in very high concentration in engineered stone, drives the pulmonary fibrosis of silicosis?
options: Asbestos fibres inhaled over many years of occupational exposure
notes: Asbestos causes asbestosis, pleural plaques and mesothelioma, not silicosis.
Coal dust causes coal workers' pneumoconiosis, not typical engineered stone disease.
Beryllium causes chronic beryllium disease, a granulomatous condition.
questions.why: Engineered stone contains over 90% crystalline silica. Ingested by alveolar macrophages, it causes inflammasome activation and nodular fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman on regular prochlorperazine for nausea develops symmetrical bradykinesia, rigidity and a tremor over 3 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Idiopathic PD typically starts asymmetrically and develops insidiously.
PSP features vertical gaze palsy and early falls, not a subacute drug-linked onset.
Essential tremor lacks bradykinesia and rigidity.
questions.why: Dopamine antagonists (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, antipsychotics) cause subacute, usually symmetrical parkinsonism. Stop the drug where possible; it generally resolves over weeks to months.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a new 2 cm firm, irregular breast lump. Which combination makes up the standard triple assessment?
options: Mammogram, ultrasound and fine-needle cytology only
notes: MRI and tumour markers are not part of standard triple assessment.
Two imaging tests are not three modalities, and core biopsy is preferred over cytology.
History and genetics do not replace examination and tissue sampling.
questions.why: Triple assessment is clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound ± mammography) and core needle biopsy for histology. Concordance of all three gives high diagnostic accuracy.

questions.stem: A child with peanut allergy develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension minutes after exposure. Which mechanism best explains this reaction?
options: Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, causing mediator release
Immune complex deposition in small vessels, activating complement and neutrophils
Allergen-specific T-cell mediated delayed cytokine release
Cytotoxic IgG binding to cell-surface antigens
notes: Describes type III hypersensitivity (e.g. serum sickness), which occurs days later.
Describes type IV hypersensitivity, which is delayed by 48-72 hours.
Describes type II hypersensitivity, such as haemolytic transfusion reactions.
questions.why: Anaphylaxis is a type I hypersensitivity: allergen cross-links IgE bound to mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine, tryptase and other mediators within minutes.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old in a remote community has weeping crusted sores on the legs and itchy burrows between the fingers. Several household members are itchy. Which treatment best addresses the underlying cause and household spread?
options: Permethrin 5% cream or oral ivermectin for the child and contacts
Oral flucloxacillin 25 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days for the child only
Oral albendazole single dose to the household
notes: Treating only the child ignores household transmission and the scabies source.
Steroids may worsen infected sores and do not treat scabies.
Albendazole treats intestinal helminths, not scabies mites.
questions.why: Scabies drives secondary impetigo in remote communities, so treat scabies for the whole household (permethrin or ivermectin) and treat sores as needed. Treating infection without controlling scabies leads to recurrence.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is found down after a 12-hour collapse. CK is 48,000 U/L, urine is dark with blood on dipstick but no red cells, K+ is 6.9 mmol/L with peaked T waves. After IV calcium gluconate, what is the next best step?
options: Insulin with glucose, and aggressive IV 0.9% sodium chloride
Fluid restriction and IV furosemide 40 mg to promote urinary potassium loss
notes: Fluid restriction would worsen kidney injury; diuretics are not first-line without volume repletion.
Bicarbonate alone is not proven and does not rapidly treat hyperkalaemia as insulin does.
Resonium is slow and inadequate for life-threatening hyperkalaemia.
questions.why: Calcium stabilises the myocardium, then insulin/glucose shifts potassium into cells while aggressive isotonic crystalloid protects the kidneys. Dialysis is needed if refractory.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has menorrhagia and easy bruising. Her father has similar problems. Platelets normal, APTT mildly prolonged, PT normal. Which test pattern best supports von Willebrand disease type 1?
options: Low vWF antigen and low vWF activity with proportionate reduction
Normal vWF antigen and activity with low factor IX activity on factor assay
Low platelet count with large platelets
Prolonged thrombin time with low fibrinogen
notes: Low factor IX is haemophilia B, X-linked, rare in women.
Large platelets with thrombocytopenia suggest Bernard-Soulier or MYH9 disorders.
Prolonged thrombin time with low fibrinogen suggests dysfibrinogenaemia or DIC.
questions.why: Type 1 vWD is a partial quantitative deficiency: vWF antigen and activity (ristocetin cofactor) are reduced proportionately, often with low factor VIII. Inheritance is autosomal dominant.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has episodes of headache, sweating, palpitations and severe hypertension. Which is the best initial biochemical test for phaeochromocytoma?
notes: That screens for primary aldosteronism.
That screens for Cushing syndrome.
That tests for carcinoid syndrome.
questions.why: Plasma free metanephrines (or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines) are the most sensitive initial tests; imaging follows biochemical confirmation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old bushwalker was bitten on the calf by an unidentified snake 1 hour ago, and a pressure immobilisation bandage is on. He has vomiting and headache. The 20-minute whole blood clotting test shows no clot. What is the best next step?
options: Remove the bandage and observe for 6 hours with repeat clotting tests hourly
notes: Observation alone is inappropriate with confirmed coagulopathy and symptoms; the bandage stays until antivenom is ready.
FFP does not neutralise venom and is reserved for life-threatening bleeding after antivenom.
Tranexamic acid does not treat venom-induced consumption coagulopathy; antivenom does.
questions.why: Systemic symptoms plus venom-induced consumption coagulopathy (no clot at 20 minutes) indicate significant envenomation and need antivenom. Factor replacement is not first-line.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has 2 years of progressive exertional dyspnoea and dry cough. He has finger clubbing and bibasal fine inspiratory crackles. HRCT shows subpleural basal honeycombing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from chronic low-grade antigen exposure
notes: Typically upper or mid-zone, centrilobular nodules and ground glass with exposure history.
Sarcoid favours hilar nodes and upper-zone perilymphatic disease.
Heart failure gives effusions and septal lines, not honeycombing.
questions.why: Older patient with clubbing, crackles and basal subpleural honeycombing (UIP pattern) on HRCT is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Antifibrotics such as nintedanib or pirfenidone slow decline.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl (16 kg) develops urticaria, stridor and pallor after eating a cashew nut. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Adrenaline 0.16 mg (1 mg/mL) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh
Adrenaline 0.16 mg (1 mg/mL) intravenous bolus over 1 minute via peripheral cannula
notes: Antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory compromise and must not delay adrenaline.
Salbutamol does not treat upper airway obstruction or shock; adrenaline comes first.
IV bolus adrenaline risks arrhythmia; reserved for specialist-monitored settings, with IM first line.
questions.why: IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh is first line for anaphylaxis; a 16 kg child gets 0.16 mg (or a 0.15 mg autoinjector). Repeat every 5 minutes if needed.

questions.stem: What is the underlying pathology of primary achalasia?
options: Loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons, causing failed LOS relaxation and aperistalsis
Hypertrophy of the upper oesophageal sphincter, causing incomplete opening on swallowing
Metaplasia of squamous to columnar epithelium
notes: This does not describe achalasia, which affects the lower sphincter and body.
This describes Barrett's oesophagus.
This describes Zenker's diverticulum.
questions.why: Degeneration of inhibitory (NO/VIP) neurons in the myenteric plexus leaves the LOS hypertensive with incomplete relaxation and aperistalsis, causing dysphagia to solids and liquids.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old is prescribed a drug that is mainly renally cleared and has a narrow therapeutic index. Which age-related change most explains the increased risk of toxicity at usual doses?
notes: First-pass metabolism and hepatic blood flow decrease with age, not increase.
Gastric acid secretion tends to fall with age and has little effect on this problem.
Albumin tends to fall with age, raising free levels of highly bound drugs; it does not increase.
questions.why: GFR falls with age, often with a normal serum creatinine because muscle mass is also reduced. Renally cleared drugs such as digoxin and lithium accumulate.

questions.stem: A patient with a large pulmonary embolism is hypoxaemic. Which mechanism is the main cause of the hypoxaemia?
options: Diffusion impairment across a thickened membrane
Anatomical right-to-left shunt through alveolar collapse
notes: Diffusion across the membrane is normal in PE; the problem is blood flow, not membrane thickness.
Alveolar collapse shunt is typical of ARDS or atelectasis, not the primary mechanism in PE.
Patients with PE usually hyperventilate, with low or normal PaCO2, not hypoventilate.
questions.why: Obstructed pulmonary arteries leave ventilated alveoli unperfused (dead space), and blood diverted to other regions is relatively under-ventilated, producing V/Q mismatch. PaCO2 is often low from hyperventilation.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has hesitancy, weak stream and nocturia. Benign prostatic hyperplasia causes these symptoms mainly by enlargement of which zone of the prostate?
notes: The peripheral zone is where most cancers arise and is palpable on DRE; it is not the main site of BPH.
The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is rarely the site of hyperplasia or cancer.
The anterior fibromuscular stroma has no glandular tissue so is not the site of BPH.
questions.why: BPH arises in the transition zone surrounding the urethra, so it compresses the prostatic urethra. Most prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old abattoir worker has had 3 weeks of fever, sweats and headache. ALT is raised, CRP is high and chest X-ray is clear. Q fever serology is positive for acute infection. Echocardiography is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
notes: Coxiella is an intracellular organism and beta-lactams are ineffective.
A single dose is inadequate for systemic infection.
This long regimen is for chronic Q fever or endocarditis, which is not present here.
questions.why: Acute Q fever without valvular disease is treated with doxycycline for 14 days. Doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine for 18 months is for Q fever endocarditis or chronic disease.

questions.stem: Which of these adults with a burn meets ANZBA criteria for referral to a burn centre?
options: 5% TBSA superficial sunburn to the back
8% TBSA partial-thickness scald to the thigh
3% TBSA partial-thickness burn to the hand
notes: Superficial burns are not counted, and 5% is below threshold.
8% partial-thickness to the thigh is below the 10% adult threshold.
Superficial 1% burn does not meet criteria.
questions.why: ANZBA referral criteria include burns involving the hands, face, feet, genitalia, perineum or major joints, regardless of size (partial thickness or deeper), and >10% TBSA in adults.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old asymptomatic man asks about PSA testing. He has no family history. After discussing benefits and harms, he chooses testing and the PSA is 2.0 ng/mL. What is the most appropriate recommendation under current Australian guidelines?
notes: Referral is for PSA 3.0 ng/mL or above, or an abnormal exam.
Biopsy isn't done on a low PSA, and MRI usually precedes it.
Three-monthly testing isn't needed and increases overdiagnosis.
questions.why: Australian guidelines (2025) advise men 50–69 who choose testing to have PSA every 2 years; a PSA under 3.0 ng/mL is repeated in 2 years. Higher results prompt further assessment, usually MRI.

questions.stem: Ovarian torsion twists the vascular pedicle and cuts off blood flow to the ovary. Which peritoneal fold carries the ovarian artery and vein to the ovary?
notes: The round ligament runs from the uterine fundus to the labium majus and carries no ovarian vessels.
The ovarian ligament joins ovary to uterus and holds only small anastomotic branches, not the main ovarian supply.
The cardinal ligament supports the cervix and carries uterine vessels, not ovarian vessels.
questions.why: The suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament carries the ovarian vessels, nerves and lymphatics from the pelvic brim. Twisting of this pedicle causes venous then arterial occlusion.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with cancer pain takes modified-release oral morphine 60 mg twice daily. Her GP wishes to switch to oral oxycodone. Using standard equianalgesic ratios (oral morphine:oxycodone 3:2), what total daily oxycodone dose is approximately equivalent?
notes: 40 mg would be a 3:1 conversion, which underestimates the equivalent dose.
60 mg treats the single morphine dose as the daily total, or uses a 2:1 ratio.
120 mg ignores the conversion and gives the morphine dose, risking overdose.
questions.why: Total morphine is 120 mg/day; dividing by 1.5 gives about 80 mg oxycodone per day. Dose reduction for incomplete cross-tolerance is often applied, so titrate to response.

questions.stem: What is the underlying mechanism of Graves disease?
options: Destruction of follicles releasing stored hormone
notes: Describes toxic adenoma, which gives focal uptake.
Describes thyroiditis, with low uptake and transient thyrotoxicosis.
Rare TSHoma gives high TSH, unlike Graves where TSH is suppressed.
questions.why: Graves disease is caused by TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies, producing diffuse goitre, hyperthyroidism, orbitopathy and diffuse increased uptake on scintigraphy.

questions.stem: Which action of digoxin on the cardiac myocyte underlies both its positive inotropy and its toxicity?
options: Inhibition of the Na-K-ATPase pump, raising intracellular calcium
Blockade of L-type calcium channels, reducing calcium entry during the plateau phase
notes: That is the action of verapamil and diltiazem.
That is the action of beta-blockers.
Potassium channel opening is not digoxin's mechanism.
questions.why: Digoxin inhibits Na-K-ATPase, raising intracellular sodium, reducing calcium extrusion via the Na-Ca exchanger and increasing contractility. Hypokalaemia increases toxicity.

questions.stem: Why are beta-lactam antibiotics alone inadequate for Legionella or Mycoplasma pneumonia?
options: They are intracellular or lack a cell wall
They are cleared by the kidneys too rapidly to reach effective serum concentrations
notes: Renal clearance is not the reason for ineffectiveness.
Beta-lactams penetrate lung adequately for typical pathogens.
Exotoxin production is not what makes these organisms resistant.
questions.why: Legionella is intracellular and Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so atypical cover needs macrolides, doxycycline or fluoroquinolones.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has fatigue and arthralgia of the second and third MCP joints. Ferritin is 1200 µg/L and transferrin saturation 80%. What is the next test?
options: Bone marrow biopsy with iron staining to quantify body stores
notes: Bone marrow biopsy is not needed for diagnosis.
Caeruloplasmin is for Wilson disease.
Hepatitis A is unrelated to iron overload.
questions.why: Raised ferritin with transferrin saturation above 45% suggests haemochromatosis; HFE genotyping (C282Y homozygosity) confirms it.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old tall, thin man has 1 day of right pleuritic chest pain. Obs: RR 16, SpO2 98% on air, HR 76, BP 120/75. CXR shows a 1.5 cm apical rim, no effusion. No prior lung disease. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Intercostal catheter with underwater seal drainage and inpatient admission
Observation with outpatient review and analgesia
notes: Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise.
Drainage is not needed for a small, stable primary pneumothorax.
Pleurodesis is for recurrence prevention, not a first episode.
questions.why: A small, minimally symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a stable patient can be observed with analgesia and early review. Aspirate or drain if breathless or large.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman born in India is to start adalimumab for rheumatoid arthritis. Her chest X-ray is normal and she has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate screening test for latent TB?
options: Interferon-gamma release assay (or tuberculin skin test)
Serum TB antibody test performed on a venous blood sample before starting therapy
notes: Gram stain is not used; active TB would need acid-fast stain and culture.
Serological TB antibody tests are not recommended and are unreliable.
Delaying and relying on imaging alone will miss latent infection.
questions.why: Before biologics, screen for latent TB with an IGRA or TST plus chest X-ray. Treat latent TB first if positive, after excluding active disease.

questions.stem: Which feature of gentamicin pharmacology underlies once-daily dosing with level monitoring?
options: Concentration-dependent killing with a post-antibiotic effect
Time-dependent killing above the MIC for most of the dosing interval
Bacteriostatic action by binding the 50S subunit
notes: Time-dependent killing describes beta-lactams, not aminoglycosides.
Gentamicin is renally excreted unchanged, not hepatically metabolised.
Gentamicin binds the 30S subunit and is bactericidal.
questions.why: Aminoglycosides kill in a concentration-dependent manner with a post-antibiotic effect, so high peaks with a low trough limit toxicity. Trough levels guide nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity risk.

questions.stem: A woman with treated hypothyroidism on levothyroxine confirms a pregnancy at 5 weeks. TSH is 3.5 mIU/L. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Increase levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in 4 weeks
Continue the same dose and recheck TSH at the postnatal visit after delivery
notes: Untreated maternal hypothyroidism risks miscarriage and impaired fetal neurodevelopment.
Stopping risks fetal harm; the fetus depends on maternal T4 in the first trimester.
Combination T3 therapy is not recommended.
questions.why: Levothyroxine requirements rise in early pregnancy (often 25–30%). Increase the dose promptly and monitor TSH every 4 weeks, aiming for the lower pregnancy-specific range (about under 2.5–4 mIU/L).

questions.stem: A 19-year-old has appendicitis. Early in the illness she feels dull central abdominal pain, which later moves to the right iliac fossa. What best explains the later localised pain?
options: Referred pain from nerve root irritation in the lumbar spine as the appendix swells
Inflamed appendix irritating the parietal peritoneum
Progressive distension of the caecum causing persistent midgut visceral pain
Mesenteric ischaemia of the terminal ileum from venous congestion around the appendix
notes: Not a spinal referred pain; the shift reflects peritoneal involvement.
Caecal distension is not the mechanism of localisation in appendicitis.
Ischaemia of the terminal ileum is not the cause of the shift.
questions.why: Early visceral pain from the midgut-derived appendix is poorly localised (periumbilical, T10). Once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, somatic pain localises to the right iliac fossa.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has heavy periods and fatigue. Hb is 98 g/L, MCV 71 fL, ferritin 6 microgram/L. She has taken oral iron before without GI intolerance. What is the best initial management?
options: Oral iron on alternate days or daily, and treat the menorrhagia
Immediate red cell transfusion of two units followed by repeat haemoglobin in 24 hours
Intravenous iron infusion as first-line therapy for all patients with iron deficiency
Intramuscular vitamin B12 injections alternate days for two weeks, then every 3 months
notes: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic instability or severe symptomatic anaemia; she is stable with Hb 98.
IV iron is for intolerance, malabsorption, ongoing losses exceeding oral replacement or need for rapid repletion, not routine first-line.
B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis; her picture is microcytic with very low ferritin.
questions.why: Oral iron is first-line for uncomplicated iron deficiency when tolerated; alternate-day dosing improves absorption. Also address the cause (menorrhagia) and recheck Hb in 2–4 weeks.

questions.stem: What is the main mechanism of airway obstruction in obstructive sleep apnoea?
options: Loss of pharyngeal dilator muscle tone during sleep causing upper airway collapse
Absent central respiratory drive to the diaphragm with reduced brainstem output in sleep
Bronchospasm of the small airways during REM sleep causing expiratory flow limitation
Laryngeal oedema from nocturnal acid reflux causing fixed upper airway narrowing
notes: Absent effort with no drive describes central sleep apnoea, not OSA.
Bronchospasm is lower airway disease, not the mechanism of OSA.
Reflux can aggravate symptoms but is not the mechanism of OSA.
questions.why: In sleep, pharyngeal dilator tone falls and a narrowed, fatty or crowded airway collapses despite ongoing respiratory effort.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man has enlarging hands and jaw, new sweating and carpal tunnel symptoms. Fasting IGF-1 is markedly raised. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
options: Failure of GH suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test
Random serum GH measurement taken in the morning on two separate occasions
Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test with 8 am serum cortisol measurement
Insulin tolerance test with serial GH and cortisol measurements over two hours
notes: Random GH is pulsatile and cannot confirm or exclude acromegaly.
This tests for Cushing syndrome.
This tests for GH or ACTH deficiency, the opposite problem.
questions.why: Acromegaly is confirmed by GH failing to suppress (nadir above about 1 mcg/L) after 75 g oral glucose, with raised IGF-1. Random GH is pulsatile and unreliable.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman presents 9 hours after waking with left hemiparesis and gaze deviation. CT shows no haemorrhage. CT angiography shows right proximal middle cerebral artery occlusion; CT perfusion shows a small core with a large penumbra. What is the best management?
options: Intravenous thrombolysis only, as treatment is permitted within 24 hours of symptom onset
Endovascular clot retrieval, as perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue
Antiplatelet therapy alone with aspirin, as the treatment window has passed
Conservative care with supportive measures, as thrombectomy is limited to 6 hours
notes: Thrombolysis is not a standard option at 9 hours, and does not replace retrieval for proximal LVO.
Antiplatelet alone would miss a treatable large vessel occlusion with salvageable brain.
The 6-hour limit has been extended to 24 hours with perfusion imaging selection.
questions.why: Extended-window ECR (up to 24 hours) is indicated for large vessel occlusion with a favourable core-penumbra mismatch on perfusion imaging.

questions.stem: A GP discovers they prescribed 10 times the intended dose of a drug to a patient, who has taken one dose and is well. After ensuring patient safety, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Open disclosure to the patient and report via the incident system
Alter the medical record to show the intended dose, then arrange a routine review
Wait to see whether harm occurs before telling the patient, then document the outcome
Report only to the pharmacist who dispensed it and ask them to correct the script
notes: Altering records is dishonest and unprofessional; add a clear, dated entry instead.
Open disclosure is required even without harm and should be prompt.
The pharmacist may help but does not replace disclosure to the patient and incident reporting.
questions.why: After a medication error, ensure safety, then use open disclosure (explain, apologise) and report the incident for learning. Records must never be altered.

questions.stem: Why does an ACE inhibitor cause hyperkalaemia, particularly in a patient with reduced renal function?
options: Lower angiotensin II reduces aldosterone, decreasing distal potassium secretion
It directly blocks the Na-K-ATPase pump in muscle, reducing cellular potassium uptake
It inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the loop of Henle, lowering potassium loss
It increases proximal tubular potassium reabsorption through raised bradykinin levels
notes: ACE inhibitors do not block the Na-K-ATPase; digoxin does.
That is loop diuretic action, which causes hypokalaemia.
Bradykinin accumulation causes cough and angioedema, not hyperkalaemia.
questions.why: Less angiotensin II means less aldosterone, so less potassium secretion in the collecting duct. Reduced GFR further limits potassium excretion.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man arrives with an open tibial fracture with a 3 cm contaminated wound. Tetanus status is unknown. Alongside wound cover and splinting, what is the most important early drug management?
options: Oral cefalexin for 5 days started after wound closure in the emergency department
Intravenous flucloxacillin only after wound culture results return, then for 48 hours
Intravenous cefazolin within 1 hour plus tetanus prophylaxis
Topical antibiotic ointment to the wound and clinic review in 48 hours
notes: Oral therapy is inadequate for initial open fracture cover.
Waiting for cultures delays the time-critical dose.
Topical agents do not replace systemic antibiotics and delay is harmful.
questions.why: Open fractures need IV antibiotics (such as cefazolin) as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour, plus tetanus toxoid and immunoglobulin if status unknown and wound contaminated.

questions.stem: In classic acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (Guillain-Barré), which structure is the main target of the immune attack?
notes: Receptor antibodies at the NMJ cause myasthenia gravis.
Anterior horn cell loss occurs in poliomyelitis and motor neurone disease.
Central myelin is targeted in multiple sclerosis.
questions.why: AIDP is an immune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves and roots, often after Campylobacter or viral infection, causing slowed conduction and areflexia.

questions.stem: A primiparous woman, 5 days postpartum, is confused, euphoric, and sleepless, with delusions that her baby is special and hears voices. She has no insight. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Urgent psychiatric admission, ideally mother-baby unit, with antipsychotic
Sertraline 50 mg daily with outpatient review by the perinatal team in two weeks
notes: An antidepressant alone is inadequate for psychosis and may worsen possible bipolar illness.
Blues is mild, transient, and does not involve psychosis.
Psychotherapy alone is inappropriate for acute psychosis without insight and with risk to mother and baby.
questions.why: Rapid onset psychosis in the first weeks postpartum suggests puerperal psychosis, a psychiatric emergency with risks of suicide and infanticide. It needs admission, ideally to a mother-baby unit, and antipsychotic or mood stabiliser treatment.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has tender red shins, ankle arthralgia and fever. Chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lungs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Lymphoma is possible but is less likely with this triad and a young woman with erythema nodosum.
Primary TB usually causes unilateral adenopathy.
GPA causes cavitating nodules and renal or sinus disease, not hilar nodes.
questions.why: Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and arthralgia define Löfgren syndrome, an acute sarcoidosis with good prognosis, often self-resolving and managed with NSAIDs.

questions.stem: What is the underlying pathology of type 1 diabetes mellitus?
options: Peripheral insulin resistance with relative deficiency
Excess glucagon secretion from an alpha-cell tumour
Impaired incretin response from the gut
Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
notes: This describes type 2 diabetes.
Glucagonoma is rare and not the cause of type 1 diabetes.
Reduced incretin effect is a feature of type 2 diabetes.
questions.why: Type 1 diabetes results from T-cell-mediated autoimmune destruction of beta cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency and ketosis-proneness.

questions.stem: Which type of ultraviolet radiation is the main cause of sunburn and direct DNA damage producing cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers?
notes: UVA penetrates deeper and causes ageing and indirect oxidative damage, but less sunburn.
Infrared causes heat, not DNA dimers.
UVC is absorbed by the ozone layer and doesn't reach the ground.
questions.why: UVB is absorbed in the epidermis and causes sunburn and pyrimidine dimers. UVA penetrates deeper, contributing to photoageing and indirect damage.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has exertional chest tightness, relieved by rest. Resting ECG and troponin are normal. She has low-intermediate pretest probability of coronary disease. Which test is most appropriate?
notes: Invasive angiography is reserved for high-risk features or positive non-invasive testing.
A resting echo does not assess for inducible ischaemia or coronary anatomy.
Waiting leaves symptomatic angina uninvestigated.
questions.why: CT coronary angiography has a high negative predictive value and suits low-to-intermediate pretest probability of obstructive CAD, allowing exclusion of disease.

questions.stem: Why does intravenous calcium gluconate protect against arrhythmia in hyperkalaemia?
options: It drives potassium into cells by stimulating the sodium-potassium ATPase pump
It stabilises the cardiac myocyte membrane potential
It binds potassium in the gut
notes: Insulin with glucose and salbutamol shift potassium, not calcium.
Diuretics increase renal excretion; calcium acts on the membrane.
Resonium-type binders act in the gut; calcium does not.
questions.why: Calcium raises the threshold potential, restoring the gap to resting membrane potential; it does not lower serum potassium, so a shift agent is still needed.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has sputum smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis confirmed in Australia. He lives with his wife and two children. What is the most appropriate public health action?
options: Notify the state health authority and begin contact tracing
Notify only if drug resistance is confirmed on culture and susceptibility testing
Advise household contacts to take isoniazid empirically
Contact trace only after culture results are final
notes: Notification is required for all cases, not just resistant ones.
Contacts are screened first; treatment is based on results and TB service advice.
Tracing starts on smear-positive diagnosis; waiting delays identifying secondary cases.
questions.why: TB is notifiable in Australia on diagnosis; state TB services lead contact tracing and screen household contacts promptly, without waiting for culture.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has sharp central chest pain, worse lying flat and relieved by sitting forward, after a viral illness. ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Prednisolone 50 mg daily alone, tapered over several weeks
notes: Corticosteroids alone increase recurrence risk and are reserved for refractory cases or contraindications to NSAIDs.
Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression is not an occlusive coronary lesion; PCI is not indicated.
Anticoagulation is not indicated and risks haemopericardium.
questions.why: Acute viral pericarditis is treated with an NSAID (aspirin or ibuprofen) plus colchicine, which reduces recurrence. Steroids are second-line, and rest from exercise is advised.

questions.stem: Which thyroid function pattern indicates primary hypothyroidism?
notes: Suggests central (pituitary or hypothalamic) hypothyroidism.
Suggests primary hyperthyroidism.
Suggests TSH-secreting adenoma or thyroid hormone resistance.
questions.why: In primary hypothyroidism, loss of negative feedback from low thyroxine raises TSH. Low TSH with low free T4 suggests central hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman collapses. She is pale and confused, BP 70/40 mmHg, HR 30/min. ECG shows complete heart block with a wide-complex escape rhythm. IV atropine 600 microgram has no effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
notes: Cardioversion treats tachyarrhythmias, not bradycardia.
Amiodarone slows conduction further and is unsafe in heart block.
Digoxin slows AV conduction and would worsen the block; it is also too slow to act.
questions.why: Unstable bradycardia unresponsive to atropine needs pacing (transcutaneous, then transvenous), with adrenaline infusion as a bridge. Complete heart block with a wide escape is usually atropine-resistant.

questions.stem: In a healthy adult, blood alcohol falls at a roughly constant rate of about one standard drink an hour, regardless of concentration. What explains this?
options: Rapid renal clearance of unchanged alcohol, proportional to plasma concentration
notes: Under 10% of alcohol is excreted unchanged, and clearance is not first-order.
CYP2E1 contributes only minor metabolism, and the pattern is saturable not first-pass.
Ethanol is water-soluble and distributes into total body water, not fat.
questions.why: Alcohol dehydrogenase saturates at low concentrations, so elimination is zero-order: a constant amount per hour, not a constant fraction.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer is diagnosed with proximal DVT. eGFR is normal and he has no GI luminal tumour concerns. What is the best anticoagulant choice?
notes: Warfarin is inferior to LMWH/DOAC in cancer-associated VTE.
Aspirin is not adequate treatment for acute proximal DVT.
Proximal DVT needs anticoagulation to prevent extension and pulmonary embolism.
questions.why: For cancer-associated VTE, DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) or LMWH are preferred over warfarin. Continue while the cancer is active or under treatment, at least 3–6 months.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old presents with low mood. In a HEADSS assessment, which approach is most appropriate when asking about sensitive topics?
options: Interview the adolescent alone after explaining the limits of confidentiality
Interview with a parent present throughout to support the adolescent and verify history
Ask about suicide only if the adolescent raises it
Ask the sensitive questions first to build urgency
notes: A parent present often inhibits honest disclosure about drugs, sex and mood.
Asking about suicide does not increase risk and should be asked directly in low mood.
Begin with non-threatening domains such as home and education to build rapport before sensitive topics.
questions.why: HEADSS is best done with the adolescent alone, after explaining confidentiality and its limits (risk of serious harm). Start with less sensitive topics (home, education) and ask directly about self-harm and suicide.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73m² (stable CKD). She takes metformin 1 g bd. What is the most appropriate action?
notes: The full dose is unsafe at this eGFR.
Dose reduction applies at eGFR 30 to 45, not below 30.
Glibenclamide risks prolonged hypoglycaemia in renal impairment and is avoided in older adults.
questions.why: Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 because of the risk of lactic acidosis. Dose reduction is advised at eGFR 30 to 45.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child in the Kimberley has fever, then drowsiness and seizures after wet-season flooding. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. Murray Valley encephalitis is suspected. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Intravenous ribavirin for 10 days, started in hospital
notes: Ribavirin has no proven benefit for flaviviruses.
Doxycycline is antibacterial.
Oseltamivir acts on influenza only.
questions.why: No specific antiviral exists for Murray Valley encephalitis or Japanese encephalitis; management is supportive, including seizure control and ICU care. Prevention is by mosquito avoidance.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has her first cervical screening test. Oncogenic HPV type 16 is detected and liquid-based cytology is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the cervical screening test in 12 months
Repeat the cervical screening test in 5 years
notes: A 12-month repeat applies to oncogenic HPV types other than 16/18 with negative or low-grade cytology.
Five-yearly screening applies only when oncogenic HPV is not detected.
Early repeat HPV testing is not used for HPV 16/18; these patients go straight to colposcopy.
questions.why: HPV 16 or 18 detected is higher risk regardless of cytology and needs direct referral for colposcopy. A 12-month repeat applies to other oncogenic types with negative or low-grade cytology.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains exertional syncope in a patient with severe aortic stenosis?
options: Fixed cardiac output with exercise-induced peripheral vasodilation
Excess vagal tone during exertion causing sinus arrest and sudden bradycardia
notes: Not the mechanism in aortic stenosis; there is no thromboembolic source in this setting.
Vagal sinus arrest underlies reflex syncope, not fixed outflow obstruction.
Haemorrhage is not part of the mechanism in aortic stenosis.
questions.why: Fixed outflow obstruction prevents cardiac output rising as exercise vasodilates peripheral vessels, so cerebral perfusion falls. Exertional syncope is a cardiac red flag.

questions.stem: A nulliparous woman at 39 weeks is fully dilated with an epidural, pushing for 2 hours with a persistent occipito-anterior head at +2 station. The CTG is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue passive descent and active pushing for a further 2 hours, then reassess
Assisted vaginal birth by an experienced operator after assessment
Start oxytocin to augment second stage only
notes: Prolonged pushing without descent increases maternal and fetal morbidity.
Caesarean is not first line when the head is low and instrumental birth is feasible.
Oxytocin may help but this woman has already had a long second stage; assessment for assisted birth is needed.
questions.why: Prolonged second stage in a nullip (about 3 hours with epidural, with no progress) warrants senior review; with an engaged OA head and normal CTG, instrumental birth is appropriate.

questions.stem: Which mechanism underlies Gilbert syndrome?
options: Reduced hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity impairs bilirubin conjugation
Defective canalicular excretion of conjugated bilirubin across hepatocyte membrane
Impaired hepatic uptake due to biliary obstruction
Increased red cell haemolysis overwhelming conjugation
notes: That describes Dubin-Johnson syndrome, with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
Obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin and cholestatic enzymes.
Haemolysis is not the cause in Gilbert syndrome; haemoglobin and reticulocytes are normal.
questions.why: Gilbert syndrome is a UGT1A1 promoter variant giving about 30% enzyme activity. Unconjugated bilirubin rises with fasting or illness, and other liver tests are normal.

questions.stem: Antenatal corticosteroids are given to a woman at 30 weeks in threatened preterm birth. What is the main mechanism by which they reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?
options: Induce fetal type II pneumocyte maturation and surfactant production
Relax fetal bronchial smooth muscle and increase airway diameter during first breaths
notes: Not the mechanism; steroids act on structural and surfactant maturation, not bronchial tone.
Steroids promote lung liquid absorption at birth, not increased secretion.
Steroids have no tocolytic effect; that is a separate intervention.
questions.why: Corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation by stimulating type II pneumocytes to produce surfactant (and thin alveolar septa), reducing RDS, IVH and NEC.

questions.stem: Which mechanism most directly links visceral obesity to type 2 diabetes?
options: Free fatty acid excess causing insulin resistance in liver and muscle
Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells mediated by islet-directed T lymphocytes
notes: That causes type 1 diabetes.
GLP-1 is not increased in a way that explains this; it would be protective.
Adiponectin is reduced, not raised, in obesity.
questions.why: Visceral fat releases free fatty acids and inflammatory cytokines, causing hepatic and muscle insulin resistance. Adiponectin falls in obesity.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has ptosis and diplopia worsening by evening, improved by rest. Pupils are normal. What is the most specific initial blood test?
options: Anti-dsDNA antibodies by Crithidia immunofluorescence assay
notes: Anti-dsDNA relates to lupus.
CK is raised in myopathies and is typically normal in myasthenia.
Anti-GAD relates to stiff-person syndrome and type 1 diabetes.
questions.why: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with normal pupils suggest myasthenia gravis; AChR antibodies are positive in about 85% of generalised disease. Also image the thymus with CT.

questions.stem: A patient has been on a stable lithium dose for years. When should a blood sample be taken to measure the lithium level correctly?
options: 12 hours after the last dose, before the next dose
1 hour after the dose, at the expected peak serum concentration
Any time, as lithium has no peak
notes: One hour after the dose captures the peak, giving falsely high values.
A 4-hour sample is not standardised and is near peak.
Timing matters because levels vary with absorption and clearance.
questions.why: Lithium levels are taken as a trough about 12 hours after the last dose, at steady state (about 5 days after a change). The usual target is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L.

questions.stem: Histology of a papillary thyroid carcinoma is reported. Which nuclear feature is most characteristic of this tumour?
options: Vascular and capsular invasion with follicles
Hürthle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm
notes: Amyloid stroma with C-cell nests describes medullary carcinoma, derived from parafollicular C cells.
Vascular and capsular invasion defines follicular carcinoma, which spreads haematogenously.
Hürthle cells characterise oncocytic (Hürthle cell) neoplasms, not papillary carcinoma.
questions.why: Papillary carcinoma shows optically clear 'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei, grooves and pseudo-inclusions, often with psammoma bodies. It spreads via lymphatics to cervical nodes.

questions.stem: What is the basic pathophysiology of gestational diabetes mellitus?
options: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells in pregnancy, with islet autoantibodies
Placental hormone-induced insulin resistance with inadequate beta-cell compensation
Lowered renal threshold for glucose reabsorption in pregnancy
notes: Autoimmune destruction describes type 1 diabetes, not typical GDM.
Lowered renal threshold causes glycosuria, which is common in pregnancy but does not cause hyperglycaemia.
Fetal hyperinsulinism is a result of maternal hyperglycaemia, not its cause.
questions.why: Placental hormones (human placental lactogen, progesterone, cortisol) increase insulin resistance; GDM occurs when maternal beta cells cannot compensate.

questions.stem: Tenofovir disoproxil with emtricitabine is used as HIV PrEP. What is their shared mechanism of action?
options: Integrase strand transfer inhibition blocking viral DNA integration into host DNA
notes: Integrase inhibitors include dolutegravir.
Protease inhibitors include darunavir.
CCR5 antagonists include maraviroc.
questions.why: Both are nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitors that terminate proviral DNA chain elongation, preventing establishment of infection.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman is 20 weeks pregnant and has a positive syphilis serology after an outbreak-area screen. She has no symptoms or prior treatment and the stage is unknown (likely latent, over 2 years). Which is the best management?
options: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IM weekly for 3 doses
Single dose of azithromycin 2 g orally
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 28 days
Defer treatment until after delivery and treat the neonate
notes: Azithromycin is unreliable due to resistance and not recommended.
Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Delaying treatment risks congenital syphilis and stillbirth.
questions.why: Pregnant women with late or unknown-duration latent syphilis need benzathine benzylpenicillin weekly for 3 doses, which prevents congenital syphilis. Doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman has a tender irreversible groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, with vomiting and abdominal distension. What is the best management?
options: Attempt gentle manual reduction at home, then book elective repair if it succeeds
notes: Reduction risks reducing necrotic bowel.
Delay risks bowel ischaemia.
A truss is inappropriate with obstruction or a femoral hernia.
questions.why: Femoral hernias have a high strangulation risk. An irreducible tender one with obstruction needs urgent resuscitation and emergency surgery.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old had diet-controlled gestational diabetes and gave birth 2 days ago. Her glucose readings are now normal. Which test is recommended 6 to 12 weeks postpartum?
options: No testing if inpatient glucose levels normalised
notes: HbA1c can be unreliable early postpartum and is less sensitive; OGTT is preferred at this stage.
A random glucose is insensitive for detecting diabetes.
Normal early postpartum glucose does not exclude persistent diabetes; testing is still needed.
questions.why: Women with GDM need a 75 g OGTT at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum to detect persisting diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance. Then screen regularly (every 1 to 3 years) for type 2 diabetes.

questions.stem: Screening detects a cancer 2 years earlier than symptoms would, but death occurs at the same age as without screening. Five-year survival from diagnosis appears improved. Which bias explains this?
notes: Length-time bias is over-detection of slow-growing, indolent cancers by screening; death timing is not the issue here.
Selection bias concerns how participants are chosen, such as healthy volunteers.
Recall bias concerns differential memory of exposures in case-control studies.
questions.why: Earlier diagnosis lengthens measured survival without delaying death. Mortality, not survival from diagnosis, should be used to evaluate screening.

questions.stem: A baby is born at term to a mother who is HBsAg positive. What is the most appropriate management in the first 12 hours?
options: Hepatitis B vaccine at 2 months only
Hepatitis B vaccine only, given within 7 days of birth, then at 2 and 4 months
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine, at separate sites
Oral antivirals for the infant for 6 months
notes: Far too late; the birth dose is needed within 12 hours.
Vaccine alone within 7 days is too late and omits immunoglobulin.
Infant antivirals are not standard prophylaxis.
questions.why: Infants of HBsAg-positive mothers should receive hepatitis B immunoglobulin and the birth-dose vaccine within 12 hours of birth, at separate sites, then complete the schedule.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes takes metformin and empagliflozin. She has 2 days of vomiting and poor intake. Glucose 8 mmol/L, pH 7.20, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, ketones 5 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop empagliflozin; give IV fluids and insulin with glucose infusion
Continue empagliflozin and metformin, encourage oral fluids and review in 24 hours
Give IV fluids alone as glucose is normal
Give sodium bicarbonate and restart metformin
notes: SGLT2 inhibitor must stop; oral fluids are inadequate for DKA.
Insulin is needed to suppress ketogenesis, with dextrose.
Bicarbonate is not routine and metformin should be withheld in acidosis.
questions.why: This is euglycaemic DKA: stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and treat with IV fluids and fixed-rate insulin with dextrose to clear ketones. Normal glucose does not exclude DKA.

questions.stem: Oseltamivir reduces influenza severity by inhibiting which viral target?
options: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, preventing viral genome replication in host cells
Neuraminidase, preventing release of new virions
notes: That is the target of baloxavir (cap-dependent endonuclease) or nirmatrelvir-type drugs differ; oseltamivir does not act here.
Haemagglutinin mediates attachment, but oseltamivir does not target it.
M2 blockers (amantadine) are no longer effective against circulating influenza.
questions.why: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor that blocks release of progeny virions from infected cells. It works best started within 48 hours of symptom onset.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with asthma presents with moderate exacerbation: talking in sentences, mild subcostal recession, SpO2 94% in air. Which is the best initial treatment?
options: Salbutamol 6 puffs (100 microgram) via spacer, reassess after 20 minutes
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg alone as a single dose, then reassess after 4 hours
Ipratropium alone via nebuliser every 20 minutes
notes: Steroids are added but a bronchodilator is the first-line immediate treatment.
IV magnesium is reserved for severe or life-threatening asthma not responding to initial therapy.
Ipratropium is an add-on in moderate to severe asthma, not alone.
questions.why: For moderate asthma in children, give salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer (12 if over 6 years in some protocols), repeat as needed, plus oral corticosteroid. Magnesium is for severe or life-threatening cases.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman from coastal Queensland has fever, rash and symmetrical small-joint pain and swelling of hands and ankles for 1 week after camping near wetlands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis presenting acutely with symmetrical polyarthritis
notes: RA would not cause acute fever and rash after mosquito exposure.
Q fever causes hepatitis or pneumonia, not typical polyarthritis.
Melioidosis does not cause this picture.
questions.why: Acute polyarthritis with rash and fever after mosquito exposure in coastal Australia suggests Ross River virus. Confirm with IgM serology or PCR; treat with NSAIDs.

questions.stem: Which organism causes most community-acquired urinary tract infections, using fimbriae to adhere to uroepithelium?
notes: Proteus is less common and is associated with struvite stones and alkaline urine.
S. saprophyticus is a notable cause in young sexually active women but is much less common.
Enterococcus is more typical of healthcare-associated or catheter-related infection.
questions.why: Uropathogenic E. coli, using P fimbriae to ascend from the perineum, causes about 75-80% of community UTIs.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community has cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema and BP 130/85 three weeks after impetigo. What is the expected complement finding?
notes: Normal complement would favour IgA nephropathy or ANCA vasculitis.
Low C4 suggests classical pathway activation, as in lupus nephritis.
Complement is consumed, not raised, in PSGN.
questions.why: Post-streptococcal GN activates the alternative pathway, causing low C3 with normal C4, usually normalising within 6-8 weeks. Persistent low C3 suggests another diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has palpitations. HR 190/min regular, narrow-complex, BP 118/76 mmHg, alert, no chest pain. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre fails to terminate it. What is the next step?
notes: He is haemodynamically stable, so cardioversion is not first-line.
Amiodarone is not first-line for SVT and is slower to act.
Verapamil is second-line if adenosine fails or is contraindicated.
questions.why: For stable regular narrow-complex SVT, vagal manoeuvres come first, then adenosine 6 mg rapid IV bolus with saline flush, then 12 mg. Cardioversion is reserved for instability.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old smoker has calf claudication at 200 metres and an ankle-brachial index of 0.7. Pulses are absent at the foot, with no rest pain or tissue loss. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Smoking cessation, supervised exercise, antiplatelet and statin
Urgent femoral-popliteal bypass grafting after CT angiography within 48 hours
notes: Bypass is for critical limb ischaemia or disabling claudication that fails conservative care.
Anticoagulation does not treat chronic PAD and adds bleeding risk.
Amputation is reserved for unsalvageable limbs.
questions.why: Stable claudication is managed with risk-factor control: stop smoking, supervised walking, antiplatelet and statin, and BP and diabetes control. Refer for revascularisation if there is critical limb ischaemia or lifestyle-limiting symptoms despite treatment.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old refugee from Sudan has 6 weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows right upper lobe cavitation. What is the most appropriate initial investigation and precaution?
options: Three sputum samples for TB microscopy, culture and PCR, with airborne isolation
Bronchoscopy only after a trial of amoxicillin
Mantoux test read at 48–72 hours, with droplet precautions and a mask for the patient
notes: IGRA cannot diagnose active TB and does not replace microbiological testing.
Delaying with antibiotics is inappropriate when cavitation and symptoms suggest TB.
Mantoux does not diagnose active disease, and TB needs airborne, not droplet, precautions.
questions.why: Suspected pulmonary TB needs sputum for smear, culture and nucleic acid testing (including rifampicin resistance), with airborne precautions. IGRA cannot distinguish latent from active disease.

questions.stem: Which cerebrospinal fluid pattern best fits acute bacterial meningitis?
options: Lymphocytes, mildly raised protein, normal glucose
Lymphocytes, very high protein, low glucose
Normal cells, high protein, normal glucose
notes: This is the typical viral meningitis or encephalitis pattern.
Lymphocytes with very high protein and low glucose suggest tuberculous or fungal meningitis.
This albuminocytological dissociation suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome.
questions.why: Bacteria cause a neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein and low CSF glucose (consumed by bacteria and neutrophils). Viral meningitis gives lymphocytes with normal glucose.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy has about 5 words, no pointing, poor eye contact and does not respond to his name. His mother reports he lined up cars for hours. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Audiology assessment and referral for developmental assessment
Review again at 3 years of age and refer then if speech has still not improved
Reassure the parents that boys commonly talk later and review at the 4-year check
Refer for speech therapy only after a further 6-month trial of watchful waiting
notes: Waiting delays diagnosis and intervention; early referral is recommended.
Late-talking reassurance is wrong when there are social communication red flags.
Delaying therapy is inappropriate; intervention should start without waiting for a diagnosis.
