questions.why: Language delay with social communication concerns and repetitive play suggests autism. Hearing must be tested and he should be referred early for developmental assessment without waiting.

questions.stem: Why does atrial fibrillation increase the risk of ischaemic stroke?
options: Atrial stasis promotes thrombus formation, usually in the left atrial appendage
Rapid ventricular rates often cause paradoxical embolism through the foramen ovale
Loss of atrial kick causes cerebral hypoperfusion only
Atrial fibrillation directly damages cerebral arteries
notes: Paradoxical embolism is a venous-sided mechanism and not the main one in AF.
Reduced cardiac output may cause hypotension but not the thromboembolic stroke risk.
AF does not directly damage cerebral vessels; the mechanism is embolic.
questions.why: Fibrillating atria do not contract effectively, so blood stagnates in the left atrial appendage and thrombus can embolise to the brain.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 29+0 weeks has confirmed PPROM. She is afebrile, with no contractions, and the CTG is normal. Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
options: Oral erythromycin 250 mg four times daily alone for 10 days, then stop antibiotics
IV azithromycin stat or erythromycin with IV/oral amoxicillin per local protocol
notes: Prophylactic antibiotics are recommended to prolong latency and reduce infection.
Erythromycin alone is inferior to combination regimens in standard protocols.
Co-amoxiclav is avoided in PPROM because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis.
questions.why: Antibiotics after PPROM prolong latency and reduce chorioamnionitis and neonatal morbidity. Use a macrolide plus amoxicillin per guideline; avoid amoxicillin-clavulanate (NEC risk).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis presents with haematemesis, HR 120, BP 90/60. He has been resuscitated cautiously. Besides urgent endoscopy, which pair of drugs should be started now?
notes: Tranexamic acid is not recommended and raises thrombosis risk; octreotide is an alternative but this pairing lacks antibiotics.
Beta-blockers are contraindicated in acute hypotensive bleeding; PPI alone is not variceal therapy.
Oral amoxicillin is not appropriate; IV ceftriaxone is used, and terlipressin is the preferred vasoactive agent.
questions.why: Suspected variceal bleeding needs a splanchnic vasoconstrictor (terlipressin) plus antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone) before endoscopy with band ligation. Antibiotics reduce infection and mortality.

questions.stem: Why does insulin with glucose lower serum potassium in hyperkalaemia?
options: It increases urinary potassium excretion by enhancing distal tubular secretion
It stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, shifting potassium into cells
It binds potassium in the gut lumen, increasing faecal potassium loss over hours
It stabilises the cardiac myocyte membrane potential within minutes of administration
notes: Excretion is promoted by diuretics or dialysis, not insulin.
Gut binding is the action of resins such as sodium zirconium cyclosilicate.
Membrane stabilisation is the action of calcium.
questions.why: Insulin stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in skeletal muscle, moving potassium intracellularly. The effect is temporary, so total body potassium must still be removed.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is 5 days post hip replacement. He collapses with BP 70/40 mmHg, HR 130/min, SpO2 86% and a raised JVP. Bedside echo shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle. No contraindications. What is the best next treatment?
notes: Oral DOACs are suitable for stable patients, not for shock needing rapid clot lysis.
An IVC filter is reserved for those with contraindications to anticoagulation; it does not treat shock.
Delaying reperfusion for CTPA in a peri-arrest patient is unsafe; LMWH alone is inadequate in shock.
questions.why: Haemodynamically unstable (massive) PE with RV strain warrants systemic thrombolysis, e.g. alteplase, plus unfractionated heparin, without delaying for imaging when bedside echo supports the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin is booked for elective colectomy tomorrow. Which advice about empagliflozin is best?
options: Continue it through the perioperative period
Withhold it for 3 days before surgery
Withhold it only on the morning of surgery
Switch it to glibenclamide on the day of surgery
notes: Continuing raises the risk of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis when fasting.
Omitting only on the morning is too short given the prolonged effect.
Sulfonylureas add hypoglycaemia risk while fasting and are not a recommended substitute.
questions.why: SGLT2 inhibitors are withheld for 3 days (ie the 3 days before surgery) to reduce risk of euglycaemic ketoacidosis. Restart when eating and drinking normally.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa has BMI 14 kg/m². Her HR is 38 bpm, lying and standing BP 80/50 mmHg with postural dizziness, and K+ 2.9 mmol/L. She and her parents want outpatient care. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Medical admission for stabilisation and cautious refeeding
Weekly outpatient family-based treatment with GP weight and observation checks
Oral potassium replacement and outpatient review with repeat ECG in two weeks
Admission to a psychiatric unit for intensive therapy, with medical review as needed
notes: Family-based treatment is first line for adolescents but only when medically stable.
Outpatient management is unsafe with this degree of instability and electrolyte disturbance.
She needs medical stabilisation first, with psychiatric input in parallel, not a psychiatric-only admission.
questions.why: Marked bradycardia, postural hypotension and hypokalaemia are medical instability criteria mandating admission. Start refeeding cautiously with thiamine and monitor phosphate, K+, Mg2+ and glucose.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains how GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide cause weight loss?
options: Reduced appetite via central action and delayed gastric emptying
Inhibited intestinal lipase, reducing dietary fat absorption from the gut lumen
Increased renal glucose excretion through reduced proximal tubular glucose reabsorption
Increased thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue through beta-3 receptor activation
notes: That is orlistat's mechanism.
That describes SGLT2 inhibitors, which cause modest weight loss.
Not a GLP-1 RA mechanism.
questions.why: GLP-1 RAs act on hypothalamic and brainstem centres to increase satiety and slow gastric emptying, also enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

questions.stem: In a trial, the event rate is 10% with placebo and 6% with a new drug. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one event?
notes: 4 is the ARR in percentage points, not its reciprocal.
10 is the control event rate, not related to NNT.
40 is the relative risk reduction (%), a common confusion with NNT.
questions.why: NNT = 1/absolute risk reduction = 1/0.04 = 25. Relative risk reduction is 40%, which is not the NNT.

questions.stem: How does Australian bat lyssavirus reach the central nervous system after a bite or scratch?
options: Haematogenous spread across the blood–brain barrier
Retrograde axonal transport along peripheral nerves
Spread via the cerebrospinal fluid from the gut
Aerosol spread via the olfactory epithelium only
notes: Viraemia is not the usual route; the virus travels along nerves.
The gut is not a route of entry for lyssavirus.
Aerosol transmission is rare and not the mechanism after a bite.
questions.why: Lyssaviruses replicate locally in muscle, then travel by retrograde axonal transport to the CNS. This is why prompt wound cleaning and post-exposure prophylaxis before symptoms can prevent disease.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old Aboriginal man who smokes attends for a health check. He has no known diabetes, kidney disease or cardiovascular disease. What is the most appropriate approach to his cardiovascular risk?
options: Defer formal risk assessment until he turns 45 years and then use the calculator
Defer formal risk assessment until he turns 35 years, then repeat every two years
Start a moderate-intensity statin empirically because of his smoking history
Calculate absolute CVD risk now using the 2023 Australian calculator
notes: Age 45 is the starting age for non-Indigenous Australians; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people start at 30.
The threshold for this group is 30 years, not 35.
Treatment is guided by calculated absolute risk, not by a single risk factor such as smoking.
questions.why: Absolute CVD risk assessment is recommended from age 30 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, versus 45 for others. Treatment is then guided by the calculated risk.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with non-valvular AF has hypertension and diabetes (CHA2DS2-VA 3). eGFR is 70 mL/min/1.73 m2 and he has no bleeding risk factors. What is the most appropriate stroke prevention?
notes: Aspirin alone is not recommended for AF stroke prevention.
Warfarin is second line to DOACs and adding aspirin raises bleeding without benefit.
His score of 3 clearly warrants anticoagulation.
questions.why: Anticoagulation is recommended for CHA2DS2-VA of 2 or more; DOACs such as apixaban are preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. She is hypotensive (BP 85/50 mmHg) and confused. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with a stone. After fluid resuscitation, blood cultures and IV antibiotics, what is the next best step?
notes: Cholecystectomy is for later, once the ducts are cleared; it does not treat the obstruction.
Delay for imaging is unsafe in septic obstruction; the stone is already shown.
Ursodeoxycholic acid does not relieve acute obstruction.
questions.why: Severe (Tokyo grade III) cholangitis with shock and confusion needs urgent biliary decompression, usually by ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction or stenting, alongside antibiotics.

questions.stem: Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)?
options: Volume load exceeding cardiac capacity causing hydrostatic pulmonary oedema
Donor anti-HLA antibodies activating recipient neutrophils in the pulmonary capillaries
Recipient anti-A antibodies causing complement-mediated destruction of donor red cells
Bacterial endotoxin in the stored blood product causing widespread vasodilatation
notes: This describes TRALI, a non-hydrostatic capillary leak with normal or low BP.
This describes acute haemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility.
This describes septic transfusion reaction from contaminated product.
questions.why: TACO is hydrostatic pulmonary oedema from too much volume or too rapid a rate, especially in elderly, cardiac or renal patients. It typically has hypertension and raised JVP, and responds to diuretics.

questions.stem: In the NEXUS low-risk criteria for cervical spine imaging, which feature must be absent for the spine to be clinically cleared?
notes: Active rotation is part of the Canadian C-spine rule, not NEXUS.
Age 65 or over is a Canadian rule item, not part of NEXUS.
Mechanism is part of the Canadian rule, not NEXUS.
questions.why: NEXUS criteria: no midline cervical tenderness, no focal neurological deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no painful distracting injury. Age and mechanism belong to the Canadian C-spine rule.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with HIV has a CD4 count of 60 cells/µL, 2 weeks of dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, hypoxaemia and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. LDH is raised. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Pneumococcus typically gives lobar consolidation and acute onset.
TB commonly gives cavitation or upper lobe disease and is less typical here.
Cryptococcus presents with headache and meningism.
questions.why: Subacute dry cough, hypoxia, bilateral interstitial infiltrates and raised LDH with CD4 below 200 suggest PJP. Confirm with PCR or stain of bronchoalveolar lavage; treat with high-dose co-trimoxazole.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman on postoperative day 1 after hip surgery has urine output of 0.2 mL/kg/h for 8 hours and a creatinine rise from 80 to 130 micromol/L. She is hypovolaemic with a palpable bladder? A bladder scan shows 80 mL. What is the best next step?
options: Fluid resuscitation with crystalloid and review nephrotoxins
Start a frusemide infusion at 10 mg/hour and monitor urine output hourly
notes: Frusemide does not improve outcomes and worsens hypovolaemia.
Obstruction is unlikely with a low bladder volume and no hydronephrosis evidence.
RRT is reserved for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, overload or uraemia.
questions.why: This is likely prerenal AKI from hypovolaemia. Give crystalloid, stop nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors, and monitor. Diuretics worsen hypovolaemia.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes delirium from dementia?
options: Gradual onset over several years with progressive decline in function
notes: Memory impairment occurs in both conditions.
Gradual onset over years favours dementia.
Language difficulty occurs in both and does not discriminate.
questions.why: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that fluctuates over hours to days. Dementia is gradual with preserved alertness until late.

questions.stem: What is the underlying mechanism of bleeding in placental abruption?
options: Rupture of fetal vessels running over the cervical os during membrane rupture
Rupture of maternal decidual vessels with retroplacental haematoma
Cervical ectropion trauma from the presenting part
Tearing of the uterine scar at the lower segment
notes: That describes vasa praevia, which causes fetal bleeding.
Cervical lesions cause minor bleeding and are not the mechanism of abruption.
That describes uterine rupture, a different cause of bleeding and pain.
questions.why: Abruption is premature separation of a normally sited placenta because decidual spiral vessels bleed, forming a retroplacental clot. Blood may be concealed and the uterus tender.

questions.stem: A woman has previously had pelvic inflammatory disease. Which mechanism best explains her increased risk of both ectopic pregnancy and infertility?
options: Persistent cervical mucus plugging blocking sperm entry
Scarring of the fallopian tube with loss of ciliary function and lumen patency
Reduced ovarian follicle numbers from ovarian abscess with loss of ovarian reserve
Adhesion of the endometrium causing Asherman syndrome
notes: PID does not cause cervical mucus plugging as its main fertility effect.
Ovarian reserve is not the main effect of PID; tubal damage is.
Intrauterine adhesions are not the usual result of PID and do not explain ectopic pregnancy.
questions.why: Salpingitis damages tubal mucosa and cilia and causes adhesions. Total blockage causes infertility; partial damage lets sperm through but delays the embryo, so it implants in the tube.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has 3 months of progressive dysphagia, first for solids then liquids, with 8 kg weight loss. He has long-standing reflux. What is the most appropriate first investigation?
options: Barium swallow followed by outpatient review in six weeks
notes: Barium does not give tissue and is not first line for alarm features.
Manometry is for suspected motility disorders after endoscopy excludes obstruction.
Delaying with empiric PPI is inappropriate with alarm features.
questions.why: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss suggests oesophageal cancer; urgent endoscopy with biopsy is the first test, allowing diagnosis and tissue.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old boy has projectile vomiting from pyloric stenosis. Which acid-base and electrolyte disturbance is expected?
options: Hyperchloraemic normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with hypernatraemia
notes: Acidosis would be expected with diarrhoea or bicarbonate loss, not gastric acid loss.
Gastric loss causes hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia, and alkalosis rather than acidosis.
Respiratory alkalosis is not the primary disturbance; hypoventilation compensates for the alkalosis.
questions.why: Loss of gastric HCl causes hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; volume depletion drives aldosterone, so renal K+ and H+ are lost, giving hypokalaemia and paradoxical aciduria.

questions.stem: Which mechanism chiefly stops bleeding from the placental bed after delivery?
options: Contraction and retraction of myometrial fibres compressing spiral arteries
Sustained vasoconstriction of uterine arteries by maternal catecholamine release
notes: Catecholamines have only a minor role in placental bed haemostasis.
Fibrinolysis would increase, not stop, bleeding.
The ductus venosus is a fetal structure and unrelated.
questions.why: Myometrial fibres contract and retract (living ligatures), compressing the spiral arteries. Uterine atony is therefore the commonest cause of PPH.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has acute pancreatitis with lipase 4 times normal, and ultrasound shows gallstones with a normal CBD. She is haemodynamically stable with mild disease. What is the best fluid management?
options: Moderate-rate Hartmann's solution titrated to clinical response
Nil fluids, as oral intake only
Aggressive normal saline bolus of 1 L/hour for the first 24 hours, then reassess
notes: Hypovolaemia needs IV fluids in the first 24 hours.
Aggressive fluids increase complications and have not improved outcomes.
Colloids offer no advantage over crystalloid.
questions.why: Early goal-directed moderate crystalloid resuscitation (lactated Ringer's/Hartmann's, ~1.5 mL/kg/h after bolus if hypovolaemic) is preferred; aggressive fluids increase fluid overload without benefit.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is found unresponsive after injecting heroin. RR is 4/min, SpO2 is 78%, and pupils are pinpoint. Bag-valve-mask ventilation has begun with oxygen. What is the next most appropriate step?
options: Naloxone 100 to 400 microgram IV, titrated to respiratory rate
Naloxone 2 mg IV bolus, repeated every minute until fully alert and RR normal
Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV, repeated every minute to a maximum of 1 mg
Intubation before any reversal agent is given, then ventilate
notes: Large boluses risk acute withdrawal and aspiration; titrate small doses unless there is peri-arrest.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.
Intubation is rarely needed first; a rapidly reversible cause should be treated with ventilation and naloxone.
questions.why: After ventilation support, titrate small naloxone doses to restore adequate breathing without precipitating withdrawal, agitation or pulmonary oedema. Repeat or infuse because naloxone is shorter acting than many opioids.

questions.stem: A footballer is struck on the lateral aspect of the knee, at the fibular neck. Which finding best reflects injury to the common peroneal nerve at this site?
options: Loss of ankle plantarflexion with weakness of resisted toe flexion
Foot drop with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot
Loss of sensation over the sole of the foot and heel
Weak knee extension with loss of knee jerk
notes: Plantarflexion is supplied by the tibial nerve, which is not injured at the fibular neck.
The sole is supplied by the tibial nerve (medial and lateral plantar branches).
Knee extension and knee jerk depend on the femoral nerve (L3-4).
questions.why: The common peroneal nerve winds around the fibular neck and supplies ankle dorsiflexors and evertors plus dorsal foot skin. Injury causes foot drop and dorsal foot sensory loss.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents 24 hours after condomless anal sex with a partner of unknown HIV status. He is not on PrEP. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start 28 days of PEP now, with baseline HIV testing
Wait for a 4-week HIV test before deciding whether PEP is required
Advise PEP is no longer effective after 24 hours
Start PrEP and review in 3 months
notes: Waiting delays PEP, which is time-critical.
PEP is recommended up to 72 hours.
PrEP is not a substitute for PEP after exposure.
questions.why: PEP should start as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours, after a substantial exposure. Give a 28-day course of three-drug therapy and test at baseline and follow-up.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Varenicline and combination NRT have each failed despite good adherence and counselling. She asks about vaping. What is the best advice under the 2024 Australian reforms?
options: Buy a nicotine vape from a licensed tobacconist or vape retailer
Import vapes online for lower cost
Vapes are first-line, so stop other therapy
Consider a pharmacy-supplied nicotine vape with support
notes: Retail sale of vapes, including tobacconists, is banned.
Unregulated or imported products are unlawful and not quality-assured.
Vapes are not first-line; NRT and varenicline with behavioural support come first.
questions.why: Vapes are a second-line option if evidence-based treatments have failed. They are supplied through pharmacies, not retail shops, with behavioural support and a plan to stop.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is abstinent from alcohol for one week after inpatient withdrawal. She has normal liver function and wants medication to reduce cravings. She takes no opioids. Which is the most appropriate option?
notes: Disulfiram is second-line due to toxicity and adherence issues.
Benzodiazepines are for withdrawal only, with misuse risk and no relapse-prevention role.
Baclofen is off-label second-line and that dose is excessive.
questions.why: Acamprosate (glutamate modulator) or naltrexone supports relapse prevention after withdrawal. With no opioid use, naltrexone is also suitable; acamprosate fits as the listed option.

questions.stem: Which coagulation factor is directly inhibited by the DOAC rivaroxaban?
notes: Thrombin is inhibited by dabigatran, not rivaroxaban.
Factor VIII is not a target of DOACs.
Warfarin reduces vitamin K-dependent factors including VII; rivaroxaban acts directly on Xa.
questions.why: Rivaroxaban and apixaban directly inhibit factor Xa. Dabigatran is the direct thrombin inhibitor.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old nursing home resident has massive abdominal distension and constipation. Abdominal X-ray shows a large, dilated 'coffee bean' loop arising from the pelvis toward the right upper quadrant. What is the diagnosis?
notes: Caecal volvulus is a dilated loop in the left upper quadrant, often with small bowel dilatation.
Toxic megacolon shows colitis with loss of haustra, not a coffee bean loop.
Carcinoma gives proximal colonic dilatation without a single twisted loop.
questions.why: A coffee bean loop pointing from the pelvis to the right upper quadrant is classic for sigmoid volvulus in elderly, institutionalised patients. Caecal volvulus typically displaces the loop to the left upper quadrant.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has a tibial shaft fracture after a motorcycle crash. Pain is severe and out of proportion, worse with passive toe extension, and the calf is tense. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: DVT is unlikely acutely and does not cause tense compartments with pain on passive stretch.
Fat embolism causes respiratory, neurological and petechial features, usually after 24 to 72 hours.
Nerve palsy causes foot drop and sensory loss, not escalating tense pain.
questions.why: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment after tibial fracture indicate compartment syndrome, a clinical diagnosis needing urgent fasciotomy.

questions.stem: Which laboratory finding best distinguishes DIC from isolated liver failure in a bleeding patient with prolonged PT?
options: Markedly raised D-dimer with low fibrinogen and platelets, and low factor VIII
Low factor V and normal factor VIII, with a mildly raised D-dimer and low platelets
notes: Low factor V with normal factor VIII is the pattern of liver disease.
Normal platelets and D-dimer argue against DIC.
Low factor VII only is an early vitamin K deficiency or liver pattern, not DIC.
questions.why: In DIC all factors are consumed, including factor VIII, with raised D-dimer. In liver disease factor VIII is normal or raised (endothelial synthesis) while other factors fall.

questions.stem: Which mechanism underlies type 2 (hypercapnic) respiratory failure?
notes: V/Q mismatch typically causes hypoxaemia with normal or low CO2 (type 1).
Diffusion impairment causes hypoxaemia, usually with normal CO2.
Shunt causes hypoxaemia unresponsive to oxygen, usually with normal CO2.
questions.why: Type 2 failure has PaCO2 above 45–50 mmHg (6 kPa) because of inadequate alveolar ventilation, as in COPD or neuromuscular weakness.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old banana farm worker in north Queensland has 5 days of fever, severe myalgia, headache and bilateral conjunctival suffusion after flooding. Bilirubin and creatinine are raised. Which is the best diagnostic test early in illness?
options: Blood culture on standard media at 48 hours
notes: Leptospira is fastidious and routine culture is insensitive.
Rose Bengal is used for brucellosis.
Weil-Felix is an obsolete rickettsial test.
questions.why: In the first week (leptospiraemic phase) PCR on blood detects Leptospira; serology (MAT) is often negative until after about day 7-10 and needs paired samples.

questions.stem: In paracetamol overdose, hepatic glutathione stores are depleted. Which toxic metabolite accumulates to cause hepatocyte injury?
options: Paracetamol glucuronide formed by hepatic conjugation with glucuronic acid
notes: Glucuronide is a non-toxic conjugate that is excreted.
Sulfate is a non-toxic conjugate that is excreted.
Acetaldehyde is an ethanol metabolite, not related to paracetamol.
questions.why: At high doses, glucuronidation and sulfation saturate and more drug is oxidised by CYP2E1 to NAPQI. When glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins.

questions.stem: A marathon runner collapses on a hot humid day with a core temperature of 41.5°C and confusion. Which mechanism best explains why heat loss fails in this setting?
options: High ambient humidity impairs evaporation of sweat
Peripheral vasoconstriction reduces skin blood flow and increases conduction
Hypothalamic set point rises as in fever
Reduced basal metabolic rate limits radiation
notes: Heat stress causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction; conduction is also minor.
Fever involves a raised set point; in heat stroke the set point is unchanged and regulation is overwhelmed.
Exertion raises metabolic heat production; radiation also fails when ambient temperature is high.
questions.why: In hot humid conditions evaporation, the main heat loss route when ambient temperature approaches skin temperature, fails. Heat stroke is thermoregulatory failure, not a raised set point as in fever.

questions.stem: Chronic severe aortic stenosis causes which adaptive change in the left ventricle?
options: Thinning of the wall from volume overload
notes: Wrong: eccentric hypertrophy with dilatation is the response to volume overload, as in chronic mitral or aortic regurgitation.
Wrong: wall thickening, not thinning, occurs initially; thinning and dilatation occur only late in decompensation.
Wrong: aortic stenosis loads the left ventricle; the right ventricle is affected only late via pulmonary hypertension.
questions.why: Fixed outflow obstruction raises systolic wall stress, so sarcomeres replicate in parallel and produce concentric hypertrophy, which impairs diastolic filling and raises myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.stem: A patient has taken prednisolone 20 mg daily for three months. Which mechanism explains why abrupt cessation may cause adrenal crisis?
options: Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses CRH and ACTH, causing adrenal atrophy
Prednisolone permanently destroys adrenal medullary cells
Prednisolone blocks aldosterone receptors in the distal tubule
Prednisolone induces autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase in the adrenal cortex
notes: The cortex (not medulla) atrophies, and it is reversible rather than destructive.
Prednisolone has mineralocorticoid activity; aldosterone is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system and is largely preserved.
Anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies cause autoimmune Addison disease, not steroid-induced suppression.
questions.why: Negative feedback from chronic exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses the HPA axis, so the adrenal cortex atrophies and cannot respond when the drug stops. Taper after prolonged courses.

questions.stem: A patient on long-term prednisolone develops central obesity and striae. What is the state of the patient's ACTH and endogenous cortisol?
notes: This pattern fits ACTH-dependent Cushing disease, not exogenous steroid.
Low cortisol with high ACTH is primary adrenal insufficiency.
Low ACTH with high cortisol suggests an autonomous adrenal source, not exogenous steroid.
questions.why: Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses the HPA axis by negative feedback, so ACTH and endogenous cortisol are low, and the adrenals atrophy. Prednisolone does not cross-react in most cortisol assays.

questions.stem: A man is rescued from an enclosed house fire with singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth, hoarse voice and mild stridor. What is the best next step?
options: Humidified oxygen via face mask and observe on the ward for 24 hours
Urgent early intubation by an experienced operator
Nebulised adrenaline then discharge home after four hours of observation
Bronchoscopy on the ward in the morning after overnight observation
notes: Observation risks airway loss as oedema progresses.
Adrenaline is temporising and discharge is unsafe.
Delay is dangerous with stridor; secure the airway first.
questions.why: Stridor, hoarseness and soot suggest inhalational airway burns with progressive oedema. Secure the airway early by intubation before swelling makes it impossible.

questions.stem: In the Australian health system, what does the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) do?
options: Subsidises the cost of listed prescription medicines
Pays the full cost of all private hospital admissions for concession card holders
Funds emergency care in public hospitals through state block grants
Provides rebates for GP consultations and specialist attendances
notes: Private hospital costs are covered by private health insurance, not the PBS.
Public hospitals are funded by state and federal agreements.
GP rebates are provided through the MBS, not the PBS.
questions.why: The PBS is a federal scheme that subsidises listed medicines; Medicare Benefits Schedule rebates cover medical services.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl attends a GP alone requesting contraception and asks that her parents not be told. She understands the risks, benefits and alternatives. What is the best approach?
options: Provide contraception if she is Gillick competent, maintaining confidentiality
Refuse contraception until a parent or guardian has provided written consent first
Prescribe the contraception but inform her parents once she has left the clinic
Refer to child protection services in all cases of sexual activity under 16 years
notes: Parental consent is not required for a competent minor.
Disclosing to parents breaches confidentiality without a safety justification.
Mandatory reporting depends on risk of harm, not on contraception request alone.
questions.why: A mature minor who has sufficient understanding and intelligence to fully appreciate the decision (Gillick competence) can consent, and confidentiality applies. Consider safety concerns such as coercion or abuse.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has resistant hypertension on three drugs. K+ is 3.1 mmol/L with metabolic alkalosis. Plasma renin is suppressed and aldosterone is elevated. After confirmatory testing, what is the next step to determine laterality before surgery?
notes: Metanephrines screen for phaeochromocytoma, which does not cause suppressed renin with high aldosterone.
Dexamethasone suppression tests for Cushing syndrome, not aldosterone excess.
Renal artery stenosis causes high renin, not suppressed renin.
questions.why: In confirmed primary aldosteronism, CT cannot reliably distinguish unilateral from bilateral disease, so adrenal vein sampling guides adrenalectomy decisions.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old bat carer, never vaccinated against rabies, was scratched by a flying fox. The wound was washed. Which post-exposure regimen is appropriate?
options: Observe the bat for 10 days and vaccinate only if it develops signs of illness
Tetanus booster only, with wound review by the GP in 48 hours and no other therapy
Rabies vaccine alone on days 0, 3, 7, 14, given intramuscularly in the deltoid
notes: Observation is used for some dogs/cats overseas, not for bats.
Tetanus cover may be needed but does not address lyssavirus.
Vaccine alone omits immunoglobulin, which is required in unvaccinated people.
questions.why: For unvaccinated people with a bat exposure in Australia, give rabies immunoglobulin (infiltrated around the wound) plus a 4-dose vaccine course. Bats cannot be reliably observed.

questions.stem: Oral rehydration solution works in secretory diarrhoea such as that from rotavirus because which intestinal transport mechanism remains intact?
options: Passive paracellular sodium diffusion in the colon
Sodium-hydrogen exchange in the crypt cells
notes: Paracellular diffusion is not the glucose-linked route that ORS relies on; it does not explain the effect.
Sodium-hydrogen exchange is reduced in diarrhoea and is not the target of ORS.
CFTR chloride secretion drives fluid loss in secretory diarrhoea; it is not what ORS uses.
questions.why: SGLT1 couples sodium and glucose uptake, and water follows osmotically. This pathway stays intact in gastroenteritis, which is why low-osmolarity ORS works.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old with advanced dementia lacks capacity. Her valid advance care directive refuses CPR and intubation. She has a cardiac arrest in hospital and her son demands full resuscitation. What is the correct approach?
options: Follow the valid directive and withhold CPR
Resuscitate fully because the son is next of kin and is present at the bedside
Resuscitate now and then review the directive with the family afterwards
Seek a court order from the guardianship tribunal before any decision is made
notes: A substitute decision-maker cannot override a valid applicable refusal made by the patient.
Resuscitating contravenes the patient's refusal and risks battery.
Court involvement is only needed if validity is genuinely uncertain.
questions.why: A valid, applicable advance care directive refusing treatment must be followed; it expresses the person's own decision and overrides substitute views.

questions.stem: Transient monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax) from carotid atheroembolism results from embolus to a branch of which artery?
options: Ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid
Posterior cerebral artery, a terminal branch of the basilar artery
Facial artery, a branch of the external carotid artery in the neck
Basilar artery, formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries
notes: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital cortex; occlusion causes homonymous hemianopia, not monocular loss.
The external carotid branches do not supply the retina.
Basilar disease causes brainstem and bilateral or posterior symptoms, not monocular loss.
questions.why: The ophthalmic artery arises from the internal carotid and gives the central retinal artery, so emboli from carotid plaque cause ipsilateral transient monocular blindness.

questions.stem: What is the main mechanism of exertional angina in a patient with fixed coronary stenosis?
options: Coronary vasospasm at rest causing transient reduction in epicardial blood flow
Myocardial oxygen demand exceeding supply through the narrowed artery
Acute plaque rupture with occlusive thrombus causing complete vessel occlusion
Pericardial inflammation causing pain that worsens on lying flat or inspiring
notes: Rest vasospasm describes Prinzmetal angina, not exertional angina.
Plaque rupture with thrombus causes acute coronary syndrome.
Pericarditis causes pleuritic, positional pain, not exertional.
questions.why: A fixed stenosis limits the rise in coronary flow during exertion, so increased demand outstrips supply and causes reversible ischaemia, relieved by rest.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man on sertraline took tramadol yesterday. He now has agitation, diaphoresis, temperature 38.8°C, inducible clonus and hyperreflexia. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Cease serotonergic drugs and give benzodiazepines
Dantrolene IV and oral bromocriptine with active external cooling measures
Start regular paracetamol for the fever and continue sertraline at current dose
Haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly for agitation, repeated after 30 minutes if needed
notes: Dantrolene and bromocriptine are used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome and are not first-line for serotonin syndrome.
Continuing the offending agent is unsafe, and paracetamol does not lower temperature as the heat is from muscle activity.
Antipsychotics such as haloperidol can worsen the condition and risk confusing the picture with NMS.
questions.why: Serotonin syndrome is managed by stopping serotonergic agents, supportive care and benzodiazepines for agitation. Cyproheptadine can be added if this fails; antipyretics are ineffective.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains a pleural effusion in congestive cardiac failure?
options: Raised hydrostatic pressure in pleural capillaries
Bacterial infection of the pleural space
notes: Increased permeability produces exudates, as in pneumonia or malignancy.
Lymphatic obstruction by tumour causes an exudate, not the cardiac failure mechanism.
Infection causes parapneumonic effusion or empyema, which are exudates.
questions.why: In heart failure, raised hydrostatic pressure drives protein-poor fluid into the pleural space, producing a transudate. Exudates arise from increased permeability or impaired lymphatics.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old Aboriginal man in a remote community has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate kidney screening for him?
options: Annual eGFR, urine ACR and blood pressure from age 30
No screening until age 50 unless he develops symptoms or abnormal blood pressure
Screening only if he develops diabetes
notes: Waiting until 50 misses the high early burden of CKD.
Imaging is not a screening test for CKD.
Screening is not restricted to people with diabetes.
questions.why: The CKD guideline recommends annual kidney health checks (eGFR, urine ACR, blood pressure) for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people from age 30, and earlier if other risk factors are present. At 28 he is just under this age, so the answer applies from 30 or sooner with any risk factor.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with heart failure on ramipril and furosemide takes regular ibuprofen for knee pain. He presents with weight gain, oedema and creatinine rising from 90 to 160 µmol/L. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: Direct tubular obstruction by intratubular crystal deposition and precipitation
Efferent arteriolar dilatation lowering filtration pressure
notes: Crystal nephropathy is not the NSAID mechanism here.
NSAIDs can cause minimal change or interstitial nephritis, but this haemodynamic picture is the common cause.
ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole; NSAIDs constrict the afferent.
questions.why: NSAIDs inhibit vasodilatory prostaglandins, constricting the afferent arteriole; with ACE inhibitor and diuretic ('triple whammy') GFR falls. Stop the NSAID and use paracetamol.

questions.stem: A healthy adult is having elective surgery under general anaesthetic at 1 pm. According to ANZCA fasting guidance, until when may they have clear fluids?
notes: Fasting from midnight is outdated and unnecessarily prolonged.
Six hours applies to solid food, not clear fluids.
Four hours is not the recommended cut-off for clear fluids in adults.
questions.why: ANZCA allows clear fluids until 2 hours before anaesthesia, with solids stopped 6 hours before. Clear fluids may reduce thirst, hypovolaemia and PONV.

questions.stem: Most colorectal cancers arise through the adenoma–carcinoma sequence. Which early molecular event typically initiates it?
options: TP53 mutation with loss of cell-cycle checkpoint control
notes: TP53 loss is a late event enabling progression to carcinoma.
SMAD4 loss occurs late in the sequence.
KRAS mutation follows APC loss and promotes adenoma growth.
questions.why: Biallelic APC loss (Wnt pathway activation) is the earliest event, followed by KRAS activation and later TP53 loss. Germline APC mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis.

questions.stem: In the Stanford classification of aortic dissection, which description defines a type A dissection?
options: Any dissection involving the ascending aorta
Dissection confined to the abdominal aorta
Dissection beginning distal to the left subclavian artery only
Dissection limited to the aortic arch branches
notes: Abdominal-only dissection does not involve the ascending aorta, so it is not type A.
This describes type B.
Involvement of the ascending aorta, not arch branches alone, defines type A.
questions.why: Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta regardless of the origin of the tear; type B involves only the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery.

questions.stem: Which pharmacological property of antipsychotics best explains acute dystonia and parkinsonism?
options: Serotonin 5-HT2C antagonism in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus pathway
Dopamine D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway
Histamine H1 blockade in the cortex
Muscarinic M1 agonism in the striatum
notes: 5-HT2C antagonism is linked to weight gain, not extrapyramidal effects.
H1 blockade causes sedation and weight gain.
Antipsychotics do not agonise muscarinic receptors; anticholinergic activity would reduce, not cause, EPS.
questions.why: Blocking D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway disrupts the dopamine and acetylcholine balance, causing extrapyramidal effects. Anticholinergics such as benztropine treat acute dystonia.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had 6 months of amenorrhoea, hot flushes and vaginal dryness. Pregnancy test is negative and FSH is 68 IU/L on two samples 4 weeks apart. She has no contraindications. What is the best management?
options: Short-course menopausal hormone therapy for 12 months, then cease and reassess symptoms
Bisphosphonate for bone protection and reassurance
Menopausal hormone therapy until about the age of natural menopause
No hormonal treatment because of breast cancer risk
notes: Stopping early leaves years of oestrogen deficiency, with bone and cardiovascular risk.
Bisphosphonates do not treat symptoms and are not appropriate in young women; oestrogen is the bone therapy.
Breast cancer risk concerns do not apply to replacement in POI, where benefits clearly outweigh risks.
questions.why: This is premature ovarian insufficiency. Replacing oestrogen until about age 50–51 protects bone and cardiovascular health; the breast risk applies to older women, not replacement here.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman reports a childhood rash after amoxicillin, with no airway symptoms and no recent reaction. She needs treatment for cellulitis. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Penicillin allergy assessment; flucloxacillin is likely safe if low risk
Avoid all beta-lactam antibiotics for life and document a penicillin allergy label
Give cefalexin only, as cephalosporins are always safe
Give vancomycin as the first-line option
notes: Lifelong avoidance is unnecessary for low-risk histories and drives worse outcomes.
Cross-reactivity depends on side chain; cephalosporins are not always safe, and this is not required here.
Vancomycin is inferior for MSSA and unnecessary in low-risk history.
questions.why: A remote benign rash is low risk; most such labels are not true allergy. Risk-stratify (eg PEN-FAST) and consider direct challenge or delabelling per eTG/ASCIA.

questions.stem: Which mechanism explains why opioids such as morphine relieve dyspnoea and pain in palliative care?
options: Agonism at mu-opioid receptors reducing perceived pain and air hunger
Blockade of NMDA receptors in the spinal cord only
Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase reducing prostaglandin synthesis
Antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
notes: NMDA antagonism is ketamine's action, not morphine's.
COX inhibition is the NSAID mechanism.
D2 antagonism is how haloperidol and metoclopramide work as antiemetics.
questions.why: Morphine is a mu-opioid receptor agonist; central action reduces the perception of pain and breathlessness.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with first-episode psychosis in an emergency department in Victoria refuses admission, believing he is well. He has persecutory delusions and has threatened to harm his mother. Which is the most appropriate step?
options: Assess against involuntary treatment criteria under the Mental Health Act
Discharge him with community follow-up, as he has refused voluntary treatment
Seek a court order for guardianship
Ask his mother to consent on his behalf
notes: Refusal does not prevent involuntary assessment when criteria are met and there is risk to others.
Guardianship applies to long-term incapacity decisions, not acute psychiatric treatment orders.
A relative cannot consent to involuntary treatment for a competent adult; the Act provides the pathway.
questions.why: Involuntary treatment criteria require mental illness, need for immediate treatment, risk of serious harm and no less restrictive option. A psychiatrist assesses and makes an order under the state Mental Health Act.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has 3 months of fatigue. Examination is normal. Which initial investigation set is most appropriate?
options: FBC, ferritin, TSH, glucose, UEC, LFT and coeliac serology
Morning cortisol with ACTH stimulation test and pituitary hormone profile
notes: Imaging isn't indicated without localising features.
Adrenal testing is for suggestive features, not first line.
No serology panel diagnoses chronic fatigue; it is a clinical diagnosis after exclusions.
questions.why: Initial fatigue workup is guided by history and includes FBC, ferritin, TSH, glucose, renal and liver function, and consider coeliac serology. Screen for depression, sleep and medication causes too.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has had 5 days of fever, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, rash and cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days with outpatient review
notes: Antibiotics are not effective; the cause is not bacterial infection.
Steroids alone are not standard first line; they may be adjuncts in high-risk cases.
Aspirin alone does not prevent coronary aneurysms; IVIG is essential.
questions.why: Complete Kawasaki disease is treated with single-dose IVIG 2 g/kg, ideally within 10 days of onset, plus aspirin, to reduce coronary aneurysm risk. Echocardiography is also required.

questions.stem: A patient stable on warfarin starts rifampicin for tuberculosis. Which effect on warfarin is expected, through what mechanism?
options: Raised INR from CYP2C9 inhibition reducing hepatic warfarin clearance
Lowered INR from CYP induction increasing warfarin metabolism
Raised INR from displacement from albumin only
Unchanged INR because warfarin is renally cleared
notes: Rifampicin induces rather than inhibits CYP2C9.
Protein displacement is minor and rifampicin does not act this way.
Warfarin is hepatically metabolised, not renally cleared.
questions.why: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of CYP enzymes (including CYP2C9 and 3A4), speeding warfarin clearance and lowering the INR. Dose requirements rise and the effect persists after stopping.

questions.stem: Adenosine terminates AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia. What is its mechanism of action?
options: Blocks L-type calcium channels in the AV node, slowing nodal conduction
Opens potassium channels, causing transient AV nodal block
Blocks fast sodium channels in the His-Purkinje system
Blocks beta-1 receptors in the AV node
notes: That is the mechanism of verapamil, not adenosine.
Sodium channel blockers (class I) act mainly on atrial and ventricular tissue, not the AV node.
That is the mechanism of beta-blockers such as metoprolol, which act longer than adenosine.
questions.why: Adenosine acts on A1 receptors to open K+ channels, hyperpolarising the AV node and briefly blocking conduction, which breaks the re-entry circuit. Its half-life is under 10 seconds.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old presents 6 hours after ingesting 20 g of immediate-release paracetamol in a single acute ingestion. She is asymptomatic. The 4-hour level was 1.4 times above the treatment line... Actually the 4-hour level is not available; the level taken now is above the nomogram treatment line. What is the next step?
options: Repeat level at 8 hours before deciding
Await liver function tests before treating
notes: Delay is unnecessary when the level is already above the line.
Charcoal alone is inadequate when treatment criteria are met.
LFTs are normal early and must not delay treatment.
questions.why: A level above the Australian treatment line (150 mg/L at 4 h) after a single acute ingestion warrants acetylcysteine without waiting for LFTs. Start promptly.

questions.stem: Which spirometry finding after bronchodilator confirms airflow limitation in COPD?
options: FEV1 increase of more than 12% and 200 mL
notes: A normal or high ratio with low FVC suggests restriction, not obstruction.
Raised DLCO is not diagnostic of COPD; emphysema typically lowers it.
Marked reversibility suggests asthma, and COPD is defined by incomplete reversibility.
questions.why: Persistent airflow limitation is a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 (COPD-X uses this). A restrictive pattern has a normal or high ratio.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains why finasteride reduces prostate volume?
options: Blocks alpha-1A receptors on prostatic and bladder neck smooth muscle
Inhibits conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone
notes: That is tamsulosin, which relaxes smooth muscle without shrinking the gland.
Androgen receptor antagonists such as bicalutamide are used in prostate cancer.
LH suppression is by GnRH agonists used in prostate cancer.
questions.why: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors block conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, shrinking the gland over months and lowering PSA by about half.

questions.stem: In acute ischaemic stroke, a region of brain with reduced blood flow but still viable and potentially salvageable by reperfusion is called which of the following?
notes: The core is irreversibly infarcted tissue with severely reduced flow; reperfusion cannot save it.
Watershed zones lie between arterial territories and are vulnerable to hypotension; this is a location, not salvageable tissue.
Luxury perfusion is hyperaemia of infarcted tissue after reperfusion; it is not salvageable penumbra.
questions.why: The penumbra is hypoperfused, functionally impaired but viable tissue surrounding the core. Reperfusion therapies (thrombolysis, clot retrieval) aim to save it; CT perfusion mismatch identifies it.

questions.stem: Which mechanism most commonly confers resistance to cefalexin and ceftriaxone in E. coli causing community UTI?
options: Efflux of drug via tetracycline pumps
Modification of the ribosomal binding site
notes: PBP2a alteration underlies MRSA, not Gram-negative cephalosporin resistance.
Tetracycline efflux does not explain cephalosporin resistance.
Ribosomal modification affects macrolides and aminoglycosides, not cephalosporins.
questions.why: ESBLs hydrolyse third-generation cephalosporins and penicillins in Enterobacterales; carbapenems (e.g. meropenem) are usually needed for serious infection. PBP2a (mecA) is a staphylococcal mechanism.

questions.stem: Warfarin impairs synthesis of which group of clotting factors by inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase?
notes: Factors I, V, VIII and XIII are not vitamin K dependent.
Factors VIII, XI and XII are not vitamin K dependent; this mixes intrinsic pathway factors.
Factors V and XI are not vitamin K dependent.
questions.why: Vitamin K is needed for gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S). Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, so these become inactive.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has 8 months of excessive worry, restlessness and poor sleep, diagnosed as generalised anxiety disorder. She has no other conditions. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Long-term diazepam 5 mg daily with regular review
notes: Benzodiazepines risk tolerance and dependence and are not recommended long term.
Antipsychotics are not first-line for GAD.
Beta-blockers may ease somatic symptoms but do not treat GAD.
questions.why: Psychological therapy, particularly CBT, is first-line for GAD in Australian guidelines. An SSRI or SNRI is added if therapy is unavailable or insufficient; benzodiazepines are avoided or limited to short use.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has pneumonia with a CORB score of 2 (confusion, respiratory rate 32), so it is moderate to severe. What empirical antibiotic regimen does eTG recommend?
options: Benzylpenicillin IV plus doxycycline or azithromycin
Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily alone for 5 days
notes: Oral amoxicillin alone suits mild CAP and gives no atypical cover.
Doxycycline alone is for mild CAP, not for a moderate case needing IV therapy.
Gentamicin alone has poor pneumococcal activity.
questions.why: Moderate CAP in eTG is treated with IV benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline or azithromycin for atypical cover. Severe cases need broader cover.

questions.stem: Strongyloides stercoralis can persist for decades after leaving an endemic area and cause hyperinfection with immunosuppression. What life-cycle feature explains this?
options: Autoinfection by larvae penetrating gut mucosa or perianal skin
Encystment of adult worms within skeletal muscle, persisting for decades
Egg shedding that reinfects through faecal-oral spread
notes: Muscle encystment describes Trichinella, not Strongyloides.
Strongyloides eggs hatch in the gut; larvae, not eggs, are passed and infect via skin.
Hydatid cysts are due to Echinococcus.
questions.why: Rhabditiform larvae mature into filariform larvae in the gut and reinvade, perpetuating infection. Corticosteroids can drive hyperinfection, so screen and treat before immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily. He needs elective cataract-unrelated hernia repair (low bleeding risk) with eGFR 70 mL/min. What is the most appropriate peri-procedural plan?
options: Withhold apixaban for 24 hours before; no bridging
Withhold apixaban for 5 days before; bridge with enoxaparin
Continue apixaban and give vitamin K the night before
Change to warfarin 5 days before the procedure
notes: Five days is for warfarin, and bridging is not needed with DOACs.
Vitamin K does not reverse DOACs and continuing them raises bleeding risk.
Switching to warfarin adds delay and risk without benefit.
questions.why: For low-bleeding-risk procedures with preserved renal function, omit the DOAC for about 24 hours (one dose-free day). DOACs need no bridging because of their rapid offset.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old at 32 weeks has BP 170/112 mmHg, severe headache, visual disturbance and brisk reflexes with clonus. Urine protein is 3+. Which drug is given to prevent eclampsia?
options: Diazepam 10 mg IV given slowly over several minutes
notes: Diazepam is inferior to magnesium for eclampsia and sedates mother and baby.
Phenytoin is less effective than magnesium sulfate for eclampsia.
Levetiracetam is not first-line for eclampsia prevention.
questions.why: Magnesium sulfate (4 g IV load then 1 g/h) is first-line to prevent and treat eclamptic seizures in severe pre-eclampsia. Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output.

questions.stem: Under the National Lung Cancer Screening Program, which asymptomatic person is eligible for low-dose CT screening?
options: A 62-year-old current smoker with a 35 pack-year history
A 45-year-old current smoker with a 30 pack-year history
A 66-year-old who quit 25 years ago with 40 pack-years
A 72-year-old current smoker with a 50 pack-year history
notes: Age 45 is below the 50–70 eligible range.
Quitting more than 10 years ago makes this person ineligible.
Age 72 is above the upper limit of 70.
questions.why: Eligibility is age 50–70, asymptomatic, at least 30 pack-years, and currently smoking or quit within the past 10 years. LDCT is offered every 2 years.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old Aboriginal child from a remote community has haematuria, periorbital oedema and hypertension 2 weeks after skin sores. Complement C3 is low. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: IgA nephropathy presenting with macroscopic haematuria after infection
notes: IgA nephropathy causes haematuria concurrent with infection (1–2 days), with normal C3.
Minimal change gives nephrotic syndrome without haematuria and with normal C3.
ARF follows streptococcal infection with carditis or arthritis, not nephritic syndrome.
questions.why: Post-streptococcal GN follows Group A Streptococcus skin infection after 2–3 weeks, with nephritic features and low C3. Skin sore control is the key preventive measure.

questions.stem: Ross River virus causes a polyarthritis in adults. Which mechanism best explains the joint symptoms?
options: Viral replication in synovial macrophages with an inflammatory immune response
Immune complex deposition in synovium two to three weeks after streptococcal infection
Urate crystal deposition in the joint
Direct bacterial invasion of the synovial space
notes: This describes acute rheumatic fever.
This describes gout.
Ross River is a virus, not a bacterium.
questions.why: Ross River virus, an alphavirus, infects macrophages in synovium and muscle, causing inflammatory arthritis and myalgia that can last months.

questions.stem: Which mechanism explains how an SGLT2 inhibitor such as empagliflozin lowers blood glucose and reduces the risk of heart failure hospitalisation?
options: Reduced proximal tubular glucose reabsorption causing glycosuria and natriuresis
Reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis via AMPK activation and improved insulin sensitivity
Delayed gastric emptying and suppressed glucagon release
notes: This describes sulfonylureas (and partly GLP-1 RAs); SGLT2 inhibitors act independently of insulin.
This describes metformin's main action, not SGLT2 inhibition.
This describes GLP-1 receptor agonists, not SGLT2 inhibitors.
questions.why: SGLT2 in the proximal tubule reabsorbs most filtered glucose; blocking it causes glycosuria with osmotic diuresis and natriuresis, lowering preload and intraglomerular pressure.

questions.stem: Which bruising site in a 6-month-old non-mobile infant is most concerning for non-accidental injury?
notes: Shins are common accidental sites in walking children.
Forehead bruises are common with falls.
Bony prominences are typical accidental sites.
questions.why: Bruising on the ears, neck, torso, buttocks or in a non-mobile infant is concerning. Shins, forehead and bony prominences are typical sites of accidental bruising in mobile children.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, not using contraception, is stable on sodium valproate. She wants to conceive. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Continue valproate at the current dose and add folic acid 5 mg daily only
Stop it abruptly now and use no mood stabiliser
Plan a switch to a safer alternative before conception
Valproate is safe if kept below 1000 mg daily
notes: Folate does not remove the risk.
Abrupt cessation risks relapse; switch should be planned and supervised.
Risk is dose-related but there is no safe dose.
questions.why: Valproate is highly teratogenic (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental disorders) and should be avoided in women of childbearing potential. Plan a gradual switch before conception, with contraception meanwhile.

questions.stem: A woman at 8 weeks' gestation has MCV 66 fL, normal ferritin and HbA2 5.2%. Her partner's carrier status is unknown. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Offer partner testing with FBE and haemoglobin studies
Start oral iron 100 mg daily and repeat the FBE and ferritin in 3 months
notes: Iron is not indicated with normal ferritin.
Her baby may be severely affected if the partner is a carrier.
Prenatal diagnosis is premature before partner status is known.
questions.why: Raised HbA2 indicates beta-thalassaemia trait. Test the partner promptly; if also a carrier, offer genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which feature best explains why chronic lymphocytic leukaemia often causes hypogammaglobulinaemia and recurrent infections?
options: Accumulation of dysfunctional clonal mature B cells that fail to make effective antibody
Excess T-cell suppression of neutrophil production
Loss of complement components from chronic haemolysis
notes: Neutropenia may occur from marrow infiltration, but T-cell suppression is not the main mechanism of the infection risk.
Autoimmune haemolysis can occur in CLL, but it does not explain hypogammaglobulinaemia.
The thymus is not destroyed in CLL.
questions.why: CLL is a clonal expansion of mature, functionally incompetent B cells, so normal plasma cell antibody production falls. Recurrent bacterial infections follow.

questions.stem: In tension pneumothorax, which mechanism is the main cause of cardiovascular collapse?
options: Direct compression of the coronary arteries by the expanding pleural air collection
Reduced venous return from raised intrathoracic pressure
Primary left ventricular failure from hypoxia
notes: Coronary compression is not the mechanism.
Hypoxia contributes, but obstructive shock from reduced preload dominates.
No pericardial fluid is present; this is obstructive shock but not tamponade.
questions.why: A one-way valve traps air, raising intrathoracic pressure and mediastinal shift, kinking the great veins and cutting venous return and cardiac output. Hypoxia contributes but is not the primary cause.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with heavy alcohol use presents with jaundice, fever and tender hepatomegaly. Bilirubin is 250 µmol/L, INR 2.0, AST 180 U/L, ALT 70 U/L. Infection is excluded and Maddrey score is 45. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Intravenous N-acetylcysteine infusion alone over 72 hours with supportive care
notes: NAC alone is not standard treatment for alcoholic hepatitis.
TIPS is for portal hypertension complications, not this.
UDCA has no proven benefit and is not used.
questions.why: Severe alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey ≥32) without infection or GI bleed is treated with prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days, plus nutrition and abstinence support. Lille score assesses response.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man arrives after a motorcycle crash, talking in short sentences. He has absent breath sounds on the right, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation and BP 70/40. What is the immediate management?
options: Urgent supine chest X-ray to confirm the side before any intervention
Needle or finger decompression of the right chest
notes: Delaying for imaging risks cardiac arrest.
Positive pressure ventilation without decompression worsens tension physiology.
Pericardiocentesis is for tamponade; here breath sounds are absent with tracheal deviation.
questions.why: This is tension pneumothorax, a clinical diagnosis. Immediate decompression (finger thoracostomy or needle) then intercostal catheter; do not wait for imaging.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with myasthenia gravis, a day after starting ciprofloxacin, has dysphagia, a weak cough and a falling forced vital capacity. What is the best management?
options: Admit to ICU, stop ciprofloxacin, and give IVIG or plasma exchange
Increase pyridostigmine to 60 mg six-hourly at home and review in clinic in a week
Start high-dose prednisolone alone as an outpatient
notes: Outpatient care is unsafe with bulbar and respiratory involvement.
Steroids alone can transiently worsen weakness and act too slowly.
Aminoglycosides also worsen myasthenia gravis.
questions.why: This is myasthenic crisis precipitated by a fluoroquinolone. Secure the airway with close FVC monitoring in ICU, remove the trigger and give IVIG or plasma exchange.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has headaches, itching after hot showers and a ruddy face. Haemoglobin is 205 g/L, haematocrit 0.62, platelets 520 x10^9/L, neutrophils raised. Serum erythropoietin is low. What is the most appropriate next test?
options: JAK2 V617F mutation analysis on peripheral blood
BCR-ABL1 PCR on peripheral blood, with repeat full blood count in four weeks
Bone marrow biopsy for ringed sideroblasts
notes: BCR-ABL1 is for CML; it is not the first test for erythrocytosis with low erythropoietin.
Carbon monoxide causes secondary polycythaemia with normal or high erythropoietin, and would not explain pruritus and thrombocytosis.
Ringed sideroblasts suggest myelodysplasia, not PV.
questions.why: Raised haemoglobin/haematocrit with low erythropoietin suggests polycythaemia vera; JAK2 V617F is present in over 95%. Test JAK2 first (exon 12 if negative).

questions.stem: A 22-year-old footballer collapses in a hot summer match. He is confused, core temperature 42°C, HR 140, BP 100/60. After airway and IV access, what is the most effective immediate treatment?
options: Rapid cooling by cold water immersion
Tepid water sponging with a fan, aiming to lower temperature over several hours
notes: Antipyretics act on the hypothalamic set point and are ineffective in heat stroke.
Dantrolene has no proven benefit in heat stroke.
Tepid sponging is too slow for exertional heat stroke; rapid cooling lowers mortality.
questions.why: Exertional heat stroke needs immediate rapid cooling, ideally cold or ice-water immersion, aiming to cool below 39°C quickly. Antipyretics and dantrolene do not work.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting. Which finding best confirms the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
options: Serum lipase greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal
Serum amylase above the upper limit of normal on two samples taken 6 hours apart
notes: Amylase is less specific and any mild elevation is not diagnostic.
ALP is a cholestatic marker, not diagnostic.
CRP is a nonspecific severity marker.
questions.why: Diagnosis requires two of three: typical pain, lipase (or amylase) >3 times the upper limit, and imaging findings. Lipase is more specific than amylase.

questions.stem: In septic shock, which mechanism best explains the profound hypotension despite a normal or high cardiac output early on?
options: Cytokine-mediated vasodilation and increased capillary permeability
Primary failure of the sinoatrial node
Adrenal overproduction of catecholamines causing widespread peripheral vasodilation
Direct bacterial toxin blockade of cardiac calcium channels
notes: The SA node is not the primary problem; tachycardia is typical in early sepsis.
Catecholamines cause vasoconstriction; relative adrenal insufficiency, not excess, may occur.
Myocardial depression may occur later but is not the main cause of early hypotension.
questions.why: Endotoxin and cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) induce nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation and endothelial leak, lowering systemic vascular resistance and effective volume (distributive shock).

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has pneumonia. BP is 78/40 mmHg, lactate 5.2 mmol/L. She has received 30 mL/kg crystalloid and remains hypotensive with a MAP of 55 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give a further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus
Give IV hydrocortisone as the sole therapy
notes: Repeated large boluses risk overload; vasopressors are indicated after initial resuscitation.
Dopamine is not first-line and is more arrhythmogenic than noradrenaline.
Steroids are adjunctive for ongoing vasopressor need, not sole therapy.
questions.why: Fluid-refractory septic shock needs a vasopressor, with noradrenaline first-line, targeting MAP of at least 65 mmHg. Continue antibiotics and source control.

questions.stem: A man returns from Papua New Guinea with fever. The thick film is positive, but parasitaemia must be quantified and species identified. Which film is best for identifying species and calculating percentage parasitaemia?
notes: The thick film is for sensitivity, not species or percentage.
Gram stain does not identify malaria.
Bone marrow is unnecessary.
questions.why: The thick film is more sensitive for detecting parasites, while the thin film shows red cell morphology for species identification and percent parasitaemia. A rapid antigen test or PCR supports this.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man born in Vietnam has chronic hepatitis B with compensated cirrhosis. What surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma is recommended?
options: Liver ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months
Annual multiphase CT of the abdomen with contrast, plus AFP at each visit
notes: Annual CT is too infrequent and involves radiation.
AFP alone is insensitive and 12 months is too long.
Biopsy is not a surveillance tool.
questions.why: Australian guidelines recommend 6-monthly ultrasound (with or without AFP) for people with cirrhosis and for many with hepatitis B from higher-risk groups.

questions.stem: Which process mainly explains the large fluid shift in the first 24 hours after a major burn?
options: Increased capillary permeability with loss of plasma into interstitium
Excessive renal sodium and water loss through osmotic diuresis in the first day
notes: Renal losses are not the main cause of early burn shock.
GI bleeding is a late complication, not the main early shift.
ADH is typically raised, not reduced, after burns.
questions.why: Inflammatory mediators increase capillary permeability, causing plasma and protein loss into tissue, hypovolaemia and oedema. Fluid resuscitation replaces this.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old hypertensive man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. BP is 200/110 mmHg. CT angiography shows a dissection of the ascending aorta. After analgesia and heart rate and BP control, what is the definitive management?
notes: Medical therapy alone is for uncomplicated type B dissection.
Thrombolysis is contraindicated and would be fatal.
Delay is unacceptable; type A needs immediate surgery.
questions.why: Acute type A dissection is a surgical emergency with high mortality. Meanwhile give IV beta-blockade (e.g. esmolol or labetalol) targeting HR below 60 and systolic BP 100–120 mmHg.

questions.stem: A patient on chemotherapy has an absolute neutrophil count of 0.2 x10^9/L. Which defence mechanism is mainly lost, making rapid bacterial sepsis the main risk?
notes: Antibody production is a B-cell function and is not primarily affected by neutropenia.
Complement is a plasma protein system and is unaffected by a low neutrophil count.
Cytotoxic T and NK cells handle virus-infected cells; they are not neutrophils.
questions.why: Neutrophils are the main phagocytes that ingest and kill bacteria and fungi. Their loss allows rapid bacteraemia, often with few localising signs.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old agitated man in the ED is threatening staff. Verbal de-escalation has failed and oral medication is refused. Before sedating, which action is most important?
options: Exclude hypoglycaemia with a bedside glucose
Obtain a CT brain to exclude intracranial injury before any sedation is given
Wait for urine drug screen result to confirm the intoxicant before sedating
Obtain psychiatric review and a formal capacity assessment before any sedation
notes: CT may be needed later but not before sedating and would delay care.
Drug screens are slow and rarely change immediate management.
Psychiatric review follows medical assessment and should not precede it.
questions.why: Rapidly reversible medical causes such as hypoglycaemia must be excluded early in acute behavioural disturbance, with bedside glucose and observations, without delaying needed safe sedation.

questions.stem: A woman has a breast cancer in the upper outer quadrant. To which lymph node group does most of the breast's lymph drain, making it the first site of spread?
notes: Receives a smaller share, mainly from medial and central tumours; not the main first station.
Supraclavicular nodes are a higher, later echelon; involvement indicates advanced disease.
Contralateral drainage is an uncommon route of late spread.
questions.why: About 75% of breast lymph drains to the axillary nodes, so the sentinel node is usually axillary. Internal mammary drainage is more relevant to medial tumours.

questions.stem: A woman at 8 weeks has bleeding and cramping. Ultrasound shows an intrauterine embryo with a crown–rump length of 8 mm and no fetal heartbeat. The cervical os is closed. What is the diagnosis?
notes: Threatened miscarriage has a viable pregnancy with a heartbeat.
Incomplete miscarriage means some products have been passed; here the embryo is still in situ with a closed os.
An intrauterine embryo is seen, so ectopic is not the diagnosis.
questions.why: A CRL of 7 mm or more with no heartbeat confirms embryonic demise. With the embryo retained and the os closed, this is a missed (delayed) miscarriage.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy has episodic inconsolable crying with drawing up of legs, pallor between episodes and a redcurrant jelly stool. Which test is the investigation of choice?
notes: X-ray is insensitive and may be normal; it is not the best test.
Used for malrotation, not intussusception.
Gastroenteritis does not explain colicky pain with redcurrant jelly stool and delays diagnosis.
questions.why: This is intussusception; ultrasound shows the target or doughnut sign and is the preferred diagnostic test. Treatment is by air enema reduction if stable.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with COPD has had 24 hours of fever, myalgia and cough. She tests positive for influenza A on PCR and is hypoxic on arrival to hospital. What is the most appropriate antiviral management?
options: Oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, started now
No antiviral therapy, as she presented more than 24 hours after symptom onset
Oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days, only if chest x-ray shows pneumonia
Oral nirmatrelvir with ritonavir for 5 days, started within 5 days of symptom onset
notes: She is within 48 hours and is also hospitalised, so treatment is indicated.
Treatment does not depend on radiological pneumonia.
Nirmatrelvir with ritonavir is for COVID-19, not influenza.
questions.why: Hospitalised patients with influenza should receive oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days (adjusted for renal function) as soon as possible, without waiting for confirmation.

questions.stem: Which study design is best suited to investigating the cause of a rare disease, by comparing past exposures in affected and unaffected people?
notes: Cohorts follow exposed people forward and need huge numbers for rare outcomes.
Cross-sectional surveys measure prevalence at one time and cannot establish past exposure well.
RCTs test interventions and are impractical for investigating harmful exposures.
questions.why: Case-control studies start with outcome and look back at exposure, so they are efficient for rare diseases. They give odds ratios.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents after a suspected methanol ingestion with visual blurring, HCO3 10 mmol/L and a high anion gap. Which treatment is most appropriate, after calling the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26)?
options: Activated charcoal alone, given within one hour of ingestion via nasogastric tube
Naloxone infusion titrated to respiratory rate and conscious state
Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV, repeated up to a maximum of 1 mg as needed
notes: Charcoal does not bind alcohols effectively.
Naloxone reverses opioids, not toxic alcohols.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and is not relevant here.
questions.why: Methanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formic acid. Fomepizole blocks this enzyme; haemodialysis is used for severe acidosis, visual symptoms or high levels.

questions.stem: Which structure normally acts as the dominant pacemaker of the heart because it has the fastest rate of spontaneous phase 4 depolarisation?
notes: The AV node's intrinsic rate is slower (about 40-60/min); it is an escape pacemaker only if the SA node fails.
The His bundle has a slower intrinsic rate and is only a subsidiary pacemaker.
Purkinje fibres fire at about 20-40/min and are the last-resort escape focus.
questions.why: The SA node has the steepest phase 4 slope (about 60-100 beats/min) and overdrives slower subsidiary pacemakers. If it fails, lower pacemakers take over at slower rates.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old private car driver is diagnosed with moderate obstructive sleep apnoea and excessive daytime sleepiness. According to Austroads principles, what is the most appropriate advice?
options: Do not drive until treated and sleepiness is controlled, with review
Continue driving as normal, with no need to notify the licensing authority
Stop driving permanently and surrender the licence to the licensing authority
Drive only at night when traffic is lighter and fewer hazards are present
notes: Sleepiness significantly raises crash risk; driving should stop until controlled.
Permanent restriction isn't needed if treatment works.
Night driving is no safer; sleepiness is the issue.
questions.why: Untreated OSA with excessive sleepiness is a conditional licence matter: stop driving until treated effectively and sleepiness is controlled, then review. It is not permanent.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has permanent AF with a mechanical mitral valve. Her GP considers a DOAC for stroke prevention. Which anticoagulant is appropriate?
notes: DOACs are not recommended with mechanical valves.
DOACs are not recommended with mechanical valves.
Dabigatran increased thromboembolism and bleeding in mechanical valves.
questions.why: Mechanical valves require warfarin. DOACs are contraindicated (dabigatran was inferior and harmful in the RE-ALIGN trial).

questions.stem: Why are febrile infants under 3 months at higher risk of serious bacterial infection and meningitis than older children?
options: Immature cell-mediated and humoral immunity with poor localising signs
Maternal IgG levels peak at this age and then begin to fall sharply
Fever is a poor marker of infection at this age, as most febrile infants are well
Higher gastric pH kills fewer bacteria, allowing more ingested pathogens to colonise
notes: Maternal IgG falls after birth, reaching a nadir around 3-4 months.
Fever is a significant marker; any fever of 38.0°C or more needs assessment.
Gastric pH is a minor factor; it is not the main reason.
questions.why: Neonatal and young infant immunity is immature (reduced opsonisation, neutrophil function), and signs are non-specific, so infection can disseminate silently.

questions.stem: Which HPV type pair accounts for the majority of cervical squamous cell carcinomas and is reported individually by the Australian cervical screening test?
