questions.stem: A 30-year-old asymptomatic woman has anaemia found on routine testing. Examination shows scleral icterus and splenomegaly. Her family has a history of early-onset gallstones. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: G6PD deficiency causes episodic haemolysis triggered by drugs, infection or fava beans, none mentioned here.
Thalassaemia minor causes microcytosis with mild anaemia, usually without jaundice or splenomegaly.
Pyruvate kinase deficiency is rarer and usually presents with more severe haemolysis earlier in life.
questions.why: Chronic haemolysis (anaemia, jaundice, splenomegaly) with pigment gallstones at a young age in the family fits hereditary spherocytosis, which can stay asymptomatic until adulthood.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 18-month-old boy presents with right knee swelling after playing in the park, with no obvious trauma. The mother's uncle had similar problems. Ultrasound shows haemarthrosis. The only abnormality on blood tests is a prolonged APTT of 52 seconds (normal 25–35). What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder with normal coagulation tests.
Von Willebrand disease typically causes mucosal or post-surgical/trauma bleeding, and is less often with haemarthrosis in an X-linked pattern.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a connective tissue disorder with normal coagulation tests.
questions.why: Spontaneous haemarthrosis in a young boy, an affected maternal relative (X-linked) and isolated prolonged APTT indicate haemophilia A.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient reports several months of tongue enlargement without other tongue changes, causing him to bite it constantly. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Hypoglossal palsy causes tongue deviation and atrophy, not enlargement.
Hyperthyroidism does not typically cause macroglossia (hypothyroidism can).
Mastocytosis causes skin lesions and mediator symptoms, not macroglossia.
questions.why: Amyloidosis is deposition of fibrillar protein, localised or systemic. Amyloid deposits in the tongue can cause macroglossia, with the kidneys and heart most often affected.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 29-year-old patient is diagnosed with severe aplastic anaemia. A fully HLA-matched sibling is available. What is the treatment of choice?
options: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant from the matched sibling
notes: Supportive care only bridges the problem and does not treat the marrow failure.
Autologous transplant is unsuitable because the patient's own marrow is aplastic and cannot provide healthy stem cells.
Immunosuppression is used when no matched donor exists or the patient is older, not first-line here.
questions.why: In younger patients (under about 40) with severe aplastic anaemia and a matched sibling donor, allogeneic stem cell transplant is first-line because it can cure the disease.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman fears stroke as her mother died of one. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes on gliclazide, aspirin, enalapril and atorvastatin, smokes 20 cigarettes daily and is sedentary. BP 150/80 mmHg, HbA1c 64 mmol/mol, LDL 2.8 mmol/L. Which action gives the greatest stroke risk reduction?
notes: Tighter glycaemic control mainly reduces microvascular disease, with a smaller effect on stroke.
Smoking cessation lowers risk, but the effect is smaller than treating blood pressure in this age group.
Further LDL lowering reduces stroke risk modestly compared with blood pressure control.
questions.why: Hypertension is the most influential modifiable risk factor for stroke, particularly in older women, and blood pressure lowering gives the largest stroke risk reduction.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with a BMI of 38 kg/m² has been obese since age 17. Despite a supervised 1500 kcal diet and 4 hours of aerobic exercise weekly she has lost 3 kg and needs 7 kg more. Which drug would reduce dietary fat absorption?
notes: Topiramate is an anticonvulsant that causes weight loss through appetite suppression. It does not affect fat absorption.
Liraglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. It reduces appetite and slows gastric emptying and does not block fat absorption.
Metformin is a glucose-lowering drug with modest weight effects. It does not reduce fat absorption and is not an anti-obesity agent.
questions.why: Orlistat inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases, so about 30% of dietary fat is not absorbed. It is the anti-obesity drug whose mechanism is reduced fat absorption.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with a previous bowel resection for mesenteric thrombosis has fatigue, bone pain and a Colles' fracture 3 months ago. Hb 95 g/L (microcytic), albumin 35 g/L, calcium 1.88 mmol/L, phosphate 0.65 mmol/L, ALP 224 U/L. Femoral X-ray shows radiolucent bands perpendicular to the inner cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Osteoporosis has normal calcium, phosphate and ALP and does not cause Looser zones.
Paget's disease has raised ALP but normal calcium and phosphate, with sclerotic and lytic bone enlargement, not hypocalcaemia.
Prostate metastases are typically sclerotic and would not explain low calcium and phosphate with Looser zones after bowel resection.
questions.why: Intestinal resection causes malabsorption and vitamin D deficiency, giving low calcium and phosphate, raised ALP, bone pain and fractures. Looser zones (pseudofractures) on X-ray are characteristic of osteomalacia.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has an asymptomatic 2 cm firm, smooth anterior neck lump that moves with swallowing, with no palpable lymphadenopathy. Which test is most useful for establishing whether the nodule is malignant?
notes: Thyroglobulin is not specific for malignancy and is used to monitor differentiated thyroid cancer after treatment.
CT is not first-line for a thyroid nodule and cannot reliably distinguish benign from malignant disease.
Antibodies support autoimmune thyroiditis but do not exclude cancer in a nodule.
questions.why: A solitary thyroid nodule needs cytology by fine needle aspiration (usually ultrasound-guided) to assess for malignancy, alongside TSH. A 2 cm nodule is above the usual size threshold for sampling.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy has brief episodes (<1 minute) of staring, unresponsiveness and blinking. EEG shows 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave discharges. What is the first-line treatment?
notes: Carbamazepine can worsen absence seizures.
Phenytoin can worsen absence seizures and is not used for them.
Gabapentin is ineffective for absence seizures and may aggravate them.
questions.why: This is typical absence epilepsy. Sodium valproate (or ethosuximide) is first line; note that valproate is avoided in females of childbearing potential.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman returned from Cuba 3 days ago. She has had fever, severe myalgia, arthralgia and headache since before her return. Now she has a generalised pruritic maculopapular rash with lower-limb petechiae. Platelets are 75 ×10⁹/L, Hct 0.36, WCC 4.1 ×10⁹/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Mononucleosis would show lymphocytosis, which is absent here.
Nothing in the picture suggests malaria, and Cuba is not a typical falciparum exposure.
Typhoid does not fit the clinical features and tropical exposure here.
questions.why: Fever, severe myalgia/arthralgia, rash and petechiae with thrombocytopenia and leukopenia after Caribbean travel indicate dengue.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 13-month-old with 48 hours of fever and no focus is well. Catheter urine shows leukocytes, blood, nitrites and Gram-negative bacilli; CRP is 50 mg/L. He is managed as an outpatient with oral antibiotics. Which empirical oral antibiotic is LEAST appropriate?
notes: Clavulanate overcomes many beta-lactamase-mediated resistances, so this is a reasonable choice for E. coli UTI.
Oral cephalosporins are good options for UTI caused by Gram-negative bacilli.
Active against most E. coli and a reasonable empirical option where local resistance is low.
questions.why: The likely organism is E. coli, and many strains are resistant to amoxicillin alone, so it is unsuitable for empirical UTI treatment.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 5-month-old in day care has had 3 days of watery stools (4/day), occasional vomiting, fever 38.3°C and coryza. He is partly breastfed, well hydrated and alert, with a 70 g weight loss. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Fast for 4 hours and rehydrate with oral rehydration solution
Introduce rice cereal for its astringent effect
Send a stool culture urgently to exclude a bacterial cause
Replace each stool's losses with oral rehydration solution and continue usual feeding
notes: Fasting is not recommended; early continued feeding is advised.
Rice cereal has no proven benefit and is a common myth.
Stool culture is not routinely needed in mild, self-limiting viral-type gastroenteritis.
questions.why: He is not dehydrated, so replace ongoing losses with oral rehydration solution after each stool and continue the usual diet, including breastfeeding. Fasting, dietary changes and routine stool culture are not needed.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl from Bangladesh has had 3 weeks of intermittent fever, weakness and anorexia. She has marked splenomegaly and pallor. Hb is 85 g/L, neutrophils 0.3 ×10⁹/L, platelets 54 ×10⁹/L, AST/ALT mildly raised, with polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Leukaemia is a differential, but polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia and endemic origin favour leishmaniasis.
Burkitt lymphoma usually presents with a rapidly growing mass, not hypergammaglobulinaemia with splenomegaly.
Miliary TB can cause cytopenias but does not typically cause massive splenomegaly with hypergammaglobulinaemia.
questions.why: Prolonged fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia in a child from an endemic area are characteristic of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 15-month-old boy suddenly develops perioral flushing, urticaria on the trunk and limbs, and cough after a bite of omelette. He is conscious, with suprasternal retraction, watery rhinorrhoea, bilateral reduced air entry without wheeze and capillary refill under 2 seconds. What is the correct management?
options: Priority is to cannulate a vein
Intramuscular methylprednisolone is the treatment of choice
Advise the parents to take him to an emergency department
notes: Adrenaline IM comes first; IV access is secondary and must not delay it.
Corticosteroids are adjuncts with slow onset and are not first-line.
Anaphylaxis is life-threatening; adrenaline must be given immediately, then transfer by ambulance.
questions.why: This is egg-induced anaphylaxis with respiratory involvement. IM adrenaline is the first-line treatment and must not be delayed; IV access, steroids and antihistamines come later.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy has brief episodes (under 1 minute) of staring and blinking, during which he does not respond when called. EEG shows generalised 3 Hz spike-wave discharges. Which drug is an appropriate first-line treatment?
notes: Carbamazepine can worsen absence seizures, so it is not used for them.
Phenytoin is not effective for absence seizures and may aggravate them.
Clonazepam is not first line because of sedation and tolerance; it is only a later adjunct.
questions.why: This is childhood absence epilepsy, shown by brief unresponsiveness with blinking and 3 Hz spike-wave on EEG. Ethosuximide and sodium valproate are the drugs of choice.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 77-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had slowly progressive memory loss for 2 years (MMSE 28/30 then, 24/30 now), including confusion with insulin doses. MRI shows diffuse posterior-predominant cortical atrophy. He has no hallucinations, behavioural change, parkinsonism or focal signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Frontotemporal dementia presents with early behavioural or language change and frontotemporal atrophy.
Vascular dementia needs evidence of cerebrovascular disease on history, examination or imaging, which is absent.
Lewy body dementia features early visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition and parkinsonism, none of which are present.
questions.why: Insidious, slowly progressive short-term memory loss with posterior cortical atrophy and no focal signs, hallucinations or behavioural change is typical of Alzheimer's disease.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A teenager presents with progressive parkinsonism, tremor, dystonia and behavioural change. Which disease should always be excluded because appropriate treatment can improve neurological symptoms and halt progression?
notes: No treatment currently stops the progression of Huntington's disease.
Sydenham's chorea follows streptococcal infection in younger children and usually resolves spontaneously.
Treatment of juvenile Parkinson's disease is symptomatic and does not stop progression.
questions.why: Wilson's disease should be excluded in young patients with movement and neuropsychiatric disorders, as copper chelation or zinc can halt and improve the course.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 87-year-old with chronic bronchitis and heart failure has acute calculous cholecystitis. After 4 days of fasting and IV piperacillin-tazobactam he still has fever, abdominal pain and leukocytosis. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Change antibiotics to ceftriaxone plus metronidazole.
Add gentamicin to the current treatment.
notes: Operative risk is prohibitive given age and cardiorespiratory comorbidity.
Piperacillin-tazobactam already gives broad cover; the problem is source control.
Adding an aminoglycoside does not address the undrained source and adds nephrotoxicity risk.
questions.why: In a frail, high-risk patient who fails medical therapy, the gallbladder source should be drained percutaneously. Changing antibiotics will not control an undrained infected gallbladder.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 40-year-old smoker with no other history has had 24 hours of rigors, fever of 39°C and productive cough. Chest X-ray shows right upper lobe alveolar consolidation, and community-acquired pneumonia is diagnosed. Which is the most common causative organism, which empirical therapy must cover?
notes: Mycoplasma is a common atypical cause, especially in younger patients, but is less frequent overall.
Legionella is a less common cause, important in severe disease or particular exposures.
H. influenzae is less common, seen more often in COPD patients.
questions.why: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia in adults and must always be covered by empirical treatment.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman has long-standing leg and arm tingling and burning at rest, worse in the evening, relieved by movement and causing insomnia, consistent with restless legs syndrome. Which statement is FALSE?
options: Diagnosis is based on clinical criteria
Iron studies, thyroid function, B12 and folate should be checked
Treatment is for sleep or quality-of-life impairment and does not alter disease course
Diagnosis is confirmed by muscle biopsy
notes: This is true; diagnosis is clinical.
This is true; secondary causes such as iron deficiency should be excluded.
This is true; treatment is symptomatic.
questions.why: Restless legs syndrome is a clinical diagnosis; muscle biopsy has no role in confirming it. Blood tests look for secondary causes such as iron deficiency.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient has impaired comprehension of spoken and written language, cannot name objects or repeat words, and speaks fluently but incomprehensibly with semantic and phonemic paraphasias. Which aphasia is this?
notes: Global aphasia has non-fluent speech as well as impaired comprehension.
Broca's aphasia has non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension.
Transcortical aphasias have preserved repetition.
questions.why: Wernicke's aphasia causes fluent speech with paraphasias and impaired comprehension, naming and repetition.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man presents with chronic diarrhoea and a history of three pneumonias in adulthood. Which immunological investigation is most appropriate?
options: Serum immunoglobulin levels and antibody response to vaccination
Neutrophil phagocytosis and oxidative burst testing
T-lymphocyte receptor repertoire and clonality studies
notes: Neutrophil oxidative burst testing assesses chronic granulomatous disease, which causes abscesses and fungal or catalase-positive infections.
Lymphocyte apoptosis testing is for autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, which does not fit this picture.
T-cell repertoire studies are for combined or T-cell immunodeficiency or lymphoproliferation, not recurrent bacterial pneumonia.
questions.why: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections with diarrhoea suggest antibody deficiency (e.g. CVID). Measure serum immunoglobulins and the specific antibody response to vaccines.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 49-year-old asymptomatic man has a father who died of prostate cancer. A routine check shows PSA 5.9 µg/L with free/total PSA ratio 11%, and DRE shows increased firmness of the right lobe. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Refer for prostate MRI and biopsy to assess for prostate cancer
Perform a CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Start a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor to halve the PSA
Start an LHRH analogue with an antiandrogen
notes: CT does not diagnose prostate cancer; staging comes only after histological confirmation.
A 5-ARI would mask the PSA rise and delay diagnosis of possible cancer.
Androgen deprivation therapy is not given without a tissue diagnosis and staging.
questions.why: Raised PSA, a low free/total ratio (<25%), an abnormal DRE and family history strongly suggest prostate cancer. Tissue diagnosis (usually after MRI, with biopsy) is required before any treatment or staging.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A woman at 40 weeks is in labour at 6 cm dilation with a decelerative CTG pattern. A fetal scalp blood sample gives pH 7.22. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Severe acidosis; proceed to urgent caesarean section.
Borderline result; repeat the scalp sample in 15–30 minutes.
Moderate acidosis; repeat the scalp sample in 1–2 hours.
Normal result; allow labour to continue without further sampling.
notes: Delivery is indicated for pH below 7.20, not 7.22.
Waiting 1–2 hours is too long with ongoing decelerations.
A pH of 7.22 is not in the normal range (above 7.25), so resampling is required.
questions.why: A fetal scalp pH of 7.20–7.25 is borderline (pre-pathological) and should be repeated within about 15–30 minutes. Below 7.20 is abnormal and needs delivery; above 7.25 is normal.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman seeks preconception advice. After cervical excision for a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, she had three second-trimester losses (20–22 weeks), each with painless 8 cm dilatation and bulging membranes. What is the best advice for her next pregnancy?
options: Elective cervical cerclage at about 14 weeks
notes: Atosiban is given intravenously and is not used as oral prophylaxis; the problem is a structurally weak cervix, not contractions.
Corticosteroids aid fetal lung maturity only when delivery is imminent and do not prevent cervical dilatation.
Successful pregnancy is achievable with cerclage, so advising against pregnancy is not warranted.
questions.why: Recurrent painless second-trimester dilatation is cervical insufficiency, with prior cervical excision as a risk factor. A planned (history-indicated) cerclage in the late first or early second trimester is the treatment.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man who injects drugs, recently released from prison, has a 10 mm Mantoux induration. His test was negative a year ago. He is asymptomatic, HIV negative, with a normal chest X-ray. What is the most appropriate management?
options: No treatment and annual chest X-ray
notes: Recent conversion carries a high risk of progression, so observation alone is inappropriate.
Four-drug therapy is for active TB, which has been excluded clinically and radiologically.
Rifampicin plus pyrazinamide is hepatotoxic and not recommended for latent TB.
questions.why: Recent tuberculin conversion with no active disease means latent TB infection in a high-risk person, so preventive therapy is indicated. Isoniazid for 6 months is a standard regimen.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has persistent allergic asthma, well controlled on daily inhaled budesonide and as-needed salbutamol. She is worried about teratogenicity. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop all asthma treatment, since asthma usually improves in pregnancy
Stop budesonide, as it increases malformation risk, and start oral montelukast
Continue current treatment and reassure her; good asthma control matters in pregnancy
Replace budesonide with omalizumab because it is safer in pregnancy
notes: Asthma control can worsen in pregnancy, and uncontrolled asthma harms mother and fetus. Stopping preventer therapy is unsafe.
Budesonide is not associated with increased malformations; it is the preferred inhaled steroid in pregnancy. Switching to montelukast gives no benefit.
Omalizumab is not a first-line change in a well-controlled patient, and biologics are not clearly safer than inhaled budesonide.
questions.why: Inhaled corticosteroids and salbutamol are safe in pregnancy. Uncontrolled asthma poses greater risk to mother and fetus than the drugs, so current treatment should continue.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman has 24 hours of left iliac fossa pain, fever and vomiting, with focal tenderness, a sense of fullness, guarding and rebound. Acute diverticulitis is suspected. Which statement is correct?
options: Barium enema is the safest and best initial investigation.
A contained pelvic abscess is managed by CT- or ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage.
Laparoscopic surgery is contraindicated for elective resection after an acute episode.
Elective sigmoidectomy is indicated after a first episode of uncomplicated diverticulitis.
notes: CT (or ultrasound) is the investigation of choice; contrast enema risks perforation in acute disease.
Laparoscopic elective resection is appropriate and commonly used.
Elective resection after a first uncomplicated episode is not routine; it is considered individually after recurrent episodes or persistent symptoms.
questions.why: Contained diverticular abscesses (typically >3-4 cm) are managed with antibiotics plus CT- or ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage, avoiding emergency surgery.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man had a truncal vagotomy and antrectomy with Billroth II reconstruction for peptic ulcer disease. Six weeks later, within 30 minutes of eating, he has nausea, sweating, dizziness, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Surgical conversion to an antiperistaltic Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy
notes: Octreotide is second-line, used when dietary measures fail.
Symptoms began after surgery and fit dumping; a carcinoid is not the likely cause.
Revisional surgery is a last resort after failure of dietary and medical therapy.
questions.why: This is early dumping syndrome after gastrectomy. First-line management is dietary: small frequent low-carbohydrate meals, separating fluids from solids. Octreotide and surgery are reserved for refractory cases.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has had a painful, swollen right knee with effusion for 24 hours, with fever 38°C. Bloods show neutrophilic leukocytosis and raised CRP. A diagnosis of acute monoarthritis is made. What is the most likely cause?
notes: Crystal arthritis can look similar but is less likely in a 19-year-old; septic arthritis must still be excluded first.
Reactive arthritis can present like this but is less common than septic arthritis and is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Mycobacterial arthritis usually has a chronic, indolent course rather than a 24-hour onset.
questions.why: A young man with acute febrile monoarthritis and raised inflammatory markers most likely has bacterial septic arthritis. It must always be excluded first because of the risk of joint destruction.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man presents with dyspnoea and haemoptysis. Creatinine is 620 µmol/L and anti-GBM antibodies are strongly positive. Renal biopsy shows crescents in 75% of glomeruli and linear immunoglobulin deposition on immunofluorescence. Which statement is correct?
options: This is IgA nephropathy with acute kidney injury.
Glomerular injury is caused by circulating immune complexes.
notes: IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits, not linear IgG.
Membranous nephropathy shows granular subepithelial deposits, not crescents with linear staining.
Injury is from antibodies binding the GBM (type II hypersensitivity), not circulating immune complexes.
questions.why: This is anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome). Treatment is plasma exchange with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man has a left renal mass suggestive of renal cell carcinoma. Bloods show raised ALT, ALP and alpha-2-globulin and a prolonged PT. The liver is diffusely enlarged with no focal infiltrative lesions. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Hepatotoxic substances secreted by the tumour (paraneoplastic)
notes: Metastases are excluded by the absence of focal infiltrative defects on imaging.
Tumour thrombus would present differently and more acutely.
Acute hepatitis does not fit the context of a renal tumour with this pattern.
questions.why: This is a paraneoplastic hepatic dysfunction (Stauffer syndrome) in renal cell carcinoma, with cholestasis, raised enzymes and prolonged PT but no infiltrative lesions.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old man has small palpable purpuric lesions over the shins. FBC, coagulation, creatinine and electrolytes are normal. Urine microscopy shows haematuria, which has been found before without a diagnosis. Regarding the likely underlying renal disease, which statement is FALSE?
options: Serum IgA is elevated in 20–50% of cases
Mesangial IgA deposits on renal biopsy are characteristic
Nephrotic-range proteinuria is the usual presentation
Most patients do not progress to renal failure
notes: True: serum IgA is raised in up to half of patients, though it is not diagnostic.
True: dominant mesangial IgA deposition is the defining biopsy finding.
True: roughly a quarter of patients progress to renal failure, so most do not.
questions.why: This is IgA nephropathy (with IgA vasculitis skin lesions). It typically presents with haematuria and a nephritic picture; nephrotic-range proteinuria is uncommon.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and stage 5 chronic kidney disease has suspected pulmonary embolism. Which investigation carries the greatest risk of further renal injury and should generally be avoided?
notes: Echocardiography uses no contrast and is safe, and can show right ventricular strain.
V/Q scanning uses no nephrotoxic contrast and is a suitable alternative in renal failure.
An ECG is non-invasive, needs no contrast and is safe.
questions.why: CT pulmonary angiography needs intravenous iodinated contrast, which risks further kidney injury in severe renal impairment. The other tests need no contrast, and V/Q scanning is a suitable alternative.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A woman presents to the emergency department with 24 hours of fever without a focus and appears severely unwell. She had a splenectomy 2 years ago for staging of Hodgkin lymphoma. Which organism is most frequently responsible?
notes: Pseudomonas is not an encapsulated organism classically associated with post-splenectomy sepsis.
Non-typhoidal Salmonella is a lesser concern in asplenia, mainly in sickle cell disease.
Pneumocystis is an opportunistic infection of cellular immunodeficiency, not asplenia.
questions.why: Asplenic patients are at risk of overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated organisms, and Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most frequent.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man has ataxia, headaches and a solid-cystic mass in the right cerebellar hemisphere. The resected lesion shows cells with long, thin cytoplasmic processes, fascicular and microcystic patterns, numerous vessels and Rosenthal fibres. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Rosenthal fibres can occur here, but the hair-like cell morphology and cerebellar location point to pilocytic astrocytoma.
Central neurocytoma is an intraventricular tumour of small uniform round cells, not a cerebellar tumour with Rosenthal fibres.
Cerebellar liponeurocytoma shows neuronal cells with lipidised cells, not hair-like processes with Rosenthal fibres.
questions.why: A young patient with a cystic cerebellar mass and bipolar hair-like cell processes with Rosenthal fibres and microcysts is characteristic of pilocytic astrocytoma.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man who has sex with men, living with HIV (CD4 above 200 cells/microlitre), volunteers at an AIDS support centre. He had Td 6 years ago, MMR in childhood and adolescence, and hepatitis B vaccine 3 years ago, with no hepatitis A immunity. Which vaccines should be recommended?
options: Influenza, pneumococcal, quadrivalent meningococcal (ACWY) and hepatitis A
Influenza, Td, pneumococcal and quadrivalent meningococcal (ACWY)
notes: Td was given only 6 years ago and is not yet due (booster at 10 years), and this option omits hepatitis A, which is indicated.
This list omits hepatitis A, which is indicated for a non-immune man who has sex with men.
Td is not yet due, and this option omits annual influenza and hepatitis A vaccination.
questions.why: Adults with HIV need annual influenza, pneumococcal and meningococcal ACWY vaccines, and hepatitis A is also indicated in men who have sex with men. Td and MMR are up to date, and hepatitis B was already given.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has had 6 months of exertional dyspnoea, without angina or syncope. Echo shows mean aortic gradient 55 mmHg, valve area 0.7 cm² and ejection fraction 65%. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Diuretics and more frequent specialist review
Percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty if dyspnoea worsens
Surgical aortic valve replacement with a prosthetic valve
notes: Medical therapy and surveillance allow ventricular decline and reduce survival.
Balloon valvuloplasty is only a bridge or palliation in patients unfit for surgery.
TAVI is for patients at high surgical risk or older; this man is 52 and suited to surgery.
questions.why: This is severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (area <1 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg), which needs valve replacement. A young, fit patient is best managed with surgical replacement.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 82-year-old hypertensive woman takes atenolol, hydrochlorothiazide and digoxin. She presents with atrial fibrillation and is given intravenous verapamil. ECG then shows complete atrioventricular block. What is the most likely cause?
options: Digoxin toxicity from a pharmacokinetic interaction with verapamil
Additive pharmacodynamic effect of beta-blocker, digoxin and verapamil on the AV node
notes: Verapamil does raise digoxin levels, but the question points to the additive nodal blockade of three drugs.
Hypokalaemia promotes ectopy and digoxin toxicity but is not the most likely cause of AV block here.
Verapamil alone is less likely to cause complete block; the combination with other nodal blockers is the cause.
questions.why: She is already on two AV nodal blocking drugs (atenolol, digoxin); adding verapamil, a third, produces an additive pharmacodynamic effect and complete AV block.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a childhood murmur presents with palpitations, fatigue, ankle oedema and mild hepatomegaly. SpO₂ is 97%. She has AF at 100 bpm, a 2/6 ejection systolic murmur at the pulmonary area, wide fixed splitting of S2, and RBBB. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: A VSD does not cause atrial dilatation, and wide fixed splitting of S2 is not a feature.
Aortic stenosis is a left-sided lesion and does not produce right heart overload or fixed splitting.
Mitral stenosis can cause AF but not fixed splitting of S2 or RBBB from a congenital murmur.
questions.why: A childhood murmur with right heart overload (RBBB, hepatomegaly, oedema), AF from atrial dilatation and wide fixed split S2 indicates an atrial septal defect.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient with signs of right-sided heart failure has ascites out of proportion to peripheral oedema. Which underlying condition is most likely?
options: Dilated cardiomyopathy with marked left ventricular dysfunction
notes: Aortic stenosis causes left-sided failure (dyspnoea, angina, syncope), not predominant ascites.
Dilated cardiomyopathy with LV dysfunction mainly produces left-sided congestion and pulmonary symptoms.
In pulmonary hypertension the tricuspid valve initially contains the pressure overload, so ascites out of proportion is less typical.
questions.why: Constrictive pericarditis raises right-sided filling pressures, causing retrograde hepatic congestion with ascites often out of proportion to oedema. Left-sided lesions do not typically present this way.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A previously healthy 10-month-old has had one day of acute gastroenteritis with mild dehydration, no blood or mucus in the stool, and is vomiting but taking small sips. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Intravenous rehydration, fast for 8 hours, then a bland diet
Low-osmolality oral rehydration solution and continue usual diet or feeds
Oral rehydration solution, usual feeds and 10 days of oral amoxicillin
Oral rehydration solution, then change to lactose-free formula
notes: IV fluids are for severe dehydration or failed oral/enteral rehydration. Fasting and a bland diet are not recommended.
Most gastroenteritis is viral; antibiotics give no benefit and are not indicated without a specific bacterial indication.
Routine lactose-free formula is unnecessary; usual feeding should continue.
questions.why: Mild dehydration in gastroenteritis is managed with oral rehydration solution given in small frequent amounts, continuing breast milk or the usual diet.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on sulfasalazine, prednisolone and etanercept presents with 72 hours of right facial herpes zoster involving the auricle, sparing the forehead, with conjunctival chemosis. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Outpatient oral aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir
notes: Untreated zoster in an immunosuppressed patient with eye involvement risks serious complications and dissemination.
Topical antivirals are ineffective for zoster.
Oral therapy suits immunocompetent patients without complications; this patient is immunosuppressed with ocular signs.
questions.why: She is immunosuppressed and has possible ocular involvement, so there is a high risk of complications. Admission for intravenous antiviral therapy is indicated.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with known cow's milk allergy accidentally ate yoghurt 5 minutes ago. He has facial angioedema, conjunctivitis, nasal congestion, hoarseness, mild hypotension, SpO2 93%, pallor, sweating and scattered wheeze. What is the first treatment of choice?
notes: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less reliable; adrenaline should be given intramuscularly.
Corticosteroids take hours to act and are not first line.
Salbutamol treats only the bronchospasm and does not treat the circulatory or airway compromise of anaphylaxis.
questions.why: This is anaphylaxis, so give intramuscular adrenaline (1 mg/mL, 0.01 mg/kg) first. It acts fastest, whereas corticosteroids take hours to work.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 1-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with 10 days of worsening jaundice. Total bilirubin is 120 µmol/L with an unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin of 26 µmol/L. What is the most likely cause?
notes: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated, so it would not give a mainly conjugated rise.
ABO haemolysis causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not mainly conjugated.
Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
questions.why: Most of the bilirubin is conjugated, so this is cholestatic jaundice beyond 2 weeks of age. Biliary atresia is the key diagnosis and the main indication for paediatric liver transplantation.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man has a pathological femoral fracture. Tests show Hb 95 g/L, total protein 110 g/L, albumin 20 g/L, beta-2 microglobulin 6 mg/L and creatinine 159 µmol/L. Which pair of tests is needed to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
options: Skeletal survey and bone marrow aspirate
Serum and urine electrophoresis and renal function tests
Bone marrow aspirate and serum and urine protein electrophoresis
notes: Bone marrow is needed, but a skeletal survey assesses disease extent rather than confirming the diagnosis; the monoclonal protein is still missing.
Electrophoresis finds the paraprotein, but there is no marrow sample to show clonal plasma cells; renal tests are for staging, not diagnosis.
Imaging stages disease and a fracture biopsy is not the standard route; the paraprotein and marrow plasma cell count are the key tests.
questions.why: This is multiple myeloma. Diagnosis needs clonal plasma cells from bone marrow and a monoclonal protein on serum and urine electrophoresis. Imaging and renal tests stage the disease and guide treatment after diagnosis.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman taking clopidogrel presents with headache, fatigue and lower limb petechiae. Hb 82 g/L, MCV 100 fL, platelets 25 ×10⁹/L, raised reticulocytes, numerous schistocytes, normal APTT, PT and fibrinogen, LDH 2700 U/L, bilirubin 44 µmol/L. Most likely diagnosis?
notes: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia without anaemia or schistocytes.
Drug-induced thrombocytopenia would not explain the haemolysis, schistocytes and raised LDH.
DIC would show prolonged clotting times and low fibrinogen. Here coagulation is normal.
questions.why: Thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic haemolysis (schistocytes, high LDH and bilirubin, reticulocytosis), neurological symptoms and normal coagulation is TTP. Thienopyridines such as ticlopidine and clopidogrel are known triggers.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man is in ICU in a coma after a road traffic accident. He has not improved neurologically after several days. CT shows punctate haemorrhagic lesions in the corpus callosum and grey-white matter junction. What is the diagnosis?
notes: A subdural would appear as a crescentic extra-axial collection, not punctate lesions.
Contusions are focal, larger cortical lesions (often frontal or temporal poles), not punctate callosal haemorrhages.
Hypoxic-ischaemic injury shows diffuse oedema and loss of grey-white differentiation, not punctate haemorrhages.
questions.why: Diffuse axonal injury causes early, sustained coma, often with a near-normal CT. When visible, there are punctate haemorrhages in the corpus callosum, grey-white junction and dorsolateral brainstem.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension and a year of cognitive decline presents with sudden aphasia and right hemiparesis. CT shows a left frontal lobar haematoma with no contrast enhancement. What is the most likely cause?
options: Arteriovenous malformation masked by acute haematoma
notes: AVMs typically present in young patients and would usually be seen on contrast imaging.
Hypertensive bleeds typically occur deep (putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum), not lobar, and his BP is well controlled.
A tumour is unlikely: no mass is seen, and enhancement would be expected.
questions.why: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is the commonest cause of spontaneous non-hypertensive lobar haemorrhage in older people, and is associated with cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has fever, weight loss, exertional dyspnoea, a new aortic diastolic murmur and peripheral emboli. Echocardiography shows a 1 cm aortic vegetation, and blood cultures grow penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus bovis. Which investigation is most appropriate next?
notes: Glucose tolerance testing has no link to S. bovis endocarditis.
A chest X-ray does not address the known association with colonic lesions.
Upper endoscopy is not the source to investigate; the association is with colonic neoplasia.
questions.why: Streptococcus bovis (gallolyticus) endocarditis is associated with colorectal neoplasia, so colonoscopy should be performed.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man has 8 months of cognitive decline, slowness and clumsy movements. His family report visual hallucinations. Low-dose risperidone was started and his motor state worsened markedly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Alzheimer's disease typically presents with early memory loss, and early hallucinations and parkinsonism are not typical.
Frontotemporal dementia presents with behavioural or language change, and visual hallucinations are not typical.
Vascular dementia has a stepwise course with focal deficits, and does not explain antipsychotic sensitivity.
questions.why: Dementia with Lewy bodies features cognitive decline, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and severe sensitivity to antipsychotics, even at low doses.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 29-year-old obese woman has had a month of severe bilateral pulsating headache, horizontal diplopia and brief episodes of monocular visual loss. Examination is normal apart from bilateral papilloedema. Which test confirms the likely diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
notes: Carotid ultrasound assesses extracranial vessels and does not diagnose raised intracranial pressure.
MRI is used to exclude a mass or venous thrombosis but cannot confirm raised CSF pressure.
EEG assesses seizure activity and has no role in diagnosing intracranial hypertension.
questions.why: This is idiopathic intracranial hypertension (obese young woman, papilloedema, VI nerve palsy diplopia). Once a mass is excluded, lumbar puncture shows raised opening pressure with normal CSF and confirms it.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic bronchitis is admitted with pneumonia and Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteraemia, penicillin-susceptible (MIC 0.0125 mg/L). He is given benzylpenicillin 2 million units 4-hourly but is still febrile (38°C) on day 5. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Change to ceftriaxone for greater efficacy
Continue the same treatment, as this is simply a matter of time
notes: Ceftriaxone offers no advantage against a fully penicillin-susceptible pneumococcus; the problem is the focus, not the drug.
Pneumococcus does not produce beta-lactamase, so clavulanic acid adds nothing.
With a susceptible organism and adequate dosing, persistent fever is not just a timing issue and suggests a complication such as empyema.
questions.why: The organism is fully susceptible and the dose adequate, so persistent fever suggests the antibiotic is not reaching the focus, most likely a pleural empyema, which needs to be excluded and drained.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with fever, cervical lymphadenopathy and a rash. Three weeks ago she had sexual exposure with a risk of HIV transmission. Which statement is correct?
options: A negative HIV antibody screening immunoassay excludes HIV infection
This presentation is not consistent with acute HIV infection
A positive screening immunoassay alone is enough to diagnose HIV infection
If the screening immunoassay is negative, HIV RNA PCR can still detect infection
notes: Serology can be negative in the window period, and no test excludes disease with certainty.
A mononucleosis-like illness is a classic presentation of acute (seroconversion) HIV infection.
A reactive screening test requires confirmatory testing before diagnosis.
questions.why: At 3 weeks she may be in the window period, when antibody-based tests can be negative despite acute infection. HIV RNA PCR can detect the virus in this setting.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy for leukaemia is admitted with pneumonia and started on cefepime. Chest imaging shows a peripheral infiltrate with a halo sign and crescentic meniscus (air-crescent). Pending biopsy results, which antimicrobial should be added?
notes: Ganciclovir treats CMV, which does not cause this radiological picture.
Caspofungin is not first-line for invasive aspergillosis; it is used as salvage or in combination.
Aspergillus is resistant to fluconazole, so it is not a valid option.
questions.why: Halo sign and air-crescent in a neutropenic chemotherapy patient suggest invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, treated with voriconazole.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes returns from overseas travel with 40°C fever, rigors, arthromyalgia and headache. Three days later he develops a maculopapular rash with lower limb petechiae, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia (91 ×10⁹/L) and markedly raised transaminases. Malaria testing is negative. Most likely diagnosis?
notes: Coronavirus infection typically causes respiratory symptoms and does not produce this thrombocytopenic, hepatitic picture.
Lymphocytic choriomeningitis mainly causes meningitis or flu-like illness after rodent exposure, not a petechial rash with marked transaminitis.
Chikungunya causes fever and severe arthralgia, but marked thrombocytopenia, petechiae and raised transaminases favour dengue.
questions.why: Fever, arthromyalgia, rash with petechiae, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases after travel, with malaria excluded, are classic for dengue. Thrombocytopenia and petechiae reflect capillary fragility.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man who has sex with men presents with fever and malaise. Two months ago he had a painless penile ulcer with bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy that resolved spontaneously. HIV is negative, RPR titre is 1:320 and TPHA titre is 1:128. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 24 MU daily for 14 days
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU intramuscularly weekly for 3 weeks
Ceftriaxone 2 g intramuscularly as a single dose
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g (2.4 MU) intramuscularly as a single dose
notes: Intravenous benzylpenicillin for 14 days is used for neurosyphilis, ocular or otic syphilis, not early syphilis without neurological features.
Three weekly doses are for late latent syphilis or syphilis of unknown duration, not early syphilis of less than 2 years.
Ceftriaxone is not first-line for syphilis and is the treatment for gonorrhoea.
questions.why: This is early (secondary) syphilis, with a prior chancre and high-titre positive nontreponemal and treponemal tests. Treatment is a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g (2.4 MU).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with fever of 38°C and right flank pain. Her white cell count is 25 × 10^9/L with a left shift, and abdominal ultrasound shows a staghorn calculus. Which organism is most likely to be isolated?
notes: E. coli does not produce urease, so it is not the typical organism in struvite stones.
Enterococcus faecalis is not a urease-splitting organism and is not classically linked to staghorn calculi.
Candida can cause urinary infection but is not urease-producing and is not linked to struvite stones.
questions.why: Staghorn (struvite) calculi are associated with urease-producing bacteria, most commonly Proteus, also Pseudomonas, Klebsiella and some staphylococci. Urease splits urea, raising urinary pH.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man, whose child has coeliac disease, has iron-deficiency anaemia and a recent increase in stool frequency. HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 are both negative. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
notes: Negative HLA-DQ2/DQ8 has a high negative predictive value, so serology is low yield.
Coeliac disease is very unlikely with negative HLA typing, so duodenal biopsy is not the priority.
A gluten-free diet trial is not indicated when coeliac disease is unlikely and cancer has not been excluded.
questions.why: Iron-deficiency anaemia with a change in bowel habit in a middle-aged man needs colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer. Negative HLA-DQ2/DQ8 makes coeliac disease very unlikely.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman drinking 60 g alcohol/day (more in the last month) has fever 38.5°C, jaundice, painful hepatomegaly, disorientation and asterixis, without ascites or peritonism. WBC 15×10⁹/L (90% neutrophils), Hb 100 g/L, MCV 115 fL, direct bilirubin 257 µmol/L, AST 300, ALT 120, GGT 635 U/L, prolonged PT. Most likely diagnosis?
notes: Cholecystitis presents with right upper quadrant pain and Murphy's sign, not encephalopathy and coagulopathy.
Cholangitis (Charcot's triad) is possible, but the alcohol history, macrocytosis, AST>ALT and encephalopathy favour alcoholic hepatitis.
Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised lipase, not hepatic failure features.
questions.why: Heavy alcohol use with fever, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, macrocytosis, neutrophilia and AST:ALT >2 with AST under 5× normal indicates acute alcoholic hepatitis.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A young patient has recurrent dysphagia to solids and liquids with repeated food bolus impactions but no heartburn. Endoscopy shows multiple concentric oesophageal rings with otherwise normal mucosa (trachealised oesophagus). What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Candida causes white plaques on the mucosa, usually with odynophagia and immunosuppression, not fixed rings.
CMV oesophagitis causes discrete ulcers in immunosuppressed patients, with odynophagia rather than rings.
Adenocarcinoma is uncommon in the young and presents as a mass or stricture, usually with long-standing reflux (Barrett oesophagus).
questions.why: Concentric rings (trachealised or feline oesophagus) with dysphagia and recurrent food impaction in a young patient are typical of eosinophilic oesophagitis. Biopsy confirms it.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman with extensive ulcerative colitis has a severe flare. She has had no improvement after one week of intravenous corticosteroids (prednisolone-equivalent 1 mg/kg). What is the next step?
options: Emergency subtotal colectomy, later completion proctectomy and ileoanal pouch
Add oral mesalazine 4 g daily and rectal corticosteroid
notes: Colectomy is for rescue failure, toxic megacolon or perforation, not the first step.
Azathioprine acts too slowly to rescue an acute severe flare.
Mesalazine and topical steroids are inadequate for a steroid-refractory severe flare.
questions.why: Severe UC not responding to full-dose IV corticosteroids needs rescue therapy with ciclosporin or infliximab. Surgery is reserved for failure of rescue therapy or complications.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A healthy 17-year-old athletic boy has occasional scleral icterus. He takes no drugs and has no abdominal pain. ALT, AST, GGT and ALP are normal; total bilirubin is 55 µmol/L, conjugated 7 µmol/L. No anaemia; liver ultrasound is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Rotor syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not an unconjugated rise.
Dubin-Johnson syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not an unconjugated rise.
Acute hepatitis would show clearly raised transaminases.
questions.why: Mild, intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (usually under 85 µmol/L) with normal liver enzymes and no haemolysis in a young healthy person is Gilbert syndrome, often unmasked by stress or fasting.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman on NSAIDs for joint pain has iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 110 g/L, MCV 69 fL, ferritin 18 µg/L). Coeliac serology is negative. Gastroscopy (3 cm hiatus hernia), colonoscopy to the caecum, small bowel transit and abdominal ultrasound are unremarkable. Which investigation is most appropriate next?
notes: Coeliac disease has already been made unlikely by negative serology, and a biopsy would not examine the ileum.
Angiography is invasive and reserved for active bleeding, not for occult blood loss with an unexplored small bowel.
Radioisotope scans are low-yield here and are not the standard way to survey the small bowel in occult bleeding.
questions.why: Iron deficiency anaemia needs a GI source excluded. With normal gastroscopy and colonoscopy and negative coeliac serology, the small bowel (jejunum and ileum) remains unexamined, so capsule endoscopy is next.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has incidental mild hypercalcaemia (calcium 2.75 mmol/L) with an inappropriately normal PTH (4.8 pmol/L). Her mother and paternal grandfather had parathyroid surgery but stayed hypercalcaemic. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
notes: Vitamin D status does not distinguish FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism.
Phosphate handling is altered in primary hyperparathyroidism but is not diagnostic of FHH.
PTHrP is for malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia, where PTH is suppressed, and does not fit this family history.
questions.why: This is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (autosomal dominant, calcium-sensing receptor mutation), confirmed by a low urine calcium/creatinine ratio. It is benign and not cured by parathyroidectomy.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with 10 years of type 2 diabetes takes metformin and sitagliptin and follows diet advice. Over 6 months he has lost weight and become fatigued. HbA1c has risen from 54 to 69 mmol/mol, with fasting glucose now 9.4–11.1 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Increase dietary protein and complex carbohydrate intake
notes: Dietary changes alone will not correct this degree of deterioration, and weight loss reflects insulin deficiency.
Swapping to pioglitazone is unlikely to achieve enough glucose lowering and can cause weight gain and fluid retention.
Removing metformin and substituting a sulfonylurea is a step backward; the patient needs intensification, not substitution.
questions.why: Poor control on dual therapy with weight loss and fatigue suggests relative insulin deficiency. Adding basal insulin relieves symptoms and lowers HbA1c towards target.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An immunocompromised patient with pneumonia has a halo sign and then an air-crescent (meniscus) sign on chest CT. Which organism is the most likely cause?
notes: S. aureus pneumonia causes consolidation, cavitation or pneumatoceles, not the classic halo sign.
Candida rarely causes pneumonia and is not classically linked to the halo sign.
Pseudomonas causes necrotising pneumonia, mostly in hospitalised patients, but not the classic halo or air-crescent sign.
questions.why: The CT halo sign and air-crescent sign are characteristic of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients. They are not pathognomonic; TB, some neoplasms and granulomatosis with polyangiitis can also cause them.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman had a 2 cm pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour in the tail removed by partial pancreatectomy. She has amenorrhoea for 6 months and recurrent renal colic since age 20 needing lithotripsy, and a family history of renal colic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: MEN 2A involves medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism, not pancreatic tumours or pituitary disease.
MEN 2B involves medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus.
A single somatostatinoma would not explain the amenorrhoea, recurrent stones and family history.
questions.why: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, probable prolactinoma (amenorrhoea) and hyperparathyroidism (recurrent renal stones) form the MEN 1 triad of pituitary, parathyroid and pancreatic tumours.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with severe headache, meningism, bilateral visual disturbance and ophthalmoplegia. CT shows a 2 cm sellar mass with haemorrhage, a deviated pituitary stalk and compressed gland. Which statement about her management is INCORRECT?
options: The likely diagnosis is pituitary apoplexy
High-dose corticosteroids with observation only may avoid surgery
Glucocorticoids should be given to prevent life-threatening adrenal insufficiency
Ophthalmoplegia and visual defects mean urgent surgery is never indicated
notes: This is a correct statement; the picture is classic for pituitary apoplexy.
This is a reasonable statement; conservative management with steroids is an option in selected stable patients without severe deficits.
This is correct; glucocorticoid replacement is essential because of acute secondary adrenal insufficiency.
questions.why: Visual deficits or ophthalmoplegia with reduced consciousness or instability are indications for early surgical decompression. Conservative management is considered only for milder cases.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with hypertension and heart failure has a persistent dry cough that starts as an itchy tickle in the throat. Which of her medicines is the most likely cause?
notes: Thiazides cause hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia and hyperuricaemia, not cough.
Beta blockers can cause bradycardia, fatigue and bronchospasm, but not a dry tickly cough.
Loop diuretics cause volume depletion, hypokalaemia and ototoxicity, not cough.
questions.why: A persistent dry, irritating cough is a typical ACE inhibitor adverse effect, caused by bradykinin accumulation. Hyperkalaemia is another.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is found collapsed in the street with SpO2 88% on room air and pinpoint pupils. ABG: pH 7.25, PaCO2 8.0 kPa, PaO2 7.7 kPa, HCO3 26 mmol/L, base excess −1. Na 137, Cl 100 mmol/L. What is the acid–base disturbance?
options: Venous sample; arterial interpretation is not possible
notes: Type 1 failure has hypoxaemia with normal or low PaCO2. Here PaCO2 is raised.
Bicarbonate and base excess are normal and the anion gap is normal (137 − 100 − 26 = 11), so there is no metabolic component.
The PaO2 of 7.7 kPa and the picture are consistent with an arterial sample, and nothing suggests it is venous.
questions.why: Low pH with raised PaCO2 and normal bicarbonate indicates acute, uncompensated respiratory acidosis. With pinpoint pupils, the likely cause is hypoventilation from opioid intoxication.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for pancreatic cancer is suspected of having a deep vein thrombosis of the leg. Which investigation is the most appropriate and cost-effective to confirm the diagnosis?
notes: D-dimer is commonly raised in malignancy, so it has low specificity and is unhelpful here.
MRI is costly and not first line for suspected DVT.
Venography is invasive and carries contrast risk; it is rarely used now.
questions.why: Venous duplex ultrasound is accurate, non-invasive and cheap, and allows follow-up. D-dimer is unhelpful in cancer patients as it is often raised.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites develops a pleural effusion. Pleural fluid LDH is 45 U/L (serum 220), pleural/serum protein ratio 0.3 and pleural/serum LDH ratio 0.2. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Extend fluid analysis with cell count, glucose, pH, ADA, cholesterol and culture
Continue treatment of the liver disease
notes: Extended testing is for exudates; this is a transudate.
Thoracoscopy is not indicated for a clear transudate.
Nothing suggests infection; parapneumonic effusions are exudates.
questions.why: The fluid meets transudate criteria by Light's criteria, consistent with hepatic hydrothorax from decompensated cirrhosis, so no further pleural work-up is needed; treat the liver disease.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 50-year-old has a pleural effusion: straw-coloured, pH 7.3, pleural/serum protein 0.8, pleural/serum LDH 0.9, Gram and Ziehl-Neelsen stains negative, normal lipids, mesothelial cells <5%, marked lymphocytosis without atypia, ADA 64 U/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Empyema would show purulent fluid with neutrophils, low pH and often positive Gram stain.
Mesothelioma would typically show atypical or malignant cells on cytology, and ADA would not be markedly raised.
Infarction gives a bloody or exudative effusion that is not lymphocyte-predominant with high ADA.
questions.why: This is a lymphocytic exudate with high ADA and no malignant cells, which points to tuberculous pleurisy. The main alternative for a lymphocytic exudate is malignancy.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with asthma has a severe exacerbation. After an hour of oxygen and two nebulised salbutamol doses he is no better: RR 42/min, accessory muscle use, diffuse wheeze, PEF 220 (from 310) L/min. On 28% O2, PaO2 is 7.2 kPa and PaCO2 4.7 kPa. Which is LEAST indicated?
options: Nebulised ipratropium with salbutamol every 20 minutes
notes: Hypoxaemia persists on 28% oxygen, so increasing oxygen is indicated.
Combined ipratropium and salbutamol every 20 minutes is standard for severe asthma not responding to initial treatment.
IV magnesium is an accepted adjunct in severe or life-threatening asthma not responding to initial bronchodilators.
questions.why: In severe asthma with hypoxaemia but a normal PaCO2, escalate oxygen, bronchodilators, steroids and magnesium first. NIV is not a routine step and invasive support is reserved for deterioration with hypercapnia or acidosis.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is admitted with severe pneumonia and improves on antibiotics. On day 4 of his admission he develops severe diarrhoea. What is the most likely causative organism?
options: The pneumonia-causing bacterium, now antibiotic resistant
notes: Salmonella is community-acquired from food and does not typically arise after antibiotics in hospital.
Resistance emerging within days and causing diarrhoea is implausible.
Campylobacter is a community-acquired foodborne cause, not a typical hospital antibiotic-associated one.
questions.why: Severe diarrhoea developing in hospital during or after antibiotic therapy is most commonly due to Clostridioides difficile infection.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A young man presents with a flame burn covering 10% of his body surface area, circumferential around the right arm. There is no Doppler arterial signal in the hand. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Occlusive silver sulfadiazine dressings and review of burn depth at one week
Lymphatic drainage and assessment for vascular bypass
notes: Topical dressings suit a small burn, but they ignore the limb-threatening circumferential constriction.
Bypass and lymphatic drainage don't address the constricting eschar causing the ischaemia.
Amputation is not indicated when decompression can restore perfusion.
questions.why: A circumferential burn with loss of distal pulses indicates compartment-like compression from the rigid eschar and oedema. Emergency escharotomy relieves pressure and saves the limb.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has had extensive ulcerative colitis for 15 years, in clinical remission for 3 years. He asks about colorectal cancer risk and prevention. Which advice is correct?
options: Risk is increased only if he smokes
Remission means population screening is adequate
Periodic surveillance colonoscopy with biopsies or chromoendoscopy is appropriate
Faecal occult blood testing at higher frequency than the general population is appropriate
notes: Colitis itself raises cancer risk whether or not the patient smokes.
Risk persists despite remission; population screening is insufficient.
FOBT is not adequate for surveillance in colitis, as dysplasia is often flat and may be missed.
questions.why: Extensive colitis for over 8–10 years raises colorectal cancer risk regardless of remission or smoking. Surveillance colonoscopy at intervals set by risk, with targeted biopsies (chromoendoscopy) or random biopsies, is recommended.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 18-year-old man with asthma and allergies to pollen, dust mites and cats presents with food sticking retrosternally and inability to swallow saliva. Similar episodes have resolved spontaneously. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Barrett oesophagus occurs with chronic reflux in older patients; any stricture would cause progressive dysphagia.
A Schatzki ring is possible, but the strong atopic history favours eosinophilic oesophagitis.
Infectious oesophagitis is typical in immunocompromised patients and causes odynophagia.
questions.why: Intermittent dysphagia with food impaction in a young man with marked atopy suggests eosinophilic oesophagitis.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has two weeks of progressive abdominal distension and malaise, with shifting dullness and no oedema. Diagnostic paracentesis shows 2,300 cells/µL, 60% polymorphs. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
notes: Ascites measures can wait; infection must be treated first.
Diuretics can wait until the infection is treated and are not the immediate priority.
There is no tense ascites to justify urgent drainage.
questions.why: Ascitic polymorphs above 250/µL (here about 1,380/µL) define spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Start a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) promptly, with albumin.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a colonoscopy after a positive screening test. A 2 cm pedunculated sigmoid polyp is removed by diathermy snare. Histology shows carcinoma in situ (high-grade dysplasia) confined to the polyp head. CT chest/abdomen is normal. What is the correct management?
options: Local excision of the polyp base
notes: Surgery is unnecessary for non-invasive disease that has been completely removed.
The polyp has already been removed by snare; further local excision of the base adds nothing.
Lymphadenectomy is for invasive cancer with adverse features, not in situ disease.
questions.why: Carcinoma in situ does not breach the basement membrane, so it has no metastatic potential. Complete polypectomy is curative and only endoscopic surveillance follows.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a 15 cm solid-cystic ovarian tumour found on ultrasound. Histology shows teeth, hair, intestinal, bronchial and squamous epithelium (15%), plus neuroectodermal and embryonic elements. What is the correct diagnosis?
notes: Teratocarcinoma is an outdated term implying overt malignant epithelial elements; no atypia is described here.
A mature cystic teratoma (dermoid) has only well-differentiated tissues; embryonic elements exclude it.
