Histology shows an 11 mm grade 3 invasive ductal carcinoma, two negative sentinel nodes, ER 0%, PR 0%, HER2 negative, Ki-67 70%. Staging is negative. What is the most appropriate adjuvant treatment?
options: Anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy, radiotherapy and trastuzumab
Anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy, radiotherapy and tamoxifen
Anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy and radiotherapy
Anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy, radiotherapy and an aromatase inhibitor
notes: Trastuzumab requires HER2-positive disease; this tumour is HER2 negative.
Tamoxifen requires hormone receptor positivity; this tumour is ER and PR negative.
Aromatase inhibitors work only in hormone receptor-positive tumours, regardless of menopausal status.
questions.why: This is triple-negative, high-grade breast cancer over 1 cm, so chemotherapy is indicated, and breast-conserving surgery requires adjuvant radiotherapy. Endocrine and HER2-directed therapy have no role without receptor expression.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has a normal physical examination. CT shows a mediastinal mass and a hepatic nodule. Serum lactate dehydrogenase, beta-hCG and alpha-fetoprotein are all elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Metastatic extragonadal non-seminomatous germ cell tumour
notes: Hepatocellular carcinoma can raise AFP alone, but not beta-hCG.
Seminoma may raise LDH (and mildly hCG), but AFP is normal in pure seminoma.
Lymphoma can raise LDH but does not raise beta-hCG or AFP.
questions.why: Raised beta-hCG with alpha-fetoprotein and LDH in a young man with a mediastinal mass indicates a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour. Pure seminoma does not raise AFP.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history has one month of pain along the ulnar border of the left arm and left ptosis. Chest imaging shows a left apical mass invading the second rib. What is the most appropriate treatment for the suspected diagnosis?
options: Chemotherapy alone, followed by radiotherapy without surgery
notes: Omitting surgery forgoes the curative resection achievable after induction therapy in resectable disease.
Upfront surgery is difficult with chest wall and rib invasion; induction chemoradiotherapy comes first.
Radiotherapy alone is the older approach; concurrent chemotherapy improves outcomes and is preferred.
questions.why: This is a Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumour with Horner syndrome. Induction concurrent chemoradiotherapy followed by surgical resection is the standard approach for resectable disease.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man has two months of dysphagia to solids. Endoscopy shows a partially stenosing mid-oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Endoscopic ultrasound and PET-CT show no pathological lymph nodes. What is the most appropriate management?
notes: Surgery alone gives poorer outcomes than multimodal therapy for locally advanced disease.
Surgery alone omits the neoadjuvant therapy that improves survival, whatever the operative technique.
Chemotherapy alone is inferior to combined chemoradiotherapy for squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.why: Locally advanced resectable oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma is treated with preoperative chemoradiotherapy (e.g. CROSS regimen) followed by surgery, as guidelines recommend.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with abdominal pain and upper gastrointestinal bleeding has a tumour of the gastric wall. Histology shows a spindle cell tumour with few mitoses that is CD117 positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Neurofibromas are S100 positive and are not typically CD117 positive.
Leiomyomas are smooth muscle tumours, positive for desmin and SMA and negative for CD117.
Granulocytic sarcoma is a myeloid tumour and not a spindle cell gastric tumour.
questions.why: GISTs are spindle cell tumours arising from the interstitial cells of Cajal and are characteristically CD117 (c-KIT) positive.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has had daily heartburn since youth, self-treated with antacids. Endoscopy shows mild erosive oesophagitis and a squamocolumnar junction 7 cm above the gastric folds. Distal oesophageal biopsies show intestinal-type columnar epithelium with low-grade dysplasia. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue antacids, as the oesophagitis is mild and the dysplasia low grade
Indefinite high-dose PPI, making endoscopic surveillance unnecessary
Periodic surveillance endoscopy and indefinite PPI therapy
notes: Antacids do not control acid adequately, and dysplasia needs surveillance.
PPIs do not remove the need for endoscopic surveillance.
Oesophagectomy is not indicated for low-grade dysplasia; it is reserved for invasive cancer not suitable for endoscopic therapy.
questions.why: This is Barrett's oesophagus with low-grade dysplasia. It needs endoscopic surveillance plus long-term PPI (or antireflux surgery) to limit progression.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl presents with delayed menarche and short stature, without intellectual disability. Which genetic test is routinely used to establish the likely diagnosis?
notes: NGS is for single-gene disorders and is not the routine test for suspected Turner syndrome.
FISH is targeted at specific loci and is not the routine diagnostic test here.
Microarray is for submicroscopic copy-number changes, not the routine first test for Turner syndrome.
questions.why: Delayed puberty with short stature in a girl suggests Turner syndrome (45,X), which is diagnosed by karyotype.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy with chronic kidney disease presents with vomiting, malaise and palpitations. ECG shows peaked T waves and serum potassium is 5.9 mmol/L. Intravenous calcium gluconate is given immediately. What is its purpose?
options: Shift potassium from plasma into cells
Bind circulating potassium to promote hepatic elimination
Bind circulating potassium to promote renal elimination
Antagonise the effect of potassium on the myocardial cell membrane
notes: Shifting potassium into cells is the action of insulin with glucose or salbutamol, not calcium.
Calcium does not chelate potassium, and potassium is not eliminated by the liver.
Calcium does not chelate potassium or alter renal excretion; that requires diuretics, resins or dialysis.
questions.why: Calcium gluconate does not lower serum potassium. It stabilises the cardiac myocyte membrane, reducing excitability and the risk of arrhythmia.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with moderate respiratory distress, intercostal and subcostal recession, scattered expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiration and SpO2 95% in room air. He is afebrile and has no murmur. He is kept for observation. What is the most appropriate approach to investigations?
options: Venous blood gas, white cell count and acute phase reactants
Arterial blood gas and acute phase reactants
notes: Blood tests and inflammatory markers are not routinely indicated in bronchiolitis.
Chest X-ray is not routine in typical bronchiolitis and is reserved for atypical or deteriorating cases.
Arterial gases and inflammatory markers are not indicated in a stable infant.
questions.why: This is likely bronchiolitis, a clinical diagnosis. No investigations are needed unless the infant deteriorates.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy has had pubic hair at the base of the penis for 12 months. Testicular volume and penile size have not increased, growth velocity is unchanged, and bone age is one year ahead of chronological age. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Central precocious puberty requires testicular enlargement (4 mL or more), which is absent here.
Peripheral precocious puberty would usually cause penile enlargement and more marked virilisation, not isolated pubic hair.
An androgen-secreting adrenal tumour would cause marked virilisation, rapid hair growth and penile enlargement, which he lacks.
questions.why: Pubic hair without testicular enlargement (volume under 4 mL), penile growth or growth spurt indicates premature adrenarche, due to early adrenal androgen secretion.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy has sudden-onset obsessive-compulsive disorder along with tics and chorea. Infection with which organism should be ruled out?
notes: S. viridans is a cause of endocarditis and is not linked to PANDAS.
Alpha-haemolytic streptococci include viridans group and pneumococcus; they are not linked to PANDAS.
Enterococcus is not associated with post-infectious neuropsychiatric syndromes.
questions.why: Abrupt OCD with tics or chorea in a child suggests PANDAS, a post-infectious autoimmune complication of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal (Streptococcus pyogenes) infection.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 79-year-old nursing home resident with no available history is brought to the ED. He is disoriented, has poor short-term memory and sees threatening people. He is agitated at times and drowsy and inattentive at others. Which feature best favours delirium over dementia?
notes: Visual hallucinations occur in delirium but also in dementia, such as Lewy body dementia.
Cognitive impairment is present in both delirium and dementia.
Agitation can occur in both conditions and is not specific.
questions.why: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that fluctuates over the day. A fluctuating level of consciousness or alertness distinguishes it from dementia.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has an incidental 2 cm polycystic lesion with central calcification in the pancreatic tail, not communicating with the main duct, and bilateral renal cysts. Fluid analysis is consistent with serous cystadenoma. What is the most appropriate management?
notes: Surgery is not needed for a benign, asymptomatic lesion.
Ablation is not indicated for a benign serous lesion.
Transplant has no role for benign cysts.
questions.why: Serous cystadenoma is benign and usually asymptomatic. Surgery is reserved for symptomatic lesions or diagnostic doubt, so surveillance imaging is appropriate.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 37-week pregnant woman is HBsAg positive. She asks how her newborn should be managed and whether she can breastfeed. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Hepatitis B vaccine at birth only; formula feeding
Vaccine and immunoglobulin at birth; breastfeeding only from one month
Immunoglobulin at birth only; formula feeding
Vaccine and immunoglobulin within 12 hours of birth; breastfeeding is fine
notes: Immunoglobulin is also needed for immediate passive protection.
Delaying breastfeeding is unnecessary once the infant is immunised.
Vaccine is also needed for active immunity, and formula feeding is not required.
questions.why: Infants of HBsAg-positive mothers should receive hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin at separate sites soon after birth (within 12 hours). Breastfeeding is not contraindicated as transmission risk via milk is very low.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman taking olmesartan has had 2 months of watery diarrhoea, 4 to 6 stools daily, after a 3-week NSAID course. Gastroscopy, colonoscopy and duodenal biopsies are normal. Colonic biopsies show chronic inflammation, a subepithelial collagen band over 10 µm thick and over 20 intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 epithelial cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: NSAID enteropathy affects the small bowel and does not give this colonic histology.
Olmesartan enteropathy causes duodenal villous atrophy, but the duodenal biopsies here are normal.
IBS has normal histology and no collagen band.
questions.why: Chronic watery diarrhoea with a macroscopically normal colon and a thickened subepithelial collagen band with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes is microscopic (collagenous) colitis. Budesonide is the treatment.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient treated for acute diverticulitis with amoxicillin with clavulanic acid develops fever and diarrhoea on day 5. Clostridioides difficile colitis is diagnosed, the antibiotic is stopped and metronidazole started. After 4 days there is no response, but the patient is clinically stable. What is the next step?
options: Change to oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days
Change to piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 8 hours
Fashion a loop ileostomy with antegrade colonic lavage
notes: Another broad-spectrum antibiotic would worsen C. difficile infection and has no activity against it.
Colectomy is reserved for fulminant colitis with shock, ileus, megacolon or perforation; this patient is stable.
Diverting ileostomy with lavage is a surgical option for severe or fulminant disease, not for a stable patient.
questions.why: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days is the treatment for C. difficile infection that fails to respond to metronidazole. Fidaxomicin is an alternative.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: After a road crash, an injured man opens his eyes when spoken to and says only inappropriate words. He localises pain with his right limbs, but shows abnormal extension to pain in his left limbs. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
notes: Verbal response is inappropriate words (V3), not incomprehensible sounds (V2), and the best motor response is M5, not M4.
Eye opening to voice is E3, not E2 (to pain), and the best motor response is M5, not M4.
Eye opening to voice is E3, not E2 (to pain), and inappropriate words score V3 rather than V4 (confused).
questions.why: Always score the best response in each domain. Eyes open to voice = E3, inappropriate words = V3, localising pain = M5, giving E3V3M5 (11/15).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 15-year-old is ejected after being hit by a car. He is conscious with left chest pain and dyspnoea. BP 90/60 mmHg, HR 130, SpO2 90%, RR 35, with absent breath sounds and dullness on the left. X-ray shows left rib fractures and a massive effusion. A chest drain returns 1700 mL of blood. What is the next step?
options: Analgesia, oxygen, blood transfusion and urgent surgery
Intubation, transfusion and observation, operating only if he worsens
Intubation and urgent CT scan to assess injuries
notes: Non-invasive ventilation does not secure the airway and does not control the bleeding.
Waiting for deterioration increases morbidity and mortality when immediate drainage is massive.
CT may be reasonable only if he stabilises, but with massive haemothorax haemorrhage control takes priority.
questions.why: Initial drainage over 1500 mL of blood is an indication for urgent thoracotomy per ATLS. Resuscitate with analgesia, oxygen and transfusion while arranging urgent surgery.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is a pedestrian struck by a car. He is pale and sweaty with a thready pulse, BP 90/50 mmHg, HR 127/min, RR 28/min, SpO2 92%. After 1 L of crystalloid his vitals improve transiently, then deteriorate on arrival at hospital. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate uncrossmatched group O blood (massive transfusion protocol)
Group-specific blood transfusion once typing is complete
Prepare crossmatched blood in case transfusion becomes necessary
Give a further 1 L crystalloid bolus
notes: Group-specific blood requires typing time that this unstable, ongoing-bleeding patient does not have.
Crossmatching takes too long; transfusion is already indicated, not merely possible.
More crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and worsens acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy; blood products are needed.
questions.why: Transient response to fluids in a trauma patient indicates ongoing haemorrhagic shock. With vital compromise, blood must be given immediately as uncrossmatched group O (activate the massive transfusion protocol), alongside haemorrhage control.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman taking propranolol develops stridor, rash, vomiting and hypotension (90/40 mmHg) 30 minutes after a penicillin dose. Hypotension persists after repeated IM adrenaline and IV fluids. Which additional drug is most specifically indicated?
notes: Corticosteroids have no proven role in acute resuscitation and do not address adrenaline resistance.
Antihistamines are adjuncts for skin symptoms only and do not treat refractory hypotension.
Salbutamol may help bronchospasm but does not reverse beta-blocker-related refractory hypotension.
questions.why: Beta-blockade can make anaphylaxis resistant to adrenaline, causing refractory hypotension and bradycardia. Glucagon (1–2 mg IV/IM, repeated or infused) bypasses the beta-receptor and is used in this setting.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man who migrated to Australia 4 years ago has had anxiety and low mood for 10 months, moderately affecting daily activities. He has no psychiatric history. Symptoms began after his older brother, to whom he was very close, died in a car accident. Which diagnosis is most appropriate?
notes: The symptoms are relatively mild and do not seriously impair function, which argues against major depression.
There is no history of hypomanic episodes.
Requires symptoms for at least 2 years.
questions.why: Mild anxious-depressive symptoms after an identifiable stressor, with no previous psychiatric history, fit adjustment disorder. The stressor (bereavement) and its consequences are ongoing.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 7-year-old afebrile girl has had a red face since yesterday. Today she has a confluent maculopapular rash on both cheeks, sparing the perioral area, giving a 'slapped' look, and a reticular, lacy, non-itchy rash on the trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Varicella gives itchy vesicles in crops, not a slapped-cheek and lacy rash.
Rubella causes a rash spreading from the face with postauricular lymphadenopathy, not a lacy reticular pattern.
Roseola presents with high fever for several days, then a rash on the trunk as the fever settles.
questions.why: Bilateral slapped cheeks followed by a lacy reticular truncal rash are typical of erythema infectiosum, caused by parvovirus B19.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes diagnosed 3 months ago has a BMI of 31 kg/m² and poor glycaemic control despite diet and exercise. Which of the following glucose-lowering drugs is associated with weight gain?
notes: Metformin is weight neutral or causes modest weight loss.
SGLT2 inhibitors cause weight loss through glycosuria.
GLP-1 receptor agonists cause significant weight loss.
questions.why: Pioglitazone (a thiazolidinedione) causes dose-dependent weight gain from fat accumulation and sometimes fluid retention.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A man with newly diagnosed HIV (CD4 45 cells/µL, viral load 500,000 copies/mL, negative tuberculin skin test) started an integrase inhibitor plus two NRTIs. At 3 months, viral load has fallen and CD4 is rising, but he develops fever and cervical lymphadenopathy. Node aspirate shows acid-fast bacilli and epithelioid granulomas. What is the best interpretation?
options: Lymph node tuberculosis caused by incomplete immunological recovery
Antiretroviral treatment failure with a new opportunistic infection
Opportunistic infection unmasked as part of immune reconstitution syndrome
A negative tuberculin skin test excludes tuberculosis in this patient
notes: The infection was unmasked during immune recovery; it is not a consequence of incomplete recovery.
Viral load has fallen and CD4 is rising, so this is the expected response, not treatment failure.
A negative tuberculin test does not exclude TB in severe immunosuppression because false negatives occur.
questions.why: He is responding virologically and immunologically to ART, so the TB lymphadenitis has been unmasked by immune reconstitution (IRIS). It is not caused by incomplete recovery or treatment failure.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 86-year-old woman has non-valvular atrial fibrillation and a CHADS2 score of 3. Similar patients have a stroke risk of 2.2% on warfarin versus 5.2% without. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one stroke?
notes: 3 is the ARR in percentage points, not its reciprocal.
19.2 is the reciprocal of 5.2%, i.e. not the risk difference.
49.5 does not follow from the risk difference; NNT = 1/ARR.
questions.why: Absolute risk reduction is 5.2% − 2.2% = 3.0%. NNT = 1/0.03 = 33.3.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 86-year-old woman has non-valvular atrial fibrillation and a CHADS2 score of 3. Stroke risk is 2.2% on warfarin versus 5.2% without it. What is the number needed to treat (NNT) with anticoagulation to prevent one stroke?
notes: 3 is the absolute risk reduction in percentage points, not its reciprocal.
19.2 does not result from the correct calculation (1/0.03).
49.5 does not result from the correct calculation (1/0.03).
questions.why: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction. ARR = 5.2% − 2.2% = 3% = 0.03, so NNT = 1/0.03 = 33.3.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient's arterial blood gas shows pH 7.40, PaCO2 60 mmHg and bicarbonate 36 mmol/L. What is the acid–base disturbance?
options: None, as the pH is normal
notes: A normal pH does not exclude a disorder; both PaCO2 and bicarbonate are abnormal.
Uncompensated respiratory acidosis would give a low pH and near-normal bicarbonate.
Metabolic alkalosis alone would not explain the raised PaCO2 of 60 mmHg.
questions.why: A normal pH can mask a mixed disorder. Raised PaCO2 indicates respiratory acidosis and raised bicarbonate indicates metabolic alkalosis (compensatory in chronic CO2 retention, as in COPD).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 53-year-old obese woman with migraine has repeated clinic BP readings below 140/90 mmHg. She buys a validated home BP monitor and is taught to use it correctly. Over several weeks her home readings are consistently above 140/90 mmHg. What does she have?
notes: No investigation has shown a secondary cause, so this label is unsupported.
White-coat hypertension is the reverse: raised clinic BP with normal home readings.
Resistant hypertension requires uncontrolled BP despite several drugs. She is untreated.
questions.why: Masked hypertension is normal clinic BP with elevated out-of-office BP on home or ambulatory monitoring. Her home readings stay raised over several weeks.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 18-year-old presents with oedema. Tests show proteinuria of 8 g/day without haematuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hypercholesterolaemia and normal renal function. After one month of empirical corticosteroids, he has fully recovered. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Amyloidosis causes nephrotic syndrome but is rare at this age and does not remit with steroids.
IgA nephropathy usually presents with haematuria and does not typically give a full steroid response.
Alport syndrome presents with haematuria, hearing loss and progressive renal impairment, not steroid-responsive nephrosis.
questions.why: Nephrotic syndrome with normal renal function and complete response to corticosteroids indicates minimal change disease, which responds to steroids in about 85–90% of cases.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A man with CKD G4 (eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73 m²) presents with generalised weakness. His potassium is 7.0 mmol/L and the ECG shows hyperkalaemic changes. What is the first treatment to give?
options: Insertion of a dialysis catheter to start haemodialysis
notes: Resins remove potassium slowly and do not protect the heart, so they are not first-line in an emergency.
Dialysis may be needed if the response is poor, but it takes time to set up and is not the first step.
Oral furosemide acts too slowly and is unreliable at eGFR 20. Cardiac membrane stabilisation comes first.
questions.why: In severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, IV calcium gluconate is given first to stabilise the cardiac myocyte membrane and protect against arrhythmia. It does not lower potassium, but it buys time for shifting and removal measures.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient has had an ulcerovegetating lesion of the mandibular gingiva in the molar region for 5 months. He now develops numbness of the chin. What should be ruled out as the cause?
options: Herpes virus infection in an immunosuppressed patient.
notes: Numb chin from a local tumour is direct infiltration, not paraneoplastic.
Sarcoidosis causes facial palsy, not mental nerve numbness, and does not fit a gingival tumour.
Herpes infection does not fit a chronic ulcerovegetating lesion with no immunosuppression.
questions.why: Chin numbness (mental nerve neuropathy, numb chin syndrome) here indicates direct infiltration of the inferior alveolar nerve in the mandibular canal by the local oral carcinoma, not a paraneoplastic effect.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with MEN-2A and a RET mutation has a 6 mm hypoechoic calcified thyroid nodule on ultrasound. Total thyroidectomy and neck dissection show three small nodules of uniform round cells in solid sheets with calcification and amyloid, no nuclear clearing or pseudoinclusions, synaptophysin positive, and nodal metastases. What is the diagnosis?
notes: Papillary carcinoma shows optically clear nuclei, grooves and pseudoinclusions, and lacks amyloid; these are explicitly absent here.
Follicular carcinoma shows follicular architecture with capsular or vascular invasion, not amyloid or neuroendocrine staining.
C-cell hyperplasia is a precursor lesion and does not form invasive nodules or nodal metastases.
questions.why: Multifocal medullary carcinoma arises from C cells in RET-mediated MEN-2A. Solid sheets of uniform cells with amyloid and neuroendocrine marker positivity are typical, and nodal metastases exclude simple hyperplasia.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with reflux, Raynaud phenomenon and skin induration of the hands and arms was recently started on prednisolone 20 mg daily. She now has headache and malaise, BP 200/110 mmHg and creatinine 220 µmol/L. Which autoantibody is most associated with this complication?
notes: Anti-centromere is linked to limited disease and pulmonary hypertension, with renal crisis rare.
Anti-proteinase 3 is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not scleroderma.
Anti-PM-Scl is linked to scleroderma–myositis overlap, not renal crisis.
questions.why: This is systemic sclerosis with scleroderma renal crisis, precipitated by corticosteroids. Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are most associated with diffuse disease and renal crisis.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has leg oedema, reduced urine output, fever and a malar rash for 20 days. Creatinine is 265 µmol/L, Hb 105 g/L (normocytic), leukopenia, CRP 90 mg/L, ESR 60 mm/h. Which statement about her likely condition is correct?
options: Anti-Sm antibodies are not specific for this condition
Anti-centromere antibodies are present in 90% of cases
ANA are present in only 50% of cases
Anti-dsDNA antibodies correlate with the risk of nephritis
notes: Anti-Sm antibodies are highly specific for SLE, though not sensitive.
Anti-centromere antibodies are typical of limited systemic sclerosis, not SLE.
ANA are positive in over 90% of SLE cases, so it is a sensitive screening test.
questions.why: This is SLE with renal involvement. Anti-dsDNA antibodies correlate with disease activity and the risk of lupus nephritis.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man has 3 weeks of malaise, bitemporal headache and jaw claudication, then amaurosis fugax of the left eye. The left temporal artery is thickened and pulseless. ESR is 92 mm/h and CRP is raised. Which statement about treatment of the likely diagnosis is correct?
options: Rituximab is first-line, as glucocorticoids are now second-line
Tocilizumab reduces relapses and cumulative prednisolone dose
With ischaemic symptoms, glucocorticoid doses above 30 mg/day should be avoided
Infliximab with 1 g glucocorticoid boluses is first-line for induction
notes: Glucocorticoids remain first-line in giant cell arteritis; rituximab is not standard therapy.
Visual or ischaemic involvement needs high-dose glucocorticoids (often IV pulses), not restriction to under 30 mg/day.
Infliximab has not been shown to be effective in giant cell arteritis and is not first-line.
questions.why: This is giant cell arteritis. Glucocorticoids remain first-line (pulse doses if visual involvement), and tocilizumab is the steroid-sparing agent shown to reduce relapses and cumulative steroid dose.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: After reduction of an anterior shoulder dislocation and 3 weeks in a sling, a woman has numbness over the lateral shoulder and can abduct only to 15 degrees. MRI shows an intact rotator cuff. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: The rotator cuff is intact on MRI, and this would not cause sensory loss.
Adhesive capsulitis causes pain and stiffness, especially on external rotation, not focal sensory loss.
The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus (first 15 degrees of abduction, preserved here) and has no cutaneous territory.
questions.why: Lateral shoulder sensory loss (regimental badge area) and deltoid weakness, with abduction beyond 15 degrees lost, indicate axillary nerve injury, a common complication of anterior dislocation.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had a first episode of low back pain for 3 weeks that limits her daily activities. There was no trauma, she has no known underlying disease, and neurological examination is normal. Which imaging is indicated?
options: Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine
notes: Plain films add radiation and rarely change management without red flags.
MRI is reserved for red flags or persistent radicular symptoms; incidental findings are common and can mislead.
CT gives high radiation and is not indicated without suspected fracture or other red flags.
questions.why: Acute low back pain (under 6 weeks) without red flags such as fracture, infection or malignancy does not need imaging. Management is reassurance, analgesia and staying active.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman taking the oral contraceptive pill has 2–3 days of weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia, nausea and deep rapid breathing (RR 28). BP 100/60, dry mucosa, afebrile, alert. Glucose 23 mmol/L, Na 131, pH 7.08, HCO3 8 mmol/L, ketonuria +++. What is the best management?
options: New type 2 diabetes; dyspnoea likely from pneumonia or pulmonary embolism
Diabetic ketoacidosis: IV insulin, IV fluids, supportive care and search for a precipitant
Type 1 diabetes: give bicarbonate first, then add IV insulin once acidosis corrected
Likely alcoholic ketoacidosis: measure blood alcohol before starting insulin
notes: Ketoacidosis with Kussmaul breathing explains the dyspnoea; this is not type 2 diabetes with pneumonia or PE.
Bicarbonate is not first-line and insulin must not be delayed until acidosis is corrected.
Waiting for an alcohol level would delay insulin, which must not be delayed.
questions.why: This is DKA at presentation of diabetes. Priorities are IV insulin and IV fluids, with bicarbonate only for severe acidosis; insulin should never be delayed.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man develops right buttock pain after a long car trip and cannot tolerate prolonged sitting. He has intermittent right leg numbness relieved by standing. MRI, hip X-ray, sensation and reflexes are normal. Resisted abduction and external rotation with the hip flexed to 90° reproduces the pain. Most likely diagnosis?
notes: Causes groin pain and reduced internal rotation, with abnormal hip imaging or positive FADIR; not buttock pain on sitting with normal X-ray.
Causes lateral hip or iliotibial band pain, not sciatic-type buttock pain with leg numbness.
Radiculopathy would typically give reflex or sensory changes and MRI findings, which are normal here.
questions.why: Piriformis syndrome is sciatic nerve irritation by the piriformis muscle, causing gluteal pain and paraesthesia after prolonged sitting. Pain on resisted abduction and external rotation in 90° flexion (PACE manoeuvre) with normal imaging and neurology supports it.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A haemodynamically stable 25-year-old man has a motorcycle crash with negative FAST, mild head injury (GCS 14) and a displaced intracapsular right hip fracture. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Early reduction and internal fixation, within 24–36 hours
Elective total hip arthroplasty the following Monday
Delay until the head injury improves, then elective reduction and fixation next week
Emergency bipolar hemiarthroplasty because of the risk of non-union
notes: Arthroplasty is avoided in a young patient. Delay also raises the risk of avascular necrosis.
Surgery should not be postponed in a stable patient, as delay increases the risk of avascular necrosis.
Replacement is avoided in a young patient. Fixation with reduction is preferred.
questions.why: In a young patient a displaced intracapsular fracture needs early anatomical reduction and fixation, preserving the native hip, to reduce the risk of avascular necrosis. He is stable, so surgery need not be delayed.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with asthma and atopic dermatitis develops hypotension, tachycardia, urticaria and bronchospasm after eating peanuts. Which is the first drug to give and a blood test useful for later evaluation?
options: Intramuscular promethazine first; eosinophil cationic protein
notes: Bronchodilators and other agents are adjuncts only; adrenaline must not be delayed.
Antihistamines are adjuncts and must not precede adrenaline; ECP is not the marker used.
Adrenaline is right, but eosinophil cationic protein is not the useful marker; tryptase is.
questions.why: This is anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline (0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg in adults) is first-line. Serum tryptase, taken early and again at 4–6 hours, supports the diagnosis.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with prior gastrointestinal anisakiasis after eating fish has specific IgE to Anisakis simplex of 10 kU/L. Which dietary advice is most appropriate?
options: Avoid all fish, crustaceans, molluscs and cephalopods.
Fresh fish is safe if cooked on the grill.
Commercially deep-frozen fish is safe if thoroughly cooked.
Fresh marinated or cold-smoked fish is safe.
notes: Unnecessary restriction; sensitisation is to the parasite, not to fish or other seafood.
Grilling may not heat the flesh sufficiently to kill larvae in fresh, unfrozen fish.
Marinating and cold smoking do not reliably kill larvae.
questions.why: Anisakis larvae are killed by freezing (-20°C for at least 5 days) and by cooking above 60°C. Fresh raw, marinated, smoked or lightly grilled fish should be avoided.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis has inadequate seasonal control despite oral antihistamines and intranasal corticosteroids. Which disease-modifying treatment is indicated?
options: Allergen immunotherapy (sublingual or subcutaneous) for at least 3 years
Allergen immunotherapy (sublingual or subcutaneous) for a maximum of 1 year
Omalizumab every 4 weeks for up to 1 year
Omalizumab every 4 weeks for at least 6 months
notes: One year is too short to achieve a lasting disease-modifying effect.
Omalizumab is reserved for severe allergic asthma or urticaria, not isolated rhinitis.
Omalizumab is not indicated for rhinoconjunctivitis alone.
questions.why: Allergen immunotherapy is the only treatment that modifies the natural course of allergic rhinitis and should be given for at least 3 consecutive years.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man has 3 months of fatigue and dyspnoea, now present at rest, plus exertional angina. BP is 110/80 mmHg, HR 85/min. There is a harsh systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space and bibasal crackles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Mitral regurgitation gives an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla, not a right upper sternal border murmur.
Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure, not a harsh systolic murmur with narrow-ish pulse pressure.
Ischaemic cardiomyopathy would not explain a harsh aortic-area systolic murmur; the triad of angina, dyspnoea and murmur fits aortic stenosis.
questions.why: Angina, heart failure symptoms and a harsh systolic murmur at the aortic area in an elderly patient indicate aortic stenosis; symptom onset marks a poor prognosis and need for valve replacement.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman with permanent atrial fibrillation for 10 years and preserved biventricular systolic function has episodes of symptomatic complete atrioventricular block. Which permanent pacing system is most appropriate?
notes: Atrial sensing and tracking are useless in permanent AF, so a second lead adds no benefit.
An atrial lead cannot correct AV block, and the atria are fibrillating.
CRT is for reduced LVEF with LBBB or expected high ventricular pacing burden with heart failure; function is preserved here.
questions.why: In permanent AF there is no effective atrial activity to sense or pace, so a single-chamber ventricular (VVI) pacemaker is indicated for AV block. Preserved systolic function means no CRT is needed.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man with known Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome presents with palpitations. ECG shows an irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 205 bpm consistent with pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Which drug is appropriate to terminate it?
notes: AV nodal blockers like verapamil can increase conduction down the accessory pathway and cause VF.
Digoxin is contraindicated as it may increase ventricular rate and precipitate VF.
Adenosine blocks the AV node and is ineffective or dangerous in pre-excited AF.
questions.why: In pre-excited AF, drugs prolonging the accessory pathway refractory period (procainamide, or amiodarone) are used if cardioversion is not possible. DC cardioversion is the treatment of choice if unstable.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with resistant hypertension on an ACE inhibitor, a diuretic and a calcium channel blocker has BP 149/100 mmHg, K+ 2.2 mmol/L, metabolic alkalosis and creatinine 106 µmol/L. Which statement about his likely condition is correct?
options: It is caused by autonomous aldosterone secretion from the adrenal medulla
Plasma renin activity is typically raised
Adrenal CT is part of the work-up once biochemical confirmation is obtained
Spironolactone is contraindicated in its management
notes: Aldosterone is made in the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa), not the medulla.
Renin is suppressed in primary hyperaldosteronism because of volume expansion.
Spironolactone (a mineralocorticoid antagonist) is a mainstay of medical treatment, not contraindicated.
questions.why: This is primary hyperaldosteronism. After biochemical screening (aldosterone:renin ratio) and confirmation, adrenal CT is used for subtype assessment, followed by adrenal vein sampling if surgery is considered.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman with heart failure (LVEF 25%) and an ICD is stable in NYHA class III on maximum tolerated lisinopril, carvedilol and spironolactone. BP is 118/74 mmHg, HR 78/min, with a third heart sound and no congestion. What is the most appropriate next step?
notes: Combining it with an ACE inhibitor is contraindicated because of the risk of angioedema.
Ivabradine is a later option, and the ACE inhibitor should be changed to an ARNI first.
The beta-blocker has proven mortality benefit and should not be stopped.
questions.why: In symptomatic HFrEF despite optimal ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker and MRA therapy, the ACE inhibitor should be replaced by sacubitril/valsartan. A 36-hour washout is needed because of angioedema risk.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: Ten days after hemithyroidectomy for a 1.5 cm thyroid nodule, histology shows a very cellular follicular neoplasm with invasion of adjacent blood vessels and nerves. Which statement is correct?
options: A follicular pattern is an indication for prophylactic central neck dissection
This is follicular carcinoma and completion thyroidectomy is required
Serum calcitonin distinguishes papillary from follicular carcinoma
notes: Omitting further surgery is reserved for low-risk disease, not tumours with vascular or nerve invasion.
Prophylactic neck dissection is associated with medullary carcinoma, not a follicular pattern.
Calcitonin is a marker of medullary carcinoma and does not separate papillary from follicular carcinoma.
questions.why: Invasion of vessels and nerves means follicular carcinoma with adverse features, so completion thyroidectomy followed by radioiodine assessment is appropriate. Avoiding it is reserved for low-risk tumours such as microcarcinomas under 1 cm.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 65-year-old smoker with hypertension and dyslipidaemia has cyanotic mottled toes bilaterally. CT angiography shows a 7 cm descending thoracic aortic aneurysm distal to the left subclavian artery, with mural thrombus. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Statin therapy alone to stabilise the thrombus.
Open replacement with a tubular graft and reimplantation of the supra-aortic trunks.
notes: Statins do not stabilise thrombus or prevent embolisation, and a 7 cm aneurysm needs repair.
CT angiography has already defined the anatomy; invasive aortography adds risk and delay.
Supra-aortic trunk reimplantation applies to arch disease; this aneurysm lies distal to the left subclavian artery.
questions.why: A 7 cm symptomatic aneurysm with thrombus embolising to the feet needs repair. Thoracic endovascular repair is preferred for a descending aneurysm with suitable anatomy.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 85-year-old man with permanent atrial fibrillation has 6 hours of sudden pain and coldness in the right foot. There is plantar cyanosis with partial sensory and motor deficit. The femoral pulse is palpable; popliteal and distal pulses are absent. What is the best management?
options: Avoid revascularisation because of the ischaemia time
Apply heat and wait for vascular review
notes: At 6 hours the limb is still salvageable, so revascularisation is indicated.
Heat worsens ischaemic injury, and this threatened limb needs urgent intervention, not delay.
Prostaglandins are not adequate treatment for an acute embolic occlusion.
questions.why: This is acute limb ischaemia from an embolus (AF) with a threatened limb (sensory and motor deficit), needing urgent revascularisation by embolectomy, alongside heparin.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl has had fever for 6 days. She has a maculopapular rash on the trunk and groin that is confluent but not scarlatiniform, non-purulent conjunctival injection, red lips, strawberry tongue, oedema and erythema of the hands and feet, and a 2 cm unilateral cervical node. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Measles has cough, coryza and exudate-free conjunctivitis with Koplik spots; it lacks acral oedema, red lips and a single large node.
Rubella is a milder illness with posterior auricular/occipital nodes and not prolonged high fever.
Scarlet fever has a sandpaper scarlatiniform rash and exudative pharyngitis, and the rash here is not scarlatiniform.
questions.why: Fever for 5 or more days plus rash, non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes, acral oedema/erythema and cervical lymphadenopathy fulfils the criteria for Kawasaki disease.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 6 years, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, ischaemic heart disease and prior biliary pancreatitis takes metformin, lisinopril, metoprolol, aspirin and atorvastatin. BP 151/93 mmHg, BMI 27.1 kg/m², HbA1c 8.3% (67 mmol/mol). Which add-on agent is most appropriate?
notes: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain and have no cardiovascular benefit; they are not preferred in ischaemic heart disease.
Acarbose has modest HbA1c effect, causes GI side effects, and gives no cardiovascular benefit.
Sitagliptin lowers HbA1c but has no cardiovascular or BP/weight benefit, and DPP-4 inhibitors carry a pancreatitis concern given his history.
questions.why: Empagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor, lowers HbA1c, blood pressure and weight, and reduces cardiovascular events in people with established cardiovascular disease, so it suits this patient.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since age 15 has nausea and abdominal distension, worse after meals. Evaluation is consistent with diabetic gastroparesis. Which medication is most appropriate to improve her symptoms?
notes: A proton pump inhibitor reduces acid but does not improve gastric emptying.
An antiemetic may ease nausea but is not a prokinetic and does not treat the underlying dysmotility.
Loperamide slows gut motility and would worsen gastroparesis.
questions.why: Metoclopramide is the first-line prokinetic for gastroparesis. It antagonises D2 receptors and stimulates 5-HT4 receptors, increasing gastric contractions and antropyloroduodenal coordination, and it is also antiemetic.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has his GP request a serum vitamin B12 level because of his antidiabetic medication. Which drug is he most likely taking?
notes: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain, not B12 deficiency.
Repaglinide is an insulin secretagogue and is not linked to B12 deficiency.
Pioglitazone causes fluid retention, weight gain and fractures, not B12 deficiency.
questions.why: Long-term metformin is associated with reduced vitamin B12 absorption and lower serum levels, which is reversible on stopping. Monitoring B12 is recommended, especially with neuropathy or anaemia.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An obese, asymptomatic 58-year-old man drinks alcohol moderately. Fasting plasma glucose is 8.5 mmol/L with negative urine glucose. On two later occasions weeks apart, fasting glucose is 6.6 and 7.5 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate step to confirm diabetes?
options: Perform a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test
He already meets the diagnostic criteria for diabetes
Measure HbA1c before making the diagnosis
notes: Not needed. An OGTT is reserved for equivocal results, and the fasting criteria are already met twice.
Insulin or C-peptide helps classify diabetes type. It is not a diagnostic test for diabetes.
HbA1c ≥6.5% is an alternative criterion, but it is not required when two fasting glucose results are already diagnostic.
questions.why: Diabetes is diagnosed when fasting plasma glucose is ≥7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) on two separate occasions in an asymptomatic patient. Two of his three readings (8.5 and 7.5) meet this, so no further testing is needed.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman on the oral contraceptive pill presents with fever and left hemibody paraesthesias. Hb 75 g/L, platelets 7 ×10⁹/L, LDH 1200 U/L, reticulocytes 10%, haptoglobin undetectable, direct Coombs negative, schistocytes on film, normal PT and APTT. Which diagnosis is most likely?
notes: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia has a positive direct Coombs test and no schistocytes.
Evans syndrome combines Coombs-positive haemolysis with immune thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes are absent.
Immune thrombocytopenia has no haemolysis or schistocytes, and does not explain fever or neurological symptoms.
questions.why: The picture of neurological disturbance, fever, Coombs-negative microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia fits TTP.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl has 2–3 years of slowed growth, delayed puberty (no menarche, little breast and pubic development), headaches and a left temporal partial hemianopia. Height is −2.1 SD, bone age is delayed 2 years, and FSH, LH and oestradiol are low. What is the best interpretation?
options: Hormone deficiency with optic chiasm involvement from a sellar or suprasellar lesion
Constitutional delay with a refractive error causing the visual symptoms
Isolated growth hormone deficiency, with an optometry review for glasses
notes: Turner syndrome causes high gonadotrophins and low oestradiol (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism).
Refractive errors do not cause hemianopia, and the absence of polyuria does not exclude a sellar tumour.
Growth hormone deficiency alone does not explain low gonadotrophins, and refractive error does not cause hemianopia.
questions.why: Short stature, delayed puberty with low gonadotrophins, headache and visual field defect indicate a hypothalamic–pituitary lesion (e.g. craniopharyngioma) compressing the optic chiasm. Imaging is needed.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus on hydroxychloroquine has 15 days of progressive weakness and pallor. FBC shows Hb 74 g/L and MCV 108 fL. Which test is most useful in deciding management?
notes: Haptoglobin supports haemolysis but does not show it is autoimmune, so it will not direct treatment.
B12 deficiency is a less likely cause of rapid anaemia in a young woman with SLE.
ANA is already known to be positive in SLE and does not explain the anaemia.
questions.why: Subacute anaemia with macrocytosis (reticulocytosis) in SLE suggests autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, which is confirmed by a positive direct antiglobulin test and determines treatment.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had dyspnoea for 4 days. She has a regular tachycardia, no murmurs and normal chest auscultation. Arterial blood gas: pO2 9.3 kPa, pCO2 4.3 kPa. Blood count, renal and liver function are normal. PT 90%, APTT ratio 2.0 (normal <1.2). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Factor V Leiden causes thrombosis but does not prolong the APTT, so it does not explain the coagulation result.
Haemophilia would not present with thrombosis and is very unlikely in a woman.
Acute pericarditis does not explain the hypoxaemia and does not prolong the APTT.
questions.why: Dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypoxaemia and hypocapnia suggest pulmonary embolism. A prolonged APTT with thrombosis points to lupus anticoagulant, so antiphospholipid syndrome is the most likely cause.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with 6 years of hypertension has poor control (BP 149/100 mmHg) despite an ACE inhibitor, a diuretic and a calcium channel blocker. Creatinine is 106 µmol/L, potassium 2.2 mmol/L with metabolic alkalosis; urinalysis is normal. Which statement is correct?
options: Aldosterone excess results from autonomous adrenal medullary overactivity
Bilateral adrenocortical hyperplasia is the usual cause
CT of the adrenals is part of the work-up once biochemically confirmed
notes: Aldosterone is produced by the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa), not the medulla.
The most frequent cause is an aldosterone-producing adenoma, with bilateral hyperplasia the other main cause.
Spironolactone is the medical treatment of choice.
questions.why: This is probable primary aldosteronism (resistant hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis). After biochemical confirmation, adrenal CT defines the subtype and excludes carcinoma.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman has chronic kidney disease from diabetic nephropathy. Her creatinine is 283 µmol/L and eGFR (CKD-EPI) is 14 mL/min/1.73 m². Which statement is correct?
options: She has stage 3 CKD and should start phosphate binders
She has stage 5 CKD and kidney replacement therapy should be considered
Good glycaemic control can reverse her kidney failure
Proteinuria above 500 mg/24 h is unlikely
notes: Stage 3 is an eGFR of 30–59; her eGFR of 14 is stage 5.
Glycaemic control may slow progression but will not reverse established advanced damage.
Diabetic nephropathy usually has albuminuria above 300 mg/24 h, sometimes nephrotic range.
questions.why: An eGFR below 15 mL/min/1.73 m² is stage 5 (G5) CKD, where kidney replacement therapy (or conservative care) should be discussed.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman is treated with ciprofloxacin for 5 days for uncomplicated cystitis. A week later she has malaise, arthralgia and a rash. Her eGFR is 45 mL/min/1.73 m² (100 six months ago). Urine microscopy shows leukocytes; nitrites are negative. What is the most likely cause of her renal impairment?
notes: Post-infectious GN typically follows streptococcal infection and presents with haematuria, mainly in children and older adults.
Direct tubular toxicity (crystal formation) from ciprofloxacin is very rare.
Pyelonephritis would present with fever and loin pain, and usually positive urine culture.
questions.why: Malaise, arthralgia, rash, acute kidney injury and sterile pyuria after a drug exposure suggest drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis. Antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin, are among the commonest causes.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presents with 12 hours of dark brown urine, 4–5 days after an upper respiratory tract infection. BP 150/95 mmHg, afebrile. Creatinine 71 µmol/L, urea 4.2 mmol/L, normal platelets and complement/autoimmune screen. Proteinuria 0.75 g/24 h; urine has 90% dysmorphic red cells, no white cells. Most likely diagnosis?
notes: Minimal change disease causes nephrotic-range proteinuria, not haematuria.
Post-infectious GN follows a latent period of 1–3 weeks and usually has low complement.
Interstitial nephritis shows pyuria and white cell casts, with renal impairment, and no dysmorphic red cells.
questions.why: Macroscopic haematuria coinciding with an upper respiratory infection, mild proteinuria and normal renal function is typical of IgA nephropathy.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has dysmorphic haematuria, proteinuria of 3 g/24 h, eGFR 85 mL/min/1.73 m² and sensorineural hearing loss. His maternal grandmother needed dialysis at 70, and his mother and younger sister have isolated microscopic haematuria. Which diagnosis is most likely?
notes: IgA nephropathy does not cause sensorineural deafness and is not typically inherited in an X-linked pattern with affected female relatives.
Fabry disease is X-linked and can cause proteinuria, but features are acroparaesthesias, angiokeratomas and corneal opacities rather than haematuria with deafness.
ADPKD causes large cystic kidneys, hypertension and usually little proteinuria; it is not associated with deafness.
questions.why: Haematuria, proteinuria and sensorineural deafness in a young man, with haematuria in female relatives, indicates Alport syndrome (usually X-linked, COL4A5 mutation).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 42-year-old obese woman has elevated serum, urinary and salivary cortisol. Cortisol remains elevated after an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, and ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome is suspected. Which test would best localise the cause?
notes: Petrosal sinus sampling is used to separate pituitary from ectopic ACTH-dependent disease, not adrenal causes.
Octreotide scanning is used to find ectopic ACTH-secreting neuroendocrine tumours, which are ACTH-dependent.
Ultrasound has poor sensitivity for small adrenal lesions and is not the imaging of choice.
questions.why: ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome is caused by an adrenal adenoma, carcinoma or hyperplasia, so adrenal CT is the imaging of choice. In practice, confirm a suppressed ACTH first.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man develops malaise, oliguria and headache after a respiratory infection. BP is 210/120 mmHg with grade III hypertensive retinopathy. Hb 74 g/L, platelets 85 ×10⁹/L, schistocytes on film, LDH raised, creatinine 773 µmol/L, haematuria and proteinuria. ADAMTS-13 activity is normal. No diarrhoea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Normal ADAMTS-13 activity rules out TTP, which is characterised by severely reduced activity.
DIC would show deranged coagulation (prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen) and bleeding, not described here.
Typical HUS follows a Shiga toxin-producing E. coli diarrhoeal illness, which is absent here.
questions.why: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury indicate thrombotic microangiopathy. Normal ADAMTS-13 excludes TTP, no diarrhoea argues against STEC-HUS, and no coagulopathy argues against DIC, leaving atypical HUS.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman on sertraline presents with confusion. She is euvolaemic with no oedema, BP 130/70. Na is 126 mmol/L, K 4 mmol/L, urine sodium 45 mmol/L; diuretics are excluded. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Treat as Addison disease with immediate corticosteroids
Give hypertonic saline to normalise sodium rapidly
Restrict fluids and review the sertraline
Order a brain MRI for presumed diabetes insipidus
notes: Adrenal insufficiency usually causes hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, not a euvolaemic picture.
Hypertonic saline is for severe neurological symptoms, and rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.
Diabetes insipidus causes hypernatraemia, the opposite of this picture.
questions.why: This is euvolaemic hyponatraemia from SIADH, probably drug-induced. With moderate symptoms and Na above 125 mmol/L, fluid restriction is first-line; rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has chronic kidney disease classified as G3a/A1. Which eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) values correspond to this stage?
options: eGFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR <3 mg/mmol
eGFR 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR <3 mg/mmol
eGFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR 3–30 mg/mmol
eGFR 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m² and ACR <3 mg/mmol
notes: This eGFR range is G3b, not G3a.
ACR 3–30 mg/mmol is A2 (moderately increased albuminuria), not A1.
This eGFR range is G4, not G3a.
questions.why: G3a is an eGFR of 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m², and A1 is a normal to mildly increased ACR (<3 mg/mmol).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman is brought by her family because of months of low mood and memory lapses. She herself feels well. Which sequence best describes the usual progression of symptoms in Alzheimer's disease?
options: Mood changes, behavioural symptoms, cognitive deficits.
Behavioural symptoms, motor symptoms, loss of functional independence.
Mood changes, cognitive deficits, loss of functional independence.
Behavioural symptoms, mood changes, motor symptoms.
notes: Prominent behavioural symptoms are not typically the second step before cognitive deficits; cognitive decline is the core feature.
Early behavioural and motor symptoms suggest other dementias (e.g. frontotemporal, Lewy body), not typical Alzheimer's.
Early behavioural symptoms suggest other dementias, and motor symptoms occur late in Alzheimer's disease.
questions.why: Alzheimer's disease typically begins with mood change and memory/cognitive deficits, followed by progressive loss of functional independence. Early prominent behavioural or motor symptoms should prompt consideration of other dementias.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes suddenly develops language impairment. Newly detected atrial fibrillation is found. She has fluent speech, poor comprehension, inability to repeat and difficulty naming. Which aphasia is this?
notes: Broca's aphasia is non-fluent with preserved comprehension.
Conduction aphasia has preserved comprehension, with impaired repetition.
Transcortical sensory aphasia resembles Wernicke's but repetition is preserved.
questions.why: Wernicke's aphasia is fluent with impaired comprehension, repetition and naming. Here it is likely from an embolic stroke in the dominant temporal lobe in the setting of atrial fibrillation.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman, a heavy smoker with childhood febrile seizures, has stereotyped episodes of an ascending epigastric sensation and unpleasant smell, then unresponsiveness with lip-smacking and repeated left-hand opening and closing. Episodes last 2 minutes, followed by confusion. Most likely diagnosis?
options: Focal impaired awareness seizures of temporal lobe origin
Transient ischaemic attacks in the right carotid territory
notes: TIAs cause sudden negative symptoms (weakness, numbness), not stereotyped aura, automatisms and postictal confusion.
Focal aware motor seizures preserve awareness and involve clonic motor activity; here awareness is lost.
Transient global amnesia is a single episode of isolated anterograde amnesia without automatisms or aura, in older patients.
questions.why: An epigastric rising aura with olfactory hallucination, then impaired awareness with oral and manual automatisms and postictal confusion, is classic mesial temporal lobe epilepsy. Febrile seizures in childhood are a risk factor. Formerly called complex partial seizures.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has unilateral periocular headaches that rapidly become very intense. Attacks last 30–60 minutes, occur 2–3 times daily, and come with ipsilateral tearing and rhinorrhoea. What is the most appropriate preventive treatment?
options: Oral prednisolone weaned over one month, plus verapamil 80–180 mg every 8 hours
Indomethacin 50 mg every 8 hours for one month
notes: Steroid alone is only a short bridge and is not adequate preventive therapy; verapamil is needed.
Carbamazepine is used for trigeminal neuralgia, not cluster headache.
Indomethacin is for paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua, which have shorter, more frequent attacks.
questions.why: This is cluster headache. Verapamil is the main preventive, usually started with a short tapering course of corticosteroid to cover the delay before it takes effect.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a one-year history of progressive memory loss now requiring help with daily activities. He has migraines and past self-limited focal neurological episodes. Neuropsychology shows early dementia and MRI shows severe leukoencephalopathy. Which test should be ordered?
options: Lumbar puncture for CSF amyloid and tau
notes: CSF amyloid and tau support Alzheimer disease, which does not explain migraine, focal episodes and marked leukoencephalopathy.
PSEN1 causes early-onset familial Alzheimer disease, not this vascular picture.
Progranulin mutations cause frontotemporal dementia, which presents with behavioural or language change.
questions.why: This is CADASIL, an autosomal dominant NOTCH3 small-vessel arteriopathy. It presents with migraine, recurrent strokes or TIAs, early cognitive decline and severe leukoencephalopathy.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man had a ruptured middle cerebral artery aneurysm causing subarachnoid haemorrhage, treated surgically. He recovered and walked, but one month later becomes progressively drowsy and struggles to follow commands. Which statement is correct?
options: He is at the stage when vasospasm is most frequent
The deterioration is most likely due to aneurysm rebleeding
Subacute deterioration is most likely due to hydrocephalus
Cerebral angiography is the diagnostic test of choice
notes: Vasospasm typically occurs in the first week or two after the bleed (peak days 4–14), not at one month.
Rebleeding is most likely in the first 24 hours and would present abruptly, not as a progressive decline after the aneurysm was treated.
The first-line test is non-contrast CT brain to show ventricular enlargement; angiography is not the test of choice here.
questions.why: Progressive decline in consciousness weeks after SAH suggests (communicating) hydrocephalus. Vasospasm occurs within the first 1–2 weeks, and non-contrast CT brain is the investigation of choice.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with severe traumatic brain injury and intraparenchymal haemorrhage is in ICU with an intracranial pressure monitor. Before intubation he did not open his eyes, made no sounds and extended to pain. Which statement is correct?
options: His Glasgow Coma Scale score on arrival was 7.
Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure plus intracranial pressure.
Vasogenic oedema results from cell swelling, membrane rupture and cell death.
Cerebral blood flow increases with hypercapnia and acidosis.
notes: His GCS was 4 (E1 V1 M2): extension is M2.
CPP is mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.
Cell swelling and death describe cytotoxic oedema; vasogenic oedema follows blood–brain barrier disruption.
questions.why: Hypercapnia and acidosis cause cerebral vasodilatation, raising cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An asymptomatic 31-year-old woman is 10 weeks pregnant. Her brother, aged 26, has ataxia and a confirmed expanded CAG repeat (70 repeats) in the SCA3 gene. She is considering chorionic villus sampling. What is the appropriate approach?
options: Test her genotype first; fetal testing only if she carries the mutation
No testing, as the disease is fully penetrant and she is asymptomatic so not a carrier
Test the first child after birth and offer prenatal testing in a later pregnancy
Offer fetal testing regardless of her genotype, as inheritance is maternal
notes: Being asymptomatic at 31 does not exclude carrying the mutation, as onset is variable and often later.
Waiting until after birth does not address the current pregnancy and is not the appropriate pathway.
Inheritance is autosomal dominant, not exclusively maternal, so unnecessary invasive testing would be avoided.
questions.why: SCA3 is autosomal dominant, so she has a 50% prior risk. Test her first; if she is negative the fetus cannot inherit it, and if positive chorionic villus sampling can be offered.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents after falling off an e-scooter with a closed head injury. She had no loss of consciousness or amnesia, has a mild headache without vomiting, a normal neurological examination and a GCS of 15. She takes no anticoagulants. What imaging is indicated?
notes: Non-contrast CT is for patients with red flags (such as GCS below 15, vomiting, anticoagulation or suspected skull fracture), none of which are present.
Contrast CT has no role in the acute assessment of head trauma.
Plain skull X-ray is not recommended, as it is poor at excluding intracranial injury.
questions.why: A minor head injury with GCS 15, no anticoagulant or antiplatelet use and no red flags needs no imaging, as validated decision rules (for example the Canadian CT Head Rule) show.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 61-year-old smoker with hypertension presents with 15 minutes of sudden right-hand weakness and tingling, now almost fully resolved. ECG shows sinus rhythm at 93 bpm. Regarding the most likely diagnosis, which statement is FALSE?
options: A probable cause is artery-to-artery embolism from a detached carotid plaque.
Carotid duplex ultrasound of the supra-aortic vessels is of little diagnostic use.
Brain imaging is needed to assess for infarction of the parenchyma.
Revascularisation is indicated if imaging shows symptomatic carotid stenosis >70%.
notes: True: carotid plaque embolism is a common cause of TIA in a vascular-risk patient.
True: CT or MRI brain is needed to exclude haemorrhage and detect infarction.
True: symptomatic stenosis of 70% or more is an indication for carotid endarterectomy.
questions.why: This is a TIA. The basic aetiological work-up includes duplex ultrasound of the supra-aortic (carotid) vessels, echocardiography and targeted bloods, so calling duplex of little use is false.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man develops low back pain after lifting weights at the gym. Hours later it radiates down the back of the right leg to the lateral border of the foot. He has a positive straight leg raise at 40°, an absent ankle reflex and cannot stand on tiptoe. What is the most likely cause?
