notes: L2-L3 herniation affects the L3 root, causing anterior thigh pain and a reduced knee reflex, not S1 signs.
L3-L4 herniation affects the L4 root, causing anterior thigh and medial leg pain, quadriceps weakness and a reduced knee reflex.
L4-L5 herniation affects the L5 root: dorsum of foot pain, weak dorsiflexion and hallux extension, with an intact ankle reflex.
questions.why: Pain to the lateral foot, absent ankle reflex and inability to tiptoe (plantarflexion weakness) indicate S1 radiculopathy. An L5-S1 disc herniation compresses the traversing S1 root.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman with a levonorgestrel intrauterine device has poor sleep, hot flushes and palpitations. Free T4 and TSH are normal; FSH is 95.6 IU/L, LH 21 IU/L and estradiol is below 0.07 nmol/L. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Oral oestrogen plus progestogen, continuous regimen
notes: Benzodiazepines do not treat the cause and are not appropriate for vasomotor symptoms.
Vaginal oestrogen acts locally and does not control systemic vasomotor symptoms.
Added oral progestogen is redundant with the levonorgestrel IUD, and oral oestrogen carries a higher thrombotic risk.
questions.why: Her hormone profile is menopausal (early menopause/premature ovarian insufficiency) with systemic vasomotor symptoms, so systemic oestrogen is indicated. The levonorgestrel IUD already provides endometrial protection.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A primigravida at 34 weeks has BP 165/95 mmHg and a 2-day headache. Platelets 98 ×10⁹/L, AST 356 U/L, ALT 234 U/L, LDH 878 U/L, and schistocytes on blood film. Antenatal corticosteroids were completed 24 hours ago. Fetal weight is below the 1st centile with absent end-diastolic umbilical flow. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Expectant management with antihypertensives and magnesium sulfate until platelets improve
Home antihypertensive treatment with review every 48 hours
Delay delivery until fetal lung maturity is confirmed
notes: Expectant management is not appropriate for HELLP at 34 weeks with fetal compromise.
Home management is unsafe in severe HELLP syndrome.
Fetal lung maturation has already been achieved with the completed corticosteroids, so there is no reason to delay.
questions.why: This is HELLP syndrome with severe features and a growth-restricted fetus with absent end-diastolic flow at 34 weeks. Corticosteroids are complete, so immediate delivery is indicated.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman wants contraception. She had an emergency caesarean section 7 months ago and is exclusively breastfeeding. Which statement is correct?
options: If amenorrhoeic, she needs no other contraception while breastfeeding
A levonorgestrel IUD is contraindicated within a year of caesarean section
A progestogen-only hormonal method is suitable
Combined hormonal contraception is the preferred option
notes: Lactational amenorrhoea is only reliable within 6 months postpartum; at 7 months she needs another method.
A levonorgestrel IUD is not contraindicated after caesarean section.
Oestrogen-containing contraception may reduce milk supply, so it is not preferred while breastfeeding.
questions.why: Progestogen-only methods are suitable and preferred while breastfeeding. Oestrogen-containing methods are best avoided because they may reduce milk supply.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man presents with conjunctival hyperaemia, foreign body sensation and tender preauricular lymphadenopathy. Which of the following conditions is the LEAST likely cause of this presentation?
notes: Adenoviral conjunctivitis classically causes preauricular lymphadenopathy, so it fits.
Parinaud syndrome (e.g. Bartonella, tularaemia) is an infective conjunctivitis with regional nodes, so it fits.
Chlamydial conjunctivitis causes follicles and a lymphoid response with adenopathy, so it fits.
questions.why: Preauricular lymphadenopathy is typical of infective conjunctivitis. Allergic conjunctivitis is not infectious and does not cause lymphadenopathy.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a sudden transient loss of consciousness. Which of the following has the highest diagnostic yield in determining the cause?
notes: ECG is an important screening test but yields a diagnosis in a minority and is guided by the history.
EEG has low yield unless seizure is suspected from the history.
CT brain has low yield without focal signs or head trauma.
questions.why: History, with a witness account, examination and orthostatic vital signs, is the most useful step in sorting out the cause of loss of consciousness. It guides which tests, if any, are needed.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman wears +4.00 D distance glasses in both eyes. For some weeks she has had eye pain, headache and blurred vision at night while watching television in dim light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Migraine is not tied to dim light, and eye pain with blurred vision is not typical.
Actinic keratitis follows ultraviolet exposure and is unrelated to hyperopia or dim light.
Dry eye causes burning, grittiness and foreign-body sensation, not this picture.
questions.why: Hyperopia and age over 50 give a shallow anterior chamber and thickened lens. Pupil dilation in dim light can close the angle, causing eye pain, headache, and blurred vision from corneal oedema.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has several days of profuse watery diarrhoea, 10 kg weight loss, facial flushing, presyncope and colicky abdominal pain. Bloods show hypokalaemia. Ultrasound shows a 1.5 cm mass in the pancreatic tail. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Causes hypoglycaemic symptoms, not secretory diarrhoea.
Usually clinically silent or causes mild symptoms; it does not produce this syndrome.
Causes necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes and weight loss rather than watery diarrhoea.
questions.why: Profuse watery diarrhoea with hypokalaemia and flushing, plus a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, indicates a VIPoma (Verner–Morrison syndrome).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 2-month-old has had a 3-day coryzal illness and now has moderate respiratory distress and expiratory wheeze. SpO2 is 89% in room air and RSV is isolated from a nasopharyngeal aspirate. Which treatment is most appropriate?
notes: Ribavirin has no role in routine bronchiolitis management and is not given orally.
Bronchodilators do not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis and are not recommended.
Corticosteroids have no proven benefit in bronchiolitis.
questions.why: This is RSV bronchiolitis, which is managed with supportive care. Supplemental oxygen is indicated for hypoxaemia (SpO2 persistently below about 90–92%).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted with an osteoporotic hip fracture. Regarding secondary prevention of fragility fractures, which one of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: Low adherence to treatment is associated with an increased risk of fracture.
Bone turnover markers may help with early monitoring of response to treatment.
Vitamin D monotherapy effectively reduces fractures in community-dwelling older adults.
Increasing dietary calcium or taking calcium alone does not protect against fractures.
notes: This is true: poor adherence to osteoporosis treatment is a major factor in increased fracture risk.
This is true: bone turnover markers can help with early monitoring of adherence and response to treatment.
This is true: neither increased dietary calcium nor calcium supplements alone protect against fractures.
questions.why: Vitamin D alone is not shown to reduce fractures in community-dwelling older adults. Calcium and vitamin D are given alongside antiresorptive or anabolic drugs, whose trials included them, but not as monotherapy.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has 3 months of fatigue and fever, then nasal obstruction with bloody crusting and clots, and painful right proptosis. ESR is 65 mm/h; urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria and proteinuria of 520 mg/24 h. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: EGPA features asthma, eosinophilia and neuropathy; destructive nasal and orbital disease with glomerulonephritis is less typical.
Microscopic polyangiitis causes glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis, but not granulomatous nasal or orbital disease.
Polyarteritis nodosa spares the lungs and glomeruli and does not cause nasal or orbital granulomas.
questions.why: Upper airway disease (crusting nasal mucosa, orbital mass causing proptosis) with glomerulonephritis is the classic presentation of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener's).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has 4 days of dyspnoea and tachycardia, with clear lungs, pO2 70 mmHg and pCO2 32 mmHg. Blood count, renal and liver function are normal. PT is normal, but the APTT ratio is 2 (normal <1.2). Which diagnosis is most likely?
notes: Factor V Leiden causes thrombosis but does not prolong clotting times.
Haemophilia prolongs the APTT but is not a typical cause of thromboembolism.
Pericarditis would not explain the hypoxaemia or the prolonged APTT, and lacks typical features.
questions.why: Hypoxaemia with likely pulmonary embolism plus an isolated prolonged APTT suggests antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant), which prolong phospholipid-dependent tests in vitro yet cause thrombosis.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man's father died of colon cancer at 38. Colonoscopy shows hundreds of adenomas throughout the colon. Which statement about this patient is incorrect?
options: Annual colonoscopy surveillance with colectomy at age 40 is the best management.
Without colectomy he will almost certainly develop colorectal cancer.
Each of his children has a 50% risk of inheriting the condition.
notes: This is correct: hundreds of colonic adenomas with a family history indicate FAP.
This is correct: untreated, the cancer risk approaches 100%.
This is correct: it is autosomal dominant (APC mutation), so each child has a 50% risk.
questions.why: In familial adenomatous polyposis, prophylactic colectomy is advised once polyposis is established, usually in early adulthood. Waiting until 40 is too late, as cancer typically develops around that age.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has had 1 month of shoulder and pelvic girdle pain and stiffness, worst on rising and easing with movement. She has no fever, headache or systemic upset. Examination shows painful, stiff shoulders and hips. ESR and CRP are raised. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial treatment?
notes: RA causes small-joint synovitis rather than isolated girdle stiffness at this age.
Fibromyalgia does not raise inflammatory markers.
Ankylosing spondylitis begins in young adults with inflammatory back pain, not in a 70-year-old woman.
questions.why: Age over 50, bilateral shoulder pain, morning stiffness, hip involvement and raised inflammatory markers indicate polymyalgia rheumatica, treated initially with moderate-dose corticosteroids.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with obesity, hypertension and metabolic syndrome has pain in both buttocks, the left lateral thigh to the knee and the left leg to mid-calf. It is reproduced by lifting the leg with the knee extended and relieved by flexing the knee. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Gouty arthritis of the left hip
notes: Gout causes an acute, red, hot joint and would not follow a root distribution or change with knee flexion.
Hip osteoarthritis gives groin pain worsened by weight-bearing and reduced hip rotation, not pain below the knee with a straight-leg raise.
Neurogenic claudication is provoked by walking or standing and relieved by sitting or lumbar flexion, not by a straight-leg raise.
questions.why: Pain reproduced by the straight-leg raise and relieved by knee flexion is a positive Lasègue sign, indicating lumbosacral nerve root irritation (lumbar radiculopathy).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with obesity, hypertension and metabolic syndrome has pain in both buttocks, the left trochanteric region, lateral thigh to the knee and leg to mid-calf. Pain is provoked by raising the leg with the knee extended and relieved by knee flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Gouty arthritis of the left hip
Neurogenic claudication from spinal canal stenosis
notes: Nothing suggests an acute gouty joint, and hip pathology would not give a positive straight leg raise.
Hip osteoarthritis gives pain limiting walking, stiffness and a negative Lasegue test.
Stenosis pain worsens with trunk extension (walking, standing) and eases with flexion/sitting, not with leg raise.
questions.why: Pain reproduced by straight leg raise (Lasegue) and relieved by knee flexion indicates radicular irritation in the lumbosacral region, i.e. lumbosciatica.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 35-year-old postal worker has had 24 hours of neck pain without trauma, radiating down the left arm to the hand, with paraesthesia of the radial forearm. There is no weakness, neck movement is preserved but painful, and paravertebral muscle spasm is present. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Conservative treatment with analgesia/NSAIDs, local heat and relative rest
Urgent MRI and nerve conduction studies/EMG
Urgent referral to an orthopaedic outpatient clinic
notes: Surgery is reserved for progressive deficit, myelopathy or failed prolonged conservative care. None applies here.
Imaging and EMG are not needed without red flags or persistent symptoms after conservative treatment.
Urgent referral is not needed in the absence of red flags or neurological deficit.
questions.why: This is acute cervical radiculopathy without red flags or motor deficit. Most cases settle with conservative care (about 75-90%).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 27-year-old regular runner has calf pain during prolonged running that settles within hours of rest. Physiotherapy for presumed calf muscle overload has not helped over several months. Which investigation is most useful to confirm the likely diagnosis?
options: Posterior compartment pressure measurement immediately after exercise
Doppler ultrasound to exclude lower limb arterial disease
notes: PET is not used for diagnosing exertional compartment syndrome.
Doppler can exclude arterial causes (e.g. popliteal entrapment), but the picture fits compartment syndrome, which needs pressure measurement.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy is not a standard diagnostic test for this condition.
questions.why: Recurrent exertional leg pain that resolves with rest and fails to respond to physiotherapy suggests chronic exertional compartment syndrome. Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring compartment pressures at rest and after exercise.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 27-year-old male runner has had months of right calf pain that comes on with running and eases over hours of rest. Physiotherapy for 'calf overload' has failed. Which investigation would best help confirm the diagnosis?
options: Compartment pressure measurement of the posterior leg at rest and after exercise
Doppler ultrasound to exclude lower limb arterial disease
notes: PET has no role in diagnosing exertional leg pain of this kind.
Doppler may exclude vascular causes such as popliteal entrapment, but the history fits compartment syndrome and pressure measurement is the confirmatory test.
MR spectroscopy is a research tool and is not used to diagnose compartment syndrome.
questions.why: This is chronic exertional compartment syndrome. Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring intracompartmental pressures at rest and after exertion.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man fell 2 m. He has a swollen left heel, tingling over the right anterior thigh and scrotum, and dysaesthesia in both feet. He moves both arms normally with no arm symptoms. Leg rotation and pelvic compression are painless. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Palpate the abdomen and log-roll him to examine the thoracolumbar spine
Apply a cervical collar and send for cervical spine and lower limb imaging
notes: Imaging the limb alone would miss a probable lumbar spine injury; the full secondary survey including the back comes first.
Arm function and sensation are normal, so the cervical spine is not the likely site of injury. The symptoms localise to the lumbosacral region.
An abdominal ultrasound does not address the neurological findings pointing to the lumbar spine.
questions.why: The sensory symptoms suggest a lumbar and sacral root injury, so the spine examination must be completed before imaging. He should be moved en bloc (log-roll) to palpate the thoracolumbar spine. The cervical spine appears clinically unaffected.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 95-year-old woman in a residential aged care facility, independent in basic activities of daily living and walking in the garden, has mild cognitive impairment. She falls at night and X-ray shows a displaced subcapital fracture of the right hip. What is the most appropriate treatment?
notes: Intramedullary nails are used for pertrochanteric (extracapsular) fractures.
Cannulated screws are for undisplaced fractures, and fail often when the fracture is displaced.
Non-operative care suits non-ambulatory patients with minimal pain or prohibitive surgical risk. She is mobile.
questions.why: A displaced subcapital (Garden III–IV) fracture in an elderly, mobile patient is treated surgically, usually with hemiarthroplasty, because of the high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man presents with several days of knee pain. On examination, the Thessaly test (pain with internal and external rotation of the flexed knee, weight-bearing) is positive. Which injury is most likely?
notes: ACL rupture is assessed with Lachman, anterior drawer and pivot shift tests, not the Thessaly test.
PCL rupture is assessed with the posterior drawer and posterior sag signs.
Osteoarthritis causes gradual pain, stiffness and crepitus; the Thessaly test is not used to diagnose it.
questions.why: The Thessaly test is a provocation test for meniscal injury: pain or catching on rotation of the flexed knee suggests a meniscal tear.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has had knee pain for several days. The Thessaly test (pain on internal and external rotation with the knee slightly flexed, weight-bearing on one leg) is positive. What is the most likely lesion?
notes: ACL rupture is assessed with the Lachman and anterior drawer tests.
PCL rupture is assessed with the posterior drawer and sag signs.
Degenerative arthropathy is not diagnosed by the Thessaly test.
questions.why: The Thessaly test is used to diagnose meniscal tears, with high sensitivity and specificity.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man presents with several days of knee pain. On examination, the Thessaly test (pain with internal and external rotation of the flexed, weight-bearing knee) is positive. Which injury is most likely?
notes: ACL assessment uses the Lachman and anterior drawer tests, and no trauma is described.
PCL assessment uses the posterior drawer test and sag sign, and no trauma is described.
Possible, but unlikely in a 41-year-old with an acute presentation, and the test points to a meniscus.
questions.why: The Thessaly test is a meniscal provocation manoeuvre. Joint-line pain, locking or catching on loaded rotation of the slightly flexed knee suggests a meniscal tear.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl, 3 months post-menarche, has progressive idiopathic scoliosis. Standing X-ray shows a thoracolumbar curve of 35° (Cobb angle) and Risser grade 0. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Swimming and review in three months
Review in 6 months with repeat X-ray
notes: Exercise alone does not prevent progression of a curve of this size.
Physiotherapy does not halt curve progression in a growing adolescent.
Observation alone risks progression during rapid growth.
questions.why: A Cobb angle of 25–45° in a skeletally immature patient (Risser 0) with remaining growth is an indication for bracing to prevent progression.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl, menarche 3 months ago, has idiopathic scoliosis followed since age 10 and now progressing. Examination shows a 7° rib hump on Adams test. X-ray: T4–L1 curve of 35° (Cobb), Risser 0. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Recommend swimming and review in 3 months
Refer to physiotherapy for spinal stretching
Review in 6 months with a repeat X-ray
notes: Swimming does not prevent curve progression and review is too late for a progressing curve.
Physiotherapy alone does not halt progression of a significant growing curve.
Simple observation is inadequate for a progressing 35° curve in a skeletally immature patient.
questions.why: Curves below about 50° are managed conservatively. With a progressing 35° curve and substantial growth remaining (Risser 0, recent menarche), bracing is indicated to slow progression.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted with an osteoporotic hip fracture. Regarding secondary prevention of fragility fractures, which statement is INCORRECT?
options: Low adherence to treatment is associated with increased fracture risk
Bone turnover markers may help monitor early response to treatment
Vitamin D monotherapy reliably reduces fractures in community-dwelling older people
Calcium alone, from diet or supplements, does not protect against fractures
notes: This is true; poor adherence to antiresorptives is associated with more fractures.
This is true; turnover markers such as CTX and P1NP can show early response.
This statement is true; calcium alone has not been shown to prevent fractures.
questions.why: Vitamin D alone has not been shown to reduce fractures in community-dwelling older people. Calcium plus vitamin D may modestly reduce non-vertebral fractures, mainly in deficient or institutionalised people.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man presents after a bicycle crash with facial trauma. CT shows a midface fracture involving the orbitozygomatic region, including the orbital floor. Which of the following is a common complication of this type of fracture?
notes: The TMJ is close to but not part of the orbitozygomatic complex.
Malocclusion occurs with fractures lower in the midface involving the maxilla, not typically an orbitozygomatic one.
Nasoethmoidal injuries involve the nasal bones, which lie anterior to the medial orbital rim, outside the orbit.
questions.why: Orbitozygomatic fractures often involve the orbital floor, increasing orbital volume and causing enophthalmos, as well as diplopia from inferior rectus displacement or entrapment.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with breast cancer has metastases at the intervertebral foramina between C4 and C5 and between T4 and T5. Which spinal nerves are at risk?
notes: C4 exits between C3 and C4, not C4 and C5.
T5 exits between T5 and T6, and C4 exits between C3 and C4.
T5 exits between T5 and T6, not between T4 and T5.
questions.why: There are 8 cervical nerves but 7 cervical vertebrae: C1–C7 exit above their vertebra, and C8 exits between C7 and T1. So C5 exits between C4 and C5. Thoracic nerves exit below their vertebra, so T4 exits between T4 and T5.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 56-year-old overweight man with type 2 diabetes has mild hepatomegaly and drinks alcohol only rarely. Liver biopsy shows macrovesicular fat in 50% of hepatocytes, neutrophilic inflammatory foci, Mallory hyaline and pericentral fibrosis. Which statement is correct?
options: The diagnosis is hepatic glycogenosis associated with diabetes.
The changes are irreversible and will inevitably progress to cirrhosis.
The injury is clearly alcohol-related despite the patient's denial.
Weight loss and good diabetes control may prevent progression to cirrhosis.
notes: The vacuoles are intracellular fat, not glycogen.
In the early phase the changes are reversible when the cause is removed; cirrhosis is not inevitable.
Diabetes causes similar changes, so there is no reason to disbelieve the patient.
questions.why: This is steatohepatitis (NASH), which diabetes and obesity can cause just as alcohol does. In the early stage it is reversible if the cause is removed, so weight reduction and glycaemic control are key.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An elderly woman is drowsy with faecal soiling. BP 100/60 (sitting 70/30), HR 100, Kussmaul respiration, weight 50 kg. pH 7.25, pCO2 14 mmHg, HCO3 5 mmol/L, Na 133, K 2.5, Cl 118 mmol/L, creatinine 300 µmol/L, urea 21 mmol/L. Which statement is correct?
options: Respiratory compensation for the acidosis is inadequate
Bicarbonate should never be given in any circumstances
She has acute kidney injury of prerenal cause
notes: Expected pCO2 is about 1.5 × 5 + 8 = 15.5 (±2), so a pCO2 of 14 is appropriate compensation.
Postural hypotension and tachycardia point to volume depletion, so dehydration is not excluded.
Bicarbonate is generally avoided unless pH falls below about 7.10, but 'never in any circumstances' is too absolute.
questions.why: This is a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis with hypokalaemia, consistent with diarrhoeal losses. Postural hypotension and raised urea and creatinine indicate volume depletion and prerenal AKI.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with hypertension and ischaemic heart disease presents to the emergency department with oppressive chest pain that began at rest. At triage, BP is 155/95 mmHg and SpO2 is 95% on room air. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Ask him to wait in the waiting room until tests are arranged
Transfer him directly to the resuscitation bay
Obtain a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival
Refer him directly from triage to the coronary care unit
notes: Chest pain of possible cardiac origin should not wait; he is haemodynamically stable but needs an urgent ECG.
He is stable, so resuscitation bay transfer is not needed before the ECG shows ischaemic changes.
Admission to CCU depends on ECG and troponin results; it is not decided at triage.
questions.why: Suspected acute coronary syndrome needs a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival. Management (resuscitation bay, cardiology review, CCU) then depends on the ECG findings.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer's disease, AF, depression and osteoarthritis has become more confused. She takes digoxin and warfarin (stable for 3 years), fluoxetine (4 months) and ibuprofen (1 month). BP 130/80 mmHg, HR 48/min, RR 10/min. What is the most likely cause?
notes: Progression is gradual; a sudden change with bradycardia points to a precipitant such as a drug effect.
Depression has been treated and would not explain the bradycardia.
Ibuprofen may contribute by impairing renal function, but it does not itself explain the bradycardia and confusion as well as digoxin toxicity.
questions.why: Acute confusion with bradycardia in a patient on digoxin suggests digoxin toxicity, likely precipitated by reduced renal clearance after starting an NSAID (ibuprofen).
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man has a 5 cm right colon tumour on colonoscopy. His maternal grandmother had colon cancer. Superficial biopsies show a poorly differentiated medullary carcinoma with abundant stromal inflammatory cells. Which statement is correct?
options: Chemotherapy is the treatment of choice
Prognosis depends mainly on its high degree of anaplasia
It is unlikely this tumour arose from a previous adenoma
Microsatellite instability and mismatch repair genes should be tested
notes: Colon cancer is treated primarily surgically, with adjuvant chemotherapy depending on stage.
Despite poor differentiation, medullary tumours have a relatively favourable prognosis.
Most colorectal cancers arise from adenomas, including those with microsatellite instability.
questions.why: Medullary carcinoma almost always shows microsatellite instability (Lynch syndrome or sporadic MLH1 methylation) and has a better prognosis than other poorly differentiated tumours, so mismatch repair testing is indicated.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient with recent fever and chest pain presents with dyspnoea and tachypnoea. Examination shows hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure with a preserved X descent and pulsus paradoxus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Ischaemia does not explain the raised JVP, hypotension and pulsus paradoxus triad.
Dilated cardiomyopathy causes heart failure but not pulsus paradoxus.
Aortic stenosis would present with a systolic murmur, syncope or angina, not this picture.
questions.why: Hypotension with raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus indicates tamponade. Fever and chest pain suggest an inflammatory pericardial effusion.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man presents to a regional hospital 2 hours after onset of severe chest pain. He is cold and sweaty with BP 80 mmHg systolic. ECG shows marked ST elevation in V1–V6, I and aVL. He had a stroke 4 months ago. Which reperfusion strategy is most appropriate?
options: Immediate fibrinolysis at the regional hospital
Immediate transfer to a tertiary centre for fibrinolysis
Immediate transfer to a tertiary centre for primary percutaneous coronary intervention
Haemodynamic stabilisation followed by deferred revascularisation
notes: Shock favours PCI, and the recent stroke is a relative contraindication to fibrinolysis.
Transferring a patient for fibrinolysis wastes time. If fibrinolysis were chosen, it would be given where he is.
Urgent reperfusion is indicated in STEMI with shock, so deferring it is inappropriate.
questions.why: An extensive anterior STEMI with cardiogenic shock needs urgent primary PCI regardless of delay. A stroke 4 months ago is also a relative contraindication to fibrinolysis.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man presents with syncope after 2 days of exertional dyspnoea. BP 75/50 mmHg, HR 130 sinus, SpO2 89%, troponin 1.2 µg/L, T-wave inversion V1–V4. CT pulmonary angiogram shows filling defects in both main pulmonary arteries. BP stays 70/55 mmHg an hour later. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Unfractionated heparin bolus, then systemic thrombolysis with alteplase
Enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously 12-hourly, started on clinical suspicion
Enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously 12-hourly, started once diagnosis confirmed
notes: Enoxaparin alone would suit haemodynamically stable PE, not persistent hypotension.
Same error, and anticoagulation should not wait for confirmation when suspicion is high.
Surgical embolectomy is considered only if thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails; thromboendarterectomy is for chronic disease.
questions.why: Persistent hypotension defines high-risk (massive) PE, for which systemic thrombolysis is the accepted treatment, with unfractionated heparin anticoagulation.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman with heart failure (on ramipril and furosemide) and insulin-treated type 2 diabetes presents with dyspnoea. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.45, PaO2 56 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L. What does this show?
options: Hypoxaemic respiratory failure with compensated respiratory alkalosis
Acute metabolic alkalosis with hypoxaemic, hypocapnic respiratory failure
Chronic normocapnic respiratory failure with normal acid-base balance
Chronic hypoxaemic respiratory failure with compensated metabolic acidosis
notes: Bicarbonate is not raised, so there is no metabolic alkalosis.
PaCO2 is low, not normal, and the pH is at the alkalotic end of normal.
Bicarbonate would be low in metabolic acidosis, and the primary disturbance is respiratory.
questions.why: Low PaO2 with low PaCO2 and a high-normal pH indicates hyperventilation, a primary respiratory alkalosis. Renal bicarbonate handling is beginning to compensate and keep pH near normal.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient admitted with acute pancreatitis develops tachypnoea, tachycardia, sweating and progressive cyanosis. PaO2 is 55 mmHg (PaO2/FiO2 <200), CXR shows bilateral alveolar infiltrates, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is normal and oxygen does not help. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Pneumonia would usually give focal consolidation, not diffuse bilateral infiltrates with this picture after pancreatitis.
Cardiac failure would show raised wedge pressure; here it is normal, so the oedema is non-cardiogenic.
PE does not typically cause bilateral alveolar infiltrates; the criteria described fit ARDS.
questions.why: Bilateral infiltrates, severe hypoxaemia (PaO2/FiO2 <200) refractory to oxygen and a normal wedge pressure (non-cardiogenic) define ARDS, a recognised complication of acute pancreatitis.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 17-year-old with colonic Crohn's disease on azathioprine presents with 5 days of bilateral, tender, warm, purplish-red pretibial subcutaneous nodules, with increased stool frequency and abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Rest, warm compresses to both legs and add an antidepressant
Biopsy skin away from the lesions and start opioid analgesia
Suspect drug-induced bilateral lower limb ischaemia
Adjust treatment of the underlying Crohn's disease
notes: Antidepressants and warm compresses do not address the flare driving the erythema nodosum.
Biopsy is unnecessary for typical erythema nodosum, and opioids are not indicated.
The picture is typical of erythema nodosum, not ischaemia from azathioprine.
questions.why: These are erythema nodosum lesions accompanying a Crohn's flare. Treating and controlling the bowel disease usually improves the skin lesions; biopsy is not needed.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman has fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. Hb 60 g/L, MCV 69 fL, ferritin 4 µg/L, iron 2.3 µmol/L. She has mild epigastric pain and heartburn, no vaginal bleeding. Gastroscopy shows only a small hiatus hernia without oesophagitis. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Oral iron and monitor the anaemia
Proton pump inhibitor and review at three months
notes: Iron alone treats the result without finding the source of bleeding, which may be a colorectal cancer.
A small hiatus hernia without oesophagitis does not explain severe iron deficiency; PPI alone would delay the work-up.
Capsule endoscopy is reserved for when bidirectional endoscopy is negative, as small bowel lesions are less common.
questions.why: Iron deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman is occult gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise. With a non-explanatory gastroscopy, colonoscopy is next, as colonic lesions are more common than small bowel ones.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A patient has had diarrhoea for over 4 weeks. Which feature in the history can occur in people without organic disease, such as in irritable bowel syndrome?
options: Weight loss with or without rectal bleeding
Extraintestinal features such as dermatitis or arthritis
Passage of mucus with more than 25% of bowel motions
notes: Weight loss and bleeding are alarm features of organic disease.
Nocturnal diarrhoea suggests an organic cause.
Dermatitis or arthritis suggests inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease.
questions.why: Passage of mucus is compatible with irritable bowel syndrome. Weight loss, nocturnal diarrhoea, bleeding and extraintestinal features are alarm features suggesting organic disease.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 52-year-old asymptomatic man has had raised transaminases for two years. His father died of cirrhosis. He has bronze skin pigmentation and mild hepatomegaly; glucose is 8.3 mmol/L, ferritin 950 microgram/L, transferrin saturation >45%, viral serology negative. HFE testing shows C282Y homozygosity. What is the best next step?
notes: Biopsy is reserved for uncertain diagnosis or suspected advanced fibrosis (e.g. ferritin >1000 or markedly abnormal liver tests); the diagnosis here is already established.
MRI can quantify iron but is not required when genetics and iron indices confirm the diagnosis; it would not change management.
Chelation is second-line, used only when venesection is not possible (e.g. anaemia or poor venous access).
questions.why: C282Y homozygosity with raised transferrin saturation and ferritin confirms hereditary haemochromatosis, so no biopsy is needed. Venesection is the treatment of choice.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man has idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy with mildly reduced left ventricular function (ejection fraction 48%) and chronic atrial fibrillation. Which one of the following drugs should be avoided in his treatment?
notes: Digoxin gives symptomatic benefit in heart failure and helps with rate control in AF, though it doesn't improve survival.
Anticoagulation is indicated in chronic AF to prevent thromboembolism.
ACE inhibitors block neurohormonal activation in heart failure and improve survival in systolic dysfunction.
questions.why: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis, raising vascular resistance and causing sodium and water retention with reduced renal perfusion. This can precipitate decompensated heart failure.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has exertional angina. Coronary angiography shows significant proximal stenoses in all three major coronary vessels with good distal run-off. His left ventricular ejection fraction is below 30%. What is the best management?
notes: PCI is a reasonable option for three-vessel disease with preserved LV function, but not the best choice with severe LV dysfunction.
Medical therapy alone gives poorer outcomes than surgery in multivessel disease with depressed LV function.
Transplantation is reserved for end-stage heart failure with no revascularisation option; here the targets are graftable with good distal beds.
questions.why: Three-vessel disease with severe LV dysfunction is best treated with surgical revascularisation (CABG), which improves outcomes over PCI or medical therapy when the distal vessels are suitable.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, LBBB, LVEF 26% and mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation. He remains NYHA class III despite furosemide, spironolactone, enalapril and bisoprolol. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: Implantation of a ventricular assist device.
Implantation of a cardiac resynchronisation system.
notes: Revascularisation is of little benefit here; the cardiomyopathy is idiopathic and there is no ischaemic target.
The mitral regurgitation is mild-to-moderate and likely secondary to annular dilatation, so valve replacement is not the answer.
A VAD is reserved for end-stage refractory heart failure as a bridge to transplant or destination therapy, not for this patient yet.
questions.why: Cardiac resynchronisation therapy is indicated for LVEF below 35%, wide QRS (typically LBBB) and NYHA class III-IV despite optimal medical therapy. Biventricular pacing restores synchronous contraction.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 75-year-old hypertensive, dyslipidaemic man with heart failure (EF <30%) has worsening dyspnoea over weeks. BP is 160/95 mmHg, HR 65 bpm, chest clear, JVP normal. Creatinine is 3.7 mg/dL (about 330 µmol/L) with normal electrolytes. Which drug is most appropriate to improve his prognosis?
notes: ACE inhibitors can worsen renal function and raise potassium in severe renal impairment.
ARBs carry the same risk of renal deterioration and hyperkalaemia.
Spironolactone is potassium-sparing and risks dangerous hyperkalaemia with this degree of renal failure.
questions.why: With severe renal impairment, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium-sparing MRAs risk worsening renal function and hyperkalaemia. A beta-blocker such as bisoprolol improves prognosis without these risks.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A 26-year-old asymptomatic man has a mid-systolic murmur at the aortic area and left sternal border that increases with the Valsalva manoeuvre. BP and pulses are normal. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy and deep T-wave inversion in V3–V6. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Aortic stenosis murmurs usually decrease with Valsalva, and pulses are typically reduced at that age only with severe disease.
Aortic regurgitation causes an early diastolic murmur with a wide pulse pressure.
A VSD gives a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that does not increase with Valsalva.
questions.why: A young man with a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva, left ventricular hypertrophy and deep lateral T-wave inversion is the classic picture of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Valsalva reduces preload and worsens outflow obstruction.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with hypertension was admitted 3 months ago with heart failure and atrial fibrillation (moderate LV dysfunction), and is now on furosemide and enalapril. She feels better but BP is 150/90 mmHg and AF rate is 110–120 bpm. Which treatment best improves symptoms and reduces cardiovascular mortality?
notes: Digoxin controls rate but does not reduce mortality, and aspirin is inadequate stroke prevention in AF.
Aspirin is inadequate for stroke prevention in AF, and atenolol lacks the proven survival benefit of carvedilol in heart failure.
Verapamil is contraindicated in systolic heart failure and should not be combined with beta-blockers because of the risk of conduction block.
questions.why: She has AF needing anticoagulation (warfarin) and heart failure with reduced EF needing a rate-controlling beta-blocker with proven survival benefit, such as carvedilol.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old smoker with diabetes and hypertension has right calf pain on climbing hills and prolonged walking, relieved within minutes by standing still. The right foot is well perfused but the pedal pulse is reduced. Which initial test best confirms the diagnosis and assesses severity?
notes: Imaging is reserved for planning revascularisation, not as the initial test.
Invasive angiography is used when revascularisation is being considered, not initially.
Imaging such as MR angiography is used to plan revascularisation, not initially.
questions.why: This is typical intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease. The ankle-brachial index is the first-line, non-invasive test to confirm the diagnosis and gauge severity.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has a hepatic flexure colon cancer. Her mother, an aunt (diagnosed at 45) and a grandfather also had colon cancer, suggesting Lynch syndrome. Which operation is most appropriate to reduce the risk of metachronous cancer?
notes: Segmental resection leaves colon at high risk of metachronous cancer in Lynch syndrome.
Extended resection still leaves much of the at-risk colon behind.
Removing the rectum is not needed prophylactically; it is used for FAP or rectal disease.
questions.why: The family history suggests Lynch syndrome, and conventional right hemicolectomy carries over 30% recurrence risk. Total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis is preferred; prophylactic rectal excision is unnecessary.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer (bone metastases) has good pain control on a weak opioid and NSAIDs. She now has headache unresponsive to this analgesia, and CT brain shows brain metastases. Which management is most appropriate for this pain?
options: Give extra opioid doses as needed
Add a corticosteroid such as dexamethasone
Switch to a strong opioid and continue NSAIDs
notes: Opioids do not treat the oedema causing this headache.
Extra opioid doses do not address raised intracranial pressure from vasogenic oedema.
Changing opioid and continuing NSAIDs still does not treat the cerebral oedema.
questions.why: Headache from brain metastases is due to raised intracranial pressure and vasogenic oedema, which responds to corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone 4–16 mg daily).

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy with colonic Crohn's disease on maintenance azathioprine has 5 days of tender, warm, red-purple bilateral pretibial subcutaneous nodules, with more frequent stools and abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Biopsy skin away from the lesions and prescribe opioid analgesia.
Suspect a malignant intestinal tumour as the trigger of the skin lesions.
Suspect drug-induced bilateral lower limb ischaemia.
Adjust the treatment of the bowel disease.
notes: Biopsy and opioids are not needed for typical erythema nodosum.
A malignant tumour is a very rare cause in a 17-year-old; Crohn's is far more likely.
Painful pretibial nodules with a flare are erythema nodosum, not ischaemia.
questions.why: The nodules are erythema nodosum, which here accompanies a Crohn's flare. Treating the underlying bowel disease is the correct approach.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man developed blisters on the dorsum of his hands 10 days ago after sun exposure, with skin fragility. Histology shows a subepidermal blister with PAS-positive deposits in and around superficial dermal vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Hailey–Hailey is a suprabasal acantholytic disorder of flexures, not photo-induced.
Bullous pemphigoid causes tense blisters in older patients but is not photodistributed and lacks PAS-positive vessel deposits.
Pemphigus vulgaris is an intraepidermal (suprabasal) blister with mucosal involvement, not photo-induced.
questions.why: Photodistributed blistering with skin fragility and a subepidermal blister with PAS-positive perivascular hyaline deposits is typical of porphyria cutanea tarda.
questions.credit: Adapted from MedExpQA / Antidote CasiMedicos (HiTZ), CC BY 4.0: Spanish MIR exam question and doctors’ explanation, adapted for Australian practice

questions.stem: A woman has had a 2-week itchy eruption of multiple flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules on the volar wrists, shins and lower back. She also has white reticulated lesions on the buccal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Mycosis fungoides gives patches or plaques with a chronic course, not violaceous papules with oral reticulation.
Guttate psoriasis causes small scaly pink papules after streptococcal infection, without oral lesions.
Pityriasis rosea has a herald patch and oval scaly lesions in a Christmas-tree pattern, without mucosal lesions.
questions.why: Pruritic purple polygonal flat-topped papules on flexor wrists and shins with oral Wickham striae are typical of lichen planus.
